For amplifiers the upper −3 dB frequency defines the bandwidth, and coupling capacitors create a lower cutoff as well. For a voltage-feedback op-amp the closed-loop bandwidth is roughly the gain-bandwidth product divided by the noise gain, so higher gain means less bandwidth. A single-pole system also links bandwidth to step response: the 10–90% rise time is about 0.35 divided by the −3 dB frequency, a handy conversion between time and frequency domains.

faq.q: What is the formula for the cutoff frequency of an RC filter?
faq.a: fc = 1/(2πRC). For example, 1 kΩ and 1 µF give about 159 Hz, where the output is 3 dB down with a 45° phase shift.

faq.q: Why is the cutoff frequency defined at −3 dB?
faq.a: At −3 dB the output voltage is 1/√2 of the passband value, so the delivered power is halved; this half-power point also falls exactly where the RC term equals one, giving a simple formula.

faq.q: Is the cutoff frequency the same as bandwidth?
faq.a: For a low-pass filter or amplifier, the bandwidth is usually quoted as the −3 dB cutoff frequency. For a band-pass filter it is the difference between the upper and lower −3 dB frequencies.

差動増幅回路.desc: A circuit that amplifies the difference between two inputs while rejecting components common to both, such as noise. It is used as the input stage of op-amps.

エイリアシング.desc: A phenomenon in which components above half the sampling frequency falsely appear as lower-frequency components. It is prevented with a low-pass filter before A/D conversion.

about.p: Sampling at rate fs records only one value every 1/fs seconds, and a sinusoid at frequency f produces the same samples as a suitably phased sinusoid at |f − n·fs| for any integer n. Any component above the Nyquist frequency fs/2 therefore folds back and masquerades as a lower frequency: a 10 kHz tone sampled at 12 kHz appears at 2 kHz. Once sampled, the false tone is indistinguishable from a genuine 2 kHz signal and cannot be removed. The wagon wheel that seems to turn backward on film is the same effect in time.

The sampling theorem requires fs to exceed twice the highest frequency present, so content up to 20 kHz needs more than 40 kHz. Because real filters cannot cut off instantly, systems add a transition band; audio CDs sample at 44.1 kHz, leaving 20–22.05 kHz for the filter to roll off. The anti-aliasing filter is a low-pass placed before the ADC. A Butterworth response is maximally flat in the passband, Chebyshev trades ripple for steepness, and Bessel preserves waveform shape. Oversampling widens the gap so a simple RC filter suffices, with sharp digital filtering and decimation done afterward.

Aliasing is sometimes deliberate. A band-limited signal centered at a high frequency can be sampled at more than twice its bandwidth, rather than twice its highest frequency, so that it folds down to a lower frequency. This is undersampling, or bandpass sampling: a 70 MHz signal with 10 MHz bandwidth sampled at 56 MS/s appears at 14 MHz, replacing an analog mixer. The ADC's sample-and-hold must still have enough input bandwidth for 70 MHz, and the sampling clock's jitter must be low enough for that input frequency, which is demanding.

about.h: Noise folding and other kinds of aliasing
about.p: Aliasing affects noise as well as tones: wideband noise above the Nyquist frequency folds into the baseband and raises the noise floor, which is one reason anti-aliasing filtering matters even when no interfering signal is expected. In images, undersampled fine detail produces moiré patterns, the spatial version of the same effect. In software, the word means something unrelated: pointer aliasing, where two pointers may refer to the same memory, prevents compilers from keeping a value in a register across stores, and C's restrict qualifier promises that no such overlap exists.

faq.q: How do you calculate the alias frequency?
faq.a: Find the integer multiple of the sampling rate nearest the input frequency and take the absolute difference, |f − n·fs|. For example, 10 kHz sampled at 12 kHz aliases to |10 − 12| = 2 kHz.

faq.q: What is the Nyquist frequency?
faq.a: It is half the sampling rate, the highest frequency that can be represented without aliasing. Components above it fold back into the band below it.

faq.q: Can aliasing be removed after sampling with a digital filter?
faq.a: No. Once a component has folded onto a lower frequency, it occupies the same frequency as legitimate signal, so it must be filtered out in the analog domain before sampling.

量子化誤差.desc: The error that arises when rounding a continuous analog value to a digital value with a finite number of bits. At most half of one LSB.

about.p: An N-bit analog-to-digital converter (ADC) divides its full-scale range into 2^N steps, each one least significant bit (LSB) wide. A 10-bit converter with a 1 V range has an LSB of about 0.98 mV. Every input inside a step maps to the same code, so the difference between the true input and the value the code represents rises and falls in a sawtooth pattern as the input sweeps. In an ideal converter with rounding it never exceeds ±1/2 LSB. Each extra bit halves the LSB and therefore halves the maximum error.

When the input is busy, spanning many codes and not locked to the sampling clock, the error behaves like random noise spread uniformly between −1/2 and +1/2 LSB. Its root-mean-square (rms) value is then LSB/√12, about 0.29 LSB. For a full-scale sine wave, this gives the ideal signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 6.02N + 1.76 dB, about 74 dB for 12 bits and 98 dB for 16 bits. Real converters fall short because of thermal noise, jitter and nonlinearity, which is why effective number of bits (ENOB) is quoted from measured performance.

about.h: When it behaves as distortion: dither
about.p: For small, slowly varying or periodic inputs synchronized with the sampling clock, the error is no longer random; it follows the signal and shows up as harmonic distortion and spurious tones. Adding a small random signal, called dither, of roughly one to a few LSB before conversion decorrelates the error from the signal, turning distortion into a benign noise floor. Averaging many dithered samples can then resolve values finer than one LSB. The same principle appears in audio bit-depth reduction and in error diffusion for images.

Oversampling spreads the fixed quantization noise power over a wider frequency range; filtering back to the signal band then removes part of it, gaining about 3 dB, or half a bit, per doubling of the sampling rate. Noise shaping, used in delta-sigma converters, goes further by pushing most of the noise out of the signal band before it is filtered away. Quantization error should be distinguished from other ADC errors, such as offset, gain error and differential or integral nonlinearity (DNL, INL), which come from imperfect circuits rather than finite resolution.

faq.q: What is the maximum quantization error of an ADC?
faq.a: For an ideal rounding ADC it is ±1/2 LSB, where one LSB is the full-scale range divided by 2^N.

faq.q: Why is quantization noise LSB divided by root 12?
faq.a: If the error is uniformly distributed between −1/2 and +1/2 LSB, its variance is LSB²/12, so the rms value is LSB/√12, about 0.29 LSB.

faq.q: What is the ideal SNR of a 12-bit ADC?
faq.a: Using 6.02N + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine wave, a 12-bit ADC has an ideal SNR of about 74 dB.

逐次比較型ADC.desc: An ADC that uses an internal DAC and comparator to determine one bit at a time, starting from the most significant. It balances speed, accuracy and power well.

about.h: Binary search, one bit per step
about.p: A successive-approximation-register (SAR) ADC first samples the input onto a hold capacitor. The control logic then sets the most significant bit of an internal DAC to give mid-scale, and a comparator decides whether the input is above or below it; the bit is kept or cleared accordingly. The next bit is then tried, halving the remaining range each time. After N comparisons the register holds the N-bit result, so conversion time grows only linearly with resolution.

In most CMOS SAR ADCs the DAC is an array of binary-weighted capacitors that also serves as the sampling capacitor, an approach called charge redistribution. During conversion the bottom plates of the capacitors are switched between reference voltages, and the comparator watches the resulting top-plate voltage. Because the array draws energy mainly when it switches and there is only one comparator, power scales roughly with sample rate, which is why SAR converters are popular in microcontrollers and battery-powered sensors.

At the start of acquisition the input sees a sampling capacitance of a few to tens of picofarads that must charge within a short acquisition time. Settling to within half an LSB of an N-bit converter takes about (N+1)·ln2 time constants, roughly 11.8 time constants at 16 bits. A high-impedance source cannot meet this, so a low-output-impedance op-amp driver is used together with an RC filter whose capacitor (a charge bucket) supplies the instantaneous charge kick.

about.h: SAR vs. flash and delta-sigma ADCs
about.p: A flash ADC uses 2ᴺ − 1 comparators to convert in a single step, so it is very fast but power-hungry and limited to low resolution. A delta-sigma ADC oversamples and digitally filters to reach high resolution, but its bandwidth is lower and its digital filter adds latency. SAR ADCs sit in between, commonly offering roughly 10 to 18 bits at sample rates up to a few megasamples per second, and they deliver each result with no pipeline delay, which suits multiplexed channels.

faq.q: How many clock cycles does a SAR ADC take?
faq.a: At least one comparison per bit, so N cycles for N bits, plus the acquisition time and sometimes extra cycles for redundant bits that correct early decision errors.

faq.q: Why does a SAR ADC need a driver amplifier?
faq.a: Its switched sampling capacitor draws a burst of charge at each acquisition, and a high-impedance source cannot recharge it accurately in time; a low-impedance op-amp plus an RC charge-bucket filter solves this.

faq.q: Should I use a SAR or a delta-sigma ADC?
faq.a: SAR suits medium-to-high resolution with fast, latency-free conversions and multiplexed inputs; delta-sigma suits very high resolution at low bandwidth, such as precision sensor and audio measurement.

ΔΣ型ADC.desc: An ADC that oversamples at a high rate, pushes quantization noise to high frequencies and then filters it out. Used in high-resolution applications such as audio and measurement.

1T1Cセル.desc: The DRAM memory cell that stores one bit with one transistor and one capacitor. The presence or absence of charge on the capacitor represents 0 or 1.

ビット線.desc: The wire used to read and write data in memory cells. In DRAM, the small change in bit-line potential caused by a cell's charge is amplified by a sense amplifier.

about.h: What happens on a DRAM bit line during a read
about.p: Before a read, the bit line is precharged to VDD/2. When the word line turns on a cell's access transistor, the cell capacitor Cs (about 10 fF) shares its charge with the much larger bit-line capacitance Cb, several to about ten times Cs. The bit line therefore moves only about (VDD/2)·Cs/(Cs + Cb), typically tens to about a hundred millivolts, up for a stored 1 and down for a 0. A sense amplifier, a cross-coupled latch, amplifies this small difference with positive feedback and simultaneously writes the full level back, because the read destroyed the cell's original charge.

The signal depends on the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs + Cb), and every cell attached to the bit line adds capacitance. A long bit line serving many cells would dilute the signal below what the sense amplifier can resolve reliably, so arrays are divided into segments with a limited number of cells per bit line, each served by its own sense amplifiers. This trades area for signal margin. Precharging back to VDD/2 after a row is closed takes time, specified as tRP, which adds to the latency of switching rows.

A sense amplifier compares two bit lines, one connected to the selected cell and one used as reference. In the folded architecture the pair runs side by side in the same array, so noise couples onto both lines equally and cancels; however, each word line can contact cells on only one line of the pair, which makes the cell 8F², where F is the minimum feature size. In the open architecture the pair lies in separate arrays. It is more sensitive to noise but permits a 6F² cell, and it is the mainstream arrangement today.

about.h: Bit lines in SRAM and flash
about.p: Other memories use bit lines differently. An SRAM column has a complementary bit-line pair precharged to VDD; the selected cell discharges one side slightly, and the sense amplifier fires at a difference of tens to about a hundred millivolts. Writing pulls one bit line low, and at low voltage a negative bit-line assist drives it slightly below ground. In NOR flash each cell connects in parallel to the bit line for fast random reads, while NAND flash connects only the end of a series string of cells to it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a word line and a bit line?
faq.a: A word line runs along a row and drives the gates of the access transistors, selecting which cells are connected. A bit line runs along a column and carries data between the selected cell and the sense amplifier or write driver.

faq.q: Why is the DRAM bit line precharged to VDD/2?
faq.a: Starting midway lets the bit line move up for a stored 1 and down for a stored 0 by similar amounts, so the sense amplifier can compare it against a reference line held at VDD/2.

faq.q: Why is a DRAM read destructive?
faq.a: Connecting the small cell capacitor to the much larger bit-line capacitance redistributes its charge, so the cell no longer holds its original voltage. The sense amplifier restores the data by writing the amplified level back into the cell.

ワード線.desc: The wire connected to the gates of memory-cell transistors that selects the row to read or write.

about.p: A memory array is a grid. Word lines run along the rows and connect to the gates of the cells' access transistors, while bit lines run along the columns and carry data between cells and sense amplifiers or write drivers. A row decoder selects one word line from the address, and its driver raises that line, connecting every cell in the row to its bit line at once. The word line therefore chooses which cells take part, and the bit lines carry the information. Because a word line is a long, heavily loaded wire, its RC delay limits how large an array segment can be.

Activating a DRAM word line turns on thousands of cell transistors, dumping an entire row of several kilobytes onto the sense amplifiers. The access transistor is an nMOS, so if its gate rose only to the supply, the capacitor could charge only to the supply minus the threshold voltage. Word lines are therefore driven to a boosted voltage VPP, about 2.5–3 V, generated by an on-chip charge pump. Modern cells bury the word line in a silicon trench, lengthening the effective channel to keep leakage near femtoamperes so charge survives the refresh interval of 64 ms or more.

In a six-transistor SRAM cell, the word line drives the gates of the two access transistors that connect the cross-coupled latch to a complementary bit-line pair. A read begins by precharging both bit lines, typically to the supply. When the word line rises, the side storing 0 slowly discharges its bit line, and the sense amplifier fires once a difference of tens to about a hundred millivolts develops, without waiting for a full swing. The word line is then lowered and the bit lines are precharged again for the next access.

In NAND flash, the word line is the control gate shared by a row of cells. All cells on one word line form the unit of reading and programming: one page for SLC, and several logical pages for multilevel cells, three for TLC. Programming applies a high voltage to the selected word line while unselected word lines in the string receive a lower pass voltage. In 3D NAND the word lines become stacked conductive layers, often tungsten, and the array edge is etched into a staircase so that each layer can be contacted.

faq.q: What is the difference between a word line and a bit line?
faq.a: The word line selects a row by switching on the access transistors of every cell in it. The bit lines carry data to and from those cells, running perpendicular to the word lines.

faq.q: Why is the DRAM word line driven above the supply voltage?
faq.a: The nMOS access transistor drops a threshold voltage, so a gate at the supply could only charge the capacitor partway. A boosted VPP lets the cell store a full-level 1 and preserves read margin.

faq.q: How does a NAND flash page relate to a word line?
faq.a: A page corresponds to the cells sharing one word line; in multilevel cells each word line holds one page per stored bit, so a TLC word line holds three pages.

6T SRAMセル.desc: The SRAM memory cell made of two cross-coupled inverters (four transistors) and two access transistors.

about.h: How six transistors hold a bit
about.p: A 6T SRAM cell is a latch of two cross-coupled CMOS inverters, each built from a PMOS pull-up and an NMOS pull-down, so four transistors in all. Each inverter's output drives the other's input, and this positive feedback holds one storage node high and the other low indefinitely while power is applied, with no refresh. Two NMOS access transistors, gated by the word line, connect the two storage nodes to a complementary pair of bit lines, BL and BL-bar. The cell is static but not free: its transistors still leak continuously.

For a read, both bit lines are precharged high and the word line is raised; the node storing 0 pulls its bit line down slightly, and a sense amplifier detects the small difference. Current flowing in through the access transistor lifts that 0 node, so the pull-down must be stronger than the access transistor, a cell ratio of about 1.5 to 2.5, or the cell can flip. For a write, one bit line is driven low and the access transistor must overpower the pull-up PMOS holding the node high, so the pull-up is kept weakest of the three.

A 6T SRAM cell occupies roughly 120 to 150 F², where F is the minimum feature size, while a one-transistor, one-capacitor DRAM cell is about 6 F², so SRAM is around 20 times less dense and costs far more per bit. In return it needs no capacitor or special process, is built alongside logic transistors and can be accessed in about a nanosecond, against tens of nanoseconds for DRAM. That is why on-chip caches and register files use SRAM, while main memory uses DRAM.

Because read stability and writability pull the transistor sizes in opposite directions, random variation in threshold voltage makes some cells fail as supply voltage drops, which sets a minimum operating voltage for large arrays. An 8T cell adds a two-transistor read port whose bit line only senses a storage node through a transistor gate, so reads cannot disturb the stored value. Read and write paths can then be optimized separately and can operate at the same time, improving low-voltage operation at the cost of a larger cell.

faq.q: Why does an SRAM cell have six transistors?
faq.a: Four transistors form two cross-coupled inverters that hold the bit through positive feedback, and two access transistors connect the cell to the bit lines when the word line is selected. This gives a stable, refresh-free storage element built only from logic transistors.

faq.q: Does SRAM need refresh like DRAM?
faq.a: No. The cross-coupled inverters actively restore the stored levels as long as power is supplied, so SRAM needs no refresh, although the data is lost when power is removed.

faq.q: What is the cell ratio in a 6T SRAM?
faq.a: It is the strength of the pull-down transistor relative to the access transistor, typically about 1.5 to 2.5. A high enough ratio keeps the 0 node from rising past the switching threshold during a read, preventing read upset.

不揮発性メモリ.desc: Memory that retains stored data when power is removed, such as flash memory and MRAM. DRAM and SRAM are volatile.

NOR型フラッシュメモリ.desc: Flash memory with cells connected in parallel. Random reads are fast, and it is used to store programs for microcontrollers and the like.

ウェアレベリング.desc: A technique that spreads writes so rewrites do not concentrate on particular flash blocks, extending the memory's life.

about.p: NAND flash cannot overwrite data in place: pages are programmed individually, but erasing works only on whole blocks containing many pages, and every program/erase (P/E) cycle slightly damages the tunnel oxide. Endurance therefore depends on cell type: roughly 50,000 to 100,000 cycles for single-level cells (SLC), several thousand to 10,000 for multi-level cells (MLC), a few thousand for triple-level cells (TLC) and around 1,000 for quad-level cells (QLC). If one frequently updated logical address, such as a log or file-system metadata, always hit the same block, that block would wear out long before the rest.

about.h: How it works through the FTL
about.p: The controller runs a flash translation layer (FTL) that maps logical block addresses from the host to physical pages. Each update of a logical address is written to a freshly erased page elsewhere, and the old page is merely marked invalid; garbage collection later copies remaining valid pages out of a block and erases it. Dynamic wear leveling directs new writes to free blocks with low erase counts. Static wear leveling also relocates cold data that rarely changes, so the barely worn blocks it occupies rejoin the rotation and all blocks age at a similar rate.

Garbage collection and static wear leveling write data the host never asked to write. The ratio of NAND writes to host writes, the write amplification factor, directly reduces usable endurance. Reserving spare capacity, called over-provisioning, and the host's TRIM commands, which tell the drive which data are deleted, give the controller room to work and lower the factor. Drive endurance is rated as total bytes written (TBW) or drive writes per day (DWPD), roughly capacity times rated P/E cycles divided by write amplification.

about.h: Related mechanisms and where it runs
about.p: Wear leveling only evens out wear; it works alongside other controller functions. Error-correcting codes (ECC), from BCH to low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes in modern SSDs, correct the raw bit errors that increase as cells age, and bad block management retires blocks that fail. SSDs, USB drives, SD cards and embedded eMMC devices do all of this inside their controllers, though inexpensive cards may implement it simply. When raw NAND is attached directly to a processor, flash-aware file systems or the host software must provide wear leveling instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic wear leveling?
faq.a: Dynamic wear leveling chooses lightly worn free blocks for new writes, while static wear leveling also moves rarely changed data out of lightly worn blocks so those blocks can share the write load.

faq.q: Does wear leveling increase write amplification?
faq.a: Static wear leveling adds some internal writes because it moves data the host did not change, but the gain in evenly distributed wear far outweighs that cost.

faq.q: How many write cycles can NAND flash handle?
faq.a: Roughly 50,000 to 100,000 for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and about 1,000 for QLC, depending on process and conditions.

PCM(相変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information by the difference between the crystalline (low-resistance) and amorphous (high-resistance) states of a chalcogenide material.

about.h: How set, reset and read work
about.p: A PCM cell is written with current pulses that Joule-heat a small volume of chalcogenide, typically GST (Ge2Sb2Te5). Reset uses a large, short pulse, tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, that melts the material above roughly 600 °C; quenching within nanoseconds freezes the disordered atoms into the high-resistance amorphous phase. Set uses a smaller, longer pulse that holds the material between its crystallization temperature (about 150 °C for GST) and the melting point until it crystallizes into the low-resistance phase. Reading applies a small bias that senses resistance without heating the cell enough to change it.

Because the crystalline and amorphous resistances differ by two to three orders of magnitude, PCM can store more than one bit per cell. Pulse amplitude and duration set the size of the amorphous region, producing intermediate resistance levels. The catch is resistance drift: the amorphous phase slowly relaxes, so its resistance rises roughly as a power of time (R ∝ t^ν, with ν around 0.1). Two-level storage tolerates this, but closely spaced levels can blur together, so multi-level PCM relies on write-and-verify programming, reference cells read alongside the data, and low-drift materials.

about.h: Scaling limits: reset current and thermal disturb
about.p: The reset current is PCM's main power cost, so cell designs shrink the volume that must melt. The mushroom cell, for example, forces current through a narrow heater electrode so only a small dome of GST is heated. Tight pitch brings a second problem, thermal disturb: when cells are only tens of nanometres apart, heat from a reset can partially crystallize an amorphous neighbour. Thermally insulating dielectrics around each cell help. Retention is also temperature-limited, since GST crystallizes near 150 °C, which is why Ge-rich compositions are used for automotive and other high-temperature applications.

PCM sits between NAND flash and DRAM. Its endurance of about 10^6 to 10^9 cycles beats NAND's thousands to tens of thousands but falls short of MRAM (above 10^10) and DRAM, which is effectively unlimited. Unlike MRAM, which stores data in the magnetization of a magnetic tunnel junction, and ReRAM, which forms and breaks a conductive filament in an oxide, PCM changes the atomic structure of a whole volume. In dense cross-point arrays each PCM element is paired with an ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selector that blocks sneak currents through unselected cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between PCM and ReRAM?
faq.a: Both store data as a resistance state, but PCM switches a chalcogenide between crystalline and amorphous phases using heat, while ReRAM moves ions in a metal oxide to form or rupture a narrow conductive filament. PCM therefore needs relatively large write currents to melt the material.

faq.q: Why is PCM set slower than reset?
faq.a: Reset only needs to melt the material and quench it within nanoseconds, while set must hold the material below its melting point long enough for atoms to arrange into a crystal, typically tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. Crystallization time is therefore what limits PCM write speed.

faq.q: What does GST stand for in phase-change memory?
faq.a: GST refers to germanium-antimony-tellurium chalcogenide alloys, most commonly Ge2Sb2Te5. It crystallizes quickly yet keeps a stable amorphous phase at room temperature, and the same family of materials was used in rewritable optical discs.

ReRAM(抵抗変化メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that applies voltage to form and break conductive paths in an oxide or similar material, storing information as differences in resistance.

about.p: A resistive RAM (ReRAM) cell is a metal-insulator-metal stack, typically a few nanometers of hafnium, tantalum or titanium oxide between electrodes. Fresh cells are highly resistive, so a one-time forming step applies a higher voltage that moves oxygen ions and leaves a conductive filament of oxygen vacancies. After that, normal operation only ruptures and reconnects the thin tip of the filament: reset produces the high-resistance state and set restores the low-resistance state, typically differing by ten times or more. The state persists without power, so the memory is nonvolatile.

Most practical ReRAM is bipolar: set and reset use opposite voltage polarities, with the field shuttling oxygen ions to connect or break the filament. Unipolar devices use one polarity and break the filament mainly by Joule heating, which is harder to control. Conductive-bridge RAM (CBRAM) is a related type in which silver or copper ions from an active electrode migrate through a solid electrolyte to build a metallic bridge, offering low voltage and low write energy. All of these store data as resistance, unlike flash, which stores trapped charge.

ReRAM cells are small and built from materials already used in CMOS, and they can be placed in the interconnect layers above the transistors with only a few extra process steps. That makes them attractive as embedded nonvolatile memory in microcontrollers at nodes where embedded flash, with its floating gates, becomes hard to integrate. Endurance of roughly 10^6 to 10^9 cycles beats NAND flash but falls short of DRAM. The main weakness is variability: random filament shapes spread resistance from cell to cell and write to write, which narrows read margins and makes multilevel storage difficult.

Cells are usually paired with an access transistor (1T1R), which also limits current during set so the filament does not grow too strong. Dense crosspoint arrays without transistors are possible, but current leaking through unselected cells (sneak paths) then requires a nonlinear selector device at each crossing. To tighten resistance distributions, controllers use write-verify, repeatedly pulsing and reading until the cell lands in its target window. Because resistance can be tuned in steps, ReRAM is also studied for analog in-memory computing of neural-network weights.

faq.q: How does ReRAM store data?
faq.a: By forming or breaking a nanoscale conductive filament, usually made of oxygen vacancies, in a thin oxide; the resulting low or high resistance represents the stored bit and remains without power.

faq.q: What is the forming step in ReRAM?
faq.a: A one-time application of higher-than-normal voltage that creates the initial conductive filament in a fresh, highly resistive cell, after which lower voltages switch it.

faq.q: What is the difference between ReRAM and PCM?
faq.a: Both store data as resistance, but ReRAM switches by moving ions to form or break a filament, while phase-change memory (PCM) switches a material between crystalline and amorphous phases by heating.

FeRAM(強誘電体メモリ).desc: Nonvolatile memory that stores information in the polarization direction of a ferroelectric. Writes are fast and low-power, and it is used in IC cards and the like.

about.h: How the cell stores a bit
about.p: A ferroelectric has a spontaneous electric polarization that can be flipped by an applied field and stays in place when the field is removed. Plotting polarization against field gives a hysteresis loop; the polarization left at zero field is the remanent polarization (Pr), and the field needed to flip it is the coercive field (Ec). FeRAM stores a 1 or 0 in the sign of that polarization, usually in a one-transistor, one-capacitor (1T1C) cell resembling DRAM but with a ferroelectric capacitor. The "Fe" stands for ferroelectric, not iron.

In capacitor-type FeRAM, a read pulses the cell toward a known polarization and senses the charge released onto the bit line. A cell whose polarization flips delivers noticeably more charge than one that does not, and a sense amplifier distinguishes the two. Because the read flips cells storing the opposite state, the data must be written back afterward, much as in DRAM. Every read therefore counts as a switching cycle. Unlike DRAM, though, the information lives in polarization rather than stored charge, so no refresh is needed and data survives power loss.

Writing simply flips polarization at a few volts, so FeRAM writes in tens of nanoseconds with little energy and endures about 10^12 cycles or more, far beyond flash. That suits contactless smart cards powered by harvested radio energy, meters and medical devices that log data frequently and must survive sudden power loss, and radiation-exposed equipment, since polarization is not easily upset by ionizing radiation. Its weakness is density: ferroelectric capacitors in traditional lead zirconate titanate (PZT) scale poorly, keeping capacities in the few-megabit range.

Around 2011, doped hafnium oxide was reported to become ferroelectric in a specific orthorhombic phase at about 10 nm thickness. Because HfO2 is already a standard high-k dielectric deposited by atomic layer deposition (ALD), this revived interest in embedding ferroelectric memory with advanced logic. The same films enable the ferroelectric FET (FeFET), where polarization shifts the transistor threshold voltage, and the ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJ), where polarization changes tunneling resistance. Both read without flipping the polarization, avoiding the destructive read of capacitor FeRAM.

faq.q: Does FeRAM contain iron?
faq.a: No. Fe stands for ferroelectric, a name borrowed from ferromagnetism because both show hysteresis; common materials are PZT, SBT and doped hafnium oxide.

faq.q: Why is FeRAM read destructive?
faq.a: Reading works by driving the cell toward one polarization and detecting whether it switches, which erases the original state of switched cells, so the data must be rewritten.

faq.q: What is the difference between FeRAM and MRAM?
faq.a: FeRAM stores bits as the electric polarization direction of a ferroelectric capacitor, while MRAM stores them as the magnetization direction of a magnetic tunnel junction and reads the resulting resistance.

磁気トンネル接合(MTJ).desc: A structure with a thin insulating film between two magnetic layers. Resistance is low when the layers' magnetizations are parallel and high when antiparallel. It is the storage element of MRAM.

about.p: A magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) sandwiches an insulating tunnel barrier, typically MgO about 1 nm thick, between two ferromagnetic layers such as CoFeB. One layer, the reference or pinned layer, has its magnetization fixed by an antiferromagnet or a synthetic antiferromagnet so that write currents and stray fields cannot move it. The other, the free or storage layer, can be switched between two directions. Production MTJs are stacks of more than ten films, many of which exist only to stabilize the reference layer.

Electrons cross the barrier by quantum tunneling, and in a ferromagnet majority-spin and minority-spin electrons have different numbers of available states. When the two layers are parallel, majority states on both sides match and tunneling is easy, giving low resistance. When antiparallel, majority electrons must enter minority states, so resistance is high. The tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio, (R_AP − R_P)/R_P, measures the contrast: 2 kΩ versus 5 kΩ gives 150%. Laboratory MgO junctions exceed 600% at room temperature, but production cells are around 100 to 200%, so the two states differ only two- to threefold.

In spin-transfer torque (STT) MRAM, write current flows through the junction; electrons spin-polarized by the reference layer transfer angular momentum to the free layer and flip it, with current direction selecting 0 or 1. Write current scales with cell area, which made STT the mainstream approach. Reads use the same path, so read current must stay well below the switching current to avoid read disturb. Spin-orbit torque (SOT) MRAM drives write current through a heavy-metal line such as tungsten or platinum under the free layer, separating read and write paths and allowing sub-nanosecond writes in a larger three-terminal cell.

The energy barrier holding the free layer is roughly magnetic anisotropy times volume, so it shrinks as cells shrink. Its ratio to thermal energy kT, the thermal stability factor Δ, must be about 60 or more for ten-year retention; a larger Δ also demands more write current, which sets the scaling trade-off. Perpendicular magnetic anisotropy materials help. MTJs are built between interconnect layers in the back end of line (BEOL), so they must survive about 400 °C, and the magnetic films are patterned with ion-beam etching to avoid metal redeposition on the sidewalls.

faq.q: What is the TMR ratio of a magnetic tunnel junction?
faq.a: The tunnel magnetoresistance ratio is (R_antiparallel − R_parallel) divided by R_parallel. Production MRAM junctions typically show about 100 to 200%, meaning the high-resistance state is two to three times the low one.

faq.q: What is the difference between an MTJ and a GMR spin valve?
faq.a: Both use two magnetic layers whose relative alignment sets the resistance, but a giant magnetoresistance (GMR) spin valve uses a thin metallic spacer such as copper, while an MTJ uses an insulating tunnel barrier. The tunnel barrier gives a much larger resistance change, which is why MRAM uses MTJs.

faq.q: Is MTJ-based memory volatile?
faq.a: No. The bit is stored as the direction of the free layer's magnetization, which persists without power, so MRAM built from MTJs is non-volatile as long as the thermal stability factor is high enough.

パイプライン処理.desc: A method that splits instruction processing into stages such as fetch, decode and execute, and processes several instructions at once, each offset by a stage.

about.p: A pipeline splits instruction processing into stages separated by registers, like an assembly line. The classic five-stage RISC pipeline uses instruction fetch, decode and register read, execute, memory access and write-back. While one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and a third fetched, so ideally one instruction completes every clock and throughput approaches five times that of an unpipelined design. The latency of an individual instruction does not shrink and actually grows slightly, because every instruction now passes through all the pipeline registers.

The clock period must cover the slowest stage plus register overhead: clock-to-Q delay, setup time and clock skew. If logic cannot be divided evenly, the longest stage sets the frequency and the others idle for part of each cycle. Deeper pipelines shorten each stage, but the fixed register overhead becomes a larger fraction of the period, and the penalty for mispredicted branches grows because more partially processed instructions must be discarded. Beyond a point, adding stages lowers performance and raises power, which is why pipeline depth is a balanced design choice.

about.h: Hazards and how they are handled
about.p: Three kinds of hazard interrupt the ideal flow. Structural hazards arise when two instructions need the same resource in the same cycle. Data hazards arise when an instruction needs a result that has not yet been written; forwarding, or bypassing, routes results directly from later stages, though a load followed immediately by its use still typically costs a stall cycle in the classic pipeline. Control hazards come from branches, whose outcome is known only several stages after fetch; branch prediction guesses the path and flushes the wrong instructions when it misses.

RISC instruction sets, with uniform instruction lengths and load/store architectures, were designed to pipeline cleanly; x86 processors reach similar behavior by splitting complex instructions into simple micro-operations. The same idea applies to any synchronous datapath: inserting registers to split a long critical path raises the maximum clock frequency at the cost of latency, and high-level synthesis tools expose this as a pipelining option. Software pipelining is the compiler counterpart, overlapping different loop iterations so loads, computation and stores proceed in parallel, with prologue and epilogue code around the loop.

faq.q: Does pipelining reduce the latency of an instruction?
faq.a: No. Pipelining increases throughput by overlapping instructions, but each instruction still passes through every stage and usually takes slightly longer because of register overhead.

faq.q: What are the three types of pipeline hazards?
faq.a: Structural hazards from resource conflicts, data hazards from dependences on results not yet available, and control hazards from branches. Typical remedies are duplicated resources, forwarding and branch prediction.

faq.q: Why not make the pipeline as deep as possible?
faq.a: Register overhead stays fixed while stage logic shrinks, so gains diminish, and branch mispredictions waste more work in a deeper pipeline. Power and design complexity also increase.

ノイマン型アーキテクチャ.desc: A computer organization that keeps programs and data in the same main memory and fetches and executes instructions in sequence.

命令セットアーキテクチャ(ISA).desc: The processor specification as seen by software, including the instructions and registers it supports. Examples include x86, Arm and RISC-V.

about.p: An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the contract between software and processor hardware. It defines the instructions and their bit encodings, the registers visible to programs, the data types and addressing modes, how memory accesses are ordered, the privilege levels, and how interrupts and exceptions behave. Everything the ISA defines is architectural state that machine code can observe and rely on. An assembler translates assembly mnemonics almost one-to-one into these encodings, which is why each ISA has its own assembly language.

The microarchitecture is how a particular processor implements the ISA: pipeline depth, cache sizes, branch predictors, the number of instructions issued per cycle. One ISA can be implemented by tiny low-power cores and large out-of-order cores that run the same machine code at very different speeds. In the performance equation, execution time = instruction count × cycles per instruction (CPI) × cycle time, the ISA and compiler mainly set the instruction count, the microarchitecture the CPI, and circuits and process technology the cycle time. Spectre-type attacks exploit the boundary: misspeculated architectural state is rolled back, but cache contents are not.

ISA details have lasting hardware consequences. RISC-V base instructions are a fixed 32 bits (16-bit forms only with the compressed C extension), so instruction boundaries are obvious, while x86 instructions range from 1 to 15 bytes and must be partly decoded to find where the next one starts, making wide decoders complex. x86 branches test flags set by an earlier compare; RISC-V compares two registers within the branch, leaving no implicit flag state to track. The MIPS branch delay slot showed the risk of encoding one pipeline's quirks into an ISA that outlives it.

RISC-V is an open ISA whose specification anyone may implement without license fees. It combines a small base integer set (RV32I or RV64I, about 40 instructions) with optional extensions: M for multiply and divide, A for atomics, F and D for floating point, C for compressed instructions, V for vectors, plus custom instructions. Leaving out an extension saves area but costs speed: without M, the compiler turns a C multiplication into a call to a library routine that multiplies with shifts and adds. Arm and x86 are proprietary and licensed or implemented by their owners.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ISA and a microarchitecture?
faq.a: The ISA is the specification software sees: instructions, registers and behavior. The microarchitecture is a specific hardware design that implements that specification, so two processors with different microarchitectures can run the same programs if they share an ISA.

faq.q: Are x86, Arm and RISC-V instruction set architectures?
faq.a: Yes. They are three different ISAs, so machine code compiled for one cannot run directly on another, even though each is implemented by many different processor designs.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ISA and an ABI?
faq.a: The ISA defines what the processor executes, while the ABI is a software convention on top of it covering calling conventions, data type sizes and system calls. One ISA can have several ABIs, for example for different operating systems.

分岐予測.desc: A technique that predicts the outcome of conditional branches before they execute, so later instructions can proceed without stalling the pipeline. A misprediction forces the work to be redone.

about.p: A pipelined CPU fetches new instructions every cycle, but whether a conditional branch is taken, and where it goes, is not known until it executes several stages later. Waiting would leave the pipeline idle, and roughly one instruction in five is a branch. Branch prediction instead guesses the outcome at fetch time and continues speculatively down the predicted path. If the guess is right, no time is lost; if wrong, the speculative instructions are flushed without affecting architectural state and fetch restarts on the correct path, costing a dozen to about twenty cycles in a deep pipeline.

Static schemes use fixed rules, such as predicting backward branches (loops) taken and forward branches not taken. Dynamic predictors learn from history: a table of 2-bit saturating counters, indexed by branch address, needs two wrong outcomes in a row to flip its prediction, so a loop exit causes only one miss. Better predictors combine the address with a global history of recent outcomes to capture correlations between branches. Predicting direction is only half the job; a branch target buffer (BTB) supplies the target address, and a return address stack predicts function returns.

The impact can be estimated as added cycles per instruction (CPI): branch frequency × misprediction rate × penalty. With 20% branches, 95% accuracy and a 20-cycle penalty, that is 0.2 × 0.05 × 20 = 0.2 extra CPI, a large share of a modern core's budget. This is why accuracy improvements of a percent or two matter. For branches that depend on random data and cannot be predicted, compilers and programmers sometimes use branchless code such as conditional moves, trading a little extra work for a guaranteed absence of flushes.

Mispredicted instructions are discarded architecturally, but they can still leave traces in microarchitectural state such as caches. Spectre-class attacks train the predictor so a victim speculatively reads secret data and leaks it through cache timing. Defenses include speculation barriers after sensitive bounds checks (such as x86 lfence), masking array indices, retpoline sequences for indirect branches and microcode controls on predictors. Each restriction costs performance, so they are applied selectively. Older ISAs such as MIPS used branch delay slots instead of prediction, a rule that became a burden for later designs.

faq.q: What happens when a branch is mispredicted?
faq.a: The CPU discards the instructions it fetched and executed speculatively down the wrong path and restarts from the correct target, losing roughly 10 to 20 cycles in a typical deep pipeline.

faq.q: How accurate is branch prediction in modern CPUs?
faq.a: High-performance predictors typically exceed 95% accuracy on ordinary code, although branches that depend on random data can be much harder to predict.

faq.q: What is the difference between branch prediction and speculative execution?
faq.a: Branch prediction is the guess about which way a branch goes; speculative execution is actually running instructions along that guessed path before the guess is confirmed.

パワーMOSFET.desc: A MOSFET built to handle large currents and voltages. It switches quickly and is widely used in power supply circuits and the like.

about.h: How it differs from a logic MOSFET
about.p: Most discrete power MOSFETs are vertical devices: source and gate are on top, the drain is the back of the chip, and current flows through the channel and then down through a lightly doped n-type drift region. That drift region holds the blocking voltage, and a higher voltage rating needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, which raises on-resistance. Many small cells are connected in parallel to carry large current. The p-type body, tied to the source, forms a PN junction with the drift region, creating a built-in body diode that conducts from source to drain.

When fully on, the device behaves as a resistor, RDS(on), so conduction loss is I²R: 10 A through 10 mΩ dissipates 1 W, and doubling the current quadruples it. In silicon, RDS(on) rises with temperature as carrier mobility falls, typically to about 1.5–2 times the 25 °C value at 125 °C, so loss must be estimated from the datasheet's normalized RDS(on)-versus-temperature curve. This positive temperature coefficient helps paralleled devices share current, since a hotter device conducts less.

Turning the device on means charging its gate capacitances. During the transition, the drain voltage swings and the gate drive current is consumed charging the gate-drain (Miller) capacitance Cgd, so the gate voltage stalls on the Miller plateau. Most switching loss occurs in this interval, whose length is roughly the gate-drain charge Qgd divided by gate current, so low-Qgd devices and strong gate drivers switch faster. The gate oxide is thin, so gate-source voltage is typically rated around ±20 V.

about.h: Body diode, avalanche and safe operating area
about.p: In bridges the body diode can carry freewheeling current, but in silicon its slow reverse recovery causes loss, so designs add fast external diodes or use synchronous rectification. Interrupting an inductive load releases energy ½LI², driving the drain into avalanche breakdown; avalanche ruggedness, tested by unclamped inductive switching (UIS), matters for relay, solenoid and automotive drivers without clamps. The safe operating area (SOA) chart bounds allowed voltage-current combinations; most are drawn for a 25 °C case and single pulses, so they must be derated, especially for linear-mode uses such as inrush limiting.

faq.q: How do you calculate power MOSFET conduction loss?
faq.a: Use P = I²·RDS(on), with RDS(on) taken at the expected junction temperature rather than the 25 °C datasheet headline value, since it can be 1.5–2 times higher when hot.

faq.q: What is the body diode in a power MOSFET?
faq.a: It is the parasitic PN junction between the source-connected p body and the n drift region, which conducts from source to drain. It can act as a freewheeling diode but has slow reverse recovery in silicon devices.

faq.q: What is the Miller plateau?
faq.a: The flat portion of the gate-voltage waveform during switching, when gate current goes into charging the gate-drain capacitance while the drain voltage transitions.

オン抵抗.desc: The resistance of the current path when a power device is on. The smaller it is, the lower the conduction loss.

about.p: A power MOSFET's on-resistance, RDS(on), is a series chain: the inversion channel, the JFET region between cells in planar designs, the lightly doped drift layer that holds off voltage, the substrate, and finally contacts, bond wires and package. Low-voltage devices are dominated by channel, substrate and package; devices rated at hundreds of volts by the drift layer. The channel part falls as gate voltage rises, so datasheets quote RDS(on) at a stated gate drive and temperature. Technologies are compared by specific on-resistance, resistance times active area.

While on, the switch dissipates P = I²R: 10 A through 10 mΩ gives 1 W, and doubling the current quadruples the loss. RDS(on) rises with temperature because carrier mobility falls; roughly 1.5 times the room-temperature value at 100 °C is a common rule of thumb, so thermal estimates should use hot values. This positive coefficient makes paralleling easy, since a hotter device carries less current. Near threshold, at low gate drive, the coefficient turns negative, so linear-mode operation or slow switching can still cause current crowding.

Blocking more voltage needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, which is more resistive. For silicon unipolar devices the ideal specific on-resistance scales with about the 2.5th power of breakdown voltage, so doubling the rating raises it about 5.7 times: the silicon limit. Trench gates pack more channel width per area and remove the JFET resistance. Superjunction MOSFETs use alternating p and n pillars that deplete sideways, bringing 600 V-class devices well below the limit. SiC and GaN tolerate a much higher critical field, allowing thinner, more heavily doped drift regions.

A conducting MOSFET operates in its linear region, where current is nearly proportional to VDS, so it behaves like a resistor. Bipolar transistors and IGBTs instead show an on-state voltage: a saturated BJT drops about 0.1–0.3 V, and an IGBT has a junction-related knee before its resistive slope. At low voltage, a small RDS(on) usually beats a fixed knee, so MOSFETs dominate. At several hundred volts and high current, the IGBT's conductivity modulation keeps the drop low where a silicon MOSFET's drift resistance would soar.

faq.q: Why does MOSFET on-resistance increase with temperature?
faq.a: Higher temperature increases lattice scattering, which lowers carrier mobility in both the channel and the drift layer. As a rough guide, RDS(on) at 100 °C is about 1.5 times the room-temperature value.

faq.q: How do you calculate MOSFET conduction loss from RDS(on)?
faq.a: Use P = I²·RDS(on) with the RMS current through the device and the on-resistance at the expected junction temperature. In a switching converter, the RMS current already accounts for the duty cycle.

faq.q: Why do high-voltage MOSFETs have higher on-resistance?
faq.a: A higher rating needs a thicker, more lightly doped drift layer, and for silicon the ideal on-resistance grows with about the 2.5th power of breakdown voltage. Superjunction structures and SiC or GaN devices are used to get around this.

スイッチング損失.desc: Loss that occurs while a power device switches between on and off, when voltage and current are present at the same time. It grows with switching frequency.

about.p: In a hard-switched converter driving an inductive load, the switch cannot change voltage and current simultaneously. At turn-on, current must first rise to the full load current while the voltage is still near the bus voltage, held there by the freewheeling diode; only then does the voltage fall. Turn-off reverses the sequence. During each overlap, power V × I is dissipated. With linear ramps, each transition costs about ½ × V × I × transition time: at 400 V, 10 A and 20 ns, roughly 40 µJ. Turning on and off at 100 kHz then wastes around 8 W.

Switching loss equals the energy per cycle, Eon plus Eoff, times the switching frequency, so it scales linearly with frequency. Conduction loss, I² × RDS(on) for a MOSFET or current times saturation voltage for an IGBT (insulated-gate bipolar transistor), depends on how long the device conducts but not on how often it switches. At low frequencies conduction loss dominates; as frequency rises, switching loss takes over. Designers choose frequency as a compromise, since higher frequency shrinks inductors, transformers and capacitors but raises switching loss and electromagnetic noise.

Besides voltage-current overlap, hard turn-on discharges the device's own output capacitance through its channel, and the reverse recovery charge of a silicon PN diode in the same leg adds a current spike and further loss. IGBTs also show a tail current at turn-off, which limits them to relatively low frequencies, typically up to a few tens of kHz. Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) transistors have smaller capacitances and gate charge, and SiC Schottky diodes and GaN devices have little or no reverse recovery, which is why they allow much higher switching frequencies.

Gate resistance sets how fast the gate capacitance charges, trading switching loss against voltage overshoot, ringing and electromagnetic interference; separate turn-on and turn-off resistances or active gate drivers refine that balance. Minimizing stray inductance in the power loop allows faster switching without destructive overshoot. Soft-switching topologies, such as resonant and LLC converters, arrange zero-voltage or zero-current switching so the overlap nearly disappears. Datasheet Eon and Eoff values are measured with a double-pulse test under stated voltage, current, gate resistance and temperature, and should be rescaled for the actual operating conditions.

faq.q: How do you calculate switching loss?
faq.a: Multiply the total energy per switching cycle, Eon plus Eoff from the datasheet or measurement, by the switching frequency. A rough estimate per transition is ½ × V × I × transition time for a hard-switched inductive load.

faq.q: Why does switching loss increase with frequency?
faq.a: Each switching event dissipates a roughly fixed energy, so doubling the number of events per second doubles the average power lost.

faq.q: Why do SiC and GaN have lower switching losses than silicon IGBTs?
faq.a: They switch faster thanks to smaller capacitances and gate charge, have no IGBT-style tail current, and have little or no reverse recovery, so the voltage-current overlap and related losses are much smaller.

CMOSイメージセンサー.desc: An image sensor made with a CMOS process that has an amplifier in each pixel. It is low-power, can integrate peripheral circuits, and dominates smartphone cameras and more.

about.h: From photon to voltage in a 4T pixel
about.p: Each pixel's photodiode absorbs light and collects electrons in proportion to the exposure; quantum efficiency for visible light is typically about 50–80%. In the common four-transistor (4T) pixel, a transfer transistor moves this charge to a small node called the floating diffusion (FD), a source-follower amplifier buffers the FD voltage onto a column line, a select transistor connects the row, and a reset transistor clears the FD. Conversion gain is q/C_FD, about 160 µV per electron for a 1 fF node. Neighboring pixels often share the FD and readout transistors to save area.

Interface states at the silicon/oxide surface generate dark current. The pinned photodiode buries the n-type collection region under a heavily doped p+ surface layer, which fills those states with holes and suppresses that current. The buried region also fully depletes, so charge transfer is complete, avoiding image lag. Readout uses correlated double sampling (CDS): the FD is sampled right after reset and again after transfer, and the difference removes kTC reset noise and amplifier offset, bringing read noise down to a few electrons or less. Column-parallel ADCs then digitize the signal on chip.

In a front-side illuminated (FSI) sensor, light must pass through gaps between metal wiring layers before reaching the photodiode, losing intensity and angle tolerance. A back-side illuminated (BSI) sensor thins the wafer to a few micrometers and receives light from the side opposite the wiring, which keeps sensitivity high for pixels around 1 µm and became standard in smartphone cameras. Stacked sensors go further, bonding the pixel wafer to a separate logic wafer that carries ADCs and image processing. Epitaxial silicon substrates are used for low-defect pixel regions.

A charge-coupled device (CCD) shifts charge packets across the chip to a single output amplifier, which needs several clock voltages and more power. A CMOS image sensor amplifies in each pixel and reads rows through column circuits, so it runs at lower power, reads out faster, and integrates timing, ADCs and processing on the same die. Row-by-row readout causes rolling-shutter distortion of fast motion, which global-shutter pixels avoid with in-pixel storage. Dual-conversion-gain pixels switch extra FD capacitance to cover both dim and bright scenes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CMOS image sensor and a CCD?
faq.a: A CCD moves charge across the chip to one shared output amplifier, while a CMOS image sensor converts charge to voltage inside each pixel and reads it out row by row. CMOS sensors use less power and integrate ADCs and logic, which is why they dominate phones and most cameras.

faq.q: What does BSI mean in an image sensor?
faq.a: BSI stands for back-side illumination: the wafer is thinned and light enters from the back, so it reaches the photodiodes without passing through the metal wiring layers, improving sensitivity for small pixels.

faq.q: What is correlated double sampling in a CMOS image sensor?
faq.a: It reads the floating diffusion once after reset and once after charge transfer, then subtracts the two. Reset (kTC) noise and amplifier offsets appear in both samples and cancel, leaving the true signal.

量子効率.desc: The fraction of incident photons converted into signal electrons. The higher it is, the better the sensitivity.

about.p: External quantum efficiency (EQE) counts electrons collected per incident photon. It is the product of three factors: the fraction of light not reflected at the surface, the fraction absorbed in the active material, and the fraction of generated carriers collected before they recombine. Internal quantum efficiency (IQE) leaves out the reflection and counts per absorbed photon. For light-emitting diodes the direction reverses: EQE is photons emitted per injected electron, the product of IQE and light-extraction efficiency. Datasheets that say QE usually mean EQE at a stated wavelength.

Silicon absorbs blue light within a fraction of a micrometre of the surface, red light over several micrometres and near-infrared over tens of micrometres, and becomes transparent beyond about 1.1 µm, where photon energy falls below its band gap. Blue carriers generated near the surface are easily lost to surface recombination, while long wavelengths pass through a thin photodiode unabsorbed. Visible quantum efficiency of CMOS image sensors is typically about 50 to 80%, raised by back-side illumination, anti-reflection coatings and microlenses, and some cooled scientific sensors exceed 90%.

Responsivity R, in amperes per watt, links QE to the current a photodiode produces: R = ηqλ/hc, or about η × λ[µm]/1.24. Longer wavelengths carry less energy per photon, so one watt contains more photons and gives more current at the same η. At 1.55 µm an 80% efficient detector gives about 1.0 A/W, and even a perfect one cannot exceed about 1.25 A/W. Silicon cannot absorb this wavelength, so telecom receivers use InGaAs or germanium absorbers.

about.h: Why it matters for low-light imaging
about.p: Photon arrival is random, so even a perfect detector has shot noise equal to the square root of the signal. A sensor with lower QE loses photons before noise is added, and its shot-noise-limited signal-to-noise ratio scales with the square root of QE, so halving QE is like halving exposure time. Avalanche or electron-multiplying detectors can produce more than one output electron per photon, but that is gain applied after detection; QE itself remains at most 100% in ordinary photodiodes.

faq.q: What is the difference between internal and external quantum efficiency?
faq.a: External quantum efficiency counts collected electrons per incident photon, including reflection losses. Internal quantum efficiency counts per absorbed photon, isolating the material and collection efficiency.

faq.q: How do you convert quantum efficiency to responsivity?
faq.a: Use R ≈ η × λ / 1.24, with λ in micrometres and R in A/W. For example, 80% quantum efficiency at 1.55 µm gives about 1.0 A/W.

faq.q: Can quantum efficiency exceed 100 percent?
faq.a: Not in an ordinary photodiode without gain, since at visible and infrared wavelengths each photon generates at most one collected electron-hole pair. Devices with avalanche multiplication give more output current, but that is counted as gain separate from quantum efficiency.

裏面照射型(BSI).desc: An image sensor structure in which light enters from the back of the substrate, where there is no wiring. Light is not blocked by wiring, so sensitivity stays high even with small pixels.

about.p: In a front-side illuminated (FSI) CMOS image sensor, light enters from the side where transistors and wiring are built, passing through the microlens, color filter and several metal layers before reaching the photodiode. The metal blocks and reflects part of the light, and the tall optical stack loses rays arriving at oblique angles. In a backside-illuminated (BSI) sensor the wafer is flipped after front-side processing, bonded to a support wafer, and its original substrate thinned to a few µm, so light enters from the back and reaches the photodiode without crossing any wiring.

about.h: Why BSI matters for small pixels
about.p: As pixels shrink toward about 1 µm, the openings between metal lines in an FSI pixel become a small fraction of the pixel area and the stack becomes tall relative to pixel width, so sensitivity and angular response drop sharply. BSI keeps nearly the whole pixel area open to light and shortens the optical path from microlens to silicon. It also frees the wiring from optical constraints, allowing more metal layers. These advantages made BSI the standard structure for smartphone camera sensors.

Thinning must leave a uniform silicon layer a few µm thick across the wafer. The new back surface must be passivated, because defects there generate dark current; films with fixed negative charge are commonly used to accumulate holes at that surface. Thin silicon also makes optical and electrical crosstalk between neighboring pixels more likely, which deep trench isolation between pixels reduces. Red and near-infrared light has an absorption length of several µm or more in silicon, so very thin layers lose some long-wavelength response.

Because a BSI sensor already needs a bonded support wafer, that wafer can carry useful circuitry instead of being blank silicon. Stacked image sensors bond the pixel wafer to a logic wafer containing readout, analog-to-digital conversion and image processing, each made in a process suited to its function. This allows smaller chips or more processing per pixel area, and it builds directly on the wafer bonding and thinning techniques developed for BSI.

faq.q: What is the difference between BSI and FSI image sensors?
faq.a: In FSI, light passes through the wiring layers before reaching the photodiode; in BSI, the wafer is flipped and thinned so light enters from the back, where there is no wiring. BSI therefore collects more light, especially in small pixels.

faq.q: Why must the wafer be thinned in a BSI sensor?
faq.a: Light enters from the back, so it must reach the photodiodes near the front side before being absorbed. Thinning the silicon to a few µm puts the photodiodes within the light's absorption depth.

faq.q: Do BSI sensors have any disadvantages?
faq.a: They need extra steps such as wafer bonding, thinning and backside passivation, and the thin silicon increases crosstalk risk and reduces long-wavelength response. Deep trench isolation and careful surface treatment address these.

グローバルシャッター.desc: An electronic shutter method that exposes all pixels at the same time. Unlike a rolling shutter, which reads row by row, it does not distort images of moving objects.

about.p: The rolling shutter used in many CMOS image sensors resets, exposes and reads the pixels one row at a time. Every row is exposed for the same length of time, but each row starts at a different moment, so the top and bottom of the frame are captured several to tens of milliseconds apart. As a result, fast-moving objects appear slanted, the image wobbles when the camera pans, and flickering fluorescent or LED lights show up as bands. A global shutter starts and ends exposure for all pixels at the same time, so the whole frame shows a single instant and these motion distortions do not occur.

Even if all pixels finish exposure together, they still have to be read out row by row. A global shutter pixel therefore transfers the photodiode's charge to an in-pixel storage element at the end of exposure, all pixels at once, and holds it there until its row is read. Storage can be in the charge domain, keeping the charge itself in a dedicated memory node or the floating diffusion, or in the voltage domain, converting it to a voltage held on in-pixel capacitors. Some designs can run the next exposure while the stored frame is being read. Either way, the pixel needs more transistors and storage elements than a rolling-shutter pixel.

The storage element is shielded from light, but light entering at an angle and charge generated in the substrate leak in slightly and add a false signal while the pixel waits to be read. How small this leakage is gets evaluated as parasitic light sensitivity (PLS) or shutter efficiency. Noise also tends to rise from dark current in the storage node and in designs where correlated double sampling, which cancels reset noise, is hard to apply, and the storage element takes area from the photodiode, reducing sensitivity and full-well capacity. Remedies include light-shield and doping designs that reduce leakage, and stacked sensors that move storage capacitors and circuits to a lower chip to preserve photodiode area.

Global shutters are used wherever moving things must be captured accurately: industrial inspection cameras (machine vision) imaging products on conveyors, barcode readers, position estimation for robots and drones, and motion tracking in AR/VR devices. In vehicles they are sometimes used for driver monitoring, which images the driver with short pulses of infrared LED light; aligning every pixel's exposure with a short light pulse is another advantage. Most digital cameras have combined a rolling shutter with a mechanical shutter, but in 2023 a full-frame mirrorless camera with a global shutter sensor was announced.

faq.q: What is the difference between a global shutter and a rolling shutter?
faq.a: A global shutter exposes all pixels at the same time, so the whole image captures a single instant. A rolling shutter exposes each row at a slightly different time, so fast-moving objects can appear slanted. On the other hand, rolling-shutter pixels are simpler and often have an edge in sensitivity and noise.

faq.q: How does a global shutter work?
faq.a: All pixels are reset together to begin exposure, and at the end of exposure every pixel's photodiode charge is transferred at once to a light-shielded storage element inside the pixel. The stored signals are then read out row by row. Exposing simultaneously but reading sequentially yields an image without motion distortion.

faq.q: What are the drawbacks of a global shutter?
faq.a: Because each pixel needs a storage element and extra transistors, the light-collecting area shrinks for a given pixel size, which tends to lower sensitivity and dynamic range, and pixels tend to be larger. Parasitic light leaking into storage and higher noise are further challenges. These sensors also tend to cost more.

HEMT(高電子移動度トランジスタ).desc: A transistor that uses the high-mobility two-dimensional electron gas formed at a heterojunction interface as its channel. It is used in high-frequency and high-power applications.

about.p: A HEMT is grown epitaxially as a heterojunction between a wide-band-gap barrier, such as AlGaAs or AlGaN, and a narrower-gap channel material, such as GaAs or GaN. The conduction-band offset creates a thin triangular potential well on the channel side, where electrons are confined in a sheet only a few nanometers thick: the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). A Schottky metal gate on the barrier modulates the sheet density, so the device is a field-effect transistor whose channel lies at a buried, nearly perfect crystal interface rather than at an oxide surface as in a MOSFET.

In GaAs-based HEMTs the electrons come from donors placed in the barrier, often behind an undoped spacer, so the ionized donors are separated from the undoped channel where electrons travel. This modulation doping sharply reduces impurity scattering, giving higher mobility and lower noise than a doped channel; mobility rises further on cooling as phonon scattering falls. In AlGaN/GaN no doping is needed at all: the difference in spontaneous and piezoelectric polarization induces a sheet density of about 10¹³ cm⁻², with room-temperature mobility around 2000 cm²/V·s.

GaAs HEMTs, including pseudomorphic versions with an InGaAs channel, are the classic low-noise amplifiers in satellite receivers and radio telescopes. GaN HEMTs trade some noise performance for power: GaN's wide band gap gives a breakdown field roughly ten times that of silicon, its electron saturation velocity is about 2.5×10⁷ cm/s, and the dense 2DEG supplies high current. Together these give several times the power density of GaAs, so GaN HEMTs serve base-station, radar and satellite power amplifiers and, increasingly, fast power-conversion switches.

Because the 2DEG exists with zero gate bias, a basic HEMT is normally on (depletion mode) and needs a negative gate voltage to turn off. Power circuits prefer normally-off devices for fail-safe behavior. Common fixes are a p-type GaN layer under the gate that depletes the 2DEG beneath it, a recessed gate that thins the barrier, or a cascode in which a low-voltage silicon MOSFET in series switches the HEMT off by pulling its source above its grounded gate, at the cost of an extra die and its parasitics.

faq.q: What is the difference between a HEMT and a MOSFET?
faq.a: A MOSFET's channel is an inversion layer at the silicon/oxide interface, while a HEMT's channel is a two-dimensional electron gas at an epitaxial heterojunction with little impurity or roughness scattering. HEMTs therefore reach higher electron mobility and suit high-frequency, low-noise and high-power RF work.

faq.q: Why are GaN HEMTs normally on?
faq.a: Polarization at the AlGaN/GaN interface creates the 2DEG without any gate voltage, so the channel conducts at 0 V. Normally-off operation needs a p-GaN gate, a recessed gate or a cascode with a silicon MOSFET.

faq.q: What does 2DEG mean in a HEMT?
faq.a: 2DEG stands for two-dimensional electron gas, a sheet of electrons confined in a quantum well at a heterojunction so they can move freely only in the plane of the interface. It forms the HEMT's channel.

III-V族化合物半導体.desc: Semiconductors made of group III elements (Ga, In, Al, etc.) and group V elements (As, P, N, etc.), such as GaAs, InP and GaN.

ワイドバンドギャップ半導体.desc: Semiconductors with a larger band gap than silicon, such as SiC and GaN. Their high breakdown field makes them strong for high-voltage, high-temperature operation.

GAA(ゲートオールアラウンド).desc: A transistor structure in which the gate surrounds the channel on all sides. It controls current better than FinFET and is used in the generations after FinFET.

about.h: Why wrap the gate all the way around
about.p: Short-channel effects arise when the drain's electric field reaches into the channel and competes with the gate. The scale length λ estimates how far that influence extends; gate lengths of about 5–10 λ keep it small, and every additional gated surface shrinks λ. A planar MOSFET gates one face, a FinFET three, and a gate-all-around (GAA) transistor surrounds each channel completely. This strongest electrostatic control suppresses punch-through and leakage at shorter gate lengths, and like FinFETs, GAA devices use nearly undoped channels with threshold voltage set by the gate work function.

Production GAA devices use nanosheets: silicon plates about 5 nm thick and roughly 15–50 nm wide, typically three stacked vertically about 10 nm apart, each wrapped by gate dielectric and metal. A nanosheet resembles a FinFET fin laid on its side and stacked. A FinFET's width can only change in whole fins, but sheet width can be drawn continuously in layout, using wide sheets for high-performance cells and narrow ones for low power and SRAM. More sheets add current per footprint but complicate processing and add parasitic capacitance.

Fabrication starts with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25–30% germanium. The stack is patterned into fins and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric inner spacer, which reduces gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevents shorts. After source/drain epitaxy, the dummy gate is removed and the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the silicon sheets suspended. ALD then fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

Samsung announced volume production of GAA at its 3 nm node in 2022 under the name MBCFET; TSMC adopted nanosheets at its 2 nm node and Intel at 18A as RibbonFET, making GAA the successor to the FinFET. Researchers are pursuing further steps: the forksheet, which places nMOS and pMOS sheets on either side of a thin dielectric wall; the CFET, which stacks nMOS over pMOS; and two-dimensional channel materials such as MoS2 that remain semiconducting at a single layer about 0.65 nm thick.

faq.q: What is the difference between GAA and FinFET?
faq.a: A FinFET's gate covers three sides of a vertical fin, while a GAA transistor's gate surrounds stacked horizontal sheets or wires on all sides. GAA gives stronger gate control and allows the channel width to be set continuously instead of in whole fins.

faq.q: What is a nanosheet transistor?
faq.a: It is a GAA transistor whose channels are thin horizontal silicon sheets, about 5 nm thick and tens of nanometers wide, stacked about three high with the gate filling the spaces between and around them.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used when making GAA transistors?
faq.a: SiGe layers grown between the silicon channel layers act as sacrificial spacers. They can be etched away selectively later, opening gaps so the gate dielectric and metal can wrap around each silicon sheet.

ナノシート.desc: A GAA transistor structure that stacks several thin, plate-like silicon channels vertically, each surrounded by the gate. Current can be tuned by the sheet width.

about.p: A nanosheet transistor stacks typically about three horizontal silicon channels, each around 5 nm thick and from about 15 to 50 nm wide, spaced about 10 nm apart vertically. The gate dielectric and metal fill every gap, so the gate surrounds each sheet on all four sides, which is why it is called gate-all-around (GAA). It resembles a FinFET fin turned on its side and stacked. The effective channel width is the perimeter of each sheet summed over the stack, so a wider sheet carries proportionally more current.

Fabrication begins with an epitaxial stack of alternating Si and SiGe layers, the SiGe containing about 25 to 30 percent germanium. The stack is patterned like a fin and a dummy gate is formed. The ends of the SiGe layers are recessed and filled with a dielectric such as nitride, forming inner spacers that reduce gate-to-source/drain capacitance and prevent shorts. After source/drain epitaxy and removal of the dummy gate, the SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, leaving the Si sheets suspended, and ALD fills the gaps with high-k dielectric and metal gate.

In a FinFET, fin height and width are fixed by the process, so drive strength can change only by the number of fins, a constraint called width quantization. Nanosheet width can be set continuously in layout: wide sheets for high-performance logic, narrow ones for low-power cells and SRAM, which allows finer tuning of drive current and capacitance. Gating the channel from all sides also gives stronger electrostatic control and better resistance to short-channel effects, delivering more current in the same footprint. Samsung's 3 nm generation in 2022 was the first announced volume production.
