It originally restricted six substances: lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium and two brominated flame retardants, PBB and PBDE. Four phthalate plasticizers were added later. The maximum concentration is 0.1 wt% for most substances and 0.01 wt% for cadmium. The 2011 recast, often called RoHS 2, tied compliance to CE marking and broadened the range of covered products.

Limits apply to each homogeneous material, meaning a material that cannot be mechanically separated into different materials, not to the weight of the whole product. A lead's tin plating, a solder joint, the mold compound and the die-attach material are each judged separately. A tiny amount of lead concentrated in one solder joint can therefore violate the rule even if it is a negligible fraction of the device. Suppliers document compliance through material declarations and test reports, often using X-ray fluorescence screening.

Banning lead pushed the industry from tin-lead solder to tin-silver-copper (SAC) alloys such as SAC305, which melt around 217 to 220 °C instead of 183 °C. Reflow peaks rose to about 260 °C, increasing package stress and moisture-induced cracking, so moisture sensitivity ratings and package materials had to be requalified. Pure tin lead finishes replaced tin-lead plating, which brought tin whisker growth back as a reliability concern to be managed.

Where no practical substitute exists, time-limited exemptions apply, for example high-lead solders used for die attach in some power packages and lead in certain glass and ceramic components. These exemptions are reviewed periodically. RoHS is often confused with REACH: REACH regulates chemicals themselves, requiring registration of substances made or imported at one tonne or more per year and disclosure of substances of very high concern above 0.1 wt% in articles, whereas RoHS bans specific substances in finished electrical equipment. Similar laws exist outside the EU.

faq.q: Which substances are restricted under RoHS?
faq.a: Lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB and PBDE flame retardants, and four phthalates. Most are limited to 0.1 wt% in any homogeneous material, and cadmium to 0.01 wt%.

faq.q: Does RoHS ban all lead in electronics?
faq.a: No. It limits lead to 0.1 wt% per homogeneous material, but listed exemptions still allow lead in some applications, such as certain high-lead die-attach solders and glass in components, where alternatives are not yet practical.

faq.q: What is the difference between RoHS and REACH?
faq.a: RoHS restricts a short list of hazardous substances inside electrical and electronic products. REACH is a broad EU chemicals regulation covering registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of substances across all industries.

IDM(垂直統合型デバイスメーカー).desc: A semiconductor company that does everything in-house, from design through front-end and back-end manufacturing to sales.

about.p: An IDM (integrated device manufacturer) owns the whole chain: circuit design, front-end wafer fabrication in its own fabs, back-end assembly and test, and selling the finished devices under its own name. This contrasts with the disaggregated model, in which a fabless company designs chips, a foundry fabricates wafers for many customers, and an OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company packages and tests them. Many companies sit between the extremes, so the label describes a business structure rather than a product category.

about.h: Why some products favor the IDM model
about.p: When manufacturing technology itself differentiates the product, keeping design and process teams under one roof pays off. Memory, power devices and analog chips are typical examples: cell structures, high-voltage device layouts or precision passive components are co-optimized with process steps that the company develops itself. Short feedback loops between yield analysis and design changes also speed up learning. The cost is capital: building and continuously upgrading fabs requires enormous investment, and fabs must stay highly utilized through demand cycles to remain profitable.

about.h: IDM vs. fabless, foundry and fab-lite
about.p: A fabless company owns no fabs and buys wafers from foundries, so it avoids fab capital but depends on the foundry's process and capacity. A foundry manufactures to customer designs and does not sell its own chips. A fab-lite company is a partial IDM: it keeps fabs for mature processes and products where it has unique process strengths, and outsources leading-edge products that would need the largest investments to foundries. Fab-lite is common among microcontroller, analog and power semiconductor makers seeking to limit capital burden while keeping manufacturing know-how.

An IDM can run engineering lots on its own lines and adjust the process as needed. Companies without fabs, and universities or startups, often prototype through an MPW (multi-project wafer) run, in which a foundry places designs from several customers on one mask set and shares the mask and wafer costs among them. Each participant receives only a small number of chips, which is enough for evaluation but not for volume production. These options illustrate how ownership of manufacturing shapes a company's development cycle.

faq.q: What does IDM stand for in semiconductors?
faq.a: IDM stands for integrated device manufacturer, a company that designs, fabricates, assembles, tests and sells its own chips rather than relying on foundries and outsourced assembly.

faq.q: What is the difference between an IDM and a fabless company?
faq.a: An IDM owns and runs its own wafer fabs, while a fabless company only designs chips and pays a foundry to manufacture them.

faq.q: What is a fab-lite company?
faq.a: A fab-lite company is a partial IDM that keeps some fabs, usually for mature or specialized processes, while outsourcing products that need leading-edge processes to foundries.

OSAT.desc: A company that provides back-end services such as semiconductor assembly and testing under contract.
OSAT.title: OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test) Explained
OSAT.description: An OSAT provides back-end assembly, packaging and test under contract. What OSATs do, how they fit beside foundries and IDMs, and how packaging is changing that.

about.p: An OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) company performs the back-end steps that turn finished wafers into tested, shippable chips. Typical services include wafer probing, backgrinding to thin the wafer, dicing, die attach, wire bonding or flip-chip bumping, molding, marking, and final electrical test. The front end, building transistors and interconnect on the wafer, is done by an integrated device manufacturer (IDM) or a foundry; the OSAT receives the processed wafers and returns packaged, tested parts to the chip company.

about.h: Place in the industry's division of labor
about.p: The modern supply chain splits work among fabless design companies, foundries for wafer fabrication, and OSATs for packaging and test. A fabless company may never own a factory: it sends designs to a foundry and has the resulting wafers assembled and tested by an OSAT. IDMs often keep some back-end work in house but outsource part of it for capacity or cost. Back-end work is more labor- and floor-space-intensive than wafer fabrication, and major OSAT sites are concentrated in Taiwan, China and Southeast Asia.

As scaling slows, more performance comes from packaging: flip-chip bumps, copper pillars, fan-out wafer-level packaging, silicon interposers and chiplets stacked or placed side by side. These steps use wafer-level processes such as lithography, plating and redistribution layers, so OSATs have invested in fab-like equipment, while foundries have started offering their own advanced packaging. The simple split of front end at the foundry and back end at the OSAT therefore no longer holds for the most advanced products.

faq.q: What does OSAT stand for?
faq.a: OSAT stands for outsourced semiconductor assembly and test. It refers to companies that package and test chips under contract for other semiconductor companies.

faq.q: What is the difference between an OSAT and a foundry?
faq.a: A foundry manufactures the wafers, building transistors and wiring in the front-end process. An OSAT takes finished wafers and does the back-end work of cutting, packaging and testing the chips.

faq.q: Do fabless companies need OSATs?
faq.a: Usually yes. A fabless company owns no fabrication or assembly lines, so it relies on a foundry for wafers and on an OSAT, or a foundry offering packaging, for assembly and test.

ムーアの法則.desc: The empirical rule that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years. It has served as a target for semiconductor scaling.

about.p: In 1965 Gordon Moore noted that the number of components on the most cost-effective integrated circuit was doubling about every year, and in 1975 he revised the pace to about every two years. It is an empirical observation about technology and economics, not a law of physics. The frequently quoted 18-month figure is not Moore's own and usually refers to performance rather than transistor count. Because the whole industry planned equipment, materials and design tools around this cadence, it worked partly as a self-fulfilling target.

Moore's law concerns how many transistors fit on a chip. Dennard scaling, described in 1974, explained why shrinking was so beneficial: if dimensions and supply voltage scale down by the same factor, power density stays constant while circuits get faster. Around the mid-2000s supply and threshold voltages stopped scaling, because the subthreshold swing of about 60 mV per decade at room temperature makes leakage explode at low thresholds. Clock frequencies plateaued and designers turned to multiple cores and power management, while transistor counts kept rising.

Keeping pace required repeated reinvention. Lithography moved to shorter wavelengths, immersion optics, multiple patterning and extreme ultraviolet (EUV). Transistors gained strained silicon, high-k dielectrics with metal gates, then FinFETs and gate-all-around nanosheets to keep the channel under gate control. Layout tricks such as fewer tracks per standard cell, together with 3D stacking and chiplets, add density beyond pure shrinking. Modern node names such as 5 nm or 3 nm are generation labels and no longer equal any physical gate length.

about.h: Cost per transistor and the slowdown
about.p: The underlying goal of scaling is better PPA, meaning performance, power and area, plus lower cost per transistor. For decades each node delivered all of these. Today, rising fab, mask and lithography costs and the added process steps of multiple patterning have slowed the fall in cost per transistor, and the doubling interval has stretched. The industry still advances density, but gains increasingly come from packaging, specialization and design rather than from shrinking alone.

faq.q: Is Moore's law a law of physics?
faq.a: No. It is an empirical observation and industry roadmap target describing how transistor counts have grown, roughly doubling every two years, driven by engineering and economics.

faq.q: Is Moore's law dead?
faq.a: Transistor density is still increasing, but more slowly and at higher cost per wafer, and the old link to lower cost per transistor and higher clock speed has weakened. Much of the progress now comes from new device structures, 3D integration and chiplets.

faq.q: What is the difference between Moore's law and Dennard scaling?
faq.a: Moore's law describes the growth in transistor count per chip. Dennard scaling described how shrinking transistors along with voltage kept power density constant, and it broke down when voltage stopped scaling.

ハイブリッドボンディング.desc: A technique that directly bonds copper electrodes and dielectric surfaces without bumps, providing huge numbers of connections at extremely fine pitch.

about.p: Each surface is planarized by chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) so that copper pads sit a few nanometres below the surrounding dielectric. The surfaces are cleaned and activated with plasma, aligned and pressed together, and the dielectrics bond near room temperature. A subsequent anneal strengthens that bond, while thermal expansion pushes the recessed copper pads into contact, where atomic diffusion joins them. The result is simultaneous dielectric-to-dielectric and copper-to-copper bonding with no solder, no bumps and no underfill, which is why it is called hybrid.

Solder microbumps, bonded for example by thermocompression, need space so molten solder does not bridge neighbours, which keeps their pitch at tens of micrometres, around 20 µm at best. Hybrid bonding goes below 10 µm and down to a few micrometres. Because connection count scales inversely with the square of pitch, shrinking from 40 µm to 4 µm gives 100 times more connections per area. The joints are also very short, cutting parasitic capacitance and inductance, which raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit transferred between dies.

Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) bonding joins whole wafers at once, giving high throughput and the best alignment, but it pairs good dies with bad ones and requires identical die sizes, so stacked yield is the product of both wafers' yields. Chip-to-wafer (C2W) bonding places tested, singulated known-good dies onto a target wafer, improving stacked yield and allowing different die sizes, at the cost of slower placement. Both demand sub-nanometre roughness and extreme cleanliness: a single particle of about 100 nm can leave an unbonded void millimetres across.

Stacked CMOS image sensors, which bond a pixel wafer to a logic wafer, were the first major commercial use. Processors now stack a cache SRAM die directly on the compute die, adding several times the cache capacity without enlarging the processor, and hybrid bonding is being extended to HBM memory stacks. It also connects photonic and electronic chips with minimal parasitics. These are 3D packages, stacking dies vertically, as opposed to 2.5D packages that place dies side by side on an interposer; the two are often combined in one product.

faq.q: What is the difference between hybrid bonding and microbumps?
faq.a: Microbumps join dies with small solder bumps at pitches of tens of micrometres. Hybrid bonding directly fuses copper pads and surrounding dielectric without solder, reaching pitches below 10 µm and far higher connection density.

faq.q: What pitch can hybrid bonding achieve?
faq.a: Production hybrid bonding works below 10 µm pitch, down to a few micrometres, compared with roughly 20 µm or more for solder microbumps.

faq.q: What is the difference between wafer-to-wafer and chip-to-wafer bonding?
faq.a: Wafer-to-wafer bonds entire wafers at once for speed and alignment accuracy but cannot exclude bad dies. Chip-to-wafer places only known-good dies, improving yield and allowing different die sizes, but is slower.

シリコンインターポーザ.desc: A silicon intermediate substrate that holds chips side by side and connects them densely with fine wiring. It is used to connect GPUs and HBM, among other things.

about.p: A silicon interposer is a slab of silicon processed with the same copper damascene wiring used for chip interconnect, giving lines and spaces of about 1 µm or finer in several metal layers. It is usually passive, containing wiring but no transistors. Chips such as a processor and memory stacks are attached face down with dense microbumps, and through-silicon vias (TSVs) carry power, ground and external signals down through the interposer to larger bumps on an ordinary package substrate. This arrangement, chips side by side on a shared silicon base, is called 2.5D packaging.

about.h: Why GPUs and HBM need it
about.p: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) reaches its bandwidth through width rather than per-pin speed: each stack has a 1,024-bit data bus through the HBM3 generation. HBM3 at 6.4 Gb/s per pin gives about 819 GB/s per stack, and several stacks around a GPU add up to several TB/s. That requires thousands of signal wires only millimeters long, far more than an organic package substrate with lines tens of micrometers wide can route. The interposer's fine wiring makes the connection possible, and short wires also keep energy per bit low.

An interposer must be larger than all the dies it carries, so large AI packages need interposers several times the area of a single lithography exposure field, built by stitching exposures together; this adds cost and yield risk. Alternatives trade density for cost. Silicon bridges embed small pieces of silicon in the package substrate only under die-to-die edges, as in Intel's EMIB. Organic redistribution-layer (RDL) interposers use polymer dielectric and copper, are cheaper and easier to make large, and better match the substrate's thermal expansion, but offer coarser wiring.

In 2.5D integration, dies sit side by side on an interposer and communicate laterally; in 3D integration, dies are stacked vertically and connected through TSVs or hybrid bonding. 2.5D keeps every die exposed for cooling and lets dies from different process nodes be mixed easily, while 3D gives the shortest connections and smallest footprint but concentrates heat. The two are often combined: HBM itself is a 3D stack of DRAM dies, and those stacks are placed in 2.5D fashion next to the processor on an interposer, as in TSMC's CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate).

faq.q: What is a silicon interposer used for?
faq.a: It carries several chips side by side and connects them with micrometer-scale wiring, most notably linking a GPU or AI accelerator to multiple HBM stacks with thousands of short wires.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2.5D and 3D packaging?
faq.a: 2.5D places dies side by side on an interposer or bridge, while 3D stacks dies directly on top of each other using TSVs or hybrid bonding.

faq.q: Why not use an organic substrate instead of a silicon interposer?
faq.a: Standard organic substrates have lines tens of micrometers wide and cannot route thousands of HBM signals in the available area; organic RDL interposers and silicon bridges are cheaper alternatives with somewhat lower density.

有効質量.desc: An apparent mass used to treat electrons and holes in a crystal as if they were free particles responding to external forces. It is set by the curvature of the band; a smaller effective mass tends to give higher mobility.

about.p: An electron in a crystal moves through the periodic potential of the atoms, so its response to an applied force differs from that of a free electron. Band theory absorbs this into the energy–wavevector relation E(k). Near a band edge E is roughly parabolic, E ≈ ħ²k²/2m*, and the effective mass is defined by the curvature, m* = ħ² / (d²E/dk²). A sharply curved band gives a light carrier and a flat band a heavy one. The electron's actual rest mass does not change; m* is simply the parameter that makes Newton's law F = m*a work inside the crystal.

Mobility is roughly μ = qτ/m*, where τ is the mean time between scattering events, so lighter carriers accelerate more between collisions. In lightly doped silicon at room temperature, electron mobility is about 1400 cm²/V·s and hole mobility about 450 cm²/V·s, mainly because holes are heavier. This is why a CMOS pMOS is commonly drawn 2–3 times wider than its nMOS partner to match drive current. GaAs electrons, with m* of about 0.067 times the free-electron mass, reach about 8500 cm²/V·s, which suits high-frequency amplifiers.

Near the top of the valence band the curvature is negative, so an electron there would have negative effective mass; treating the missing electron as a hole with positive charge and positive mass restores intuitive behavior, and the sign of the Hall voltage confirms it. Effective mass can also depend on direction. Silicon's conduction band has six equivalent valleys, each with a heavy longitudinal mass of roughly 0.9–1.0 m0 and a light transverse mass of about 0.19 m0. In GaAs, a strong field can push electrons into the higher, heavier L valley, the transferred-electron effect behind the Gunn diode.

Because effective mass comes from band structure, changing the lattice changes it. Tensile strain in silicon, for example from a thin layer grown on relaxed SiGe, splits the six conduction valleys so electrons crowd into those offering the light transverse mass in the transport direction, while intervalley scattering drops; electron mobility can rise by roughly 1.5–2 times. For pMOS, compressive strain from embedded SiGe source/drain regions lightens the holes. SiGe and germanium channels are pursued because their hole effective mass is intrinsically lower than silicon's.

faq.q: Is effective mass the real mass of an electron?
faq.a: No. The electron's rest mass is unchanged; effective mass is a parameter derived from band curvature that lets you use F = ma for a carrier inside the crystal's periodic potential.

faq.q: Why do holes have lower mobility than electrons in silicon?
faq.a: Holes in silicon have a larger effective mass than conduction-band electrons, so the same field accelerates them less between scattering events. The result is roughly a threefold mobility gap at room temperature.

faq.q: Can effective mass be negative?
faq.a: Yes, near the top of a band the curvature is negative, so an electron there would have negative effective mass. Physicists describe those states with holes of positive mass and positive charge instead.

縮退半導体.desc: A semiconductor doped so heavily that the Fermi level lies inside the conduction or valence band. It behaves almost like a metal and is used in tunnel diodes and low-resistance contacts.

about.p: In a nondegenerate n-type semiconductor, Ec − EF ≈ kT·ln(Nc/ND), where Nc is the effective density of states in the conduction band, about 3×10¹⁹ cm⁻³ for silicon at room temperature. As donor concentration ND approaches Nc, this gap shrinks to zero and the Fermi level enters the band. In practice silicon is treated as degenerate from roughly 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³ upward, and the usual criterion is that the Fermi level lies within a few kT of the band edge or inside the band. The same applies to p-type doping and the valence band.

The simple Boltzmann approximation to Fermi-Dirac statistics no longer holds, so formulas built on it, including n × p = ni², become inaccurate. Donor levels broaden into an impurity band that merges with the conduction band, and the band gap effectively shrinks, an effect called bandgap narrowing. Carriers no longer freeze out at low temperature, and resistivity changes little with temperature, much like a metal. Mobility, however, is low because carriers scatter strongly off the dense ionized impurities.

MOSFET sources and drains are degenerately doped to minimize series resistance. At metal-semiconductor contacts, very high doping thins the depletion region enough that carriers tunnel through the Schottky barrier, giving a low-resistance ohmic contact. A tunnel (Esaki) diode uses degenerate doping on both sides so that, at small forward bias, electrons tunnel directly between bands, producing negative differential resistance. Bipolar emitters and transparent conducting oxides such as indium tin oxide are other examples of degenerately doped materials.

In a nondegenerate semiconductor the Fermi level sits in the gap, carrier density follows dopant density through simple exponential formulas, and the material is clearly semiconducting. In a degenerate one the Fermi level sits in a band, Fermi-Dirac integrals are needed to calculate carrier density, and conduction is quasi-metallic. Device simulators switch statistics accordingly; applying nondegenerate formulas at very high doping misplaces the Fermi level and ignores bandgap narrowing, which distorts calculated built-in potentials and currents.

faq.q: At what doping level does silicon become degenerate?
faq.a: Roughly above 10¹⁸–10¹⁹ cm⁻³, when the Fermi level reaches or enters the conduction or valence band; the exact threshold depends on temperature and the criterion used.

faq.q: Why are contacts made to heavily doped regions?
faq.a: Degenerate doping makes the depletion region under the metal so thin that carriers tunnel through the barrier, turning a rectifying Schottky contact into a low-resistance ohmic contact.

faq.q: Is a degenerate semiconductor a metal?
faq.a: It behaves almost like one, with weak temperature dependence of resistivity, but it is still a doped semiconductor with lower carrier density and mobility than a true metal.

間接遷移型.desc: A band structure in which the bottom of the conduction band and the top of the valence band occur at different momenta. Transitions need a phonon, so light emission is inefficient. Silicon and germanium are typical examples.

SRH再結合(ショックレー・リード・ホール再結合).desc: Recombination of electrons and holes through deep levels (traps) in the band gap. It mainly determines minority-carrier lifetime in silicon and is accelerated by metal contamination and crystal defects.

about.p: A deep level in the band gap can capture an electron from the conduction band and then capture a hole from the valence band, annihilating the pair in two steps; emission of a trapped carrier back to its band is the competing process. The net rate is U = (np − ni²) / [τp(n + n1) + τn(p + p1)], where n1 and p1 describe trap position. Traps near midgap make n1 and p1 smallest and are therefore the most effective. The released energy goes mainly into lattice vibrations, not light.

The characteristic capture lifetime is τ = 1/(σ·vth·Nt), where σ is the capture cross-section, vth the thermal velocity and Nt the trap density, so lifetime falls in inverse proportion to trap concentration. Heavy metals such as iron and gold and crystal defects such as dislocations are typical culprits. In silicon, an indirect-gap semiconductor where radiative recombination is weak, SRH recombination dominates at moderate carrier densities and sets minority-carrier lifetime, which is commonly measured by photoconductance decay techniques.

Fast switching devices sometimes need short lifetime. Fast-recovery diodes and IGBTs introduce recombination centers deliberately, by platinum or gold diffusion or by electron or proton irradiation, so that stored minority carriers disappear quickly at turn-off. This reduces reverse recovery time and switching loss, but it also raises forward voltage drop and leakage, so the lifetime is tuned as a compromise between conduction loss and switching loss.

When np is below ni², as in a reverse-biased depletion region, the same traps run in reverse and generate electron-hole pairs. This generation current is the main source of reverse leakage in silicon pn junctions at room temperature and of dark current in image sensors. It scales with ni, which goes as exp(−Eg/2kT), so its activation energy is about half the band gap, whereas diffusion current, which goes as ni², has an activation energy close to the full gap and takes over at high temperature.

faq.q: Why are midgap traps the most effective recombination centers?
faq.a: A midgap level can capture both electrons and holes at comparable rates and rarely re-emits them thermally, so captured carriers tend to recombine rather than escape back to their band.

faq.q: What is the difference between SRH, radiative and Auger recombination?
faq.a: SRH goes through trap levels and dominates in silicon at moderate densities; radiative recombination emits a photon and is strong in direct-gap materials; Auger recombination gives the energy to a third carrier and dominates at very high carrier density.

faq.q: What shortens minority-carrier lifetime in silicon?
faq.a: Deep-level impurities such as iron and gold and crystal defects, which act as SRH recombination centers; lifetime falls roughly in inverse proportion to their density.

オージェ再結合.desc: Recombination in which the released energy is given to another carrier instead of being emitted as light. It becomes significant at high carrier densities and affects lifetime in heavily doped layers and efficiency loss in LEDs.

about.p: In Auger recombination an electron and a hole recombine and hand the released energy, roughly the band-gap energy, to a third carrier, either another electron (eeh process) or another hole (ehh process). That carrier is kicked high into its band and then loses the energy as heat by emitting phonons. The rate is commonly written R = Cn·n²p + Cp·np², with Auger coefficients Cn and Cp. In heavily doped n-type material this gives a lifetime that falls with the square of the doping.

A simple way to compare mechanisms is by how their rates scale with carrier density n under high injection: SRH recombination scales roughly with n, radiative recombination with n², and Auger recombination with n³. At low densities, SRH dominates in silicon; at very high densities from heavy doping or strong injection, Auger takes over. Auger processes also become stronger as the band gap narrows, which makes them a key loss in infrared detectors and long-wavelength lasers.

Heavily doped emitters of bipolar transistors and solar cells suffer short Auger lifetimes, which reduces emitter efficiency and increases recombination current. Power devices such as PiN diodes and IGBTs operate under high injection, where Auger recombination limits the stored carrier density. Because Auger recombination is intrinsic to the material and cannot be removed by purification, it sets the fundamental upper limit on silicon minority-carrier lifetime and contributes to the theoretical efficiency limit of silicon solar cells.

Indium gallium nitride (InGaN) LEDs reach peak efficiency at relatively low current densities of a few A/cm² and become less efficient as current rises, a phenomenon called efficiency droop. Auger recombination, growing with the cube of carrier density, and electron leakage over the active region are considered the main causes. The often-used ABC model writes internal quantum efficiency as Bn² / (An + Bn² + Cn³). High-power lighting lowers current density by using larger or multiple chips.

faq.q: Why does Auger recombination scale with the cube of carrier density?
faq.a: Three carriers must meet: an electron, a hole and a third carrier to receive the energy, so the rate is proportional to n²p or np², roughly n³ when n and p are similar.

faq.q: Does Auger recombination emit light?
faq.a: No. The energy goes to a third carrier and ends up as heat, which is why it is a non-radiative loss in LEDs and lasers.

faq.q: Is Auger recombination important in silicon?
faq.a: Yes, in heavily doped regions and under high injection, where it dominates over SRH recombination and limits lifetime regardless of material purity.

擬フェルミ準位.desc: Separate Fermi levels for electrons and holes, used to describe a semiconductor driven out of equilibrium by light or current injection. The larger the split between them, the more excess carriers there are.

拡散長.desc: The average distance minority carriers diffuse before recombining, given by L = √(Dτ) from the diffusion coefficient D and lifetime τ. It strongly affects the efficiency of solar cells and photodetectors.

about.p: When excess minority carriers are injected at one boundary of a neutral region, for example at the edge of a forward-biased pn junction or where light is absorbed, they spread out by diffusion while recombining at a rate set by their lifetime τ. Solving the steady-state continuity equation gives an exponential decay, Δn(x) = Δn(0)·exp(−x/L), with L = √(Dτ). The diffusion length is thus the distance over which the excess carrier density falls to 1/e of its starting value. The units check out: √(cm²/s × s) gives centimeters.

The diffusion coefficient follows from the mobility through the Einstein relation, D = μkT/q. Electrons in lightly doped silicon have D of about 35 cm²/s, holes about 12 cm²/s. With D = 36 cm²/s and τ = 10 µs, L = √(3.6 × 10⁻⁴ cm²) ≈ 190 µm. Lifetime varies enormously, from nanoseconds in heavily doped or contaminated material to milliseconds in very pure silicon, so L ranges from below a micrometer to millimeters. Heavy doping shortens L twice over, since both the mobility and the lifetime fall.

A light-generated carrier contributes current only if it reaches the junction's electric field before recombining. Carriers generated within roughly one diffusion length of the depletion region are collected efficiently, while those created deeper are mostly lost. Long-wavelength light is absorbed deep in silicon, so red and infrared response depends strongly on L. A diffusion length longer than the absorber thickness helps collect nearly all carriers. Metal impurities and crystal defects that create recombination centers cut the lifetime and hence L, which is why wafer purity matters so much for solar cells.

about.h: Not the same as dopant diffusion length
about.p: The same square-root form appears in process engineering as √(Dt), the characteristic distance dopant atoms move during a thermal step of time t. That D describes atoms, not carriers, and is many orders of magnitude smaller: about 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ cm²/s for boron in silicon at 1000 °C, giving about 0.1 µm in an hour. In bipolar transistors the carrier diffusion length matters again: the base is made much thinner than L so that few injected carriers recombine before reaching the collector, which keeps the current gain high.

faq.q: What is the formula for minority carrier diffusion length?
faq.a: L = √(Dτ), where D is the minority carrier diffusion coefficient and τ is the minority carrier lifetime. For example, D = 36 cm²/s and τ = 10 µs give about 190 µm.

faq.q: Why does diffusion length matter for solar cell efficiency?
faq.a: Only carriers that diffuse to the junction before recombining produce current. A longer diffusion length means carriers generated deep in the cell are still collected, raising the photocurrent.

faq.q: Does higher doping increase or decrease diffusion length?
faq.a: It decreases it. Heavier doping lowers mobility, and therefore D, and also shortens the minority carrier lifetime through faster recombination.

アインシュタインの関係式.desc: The relation D = μkT/q that links the diffusion coefficient D and mobility μ of carriers. It shows that materials with higher mobility also allow faster diffusion.

電子親和力.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the bottom of the conduction band of a semiconductor. It is used to estimate band offsets at heterojunctions and barrier heights at metal contacts.

仕事関数.desc: The energy difference between the vacuum level and the Fermi level: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a material. It affects the threshold voltage of metal gates and the height of Schottky barriers.

about.p: The work function is measured from the Fermi level to the vacuum level, whereas the electron affinity is measured from the conduction-band edge to the vacuum level. In a metal the Fermi level lies inside a band, so the work function is a single material property, typically about 4 to 6 eV and somewhat dependent on crystal face and surface cleanliness. In a semiconductor the work function equals the electron affinity plus the gap between the conduction band and the Fermi level. Silicon's electron affinity is about 4.05 eV, so its work function ranges from about 4.05 eV (heavily n-type) to 5.17 eV (heavily p-type).

When a metal touches an n-type semiconductor, the ideal (Schottky-Mott) barrier height for electrons is the metal work function minus the semiconductor's electron affinity. A high-work-function metal on n-type silicon should therefore make a rectifying Schottky contact. In practice, interface states pin the Fermi level, so barrier heights on silicon vary much less with the metal than the simple rule predicts. Ohmic contacts are therefore made mainly by heavy doping under the contact, which thins the barrier so carriers tunnel through it.

In a MOS structure, the difference between the gate and channel work functions sets the flat-band voltage, which adds directly to the threshold voltage. Polysilicon gates gave the right values automatically: n+ poly near the conduction band for nMOS and p+ poly near the valence band for pMOS. With high-k dielectrics, metal gates replaced poly, so the metals must provide effective work functions near 4.1 eV for nMOS (aluminum-containing stacks such as TiAl) and near 5.1 eV for pMOS (TiN-based stacks). FinFETs and gate-all-around devices use lightly doped channels, so stacking thin layers to tune the effective work function is the main way to offer multiple threshold options.

The effective work function of a metal gate depends on reactions at its interfaces with the high-k film, and the roughly 1000 °C anneals used to activate source and drain can shift it unpredictably. A gate-last, or replacement metal gate, flow therefore builds the transistor around a sacrificial polysilicon gate, removes it after the hot steps, and only then deposits the high-k and work-function metals. Work function also governs thermionic and photoelectric emission, and it is measured by photoemission spectroscopy or Kelvin probe techniques.

faq.q: What is the difference between work function and electron affinity?
faq.a: Work function is the energy from the Fermi level to the vacuum level; electron affinity is the energy from the conduction-band edge to the vacuum level. In a semiconductor the electron affinity is fixed by the material, while the work function changes with doping.

faq.q: Does doping change the work function of silicon?
faq.a: Yes. Doping moves the Fermi level, so silicon's work function varies from about 4.05 eV when heavily n-type to about 5.17 eV when heavily p-type.

faq.q: Why does the gate metal work function affect threshold voltage?
faq.a: The gate-to-channel work-function difference sets the flat-band voltage, which shifts the threshold voltage one-for-one. Choosing or tuning the gate metal therefore sets the threshold without heavy channel doping.

真性キャリア密度.desc: The density of thermally generated electrons and holes in an undoped semiconductor, written ni. For silicon it is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at room temperature and rises steeply with temperature. In equilibrium, n × p = ni².

about.p: Even in perfectly pure silicon, thermal energy occasionally lifts a valence electron across the band gap, leaving a hole behind, so electrons and holes appear in equal numbers. Their equilibrium density, the intrinsic carrier density ni, follows ni ∝ T^(3/2)·exp(−Eg/2kT). For silicon at room temperature ni is about 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, quoted as 1.0–1.5×10¹⁰ depending on the source, so only about one atom in 10¹² contributes a carrier. Narrower gaps give far more: germanium is about 2×10¹³ cm⁻³, while GaAs is only about 2×10⁶ cm⁻³.

In thermal equilibrium n × p = ni², whether or not the material is doped. Adding donors raises the electron density and gives holes more partners to recombine with, so holes fall in proportion. With 1×10¹⁶ cm⁻³ fully ionized donors, n ≈ 1×10¹⁶ and p = (1×10¹⁰)² / 10¹⁶ = 1×10⁴ cm⁻³. These minority carriers are a trillion times scarcer than majority carriers, yet they set junction reverse current and bipolar transistor action. The law fails away from equilibrium: under illumination or forward bias, np exceeds ni².

Because ni contains exp(−Eg/2kT), it rises steeply with temperature, roughly doubling for every 10 °C near room temperature in silicon. Minority-carrier densities rise with it, so pn-junction reverse leakage climbs rapidly when hot. The same effect makes a silicon diode's forward voltage fall about 2 mV/°C at constant current, used for on-chip temperature sensing and cancelled in bandgap references. When ni approaches the doping level, the device loses its doping-controlled behavior, one reason wide-gap SiC and GaN suit high-temperature operation.

A region is extrinsic when its doping far exceeds ni, which at room temperature happens with only tiny amounts of dopant. At diffusion temperatures, however, ni itself rises to around 10¹⁸ cm⁻³ or more, so only heavily doped regions remain extrinsic. There, the shifted Fermi level increases the population of charged point defects and the internal field pushes ionized dopants along, making diffusion coefficients concentration dependent. Arsenic profiles consequently become box-like, with flat tops and steep fronts, instead of ideal erfc or Gaussian shapes.

faq.q: What is the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at 300 K?
faq.a: About 1×10¹⁰ cm⁻³, with published values ranging roughly from 1.0 to 1.5×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ depending on the band-gap and effective-mass data used.

faq.q: Does n × p = ni² hold in a forward-biased diode?
faq.a: No. The relation holds only in thermal equilibrium; with forward bias V, the product near the junction rises to about ni² × exp(qV/kT) because carriers are being injected.

faq.q: Why does intrinsic carrier density increase with temperature?
faq.a: More thermal energy lets more valence electrons jump the band gap, and the dependence is exponential in −Eg/2kT. Wider band gaps make the rise far smaller at a given temperature.

ショットキーバリアダイオード.desc: A diode that uses a metal-semiconductor junction (Schottky junction). It has a low forward voltage and switches fast because there is no minority-carrier storage.

about.p: When a metal contacts a lightly doped semiconductor, usually n-type, electrons flow until the Fermi levels align, leaving a depletion region in the semiconductor and an energy barrier at the interface called the Schottky barrier. Ideally its height is the metal work function minus the semiconductor electron affinity, but in practice interface states partly pin it, so the measured barrier depends less on the metal than this rule predicts. Forward current flows by thermionic emission of majority carriers over the barrier, rising exponentially with voltage like a pn diode, but with no minority-carrier injection.

Because the barrier is lower than the built-in potential of a silicon pn junction, a Schottky diode conducts at about 0.2–0.4 V instead of roughly 0.7 V. Since current is carried by majority carriers only, no minority charge is stored, so reverse recovery is almost absent and switching is fast. The price is reverse leakage that is much larger than a pn diode's and rises steeply with temperature. A lower barrier gives lower forward voltage but higher leakage, so barrier height is a design trade-off. Silicon Schottky diodes are practical only up to about 200 V.

The same metal can form either a rectifying or an ohmic contact depending on doping. On lightly doped silicon the depletion region is wide and carriers must go over the barrier, giving diode behavior. On heavily doped silicon the depletion region becomes so thin that electrons tunnel straight through, and the contact behaves like a low resistance. This is why transistor source, drain and contact regions are heavily doped, and why a Schottky diode needs a lightly doped drift layer under the metal, which also sets its breakdown voltage.

Silicon Schottky diodes are standard rectifiers in low-voltage switching power supplies, where their low forward drop and fast recovery cut losses. SiC (silicon carbide) Schottky diodes rated roughly 600–1700 V serve as freewheeling diodes in inverters and power-factor-correction circuits; because they have almost no reverse-recovery current, they also reduce the turn-on loss of the complementary switch. A Schottky diode across a bipolar transistor's base-collector junction keeps it out of deep saturation, the trick behind the 74S and 74LS Schottky TTL logic families.

faq.q: Why does a Schottky diode have higher reverse leakage than a pn diode?
faq.a: Its barrier is lower than a pn junction's built-in potential, and reverse current is thermionic emission over that barrier, which is exponentially sensitive to barrier height and temperature.

faq.q: Does a Schottky diode have reverse recovery time?
faq.a: Practically none from stored charge, because it conducts with majority carriers only. What remains is a small capacitive current from charging the junction capacitance.

faq.q: Can Schottky diodes be used at high voltage?
faq.a: Silicon Schottky diodes are limited to about 200 V, but silicon carbide Schottky diodes are commercially used from about 600 V to 1700 V.

接合容量(空乏層容量).desc: Capacitance arising because the depletion layer of a PN junction acts like a parallel-plate capacitor. It decreases as reverse bias widens the depletion layer; varactor diodes use this property.

about.p: The depletion region of a pn junction contains fixed charge: ionized donors on the n side and ionized acceptors on the p side, with almost no mobile carriers in between. When the voltage across the junction changes, the edges of this region move, adding or removing charge on each side, just as charge is added to the plates of a capacitor. The small-signal capacitance per unit area is therefore C = ε/W, where W is the depletion width and ε is the permittivity of silicon, about 11.7 times that of vacuum.

For a one-sided abrupt junction, W = √(2ε(Vbi + V)/qN), where Vbi is the built-in potential, V the reverse bias and N the doping on the lightly doped side. Capacitance therefore falls roughly as 1/√(Vbi + V), so quadrupling the total voltage halves it. Circuit models write Cj = Cj0/(1 + V/Vbi)^m, with m = 1/2 for abrupt and 1/3 for linearly graded junctions. Plotting 1/C² against V gives a straight line whose slope yields N and whose intercept yields Vbi, the basis of capacitance-voltage (C-V) doping profiling.

Junction capacitance dominates under reverse bias and small forward bias. Under significant forward bias, a second effect takes over: injected minority carriers are stored near the junction, and because that stored charge changes with voltage, it behaves as diffusion capacitance, proportional to current and carrier lifetime. Diffusion capacitance can reach nanofarads at high current and limits the switching speed of diodes and bipolar transistors. The distinction matters in design: a reverse-biased junction gives a small, voltage-tunable capacitor, while a forward-biased one stores charge that must be removed before turn-off.

Varactor diodes exploit the voltage dependence to tune LC resonators in voltage-controlled oscillators and PLLs, with hyperabrupt doping profiles widening the tuning range. Photodiodes are reverse-biased partly to cut junction capacitance and speed their response, and depletion-type silicon optical modulators vary depletion width to move majority carriers, reaching tens of gigahertz. Elsewhere it is parasitic: source and drain junctions of MOSFETs load every logic node, and silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers reduce that load by placing transistors on a buried oxide instead of a bulk junction.

faq.q: Why does junction capacitance decrease with reverse bias?
faq.a: Reverse bias widens the depletion region, and since capacitance is permittivity divided by width, a wider region gives a smaller capacitance, roughly as one over the square root of voltage for an abrupt junction.

faq.q: What is the difference between junction capacitance and diffusion capacitance?
faq.a: Junction capacitance comes from fixed charge in the depletion region and dominates under reverse bias; diffusion capacitance comes from minority carriers stored under forward bias and grows with current.

faq.q: How do you measure doping from junction capacitance?
faq.a: Measure capacitance versus reverse bias and plot 1/C² against V; for an abrupt junction the slope gives the doping of the lightly doped side and the intercept gives the built-in potential.

拡散容量.desc: Capacitance in a forward-biased PN junction caused by injected minority carriers stored in the neutral regions. It grows in proportion to forward current and limits high-speed operation.

逆回復時間.desc: The time during which reverse current keeps flowing after a conducting diode is reverse-biased, until the stored minority carriers are removed. It causes switching loss and noise.

about.p: When a conducting diode is driven to reverse bias, the external circuit forces its current to fall at a rate di/dt and then reverse. The junction cannot block yet because minority carriers stored on both sides keep it forward-biased internally, so reverse current flows and rises to a peak, the peak reverse recovery current. Once the carriers near the junction are depleted, the diode starts blocking and the current decays toward zero. The time from zero crossing until the current has decayed to a specified fraction is trr.

The charge to be removed, Qrr, is roughly the forward current times the minority-carrier lifetime, so trr grows with forward current and with temperature, which lengthens lifetime. Faster di/dt raises the peak reverse current and changes the waveform. For this reason datasheets quote trr with conditions such as forward current, di/dt and temperature. General-purpose rectifiers recover in the order of microseconds, while fast-recovery types reach several tens of nanoseconds by adding lifetime-killing recombination centers.

trr is often split into the time to reach peak reverse current and the decay time after it; the ratio of decay time to rise time is called softness. A snappy diode whose current drops abruptly causes a large voltage spike across circuit inductance, ringing and electromagnetic interference (EMI). A soft diode decays more gradually. Designers therefore look at Qrr and the recovery waveform, not only at trr, when choosing a freewheeling diode.

about.h: Impact in power converters and the alternatives
about.p: In a hard-switched converter, the recovery current of the freewheeling diode flows through the transistor as it turns on, adding turn-on loss and stress that grow with switching frequency. MOSFET body diodes often recover slowly, a known issue in bridge circuits. Schottky diodes, including silicon carbide (SiC) Schottky diodes, conduct with majority carriers and store almost no minority charge, so they show essentially only a small capacitive charge instead of true reverse recovery.

faq.q: Do Schottky diodes have reverse recovery time?
faq.a: Practically none, because they conduct with majority carriers and store no minority charge; only a small junction-capacitance charge flows when they switch off.

faq.q: What is the difference between trr and Qrr?
faq.a: trr is the duration of the reverse recovery current, while Qrr is the total charge it carries; Qrr relates more directly to the switching loss caused in the circuit.

faq.q: How can I reduce diode reverse recovery losses?
faq.a: Use fast or soft-recovery diodes, Schottky or SiC Schottky diodes, lower di/dt with snubbers or gate control, or soft-switching topologies that let the diode current fall to zero before reverse voltage is applied.

伝導度変調.desc: A large drop in the resistance of a lightly doped layer when many minority carriers are injected into it. PIN diodes and IGBTs use it to combine high breakdown voltage with low on-state voltage.

about.p: A high-voltage device needs a thick, lightly doped layer to block voltage, and in the off state that layer contains few free carriers and is highly resistive. When the device conducts in forward bias, the heavily doped p and n regions on either side inject holes and electrons into it. At high injection their densities far exceed the background doping and stay roughly equal to preserve charge neutrality. Conductivity is proportional to carrier density times mobility, so the layer's resistance falls by orders of magnitude, and the voltage across it depends only weakly on its thickness.

about.h: Why power devices rely on it
about.p: In a unipolar device such as a power MOSFET or Schottky diode, only the doping supplies carriers in the drift layer, and the ideal specific on-resistance of silicon rises roughly with the 2.5th power of the breakdown voltage. Bipolar devices escape this limit. A PIN diode floods its i-layer with carriers, and an IGBT adds a p+ layer on the collector side of a MOSFET-like structure so that injected holes modulate the drift layer while the MOS gate controls the electron current. This keeps on-state voltage low at ratings from about 600 V to 6.5 kV.

The injected carriers do not vanish instantly when the device is told to turn off. A PIN diode conducts a reverse-recovery current while stored charge is swept out, and an IGBT shows a tail current as holes left in the drift layer recombine, because the MOS channel cannot extract them. Both add switching loss and limit the usable frequency. Carrier-lifetime control, for example by electron irradiation or heavy-metal diffusion, speeds switching but raises on-state voltage, a classic trade-off in power-device design.

Silicon MOSFETs carry only majority carriers, so they show no conductivity modulation, switch fast and dominate below a few hundred volts. Wide-band-gap SiC MOSFETs reach high voltage with a thin drift layer instead, competing with IGBTs at mid-to-high voltage. The effect is also used in PIN diodes as RF switches and attenuators: forward current lowers the i-layer resistance roughly in proportion to the current, while reverse bias leaves a high-resistance, low-capacitance layer.

faq.q: Why don't power MOSFETs have conductivity modulation?
faq.a: A MOSFET conducts only with majority carriers supplied by the drift-layer doping, and no minority carriers are injected. Its drift-layer resistance therefore stays high at high voltage ratings.

faq.q: Why does conductivity modulation slow down switching?
faq.a: The injected electrons and holes must be removed or recombine before the device can block voltage, which causes reverse-recovery current in diodes and tail current in IGBTs. This stored charge adds switching loss.

faq.q: How does an IGBT achieve low on-voltage at high voltage?
faq.a: Its p+ collector injects holes into the lightly doped drift layer, and together with electrons from the MOS channel they raise the carrier density far above the doping. This conductivity modulation lowers the drift-layer resistance.

トンネルダイオード(エサキダイオード).desc: A diode with very heavily doped p and n sides that shows negative resistance in forward bias due to tunneling. It was discovered by Leo Esaki in 1957.

理想係数.desc: The factor n in the diode equation I ∝ exp(qV/nkT). It is close to 1 when diffusion current dominates and close to 2 when recombination in the depletion layer dominates, so it indicates junction quality.

about.h: Where n = 1 and n = 2 come from
about.p: In the ideal diffusion picture, forward bias raises the minority-carrier concentration at each edge of the depletion region in proportion to exp(qV/kT), and the current that diffuses away into the neutral regions follows the same law, giving n = 1. Recombination inside the depletion region behaves differently: it is strongest where electron and hole densities are equal, and there each equals ni·exp(qV/2kT). The resulting recombination current goes as exp(qV/2kT), so a diode dominated by it shows n ≈ 2.

about.h: Extracting n from an I-V curve
about.p: Plot forward current on a logarithmic axis against voltage. At room temperature an ideal diode rises one decade per about 60 mV, since kT/q × ln 10 ≈ 26 mV × 2.3; a diode with ideality factor n needs n × 60 mV per decade. Formally n = (q/kT)·dV/d(ln I). Use the straight middle portion of the curve: at low current, shunt leakage distorts it, and at high current series resistance bends it over and inflates the apparent n.

Many silicon diodes show n close to 2 at low current, where depletion-region recombination is relatively important, and close to 1 at moderate current, where diffusion dominates. Under high-level injection, when injected carriers exceed the doping, n rises toward 2 again. Values above 2 point to other mechanisms such as tunneling or several junctions in series. Because recombination depends on defect density, n is used as a quick gauge of junction quality, for example in solar cells, which are often modeled with two diodes of n = 1 and n = 2.

The same thermal factor limits transistors. A MOSFET below threshold conducts by diffusion over a barrier, so its current also changes exponentially with voltage. Its subthreshold swing is (kT/q)·ln 10 × (1 + Cd/Cox), where Cd is depletion capacitance and Cox gate-oxide capacitance, giving at least about 60 mV per decade at room temperature. The bracketed factor plays the role of an ideality factor: gate voltage is only partly coupled to the channel potential.

faq.q: What does an ideality factor of 2 mean?
faq.a: It means the current is dominated by recombination through defect levels in the depletion region, or that the diode is in high-level injection, rather than by ideal minority-carrier diffusion.

faq.q: How do you calculate the ideality factor from an I-V curve?
faq.a: Take the slope of a semilog plot of forward current versus voltage in its straight region: n = (q/kT)·ΔV/Δ(ln I), or n equals the measured millivolts per decade divided by about 60 mV at room temperature.

faq.q: Why does the measured ideality factor increase at high current?
faq.a: Series resistance drops part of the applied voltage outside the junction and high-level injection changes the physics, both of which make the voltage per decade larger.

オーミック接触.desc: A metal-semiconductor contact with low resistance in both directions and a linear current-voltage relation. It is made by heavily doping the semiconductor surface so carriers can tunnel through the barrier.

飽和領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are forward-biased. The collector-emitter voltage falls to about 0.1-0.3 V, corresponding to a switch in the on state.
飽和領域.title: Saturation Region of a BJT (vs. MOSFET Saturation)
飽和領域.description: In BJT saturation both junctions are forward-biased and VCE drops to about 0.1–0.3 V: a switch's on state. Why MOSFET 'saturation' means something different.

about.p: A bipolar transistor has four operating regions defined by its two junctions. In the active region the base-emitter junction is forward-biased and the base-collector junction reverse-biased, and IC ≈ hFE × IB. If the base current is raised until the collector circuit cannot supply hFE × IB, for example when VCC/RC is smaller, the collector voltage falls until the base-collector junction also becomes forward-biased. That is saturation. Collector current is now set by the external circuit and barely increases with more base current, and the ratio IC/IB, called the forced beta, falls below hFE.

about.h: Saturation as the on state of a switch
about.p: Because the two forward-biased junctions largely cancel, the collector-emitter voltage VCE(sat) is only about 0.1–0.3 V, close to a closed switch, and the conduction loss is about VCE(sat) × IC. Designers guarantee saturation by driving base current several times IC/hFE(min), often 2–10 times. The cost appears at turn-off: in saturation excess minority charge is stored in the base and collector, and it must be removed before the transistor can leave saturation, delaying switching. Schottky clamps or avoiding deep saturation are classic ways to speed this up.

The same word describes a very different condition in a MOSFET. A long-channel nMOSFET with VGS > Vth enters saturation when VDS ≥ VGS − Vth: the channel pinches off at the drain end, and the drain current becomes nearly independent of VDS, following ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)². Here the current is saturated, not the voltage. In short-channel devices velocity saturation makes current saturate at lower VDS and pushes the dependence on overdrive toward linear, so detailed compact models are used for design.

For amplifiers, the useful operating regions correspond across the two devices: MOSFET saturation plays the role of the bipolar active region, where the output current is controlled by the input and is relatively insensitive to output voltage. For switches, bipolar saturation corresponds to the MOSFET triode (linear) region, where the device behaves like a low resistance. Mixing these up is a common source of confusion. An amplifier must keep a bipolar transistor out of saturation, but must keep a MOSFET in saturation, with VDS above VGS − Vth setting the minimum output swing.

faq.q: What is VCE(sat) of a bipolar transistor?
faq.a: VCE(sat) is the collector-emitter voltage when the transistor is saturated, typically about 0.1–0.3 V for small silicon devices, rising at high current because of collector resistance. It sets the on-state voltage drop and conduction loss of a BJT switch.

faq.q: Is the saturation region of a BJT the same as that of a MOSFET?
faq.a: No. BJT saturation has both junctions forward-biased and acts like a closed switch, whereas MOSFET saturation is the pinched-off region with nearly constant drain current used for amplification. The MOSFET region analogous to BJT saturation is the triode or linear region.

faq.q: Why is a bipolar transistor slow to turn off from saturation?
faq.a: In saturation, excess minority carriers are stored in the base and collector regions. This stored charge must be removed before the collector current can fall, which adds a storage delay to turn-off.

遮断領域.desc: The state of a bipolar transistor in which both junctions are reverse-biased and almost no collector current flows. It corresponds to a switch in the off state.
遮断領域.title: Cutoff Region of a BJT: Bias Conditions and Switching
遮断領域.description: In cutoff both BJT junctions are reverse-biased and almost no collector current flows: a switch's off state. Bias conditions and how it is entered and left.

about.p: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has four operating regions set by its two junctions. In the forward-active region the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased; in saturation both are forward biased; in cutoff both are reverse biased. In practice a silicon transistor is effectively in cutoff whenever VBE is below about 0.5 V, because forward current is then negligible. Only junction leakage, on the order of nanoamperes, reaches the collector, so the collector-emitter path behaves like an open switch.

about.h: Cutoff as the off state of a switch
about.p: In switching circuits a BJT alternates between cutoff (off) and saturation (on). In cutoff almost no collector current flows, so there is no drop across the load resistor and VCE rises to nearly the supply voltage; power dissipation is close to zero. If the base is left floating, collector-base leakage flows into the base and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may not turn off fully, especially when hot, since leakage rises steeply with temperature. A resistor between base and emitter diverts this leakage and guarantees cutoff.

Switching speed depends on how fast the transistor crosses between regions. Turning on from cutoff requires charging the junction capacitances until VBE reaches about 0.6–0.7 V before collector current rises, a delay time. Turning off from saturation is slower, because excess minority charge stored in the base must be removed before the transistor can return to cutoff (the storage time). Circuits that keep the transistor out of deep saturation, such as Schottky-clamped transistors, shorten this turn-off delay.

For a MOSFET, the comparable off state is VGS below the threshold voltage, although subthreshold current still flows and is usually larger than BJT cutoff leakage in scaled devices. Note that the word saturation means different things for the two devices: BJT saturation is the fully on switch state, whereas MOSFET saturation corresponds to the BJT's active region. The cutoff region is also unrelated to the cutoff frequency (fT), which is the frequency at which current gain falls to one.

faq.q: What are the conditions for a BJT to be in the cutoff region?
faq.a: Both the base-emitter and base-collector junctions are reverse biased, or in practice VBE is below about 0.5 V for silicon. Collector current is then limited to leakage of around nanoamperes.

faq.q: Why put a resistor between base and emitter?
faq.a: With a floating base, collector-base leakage flows through the base-emitter junction and is amplified by the current gain, so the transistor may conduct slightly. The resistor shunts that leakage away so the transistor stays firmly in cutoff.

faq.q: Is the cutoff region related to the cutoff frequency?
faq.a: No. The cutoff region is a DC bias state where the transistor is off, while the cutoff frequency (fT) is the frequency at which the transistor's small-signal current gain drops to one.

カレントミラー回路.desc: A circuit that uses two matched transistors to copy the current flowing in one into the other (or at a fixed ratio). It is widely used for bias current sources and active loads in analog ICs.

トランジション周波数.desc: The frequency at which the common-emitter current gain falls to 1, written fT. It is a key indicator of a transistor's high-frequency performance.
トランジション周波数.title: Transition Frequency (fT) of a Transistor Explained
トランジション周波数.description: fT is the frequency at which a transistor's common-emitter current gain falls to 1. What sets it, how it is measured, and what it says about RF performance.

about.h: How fT is defined and measured
about.p: The transition frequency fT is the frequency at which the common-emitter current gain |hfe|, measured with the output AC-shorted, falls to 1 (0 dB). At low frequencies the gain is a nearly constant β0, but above the beta cutoff frequency fβ it falls in inverse proportion to frequency (−20 dB/decade). In that region |hfe| × f is nearly constant, so fT ≈ β0·fβ, and fT can be viewed as the gain-bandwidth product of the current gain. In practice, fT is usually found by measuring |hfe| at a frequency f below fT and taking fT = |hfe| × f, or by extrapolating the current gain derived from S-parameters along the −20 dB/decade slope.

The reciprocal of fT corresponds to the total time for a signal to travel from emitter to collector, roughly 1/(2πfT) ≈ (Cje + Cμ)/gm + τB + τC. The first term is the time to charge the junction capacitances. τB is the time minority carriers take to cross the base, about WB²/(2Dn) for a uniformly doped base of width WB with diffusion coefficient Dn. τC is the transit time through the collector depletion region. In the small-signal equivalent circuit this becomes fT ≈ gm/(2π(Cπ + Cμ)), where Cπ includes the base diffusion capacitance. Thinning the base, or grading the Ge content in a SiGe HBT to accelerate electrons, mainly serves to shorten τB.

about.h: How fT depends on collector current
about.p: fT varies strongly with bias. Because gm is proportional to collector current IC, at low currents the capacitance-charging time (Cje + Cμ)/gm dominates and fT rises as IC increases. At excessive current density, however, the charge of electrons flowing through the collector cancels the field in the depletion region and the effective base spreads toward the collector. This Kirk effect (base pushout) abruptly lengthens τB and fT falls, so fT peaks at a particular IC. Datasheet fT values are specified at a given IC and VCE, so the actual fT differs if a circuit operates at a different bias point.

about.h: fT vs. fmax, and fT in MOSFETs
about.p: fT is a current-gain metric and barely reflects the base resistance rb. The maximum oscillation frequency fmax, where power gain falls to 1, is roughly √(fT/(8π·rb·Cμ)) and drops when rb or Cμ is large, so amplifier and oscillator capability is judged with fmax as well. The fT definition also applies to MOSFETs and HEMTs, where fT ≈ gm/(2π(Cgs + Cgd)). In the long-channel approximation neglecting Cgd, fT ≈ 3μ(VGS − Vth)/(4πL²), inversely proportional to the square of gate length L; in short channels with strong velocity saturation it approaches vsat/(2πL), so fT rises with scaling.

faq.q: What is the transition frequency, in simple terms?
faq.a: It is the frequency at which the common-emitter current gain falls to 1, a measure of the upper limit up to which a transistor can amplify current. Written fT, it is also called the current-gain cutoff frequency or unity-gain frequency. The higher it is, the higher the frequencies the transistor can amplify.

faq.q: Is fT the same as the gain-bandwidth product?
faq.a: Above the beta cutoff frequency fβ, current gain falls in inverse proportion to frequency, so |hfe| × f is nearly constant, and that value is fT. In this sense fT is the gain-bandwidth product of the current gain, with fT ≈ β0·fβ. It is, however, a different quantity from the gain-bandwidth product of a whole circuit such as an op amp.

faq.q: How do fT and fmax differ?
faq.a: fT is the frequency at which current gain falls to 1; fmax is where power gain falls to 1. fmax depends strongly on base resistance and collector-base capacitance, and depending on device structure it can be higher or lower than fT.

エミッタフォロワ.desc: A common-collector amplifier. Its voltage gain is about 1, but its high input impedance and low output impedance make it a buffer that drives the next stage without loading the signal.

about.p: In an emitter follower, the signal drives the base, the output is taken from the emitter, and the collector goes to the supply, which is AC ground, so the collector is common to input and output. The emitter sits one base-emitter drop (VBE, about 0.7 V) below the base and tracks it. The small-signal gain is RE/(RE + re), where RE is the total emitter load and re = 1/gm, about 26 Ω at 1 mA. Gain is therefore slightly below 1 and non-inverting. The stage provides current gain of about hFE + 1 rather than voltage gain.

The base current is only about 1/(hFE + 1) of the emitter current, so the load seen from the input is magnified: the input resistance is roughly (hFE + 1) times the emitter load plus re. Looking back from the output, the source resistance is divided by (hFE + 1) and re is added. With hFE = 100, a 1 kΩ load presents about 100 kΩ at the input, and a 10 kΩ source appears as roughly 125 Ω at the output. This lets a high-impedance source drive a low-impedance load without its signal being pulled down.

A follower biased by a resistor or current source to the negative supply can pull the output up strongly but can pull it down only with that bias current, so large swings into heavy loads clip on one side. Complementary push-pull followers, an NPN sourcing and a PNP sinking current, solve this and are the classic output stage of amplifiers and power supplies; they need a small bias to avoid crossover distortion. The VBE level shift also drifts by about −2 mV/°C. A Darlington pair, two followers in cascade, raises input impedance further.

The MOSFET counterpart is the source follower, or common-drain stage. Its input is a gate, so input impedance is essentially infinite, and its output impedance is about 1/gm. Because a MOSFET has lower gm than a bipolar transistor at the same current, its output impedance is higher, and its gain gmRs/(1 + gmRs) is further reduced by the body effect. Its level shift, VGS, is also larger than VBE and varies more between devices. The bipolar follower therefore drives loads better, while the source follower draws no input current.

faq.q: Why use an amplifier with a voltage gain of 1?
faq.a: Because it transforms impedance: it presents a high input impedance to the source and a low output impedance to the load, so a weak source can drive a heavy load without losing signal.

faq.q: Is an emitter follower the same as a common-collector amplifier?
faq.a: Yes. The two names describe the same circuit; the collector is at AC ground and common to input and output, and the emitter voltage follows the base.

faq.q: What is the output impedance of an emitter follower?
faq.a: Approximately re + Rs/(hFE + 1), where re = 1/gm (about 26 Ω at 1 mA) and Rs is the source resistance driving the base.

ダーリントン接続.desc: A connection that feeds the emitter current of one transistor into the base of a second. The overall current gain is roughly the product of the two, so a small base current can control a large current.

クロスオーバーひずみ.desc: Distortion in a class-B push-pull amplifier near 0 V, where neither transistor conducts during the handover between positive and negative half-cycles. Class-AB biasing with a small idle current reduces it.

about.h: Where the dead zone comes from
about.p: A class-B output stage pairs an NPN emitter follower for positive half-cycles with a PNP emitter follower for negative ones, with both bases driven by the same signal. A transistor conducts only when its base-emitter voltage reaches about 0.6 to 0.7 V, so for inputs between roughly −0.6 V and +0.6 V neither device conducts and the output stays near zero. The waveform is flattened at every zero crossing, creating a kink that produces higher-order harmonics, which are particularly audible.

about.h: Why it is worst at low signal levels
about.p: The dead zone is a fixed voltage band, so it represents a large fraction of a small signal but a tiny fraction of a large one. Unlike clipping, which grows with amplitude, crossover distortion is therefore most noticeable at low volume and in quiet passages, and percentage distortion figures measured at full power can hide it. It is also hard to remove completely with negative feedback, because the kink is sharp and loop gain falls at higher frequencies.

The standard fix is to bias the two bases about two base-emitter drops apart, roughly 1.2 V, using two diodes or a VBE multiplier, so a small quiescent current flows through both transistors at idle. Each device then stays slightly on through the crossover region, and the handover becomes smooth. Small emitter resistors and thermal coupling of the bias element to the output transistors' heatsink keep the idle current stable as temperature rises, preventing thermal runaway.

about.h: Efficiency vs. distortion across amplifier classes
about.p: Class A conducts continuously, giving low distortion but a theoretical maximum efficiency of only 25% with a resistive load (50% with transformer coupling) and heat even without a signal. Class B idles at almost no current and reaches π/4, about 78.5%, but suffers crossover distortion. Class AB sits between them, behaving like class A for small signals and like class B for large ones, which is why most linear audio output stages use it. Class D switching amplifiers achieve higher efficiency still.

faq.q: How do you eliminate crossover distortion?
faq.a: Bias the output transistors into class AB with diodes or a VBE multiplier so a small idle current flows, and place the output stage inside a negative-feedback loop to reduce the remaining error.

faq.q: Does a class AB amplifier have crossover distortion?
faq.a: Much less than class B, because both transistors conduct around zero crossing; some residual distortion remains if the bias current is too low or drifts with temperature.

faq.q: Why is crossover distortion more noticeable at low volume?
faq.a: The dead zone of about ±0.6 V is fixed, so it is a much larger share of a small signal than of a large one.

ミラー効果.desc: The effect by which a capacitance between the input and output of an inverting amplifier appears (1 + gain) times larger from the input. It degrades the high-frequency response of common-emitter and common-source stages.

about.p: Consider a capacitor C connected between the input and output of an inverting amplifier with voltage gain −Av. When the input rises by v, the output falls by Av·v, so the voltage across the capacitor changes by (1 + Av)·v. The input must therefore supply (1 + Av) times the charge it would for a grounded capacitor, and the capacitor appears at the input as C(1 + Av). Seen from the output the same capacitor looks roughly like C(1 + 1/Av), close to C itself. This equivalent input capacitance is often called the Miller capacitance.

In a common-emitter stage the base-collector capacitance Cμ is multiplied this way; in a common-source stage it is the gate-drain capacitance Cgd, which includes gate-to-drain overlap capacitance. With Cμ = 2 pF and a gain of 100, the input sees about 200 pF. Together with the source resistance Rs it forms a low-pass pole near 1/(2π·Rs·C_Miller), which often sets the upper bandwidth of the stage. Higher gain therefore directly costs bandwidth, which is why high-gain inverting stages driven from high-impedance sources are slow.

The classic remedy is the cascode: a common-base (or common-gate) transistor stacked on the input device holds the input transistor's collector or drain at a nearly constant voltage. The input device then has a voltage gain of only about one, so its feedback capacitance is barely multiplied, while the overall stage keeps high gain. A common-base stage alone also avoids the problem because its base is AC-grounded. Lowering the driving source resistance raises the pole frequency, and choosing devices with small feedback capacitance helps as well.

about.h: When the Miller effect is useful
about.p: The same multiplication is exploited on purpose in op-amp frequency compensation. A small capacitor placed across a high-gain inverting stage behaves like a large one, creating a dominant pole at a low frequency so that the gain falls below unity before other poles add much phase shift. This keeps the amplifier stable even as a unity-gain follower without needing a physically large capacitor on chip. In power MOSFET switching, the Miller effect also explains the plateau in gate voltage while the drain voltage swings and Cgd is being charged.

faq.q: What is Miller capacitance?
faq.a: Miller capacitance is the enlarged input capacitance, about C(1 + |Av|), that a capacitor bridging the input and output of an inverting amplifier presents to the signal source. For transistors the bridging capacitor is usually Cμ (bipolar) or Cgd (MOSFET).

faq.q: Why does a cascode amplifier reduce the Miller effect?
faq.a: In a cascode the input transistor drives the low impedance of a common-base or common-gate device, so its own voltage gain is about one. The feedback capacitance is then multiplied only by about two instead of by the full stage gain.

faq.q: Does the Miller effect occur in non-inverting amplifiers?
faq.a: The large multiplication requires an inverting gain; with a follower whose gain is near +1, the voltage across the bridging capacitor barely changes and its effective input capacitance actually shrinks. That is why emitter and source followers have good high-frequency behavior.

チャネル長変調.desc: In a saturated MOSFET, raising the drain voltage moves the pinch-off point toward the source, shortening the effective channel and slightly increasing drain current. It makes the output resistance finite.

about.h: Why drain current keeps rising in saturation
about.p: When VDS exceeds VGS − Vth, the inversion layer vanishes at the drain end of the channel, a condition called pinch-off. Further increases in VDS are absorbed by a short depletion region between the pinch-off point and the drain, and that region widens as VDS grows. The pinch-off point therefore moves toward the source, leaving a conducting channel of effective length L − ΔL. Since drain current is inversely proportional to channel length and the voltage across the remaining channel stays near VGS − Vth, the current rises slightly instead of staying perfectly flat.

about.h: The λ model and output resistance
about.p: Channel-length modulation is usually modeled by adding a factor to the square-law equation: ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)²(1 + λVDS), where λ is the channel-length modulation coefficient.
