The slope of ID versus VDS is about λID, so the small-signal output resistance is ro ≈ 1/(λID). Because ΔL is a larger fraction of a short channel, λ is roughly inversely proportional to L, and doubling L roughly doubles ro. In short-channel devices, drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) adds to the output conductance as well.

about.h: Why it matters for analog design
about.p: The intrinsic gain of a single transistor is gm·ro, and with gm = 2ID/(VGS − Vth) this becomes 2/(λ(VGS − Vth)). In highly scaled transistors it is only about 10–20, which is not enough for many amplifiers. Designers respond by using longer-than-minimum channel lengths in analog blocks, stacking cascode devices to multiply output resistance, and using multiple gain stages. Channel-length modulation also degrades current mirrors: a mismatch in drain voltage between the reference and output devices produces a current error proportional to λ.

about.h: Channel-length modulation vs. the Early effect
about.p: Bipolar transistors show an analogous effect called the Early effect, or base-width modulation. A higher collector-emitter voltage widens the collector-base depletion region, narrowing the neutral base and slightly increasing collector current. Its strength is expressed by the Early voltage VA, the point where extrapolated output curves meet the voltage axis, giving ro ≈ VA/IC. For MOSFETs the equivalent quantity is 1/λ, sometimes also called an Early voltage. Both effects tilt the otherwise flat output characteristics and limit the voltage gain available from a single device.

faq.q: What is lambda (λ) in the MOSFET drain current equation?
faq.a: λ is the channel-length modulation coefficient, which describes how much saturation drain current rises per volt of VDS through the factor (1 + λVDS). Its inverse behaves like an Early voltage and sets the output resistance ro ≈ 1/(λID).

faq.q: Why do analog circuits use longer channel lengths?
faq.a: Channel-length modulation is weaker in long channels because the pinch-off shift is a smaller fraction of L. Longer devices therefore have higher output resistance and intrinsic gain, along with better matching.

faq.q: What is the difference between channel-length modulation and the Early effect?
faq.a: Both make output current rise with output voltage and give a finite output resistance. Channel-length modulation shortens the effective channel of a MOSFET, while the Early effect narrows the neutral base of a bipolar transistor.

速度飽和.desc: Under strong electric fields, carrier drift velocity stops increasing in proportion to the field and levels off at about 1×10⁷ cm/s. In short-channel MOSFETs it makes drain current smaller than the square law predicts.
速度飽和.title: Velocity Saturation in MOSFETs: Physics and Effect on Current
速度飽和.description: At high fields carrier velocity levels off near 1×10⁷ cm/s, pulling short-channel MOSFET current below the square law. How it differs from pinch-off.

about.p: At low electric field, carrier drift velocity is v = μE, so 1000 cm²/V·s at 100 V/cm gives 1×10⁵ cm/s. As the field rises, carriers gain energy faster than ordinary scattering removes it, until they lose energy mainly by emitting optical phonons. The velocity then levels off. For electrons in silicon the departure from linearity becomes noticeable above roughly 10⁴ V/cm, and the saturated velocity is about 1×10⁷ cm/s at room temperature; holes saturate at a somewhat lower velocity. A common empirical fit is v = μE/(1 + E/Ec), with critical field Ec = vsat/μ.

about.h: What it does to MOSFET current
about.p: Lateral fields in short channels are large: 1 V across 50 nm is 2×10⁵ V/cm, well beyond the critical field. A long-channel MOSFET follows the square law, ID = (1/2)μCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)². When carriers are fully velocity saturated, the current approaches ID ≈ W·Cox·vsat·(VGS − Vth), linear in overdrive and nearly independent of channel length. Real devices sit between the two limits, which the alpha-power law captures with an exponent between 1 and 2, closer to 1 for very short channels.

In a long-channel device, current saturates when VDS reaches VGS − Vth and the channel pinches off at the drain end. In a short-channel device, carriers reach saturation velocity first, so the current saturates at a smaller VDS than VGS − Vth. Transconductance stops rising with overdrive and tends toward W·Cox·vsat, and shortening the gate gives less extra current than simple scaling predicts. Mobility degradation and parasitic source and drain resistance add further deviations, so practical design relies on compact models such as BSIM rather than the square law.

Saturation velocity is a key material figure of merit for high-frequency and power devices. GaN's electron saturation velocity, about 2.5×10⁷ cm/s, contributes to its strength in high-frequency power transistors. GaAs behaves differently: at high field, electrons transfer to a higher, heavier conduction-band valley and actually slow down, giving a region of negative differential mobility that Gunn diodes exploit to build microwave oscillators.

faq.q: What is the saturation velocity of electrons in silicon?
faq.a: About 1×10⁷ cm/s at room temperature. Drift velocity stops being proportional to field at fields above roughly 10⁴ V/cm and approaches this value.

faq.q: Why does velocity saturation make MOSFET drain current linear in gate voltage?
faq.a: Once carriers move at a fixed maximum velocity, current equals channel charge times that velocity. The channel charge is proportional to VGS − Vth, so the current becomes roughly linear rather than quadratic in overdrive.

faq.q: What is the difference between velocity saturation and pinch-off?
faq.a: Pinch-off is the long-channel mechanism in which the channel vanishes at the drain end once VDS reaches VGS − Vth. Velocity saturation is a field-driven limit on carrier speed that makes short-channel current saturate at a lower VDS.

相互コンダクタンス.desc: The ratio of the change in drain current to the change in gate voltage, written gm. It expresses a transistor's amplifying ability; amplifier gain is roughly gm times the load resistance.

about.p: Transconductance gm is the small-signal ratio of output current change to input voltage change, measured in siemens. For a bipolar transistor gm = IC/VT, where VT = kT/q is about 26 mV at room temperature, so 1 mA gives about 38 mS regardless of device size. For a long-channel MOSFET in saturation, gm = 2ID/(VGS − Vth) = √(2μCox(W/L)ID). Since the overdrive VGS − Vth is usually more than 0.1 V, roughly four times VT, a bipolar transistor delivers about 2–4 times more gm at the same current, one reason bipolars remain popular in low-noise, high-gain analog circuits.

A common-emitter or common-source stage converts the input voltage into a current gm·vin, and a load resistance converts it back into a voltage, so the gain is about −gm·RL. With gm = 40 mS and RC = 5 kΩ the gain is about 200. For a bipolar stage this equals IC·RC/VT, so gain is set by the DC voltage across the load. The transistor's own output resistance ro sits in parallel with the load, so the gain can never exceed the intrinsic gain gm·ro, which is thousands for bipolars but much smaller for short-channel MOSFETs.

The ratio gm/ID measures how much transconductance each ampere of bias current buys. A bipolar transistor reaches 1/VT, about 38 V⁻¹. A MOSFET approaches about 25–30 V⁻¹ in weak inversion and falls toward 10 V⁻¹ or less in strong inversion. High gm/ID saves power but needs a wide device with large capacitance and lower transit frequency, while low gm/ID gives speed at the cost of current. The gm/ID design method sizes analog MOSFETs by picking this ratio first and reading width and other parameters from simulated lookup tables.

Beyond gain, gm sets several other key figures. The transit frequency of a MOSFET is roughly fT ≈ gm/(2πCgs), so speed depends on gm per unit capacitance. The input-referred thermal noise voltage of a transistor falls as gm rises, which is why low-noise front ends bias their input devices at high current. The output impedance of a follower is about 1/gm. In short-channel MOSFETs velocity saturation makes gm grow only slowly with overdrive, so simply raising the gate voltage gives diminishing returns.

faq.q: What is the unit of transconductance?
faq.a: Siemens (S), the inverse of ohms, since it is a current divided by a voltage; transistor values are usually quoted in millisiemens or microsiemens. The older unit name mho means the same thing.

faq.q: Why does a BJT have higher transconductance than a MOSFET at the same current?
faq.a: A BJT's gm is IC/VT with VT about 26 mV, while a strongly inverted MOSFET's gm is 2ID divided by an overdrive voltage that is typically 0.1 V or more, so the MOSFET gets less gm per unit current.

faq.q: Does transconductance increase with current?
faq.a: Yes. In a BJT gm is proportional to collector current, while in a long-channel MOSFET in strong inversion it grows roughly with the square root of drain current.

DIBL.desc: Short for drain-induced barrier lowering. In short-channel MOSFETs, a higher drain voltage lowers the potential barrier at the source, reducing the threshold voltage and increasing off-state leakage.
DIBL.title: DIBL (Drain-Induced Barrier Lowering): Cause and Measurement
DIBL.description: DIBL lowers a short-channel MOSFET's threshold voltage as drain voltage rises, raising leakage. Its cause, how it is measured in mV/V, and how to suppress it.

about.h: How drain voltage lowers the barrier
about.p: In an off-state nMOSFET, electrons in the source are held back by a potential barrier at the source end of the channel, and the gate controls its height. In a long-channel device the drain is too far away to influence that barrier. When the gate is short, the drain's depletion region and electric field reach toward the source through the silicon, a two-dimensional electrostatic effect, and pull the barrier down. More electrons then spill over it, so the transistor turns on at a lower gate voltage: the threshold voltage falls as drain voltage rises.

DIBL is quoted as the threshold shift per volt of drain bias, in mV/V: the threshold is extracted at a small drain voltage, such as 50 mV, and again at the full supply voltage, and the difference is divided by the change in drain voltage. Advanced transistors keep it to a few tens of mV/V or less. Because subthreshold current rises exponentially as threshold drops, DIBL multiplies off-state leakage: as an illustration, 80 mV/V at a 1 V supply with a subthreshold swing of 80 mV/decade raises leakage about tenfold compared with a device without DIBL.

DIBL is one of several short-channel effects. Threshold roll-off is the drop in threshold with shorter gate length even at low drain bias; DIBL is the additional dependence on drain voltage. Punch-through is the extreme case where source and drain depletion regions merge and current flows deep below the gate control. GIDL (gate-induced drain leakage) is different again: band-to-band tunneling at the drain edge under a strong gate-to-drain field, which grows as the gate is driven more negative. In analog circuits DIBL also lowers output resistance, alongside channel-length modulation, reducing intrinsic gain.

Every remedy aims to strengthen the gate's control of the channel relative to the drain's. Thinner equivalent gate dielectrics, made possible by high-k materials, couple the gate more tightly. Shallow source/drain extensions and halo or pocket implants, which raise doping near the junction edges, limit how far drain fields penetrate. The most effective step is changing the geometry: thin-body SOI (silicon on insulator), FinFETs and gate-all-around nanosheets surround a thin channel with gate on several sides, so there is no deep silicon path through which the drain field can reach the source.

faq.q: What is the unit of DIBL?
faq.a: Millivolts per volt (mV/V): the threshold voltage shift divided by the change in drain voltage used to measure it.

faq.q: What is the difference between DIBL and channel length modulation?
faq.a: DIBL lowers the threshold voltage as drain voltage rises, mainly affecting off-state leakage and threshold; channel-length modulation shortens the effective channel in saturation, raising on-current gradually. Both reduce output resistance in short devices.

faq.q: Why do FinFETs have lower DIBL than planar MOSFETs?
faq.a: The gate wraps around a thin fin on three sides, so it controls the channel potential much more strongly and the drain field cannot easily reach the source through deep silicon.

GIDL(ゲート誘起ドレインリーク).desc: Off-state leakage caused by band-to-band tunneling in the strong field where the gate overlaps the drain. It is a concern for data retention in DRAM, among others.
GIDL(ゲート誘起ドレインリーク).title: GIDL (Gate-Induced Drain Leakage): Cause and DRAM Impact
GIDL(ゲート誘起ドレインリーク).description: GIDL is off-state leakage from band-to-band tunneling where the gate overlaps the drain. How to recognize it, why DRAM retention cares, and how to control it.

about.p: Consider an off nMOS with its gate at 0 V or below and its drain at a high voltage. In the region where the gate overlaps the heavily doped drain, the large gate-to-drain voltage creates a strong vertical field that depletes the drain surface and bends the energy bands so steeply that the valence band on one side lines up with the conduction band a few nanometres away. Electrons then tunnel band to band. They are collected by the drain, while the generated holes flow to the body, so GIDL (gate-induced drain leakage) appears as drain-to-body current.

On a log-scale drain current versus gate voltage plot, ordinary subthreshold leakage keeps falling as the gate is driven further off. GIDL does the opposite: making the gate more negative for an nMOS, or raising the drain voltage, increases the gate-to-drain field, so the off-current turns upward again. The total leakage therefore has a minimum at some intermediate gate voltage. GIDL is also distinct from DIBL (drain-induced barrier lowering), which lowers the threshold voltage and increases subthreshold current rather than adding a tunneling path.

A DRAM cell must hold its charge for tens of milliseconds between refreshes, so its access transistor must leak extremely little. Charge escapes mainly through subthreshold leakage and junction leakage at the storage node, which includes GIDL. Driving the word line slightly negative when the cell is off suppresses subthreshold current but raises the gate-to-drain voltage and therefore GIDL, so the two must be balanced. Because a small tail of the leakiest cells sets the refresh period, designers ease the fields with buried-gate cell transistors and carefully shaped junction doping.

GIDL grows with the electric field at the gate edge, so the remedies reduce that field: lighter or graded doping where the drain meets the gate edge, reduced gate-to-drain overlap, a thicker dielectric at the gate corner, and limits on how far the gate is driven negative. Thin gate dielectrics make the field and the GIDL stronger. The same mechanism can also be useful; some 3D NAND designs deliberately generate holes by GIDL to raise the channel potential during erase.

faq.q: What is the difference between GIDL and DIBL?
faq.a: GIDL is a leakage current from band-to-band tunneling in the gate-drain overlap region, and it grows as the gate is driven further off. DIBL is drain voltage lowering the source barrier, which reduces the threshold voltage and increases subthreshold current.

faq.q: Why does GIDL increase with negative gate voltage?
faq.a: For an nMOS, a more negative gate raises the gate-to-drain voltage, increasing the vertical field and band bending at the drain edge. Stronger band bending makes band-to-band tunneling more likely, so leakage rises.

faq.q: Is GIDL part of subthreshold leakage?
faq.a: No. Subthreshold leakage is carrier diffusion over the source barrier, while GIDL is a tunneling current at the drain, usually grouped with junction leakage. They respond to gate voltage in opposite directions.

パンチスルー.desc: A condition in which the source and drain depletion regions merge and current flows that the gate cannot control. It occurs when the channel is too short or the substrate doping is too low.
パンチスルー.title: Punch-Through in MOSFETs: Cause, vs. DIBL, and Prevention
パンチスルー.description: Punch-through: source and drain depletion regions merge and current flows the gate can't control. How it differs from DIBL and avalanche, and how to prevent it.

about.h: How punch-through develops in a MOSFET
about.p: When drain voltage is applied, the drain-to-body junction is reverse biased and its depletion region spreads toward the source. Depletion width grows roughly with the square root of voltage divided by doping, so a short channel and lightly doped substrate let it reach the source-side depletion region. Once the two merge below the surface, the drain itself pulls down the potential barrier that normally holds back source carriers. Current then flows deep in the substrate, where the gate field is weak, so the transistor cannot be switched off and drain current climbs steeply with drain voltage.

about.h: Punch-through vs. DIBL and avalanche breakdown
about.p: Punch-through is the extreme case of drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL). With moderate DIBL, the drain only partly lowers the source barrier, so threshold voltage falls as drain voltage rises and the subthreshold swing worsens. In punch-through the barrier in the subsurface region effectively disappears and gate control is lost. It is a purely electrostatic effect and needs no impact ionization, unlike avalanche breakdown, where carriers gain enough energy in a high field to generate new electron-hole pairs.

about.h: How process and structure suppress it
about.p: The usual cure is more doping exactly where the depletion regions would meet, without raising doping at the channel surface, which would increase threshold voltage and cut mobility. Halo (pocket) implants, tilted about 20–45°, place channel-type dopant under the source/drain edges. Retrograde wells use implants of hundreds of keV to MeV to put peak doping deep below the surface. Bulk FinFETs add a heavily doped punch-through stopper at the fin base, which the gate cannot control. SOI substrates and gate-all-around (GAA) structures remove the uncontrolled path altogether.

Bipolar transistors suffer a similar failure. A thin base reduces recombination and raises current gain and speed, but at high collector-base reverse voltage the collector depletion region can spread across the whole base and reach the emitter depletion region. The base potential barrier then collapses and collector current rises uncontrollably, which caps the usable breakdown voltage. Base width and base doping are therefore chosen together, trading current gain and high-frequency performance against punch-through voltage.

faq.q: What is the difference between punch-through and avalanche breakdown?
faq.a: Punch-through happens when the drain and source depletion regions merge and the source barrier collapses, which is purely electrostatic. Avalanche breakdown happens when carriers in a high field create new electron-hole pairs by impact ionization, multiplying the current.

faq.q: How do halo implants prevent punch-through?
faq.a: Halo implants add extra dopant of the substrate type locally under the edges of the source and drain. This narrows the drain depletion region near the channel ends, so it cannot reach the source, while leaving the rest of the channel lightly doped.

faq.q: Why do bulk FinFETs need a punch-through stopper?
faq.a: The gate wraps only the upper part of the fin, so the lower part near the substrate offers a leakage path the gate cannot shut off. A heavily doped layer of the opposite type at the fin base blocks this path.

フラットバンド電圧.desc: The gate voltage at which the bands at the semiconductor surface of a MOS structure are flat. It is set by the work-function difference between gate and substrate and by charges in the oxide, and is one component of the threshold voltage.

about.h: Why the bands bend at zero bias
about.p: In a MOS structure the gate and the semiconductor usually have different work functions. In equilibrium their Fermi levels must line up, so the work-function difference φms appears as a potential split between the oxide and the semiconductor surface, bending the bands even with the gate grounded. Charge in the dielectric adds to this: fixed charge near the interface, mobile ions such as sodium, trapped charge and charged interface states all induce opposite charge in the semiconductor. The flat-band voltage VFB is the gate voltage that exactly cancels these effects, leaving the surface neither accumulated nor depleted.

about.h: The formula and its role in threshold voltage
about.p: For charge Qox located at the oxide-silicon interface, VFB = φms − Qox/Cox; charge distributed inside the oxide counts less the closer it sits to the gate. Threshold voltage builds on it: for an nMOS device, Vth = VFB + 2φF + Qdep/Cox, where φF is the Fermi potential and Qdep the depletion charge at strong inversion. Any shift in VFB therefore moves Vth one for one. For an n+ polysilicon gate on p-type silicon of moderate doping, φms is roughly −0.9 V, and positive oxide charge pushes VFB further negative.

about.h: Setting it with the gate metal
about.p: In high-k/metal-gate transistors, choosing the gate work function is the main lever on VFB and thus on Vth. nMOS devices need a work function near the silicon conduction band, around 4.1 eV, and pMOS devices one near the valence band, around 5.1 eV. Stacks of thin metal layers of different composition and thickness give several threshold flavors on one chip for high-speed and low-leakage circuits.

A capacitance-voltage (C-V) sweep of a MOS capacitor moves through accumulation, depletion and inversion. Accumulation capacitance gives Cox and hence oxide thickness, and VFB is read where the curve reaches the flat-band capacitance, the series combination of Cox and the semiconductor's capacitance at flat band. Comparing measured VFB with the expected φms gives the effective oxide charge. A VFB shift after bias-temperature stress reveals mobile ion contamination, while stretch-out of the curve indicates interface traps, which makes VFB a routine process-control check.

faq.q: What determines the flat-band voltage of a MOS capacitor?
faq.a: The work-function difference between gate and semiconductor and the charges in the oxide and at the interface. For interface charge it is VFB = φms − Qox/Cox.

faq.q: Is flat-band voltage the same as threshold voltage?
faq.a: No. Flat band is the gate voltage where the surface bands are flat, while threshold is where strong inversion begins. Threshold equals VFB plus the voltage needed to bend the bands by 2φF and support the depletion charge.

faq.q: How is flat-band voltage measured?
faq.a: From a C-V measurement on a MOS capacitor: the gate voltage at which the capacitance equals the calculated flat-band capacitance is taken as VFB. Shifts in VFB reveal changes in oxide charge.

LDD構造.desc: Short for lightly doped drain. The drain is made lightly doped only at its edge next to the gate, relaxing the electric field and suppressing hot-carrier degradation.

基板バイアス効果.desc: An increase in threshold voltage when reverse bias is applied between source and substrate (body), because the depletion charge grows. Also called the substrate bias effect; it is sometimes used to tune the threshold.

about.p: In an n-channel MOSFET the gate must first support the negative charge of the depletion region under it before an inversion layer can form. When the source-to-body junction is reverse-biased (VSB greater than zero, meaning the body is negative relative to the source), the depletion region widens and holds more charge, so a larger gate voltage is needed to reach inversion. The textbook expression is Vth = Vth0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)), where the body-effect coefficient γ = √(2qεSi·NA)/Cox grows with heavier substrate doping and with thicker gate oxide.

about.h: Where the body effect shows up in circuits
about.p: In a stack of series nMOS transistors, such as a NAND gate pull-down, only the bottom device has its source at ground. The upper devices see raised source potentials, so their Vth rises and they conduct less current. In a single nMOS pass transistor with its gate at VDD, the output can only rise to about VDD − Vth, and because Vth increases as the source climbs, the final level is lower still. In a source follower, the body effect adds a back-gate transconductance gmb that pulls the voltage gain further below 1.

Analog designers often express the body effect as the ratio gmb/gm, which for bulk transistors is commonly in the range of roughly 0.1 to 0.3 depending on doping and bias. A source follower in a common p-substrate process, where the nMOS body is tied to ground, has its gain limited to about gm/(gm + gmb) even with an ideal load. Placing the transistor in its own well and tying body to source removes the effect, at the cost of extra area and well capacitance.

about.h: Body bias as a tuning knob
about.p: The same physics is used deliberately. Reverse body bias raises Vth to cut subthreshold leakage in standby, and forward body bias lowers Vth to gain speed, which also lets designers compensate for process variation after fabrication. The knob depends on the device structure. In FinFETs the thin fin is controlled almost entirely by the gate, so body biasing has little effect, whereas FD-SOI (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator) transistors with a thin buried oxide allow a wide back-bias tuning range.

faq.q: Is the body effect the same as the substrate bias effect?
faq.a: Yes. Both names describe the change in MOSFET threshold voltage caused by a voltage between source and body (substrate); reverse bias raises Vth and forward bias lowers it.

faq.q: Why does the body effect reduce the gain of a source follower?
faq.a: As the output (source) moves, the source-to-body voltage changes and shifts Vth, which acts like a second transconductance gmb opposing the signal. The gain becomes roughly gm/(gm + gmb) instead of approaching 1.

faq.q: How can the body effect be eliminated?
faq.a: Connecting each transistor's body to its own source removes VSB, but this requires the device to sit in a separate well, which costs area and is only possible for the well-type transistor in a given process.

貫通電流.desc: Current that flows from supply to ground in a CMOS gate during the brief time while the input switches and both the pMOS and nMOS are on. Also called crowbar current, it adds to power consumption.

about.h: How short-circuit current flows in CMOS
about.p: In a CMOS inverter, only the pMOS is on when the input is 0 and only the nMOS is on when it is 1, so in steady state there is always an off transistor between supply and ground and almost no current flows. During an input transition, however, while the input voltage is above the nMOS threshold voltage and below the supply voltage minus the magnitude of the pMOS threshold voltage, both transistors are on at once and current flows directly from supply to ground. This is short-circuit current, also called crowbar current. In circuits whose supply voltage is below the sum of the two threshold voltages, the two transistors are not on simultaneously, so almost no short-circuit current flows.

about.h: Effect on power and how to reduce it
about.p: Short-circuit power grows as input rise and fall times get slower, because both transistors stay on longer. It is also proportional to the number of transitions, so it rises with operating frequency. If input and output transition times are similar, it typically stays at roughly 10% or less of total dynamic power. Logic design tools therefore set an upper limit on signal transition time (max transition) and insert buffers where long wires slow the transitions. Lowering the supply voltage narrows the voltage range in which both transistors conduct, which also reduces short-circuit current.

about.h: When inputs linger at intermediate voltages
about.p: If an input stays at an intermediate voltage for a long time, short-circuit current keeps flowing, raising supply current and heat, and the output may oscillate. Typical causes are floating inputs connected to nothing, slowly changing signals, undefined signals from powered-down blocks, and signals between blocks at different supply voltages. Countermeasures include tying unused inputs with pull-up or pull-down resistors, receiving slow signals with hysteretic Schmitt-trigger inputs, and inserting isolation cells at the outputs of blocks that can be powered down and level shifters where voltages differ. Datasheet limits on input transition time also exist to keep this current down.

In inverters and half-bridges, if the upper and lower switches are on at the same time, the supply is shorted through both switches and a very large current flows. This current is also called shoot-through current, or an arm short. Because it can destroy the devices, and because switches take time to turn off, a dead time with both switches off is inserted between turning one off and turning the other on. A fast voltage change from the other switch's transition can also couple through the gate-drain capacitance, raise the gate voltage and turn a switch on unintentionally, which is prevented with negative gate voltage or a Miller clamp.

faq.q: What else is short-circuit current called?
faq.a: In CMOS circuits it is called short-circuit current or crowbar current; the Japanese term is kantsu denryu. The current that flows when the upper and lower switches of an inverter or half-bridge are on at the same time is usually called shoot-through current.

faq.q: How can short-circuit current be reduced?
faq.a: In CMOS circuits the basics are to keep input transitions fast, inserting buffers to meet transition-time limits, to eliminate floating inputs, and to use Schmitt-trigger inputs for slow signals. In power circuits, set an appropriate dead time and design the gate drive so switches do not turn on by mistake.

faq.q: How does short-circuit current differ from leakage current?
faq.a: Short-circuit current is a switching-related current that flows only during the brief time when both the pMOS and nMOS are on as the input changes. Leakage current, such as subthreshold current and gate leakage, keeps flowing even when transistors are off, consuming power even when the circuit is idle.

トランスミッションゲート.desc: An analog switch made of an nMOS and a pMOS connected in parallel. The nMOS passes 0 well and the pMOS passes 1 well, so both values pass without voltage loss.

about.h: Why a single transistor falls short
about.p: An nMOS switch with its gate at VDD passes a 0 fully, but when passing a 1 its source rises until the gate-source voltage drops to the threshold voltage, stopping near VDD − Vth, and the body effect lowers this level further. A pMOS switch is the mirror image: it passes a strong 1 but a weak 0 that stops near |Vth| above ground. A degraded high level can leave the next stage's pMOS partly on, wasting static current, so single-transistor switches are used with care.

A transmission gate places an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel and drives their gates with complementary control signals, C and its inverse. When the gate is on, the nMOS handles signals near ground and the pMOS handles signals near VDD, so the combined switch passes the full range from rail to rail. The on-resistance of the pair also varies less across the signal range than either device alone. Because current can flow either way, the switch is bidirectional.

In digital logic, two transmission gates make a compact 2-to-1 multiplexer, and they appear in XOR gates, D latches and master-slave flip-flops, often with fewer transistors than a static CMOS equivalent. In analog and mixed-signal circuits they act as analog switches for routing signals, in sample-and-hold circuits and in switched-capacitor filters; the classic 4066 quad bilateral switch is built on this principle. A transmission gate needs an inverter, or a complementary signal, to generate its second control phase.

A transmission gate is a passive switch with no gain, so it cannot restore a weak signal or drive a heavy load. Each switch adds series resistance and capacitance, and the delay of a chain grows roughly with the square of the number of stages, so buffers are inserted every few gates. Signals must stay within the supply rails, or the source and drain junctions become forward-biased. When the switch turns off, channel charge injection and clock feedthrough disturb the voltage on high-impedance nodes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a transmission gate and a pass transistor?
faq.a: A pass transistor is a single nMOS or pMOS and loses a threshold voltage on one logic level; a transmission gate combines both types in parallel and passes 0 and 1 without that loss.

faq.q: How many transistors does a transmission gate use?
faq.a: Two, one nMOS and one pMOS, plus an inverter (two more transistors) if the complementary control signal is not already available.

faq.q: Can a transmission gate pass analog signals?
faq.a: Yes. It is bidirectional and passes voltages anywhere between the supply rails, which is why CMOS analog switches and multiplexers are built from transmission gates.

メタステーブル.desc: A state in which a flip-flop's output stays between 0 and 1 for a while when setup or hold time is violated. Asynchronous signals are passed through two flip-flops (a synchronizer) to guard against it.

about.h: Why a flip-flop can hang between 0 and 1
about.p: A flip-flop stores its state in cross-coupled inverters, which have two stable points and one unstable balance point in between. If the data input changes inside the window defined by the setup time (before the clock edge) and hold time (after it), the latch can be left near that balance point. Positive feedback then amplifies the small imbalance with a time constant τ, but the closer it starts to balance, the longer resolution takes, with no hard upper bound. The output may sit at an intermediate voltage or switch late, and the final value is unpredictable.

With an asynchronous input, metastability can only be made rare, not prevented. A two-flip-flop synchronizer gives the first stage almost one clock period to resolve before the second stage samples it. Mean time between failures is approximately MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data), where t_r is the available resolution time and τ and T_0 depend on the flip-flop. Because t_r sits in an exponent, a third stage adds about one period and multiplies MTBF enormously: with τ = 20 ps, an extra 1 ns gives a factor of e^50, over 10^21.

about.h: What a synchronizer does not fix
about.p: Each synchronized bit may capture a change one cycle early or late, so a multi-bit value such as 0111 to 1000 can arrive as 1111 or 0000. Counters therefore cross in Gray code, where only one bit changes per step, as with asynchronous FIFO pointers; arbitrary data uses a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO. A short pulse from a fast domain can fall between slow-clock edges and vanish, so it must be stretched or converted to a toggle. Crossing signals should come straight from a flip-flop, because a combinational glitch can be captured as a valid value.

In a single synchronous clock domain, a setup violation means the data path is too slow, and static timing analysis finds it; slowing the clock or speeding the path fixes it. Across asynchronous clocks there is no fixed phase relationship, so violations happen eventually no matter how fast the logic is, and timing analysis cannot close them. That is why designs rely on CDC (clock domain crossing) verification, where tools find every crossing and check for a proper synchronizer, Gray-coded pointer or handshake. Such bugs are rare, so ordinary simulation seldom catches them.

faq.q: What causes metastability in a flip-flop?
faq.a: Data changing within the setup-and-hold window around the clock edge, which leaves the internal latch near its unstable balance point. It is unavoidable when the input is asynchronous to the clock.

faq.q: Why are two flip-flops used to synchronize an asynchronous signal?
faq.a: The first flip-flop may go metastable, and the second samples it a full clock period later, by which time it has almost certainly resolved. This raises MTBF exponentially but does not make failure impossible.

faq.q: Can a synchronizer be used for a multi-bit bus?
faq.a: Not bit by bit, because different bits can be captured on different cycles and produce an invalid intermediate value. Use Gray code for counters, or a handshake or asynchronous FIFO for general data.

グレイコード.desc: A code in which successive values differ in only one bit. It prevents read errors in rotary encoders and when passing counter values between different clock domains.

about.h: Converting between binary and Gray code
about.p: The usual Gray code is the reflected binary code, built by listing the n-bit sequence, appending its mirror image and prefixing 0 to the first half and 1 to the second. Conversion from binary B is a single expression: G = B XOR (B >> 1), so each Gray bit below the most significant one is the XOR of two neighboring binary bits. Converting back takes a running XOR from the most significant bit down: the top bit is copied, and each lower binary bit is the previous binary bit XOR the current Gray bit. For three bits the sequence is 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100.

about.h: Why one-bit changes matter in encoders
about.p: In plain binary, stepping from 0111 to 1000 flips four bits at once. A rotary or linear absolute encoder reads each bit from its own track, and the transitions on those tracks never line up perfectly, so a reading taken at the boundary can mix old and new bits and report a value far from either position. With Gray code only one track changes at each step, so a reading at the boundary can only be the old or the new value, both of which are correct to within one step.

An asynchronous FIFO passes data between two clock domains, and each side must see the other's read or write pointer to compute full and empty flags. Sending a binary pointer through synchronizer flip-flops is unsafe because several bits may change together and be captured at different clock edges, producing a pointer value that never existed. A Gray-coded pointer changes one bit per increment, so even if that bit is caught mid-transition, the receiving side gets either the old or the new pointer. This works only when the pointer advances by one per clock and the counter wraps at a power of two.

about.h: Gray code in flash memory and Karnaugh maps
about.p: Multi-level cell (MLC) and triple-level cell (TLC) NAND flash store two or three bits as one of four or eight threshold-voltage states. Wear and interference broaden the state distributions, and a misread almost always lands in a neighboring state. Assigning bit patterns in Gray order, such as 111, 110, 100, 101, 001, 000, 010, 011 for TLC, turns each such misread into a single-bit error that error-correcting code handles cheaply. Karnaugh maps use the same ordering on their axes so that physically adjacent cells differ by one variable and can be grouped.

faq.q: How do you convert binary to Gray code?
faq.a: XOR the binary number with itself shifted right by one bit: G = B XOR (B >> 1). The most significant bit stays the same, and every other Gray bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits.

faq.q: Why are FIFO pointers Gray-coded for clock domain crossing?
faq.a: A Gray-coded pointer changes only one bit per increment, so a synchronizer that samples it during a transition still yields either the old or the new value. A binary pointer can change many bits at once and be captured as a completely wrong value.

faq.q: What is the difference between Gray code and BCD?
faq.a: Gray code is an ordering of binary patterns in which successive values differ by one bit. BCD (binary-coded decimal) encodes each decimal digit separately in four bits and has no one-bit-change property.

2の補数.desc: The usual binary representation of negative integers. Inverting all bits and adding 1 negates a number. n bits cover −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, and the same adder can be used for subtraction.

about.p: In n-bit two's complement, every bit has its usual binary weight except the most significant bit, which carries weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. In 4 bits, 1111 therefore reads as −8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = −1, and 1000 is −8. To negate a value, invert every bit and add 1: +1 (0001) becomes 1110, then 1111. Zero has a single pattern, which leaves one more negative value than positive, so the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1: −128 to +127 in 8 bits and −32,768 to +32,767 in 16 bits.

Two's complement arithmetic is simply binary arithmetic modulo 2ⁿ, so one adder handles signed and unsigned numbers identically, and only the interpretation of the result differs. Subtraction A − B becomes A + (inverted B) + 1, implemented by inverting B and setting the adder's carry-in to 1. Sign-magnitude, where 1001 means −1 in 4 bits, has two zeros and needs separate add and subtract logic, and ones' complement also has two zeros and an end-around carry. Booth multipliers likewise rely on two's complement to generate negative partial products cheaply.

Signed overflow happens only when two operands of the same sign produce a result of the opposite sign, for example 0111 + 0001 = 1000 (7 + 1 giving −8) in 4 bits; adding numbers of opposite sign never overflows. Hardware detects it as the XOR of the carry into and the carry out of the most significant bit, reported as the V (overflow) flag. The C (carry) flag instead signals unsigned overflow. The asymmetric range creates corner cases: negating or taking the absolute value of the most negative number, or computing −128 × −1 in 8 bits, overflows.

Widening a two's complement value copies its sign bit into the new upper bits. A RISC-V addi immediate is a 12-bit field covering −2048 to 2047; −1 is stored as 0xFFF and sign-extends to 0xFFFFFFFF, whereas zero-filling would give 4095. An arithmetic right shift also replicates the sign bit, so 1111 1000 (−8) becomes 1111 1100 (−4); for negative odd values it rounds toward negative infinity, so −7 shifted right by one gives −4, while integer division in C truncates toward zero to −3. Offset binary, common at ADC outputs, differs from two's complement only by an inverted MSB.

faq.q: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?
faq.a: Write the positive value in binary with the chosen number of bits, invert every bit, then add 1. For example, −5 in 8 bits is 00000101 → 11111010 → 11111011.

faq.q: How can you tell if two's complement addition overflowed?
faq.a: Overflow occurs when two positives give a negative or two negatives give a positive, which hardware detects when the carry into the MSB differs from the carry out of it. The carry-out alone indicates unsigned overflow, not signed overflow.

faq.q: Why is the range of 8-bit two's complement −128 to 127 and not symmetric?
faq.a: Zero uses one of the 256 patterns with a 0 sign bit, leaving 127 positive values, while all 128 patterns with a 1 sign bit are negative. As a result +128 cannot be represented.

カルノー図.desc: A diagram that arranges a truth table so that adjacent cells differ in one bit. Grouping neighboring 1s lets you simplify a logic expression visually.

about.p: A Karnaugh map has one cell per row of the truth table: 4 cells for two variables, 8 for three and 16 for four, typically drawn as a 4 × 4 grid with two variables along each side. The row and column labels run in Gray-code order, 00, 01, 11, 10, so neighboring cells differ in exactly one variable. Opposite edges are also adjacent, since 10 and 00 differ by one bit, so the map behaves like a surface that wraps around in both directions.

Circle rectangular groups of 1s whose sizes are powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 cells. A group of 2ᵏ cells eliminates k variables, so groups should be as large as possible, and they may overlap. Each group becomes a product term containing only the variables that stay constant within it, and ORing the groups gives a minimal sum of products. Grouping the 0s instead yields a product of sums. Don't-care cells may be included in a group whenever that makes the group larger.

Take a four-variable function of A, B, C and D that is 1 only for minterms 0, 2, 8 and 10, that is, ABCD = 0000, 0010, 1000 and 1010. With AB labeling the rows and CD the columns, these sit in the four corner cells. Because the edges wrap around, the corners form one group of four. Within it A and C both change while B and D stay 0, so the whole function reduces to the single term B̄D̄.

Karnaugh maps also reveal static hazards: if two adjacent 1s are covered by different groups with no group spanning both, the output can glitch briefly when the input moves between them, and adding the redundant bridging group removes the glitch. Manual maps become unwieldy beyond four or five variables. Larger functions are minimized with the tabular Quine-McCluskey method or heuristic algorithms such as those in logic synthesis tools, which also handle multiple outputs and real gate libraries.

faq.q: Why are Karnaugh map labels in Gray code order?
faq.a: Gray code changes one bit between neighbors, so physically adjacent cells differ in one variable, and that variable drops out when the cells are grouped.

faq.q: How many variables can a Karnaugh map handle?
faq.a: Comfortably up to four, and five or six with stacked or mirrored maps; beyond that the Quine-McCluskey method or software minimizers are used.

faq.q: Is the minimal expression from a Karnaugh map unique?
faq.a: Not always. Some functions have several equally minimal groupings, all of which are correct.

マルチプレクサ.desc: A circuit that selects one of several inputs according to select signals and passes it to the output. The reverse, routing one input to one of several outputs, is a demultiplexer.

about.p: A 2:1 multiplexer (mux) outputs Y = S'·A + S·B: input A when the select signal S is 0 and input B when S is 1. With n select bits a mux chooses among 2ⁿ inputs, so an 8:1 mux needs three select lines. In CMOS, muxes are built from AND-OR or NAND-NAND logic, from transmission gates, or as trees of 2:1 muxes for wide inputs. A mux is also a universal logic element: tying its data inputs to the constants of a truth table makes a 2ⁿ:1 mux implement any n-input Boolean function.

Processor datapaths are full of muxes: they select ALU operands from registers or immediates, forward results through bypass paths to avoid pipeline stalls, choose the next program counter and switch shared buses. FPGA logic blocks implement arbitrary functions with lookup tables (LUTs), which are small memories read out through a mux tree. In design for testability, scan flip-flops add a mux at the data input so the flip-flops can be chained into shift registers in test mode. On boards, analog multiplexers share one ADC among several sensors, and I2C multiplexers separate devices with identical addresses.

In Verilog or VHDL, a conditional assignment, if statement or case statement usually synthesizes to a multiplexer. A long if/else-if chain implies priority, giving a series of 2:1 muxes with long delay, while a case statement on mutually exclusive values tends to become a single wide parallel mux, although modern synthesis tools often optimize either form. A common pitfall is leaving some branch without an assignment in combinational logic, which infers a latch to hold the old value instead of a pure mux.

A demultiplexer does the reverse of a multiplexer: it routes one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs chosen by the select bits. A decoder converts an n-bit code into 2ⁿ one-hot lines and is in effect a demultiplexer with its data input held at 1; decoders drive the select logic of large muxes and memory word lines. In communications, multiplexing more generally means sharing one channel among several signals by time, frequency or code.

faq.q: How many select lines does an 8-to-1 multiplexer need?
faq.a: Three, because 2³ = 8. In general a mux with 2ⁿ data inputs needs n select lines.

faq.q: What is the difference between a multiplexer and a demultiplexer?
faq.a: A multiplexer selects one of several inputs and passes it to a single output. A demultiplexer takes a single input and steers it to one of several outputs.

faq.q: How can a multiplexer implement any logic function?
faq.a: Connect the select lines to the function's input variables and tie each data input to 0 or 1 according to the truth table. The mux then outputs the correct table entry for every input combination, which is how FPGA lookup tables work.

デコーダ.desc: A circuit that activates exactly one of 2ⁿ outputs according to an n-bit input. It is used to select the row addressed in a memory. The reverse function is an encoder.

about.p: An n-to-2ⁿ decoder has one output for every possible input code. Each output is an AND of the input bits, each taken true or complemented, so it goes active for exactly one combination: output k is the minterm for code k. A 2-to-4 decoder needs four 2-input AND gates plus inverters; a 3-to-8 decoder needs eight 3-input gates. Many decoders add an enable input and use active-low outputs, and the enable lets small decoders be cascaded into larger ones. Since every minterm is available, a decoder followed by OR gates can implement any combinational function of its inputs.

An encoder does the reverse: it converts one active line out of 2ⁿ into an n-bit code. A plain encoder gives a wrong result if two inputs are active at once, so a priority encoder reports the highest-priority active input instead. A demultiplexer is a decoder whose enable carries data, routing one input signal to the output chosen by the select bits. A multiplexer can be viewed as a decoder whose outputs gate the data inputs into a common OR. Code converters such as a BCD-to-seven-segment driver are also called decoders even though their outputs are not one-hot.

Every memory array uses decoders: the row decoder turns the row address into one active word line, and the column decoder selects which bit lines connect to the sense amplifiers and I/O. Driving thousands of word lines with single wide AND gates would be slow, so large decoders use predecoding: the address is split into groups of two or three bits, each group is decoded into a few one-hot lines, and a small gate at each row combines one line from each group. Address-decoder faults are among the faults that March tests are designed to catch.

In a CPU, the instruction decoder interprets opcode fields and generates control signals; high-performance x86 cores decode variable-length instructions into simpler micro-operations and may cache them to avoid decoding again. A video decoder is a dedicated hardware block that decompresses video streams far more energy-efficiently than running the same algorithm in software on a general-purpose core. These are much larger circuits than a binary decoder, but they share the idea of translating an encoded input into the signals that act on it.

faq.q: How many outputs does a 4-bit decoder have?
faq.a: A 4-to-16 decoder has 2⁴ = 16 outputs, and exactly one of them is active for each 4-bit input code. In general an n-bit decoder has 2ⁿ outputs.

faq.q: What is the difference between a decoder and an encoder?
faq.a: A decoder converts an n-bit code into one active line out of 2ⁿ, while an encoder converts one active line out of 2ⁿ back into an n-bit code. A priority encoder handles cases where several inputs are active.

faq.q: Is a demultiplexer the same as a decoder?
faq.a: They are closely related: a decoder with an enable input becomes a demultiplexer when the enable is used as the data input. The select bits then choose which output receives the data.

シフトレジスタ.desc: A chain of flip-flops that moves data one bit to the next stage on each clock. It is used for serial-parallel conversion and as the scan chain in scan testing.

about.h: How a shift register is built
about.p: A shift register chains D flip-flops so that each output feeds the next input, and all share one clock. On every active edge each bit moves one stage along the chain. Variants are classified by how data enter and leave: serial-in serial-out acts as a delay line, serial-in parallel-out collects incoming bits into a word, parallel-in serial-out loads a word and shifts it out, and some designs also shift in both directions. In HDL the stages must be written with nonblocking assignments, as in q1 <= d; q2 <= q1;.

Serial-parallel conversion is the classic use. High-speed serial links (SerDes, serializer/deserializer) convert wide parallel buses into a few very fast serial lanes and back, reducing wire and pin count. A simple serial-in parallel-out chip such as the 74HC595 lets a microcontroller drive many LEDs from three pins. In chip testing, scan design connects a block's flip-flops into scan chains: in test mode the flip-flops form a shift register so test patterns can be shifted in, one functional clock applied, and the captured responses shifted out.

Feeding outputs back to the input turns a shift register into a counter. A ring counter recirculates a single 1 and has n states with n flip-flops. A Johnson, or twisted-ring, counter feeds back the inverted last output and cycles through 2n states, such as 000, 100, 110, 111, 011, 001 for three stages. Only one bit changes between neighboring states, so each state can be decoded with a two-input gate with little risk of glitches, and the outputs provide evenly staggered clock phases.

A linear feedback shift register (LFSR) feeds the XOR of selected outputs, called taps, back to the input. With properly chosen taps an n-bit LFSR steps through all 2ⁿ − 1 nonzero states before repeating, a maximal-length sequence that looks random. Built only from flip-flops and XOR gates, LFSRs generate test patterns and compact responses in built-in self-test (BIST), compute cyclic redundancy checks (CRC) and scramble data on communication links. Their output is fully predictable from a few bits, so they are not suitable for cryptographic randomness.

faq.q: What is a shift register used for?
faq.a: Shift registers are used for converting between serial and parallel data, building delay lines and counters, generating pseudo-random sequences as LFSRs, and forming the scan chains used to test chips.

faq.q: How many states does a Johnson counter have?
faq.a: A Johnson counter built from n flip-flops cycles through 2n states, twice as many as a ring counter with the same number of flip-flops.

faq.q: Why must a shift register in Verilog use nonblocking assignments?
faq.a: With blocking assignments each stage is updated immediately, so the next stage receives the new value in the same clock and the chain collapses to a single stage; nonblocking assignments make every stage take the value from before the edge.

全加算器.desc: A circuit that adds two bits plus a carry-in from the lower digit and outputs a sum and a carry-out. A version without carry-in is a half adder. Chaining full adders makes a multi-bit adder.

about.p: A full adder adds three one-bit inputs, A, B and a carry-in Cin, and produces a sum S and a carry-out Cout whose combined value equals the number of inputs that are 1. The sum is the parity of the inputs, S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, and the carry is their majority, Cout = AB + BC + CA. A half adder handles only two inputs, with sum A ⊕ B and carry AB, so a full adder can be built from two half adders plus an OR gate that merges their carries.

Chaining n full adders, with each carry-out feeding the next carry-in, makes an n-bit ripple-carry adder. It is small and regular, but the highest bit cannot settle until the carry has rippled through every stage, so delay grows linearly with width: a 64-bit adder takes about 64 full-adder delays, too slow for a GHz processor datapath. The same chain also subtracts. Inverting B and setting the lowest carry-in to 1 computes A + (¬B + 1), which is A − B in two's complement, so an ALU uses one adder for both operations.

Fast adders compute carries without waiting for the ripple. Each bit position generates a carry when G = AB and propagates an incoming carry when P = A ⊕ B. A carry-lookahead adder expands the carry recurrence in terms of G and P for groups of bits. A carry-select adder computes upper sums for both possible carry-ins and picks one when the real carry arrives. Parallel-prefix adders, such as the Kogge-Stone adder, combine G and P in a tree so carry delay grows with log2 n, at the cost of much more wiring and area.

about.h: Where full adders appear beyond adders
about.p: Multipliers add many partial products at once, and there the full adder is used as a 3:2 compressor: it takes three bits of equal weight and outputs a sum bit plus a carry bit of the next weight. Trees of such carry-save adders, such as Wallace or Dadda trees, reduce many rows to two before a single fast adder produces the final result. At the transistor level, a common static CMOS implementation is the 28-transistor mirror adder, which shares carry logic and generates the sum from the inverted carry.

faq.q: What is the difference between a half adder and a full adder?
faq.a: A half adder adds two bits and produces a sum and carry, while a full adder adds two bits plus a carry-in from the lower position. Only the full adder can be chained to add multi-bit numbers.

faq.q: What are the Boolean expressions for a full adder?
faq.a: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = AB + BC + CA, which is equivalently AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). The carry-out is the majority function of the three inputs.

faq.q: How many half adders make a full adder?
faq.a: Two. The first adds A and B, the second adds that sum to Cin, and an OR gate combines the two carry outputs into Cout.

セットアップ時間.desc: The minimum time before the active clock edge during which a flip-flop's data input must be stable. Paths that cannot meet it limit the maximum operating frequency.

about.p: An edge-triggered flip-flop is typically built from two latches. Before the clock edge, the input must pass through the first latch and its internal nodes must settle so the value is firmly held when that latch closes. If data changes too close to the edge, the flip-flop may capture the old value, the new one, or go metastable, taking unpredictable time to resolve. Setup time is the required stable interval before the edge and hold time the interval after it. Both are characterized per cell and vary with slew and operating conditions.

Data launched at one edge must arrive at least the setup time before the next capture edge. Arrival time is clock-to-output plus logic delay; required time is the period, adjusted for clock skew, minus setup time and clock uncertainty. Slack is required minus arrival, and negative slack is a violation. With a 2.0 ns period, 0.2 ns clock-to-output, 1.4 ns of logic and 0.1 ns setup, slack is 0.3 ns. The slowest path, the critical path, sets the maximum frequency: a 2.5 ns total allows 400 MHz.

Setup is a maximum-delay check against the next edge, so a violation disappears if the clock is slowed, or the path is shortened by pipelining, reducing logic depth, upsizing cells or using low-threshold-voltage cells. Hold is a minimum-delay check against the same edge and does not depend on frequency, so it is repaired by adding delay. The two pull in opposite directions: capture-clock skew that helps setup hurts hold. Under on-chip variation (OCV) derating, setup assumes a slow launch side and an early capture clock; hold reverses this.

A multicycle path of 2 moves the capture edge two periods away, valid only if logic such as an enable really captures every other cycle. A half-cycle path, launched on the rising edge and captured on the falling edge, gets only half a period. Latches allow time borrowing: data arriving after the latch opens still passes if it arrives before closing, taking time from the next stage. At chip boundaries, set_input_delay and set_output_delay describe time spent outside the chip. Useful skew deliberately delays a capture clock to rebalance adjacent stages.

faq.q: What is the difference between setup time and hold time?
faq.a: Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge, and hold time is how long it must stay stable after the edge. Setup limits maximum frequency, while hold violations are independent of clock frequency.

faq.q: How do you calculate setup slack?
faq.a: Slack = required time − arrival time, where arrival time is clock-to-output plus logic delay and required time is the clock period (adjusted for skew) minus setup time and clock uncertainty. Positive slack means the path meets timing.

faq.q: Can a setup violation be fixed by lowering the clock frequency?
faq.a: Yes, a longer period gives the data more time to arrive, so setup violations disappear at a low enough frequency. Hold violations do not, which makes them more dangerous once silicon is built.

ホールド時間.desc: The minimum time after the active clock edge during which a flip-flop's data input must stay unchanged. Violations are not fixed by lowering the clock frequency, so delay is added to the path.

about.p: A flip-flop needs its data input to stay unchanged for a short window after the active clock edge while the internal latch closes; that minimum interval is the hold time. Setup time is the mirror requirement before the edge. The danger for hold comes from the same edge that captures data: it also launches new data from the upstream flip-flop, and if that new value races through a very short path, it can overwrite the value being captured. Either violation can produce a wrong value or drive the flip-flop into metastability.

Hold analysis uses the fastest case: minimum clock-to-output delay plus minimum logic and wire delay must exceed the hold time, adjusted for when the capture clock actually arrives. With 0.08 ns clock-to-output, 0.02 ns of logic, 0.05 ns hold time and a capture clock 0.1 ns late, arrival is 0.10 ns against a requirement of 0.15 ns, a −0.05 ns violation. Board-level interfaces follow the same logic, using the transmitter's minimum clock-to-output; if a datasheet omits it, assuming 0 ns is the safe choice.

about.h: Why slowing the clock does not help
about.p: For an ordinary path launched and captured by the same clock edge, the clock period does not appear in the hold equation, so lowering the frequency leaves the violation unchanged. A chip shipped with a real hold violation can be unusable at any speed. The standard fix is inserting buffers or delay cells on the short data path, usually after clock tree synthesis when actual skew is known. Paths with little or no logic, such as shift registers and scan chains, are the classic hold risks, and positive clock skew makes them worse.

Hold time is a characterized property of each flip-flop design and depends on input slew, load and process corner. It can be very small, zero or even negative, meaning the data may change slightly before the clock edge without harm, because of internal delays between the clock pin and the sampling point. A negative hold time makes hold easier to meet but does not eliminate the check, since clock skew and on-chip variation still shift the effective requirement at every endpoint.

faq.q: What is the difference between setup time and hold time?
faq.a: Setup time is how long data must be stable before the clock edge, and hold time is how long it must remain stable after the edge. Setup is violated by paths that are too slow and hold by paths that are too fast.

faq.q: Can a flip-flop have a negative hold time?
faq.a: Yes. Internal delays can mean the data is effectively sampled slightly before the external clock edge, so the data may change just before the edge without error; the library then reports a negative hold value.

faq.q: How do you fix a hold time violation?
faq.a: Add delay to the short data path with buffers or delay cells, or reduce the skew that makes the capture clock late. Changing the clock frequency has no effect on a same-edge hold check.

クロックスキュー.desc: The difference in arrival time of the same clock signal at different flip-flops. Because it changes setup and hold margins, clock tree synthesis keeps it small.

about.p: In a synchronous circuit one clock source feeds thousands to millions of flip-flops through a network of wires and buffers. Differences in wire length, wire resistance and capacitance, buffer load, and local variations in process, voltage and temperature make the same clock edge arrive at slightly different times at different flip-flops. That spatial difference in arrival time is clock skew. It should not be confused with jitter, which is the variation of the clock edge's timing from cycle to cycle at a single point. What matters for timing is the skew between each pair of flip-flops that pass data to each other.

Define skew as the capture clock's arrival minus the launch clock's arrival. A late capture clock gives data more time, helping setup: the condition becomes period + skew ≥ clock-to-output + logic delay + setup time. For a 2.0 ns period, 0.2 ns clock-to-output, 1.4 ns logic and 0.1 ns setup, slack is 0.3 ns at zero skew and 0.4 ns with 0.1 ns positive skew. The same late capture hurts hold, because new data can overwrite the old before the capture flip-flop has latched it: minimum clock-to-output plus minimum logic delay must exceed hold time plus skew.

about.h: Controlling skew with clock tree synthesis
about.p: Clock tree synthesis (CTS) builds the chip-wide distribution network, choosing buffer locations and balancing wire lengths and loads so that skew stays within tens of picoseconds. Common structures include symmetric H-trees, buffered trees and grid-like clock meshes that short many branches together. Static timing analysis then checks every path with the actual computed clock arrivals and adds derating for on-chip variation. Designers sometimes introduce intentional, or useful, skew, delaying the capture clock of a critical path to borrow time from a neighboring path that has slack to spare.

A setup violation can be fixed after fabrication by lowering the clock frequency, since a longer period gives data more time. A hold violation cannot, because the hold condition does not include the clock period at all; it is a race between the new data and the clock edge in the same cycle. That is why skew-induced hold problems are fixed before tape-out by inserting delay buffers on short paths. At board level the same arithmetic applies to chip-to-chip interfaces, where clock skew and jitter must be subtracted from the timing budget.

faq.q: What is the difference between clock skew and clock jitter?
faq.a: Skew is a difference in clock arrival time between different locations in the same cycle, while jitter is the variation of the clock edge time from cycle to cycle at one location.

faq.q: Is clock skew always bad?
faq.a: No. Positive skew gives a path more setup time, and designers sometimes add intentional useful skew to balance timing, but any skew that helps setup reduces hold margin on the same path.

faq.q: Can a hold violation be fixed by slowing the clock?
faq.a: No. Hold timing does not depend on the clock period, so it must be fixed by adding delay to the short data path or reducing skew.

グリッチ.desc: An unwanted momentary pulse on an output, caused for example by differing delays along signal paths. In combinational logic it is also called a hazard; in DACs it appears when the code changes.

about.h: How a hazard creates a glitch
about.p: A glitch appears when one input change reaches an output through paths of different delay. Consider F = A·B + (not A)·C with B and C both 1: F should stay 1 as A switches, but if the inverted path is slower, both product terms can be 0 for an instant and F dips briefly. This is a static-1 hazard. Adding the redundant consensus term B·C removes it. A dynamic hazard is an output that should change once but bounces several times before settling.

In synchronous logic, a glitch on a data path is functionally harmless if it settles before the capturing clock edge, which static timing analysis guarantees. It still wastes dynamic power, because every spurious transition charges and discharges capacitance, and deep arithmetic logic can produce many of them. Glitches become real failures on clocks, asynchronous resets or sets, and signals leaving the chip, where a brief pulse can be taken as a real event. Such signals should therefore come directly from flip-flop outputs, which is one reason Moore-machine outputs are preferred for critical controls.

Gating a clock with a plain AND gate is risky: if the enable changes while the clock is high, the output can produce a truncated or extra pulse. Static timing analysis applies clock gating checks to ensure the enable is stable before the clock rises and held until it falls. Standard designs avoid the problem with integrated clock gating cells, which latch the enable while the clock is low so it can only change during the low phase.

In a digital-to-analog converter (DAC), bits switching at slightly different times create brief wrong codes at the output. The worst case is the midscale major carry, from 0111... to 1000..., where every bit changes. Glitch energy is specified as glitch impulse area, and it is reduced by thermometer-coding the upper bits, matching switch drivers and adding a deglitching sample-and-hold. Glitches can also be weaponized: fault injection attacks insert deliberate glitches into a chip's clock or supply to make it skip instructions such as a signature check.

faq.q: What is the difference between a glitch and a hazard?
faq.a: A hazard is the property of a logic circuit that allows a momentary wrong output when inputs change; the glitch is the actual spurious pulse that appears. The terms are often used interchangeably.

faq.q: Are glitches a problem in synchronous designs?
faq.a: On ordinary data paths they are harmless as long as they settle before the clock edge, though they add power consumption. On clocks, asynchronous resets and off-chip control signals they can cause real malfunctions.

faq.q: Why is DAC glitch worst at midscale?
faq.a: At the midscale transition every bit changes at once, so small timing mismatches between the most significant bit and the rest briefly produce codes far from either the old or new value.

トライステートバッファ.desc: A buffer that can output 0, 1 or a disconnected high-impedance state. It prevents output conflicts when several circuits share one bus.

仮想短絡(イマジナリーショート).desc: The property of an ideal op-amp with negative feedback that its two input voltages become nearly equal. Although no current flows between them, they can be treated as shorted, which makes gain calculations simple.

about.h: Why the inputs end up equal
about.p: An op-amp's output is Vout = A(V+ − V−), where the open-loop gain A is very large, about 10⁵ to 10⁶ for typical real devices at low frequency. With negative feedback the circuit settles where the output is finite, so the input difference must be Vout/A. For an output of 10 V and A = 10⁵, the inputs differ by only 100 µV. In ideal analysis A is infinite, the difference becomes zero, and the two inputs can be treated as being at the same voltage.

In an inverting amplifier the non-inverting input is grounded, so the virtual short puts the inverting input at 0 V; this special case is called a virtual ground. The input current is then Vin/R1. Because an ideal op-amp input draws no current, all of it flows through the feedback resistor Rf, giving Vout = −(Rf/R1)·Vin. The same two rules give the non-inverting gain of 1 + Rf/R1 and analyze summing amplifiers, integrators and differential amplifiers.

about.h: Virtual short vs. a real short
about.p: A real short would let current flow between the inputs; a virtual short does not. Analysis therefore uses two separate ideal-op-amp assumptions together: the inputs are at equal voltage because of feedback and high gain, and no current enters either input because of the infinite input impedance. Confusing the two, for example by letting current flow from one input to the other, gives wrong answers. The equality is maintained actively by the output, not by any connection.

The virtual short holds only while negative feedback is working. If the output saturates at a supply rail, is slew-rate limited or the signal frequency is so high that the loop gain has fallen, the inputs separate. Comparators and Schmitt triggers run open loop or with positive feedback, so their inputs are deliberately unequal. Real op-amps also have an input offset voltage, from microvolts to a few millivolts, that appears as a small, constant difference between the inputs.

faq.q: What is the difference between virtual short and virtual ground?
faq.a: Virtual short is the general property that both inputs sit at the same voltage under negative feedback; virtual ground is the case where one input is grounded, so the other is held at 0 V.

faq.q: Does current flow through a virtual short?
faq.a: No. The inputs are at the same voltage but not connected, and an ideal op-amp draws no input current.

faq.q: Why can't the virtual short be used for a comparator?
faq.a: A comparator has no negative feedback, so its output swings to a rail and nothing forces the inputs to the same voltage.

スルーレート.desc: The maximum rate at which an op-amp's output voltage can change, expressed in V/µs. If it is insufficient for large, high-frequency signals, the waveform distorts.

about.p: In a typical two-stage op-amp, a fast, large input step overloads the input differential pair, which then steers its entire tail current I to one side. That current, the most the stage can deliver, charges the compensation capacitor Cc, so the output can ramp no faster than SR = I/Cc. Instead of following the input with a smooth exponential, the output moves as a straight-line ramp until the error shrinks and linear operation resumes. Rising and falling slew rates can differ, and datasheets give slew rate in V/µs under stated gain and load conditions.

A sine wave Vp·sin(2πft) has a maximum slope of 2πf·Vp, at its zero crossings. If that slope exceeds the slew rate, the output cannot keep up and turns into a triangle-like wave. The highest undistorted frequency, called the full-power bandwidth, is therefore f = SR/(2πVp). An op-amp with 0.5 V/µs delivering a 10 V peak sine is limited to about 8 kHz; forgetting the 2π gives an incorrect 50 kHz. Halving the amplitude doubles the usable frequency, so slew limits bite hardest on large signals.

The gain-bandwidth product (GBW) describes small-signal, linear behavior, while slew rate is a large-signal, nonlinear limit, and the two must be checked separately. Suppose an amplifier with a GBW of 1 MHz runs at a gain of 10: its small-signal bandwidth is about 100 kHz, but a 10 V peak output at 100 kHz needs a slew rate of at least 2π × 100 kHz × 10 V ≈ 6.3 V/µs. If the part offers only 0.5 V/µs, large signals distort long before the small-signal bandwidth is reached.

Because GBW = gm1/(2πCc) and SR = I/Cc, the two are linked through the ratio of tail current to input-pair transconductance. A bipolar input pair gives a high gm per unit current, so it tends to have a low slew rate for its bandwidth; emitter degeneration or MOS input pairs with larger overdrive raise slew rate at the same GBW. Typical values range from below 1 V/µs in low-power general-purpose op-amps to well over 1,000 V/µs in high-speed amplifiers, which often use current-feedback or class-AB input structures.

faq.q: How do I calculate the slew rate needed for a sine wave?
faq.a: Multiply 2π by the frequency and by the peak output voltage: SR ≥ 2πf·Vp. A 10 V peak sine at 20 kHz needs at least about 1.3 V/µs, plus some margin.

faq.q: What does slew rate distortion look like?
faq.a: A sine wave becomes triangular because the output can only change at a fixed maximum rate, and step responses show straight-line ramps instead of smooth exponential settling.

faq.q: Is slew rate the same as bandwidth?
faq.a: No. Bandwidth (set by GBW) limits small signals linearly, while slew rate limits how fast large signals can swing; a part can have enough GBW and still distort large signals.

利得帯域幅積(GBW).desc: The product of an op-amp's gain and bandwidth, which stays roughly constant. With a GBW of 1 MHz, for example, a gain-of-10 circuit has a bandwidth of about 100 kHz.

about.h: Why gain times bandwidth is constant
about.p: Most general-purpose op-amps are internally compensated so that a single dominant pole sets the open-loop response. The open-loop gain A0, often around 100 dB, stays flat up to a pole frequency fp of a few to tens of hertz and then falls at −20 dB per decade. Above fp, gain is inversely proportional to frequency, so gain multiplied by frequency stays at A0 × fp. That product is the gain-bandwidth product (GBW), and it also approximately equals the unity-gain frequency where open-loop gain reaches 1. For example, 10⁵ gain with a 10 Hz pole gives a 1 MHz GBW.

With negative feedback, the closed-loop bandwidth is roughly GBW divided by the noise gain, which for a voltage-feedback op-amp is 1 + Rf/Rg, the non-inverting gain of the feedback network. A non-inverting amplifier with gain 10 on a 1 MHz part therefore reaches about 100 kHz. An inverting amplifier with gain −10 has a noise gain of 11, so its bandwidth is about 91 kHz. To get high gain and wide bandwidth together, choose a part with higher GBW or split the gain across two or more stages, each with a modest gain.

The closed-loop −3 dB frequency is not where the amplifier stops working well; there the gain is already down about 30% and the output lags by 45°. What matters below it is the loop gain, approximately GBW divided by the product of frequency and noise gain, because loop gain is what suppresses distortion, gain error and output impedance. It falls as frequency rises: at one-tenth of the closed-loop bandwidth it is only about 10, so feedback reduces distortion only about tenfold and the phase shift is already near 6°. Low-distortion and precision circuits therefore choose GBW with large margin.

The constant-GBW rule applies to dominant-pole, voltage-feedback op-amps in small-signal operation. Decompensated op-amps trade stability for speed and are specified only above a minimum closed-loop gain. Current-feedback amplifiers do not follow the rule: their bandwidth is set mainly by the feedback resistor and stays nearly constant over a range of gains. Large signals are limited by slew rate rather than GBW, so a circuit can meet its small-signal bandwidth yet distort at full amplitude. Additional poles near the unity-gain frequency also reduce phase margin, causing peaking.

faq.q: Is gain-bandwidth product the same as unity-gain bandwidth?
faq.a: For a dominant-pole compensated op-amp they are nearly equal, since the open-loop gain falls at −20 dB/decade all the way to unity. They differ when other poles lie close to the unity-gain frequency.

faq.q: How do you calculate bandwidth from GBW?
faq.a: Divide GBW by the noise gain, 1 + Rf/Rg. A 1 MHz op-amp in a non-inverting gain of 10 gives about 100 kHz; an inverting gain of −10 gives about 91 kHz.

faq.q: What GBW do I need for my amplifier?
