faq.a: At minimum, the noise gain times the highest signal frequency, but for low distortion and small phase error choose several to many times more, and check slew rate separately for large signals.

CMRR(同相信号除去比).desc: The ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain in a differential amplifier. The larger it is, the better the circuit rejects noise that appears equally on both inputs.

about.p: A differential amplifier should respond only to the difference between its inputs. The common-mode rejection ratio is the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain, CMRR = |Ad/Acm|, usually given in decibels as 20·log10 of that ratio. Op-amps typically offer 80–120 dB at low frequency. A useful way to read it: with 100 dB, a ratio of 100,000, a 1 V shift in the common-mode voltage looks like only about 10 µV of differential input error. Higher CMRR means better immunity to noise picked up equally on both wires, such as interference on long cables or ground differences.

about.h: What limits it inside the amplifier
about.p: In a differential pair, the tail current source splits its current between the two transistors according to the input difference; if both inputs move together, the split ideally stays the same. Real circuits fall short because the tail source has finite output impedance, so its current changes slightly with common-mode voltage, and because the two transistors and their loads are never perfectly matched, so that change is converted into a differential output. At higher frequencies, parasitic capacitance at the tail node lowers its impedance, which is why CMRR drops as frequency rises.

A single op-amp with four resistors makes a simple difference amplifier, but its CMRR is usually limited by resistor matching rather than by the op-amp. In the worst case it is about (1 + G)/(4ε), where G is the differential gain and ε the resistor tolerance. With 1% resistors and unity gain, that is only about 50, or 34 dB. The three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier fixes this: two input op-amps provide high input impedance and gain, raising the differential signal before a laser-trimmed or on-chip-matched difference stage, so CMRR above 100 dB is achievable.

about.h: CMRR vs. PSRR and common-mode range
about.p: Two related specifications are often confused with CMRR. The power-supply rejection ratio (PSRR) describes how well the amplifier ignores changes in its supply voltage, not in its input common-mode voltage. The input common-mode voltage range is the span over which the inputs can sit while the amplifier still works properly at all; CMRR is only meaningful inside that range. Exceeding it, for example driving a non-rail-to-rail input near the supply, causes gross errors that no CMRR figure predicts. Datasheets give each of these specs separately, usually with graphs versus frequency.

faq.q: What is a good CMRR value?
faq.a: General-purpose op-amps typically specify 80–120 dB at DC, and instrumentation amplifiers can exceed 100 dB. What matters is the value at the frequency of the interference you need to reject, since CMRR falls with frequency.

faq.q: How do you convert CMRR from dB to a ratio?
faq.a: Ratio = 10^(dB/20). For example, 80 dB is 10,000 and 100 dB is 100,000, meaning a common-mode change is attenuated by that factor relative to a differential signal.

faq.q: Why is my difference amplifier's CMRR so low?
faq.a: In a single op-amp difference amplifier, mismatch among the four resistors usually dominates; 1% resistors can limit CMRR to around 34 dB at unity gain. Use tightly matched resistor networks or an instrumentation amplifier.

PSRR(電源電圧変動除去比).desc: A measure of how little supply-voltage variation reaches a circuit's output. The larger it is, the more immune the circuit is to supply noise.

about.p: PSRR compares a change on a supply rail with the change it causes at the circuit's output, and it is quoted in decibels using 20 log₁₀ because it is a ratio of voltages. A PSRR of 60 dB therefore means a supply disturbance is attenuated about 1000 times, and 80 dB means 10,000 times. Datasheets often give separate values for the positive and negative rails, and some refer the result to the input by dividing by the closed-loop gain. Sign conventions differ between vendors, so the same part may be listed as +60 dB or −60 dB; what matters is the magnitude.

In an op-amp or a low-dropout regulator (LDO), supply rejection comes mainly from the feedback loop, which senses and corrects whatever the supply couples into the signal path. Loop gain drops as frequency rises, so less correction is available, while parasitic capacitances open direct paths from the supply to the output. The result is a curve, not a single number: a device with 80–100 dB at low frequency may offer only 20–30 dB at several hundred kilohertz. That is exactly where switching-regulator ripple and its harmonics tend to sit.

To estimate output ripple, convert PSRR to a linear ratio with 10^(PSRR/20) and divide the input ripple by it: 100 mV of 1 kHz ripple through 60 dB leaves about 0.1 mV. Using 10 log₁₀, which applies to power ratios, gives an answer a thousand times too small. Always read the PSRR at the actual ripple frequency from the datasheet graph. When an LC filter precedes an LDO, their attenuations multiply, so in decibels they roughly add, although source and load impedances keep this from being exact.

about.h: PSRR vs. CMRR and line regulation
about.p: Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) describes how well an amplifier ignores a voltage that appears equally on both of its inputs; PSRR describes how well it ignores changes on its power pins. The two are often confused because both are rejection ratios in decibels. Line regulation, a regulator specification, is the static or slow-change version of PSRR, usually given as output change per volt of input change. PSRR is the dynamic counterpart that tells you how much ripple and noise get through at each frequency.

faq.q: How do I calculate output ripple from PSRR in dB?
faq.a: Divide the input ripple amplitude by 10^(PSRR/20), using the PSRR value at the ripple frequency. For example, 60 dB corresponds to a factor of 1000, so 100 mV of ripple becomes about 0.1 mV.

faq.q: Why doesn't my LDO remove switching regulator ripple?
faq.a: LDO PSRR is usually high only at low frequencies and can drop to a few tens of dB at the hundreds of kilohertz where switching ripple sits. Adding an LC or ferrite filter before the LDO, or choosing an LDO specified for high-frequency PSRR, is the usual fix.

faq.q: Is PSRR positive or negative in dB?
faq.a: Both forms appear because vendors define the ratio in opposite directions. Treat the magnitude as the rejection: a larger magnitude means less supply noise reaches the output.

位相余裕(フェーズマージン).desc: How far the phase lag is from 180° at the frequency where the feedback loop gain is 1 (0 dB). A small margin causes ringing, and zero or negative margin causes oscillation; 45-60° or more is a common target.

about.p: Take the loop gain T = Aβ, the gain a signal sees going once around the feedback loop. At the crossover frequency where the magnitude of T falls to 1 (0 dB), phase margin is how far the phase lag still is from 180 degrees: with 120 degrees of lag, the margin is 60 degrees. Gain margin is the companion measure, how far the loop gain is below 0 dB at the frequency where the lag reaches 180 degrees. Both are read from a Bode plot of the loop gain, not of the closed-loop response.

about.h: What the number means in practice
about.p: Zero margin means the loop sustains oscillation, and negative margin means the oscillation grows. Small positive margins show up as peaking in the closed-loop frequency response and overshoot with ringing in the step response. Around 45 degrees, overshoot is clearly visible; around 60 degrees, the response is fast with only slight overshoot, which is why 45 to 60 degrees or more is the usual target. Very large margins are stable but often mean bandwidth has been given away.

about.h: Where the phase lag comes from
about.p: Each pole in the loop contributes up to 90 degrees of lag, so two poles near the crossover frequency push the total toward 180 degrees. Dominant-pole compensation places one pole at a very low frequency, a few to tens of hertz in general-purpose op-amps, often using the Miller effect so a small on-chip capacitor suffices. Gain then falls at −20 dB per decade and crosses 0 dB well before the next pole adds much lag. With a single second pole, placing it about 1.7 times above crossover gives roughly 60 degrees of margin. The cost is lower bandwidth and slew rate.

about.h: Why the voltage follower is the worst case
about.p: With feedback fraction β = 1, loop gain equals the full open-loop gain and crossover occurs at the highest frequency, closest to the op-amp's internal poles. Higher closed-loop gain means smaller β, a lower crossover and more margin, so decompensated op-amps are specified as stable only above a minimum gain. Capacitive loads, which form an extra pole with the output resistance, and delays in the loop also erode margin. The same analysis applies to voltage regulators and phase-locked loops.

faq.q: What is a good phase margin for an amplifier?
faq.a: A common target is 45 to 60 degrees or more. About 60 degrees gives a fast step response with little overshoot, while much less than 45 degrees causes noticeable ringing.

faq.q: What is the difference between phase margin and gain margin?
faq.a: Phase margin is the distance from 180 degrees of lag at the frequency where loop gain is 0 dB. Gain margin is how far the loop gain is below 0 dB at the frequency where the lag reaches 180 degrees.

faq.q: Why is an op-amp less stable at unity gain?
faq.a: At unity gain the whole output is fed back, so the loop gain crosses 0 dB at the highest frequency, where the op-amp's higher poles add the most phase lag. Higher closed-loop gain lowers the crossover frequency and increases phase margin.

計装アンプ(インスツルメンテーションアンプ).desc: A differential amplifier, typically built from three op-amps, with high input impedance and high CMRR. It amplifies small differential signals from sensors with high accuracy.

トランスインピーダンスアンプ.desc: An amplifier that converts an input current to a voltage. The current enters the op-amp's inverting input and a feedback resistor turns it into a voltage. It is used to read photodiode signals.

about.h: How the circuit converts current to voltage
about.p: A transimpedance amplifier (TIA) feeds the input current into the inverting input of an op-amp whose non-inverting input is grounded. Negative feedback keeps the inverting input at a virtual ground, so the current has nowhere to go except through the feedback resistor Rf, and the output becomes −Iin × Rf. With 1 µA and 1 MΩ the output is 1 V. The gain is therefore measured in ohms, or volts per ampere, which is why it is called a transimpedance. A photodiode connected here sees almost 0 V across it regardless of light level.

about.h: TIA vs. a simple load resistor
about.p: A photodiode current could be turned into a voltage with just a resistor to ground, but then the diode voltage changes with the signal, and the diode's junction capacitance must charge through that resistor. A large resistor for high gain then means a slow RC response and a light-dependent operating point. In a TIA the op-amp holds the diode voltage nearly constant, so the effective input impedance is roughly Rf divided by the amplifier's open-loop gain. That decoupling of gain from input impedance is what improves both speed and linearity.

Larger Rf gives more output per microamp and lowers the resistor's relative thermal-noise contribution, but it also slows the circuit. The photodiode and op-amp input capacitance combine with Rf to put a zero in the feedback network's noise gain, which can cause peaking or oscillation. A small capacitor Cf across Rf restores phase margin and sets the bandwidth near 1/(2π Rf Cf). A common first estimate for the achievable bandwidth is the square root of the op-amp gain-bandwidth product divided by 2π Rf times the total input capacitance.

Every optical receiver starts with a TIA directly after the photodiode. A received power of about 0.1 mW yields roughly 0.1 mA, too small for the decision circuit, so the TIA converts and amplifies it while providing bandwidths of tens of gigahertz with low noise. It is placed right beside the photodiode to minimize interconnect capacitance, and is usually followed by limiting or variable-gain stages. Slower TIAs with megohm-range feedback resistors read ambient-light sensors, laboratory photodetectors and CT-scanner detector channels.

faq.q: Why is a capacitor placed across the feedback resistor in a transimpedance amplifier?
faq.a: Photodiode and amplifier input capacitance create a phase shift that can make the loop ring or oscillate. The feedback capacitor adds compensation and also sets the circuit's bandwidth.

faq.q: What are the units of transimpedance gain?
faq.a: Ohms, since gain is output voltage divided by input current. A 100 kΩ TIA produces 0.1 V for every microamp of input current.

faq.q: Why use a TIA instead of a resistor to read a photodiode?
faq.a: The TIA keeps the photodiode at a nearly fixed voltage, so its capacitance is not repeatedly charged and the response stays fast and linear even with high gain.

バンドギャップ基準電圧回路.desc: A circuit that adds a diode voltage that falls with temperature to a voltage that rises with temperature, producing a reference of about 1.2 V that barely depends on temperature. It is widely used in ADCs and power ICs.

PLL(位相同期回路).desc: A circuit that detects the phase difference from a reference clock and controls an oscillator to produce a clock locked to the reference, for example at an integer multiple of its frequency. It is used to generate CPU clocks and synthesize radio frequencies.

about.p: A typical PLL contains a phase-frequency detector (PFD), a charge pump, a loop filter, a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) and a feedback divider. The PFD compares the reference clock with the VCO output divided by N and emits up or down pulses proportional to their phase difference. The charge pump turns these into current, which the loop filter integrates into the VCO control voltage. Negative feedback adjusts the VCO until the divided output matches the reference in phase, at which point the output frequency is exactly N times the reference, for example multi-GHz from a 25 MHz crystal.

In an integer-N PLL the output can move only in steps equal to the reference frequency, so fine channel spacing forces a low reference and therefore a narrow, slow loop. A fractional-N PLL switches the divide ratio between neighboring integers, typically under control of a delta-sigma modulator, so the average ratio can be a fraction. This gives fine frequency resolution with a high reference frequency. The cost is quantization noise and fractional spurs that the loop filter and careful design must suppress.

Loop bandwidth sets a key trade-off. Within the bandwidth, output phase noise follows the reference multiplied by N, which raises it by 20·log10(N) dB; outside, it follows the free-running VCO. A wider loop locks faster and suppresses VCO noise better, but for stability the bandwidth is normally kept well below the reference frequency, often a tenth or less. Ring-oscillator VCOs are compact and tune over a wide range but are noisy; LC-tank VCOs give much lower phase noise at the cost of inductor area.

about.h: PLL vs. DLL and where they appear
about.p: PLLs generate processor and memory-interface clocks, the local oscillators of radio transceivers, the at-speed test clocks applied after scan loading, and the recovered clock in clock and data recovery (CDR) circuits of serial links. MEMS oscillators also pair a silicon resonator with a PLL to produce programmable frequencies. A delay-locked loop (DLL) is the closest relative: instead of an oscillator it adjusts a delay line to align a clock's phase. Because it does not oscillate, a DLL accumulates no jitter, but it cannot easily multiply frequency.

faq.q: How does a PLL multiply frequency?
faq.a: A divider in the feedback path divides the VCO output by N before it is compared with the reference. When the loop locks, the divided signal equals the reference frequency, so the VCO runs at N times the reference.

faq.q: What is the difference between a PLL and a DLL?
faq.a: A PLL controls an oscillator and can synthesize new frequencies, while a DLL controls a delay line to shift the phase of an existing clock. DLLs are simpler and do not accumulate jitter but generally cannot multiply frequency.

faq.q: What is a fractional-N PLL?
faq.a: It is a PLL whose divider alternates between integer ratios so the average ratio is fractional. This allows fine frequency steps without lowering the reference frequency, at the cost of extra spurs and noise.

シュミットトリガ.desc: A circuit whose switching threshold differs for rising and falling inputs (hysteresis). Its output does not chatter even with slowly changing or noisy signals.

about.p: A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback. In the common inverting form, the input drives the inverting input while a divider from the output feeds a fraction of the output voltage back to the non-inverting input. When the output is high, that fraction sets a higher threshold; when it is low, the threshold moves down. With output swings of ±Vsat and a divider of R2 from output to the non-inverting node and R1 from that node to ground, the thresholds are ±Vsat·R1/(R1+R2) and the hysteresis width is twice that.

A comparator with a single threshold toggles every time noise carries a slowly moving signal back and forth across that threshold, producing a burst of output edges known as chattering. In a Schmitt trigger, the moment the output switches, the threshold jumps away from the input, so noise smaller than the hysteresis width cannot switch it back. The design rule is to make the hysteresis larger than the expected peak-to-peak noise, while keeping it small enough that the shifted thresholds do not cost too much sensitivity or timing accuracy.

about.h: Schmitt inputs vs. ordinary logic inputs
about.p: A standard CMOS logic input has one switching point near half the supply. If the input edge is slow, it lingers in the region where both the pull-up and pull-down transistors conduct, drawing extra current and possibly oscillating. Gates with Schmitt-trigger inputs, such as the 74HC14 hex inverter, have separate rising and falling thresholds and tolerate slow or noisy edges. Many microcontroller input pins include a Schmitt trigger for the same reason, which helps with long cables, RC-filtered signals and reset lines.

Mechanical switch contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when closed. A resistor-capacitor filter slows the bouncing waveform, and a Schmitt trigger turns it back into one clean edge; software debouncing that waits and rereads is the alternative. A single Schmitt inverter with a resistor from output to input and a capacitor from input to ground forms an RC relaxation oscillator: the capacitor charges and discharges between the two thresholds, so the frequency depends on RC and on the hysteresis. Schmitt triggers also square up sine waves and sensor signals.

faq.q: What is hysteresis in a Schmitt trigger?
faq.a: It is the difference between the rising-input threshold and the falling-input threshold. The output only changes state when the input crosses the far threshold, which gives immunity to noise smaller than that gap.

faq.q: How do you debounce a button with a Schmitt trigger?
faq.a: Place an RC low-pass filter between the switch and a Schmitt-trigger input. The filter smooths the bounces into a slow ramp, and the hysteresis converts that ramp into a single clean transition.

faq.q: What is the difference between a comparator and a Schmitt trigger?
faq.a: A plain comparator switches at one threshold and can chatter on noisy inputs. A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback, giving two thresholds and a clean single transition.

1/f雑音(フリッカ雑音).desc: Noise that grows larger at lower frequencies. In MOSFETs it comes from traps at the gate-oxide interface capturing and releasing carriers, and it matters in low-frequency analog circuits.

熱雑音(ジョンソン雑音).desc: Noise caused by the thermal motion of electrons in a resistor. Its mean-square voltage is 4kTRΔf, proportional to temperature, resistance and bandwidth.

about.p: Electrons in any resistor jiggle randomly with thermal energy, producing a tiny fluctuating voltage across its terminals even when no current flows. This thermal noise, also called Johnson-Nyquist noise, is white, meaning its power spectral density is flat over the frequencies of interest, and its amplitude follows a Gaussian distribution. Its mean-square voltage is 4kTRΔf, where k is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature, R the resistance and Δf the bandwidth. Equivalently, it can be modeled as a noise current with mean square 4kTΔf/R in parallel with the resistor.

A 1 kΩ resistor at room temperature produces about 4 nV/√Hz, or about 0.57 µVrms over a 20 kHz audio bandwidth; since voltage noise scales with the square root of resistance, 100 kΩ gives about 40 nV/√Hz. When a voltage is sampled onto a capacitor through a switch, the resistor's noise density and the RC bandwidth cancel, leaving √(kT/C) regardless of switch resistance, about 64 µVrms for 1 pF. Halving kT/C noise requires four times the capacitance, which costs area and power in high-resolution ADCs and image sensors.

about.h: Thermal noise vs. shot noise and 1/f noise
about.p: Thermal noise exists in any resistance at equilibrium. Shot noise, by contrast, arises from discrete charges crossing a barrier such as a PN junction and requires current, with mean-square current 2qIΔf. Flicker or 1/f noise rises at low frequencies; in MOSFETs it comes mainly from traps at the gate dielectric interface, and its corner frequency, where it equals thermal noise, ranges from kHz to MHz. Fixed-pattern noise in image sensors is not temporal noise at all but repeatable pixel-to-pixel variation.

Since thermal noise depends on R, T and bandwidth, designers use lower resistances where possible, limit bandwidth to what the signal needs and, in radio astronomy or quantum-computer readout, cool amplifiers to cryogenic temperatures. Image sensors remove the kT/C reset noise with correlated double sampling, and ADC designers budget thermal noise against the ideal quantization-limited SNR of 6.02N + 1.76 dB. Thermal noise can also be useful: its unpredictability makes it a physical entropy source for on-chip true random number generators.

faq.q: What is the formula for thermal noise voltage?
faq.a: The RMS thermal noise voltage of a resistor is √(4kTRΔf), where k is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature, R the resistance and Δf the bandwidth. At room temperature, 1 kΩ gives about 4 nV/√Hz.

faq.q: Does thermal noise occur without current flowing?
faq.a: Yes. Thermal noise comes from the random thermal motion of carriers and exists in any resistor at a temperature above absolute zero, even with no applied current, unlike shot noise.

faq.q: What is kT/C noise?
faq.a: It is the thermal noise left on a capacitor after sampling through a switch, with RMS value √(kT/C) independent of the switch resistance. For 1 pF at room temperature it is about 64 µV.

LDO.desc: Short for low-dropout regulator: a linear regulator that works with only a small difference between input and output voltage. It is low-noise, but the voltage difference times the current is lost as heat.

about.p: A low-dropout regulator (LDO) is a linear regulator: an error amplifier compares a fraction of the output voltage, taken from a resistor divider, with a stable reference such as a bandgap, and drives the pass transistor so the output stays at the set value. The pass device behaves like a continuously adjusted resistor. A PMOS (or PNP) pass device can be turned fully on simply by pulling its gate toward ground, which lets it stay in regulation with only 0.1 to 0.3 V across it, whereas classic NPN-follower regulators need roughly 1.5 to 2 V or more of headroom.

The minimum input is the output voltage plus the dropout voltage at the actual load current and temperature; a 3.3 V LDO with 300 mV maximum dropout needs at least 3.6 V in. Because input and output currents are essentially equal, efficiency is roughly Vout divided by Vin, so 1.8 V to 1.0 V gives about 56%. The rest, (Vin - Vout) times the load current, becomes heat, which must be checked against the package's thermal resistance. At light loads the regulator's own quiescent current dominates battery drain.

Power supply rejection ratio (PSRR) expresses how much input ripple is suppressed, as a voltage ratio in dB using 20·log10: 60 dB means ripple is divided by 1000. PSRR is highest at low frequency and falls as the error amplifier's gain rolls off, sometimes to 20 to 30 dB at several hundred kHz. When an LDO cleans up a switching regulator's output, check PSRR at the switching frequency. Output noise, largely from the reference, matters for PLLs, ADC references and RF circuits, and some LDOs provide a noise-reduction capacitor pin.

A switching regulator chops the input at hundreds of kHz to several MHz and transfers energy through an inductor, reaching roughly 80 to 95% efficiency even for large voltage steps, and can also boost or invert. It produces switching ripple and electromagnetic noise. An LDO only steps down and wastes the difference as heat, but it is small, quiet and fast to respond to load changes. A common design steps down efficiently with a switcher, then follows it with an LDO for noise-sensitive loads. LDOs are also integrated on chip to supply separate voltage domains.

faq.q: What is the dropout voltage of an LDO?
faq.a: It is the smallest input-to-output voltage difference at which the regulator can still hold its output at the specified value. It rises with load current and often with temperature, so use the datasheet value at your operating conditions.

faq.q: How do I calculate LDO efficiency and power loss?
faq.a: Efficiency is approximately Vout divided by Vin, ignoring quiescent current. The power lost as heat is (Vin - Vout) times the load current; for example, 5 V to 3.3 V at 0.5 A dissipates about 0.85 W.

faq.q: Should I use an LDO or a switching regulator?
faq.a: Use a switching regulator when the voltage drop or current is large and efficiency matters. Use an LDO when the drop is small, the load is noise-sensitive, or simplicity and low ripple are more important than efficiency.

コンパレータ.desc: A circuit that compares two input voltages and outputs the result as a binary high or low. It is also a basic building block of ADCs.

about.p: Both have a differential input and very high gain, but they are optimized for opposite jobs. An op-amp is designed for stable linear operation with negative feedback and recovers slowly once its output saturates. A comparator runs open loop, spends almost all its time saturated at one rail or the other, and is built to switch quickly and recover cleanly, often with an open-drain or logic-level output that drives digital inputs directly. Using an op-amp as a comparator works for slow signals but usually gives long and unpredictable propagation delay.

When a noisy or slowly varying input hovers near the threshold, a plain comparator can toggle many times as noise crosses back and forth, a problem called chattering. Adding positive feedback creates two thresholds: a higher one for a rising input and a lower one for a falling input. The gap between them, the hysteresis, must exceed the noise amplitude. This arrangement is a Schmitt trigger, also available as logic gates such as the 74HC14, and is used for switch inputs, zero-crossing detection and RC relaxation oscillators.

Input offset voltage sets how far apart the inputs must be before the decision is reliable, and in an ADC it appears directly as offset error. Propagation delay, often specified for a given input overdrive, sets maximum speed; small overdrive gives longer delay. Input common-mode range, supply current and output type complete the picture. Inside ADCs, comparators are usually clocked: a preamplifier followed by a regenerative latch of cross-coupled inverters that amplifies a tiny difference to full logic levels. If the input difference is extremely small, the latch can take too long to resolve, which is metastability.

Every analog-to-digital converter ends in comparator decisions, and the architectures differ in how many they use. A flash ADC needs 2^N − 1 comparators, seven for 3 bits and 255 for 8 bits, which makes it fast but power-hungry. A successive-approximation (SAR) ADC reuses one comparator N times, comparing the input with an internal DAC from the most significant bit down. Pipelined ADCs use a few comparators per stage with redundancy for digital correction, and column-parallel image-sensor ADCs pair a comparator with a counter against a shared ramp.

faq.q: Can I use an op-amp as a comparator?
faq.a: For slow, non-critical signals it often works, but op-amps recover slowly from saturation and may not produce clean logic levels, so a dedicated comparator is better when speed or clean edges matter.

faq.q: Why add hysteresis to a comparator?
faq.a: Hysteresis gives separate rising and falling thresholds so noise near the switching point cannot make the output toggle repeatedly.

faq.q: How many comparators does an N-bit flash ADC need?
faq.a: 2^N − 1, so a 3-bit flash ADC needs 7 and an 8-bit one needs 255.

時定数.desc: A quantity describing how fast a circuit such as an RC network responds to a step; for an RC circuit τ = RC. The response reaches about 63% of its final value after τ and has nearly settled after about 5τ.

about.p: When a step voltage charges a capacitor through a resistor, the capacitor voltage follows V(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = RC. At t = τ the exponent is −1, so the voltage reaches 1 − 1/e, about 63% of its final value. It reaches about 86% at 2τ, 95% at 3τ, 98% at 4τ and over 99% at 5τ, which is why 5τ is treated as settled. Discharge mirrors this, falling to about 37% after one time constant. If the initial slope continued unchanged, the voltage would reach its final value in exactly τ.

Any first-order system has a time constant. For a resistor and inductor, τ = L/R, and the current rather than the voltage rises exponentially. Thermal systems behave the same way, with τ equal to thermal resistance times heat capacity, which explains why a chip and its heat sink take seconds or longer to warm up. The time constant also links time and frequency: a first-order low-pass filter has its −3 dB cutoff at 1/(2πτ), and its 10–90% rise time is about 2.2τ.

With 10 kΩ and 1 µF, τ is 10 ms, a useful scale for reset delays and switch debouncing. An open-drain line with a 10 kΩ pull-up and 100 pF of wiring capacitance has τ = 1 µs. Lowering the pull-up to 1 kΩ makes rising edges ten times faster, but then 3.3 mA flows from a 3.3 V supply whenever the output is low, which can push the low-level voltage above its specified limit if the driver's rated sink current is exceeded.

When a precise final value matters, the required number of time constants is ln(1/ε), where ε is the allowed fractional error. Settling to 1% takes about 4.6τ, and settling to half a least-significant bit of an N-bit converter takes (N+1)·ln2 time constants, roughly nine for 12 bits. This is why sample-and-hold acquisition times, reference-capacitor charging and filter delays are all specified as multiples of an RC product, and why a higher source resistance directly lengthens the time an analog-to-digital converter must wait.

faq.q: How do you calculate the time constant of an RC circuit?
faq.a: Multiply resistance in ohms by capacitance in farads to get τ in seconds. For example, 10 kΩ and 1 µF give 10 ms.

faq.q: Why is 5 time constants considered fully charged?
faq.a: After 5τ the remaining error is e^−5, less than 1%, which is negligible for most purposes. Precision circuits may need more, such as about 9τ for 12-bit accuracy.

faq.q: What is the relationship between time constant and cutoff frequency?
faq.a: For a first-order RC low-pass filter, the cutoff frequency is 1/(2πτ). A 1 ms time constant gives a cutoff of about 159 Hz.

ENOB(有効ビット数).desc: The real performance of an ADC, including noise and distortion (SINAD), expressed as the bit count of an ideal ADC. A 12-bit ADC with an ENOB of around 10 bits is not unusual.

about.p: An ideal N-bit ADC (analog-to-digital converter) still has quantization error, which behaves like noise with an rms value of LSB/√12. Comparing that with the rms value of a full-scale sine gives the ideal signal-to-noise ratio, 6.02N + 1.76 dB: about 74 dB at 12 bits and 98 dB at 16 bits. ENOB runs this formula backwards using the measured SINAD (signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio): ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02. A 12-bit converter measuring 62 dB SINAD therefore has an ENOB of about 10 bits, and a 16-bit part with 74 dB behaves like an ideal 12-bit one.

Real converters add several error sources on top of quantization. Thermal noise in the sampling switch, comparators and reference adds random noise. Nonlinearity in the transfer curve, from capacitor mismatch or amplifier gain error, creates harmonic distortion. Clock jitter turns timing uncertainty into amplitude error that grows with input frequency: the jitter-limited SNR is about −20·log10(2π·fin·σj), so 1 ps rms jitter caps SNR near 64 dB for a 100 MHz input. This is why ENOB usually falls as input frequency rises, and why the test frequency in a datasheet matters.

ENOB is normally measured with a spectrally pure sine wave close to full scale, capturing a record of samples and computing an FFT (fast Fourier transform). Everything that is not the fundamental, apart from DC, counts as noise and distortion in SINAD. If the test signal is smaller than full scale, SINAD drops roughly decibel for decibel, so some datasheets quote ENOB normalized to full scale. Related specs separate the pieces: SNR excludes harmonics, while SFDR (spurious-free dynamic range) is the gap between the signal and the largest single spur.

Resolution is just the number of output bits; ENOB is how many of them carry real information under specified conditions. The two can differ by several bits in fast converters. ENOB of a raw converter cannot meaningfully exceed its resolution, because quantization noise alone sets the ceiling, but oversampling and digital filtering can raise effective resolution within a narrower band: averaging four samples of uncorrelated noise improves SNR by about 6 dB, roughly one bit. ENOB also appears in common ADC figures of merit, which divide power by sampling rate times 2^ENOB.

faq.q: How do you calculate ENOB from SNR or SINAD?
faq.a: ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02, with SINAD in dB. Using SNR instead of SINAD gives a value that ignores distortion, so it overstates ENOB when harmonics are significant.

faq.q: Why is ENOB lower than the ADC's resolution?
faq.a: Thermal noise, distortion from nonlinearity, and clock jitter all add error beyond ideal quantization noise, so the converter performs like an ideal ADC with fewer bits.

faq.q: Why does ENOB decrease at high input frequencies?
faq.a: Clock jitter error grows in proportion to input frequency, and the sampling circuit's bandwidth and settling limits add distortion, so SINAD and ENOB fall as the input frequency rises.

DNL(微分非直線性).desc: The error in each code step width of an ADC relative to the ideal 1 LSB. When it reaches −1 LSB, a missing code occurs.

about.p: An ideal N-bit converter divides its full-scale range into 2ᴺ equal steps of 1 LSB (least significant bit). For an analog-to-digital converter (ADC), each output code should therefore correspond to an input interval exactly 1 LSB wide. Differential nonlinearity (DNL) is the error of each actual code width, expressed in LSB: DNL = (actual width − 1 LSB) / 1 LSB. A code 1.5 LSB wide has DNL = +0.5 LSB, and one 0.7 LSB wide has −0.3 LSB. For a digital-to-analog converter (DAC), the same idea applies to the size of each output step.

When a code's DNL reaches −1 LSB its width shrinks to zero, so that code never appears no matter how the input is swept: a missing code. A guarantee of "no missing codes" at a given resolution is therefore equivalent to DNL staying above −1 LSB. Large positive DNL, beyond about +1 LSB, wastes resolution because one wide code covers what should be several. For a DAC, DNL above −1 LSB guarantees monotonicity, meaning the output never falls when the code rises. Errors cluster at major carry transitions, such as 0111…1 to 1000…0, where mismatched binary-weighted elements swap.

about.h: DNL vs. INL, offset and gain error
about.p: Offset error shifts the whole transfer curve and gain error changes its slope; both are linear and can be removed with a two-point calibration. Integral nonlinearity (INL) is the maximum deviation of the actual curve from a straight line, drawn either through the endpoints or as a best fit, and at any code it equals the running sum of DNL up to that code. A converter can thus have small DNL everywhere yet large INL if small errors accumulate in one direction. INL shows up as harmonic distortion on large signals, while DNL governs small-step accuracy and missing codes; neither is fixed by simple calibration.

about.h: Measuring DNL and designing it down
about.p: The histogram, or code-density, method feeds the ADC a signal with known amplitude distribution and counts how often each code occurs. With a slow ramp or triangle every code should receive the same count, so each code's count divided by the average, minus one, gives its DNL; a sine wave is easier to make pure but needs correction for its peak-weighted distribution. Summing DNL gives INL. On the design side, thermometer-coded current-steering DACs and resistor-string DACs are monotonic by construction, and segmenting upper bits into equal-weight elements reduces DNL at major transitions.

faq.q: What does a DNL of ±0.5 LSB mean?
faq.a: Every code width lies between 0.5 and 1.5 LSB, so no code is missing and none is wider than one and a half ideal steps. It is a common specification for good-quality converters.

faq.q: What is the difference between DNL and INL?
faq.a: DNL is the error of each individual step width, while INL is how far the whole transfer curve wanders from a straight line. INL at a code is essentially the accumulated DNL up to that point.

faq.q: Does DNL greater than −1 LSB guarantee no missing codes?
faq.a: Yes. A missing code is precisely a code whose width has shrunk to zero, which corresponds to DNL = −1 LSB, so keeping every DNL above −1 LSB rules it out.

INL(積分非直線性).desc: The maximum deviation of an ADC's or DAC's actual transfer characteristic from the ideal straight line. It corresponds to the accumulated DNL.

about.h: How INL is measured against a line
about.p: For an analog-to-digital converter (ADC), INL is evaluated at each code transition (or code center) as the distance from a reference straight line, expressed in least significant bits (LSB); the datasheet figure is the worst case over all codes. The line can be the endpoint line, drawn through the first and last transitions, or a best-fit line chosen to minimize deviations. Both remove offset and gain error, so INL describes only the curve's shape. A best-fit specification usually gives a smaller number, so check which definition a datasheet uses before comparing parts.

Differential nonlinearity (DNL) is how far each individual step width differs from the ideal 1 LSB. INL is essentially the running sum of DNL, so many small errors of the same sign can add up to a large INL, while random errors tend to partially cancel. The two answer different questions: DNL governs missing codes, which occur when a code's width shrinks to zero (DNL of -1 LSB), whereas INL measures how far the overall transfer curve wanders from straight. A converter can have excellent DNL and still show a large bow.

about.h: Why INL is hard to calibrate away
about.p: Offset and gain errors are linear, so a two-point calibration at zero and a known voltage removes them. INL is a curvature or S-shape that varies code by code, and fixing it needs a multipoint lookup table or calibration built into the converter. Its typical sources are mismatch between capacitors or resistors that set the binary weights, amplifier nonlinearity and voltage-dependent components. On large signals, a bow-shaped error mainly creates second-harmonic distortion and an S-shaped error third-harmonic distortion, degrading total harmonic distortion in audio and measurement systems.

In the histogram method, an ADC receives a signal with a known amplitude distribution and the occurrences of each output code are counted. A slow ramp or triangle wave gives nearly equal counts per code; a sine wave is easier to generate cleanly but dwells near its peaks, so counts are corrected against its theoretical distribution. Each code's relative count gives its width, and hence DNL, and accumulating DNL gives INL. DAC INL is measured more directly, by stepping through codes and reading each output with a precise voltmeter.

faq.q: What is the difference between INL and DNL?
faq.a: DNL is the error in each individual step width relative to 1 LSB, while INL is the deviation of the whole transfer curve from a straight line. INL roughly equals the accumulated DNL.

faq.q: Can INL be removed by calibration?
faq.a: Not with a simple two-point calibration, which only fixes offset and gain. Correcting INL requires multipoint correction such as a lookup table, or calibration circuitry inside the converter.

faq.q: What is the difference between endpoint and best-fit INL?
faq.a: Endpoint INL is measured from a line through the first and last code transitions, while best-fit INL uses a line chosen to minimize the deviations. The best-fit value is usually smaller for the same device.

ミッシングコード.desc: A defect in which an ADC never outputs a particular code no matter how the input varies. It occurs when DNL reaches −1 LSB.

about.p: An ADC divides its input range into code bins separated by transition voltages. Ideally every bin is exactly 1 LSB wide. Differential nonlinearity (DNL) is each bin's actual width minus 1 LSB: a bin 1.5 LSB wide has DNL = +0.5 LSB. When DNL reaches −1 LSB the bin has zero width; its two transitions coincide and no input voltage produces it. That is a missing code. Because the bin widths must add up to the full range, a missing code is often accompanied by a neighboring code that is too wide.

Missing codes usually appear at major carry transitions, where many bits change at once, such as from 0111…1 to 1000…0. In a SAR (successive-approximation register) ADC, the internal capacitive DAC (digital-to-analog converter) sets the decision levels; if an upper-bit weight is slightly too small compared with the sum of the lower bits, the code just below that transition can vanish, while an oversized weight creates an extra-wide code instead. Pipeline and subranging ADCs are vulnerable to comparator offsets between stages, which is why they add redundancy and digital error correction to guarantee no missing codes.

Missing codes are found with a histogram test: a slow ramp or a sine wave is applied, many samples are collected, and the number of hits per code is counted. With a ramp, each code's count is proportional to its width; with a sine the counts are corrected for the sine's amplitude distribution. A code with zero hits is missing. Datasheets state a resolution with guaranteed no missing codes, for example 16-bit output with no missing codes at 16 or perhaps 15 bits, which is equivalent to guaranteeing DNL greater than −1 LSB at that resolution.

about.h: Missing codes vs. INL and DAC monotonicity
about.p: Integral nonlinearity (INL) is the accumulated deviation of the transfer curve from an ideal straight line; an ADC can have several LSB of INL and still produce every code, so INL does not directly determine missing codes. In a DAC the analogous concern is monotonicity: if DNL stays above −1 LSB, the output never decreases when the code increases. Missing codes matter most in control loops, where a skipped code acts as a sudden jump in loop gain that can cause limit cycling, and in measurement systems that build histograms of codes.

faq.q: What does 'no missing codes' mean on an ADC datasheet?
faq.a: It guarantees that every output code occurs for some input voltage at the stated resolution, which is equivalent to DNL staying greater than −1 LSB.

faq.q: Can INL cause missing codes?
faq.a: Not directly. INL is accumulated deviation from a straight line, while missing codes come from a single code bin shrinking to zero width, which is a DNL condition.

faq.q: How do you test an ADC for missing codes?
faq.a: Apply a slow ramp or a sine wave, collect a large number of samples, and build a histogram of output codes; any code with zero occurrences is missing.

フラッシュ型ADC.desc: The fastest type of ADC, which compares the input against many comparators at once. N bits need 2ᴺ − 1 comparators, so the circuit grows rapidly with resolution.

about.p: A flash analog-to-digital converter (ADC) uses a resistor ladder to generate 2ᴺ − 1 reference voltages spaced one least-significant bit (LSB) apart and gives each tap its own comparator. All comparators see the input at the same instant, so every comparator below the input level outputs 1 and every one above outputs 0. This pattern is a thermometer code, which an encoder converts to an N-bit binary word. The whole conversion takes one comparator decision plus encoding, which is why flash converters reach several gigasamples per second.

about.h: Why it scales poorly with resolution
about.p: Every extra bit doubles the number of comparators: 7 for 3 bits, 255 for 8 bits and 1023 for 10 bits. Area and power grow in proportion, and the combined input capacitance of all those comparators makes the converter hard to drive at high frequency. Accuracy also gets harder, because each comparator's offset must stay well below 1 LSB, and the LSB halves with every added bit. In practice, standalone flash converters are therefore limited to about 6–8 bits.

Comparator offsets and small timing mismatches can leave an isolated 0 inside the run of 1s in the thermometer code, an error called a bubble. A naive encoder can turn a bubble into a large output error, so practical designs add bubble-correction logic, for example by checking three adjacent comparators, or encode through Gray code to limit the damage. A comparator whose input sits almost exactly on its threshold may also take too long to resolve, a metastability problem that latches and pipelining help contain.

A successive-approximation (SAR) ADC uses one comparator and N clock cycles to perform a binary search, trading speed for low power and area. Pipelined and subranging ADCs split the conversion into stages, each containing a small flash sub-converter of a few bits, reaching higher resolution at high speed with far fewer comparators. Delta-sigma converters go further toward resolution and lower bandwidth. The flash converter thus survives both as the fastest standalone option at low resolution and as a building block inside other architectures.

faq.q: How many comparators does an N-bit flash ADC need?
faq.a: It needs 2ᴺ − 1 comparators, one for each threshold between adjacent codes. A 3-bit flash ADC uses 7, and an 8-bit one uses 255.

faq.q: Why are flash ADCs limited to low resolution?
faq.a: Comparator count, power, area and input capacitance double with every bit, while comparator offsets must shrink with the LSB. Beyond roughly 8 bits, pipelined or SAR architectures are more practical.

faq.q: What is a thermometer code in an ADC?
faq.a: It is the raw output of the comparator bank, a string of 1s up to the input level followed by 0s above it. An encoder converts it into a binary number.

パイプライン型ADC.desc: An ADC that splits conversion into stages, each resolving a few bits and passing the residue to the next, like an assembly line. It combines high speed with medium to high resolution.

サンプルホールド回路.desc: A circuit that captures (samples) the input voltage at an instant and holds it constant until AD conversion finishes. It is built from a switch and a capacitor.

about.p: The core of the circuit is an analog switch, usually a MOSFET or a CMOS transmission gate, in series with a capacitor, often followed by a buffer. In track mode the switch is closed and the capacitor voltage follows the input. At the sampling instant the switch opens, and the capacitor holds the voltage present at that moment while the converter works on it. Because the output follows the input during tracking, many circuits are more precisely called track-and-hold; in successive-approximation (SAR) ADCs the capacitive DAC array itself performs this function.

Most converters take some time to produce a result, and if the input moves by more than about half a least-significant bit (LSB) during that time, the code is wrong. A full-scale 10 kHz sine wave has a maximum slope of π × 10 kHz × full scale, so staying within half an LSB at 12 bits leaves only about 4 ns. A sample-and-hold freezes the input so the conversion time no longer matters; what matters instead is how precisely the switch opens, set by aperture delay and aperture jitter.

Acquisition time is the time needed in track mode for the capacitor to settle to the input within a specified error. It is RC settling through the source and switch resistance, so reaching half an LSB takes (N+1)·ln2 time constants, about nine at 12 bits; too short a time leaves part of the previous sample behind, causing crosstalk between multiplexed channels. In hold mode, leakage causes droop at a rate of leakage current divided by capacitance, and charge injection from the opening switch adds a small step called pedestal error.

The capacitor size is a trade-off. Sampling freezes thermal noise with an RMS value of √(kT/C), about 64 µV for 1 pF at room temperature, so higher resolution needs larger capacitance. A larger capacitor also reduces droop and the relative size of the pedestal step. On the other hand, it takes longer to charge, demands more current from the driving amplifier and widens the kickback seen by the source at each sampling instant. High-speed designs often use bootstrapped switches whose on-resistance stays nearly constant over the signal range.

faq.q: What is the difference between track-and-hold and sample-and-hold?
faq.a: A track-and-hold output follows the input continuously during the track phase, while a strict sample-and-hold takes a brief sample and presents only held values. In practice the terms are used almost interchangeably for ADC front ends.

faq.q: Why does high source impedance cause ADC errors?
faq.a: The hold capacitor must charge through the source resistance during the acquisition window. A larger resistance lengthens the RC time constant, so the capacitor may not settle fully and the reading carries an error or residue from the previous channel.

faq.q: What is aperture jitter?
faq.a: It is random variation in the exact moment the sampling switch opens. Because a fast-changing input moves during that uncertainty, jitter adds noise that grows with input frequency.

R-2Rラダー型DAC.desc: A DAC built from a ladder of only two resistor values, R and 2R. It needs few resistor types, and the resistor ratio does not grow as bits are added.

オーバーサンプリング.desc: Sampling at a rate well above what the signal requires (twice its bandwidth). It spreads quantization noise over a wider band and reduces noise in the signal band; it is the basis of delta-sigma ADCs.

about.h: Why sampling faster lowers in-band noise
about.p: Quantization adds an error whose total power is fixed by the step size, about one step squared over twelve, and is roughly spread evenly from DC to half the sampling frequency. The oversampling ratio (OSR) is the sampling rate divided by twice the signal bandwidth. Raising the OSR spreads the same noise over a wider band, so the portion inside the signal band falls by 10 log10(OSR) dB, and a digital filter removes the rest. Quadrupling the rate gives about 6 dB, or one extra bit. This assumes the error is noise-like rather than correlated with the signal, which sometimes requires added dither.

Plain oversampling is inefficient: one extra bit costs a fourfold rate increase and two bits cost sixteenfold. A delta-sigma (ΔΣ) modulator adds a feedback loop with integrators that pushes quantization noise toward high frequencies, away from the signal band. For a modulator of order L, each doubling of the OSR improves in-band signal-to-noise ratio by about 6L + 3 dB, roughly 9 dB for first order and 15 dB for second order. With OSRs in the tens to hundreds, even a 1-bit quantizer can deliver more than 20 bits of resolution at low frequencies, with little dependence on analog component matching.

An oversampling converter does not deliver its raw samples. A digital decimation filter removes the noise above the signal band and reduces the output rate to roughly the Nyquist rate, turning many coarse samples into fewer high-resolution ones. This filter accounts for the latency of ΔΣ converters, which makes them unsuitable for fast control loops and multiplexed channels. A side benefit is on the analog side: because the sampling rate is far above the signal band, frequencies that would alias are far away, so the analog anti-aliasing filter can be a simple, gentle one.

Nyquist-rate converters such as flash, pipelined and successive-approximation register (SAR) ADCs sample at about twice the signal bandwidth and convert each sample independently. A SAR ADC, for instance, resolves one bit per comparison, giving 8 to 18 bits at rates from kilosamples to tens of megasamples per second, which suits microcontrollers. Oversampling converters trade conversion speed for resolution and are found in audio, precision instrumentation and sensor readout. The same principle appears in software too: averaging many samples from a Nyquist-rate ADC and decimating can add resolution, provided enough noise is present to act as dither.

faq.q: How much does oversampling improve ADC resolution?
faq.a: Without noise shaping, each doubling of the sampling rate lowers in-band quantization noise by about 3 dB, so a fourfold increase gains roughly 6 dB, or one bit. Delta-sigma converters add noise shaping to gain much more per doubling.

faq.q: What is the difference between oversampling and noise shaping?
faq.a: Oversampling spreads a fixed amount of quantization noise over a wider band so less of it falls in the signal band. Noise shaping uses feedback to move the noise itself toward high frequencies, multiplying the benefit of oversampling.

faq.q: What is the oversampling ratio?
faq.a: The oversampling ratio is the sampling frequency divided by the Nyquist rate, that is, twice the signal bandwidth. Delta-sigma ADCs typically use ratios from tens to hundreds.

ノイズシェーピング.desc: A technique that uses a feedback loop to push quantization noise toward high frequencies, lowering noise in the signal band. Delta-sigma ADCs combine it with oversampling to achieve high resolution.

about.p: In a delta-sigma (ΔΣ) modulator, the quantizer sits inside a feedback loop with a loop filter, often one or more integrators. The loop subtracts the quantized output from the input and accumulates the error, so over time the average output follows the input. In the frequency domain the signal passes with little change, while quantization noise is multiplied by a noise transfer function that is small at low frequencies and large at high frequencies. For a first-order loop that function is 1 − z⁻¹, a simple high-pass characteristic.

about.h: Why oversampling alone is not enough
about.p: Quantization noise power is fixed by the quantizer step size. Sampling faster spreads it over a wider bandwidth, so the in-band portion falls by 10 log₁₀ of the oversampling ratio: about 3 dB, or half a bit, per doubling, and about 6 dB, one bit, for a fourfold rate increase. Gaining two bits this way needs 16 times the rate. With noise shaping, each doubling of the oversampling ratio improves in-band noise by roughly 9 dB for a first-order loop and 15 dB for a second-order loop, so higher-order shaping is far more efficient.

Noise pushed above the signal band is removed by a digital low-pass decimation filter, which also reduces the output rate to near the Nyquist rate. Even a 1-bit quantizer can then yield more than 20 bits of resolution at low frequencies, and since a two-level quantizer is inherently linear, accuracy depends little on matching of analog components. The costs are a modulator clock far above the signal bandwidth and the latency of the decimation filter, so ΔΣ ADCs suit audio, instrumentation and sensor readout rather than high-speed sampling.

Higher-order loops suppress in-band noise more strongly, but loops above second order with a single-bit quantizer can become unstable, so designers use multi-bit quantizers, carefully scaled loop filters or cascaded (MASH) structures. Noise shaping also appears outside ADCs. ΔΣ DACs drive audio outputs from few-level signals, fractional-N phase-locked loops use a ΔΣ modulator to shape the noise of a divider ratio that toggles between integers, and error diffusion dithering in image printing pushes quantization error to high spatial frequencies.

faq.q: What is the difference between oversampling and noise shaping?
faq.a: Oversampling spreads a fixed amount of quantization noise over a wider band, giving only about 3 dB per doubling of sample rate. Noise shaping uses feedback to move that noise out of the signal band, giving much larger improvement for the same oversampling ratio.

faq.q: Why do delta-sigma ADCs use a 1-bit quantizer?
faq.a: A two-level quantizer is inherently linear, so the converter's accuracy does not rely on precisely matched components; noise shaping and oversampling recover the resolution.

faq.q: Why are delta-sigma ADCs not used for very high-speed signals?
faq.a: They must sample many times faster than the signal bandwidth and need a decimation filter that adds latency, which limits them to low and moderate bandwidths.

ナイキスト周波数.desc: Half the sampling frequency. Components above it are folded back to lower frequencies when sampled (aliasing).

about.p: When a signal is sampled at rate fs, the samples cannot distinguish a frequency f from f plus or minus any multiple of fs. Every input component therefore appears somewhere between 0 and fs/2, the Nyquist frequency, folded back like paper on a crease at each multiple of fs/2. A 10 kHz sine sampled at 12 kHz, for instance, lies above the 6 kHz Nyquist frequency and shows up at |12 − 10| = 2 kHz. The samples are then identical to those of a genuine 2 kHz tone, and no later processing can separate them.

The two terms are easy to mix up. The Nyquist frequency is a property of the sampler: half the sampling rate, fs/2. The Nyquist rate is a property of the signal: twice its highest frequency component, the minimum sampling rate the sampling theorem requires. Sampling 20 kHz audio therefore needs a rate above 40 kHz. A component sitting exactly at fs/2 is ambiguous, because the sampled amplitude depends on its phase and may even be zero, which is why the theorem requires sampling strictly faster than twice the highest frequency.

Because aliasing cannot be undone, a low-pass anti-aliasing filter is placed before the ADC to remove content above the Nyquist frequency. Real filters need a transition band between passband and stopband, so the sampling rate is chosen with margin: audio CDs sample at 44.1 kHz for a 20 kHz band, leaving the region from 20 to 22.05 kHz for the filter's rolloff. Sampling much faster than necessary, called oversampling, pushes the Nyquist frequency far above the signal band, so a simple first- or second-order RC filter is enough and a digital filter does the sharp cutoff afterward.

about.h: Deliberate aliasing and the DAC side
about.p: Aliasing is not always an error. In undersampling, or bandpass sampling, a narrowband signal in a higher Nyquist zone, such as an intermediate-frequency carrier in a radio receiver, is deliberately sampled below twice its frequency so that it folds down to a convenient lower frequency. This works only with a bandpass filter in front and an ADC whose analog bandwidth and clock jitter are good enough for the high input frequency. On the output side, a DAC produces images at fs ± f, which a reconstruction low-pass filter removes.

faq.q: What is the difference between Nyquist frequency and Nyquist rate?
faq.a: The Nyquist frequency is half of the sampling rate, the highest frequency a given sampler can represent. The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency in the signal, the minimum sampling rate needed to capture it.

faq.q: How do you calculate the alias frequency?
faq.a: Find the multiple of the sampling rate nearest to the input frequency and take the absolute difference. For example, 10 kHz sampled at 12 kHz appears at |12 − 10| = 2 kHz.

faq.q: Why is CD audio sampled at 44.1 kHz instead of 40 kHz?
faq.a: Human hearing extends to about 20 kHz, and the extra margin above 40 kHz gives the anti-aliasing filter a transition band from 20 to 22.05 kHz, since no real filter can cut off instantly.

ジッタ.desc: Small fluctuations in the timing of clock or signal edges from their ideal positions. When sampling high-frequency signals, even slight jitter causes large voltage errors.

about.p: Jitter can be measured several ways: period jitter is the variation of each cycle's length, cycle-to-cycle jitter is the change between adjacent periods, and time interval error is each edge's deviation from an ideal clock. By origin, random jitter comes from thermal and other noise, is roughly Gaussian and unbounded, and is quoted as an rms value. Deterministic jitter is bounded and includes data-dependent jitter from intersymbol interference, periodic jitter from supply or crosstalk coupling, and duty-cycle distortion. In the frequency domain, the same phenomenon appears as phase noise, which can be integrated over a band to give rms jitter.

If the sampling instant shifts by Δt, the signal's change during Δt becomes error. A sine wave's slope grows with frequency, so jitter caps SNR at −20·log₁₀(2π·f·tj) regardless of resolution. Holding 70 dB on a 100 MHz input requires jitter below about 0.5 ps. That is why measured ENOB of a high-speed ADC drops at high input frequencies even when quantization noise, set by 6.02N + 1.76 dB, would allow more. In undersampling receivers, the jitter budget is set by the input frequency, not the lower sample rate, making it especially strict.

about.h: Jitter vs. skew in digital timing
about.p: Skew is the difference in clock arrival time between flip-flops at different locations, a mostly static, spatial effect set by the clock tree. Jitter is the variation of a clock edge over time at one point. Static timing analysis covers jitter with clock uncertainty, a margin subtracted from the available time; before clock tree synthesis it also includes expected skew. Period jitter matters for setup, where launch and capture are one cycle apart, but largely cancels in hold checks, where both sides use the same edge.

On a serial link, jitter narrows the horizontal opening of the eye diagram, leaving less time margin for the receiver's sampling point. Because random jitter is unbounded, total jitter is specified at a target bit error rate; at 10⁻¹² it is commonly estimated as the deterministic part plus about 14 times the rms random jitter. Clock and data recovery circuits track slow jitter but not fast jitter, so standards specify jitter tolerance masks. In a different role, jitter is a resource: on-chip true random number generators harvest ring-oscillator jitter as entropy.

faq.q: What is the difference between jitter and skew?
faq.a: Skew is a difference in clock arrival time between two locations, largely fixed by the clock tree. Jitter is the cycle-by-cycle variation of edge timing at a single point, caused mainly by noise.

faq.q: How does clock jitter limit ADC performance?
faq.a: Jitter turns timing error into voltage error proportional to the signal's slope, limiting SNR to about −20·log₁₀(2π·f·tj). For a 100 MHz input, about 0.5 ps rms jitter already caps SNR near 70 dB.

faq.q: What is the difference between random and deterministic jitter?
faq.a: Random jitter comes from noise, follows a roughly Gaussian distribution and is unbounded, so it is specified as an rms value. Deterministic jitter is bounded and has identifiable causes such as intersymbol interference, crosstalk or duty-cycle distortion.

プリチャージ.desc: Charging the bit lines to a set potential (half the supply voltage in DRAM, for example) before a read. In DRAM it also means closing the open row to prepare for activating the next one.

about.h: Precharge in the DRAM read path
about.p: Each DRAM sense amplifier sits on a pair of bit lines that are equalized to half the array supply, VDD/2, before a row is opened. When a word line turns on, the cell capacitor shares its charge with the much larger bit-line capacitance and nudges that line slightly up for a stored 1 or down for a 0. Starting from the midpoint makes the two cases symmetric, and the sense amplifier compares the disturbed line with its untouched partner, then drives both to full logic levels, restoring the cell in the process.

At the command level, precharge (PRE) closes the open row of a bank, letting the word line turn off and the bit lines return to VDD/2 so a different row can be activated. A typical access sequence is activate (ACT), wait tRCD, read or write, then precharge, and wait tRP before the next activate. The row cycle time tRC is tRAS plus tRP. Read and write commands can also carry auto-precharge, closing the row automatically, and a precharge-all command closes every bank, which is required before an all-bank refresh.

While a row stays open its data sits in the sense amplifiers, so another access to that row needs only a column command and the CAS latency. Accessing a different row in the same bank instead costs precharge, activation and column access, roughly tRP + tRCD + CL. Memory controllers therefore choose policies: leave pages open when accesses show locality, or precharge early when access is random. They also reorder queued requests to favor row hits. In DDR4 and DDR5 parts, tRP is usually a figure close to the CAS latency.

The word appears in other contexts too. SRAM bit lines are typically precharged high, usually to VDD, and a read is detected as one line discharging slightly. Dynamic (domino) logic precharges an internal node high during one clock phase and conditionally discharges it during the evaluate phase. In power electronics, precharging means charging a large DC-link capacitor bank slowly through a resistor to limit inrush current before closing the main contactor. The common idea is preparing a node at a known voltage before the real operation begins.

faq.q: What is tRP in RAM timings?
faq.a: tRP is the row precharge time, the minimum delay between a precharge command and the next activate to the same bank. It is usually the third number in timings written like CL-tRCD-tRP.

faq.q: Why are DRAM bit lines precharged to VDD/2?
faq.a: A cell can then pull the bit line either up or down by a similar small amount, so the sense amplifier sees symmetric signals for 1 and 0 against the midpoint reference.

faq.q: What is the difference between precharge and refresh in DRAM?
faq.a: Precharge closes an open row and resets the bit lines; refresh periodically reads and rewrites rows so their leaking charge is restored. A refresh internally involves activation and precharge of the rows it touches.

ロウハンマー.desc: A DRAM phenomenon in which repeatedly activating the same row in a short time drains charge from cells in neighboring rows and flips their data. Because it can be exploited in attacks, countermeasures are built into DRAMs and memory controllers.

about.p: DRAM cells store data as charge that slowly leaks, which is why each row is refreshed within a fixed window, typically 64 ms. Activating a row swings its word line, and repeated activation of the same aggressor row couples electrically into physically adjacent victim rows and promotes charge migration that speeds their leakage. If an aggressor is activated tens of thousands of times before the victims are refreshed, some victim cells lose enough charge to flip. Hammering the two rows on either side of a victim (double-sided) is more effective, and denser cells are more susceptible.

Rowhammer needs no special privileges, only ordinary memory reads issued fast enough that they reach DRAM instead of hitting in cache, for example by flushing or evicting the cache lines. After it was widely reported in 2014, researchers showed it could cross isolation boundaries: flipping bits in page-table entries to gain kernel privileges, corrupting data belonging to other processes or virtual machines, and triggering flips from sandboxed code. A hardware reliability flaw thus became a software-exploitable vulnerability.

Target row refresh (TRR) tracks frequently activated rows inside the DRAM or controller and refreshes their neighbors early. DDR5 adds refresh management (RFM), in which the controller counts activations and grants the DRAM extra time for such refreshes. Simply raising the refresh rate helps but costs bandwidth and power. Error-correcting code (ECC) can detect and fix single-bit flips, but several flips in one word can defeat common schemes. Research has shown that simple trackers can be bypassed by hammering many rows at once, so layered defenses are used.

Soft errors from alpha particles or cosmic-ray neutrons are random in time and location, and ECC with scrubbing is designed around that statistical behavior. Rowhammer is different: it is induced by a specific access pattern, it tends to recur in the same vulnerable cells, and an attacker can aim it at chosen addresses. That repeatability is what makes it dangerous, and why defenses focus on detecting suspicious activation patterns rather than only correcting errors after they occur.

faq.q: Does ECC memory stop Rowhammer?
faq.a: ECC makes attacks harder by correcting single-bit flips and detecting some multi-bit ones, but it is not a complete fix. Multiple flips in one word can escape correction, so ECC is combined with refresh-based mitigations.

faq.q: What is TRR in DRAM?
faq.a: Target row refresh is a mitigation that identifies rows activated unusually often and refreshes their neighboring rows before enough charge leaks to flip bits.

faq.q: Is Rowhammer still a problem with DDR5?
faq.a: DDR5 adds mechanisms such as refresh management to help, but cells keep shrinking and susceptibility generally rises with density. Mitigation is an ongoing effort shared between DRAM makers, controllers and system software.

DDR SDRAM.desc: Synchronous DRAM that transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges. Successive generations such as DDR4 and DDR5 have raised the data rate. It is the standard main memory of PCs and servers.

about.h: Double data rate and how it is counted
about.p: Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) takes commands on clock edges, which allows pipelined commands and burst transfers. DDR SDRAM additionally moves data on both rising and falling edges, so its speed is quoted in megatransfers per second (MT/s): DDR4-3200 uses a 1600 MHz clock to make 3200 MT/s. Peak bandwidth is the data rate times the bus width, so a 64-bit (8-byte) channel at 3200 MT/s delivers 25.6 GB/s. Real sustained bandwidth is lower because of row switches, refresh and bus turnarounds.

about.h: How the slow array keeps up
about.p: The memory array itself runs far slower than the interface. DDR bridges the gap with prefetch: each internal access fetches several words in parallel, which are then serialized onto the pins. The prefetch grew from 2n in DDR to 4n in DDR2 and 8n in DDR3 and DDR4, while DDR5 uses a burst length of 16. Data is captured with a data strobe (DQS) that travels alongside the data lines, so timing references and data experience similar delays, a source-synchronous scheme.

Each generation raised data rates and lowered supply voltage to save power: roughly 2.5 V for DDR, 1.8 V for DDR2, 1.5 V for DDR3, 1.2 V for DDR4 and 1.1 V for DDR5, where parts exceed 6400 MT/s. DDR5 also splits each module into two independent 32-bit subchannels, moves voltage regulation onto the module with a power-management IC, and adds on-die error correction inside the chips. Generations are not interchangeable: modules differ in key position, signaling and voltage.

about.h: DDR vs. LPDDR, GDDR and HBM
about.p: Standard DDR is optimized for capacity and cost on removable modules in PCs and servers. LPDDR targets phones and laptops with low-power states and is usually soldered next to the processor. GDDR serves graphics cards with very high per-pin data rates on point-to-point links, trading capacity for bandwidth. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks DRAM dies with through-silicon vias and connects them through a very wide interface on an interposer. All share the same DRAM cell and row-column access principles.

faq.q: Why is DDR4-3200 called 3200 when the clock is 1600 MHz?
faq.a: Data is transferred on both clock edges, so 1600 MHz yields 3200 million transfers per second. The number in the name is the data rate in MT/s, not the clock frequency.

faq.q: How do you calculate DDR memory bandwidth?
faq.a: Multiply the data rate in MT/s by the bus width in bytes and by the number of channels. One 64-bit channel of DDR4-3200 gives 3200 × 8 = 25,600 MB/s, or 25.6 GB/s peak.

faq.q: Can DDR5 memory be used in a DDR4 slot?
faq.a: No. The modules have different key notch positions, pinouts and supply arrangements, so they neither fit nor work in each other's slots.

LPDDR.desc: Short for low-power DDR: a DRAM standard for smartphones and laptops with lower supply voltages and enhanced power-saving features.

about.h: Where the power savings come from
about.p: LPDDR (low-power double data rate) DRAM saves energy in several ways. Its supply and I/O voltages are lower than those of desktop DDR, and dynamic power in the interface scales with the square of voltage. When the device is idle, deep low-power states switch off most internal circuitry, partial-array self-refresh refreshes only the banks that hold data, and temperature-compensated self-refresh lengthens the refresh interval when the chip is cool, because DRAM cells leak more slowly at low temperature. Phones spend most of their time idle, so these standby features matter as much as active power.

LPDDR is designed for short point-to-point links. The DRAM is stacked on top of the application processor (package-on-package, PoP) or soldered right next to it, so traces are only millimetres long and need little drive strength. The interface is split into narrow channels, 16 bits wide since LPDDR4, which lets a processor access several channels independently. Because the memory is soldered rather than plugged into a DIMM socket, capacity in an LPDDR-based laptop or phone is normally fixed at purchase and cannot be upgraded later.

about.h: LPDDR vs. DDR, GDDR and HBM
about.p: All four are DRAM standards defined by JEDEC, but they optimize different things. Standard DDR on DIMMs prioritizes capacity and upgradability for desktops and servers. LPDDR prioritizes energy per bit and standby power for battery-powered devices, while still reaching high data rates; LPDDR5X runs at 8533 MT/s and beyond. GDDR pushes per-pin speed for graphics cards, and HBM stacks dies with a very wide interface on a silicon interposer for maximum bandwidth. LPDDR generation numbers do not map one-to-one onto DDR: LPDDR4 and DDR4 use different interfaces and protocols.

faq.q: What does LPDDR stand for?
faq.a: LPDDR stands for low-power double data rate, a family of mobile DRAM standards published by JEDEC. Double data rate means data is transferred on both edges of the clock.

faq.q: Can LPDDR memory be upgraded?
faq.a: Usually not. LPDDR is soldered to the board or stacked on the processor package to keep wiring short, so the installed capacity is fixed when the device is built.

faq.q: Is LPDDR slower than DDR?
faq.a: Not necessarily; recent LPDDR generations reach data rates comparable to or higher than desktop DDR. The main trade-offs are capacity, which is limited by the soldered packages, and the lack of upgradeable modules.

CASレイテンシ.desc: The number of clock cycles in DRAM from a read command (specifying the column address) until data appears at the output, abbreviated CL. Smaller values mean a faster response.

about.p: CAS stands for column address strobe. A DRAM read first activates a row, copying it into the sense amplifiers, and then issues a read command carrying the column address. The CAS latency (CL) is the number of clock cycles from that read command until the first data appears at the output. After that, the rest of the burst follows on successive clock edges. Because CL is counted in cycles, the actual delay in nanoseconds is CL multiplied by the clock period, and a smaller CL is faster only when the clock speed is the same.

For DDR memory the data rate is twice the clock frequency, so DDR4-3200 transfers 3200 million times per second on a 1600 MHz clock with a period of 0.625 ns. CL22 then corresponds to 22 × 0.625 ns ≈ 13.75 ns. DDR3-1600 runs an 800 MHz clock with a 1.25 ns period, so CL11 is also about 13.75 ns. The larger CL number of the newer generation hides an essentially unchanged delay, because the speed of the memory cell array improves little between generations while the interface clock keeps rising.

about.h: Where CL fits among DRAM timings
about.p: CL is only one part of an access. If the needed row is not open, the controller must first precharge the bank to close the old row (tRP), then activate the new one and wait the RAS-to-CAS delay (tRCD) before issuing the read, and only then wait CL. Timings are often quoted together, such as CL-tRCD-tRP. A page hit, where the row is already open in the sense amplifiers, needs only CL, so memory controllers reorder requests to group accesses to the same row and increase the fraction of hits.

CAS latency describes how long the first word takes, while bandwidth describes how fast data streams once it starts. Faster memory generations mainly raise bandwidth by increasing the data rate and burst length; first-word latency in nanoseconds has stayed in a similar range. Workloads that stream large blocks benefit from bandwidth, while pointer chasing and random accesses that miss in the processor's caches are more sensitive to latency. Comparing modules therefore requires converting CL to nanoseconds and also considering the other timings, not just the CL number.

faq.q: What does CAS latency mean for RAM?
faq.a: CAS latency is the number of memory clock cycles between a read command with a column address and the first data output. Multiplying it by the clock period gives the actual delay in nanoseconds.

faq.q: Is lower CAS latency always faster?
