faq.a: Only at the same clock speed. A higher-frequency module with a larger CL can have the same or lower latency in nanoseconds, so CL must be converted using the clock period before comparing.

faq.q: Why are CAS latency numbers larger for newer DDR generations?
faq.a: The DRAM cell array's response time in nanoseconds has changed little, while the clock period keeps shrinking. More clock cycles are therefore needed to cover about the same delay.

バンク.desc: One of several independently operating sections inside a DRAM. Overlapping activation and access across different banks raises effective performance.

about.h: Why DRAM is split into banks
about.p: Accessing DRAM involves several slow steps. An activate command opens a row, copying it into the bank's sense amplifiers, often called the row buffer; reads and writes then select columns from that row; finally a precharge closes the row and readies the bit lines. Activation and precharge each take over ten nanoseconds. A bank is an independent array with its own row buffer, so while one bank is activating or precharging, another can be transferring data. Interleaving accesses across banks hides these latencies and keeps the data bus busy.

DDR4 devices have 16 banks arranged in four bank groups, and DDR5 doubles this to 32. Bank groups add a timing rule: consecutive column accesses to different groups can be issued closer together than accesses within the same group, so controllers spread traffic across groups. Each bank can hold a different open row, which also raises the chance that a request hits an already-open row (a page hit) instead of paying for another activate. A bank is distinct from a rank, which is a set of chips sharing a chip select on a module.

DRAM cells leak, so every row must typically be refreshed within 64 ms. A bank under refresh cannot serve accesses, and as capacity grows each refresh command covers more rows and lasts longer, a time known as tRFC. For 16 Gbit-class devices, refresh can cost from several percent to about 10% of performance, along with extra power. Per-bank refresh reduces the impact by refreshing one bank while the others remain available, and research has explored refreshing rows with long retention less often.

The word also appears in GPU programming with a related idea. CUDA shared memory is divided into 32 banks assigned in rotation every 4 bytes, and each bank serves one address per access. If the 32 threads of a warp hit distinct banks, the access completes at once; if several threads hit different addresses in one bank, the accesses are serialized, a bank conflict. Reading down a column of a 32 × 32 float tile puts every element in one bank; padding the tile to 32 × 33 shifts each row by one bank and removes the conflict.

faq.q: How many banks does DDR5 have?
faq.a: DDR5 devices have 32 banks, organized into bank groups, compared with 16 banks in four bank groups for DDR4.

faq.q: What is the difference between a DRAM bank and a rank?
faq.a: A bank is an independently operating array inside a single DRAM chip. A rank is a set of chips on a module that share a chip select and together supply the full data width, and each chip in it contains its own banks.

faq.q: What is a shared memory bank conflict?
faq.a: It occurs when threads in a GPU warp access different addresses that map to the same shared-memory bank, forcing the hardware to serialize the accesses. Padding arrays or changing the access pattern usually avoids it; all threads reading the same address is a broadcast and not a conflict.

ECC(誤り訂正符号).desc: A scheme that adds redundant bits to data so that bit errors can be detected and corrected on readout. It is used in server memory, flash memory and inside DDR5 chips, among others.

about.p: A single parity bit detects an odd number of flipped bits but cannot locate the error, and two flips cancel out. Hamming codes add several parity bits, each covering an overlapping subset of data bits; on readout the recomputed checks form a syndrome that points to a single erroneous bit so it can be flipped back. One more overall parity bit distinguishes a correctable single error from a detected-only double error: SECDED (single error correction, double error detection). Protecting 64 data bits takes 8 check bits, giving the familiar 72-bit memory word.

ECC modules carry extra chips for the check bits: nine x8 chips form a 72-bit rank, and in DDR5 each 32-bit subchannel becomes 40 bits wide. The memory controller encodes on write and checks on read. DDR5 also adds on-die ECC, 8 check bits per 128 data bits inside each die, but it is invisible outside the chip and does not cover transfer errors, so it does not replace system ECC. Chipkill-type codes survive a whole failed chip, and controllers commonly scrub memory so single-bit errors are fixed before a second accumulates.

The classic target is the soft error: alpha particles from package materials or cosmic-ray neutrons generate charge that flips a bit without damaging the device, and neutron flux grows strongly with altitude. ECC also absorbs cells with variable retention time, occasional Rowhammer flips and stochastic STT-MRAM write failures. An error beyond the code's capability, such as a 2-bit error under SECDED, is reported as uncorrectable, and the system discards the data or moves to a safe state. Logging corrected errors helps spot failing parts early.

NAND flash has much higher raw bit error rates, rising with program/erase wear and with more bits per cell, so controllers use stronger codes such as BCH or LDPC that correct many bits per block; Gray-coded state assignments keep a misread into a neighbouring state to one bit. Serial links use forward error correction (FEC) when signalling leaves little margin, as with PAM4 in PCI Express 6.0. In automotive chips the ECC logic is itself a safety mechanism, and a fault in it is a latent fault that BIST must find.

faq.q: What is the difference between ECC memory and DDR5 on-die ECC?
faq.a: On-die ECC corrects single-bit errors inside each DRAM chip and outputs only corrected data, while ECC memory adds extra chips so the memory controller checks the whole word, including errors that occur on the bus. Servers rely on the latter even with DDR5.

faq.q: Can SECDED ECC correct a 2-bit error?
faq.a: No. It corrects any single-bit error and detects, but cannot correct, a 2-bit error, which is reported as uncorrectable. Stronger symbol-based codes such as Chipkill are needed to survive multi-bit failures from one chip.

faq.q: How many check bits does ECC memory use for 64 bits of data?
faq.a: Standard SECDED uses 8 check bits per 64 data bits, so each word is 72 bits wide. That is why an ECC module built from x8 chips has nine chips per rank instead of eight.

冗長救済.desc: Replacing rows or columns that contain defective memory cells with spare rows or columns prepared in advance. The defect locations are found by testing and the switch is made with fuses or similar. It greatly improves yield.

about.p: A DRAM die contains billions of cells, and the chance that every one of them is defect-free is small. Without repair, a single bad cell or a shorted word line would scrap the whole chip, and yields of high-capacity memory would be untenable. Designers therefore add spare rows and spare columns to each memory array. Redundancy repair replaces rows or columns that contain defective cells with these spares, so a die with a limited number of faults can still be shipped as a fully working part.

At wafer test, memory testers write and read patterns across all addresses and build a fail bit map showing which bits failed. A redundancy analysis program then decides how to cover every failing bit with the available spare rows and columns; a single failing bit can be fixed by either, while a failing line needs a matching spare line. The chosen addresses are stored in fuses, either laser-cut metal fuses or electrically programmed fuses and antifuses. On each access, comparators check the incoming address against the stored ones and redirect matches to a spare.

Laser fuses can only be cut at wafer level, but electrically programmable elements allow fixes later. Post-package repair (PPR) lets a failing row discovered after assembly be remapped to a spare, and some memory standards let a system perform this in the field. This catches defects introduced by packaging stress or found in burn-in. The design must balance spare count against cost: each spare row or column takes area, and the address comparison adds a small delay to the access path.

about.h: Fail bit maps as a diagnostic
about.p: The fail bit map is useful beyond repair. The shape of the failures hints at their physical cause: isolated single bits suggest weak cells or point defects, complete rows or columns suggest broken or shorted word lines or bit lines, and clusters suggest particles or local process problems. Failure analysis engineers correlate these signatures with inline inspection data to find the responsible process step. The same redundancy approach is used in large SRAM caches on processors, where spare rows or columns recover yield on dies with large memory area.

faq.q: How does DRAM redundancy repair work?
faq.a: Testing identifies the addresses of failing rows or columns, those addresses are stored in fuses or antifuses, and on-chip comparators redirect any access to them to built-in spare rows or columns.

faq.q: What is post-package repair (PPR)?
faq.a: Post-package repair is a feature that lets a failing DRAM row be remapped to a spare row after the chip is packaged, using electrically programmable elements instead of wafer-level laser fuses.

faq.q: What is a fail bit map?
faq.a: A fail bit map is a map of which memory bits failed at which addresses; it is used to plan redundancy repair and to infer the physical cause of defects from the failure pattern.

メモリウォール.desc: The problem that memory bandwidth and latency improve more slowly than processor performance, limiting overall performance. HBM, larger caches and advanced packaging are used to address it.

about.p: Processor performance grew quickly for decades, first through clock speed and later through more cores and wider vector units, while DRAM was optimized mainly for density and cost per bit. DRAM access latency has stayed in the tens of nanoseconds, so at clock rates of several gigahertz a miss to main memory costs hundreds of cycles. The phrase memory wall was popularized in the mid-1990s to warn that this widening gap, not the processor core, would ultimately limit system performance.

The problem has two faces. Latency hurts code with dependent accesses, such as following pointers through a linked structure, where each load must finish before the next address is known. Bandwidth hurts streaming code that touches lots of data per operation. The roofline model captures the bandwidth side: attainable performance is the lower of peak compute and memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity, the number of operations performed per byte moved. Code with low arithmetic intensity never reaches peak compute, however many cores are available.

about.h: Why AI workloads hit it hard
about.p: Large neural networks hold billions of weights, and generating one token at small batch sizes reads essentially every weight once while doing only a multiply and an add with each. With 16-bit weights that is about one operation per byte, while modern accelerators can perform hundreds of operations for each byte their memory delivers. The compute units therefore wait on memory. Batching requests, quantizing weights to fewer bits and keeping data on chip all raise arithmetic intensity or cut the bytes moved.

Multilevel caches exploit locality so most accesses never reach DRAM, and hardware prefetchers fetch data before it is requested. Out-of-order cores and GPUs with thousands of threads keep many misses in flight to hide latency. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) placed beside the processor with advanced packaging, and large caches stacked on the die, raise bandwidth directly. Processing-in-memory and near-memory computing take the opposite route, moving some computation to where the data already lives instead of moving the data.

faq.q: Is the memory wall about latency or bandwidth?
faq.a: Both. Latency limits programs that make dependent memory accesses, while bandwidth limits programs that stream large amounts of data relative to the computation they do.

faq.q: How does HBM help with the memory wall?
faq.a: HBM stacks DRAM dies next to the processor and uses a very wide interface, giving much higher bandwidth than conventional DIMMs. It mainly attacks the bandwidth side; latency stays in the same tens-of-nanoseconds range.

faq.q: Why are large language models memory-bound?
faq.a: During generation at small batch sizes, each weight is fetched from memory and used for only a couple of operations. The accelerator can compute far faster than memory can supply the weights.

DIMM.desc: A memory module that mounts several DRAM chips on a small board so it can be plugged into a slot in a PC or server.

about.h: Structure and the origin of the name
about.p: A DIMM (dual inline memory module) is a memory module that mounts several DRAM chips on a long, narrow printed circuit board so it can be plugged into a motherboard slot. On the earlier SIMM, the contacts on the front and back of the board were connected to the same signals; on a DIMM they carry different signals, hence 'dual'. Besides the DRAM chips, the board carries a small nonvolatile memory called the SPD, which records capacity, speed, timing and other information that the motherboard reads at startup to configure the memory. The position of the notch in the contact edge differs by generation, so a module of the wrong generation cannot be inserted by mistake.

Ordinary DIMMs for desktop PCs do not buffer signals and are also called UDIMMs (unbuffered DIMMs). Laptops use the shorter, smaller SO-DIMM. Servers use RDIMMs, which re-drive command and address signals through a register so that many chips can be driven, and LRDIMMs, which also buffer the data signals, allowing larger capacities. Modules with error correction (ECC) use a 72-bit width: 64 data bits plus 8 ECC bits. In DDR5, each module is split into two independent 32-bit subchannels, and the power circuitry (PMIC) is also mounted on the module.

A DIMM's capacity is set by the capacity and number of DRAM chips on it. For example, a module with eight 16 Gb chips of 8-bit data width (x8) holds 16 Gb × 8 = 128 Gb = 16 GB. A set of chips that together provide the 64-bit data width is called a rank, and adding ranks increases capacity. Peak bandwidth is data rate times data width: a DDR4-3200 DIMM gives 3200 MT/s × 8 bytes = 25.6 GB/s, and DDR5-4800 gives 38.4 GB/s. Populating a DIMM on each of the CPU's memory channels multiplies bandwidth by the number of channels.

DIMMs of different generations, such as DDR4 and DDR5, differ in notch position, voltage and signaling and are not compatible. Even within a generation, RDIMMs and UDIMMs cannot be mixed, and whether ECC works depends on CPU and motherboard support. When DIMMs of different speeds are mixed, they generally run at the speed of the slowest. Installing more DIMMs on one channel increases the signal load and can lower the maximum supported speed. For laptops, JEDEC has also standardized CAMM2, a new thin module form factor that is easier to run at high speed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a DIMM and an SO-DIMM?
faq.a: Both are plug-in memory modules carrying DRAM chips. A DIMM is the longer type for desktop PCs and servers, and an SO-DIMM (small outline DIMM) is the shorter type for laptops and small PCs. They differ in pin count and notch position and do not fit each other's slots.

faq.q: What is the difference between an RDIMM and a UDIMM?
faq.a: An RDIMM re-drives command and address signals through a register on the module before distributing them to the DRAM chips, so it can drive many chips reliably and is used in high-capacity servers. A UDIMM has no buffer and is mainly used in PCs. They are electrically different and cannot be mixed in the same system.

faq.q: What does 'dual' in DIMM mean?
faq.a: It means the contacts on the front and back of the board each carry separate signals. On the previous generation, the SIMM (single inline memory module), the front and back contacts were connected to the same signals. It is unrelated to dual-channel memory, which means using two memory channels.

3D NAND.desc: NAND flash in which memory cells are stacked vertically in many layers to increase capacity. It was introduced to get past the limits of planar scaling, and layer counts now exceed 200.

about.h: From planar cells to vertical strings
about.p: Planar NAND flash ran into limits around the 15 nm generation: each cell held only a handful of stored electrons, and coupling between neighboring cells grew severe. 3D NAND, which entered mass production around 2013 with 24 layers, turns the cell string vertical instead. A thick stack of alternating insulating and word-line layers is deposited, and cylindrical memory holes about 100 nm wide are etched through it, several micrometers deep. The channel runs up the hole, each layer forms the gate of one cell around it, and capacity grows by adding layers rather than by shrinking cells. Products now exceed 200 layers.

Most 3D NAND stores charge in a charge-trap layer of silicon nitride rather than a conductive floating gate. A silicon oxide, nitride, oxide (ONO) stack is deposited conformally on the hole wall, followed by a thin polysilicon channel. Charge stays localized in nitride traps, so a single defect cannot drain the whole cell and interference with neighbors is low. In stacks built from alternating oxide and nitride, the sacrificial nitride is later removed through slits with hot phosphoric acid, and the cavities are filled with tungsten by CVD from WF6 to form the word lines.

about.h: Process challenges at high layer counts
about.p: Memory holes have aspect ratios of 50 to 100, so etching them is the defining challenge. Amorphous-carbon hard masks several micrometers thick are needed, and holes tend to bow, twist or taper; cryogenic etching is being adopted to keep them straight and fast. Very tall stacks are split into two or more decks whose holes are aligned and joined, known as string stacking. Contacting hundreds of word lines requires a staircase at the array edge, formed by repeated etch and resist trim. Measuring hole shapes without cross-sectioning has prompted X-ray scattering methods such as CD-SAXS.

about.h: Putting the periphery under the array
about.p: Sense amplifiers, page buffers and other peripheral circuits originally sat beside the cell array. Building them first and stacking the array on top, in approaches called CMOS under Array or Periphery under Cell, saves roughly 20 to 30% of die area, though the periphery must then survive the thermal steps of array formation. Another approach fabricates the array and the peripheral CMOS on separate wafers and bonds them, letting each use its own optimized process and allowing parallel processing. Combined with three or four bits per cell (TLC or QLC), these steps drive cost per bit down.

faq.q: What is the difference between 2D NAND and 3D NAND?
faq.a: 2D (planar) NAND places cells side by side on the wafer surface and gains density by shrinking them. 3D NAND stacks cells vertically along channels in deep holes and gains density by adding layers, which avoids the interference and charge-count limits of tiny planar cells.

faq.q: How many layers does 3D NAND have?
faq.a: The first products had 24 layers, and mass-production devices now exceed 200 layers, with higher counts appearing. Very tall stacks are built in two or more decks joined together.

faq.q: Why does 3D NAND use charge-trap cells?
faq.a: A silicon nitride charge-trap layer can be deposited continuously on the walls of the memory holes, and its localized charge is less vulnerable to a single oxide defect and causes less interference. These traits suit vertically stacked strings better than conductive floating gates.

フローティングゲート.desc: An electrode in a flash memory cell that is completely surrounded by insulator. Storing electrons on it shifts the transistor's threshold voltage, so data is kept even without power.

about.p: A floating-gate flash cell is a MOSFET with two stacked gates. The lower one, the floating gate, is usually polysilicon and is completely isolated: a thin tunnel oxide separates it from the channel, and an inter-poly dielectric separates it from the control gate above. The inter-poly dielectric is typically an ONO (oxide/nitride/oxide) stack, because oxide grown thermally on doped polysilicon is rough and has lower breakdown strength. The control gate couples to the floating gate capacitively, so the voltage on the floating gate is a fraction of the control-gate voltage set by the coupling ratio.

about.h: How stored charge shifts the threshold
about.p: Electrons on the floating gate are negative charge that cancels part of the control-gate voltage, so a higher voltage is needed to invert the channel and the threshold voltage rises. Programming adds electrons and raises the threshold; erasing removes them and lowers it. Reading applies a fixed voltage between the two threshold levels and checks whether current flows. In NAND, the erased, low-threshold state is conventionally read as 1, so erased flash reads as 0xFF. Multi-level cells divide the threshold window into more levels to store several bits per cell.

Because the floating gate has no electrical contact, charge must cross an insulator. Fowler-Nordheim tunneling, driven by a strong field across the tunnel oxide at a high voltage applied to the control gate or substrate, is used for both program and erase in NAND. NOR flash typically programs by channel hot-electron injection, where electrons accelerated near the drain gain enough energy to surmount the oxide barrier. Since the surrounding insulators are thick enough to block leakage at normal voltages, the charge is retained for around ten years without power. Repeated cycling gradually damages the tunnel oxide, limiting endurance.

A conductive floating gate shares its charge across the whole electrode, so a single leakage path through a defect in the tunnel oxide can drain all of it, and closely packed floating gates couple capacitively to their neighbors. Charge-trap cells instead store electrons in traps within an insulating silicon nitride layer, where the charge stays localized. The SiO2/SiN/SiO2 stack can be deposited continuously on the walls of vertical channel holes, which is why charge trapping is widely used in 3D NAND, while floating gates dominated planar flash.

faq.q: Why does a floating gate keep data without power?
faq.a: The floating gate is completely surrounded by insulators that electrons cannot cross at normal operating voltages, so injected charge stays trapped for years. Only high programming or erase voltages make it tunnel through the oxide.

faq.q: What happens to the threshold voltage when a flash cell is programmed?
faq.a: Programming adds electrons to the floating gate, and their negative charge raises the threshold voltage. Erasing removes them and lowers the threshold again.

faq.q: What is the difference between a floating gate and a charge trap?
faq.a: A floating gate is a conductive polysilicon electrode that holds charge spread across it, while a charge-trap cell stores charge in localized traps within an insulating silicon nitride layer. Charge trapping is more tolerant of single oxide defects and is easier to build in 3D NAND.

電荷トラップ型セル.desc: A flash memory cell that stores electrons in traps within an insulating film such as silicon nitride instead of in a floating gate. It is mainly used in 3D NAND.

FNトンネル電流(ファウラー・ノルドハイム).desc: Current that flows when a strong electric field lets electrons tunnel through the triangular barrier of a thin insulator. It is used to program and erase NAND flash.

ガベージコレクション.desc: In an SSD, moving the still-valid data out of blocks that contain invalid data and then erasing those blocks to create free space.

about.p: NAND flash reads and programs in pages of around 16 KB but can erase only whole blocks of hundreds of pages, several to tens of megabytes, because erasure applies high voltage to an entire well. A page cannot be overwritten in place. When the host updates data, the SSD controller writes the new version to a free page, updates its logical-to-physical map in the flash translation layer (FTL), and marks the old page invalid. Over time blocks fill with a mix of valid and invalid pages, and free blocks run out unless space is reclaimed.

The controller selects victim blocks, typically those with the most invalid pages because they need the least copying. It copies the remaining valid pages to another block, updates the mapping, erases the victim and returns it to the free pool. Ideally this runs in the background during idle time; if free blocks are exhausted it must run in the foreground, stalling host writes. The fuller the drive, the fewer invalid pages each victim holds, so more copying is needed per block reclaimed and write performance drops.

Every valid page moved during collection is an extra write the host never asked for. The write amplification factor (WAF) is the ratio of data written to flash to data written by the host, and under small random writes it can reach several times. Because each NAND block tolerates only a limited number of program/erase cycles, a high WAF shortens drive life as well as consuming bandwidth. Garbage collection is distinct from wear leveling, which spreads erase cycles evenly across blocks, though controllers coordinate the two.

Three levers reduce the burden. TRIM, or Deallocate in NVMe, lets the operating system report deleted ranges, so the drive can treat those pages as invalid instead of copying them. Over-provisioning installs more flash than the user-visible capacity; 512 GiB of NAND sold as a 480 GB drive leaves about 14% spare, giving collection room to work, and enterprise drives reserve more. Data compression in some controllers reduces the volume written. Together they lower WAF, stabilize write speed and extend endurance.

faq.q: What is the difference between TRIM and garbage collection?
faq.a: TRIM is a command from the operating system telling the SSD which logical blocks are no longer in use. Garbage collection is the drive's internal process of copying valid data and erasing blocks; TRIM makes it cheaper by marking deleted data invalid so it is not copied.

faq.q: Why does an SSD slow down when it is nearly full?
faq.a: With little free space, victim blocks still hold many valid pages, so garbage collection must copy more data per erased block and often runs in the foreground, increasing write amplification and stalling host writes.

faq.q: Is SSD garbage collection the same as garbage collection in programming languages?
faq.a: Only by analogy. Language runtimes reclaim unreachable memory objects, while an SSD reclaims flash blocks by relocating valid pages and erasing the rest, a requirement imposed by NAND's block-level erase.

TRIM.desc: A command by which the operating system tells an SSD which areas belong to deleted files. Knowing which data is no longer needed makes garbage collection more efficient.

about.h: Why an SSD needs to be told
about.p: An SSD's controller runs a flash translation layer (FTL) that maps the logical block addresses used by the operating system to physical flash pages. Deleting a file only updates the file system's own bookkeeping; the SSD receives no write and still considers the old data valid. During garbage collection, the drive therefore keeps copying data that nobody will ever read again, wasting time and flash endurance. TRIM closes this information gap: the operating system sends the address ranges that no longer hold useful data, so the drive can stop preserving them.

On receiving TRIM, the FTL removes the mapping for those logical addresses and marks the corresponding physical pages invalid. The data is not necessarily erased immediately; erasure happens later, block by block, when garbage collection reclaims the space. Blocks containing mostly invalid pages can then be erased with little or no copying, which reduces write amplification and keeps write performance steady as the drive fills. Depending on the drive, reading a trimmed address afterward may return zeros or undefined data, so deleted files on SSDs are typically much harder to recover than on hard disks.

about.h: Interfaces and how it is issued
about.p: TRIM is the name of the ATA (SATA) command option; SCSI and SAS systems use UNMAP, and NVMe provides the same function through the Deallocate option of its Dataset Management command. Operating systems issue it either continuously, sending a discard as each file is deleted, or in periodic batches, which avoids slowing down deletions. Layers between the file system and the drive, such as some RAID or disk-encryption setups and virtual disks, must pass the command through for it to reach the flash, and may need to be configured to do so.

TRIM is only a hint from the host; garbage collection is the drive's internal process that actually relocates valid data and erases blocks, and it runs with or without TRIM. In semiconductor fabrication, resist trimming is an unrelated plasma process that thins resist lines below the exposure limit, and laser trimming adjusts resistor values in analog chips. Conventional hard disks overwrite data in place and do not need TRIM, although thin-provisioned storage uses the equivalent unmap command to reclaim space.

faq.q: Does TRIM erase data immediately?
faq.a: Not necessarily. TRIM marks the data as invalid and removes its address mapping; the physical erase happens later when garbage collection reclaims the block, though reads of trimmed addresses may already return zeros.

faq.q: Do NVMe SSDs support TRIM?
faq.a: Yes, through the Deallocate option of the NVMe Dataset Management command, which does the same job; operating systems usually still call it TRIM or discard.

faq.q: Is TRIM needed on a hard disk drive?
faq.a: Conventional hard drives can overwrite sectors in place, so they do not benefit from TRIM; it matters for flash storage, where blocks must be erased before reuse.

リードディスターブ.desc: In NAND flash, the gradual shift in threshold voltage of unread cells caused by the weak voltage applied to them when the same block is read many times.

about.h: Why reading one page stresses its neighbors
about.p: NAND flash cells are connected in series in strings. To read one word line, the selected cell's gate receives a read voltage while every other word line in the block receives a pass voltage of several volts, high enough to turn those cells fully on regardless of their stored data. That pass voltage creates a weak field across the tunnel oxide of the unselected cells, and each read injects a tiny amount of charge into their storage layer. Over many reads, their threshold voltages creep upward. Erased cells, with the lowest threshold voltage, are typically the most vulnerable.

about.h: When read disturb becomes a problem
about.p: A single read causes a negligible shift, but read disturb becomes significant after tens to hundreds of thousands of reads of the same block. It therefore hits blocks holding data that is read very often but rarely rewritten, such as boot code or hot lookup tables. Cells that store multiple bits (MLC, TLC, QLC) are more sensitive because the threshold voltage windows separating their states are narrow, and cells worn by many program/erase cycles are more susceptible still.

Controllers keep a read counter per block. As the count approaches a limit, or when error correction (ECC) starts reporting more corrected bits, the controller copies the data to a fresh block and later erases the old one, a process often called read reclaim or refresh. The shift is caused by added charge, not by permanent damage, so erasing and rewriting the block resets it. Read-retry, which re-reads with shifted reference voltages, can also recover pages whose distributions have moved.

about.h: Read disturb vs. retention and other memories
about.p: Read disturb raises threshold voltages and depends on how often a block is read; retention loss lowers them as stored charge leaks away over time, even if the data is never touched. The term also appears in other memories. In STT-MRAM the read current flows through the same magnetic tunnel junction used for writing, so it must stay well below the switching current or it may flip the bit, yet too small a current weakens the signal. In SRAM, read stability describes the related risk that accessing a cell upsets its stored value.

faq.q: What is read disturb in NAND flash?
faq.a: Read disturb is the gradual upward shift in the threshold voltage of unselected cells in a NAND block caused by the pass voltage applied to them on every read. After enough reads, it can flip stored bits.

faq.q: Is read disturb permanent damage?
faq.a: No. The shift comes from extra charge injected into the cells, so erasing the block and rewriting the data restores normal margins, unlike wear from program/erase cycling.

faq.q: What is the difference between read disturb and data retention errors?
faq.a: Read disturb adds charge and raises threshold voltages in proportion to how many reads a block sees. Retention errors come from charge leaking out over time, which lowers threshold voltages even when the data is not accessed.

書き込み増幅(ライトアンプリフィケーション).desc: The amount of data actually written to flash exceeding what the host wrote, because of garbage collection and similar operations. The larger it is, the shorter the SSD's life.

about.h: Where the extra writes come from
about.p: NAND flash is programmed in pages but erased only in much larger blocks containing hundreds or more pages, and a page cannot be overwritten in place. When the host updates data, the SSD writes the new version to a fresh page and marks the old one invalid. To reclaim space, garbage collection picks a block with many invalid pages, copies its remaining valid pages elsewhere, and erases it. Those copies are writes the host never asked for. Wear leveling, which moves rarely changed data off lightly worn blocks, and the drive's own mapping-table updates add more.

The write amplification factor (WAF) is the amount of data written to flash divided by the amount written by the host. Large sequential writes tend to invalidate whole blocks at once, so garbage collection has little to copy and WAF stays near 1. Small random writes scatter invalid pages across many blocks, so each reclaimed block still holds much valid data and WAF can reach several. The fuller the drive and the less spare area it has, the fewer mostly-empty blocks are available, and write amplification and performance loss both grow.

Each flash block survives only a limited number of program/erase cycles, so write amplification directly consumes endurance. As a simple illustration, if a 1 TB drive's flash could withstand 1,000 cycles, its raw budget would be about 1 PB of flash writes; at a WAF of 3, the host could write only about a third of that. Drive endurance ratings in terabytes written already assume some typical workload WAF, so a workload dominated by small random writes can wear a drive out faster than its rating suggests.

TRIM tells the drive which data is obsolete so garbage collection does not copy it. Over-provisioning, spare flash capacity hidden from the host, gives garbage collection more free blocks to work with, so victim blocks contain fewer valid pages; enterprise drives reserve a larger share for this reason. Controllers that compress data before writing can push the effective WAF below 1 for compressible data. Writing in large, aligned, sequential chunks and separating short-lived from long-lived data in different blocks also help, which is the idea behind zoned storage interfaces that let the host place data deliberately.

faq.q: What is a good write amplification factor?
faq.a: A WAF near 1 is ideal and typical for sequential workloads; small random writes on a nearly full drive can push it to several. Lower is better for both endurance and sustained write speed.

faq.q: Can write amplification be less than 1?
faq.a: Yes, if the controller compresses or deduplicates data, it can write less to flash than the host sent, giving an effective WAF below 1 for compressible data.

faq.q: Does over-provisioning reduce write amplification?
faq.a: Yes. Extra spare area means garbage collection can choose blocks with fewer valid pages to copy, which lowers WAF, especially under random write workloads.

SLC(シングルレベルセル).desc: A flash format that stores one bit per cell. With only two threshold-voltage states it is faster and more durable than multi-level formats.

about.h: How an SLC cell stores one bit
about.p: A flash cell is a transistor whose threshold voltage (Vt) shifts according to how much charge sits in its floating gate or charge-trap layer. Programming pushes electrons through the thin tunnel oxide, raising Vt; erasing removes them, lowering it. A single-level cell (SLC) uses only two Vt states, erased and programmed, so a read needs just one reference voltage placed in the wide gap between the two distributions. Large margin means the cell can be programmed with fewer verify steps and read reliably even as the distributions broaden with wear, age or temperature.

about.h: SLC vs. MLC, TLC and QLC
about.p: Storing N bits per cell requires 2ᴺ distinguishable Vt states: 2 for SLC, 4 for multi-level cell (MLC), 8 for triple-level cell (TLC) and 16 for quad-level cell (QLC). The usable window is only a few volts in every case, so the spacing between states shrinks rapidly as N grows. Multi-level cells therefore need finely stepped program-and-verify sequences and several read references, making them slower, and their narrow margins tolerate less degradation. In exchange they store two to four times more data on the same cells, lowering cost per bit, which is why TLC dominates mainstream SSDs.

Each program or erase drives electrons through the tunnel oxide at fields around 10 MV/cm. Over many cycles some charge becomes trapped and new defects form, narrowing the Vt window and enabling stress-induced leakage current (SILC), which lets stored charge escape. SLC's wide gap absorbs much more of this damage before reads fail. Typical endurance is about 50,000–100,000 program/erase cycles for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and roughly 1,000 for QLC. SLC also retains data better and copes with higher temperatures.

Native SLC NAND appears in industrial, automotive and embedded systems that need high endurance and retention more than capacity, and low-latency SLC devices serve some roles between DRAM and conventional NAND. More commonly, consumer TLC and QLC SSDs run part of their free space in SLC mode, often called pseudo-SLC or an SLC cache. Writes land there quickly and are later folded into denser storage during idle time. When a long transfer fills the cache, speed drops to the slower native TLC or QLC rate, which is why large copies can slow midway.

faq.q: Is SLC better than TLC?
faq.a: SLC is faster, more durable and more reliable, but it stores one third as much data per cell, so it costs much more per gigabyte. TLC is the better value for typical consumer and data-center use.

faq.q: How many write cycles does SLC NAND last?
faq.a: Typical SLC NAND is rated for roughly 50,000 to 100,000 program/erase cycles per block, an order of magnitude or more beyond TLC. Drive-level endurance also depends on wear leveling and spare area.

faq.q: What is an SLC cache in an SSD?
faq.a: It is a region of TLC or QLC flash temporarily operated with one bit per cell so incoming writes complete quickly. Data is later rewritten into the denser format, and once the cache is full, writes slow to the native speed.

TLC(トリプルレベルセル).desc: A flash format that stores three bits per cell, distinguishing eight threshold-voltage states. It lowers cost per bit but reduces endurance. Four bits per cell is QLC.

about.p: A flash cell stores data as the threshold voltage of its transistor, set by how much charge sits in the floating gate or charge-trap layer. Triple-level cell (TLC) flash programs each cell to one of eight threshold-voltage windows, encoding three bits, and reading a cell requires comparing it against seven reference voltages. The three bits are mapped to separate logical pages on the same word line, often called lower, middle and upper pages. Adjacent states are assigned Gray-coded patterns that differ in only one bit, so the common error of reading a neighboring state corrupts just one bit.

about.h: Why more bits cost endurance and speed
about.p: Squeezing eight states into the same voltage window leaves narrow gaps between them. Programming must therefore proceed in small incremental pulses, each followed by a verify read, which makes TLC writes slower than single-level cell (SLC) writes. Each program and erase also drives electrons through the tunnel oxide at high field, gradually trapping charge and broadening distributions until neighbors overlap. Typical endurance is about 100,000 cycles for SLC, several thousand to 10,000 for MLC, a few thousand for TLC and about 1,000 for QLC; data retention also suffers as gaps narrow.

Controllers hide TLC's weaknesses. An SLC cache runs part of the free space in one-bit mode so incoming writes land quickly, then migrates data to TLC blocks when the drive is idle; sustained writes that overflow the cache drop to the slower native speed. Strong error-correcting codes recover from bit errors that grow with wear, wear leveling spreads erases evenly across blocks, and spare area gives garbage collection room to work. Drive endurance is rated as total bytes written (TBW) or drive writes per day (DWPD) rather than raw cell cycles.

about.h: TLC vs. SLC, MLC and QLC
about.p: Bits per cell trade density against robustness: SLC stores one bit, MLC two, TLC three and quad-level cell (QLC) four. For the same number of cells, TLC holds three times the data of SLC, which is why it has become the mainstream choice for SSDs, usually built in 3D NAND with cells stacked in many layers. QLC pushes cost per bit lower for read-heavy, high-capacity storage, while SLC and SLC-mode operation remain in industrial and automotive parts that need maximum endurance and temperature tolerance.

faq.q: How many voltage states does TLC flash use?
faq.a: Eight threshold-voltage states, which encode three bits per cell and require seven reference levels to read.

faq.q: How many write cycles can TLC NAND endure?
faq.a: Typically a few thousand program/erase cycles, compared with roughly 100,000 for SLC and around 1,000 for QLC.

faq.q: Why does a TLC SSD slow down during long file copies?
faq.a: Writes first go to a fast SLC-mode cache; once a long transfer fills it, the drive must write directly in TLC mode, which is much slower.

NVMe.desc: An interface standard for fast access to SSDs connected over PCI Express. It processes many commands in parallel and has lower latency than SATA, which was designed for HDDs.

about.h: Why SSDs needed a new interface
about.p: SATA SSDs use AHCI, a host interface designed for hard disks: one command queue holding up to 32 commands, behind a link that tops out around 600 MB/s. Flash memory can service many requests in parallel, so this became the bottleneck. NVMe (NVM Express) is a protocol designed for non-volatile memory attached directly to PCI Express. It supports up to 64K I/O queues, each up to 64K commands deep, uses a compact command set, and lets each CPU core own its own queues, cutting software overhead and lock contention.

NVMe queues are rings in host memory. To issue a read or write, the driver places a 64-byte command in a submission queue and writes the new tail position to a doorbell register on the device. The controller fetches commands by DMA, moves the data directly to or from host memory, and writes a 16-byte entry to the paired completion queue, typically signaling the host with an MSI-X interrupt. The host then updates the completion queue's head doorbell. Host and device advance independently, so many transfers are in flight at once.

Because NVMe rides on PCIe, its bandwidth follows the link generation and lane count: about 7 GB/s for PCIe 4.0 x4 drives and over 10 GB/s with PCIe 5.0 x4. Protocol latency is a few microseconds, small compared with flash read times of tens of microseconds. NVMe drives come as compact M.2 cards, 2.5-inch U.2 drives and add-in cards. Note that M.2 is only a connector: an M.2 slot may carry SATA or PCIe, so an M.2 SSD is not necessarily NVMe. NVMe over Fabrics extends the protocol across networks.

Besides reads and writes, NVMe defines administrative commands for creating queues, identifying the controller, managing namespaces and updating firmware. The Deallocate operation, part of the Dataset Management command, is the NVMe equivalent of ATA TRIM: it tells the SSD which logical blocks no longer hold useful data, so garbage collection can erase them without copying. This reduces write amplification, which improves sustained write performance and extends flash endurance.

faq.q: What does NVMe stand for?
faq.a: NVMe stands for Non-Volatile Memory Express, also written NVM Express. It is a host interface and command protocol for accessing SSDs and other non-volatile memory over PCI Express.

faq.q: What is the difference between an NVMe SSD and a SATA SSD?
faq.a: A SATA SSD uses the AHCI protocol with a single 32-command queue and a link limited to about 600 MB/s. An NVMe SSD connects over PCIe with thousands of parallel queues, giving several to more than ten gigabytes per second and lower software latency.

faq.q: Does NVMe support TRIM?
faq.a: Yes. NVMe provides the same function through the Deallocate attribute of the Dataset Management command, which operating systems issue when files are deleted.

STT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that writes by flipping the magnetization of the MTJ's free layer using the spin-transfer torque of a spin-polarized current. It is in volume production as embedded non-volatile memory.

about.p: Each bit is a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ): two ferromagnetic layers, typically CoFeB, separated by an MgO tunnel barrier about a nanometer thick. The reference layer's magnetization is fixed, while the free layer's can point either way. When the two are parallel, electrons tunnel easily and resistance is low; when antiparallel, resistance is higher, and the relative difference is the tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio. A cell usually pairs one access transistor with one MTJ, built in the back-end interconnect layers, and is read by comparing its resistance with a reference.

Electrons flowing from the reference layer into the free layer are spin-polarized by the reference layer, and they transfer angular momentum to the free layer, pulling its magnetization parallel. Reversing the current direction drives it antiparallel, because electrons whose spin opposes the reference layer are reflected back into the free layer, so the access transistor must pass current both ways. Earlier MRAM switched bits with magnetic fields from nearby write lines, and the needed current grew as cells shrank. With spin-transfer torque, the write current scales down roughly with junction area, which is why the approach became mainstream.

Retention depends on the energy barrier between the two magnetization states relative to thermal energy, kT. In-plane MTJs rely on an elongated cell shape for that barrier, which weakens as cells shrink. Perpendicular MTJs use the perpendicular magnetic anisotropy that arises at the CoFeB/MgO interface, so even small round cells stay thermally stable while switching at lower current. There is still a trade-off: a higher barrier gives longer retention but generally needs more write current, so devices are tuned differently for code storage and for cache-like use.

Thermal fluctuation makes switching stochastic, so a pulse of a given current and width occasionally fails to flip the bit. Raising current lowers this write error rate but stresses the thin MgO barrier toward breakdown, so designs combine current and pulse-width margins, verify-and-rewrite and error-correcting code (ECC). Reading also passes current through the junction, which exerts torque, so read current must stay well below the switching current to avoid read disturb, yet large enough for a fast, reliable sense.

faq.q: How is data read in STT-MRAM?
faq.a: A small current is passed through the MTJ and its resistance is compared with a reference: parallel magnetization gives low resistance and antiparallel gives high resistance. The read current is kept well below the write current to avoid flipping the bit.

faq.q: Why do STT-MRAM cells use perpendicular MTJs?
faq.a: Perpendicular anisotropy from the CoFeB/MgO interface keeps small, round cells thermally stable without relying on cell shape, and it allows lower switching current. In-plane cells lose stability as they shrink.

faq.q: Is STT-MRAM non-volatile?
faq.a: Yes. Data is stored as the magnetization direction of the free layer, which is retained without power, so no refresh is needed as it is in DRAM.

SOT-MRAM.desc: MRAM that flips magnetization by spin-orbit torque from a current in a heavy-metal layer. The write and read current paths are separate, giving fast, durable writes.

カルコゲナイド.desc: A compound containing group 16 elements such as sulfur, selenium or tellurium. It is used as the recording material of phase-change memory (such as GST) and in selectors (OTS) that switch on abruptly above a threshold voltage.

about.p: The chalcogens are the group 16 elements: oxygen, sulfur, selenium and tellurium. Although oxygen belongs to the group, oxides are normally treated as their own class, so in electronics a chalcogenide usually means a compound built on sulfur, selenium or especially tellurium, combined with elements such as germanium, antimony or arsenic. Many of these compounds readily form glasses, meaning amorphous solids that remain stable at room temperature, and some can be switched back and forth between amorphous and crystalline phases with heat. That combination is what makes them useful in memory devices.

In phase-change memory (PCM) the cell is a small volume of a chalcogenide such as Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) heated by the cell current itself. A short, high-current RESET pulse melts the region and the rapid cool-down freezes it as high-resistance amorphous material. A longer, more moderate SET pulse holds it above the crystallization temperature but below melting, so it recrystallizes within tens of nanoseconds into a low-resistance state. Reading uses a small voltage that does not disturb the phase. Because the two states differ in resistance by two to three orders of magnitude, intermediate levels can hold more than one bit.

Amorphous chalcogenides show threshold switching: above a threshold voltage they snap into a conducting state within nanoseconds, and they return to high resistance once the current falls below a holding value. In PCM this effect is what lets enough current flow through an amorphous cell to heat and crystallize it. An ovonic threshold switch (OTS) uses a composition that switches this way but does not crystallize, so it stores nothing and acts purely as a selector. Placed in series with each storage element in a cross-point array, its very low off-current suppresses sneak paths through unselected cells, which makes stacked arrays practical.

GST crystallizes at roughly 150 °C, so data held in the amorphous state can be lost at high temperature; Ge-rich compositions raise that limit for automotive and other hot environments, where stored data must survive long periods at elevated temperature. The RESET operation needs a relatively large current to melt the material, which constrains the size of the access device and the power budget. The resistance of the amorphous phase also drifts slowly upward after programming, which complicates multi-level storage because the gaps between levels shift over time.

faq.q: Is oxygen a chalcogen?
faq.a: Yes, oxygen is a group 16 element and therefore a chalcogen, but oxides are conventionally treated separately. In device engineering, chalcogenide almost always refers to sulfides, selenides and tellurides.

faq.q: What is GST in phase change memory?
faq.a: GST is a germanium-antimony-tellurium chalcogenide, typically Ge2Sb2Te5. It switches between a low-resistance crystalline phase and a high-resistance amorphous phase when heated by current pulses, and that resistance difference stores the data.

faq.q: What is the difference between an OTS and a phase-change cell?
faq.a: Both are chalcogenides that threshold-switch, but a phase-change cell crystallizes and keeps its new state, while an OTS stays amorphous and returns to high resistance once the current is removed. The OTS is therefore used as a selector, not as storage.

フォーミング.desc: An initialization step for ReRAM in which a relatively high voltage is first applied after fabrication to create the conductive filament that later switches resistance.

クロスポイント型メモリ.desc: Memory with a storage element at each intersection of row and column lines. It is very dense, but a selector is placed in series with each element to stop current sneaking through unselected cells.

ストレージクラスメモリ.desc: Non-volatile memory intended to bridge the gap in speed, capacity and cost between DRAM and NAND flash. Products based on 3D XPoint were the best-known example.

about.h: The gap it is meant to fill
about.p: DRAM answers in tens of nanoseconds but is volatile and relatively expensive per bit, while NAND flash is cheap and non-volatile but needs tens of microseconds to read, roughly a thousand times longer. Storage-class memory (SCM) aims at the space between: non-volatile, denser and cheaper than DRAM, and orders of magnitude faster than NAND. Candidate technologies also avoid flash's erase-before-write, allowing data to be updated in place, and generally offer much higher write endurance than NAND.

SCM can sit on the memory bus as modules that the processor reads and writes with ordinary load and store instructions, byte by byte. Used this way it acts as large persistent memory, but software must explicitly flush data out of the CPU caches to be sure it has reached the non-volatile medium. Alternatively, it can sit behind a storage interface such as NVMe as a very fast solid-state drive, where it is accessed in blocks and much of the latency comes from the interface and software stack rather than the medium.

The best-known example, 3D XPoint, was developed by Intel and Micron and sold as Optane. It stacked resistive storage elements, widely believed to be phase-change based, with ovonic threshold switch (OTS) selectors at the crossings of word lines and bit lines, with no transistor in each cell. Other candidates include phase-change memory, resistive RAM (ReRAM) and magnetoresistive RAM (MRAM), although MRAM's larger cells suit it better to embedded memory. Low-latency single-level-cell (SLC) NAND is a flash-based approach to part of the same space.

To succeed, SCM has to be clearly cheaper than DRAM and clearly faster than NAND at the same time, while both incumbents keep improving: NAND cost falls as 3D layer counts rise, and DRAM keeps scaling. Applications also needed software changes to exploit persistent memory. Optane products never reached a large market, and their discontinuation was announced in 2022. Much of the tier is now served by low-latency SLC NAND and by memory attached through Compute Express Link (CXL), which expands capacity behind a standard interconnect.

faq.q: Is Intel Optane DRAM or flash?
faq.a: Neither. Optane used 3D XPoint, a non-volatile crosspoint memory believed to be based on phase change, positioned between DRAM and NAND flash in speed and cost.

faq.q: Is storage-class memory volatile?
faq.a: No. By definition it is non-volatile, keeping its data without power, which is the main thing that separates it from DRAM.

faq.q: What replaced Intel Optane?
faq.a: No single technology took its place. Low-latency SLC NAND SSDs cover much of the fast-storage role, and CXL-attached memory addresses capacity expansion beyond DRAM slots.

3D XPoint.desc: Cross-point non-volatile memory jointly developed by Intel and Micron. It stacked phase-change material with OTS selectors and was sold as Optane, but the business was wound down in 2022.

FeFET(強誘電体トランジスタ).desc: A transistor with a ferroelectric gate insulator. Its threshold voltage depends on the polarization direction, so a single transistor can store data non-volatilely and be read non-destructively.

TMR比.desc: In an MTJ, the difference between the resistances in the parallel and antiparallel states divided by the parallel-state resistance. The larger it is, the easier it is to tell 0 from 1; MgO barriers give large values.

about.p: A magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ) has two ferromagnetic layers separated by an insulating barrier about a nanometer thick. Its resistance is low when the magnetizations are parallel and high when they are antiparallel. The tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) ratio is (R_AP − R_P)/R_P: with R_P = 2 kΩ and R_AP = 5 kΩ it is 150%. Equivalently, R_AP/R_P = 1 + TMR, so 100–200% means the two states differ by only two to three times. An older pessimistic definition divides by R_AP instead and can never exceed 100%.

about.h: Why MgO barriers give high values
about.p: Early MTJs with amorphous aluminum-oxide barriers reached TMR ratios of tens of percent at room temperature. Crystalline magnesium oxide (MgO) barriers grown with matching cobalt-iron-boron (CoFeB) electrodes changed this: the ordered barrier preferentially transmits electron states of a particular symmetry, which are strongly spin-polarized in the electrodes, a process called coherent tunneling. After an anneal crystallizes the electrodes against the MgO, ratios of several hundred percent become possible, and values above 600% at room temperature have been reported in laboratory devices.

Memory products typically operate around 100–200%. Cells are tiny, so edge damage and variation matter, and the stack must survive back-end processing temperatures. The barrier must also be very thin to keep the resistance-area product low, because spin-transfer-torque (STT) writing drives current through it. TMR also falls as bias voltage rises, noticeably so at a few hundred millivolts, and it decreases with temperature. The ratio quoted for a material stack is therefore an upper bound on the signal a circuit actually sees.

about.h: Read margin and the TMR vs. GMR distinction
about.p: Reading compares the cell current against a reference set between the two states, using a current well below the write current so the read does not disturb the stored bit. Because the states differ by only two to three times and every cell's resistance varies, the margin is tighter than in DRAM or flash, and sense amplifiers and reference design are critical. Giant magnetoresistance (GMR), which uses a metallic spacer rather than a tunnel barrier, gives much smaller ratios and found its main use in hard-disk read heads.

faq.q: What is a typical TMR ratio in MRAM?
faq.a: Production MRAM typically operates around 100–200%, meaning the high-resistance state is two to three times the low-resistance state. Laboratory MgO junctions have shown much higher values.

faq.q: How do you calculate the TMR ratio?
faq.a: Subtract the parallel-state resistance from the antiparallel-state resistance and divide by the parallel-state resistance. For 2 kΩ and 5 kΩ, (5 − 2)/2 = 150%.

faq.q: What is the difference between TMR and GMR?
faq.a: Both are resistance changes that depend on relative magnetization. TMR comes from spin-dependent tunneling through an insulating barrier and gives large ratios, while GMR uses a conducting metal spacer and gives smaller ratios.

インメモリコンピューティング.desc: Performing computations such as multiply-accumulate inside the memory array to cut data movement between memory and processor. Research is under way on using resistive elements and the like for AI inference.

スーパースカラ.desc: A processor design that issues and executes several instructions per clock cycle. It has multiple execution units and processes independent instructions in parallel.

about.p: A superscalar processor fetches and decodes several instructions per clock, checks which of them depend on one another, and dispatches the independent ones to multiple execution units such as integer ALUs, load/store units, floating-point units and branch units. Its throughput can therefore exceed one instruction per clock, meaning instructions per clock (IPC) above 1 or clocks per instruction (CPI) below 1. A 2 GHz core averaging a CPI of 0.5 executes 4 billion instructions per second. Recent high-performance cores are roughly 6 to 10 instructions wide.

Pipelining overlaps the stages of successive instructions and at best completes one per clock; a superscalar core effectively runs several pipelines side by side. Very long instruction word (VLIW) machines also execute several operations per cycle, but the compiler finds the parallelism and packs it into each instruction, whereas a superscalar core finds it in hardware at run time, so existing binaries benefit without recompilation. Superscalar issue can be in-order or, in most high-performance cores, combined with out-of-order execution and register renaming.

Real programs offer limited instruction-level parallelism: data dependencies, branches and cache misses stall issue slots, so branch prediction, out-of-order windows and large caches are needed to keep wide machines busy. The hardware cost also rises steeply. Dependency checks and result-forwarding paths among simultaneously issued instructions grow roughly with the square of the width, and register files need more ports. Beyond a point, each extra slot adds little IPC for considerable area, power and timing difficulty.

Issuing many instructions per cycle requires decoding many per cycle. Fixed-length instruction sets make this easy because instruction boundaries are known in advance. Variable-length sets such as x86 must first find the boundaries, then split complex instructions into simpler micro-operations; many cores keep a micro-op cache so frequently executed code can skip decoding. Superscalar execution is also distinct from multicore and SIMD, which exploit parallelism across threads and across data elements rather than among neighboring instructions.

faq.q: What is the difference between superscalar and pipelined processors?
faq.a: A pipelined processor overlaps the stages of consecutive instructions and completes at most about one per clock. A superscalar processor has multiple pipelines and execution units, so it can issue and complete several instructions per clock.

faq.q: What is IPC in a CPU?
faq.a: IPC means instructions per clock, the average number of instructions completed per cycle and the inverse of CPI. Performance is proportional to IPC times clock frequency for a given instruction count.

faq.q: Is superscalar the same as multicore?
faq.a: No. Superscalar execution runs several instructions from one thread in parallel inside a single core, while multicore puts several cores on a chip to run separate threads.

アウトオブオーダー実行.desc: Executing instructions as soon as their dependencies allow, in a different order from the program, to improve performance. Results are committed in program order through a reorder buffer.

about.p: The front end still fetches and decodes instructions in program order. Each instruction is then renamed, given an entry in the reorder buffer (ROB) and placed in an issue queue. Scheduling logic watches for instructions whose source operands are ready and sends them to free execution units, regardless of their position in the program. An instruction waiting for a slow load sits aside while later, independent instructions run. Results are held until the ROB retires instructions in their original order, so software sees exactly the behavior of a sequential machine. The window spans hundreds of instructions in high-performance cores.

Programs reuse a small set of architectural registers, which creates false dependences: a later write must not overtake an earlier read or write of the same register. Register renaming maps each new value to a fresh physical register, leaving only true data dependences, where an instruction actually needs a value computed by another. In-order commit through the ROB gives precise exceptions and lets the core execute past predicted branches, discarding wrong-path work on a misprediction. ISA details matter here; RV64I sign-extends lw results into the full register precisely so the upper bits never depend on the register's previous value.

The biggest payoff comes during cache misses. An in-order core stalls behind a missing load; an out-of-order core keeps finding independent work and can issue further loads whose misses overlap with the first. That requires a non-blocking cache, which tracks outstanding misses in miss status holding registers (MSHRs) and keeps serving hits meanwhile. The number of misses and the latency of each are unchanged, but overlapping them hides much of the cost. Together with superscalar issue, branch prediction and large caches, this raises IPC (instructions per clock), and performance scales with IPC times frequency.

about.h: Out-of-order vs. superscalar, and the cost
about.p: Superscalar describes width, issuing several instructions per cycle; out-of-order describes the order in which they execute. A core can be in-order superscalar, and recent high-performance cores combine both at roughly 6–10 instructions wide. The cost is large: dependency checking grows roughly with the square of width, and renaming tables, wakeup logic and the ROB add area and energy to every instruction. That is why efficiency cores in phone SoCs are smaller and simpler, and why GPUs spend that silicon on many simple arithmetic units for throughput instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between out-of-order execution and superscalar?
faq.a: Superscalar means issuing multiple instructions per clock; out-of-order means executing them in an order other than program order when dependences allow. The two are independent ideas that high-performance cores usually combine.

faq.q: Why do out-of-order CPUs need a reorder buffer?
faq.a: Instructions finish out of order, but the architectural state must update in program order so exceptions are precise and mispredicted work can be discarded. The reorder buffer holds results until each instruction can retire in order.

faq.q: Does out-of-order execution reduce cache misses?
faq.a: No. It hides miss latency by doing independent work, including issuing other misses in parallel, while the miss is serviced; the number of misses stays the same.

TLB(変換索引バッファ).desc: A small cache that holds recent virtual-to-physical address translations. It avoids walking the page tables in memory on every access, speeding up address translation.

about.p: On every fetch, load and store, the memory management unit (MMU) splits the virtual address into a virtual page number and a page offset; with 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset and pass through untranslated. On a TLB hit, the stored physical page number is joined to the offset and permissions are checked in the same step. On a miss, a page-table walk reads the tables in memory, up to four levels for 48-bit addresses with 4 KB pages, and refills the entry. A page fault occurs only if the page-table entry is invalid or forbids the access.

TLB reach is entries times page size: 64 entries of 4 KB cover only 256 KB, while the same 64 entries holding 2 MB huge pages cover 128 MB. Because TLBs hold only tens to thousands of entries, programs with large or scattered working sets, such as databases and virtual machines, can spend a noticeable share of time walking page tables. Remedies include huge pages, a larger second-level TLB behind small first-level ones, keeping page-table entries in the data caches, and better locality.

about.h: TLB vs. page table vs. data cache
about.p: The page table is the authoritative mapping, built by the operating system per process and stored in memory; the TLB caches recently used entries from it, so it holds translations, not data. Data caches are separate but cooperate closely: many L1 caches are virtually indexed and physically tagged (VIPT), selecting the set with untranslated offset bits so the set read and TLB lookup run in parallel, then comparing the physical tag. A cache miss is handled in hardware, whereas a page fault is an exception serviced by the OS.

Processes reuse the same virtual addresses, so stale translations must not survive an address-space change. Without tags the TLB is flushed on every switch, causing a burst of misses; tagging entries with an address space identifier (ASID) lets them be reused when a process returns. Mapping the kernel into every address space means system calls need no switch. When the OS changes a mapping, it must invalidate matching entries on every core that may hold them. With nested paging and four-level tables in both guest and host, one miss can cost up to 24 memory accesses.

faq.q: What happens on a TLB miss?
faq.a: The MMU (or an OS handler on some architectures) walks the page tables in memory to find the translation, installs it in the TLB and retries the access. If the page-table entry is invalid or the access is not allowed, a page fault is raised instead and the OS takes over.

faq.q: How do you calculate TLB reach?
faq.a: Multiply the number of TLB entries by the page size. For example, 64 entries × 4 KB = 256 KB, while 64 entries × 2 MB = 128 MB, which is why huge pages reduce TLB misses.

faq.q: Is the TLB part of the CPU cache?
faq.a: It is a cache, but of address translations rather than data. It sits beside the L1 caches and is usually looked up in parallel with them, but it never holds the memory contents themselves.

SIMD.desc: Short for single instruction, multiple data: one instruction performs the same operation on several data elements at once. It speeds up image processing and AI calculations.

about.p: A SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) unit treats a wide register as a set of independent lanes. A 128-bit register holds four 32-bit values, and a 512-bit register holds sixteen; one add instruction adds all lanes in parallel. Instruction-set extensions such as x86 SSE and AVX and Arm NEON and SVE provide integer and floating-point lane operations, along with loads, shuffles and comparisons. In Flynn's taxonomy SIMD sits beside SISD, an ordinary sequential processor, and MIMD, multiple cores running independent instruction streams. Image filters, video codecs and matrix math typically speed up several-fold or more.

Compilers auto-vectorize loops that apply the same operation to each array element. The key condition is no loop-carried dependence: in a[i] = a[i-1] + b[i], each element needs the previous result, so lanes cannot run simultaneously. Data should be contiguous, and possible pointer overlap (aliasing) can make the compiler give up. A trip count unknown at compile time is not a barrier; the vector loop handles full chunks and a short remainder loop handles the rest. Media code also uses saturating arithmetic, where 8-bit signed 127 + 1 clamps to 127 instead of wrapping to −128.

An array of structures (AoS) stores each record's fields together, such as x, y, z and mass. A loop that reads only x then wastes most of each cache line and needs gather or shuffle work to fill vector lanes. A structure of arrays (SoA) keeps all x values contiguous, so every fetched line is fully used, memory traffic can drop sharply, and one vector load fills the lanes directly. The same layout lets adjacent GPU threads read adjacent addresses, which coalesces their memory accesses.

With CPU SIMD, the programmer or compiler explicitly uses fixed-width vector instructions, so code is written with the vector width in mind. GPU SIMT (single instruction, multiple threads) lets the programmer write ordinary code for one thread; the hardware groups threads, commonly 32, to run in lockstep on shared instruction issue. When threads in a group branch differently, the hardware executes each path in turn with inactive threads masked, so code still works but efficiency drops. Underneath, both rely on the same principle of amortizing one instruction over many data elements.

faq.q: What does SIMD stand for and what does it do?
faq.a: Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction operates on several data elements packed into a wide register, such as four 32-bit numbers in a 128-bit register.

faq.q: Why does my loop not auto-vectorize?
faq.a: Common reasons are a loop-carried dependence where an iteration needs the previous one's result, non-contiguous memory access, or possible pointer aliasing that the compiler cannot rule out.

faq.q: What is the difference between SIMD and SIMT?
faq.a: SIMD uses explicit fixed-width vector instructions on a CPU. SIMT, used by GPUs, runs scalar per-thread code on groups of threads in lockstep, with hardware handling branch divergence.

DMA(ダイレクトメモリアクセス).desc: A mechanism that transfers data directly between peripherals and memory without going through the CPU, so the CPU can do other work during large transfers.

about.p: In programmed I/O the CPU moves every word itself with load and store instructions. With direct memory access (DMA), the CPU instead programs a DMA controller, or the device's own DMA engine, with a source, a destination, a length and a trigger, then goes back to other work. The controller takes control of the bus, moves the data and raises a completion interrupt. In a microcontroller, for example, a timer can trigger an ADC conversion at fixed intervals and DMA can store each result into an array, waking the CPU only when the buffer is full.

Network cards and NVMe SSDs use descriptor rings: circular tables in main memory whose entries give a buffer address and length. The CPU fills free descriptors and writes once to a device register, often called a doorbell, to say how far it has written. The device reads the descriptors by DMA, performs the transfers itself and marks finished entries complete. CPU and device thus advance many transfers without waiting for each other, and lists of scattered buffers can be handled in one operation, known as scatter-gather.

DMA bypasses the CPU caches, so the two views of memory can disagree. Where hardware does not keep them coherent, the driver writes dirty cache lines back to memory before a device reads a buffer, and invalidates the cached range before the CPU reads data a device has written, so stale values are not used. The operating system may also move or swap out ordinary pages at any time, so buffers for DMA are pinned in place; pinned host memory lets a GPU transfer data without an intermediate copy and overlap transfers with computation.

Because DMA writes memory directly, a faulty or malicious device could overwrite kernel data or read encryption keys, a particular concern for devices attached through fast external ports. An IOMMU (input-output memory management unit) does for devices what the MMU does for the CPU: it translates the addresses devices use into physical addresses and blocks access outside the regions the operating system has granted. It also lets scattered physical pages appear contiguous to a device and makes it safe to assign a device directly to a virtual machine.

faq.q: What does DMA stand for?
faq.a: DMA stands for direct memory access, a mechanism that lets peripherals transfer data to and from main memory without the CPU copying each word, so the CPU can do other work during the transfer.

faq.q: What is the difference between DMA and programmed I/O?
faq.a: In programmed I/O the CPU reads or writes every data word to the device itself. With DMA the CPU only sets up the transfer and is notified when it finishes, which saves CPU time for large or frequent transfers.

faq.q: Why must the cache be invalidated after a DMA transfer into memory?
faq.a: On systems without hardware cache coherence, the CPU's cache may still hold old copies of that memory range. Invalidating it forces the CPU to read the new data the device wrote.

割り込み.desc: A CPU mechanism that temporarily suspends the current task to handle a request, for example from an external device, and then returns to the original task.

about.h: What happens when an interrupt is taken
about.p: When a device, timer or other source raises an interrupt and it is enabled, the CPU saves the address of the next instruction together with state such as the privilege mode and interrupt-enable bit in dedicated registers. It obtains a vector number for the cause, reads the handler's start address from the interrupt vector table set up by the OS, and jumps there. The handler saves the registers it uses, services the device, clears the interrupt source, restores state, and returns with a special instruction such as RISC-V mret or sret, which restores the mode and return address atomically.

Interrupts are asynchronous: a timer tick or network packet arrives regardless of which instruction is running. Exceptions such as page faults, division by zero or a deliberate system call (RISC-V ecall) are synchronous, caused by a specific instruction. Polling, in which the CPU repeatedly reads device status, is the alternative to interrupts. Interrupts are better when events are rare or the CPU should sleep, but each costs state saving and a jump, so at very high event rates, as in fast networking, batched polling can be more efficient.

An interrupt controller arbitrates simultaneous requests, often with a priority encoder, and with nesting a higher-priority interrupt can preempt a lower-priority handler, as in the Arm Cortex-M NVIC. Software can mask interrupts, but a non-maskable interrupt (NMI) is reserved for serious events such as uncorrectable memory errors or watchdog timeouts. Worst-case interrupt latency is set mostly by the longest section that runs with interrupts disabled, so operating systems split handling into a short urgent part and deferred work done later with interrupts enabled. PCI Express devices signal interrupts by memory writes (MSI) instead of dedicated wires.

Handlers should be short: no printf or waiting loops, just moving data to a buffer or setting a flag for the main loop. Variables shared with a handler must be declared volatile, or the compiler may read them only once. Read-modify-write updates like reg |= mask can lose a bit changed by a handler in between, and an 8-bit microcontroller reading a 32-bit counter can see half-updated bytes; disabling interrupts briefly fixes both. A periodic timer interrupt, for example 16 MHz divided by 16 counting to 1000 for 1 ms, provides the system tick.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?
faq.a: An interrupt is asynchronous and comes from outside the instruction stream, such as a timer or I/O device. An exception is synchronous, triggered by executing a particular instruction, such as a page fault, illegal instruction or system call.

faq.q: What is an interrupt vector table?
