about.p: When light exceeds the full well, excess charge spills into neighboring pixels and bright areas spread, which is called blooming; in CCDs it can also appear as smear along the transfer direction. CMOS pixels provide an overflow path, often through the reset transistor, to drain excess charge. Full well is commonly measured with the photon transfer curve: in electrons the shot-noise variance equals the mean, so plotting variance against mean gives conversion gain from the slope, and the point where variance stops rising and collapses marks saturation.

faq.q: What is full-well capacity in an image sensor?
faq.a: It is the maximum number of photoelectrons one pixel can store before it saturates and highlights clip. Typical values range from a few thousand electrons in small pixels to around 100,000 in large ones.

faq.q: How does full-well capacity affect dynamic range?
faq.a: Dynamic range is roughly full-well capacity divided by read noise. For example, 6000 electrons with 2 electrons of read noise gives 3000:1, or about 70 dB.

faq.q: Why do smaller pixels have lower full-well capacity?
faq.a: A smaller photodiode has less area and volume in which to store charge, so it saturates at fewer electrons. It also collects less light, which reduces sensitivity.

ToF(Time of Flight).desc: Measuring distance from the time light takes to travel to an object and back. ToF sensors are used in face recognition, robotics and automotive LiDAR.

about.h: The basic relation and its timing demands
about.p: Distance equals the speed of light times the round-trip time divided by two, because the light travels out and back. A target 1 m away returns light after about 6.7 ns, and a LiDAR echo arriving after 400 ns means about 60 m; forgetting the factor of two gives 120 m. The challenge is timing precision: a 1 cm change in distance shifts the round trip by only about 67 ps. Sensors therefore either time individual pulses with very fast detectors and circuits or measure the phase of modulated light.

A direct ToF (dToF) sensor fires short laser pulses and timestamps the returning photons, typically with single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) and time-to-digital converters. Because a single pulse may return only a few photons among ambient-light counts, the measurement is repeated many times and the arrival times are collected in a histogram whose peak marks the target distance. This approach suits long ranges and is common in automotive and robotic LiDAR, where a scanning or flash laser builds a 3D point cloud.

An indirect ToF (iToF) sensor illuminates the scene with light modulated at tens of megahertz and measures the phase shift of the returning signal. Each pixel steers photo-generated charge into two or more storage nodes, or taps, during different phase windows, and the charge ratios give the phase. Distance follows from the phase and modulation frequency, but it wraps around: at 20 MHz the unambiguous range is 7.5 m, so several frequencies are often combined. iToF gives dense depth maps at short range, while multipath reflections and strong sunlight are its main error sources.

ToF systems use near-infrared light around 850 nm or 940 nm so the illumination is invisible; 940 nm also falls in a dip of the sunlight spectrum caused by atmospheric water absorption. Silicon absorbs these wavelengths weakly, with absorption depths of about 20 µm at 850 nm and over 50 µm at 940 nm, so thin photodiodes lose much of the light. Pixels add light-trapping surface textures and deeper collection regions. Eye-safety limits on laser power and scattering in fog or heavy rain further limit range.

faq.q: What is the difference between direct ToF and indirect ToF?
faq.a: Direct ToF times short light pulses with fast detectors such as SPADs, which suits long range. Indirect ToF measures the phase shift of continuously modulated light, giving dense, high-resolution depth at shorter range.

faq.q: How do you calculate distance from time of flight?
faq.a: Multiply the speed of light by the measured round-trip time and divide by two. For example, 400 ns gives 3×10⁸ m/s × 400 ns ÷ 2 = 60 m.

faq.q: Why do ToF sensors use 940 nm light?
faq.a: Near-infrared light is invisible, and around 940 nm sunlight is weakened by atmospheric water absorption, which reduces ambient-light interference outdoors. The drawback is that silicon absorbs 940 nm light weakly.

SPAD(単一光子アバランシェダイオード).desc: A photodetector biased above breakdown so that even a single photon triggers a large avalanche pulse. It is used for ranging, such as in LiDAR.

about.p: A single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) is reverse-biased above its breakdown voltage by an excess bias, typically a few volts. In this Geiger mode a single photogenerated carrier can trigger a self-sustaining avalanche that produces a large, easily detected current pulse. The pulse looks the same whether one photon or several arrived, so the device counts events rather than measuring intensity. Because the avalanche would otherwise continue, a quench circuit, either a series resistor (passive) or an active sensing circuit, lowers the bias to stop it and then restores the bias.

Photon detection probability is the chance that an arriving photon produces a pulse. Dark count rate counts avalanches triggered by thermally generated or tunneling carriers with no light at all. Afterpulsing happens when carriers trapped during one avalanche are released after recharge and trigger a false pulse. Dead time, while the diode is being quenched and recharged, limits the maximum count rate. Timing jitter, often tens to hundreds of picoseconds, sets ranging precision. Raising the excess bias improves detection probability but also increases dark counts and afterpulsing.

about.h: SPAD vs. APD vs. PIN photodiode
about.p: A PIN photodiode has no internal gain: each absorbed photon yields at most one electron-hole pair, and an external amplifier must lift the signal above noise. An avalanche photodiode (APD) operates just below breakdown in linear mode, multiplying the photocurrent tens to hundreds of times while keeping the output proportional to the light. A SPAD crosses breakdown and gives up proportionality for effectively unlimited gain on each detection, which is what makes single-photon counting and precise photon timing possible.

Direct time-of-flight LiDAR and smartphone ranging sensors fire a short laser pulse and time the returning photons with a time-to-digital converter; every nanosecond of round trip corresponds to 15 cm of distance. Because individual detections are noisy, many pulses are accumulated into a histogram, a technique known as time-correlated single-photon counting. The same method measures fluorescence lifetimes, and SPADs also appear in quantum optics. Silicon SPADs can be built in CMOS processes as large arrays, often stacked on logic chips.

faq.q: What is the difference between an APD and a SPAD?
faq.a: An APD is biased below breakdown and gives an output proportional to light intensity with moderate gain. A SPAD is biased above breakdown, so each detected photon produces a full-size pulse that is counted digitally.

faq.q: What is dark count rate in a SPAD?
faq.a: It is the rate of avalanche pulses that occur without any light, caused by thermally generated or tunneling carriers. It sets the noise floor and rises with temperature and excess bias.

faq.q: Why does a SPAD need a quenching circuit?
faq.a: Above breakdown the avalanche sustains itself, so the bias must be pulled down to stop it and then restored before the next photon can be detected.

積層型CMOSイメージセンサ.desc: An image sensor whose pixel array and signal-processing circuitry are made on separate chips and bonded together. Each can use the most suitable process, making the chip smaller and processing faster.

インゴット.desc: A cylindrical single-crystal block grown by the CZ method or similar, before it is cut into wafers. The ends are removed and the outside is ground to a uniform diameter before slicing.

about.p: In the Czochralski (CZ) method, high-purity polysilicon is melted in a quartz crucible just above silicon's melting point of about 1414 °C. A seed crystal is dipped into the melt and slowly pulled upward while seed and crucible rotate in opposite directions, which evens out the temperature around the axis and yields a cylindrical crystal. A thin neck first lets dislocations grow out, then the diameter widens through the shoulder, or crown, into the constant-diameter body. A camera tracks the bright meniscus ring at the crystal–melt boundary, and pull rate and heater power are adjusted to hold diameter constant.

about.h: Doping and segregation along the ingot
about.p: Dopants are added to the melt: boron for p-type, phosphorus, arsenic or antimony for n-type. Most dopants have a segregation coefficient k below 1, meaning the growing crystal accepts less impurity than the melt holds, so the rejected dopant builds up in the shrinking melt and the later-grown part of the ingot is more heavily doped and lower in resistivity. Phosphorus has k of about 0.35, arsenic about 0.3 and antimony about 0.023, while boron's value of about 0.8 keeps p-type ingots fairly uniform. Only sections within the resistivity specification become product.

Only the constant-diameter body is used; the crown and the tail are cut off. The tail is deliberately tapered into a cone before the crystal leaves the melt, because abrupt separation of a full-diameter crystal causes thermal shock that creates slip dislocations, which can propagate back into the body by roughly one diameter. Pull rate also affects crystal quality, because the ratio of growth rate to temperature gradient (V/G) decides whether vacancy- or interstitial-type point defects dominate, so diameter control must not compromise it. Oxygen dissolved from the quartz crucible is incorporated as well and is measured along the ingot.

The ingot is cropped, ground to an exact diameter and given an orientation notch or, on older sizes, a flat. A multi-wire saw with hundreds of parallel wires about 0.1 mm thick then slices it into hundreds of wafers just under 1 mm thick in one run of several hours. The wafers are edge-beveled, lapped or ground for flatness, etched to remove the sawing damage layer and polished to a mirror finish before cleaning and inspection. Float-zone (FZ) growth, which uses no crucible, produces ingots with very low oxygen, favored for high-resistivity and some power devices.

faq.q: Why are silicon wafers round?
faq.a: The CZ crystal is pulled while rotating, so it grows as a cylinder and slices into round wafers. Round substrates also suit spin coating, polishing and other rotation-based processes.

faq.q: How is a silicon ingot cut into wafers?
faq.a: After grinding to diameter, the ingot is sliced with a multi-wire saw that cuts hundreds of wafers simultaneously using fine wires carrying abrasive slurry or fixed diamond. Lapping, etching and polishing then remove the saw damage.

faq.q: Why does resistivity change from the top to the bottom of an ingot?
faq.a: Most dopants segregate into the melt as the crystal grows, so the melt becomes richer in dopant over time and the bottom of the ingot ends up more heavily doped. Boron, with a segregation coefficient near 1, shows this effect least.

SOIウエハ.desc: A wafer with a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide (BOX) layer over a silicon substrate. It is made, for example, by bonding a hydrogen-implanted wafer and splitting it. Its low parasitic capacitance suits FD-SOI devices and MEMS.

about.p: A silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafer stacks three layers: a thin single-crystal device layer on top, a buried oxide (BOX) layer of silicon dioxide beneath it, and a thick handle wafer that provides mechanical support. Thicknesses vary widely by application. Fully depleted SOI (FD-SOI) transistors use a device layer of roughly ten nanometers on a thin BOX, silicon photonics commonly uses about 220 nm of silicon on a BOX around 2 µm thick, and micro-electro-mechanical systems (MEMS) may use device layers several micrometers thick or more.

The Smart Cut process dominates for thin layers. A donor wafer is thermally oxidized and implanted with hydrogen ions to a depth of a few hundred nanometers, then bonded to a handle wafer. Annealing at a few hundred degrees Celsius makes the hydrogen form microcavities that link up and split the donor at the implant depth, leaving a thin silicon film on oxide. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) and annealing finish the surface, and the donor can be reused. Older methods include oxygen implantation (SIMOX) and bonding followed by grinding and etch-back.

The buried oxide isolates each transistor from the substrate, cutting junction capacitance and leakage and eliminating the latch-up paths of bulk CMOS. In FD-SOI the channel is thin enough to be fully depleted, improving electrostatic control, and a voltage applied beneath the thin BOX acts as a back gate to tune threshold voltage. In silicon photonics, the large refractive-index contrast between silicon and oxide confines light in compact waveguides, and InP laser material can be bonded onto the wafer for heterogeneous integration. MEMS processes use the BOX as an etch stop.

about.h: Drawbacks and contrasts with bulk silicon
about.p: SOI wafers cost more than bulk wafers, which limits them to applications where the benefits pay off. Silicon dioxide conducts heat roughly a hundred times worse than silicon, so transistors on SOI suffer self-heating. In partially depleted SOI, where the body is thicker than the depletion region, the undepleted body floats electrically and causes history-dependent effects, including the so-called kink in output characteristics. FD-SOI avoids most of the floating-body problem but needs very tight control of device-layer thickness, since it directly affects threshold voltage.

faq.q: What is the BOX layer in an SOI wafer?
faq.a: BOX stands for buried oxide, the silicon dioxide layer between the thin device silicon and the handle wafer. It electrically isolates devices from the substrate and serves as optical cladding in silicon photonics.

faq.q: What is the Smart Cut process?
faq.a: It is a layer-transfer method in which hydrogen is implanted into an oxidized wafer, the wafer is bonded to a handle, and annealing splits it at the implant depth to leave a thin silicon film on oxide.

faq.q: Why is SOI used for silicon photonics?
faq.a: The buried oxide has a much lower refractive index than silicon, so the top silicon layer can act as a tightly confining waveguide core that is compatible with standard fabrication tools.

シーメンス法.desc: A method that reduces trichlorosilane with hydrogen to deposit high-purity polycrystalline silicon on heated silicon rods. It is the main way to make raw silicon for semiconductors.

about.p: The starting material is metallurgical-grade silicon, about 98% pure, made by reducing quartz with carbon in an electric arc furnace. Reacting it with hydrogen chloride produces trichlorosilane (SiHCl₃), which is liquid at room temperature and boils at about 32 °C. Converting silicon to a volatile compound is the key step, because it allows purification by fractional distillation, separating out the chlorides of boron, phosphorus and metals. Boron and phosphorus are especially important to remove, since they act as dopants in the final silicon.

Purified trichlorosilane is mixed with hydrogen and fed into a bell-jar reactor containing thin silicon rods, typically arranged as inverted U shapes. Electric current passed through the rods heats them to about 1100 °C, and trichlorosilane is reduced by hydrogen on their surfaces, depositing silicon and releasing hydrogen chloride. The rods thicken slowly over days, and the reactor walls are cooled so silicon deposits only on the rods. By-products such as silicon tetrachloride are converted back into trichlorosilane and recycled.

The resulting polysilicon reaches about 11N, 99.999999999% purity, with total impurities around 0.01 parts per billion, because even trace metals shorten carrier lifetime and increase leakage. Solar-grade silicon tolerates roughly 6N to 9N. The process is very energy intensive: the rods must be held near 1100 °C for long periods while they radiate heat to the cooled walls. The rods are broken into chunks to charge Czochralski (CZ) crystal growth, or used whole as feed rods for float-zone (FZ) growth.

The main alternative uses a fluidized-bed reactor, in which silane (SiH₄) or a chlorosilane decomposes onto small seed granules kept suspended by flowing gas. It runs continuously, uses considerably less energy and produces granular polysilicon that pours easily into crucibles. Its product has been used mostly for solar cells, because controlling contamination and surface quality is harder than with Siemens rods. For electronic-grade silicon, the Siemens process remains the standard route.

faq.q: Why is silicon converted to trichlorosilane in the Siemens process?
faq.a: Trichlorosilane is a volatile liquid that can be purified by distillation far more effectively than solid silicon can be refined. It is then reduced back to silicon in pure form.

faq.q: What does 11N purity mean for polysilicon?
faq.a: It means eleven nines, 99.999999999% silicon, leaving impurities at roughly 0.01 parts per billion. This level is required for semiconductor-grade crystal growth.

faq.q: Why is the Siemens process so energy intensive?
faq.a: Silicon rods must be kept around 1100 °C for days while deposition proceeds slowly, and much of that heat is lost by radiation to the cooled reactor walls.

偏析係数.desc: The ratio of impurity concentration in the crystal to that in the melt during solidification. For most impurities it is below 1, so they concentrate in the melt and the later part of a CZ crystal has higher impurity levels.
偏析係数.title: Segregation Coefficient (k0) in Silicon Crystal Growth
偏析係数.description: The impurity level in the crystal divided by that in the melt. Typical values, why CZ ingot tails are more heavily doped, and effective vs. equilibrium k.

about.p: When a crystal solidifies from a melt, an impurity is incorporated at a concentration different from that in the liquid. The equilibrium segregation coefficient k0 is the ratio of concentration in the solid to concentration in the liquid at the growth interface. For dopants in silicon, boron is about 0.8, phosphorus about 0.35, arsenic about 0.3 and antimony about 0.023. Transition metals such as iron have coefficients many orders of magnitude below 1, so they are strongly rejected into the melt, which is why crystal growth itself purifies silicon.

about.h: Why the tail of a CZ ingot is more heavily doped
about.p: In Czochralski (CZ) growth, the rejected dopant accumulates in a shrinking volume of melt, so the melt concentration rises and each later slice of crystal is more heavily doped. Under ideal mixing this follows the normal-freezing (Scheil) relation, Cs = k C0 (1 − f)^(k − 1), where C0 is the initial melt concentration and f the fraction already solidified. With k near 0.8, boron gives a fairly flat resistivity along the ingot, while phosphorus and especially antimony vary much more. Only the length within the resistivity specification becomes product.

The equilibrium value assumes the rejected impurity mixes instantly into the bulk melt. In reality a thin boundary layer forms at the interface, the impurity piles up in it, and the crystal incorporates more than k0 predicts. The resulting effective coefficient lies between k0 and 1 and rises with faster pulling and weaker melt stirring. Crystal and crucible rotation rates and pull speed therefore influence both the axial dopant profile and radial uniformity, and unsteady growth can leave periodic dopant variations known as striations.

The same idea applies across the interface between silicon and its thermal oxide, where the coefficient m is usually defined as concentration in silicon divided by concentration in oxide. Boron has m of about 0.3, so the growing oxide takes it up and the silicon surface is depleted, an effect called pile-down. Phosphorus and arsenic, with m around 10, are rejected by the oxide and accumulate in the silicon just below the interface, called pile-up. Device designers account for these shifts when setting channel doping and threshold voltage.

faq.q: Why is boron used for p-type CZ silicon?
faq.a: Boron is a group III acceptor with a segregation coefficient of about 0.8, close to 1, so its concentration stays relatively uniform from the top to the bottom of the ingot. That makes it easy to hit a resistivity target over most of the crystal.

faq.q: What is the segregation coefficient of phosphorus in silicon?
faq.a: It is about 0.35 for melt growth, so phosphorus concentrates in the melt and later portions of an n-type CZ ingot have noticeably lower resistivity than the seed end.

faq.q: What is dopant pile-up during oxidation?
faq.a: Dopants such as phosphorus and arsenic that prefer silicon over oxide are pushed ahead of the moving Si/SiO2 interface and accumulate in the silicon beneath it. Boron does the opposite and is depleted from the silicon surface.

ネッキング.desc: Growing a thin neck just after the seed at the start of CZ pulling. It lets dislocations created by thermal shock when the seed touches the melt escape, giving a dislocation-free crystal.
ネッキング.title: Necking (Dash Neck) in CZ Silicon Crystal Growth
ネッキング.description: Necking grows a thin neck right after the seed so dislocations from thermal shock grow out, giving a dislocation-free ingot. How it works and why it matters.

about.p: When a silicon single crystal is pulled by the CZ (Czochralski) method, dipping the seed crystal into melt at the melting point (about 1414 °C) introduces many dislocations at the seed tip through thermal shock from the sudden temperature difference. If the crystal were grown wide right away, those dislocations would carry through the entire crystal. So at the start of pulling, the diameter is narrowed to about 3–5 mm. This is necking, and the thin section is called the neck. Because W. C. Dash reported the method in 1958, it is also called the Dash method or Dash necking, and it remains essential for producing today's dislocation-free silicon crystals.

about.h: Why a thin neck removes dislocations
about.p: Dislocations in silicon move mainly along {111} planes and extend at an angle to the growth direction. In a thin neck, these angled dislocations reach the side surface of the crystal within a short distance and exit. Once the dislocations are gone partway along the neck, growth can continue dislocation-free even after the diameter is widened. A dislocation-free crystal shows growth lines on its surface (four for a <100> crystal), and whether these lines continue unbroken is monitored as an indicator of dislocation-free growth. If the lines disappear, the crystal is judged to have lost its dislocation-free structure.

about.h: Where it fits in the pulling process
about.p: CZ pulling proceeds through seed dipping, necking, the shoulder (crown) that widens the diameter to the target, the body grown at constant diameter, and the tail (end cone), in which the diameter is gradually reduced before the crystal is separated from the melt. The tail is tapered because an abrupt separation would introduce dislocations by thermal shock, which could propagate back up into the dislocation-free body. If dislocation-free growth is lost partway through the body, the rest cannot be used for wafers, and the crystal may be remelted and the pull restarted.

about.h: Challenges at large diameters, and another meaning
about.p: A 300 mm ingot can weigh hundreds of kilograms, yet it hangs from a neck only a few millimeters in diameter while being pulled. As diameters and weights grow further, neck strength approaches its limit, so researchers have explored seeds heavily doped with impurities, which resist thermal-shock dislocations and allow a dislocation-free thick neck, as well as mechanically supporting the crystal. The FZ (float zone) method also forms a neck after the seed to eliminate dislocations. Note that in materials mechanics, necking means something different: the local narrowing of a specimen during a tensile test.

faq.q: What is necking?
faq.a: It is the step at the start of single-crystal pulling in which the crystal just after the seed is grown narrowed to a few millimeters in diameter. It lets dislocations introduced by thermal shock when the seed touches the melt escape from the crystal, so that a dislocation-free crystal can then be grown.

faq.q: What is Dash necking?
faq.a: It is the method shown by W. C. Dash in 1958 for obtaining dislocation-free silicon single crystals by removing dislocations with a thin neck. It is still used as a basic step in single-crystal production by the CZ and FZ methods.

faq.q: What happens if the neck is too thin?
faq.a: Dislocations escape more easily, but the neck's strength to support the crystal's weight drops, and it may be unable to hold a heavy ingot. The diameter is therefore chosen to be thin enough to remove dislocations yet thick enough to bear the weight.

MCZ法(磁場印加CZ法).desc: A CZ variant that applies a magnetic field to the crucible to suppress melt convection. It makes the oxygen concentration in the crystal easier to control and is used for large-diameter crystals.

酸素析出物(BMD).desc: Tiny defects formed inside a CZ silicon wafer when its oxygen precipitates during heat treatment. Also called BMDs (bulk micro defects), they serve as gettering sites that capture metal impurities.

about.p: Czochralski (CZ) silicon is pulled from a melt held in a quartz crucible, which dissolves and releases oxygen into the crystal, giving interstitial oxygen concentrations on the order of 10¹⁸ cm⁻³. At typical device-processing temperatures this oxygen is supersaturated, so during heat treatment it clusters into silicon-oxide precipitates. Nucleation is favored at lower temperatures and growth at higher ones. Because the oxide occupies more volume than the silicon it replaces, growing precipitates emit silicon interstitials and strain the lattice, often producing punched-out dislocations or stacking faults around them. Float-zone silicon, grown without a crucible, contains little oxygen.

about.h: Intrinsic gettering and the denuded zone
about.p: Precipitates and their strained surroundings act as sinks for fast-diffusing metals such as iron, copper and nickel, which are captured in the bulk as the wafer cools instead of degrading junctions and gate oxides near the surface. This is intrinsic gettering. It works only if the top layer of tens of micrometers, where devices are built, stays free of precipitates. That denuded zone was classically formed by a high-low-high anneal: oxygen out-diffuses near the surface, then nuclei form and grow in the bulk. Rapid thermal anneals that engineer the vacancy profile are a modern alternative.

BMD density is typically controlled to about 10⁸ to 10¹⁰ cm⁻³. Too few precipitates give weak gettering; too many, or precipitates too close to the surface, cause junction leakage and can nucleate oxidation-induced stacking faults. Large precipitates also lower the wafer's resistance to slip and warpage during high-temperature steps. Modern processes have small thermal budgets, so precipitates may not nucleate on their own. Adding trace nitrogen, about 10¹³ to 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, during crystal growth promotes nucleation, shrinks vacancy-cluster voids (COPs) and strengthens the wafer, with negligible electrical effect.

Extrinsic gettering uses deliberately introduced sinks outside the device region, such as backside mechanical damage or a polysilicon film on the back, while heavily doped substrates also attract certain metals. Epitaxial wafers combine approaches: a lightly doped p-type epi layer on a p+ substrate provides a surface nearly free of precipitates and COPs, and the substrate below handles gettering while also suppressing CMOS latch-up. BMD density is commonly evaluated by preferential etching of cleaved cross-sections and counting the revealed pits, or by infrared light-scattering techniques.

faq.q: What is a BMD in a silicon wafer?
faq.a: A bulk micro defect is an oxygen precipitate, often with associated dislocations or stacking faults, that forms inside a CZ wafer during heat treatment. Controlled BMDs serve as gettering sites for metal contamination.

faq.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic gettering?
faq.a: Intrinsic gettering uses oxygen precipitates inside the wafer bulk as sinks for metals. Extrinsic gettering uses sinks introduced from outside, such as backside damage, a backside polysilicon layer or a heavily doped substrate.

faq.q: Why must the wafer surface be free of oxygen precipitates?
faq.a: Devices are built in the top few micrometers, and precipitates or the defects around them there would cause junction leakage and oxide problems. A precipitate-free denuded zone keeps the active region clean while the bulk does the gettering.

DZ(無欠陥層).desc: A layer near the wafer surface with few defects such as oxygen precipitates, made by out-diffusing oxygen during heat treatment. Devices are built in this layer while precipitates deeper inside provide gettering.

スリップ.desc: A defect in which crystal planes shift and dislocations form under stress from temperature differences or the wafer's own weight during high-temperature processing of large wafers. It can cause problems such as overlay errors.

about.p: Silicon is brittle at room temperature but becomes much softer at the temperatures used for oxidation, diffusion and annealing. If shear stress in the wafer exceeds the critical value at that temperature, dislocations are created and glide on {111} planes, permanently shifting one part of the crystal relative to another. The stress comes from temperature differences across the wafer, for example when the edge heats or cools faster than the centre during a rapid ramp, and from the wafer's own weight concentrated at the points where it rests on a boat or support pins.

about.h: Why large wafers are more vulnerable
about.p: Gravitational stress rises with wafer diameter because a larger, heavier disk spans a greater distance between supports, and radial temperature gradients are harder to suppress across a bigger area. Slip therefore typically starts near edge contact points and appears as families of straight lines; on a (100) wafer they run along the two perpendicular ⟨110⟩ directions, where the {111} slip planes intersect the surface. X-ray topography and surface inspection are used to detect it. Rapid thermal processing, with its fast ramps, is a common place to meet slip problems.

Dislocations crossing active regions provide paths for junction leakage and act as recombination centres, especially once metal impurities collect on them, so dies cut by slip lines often fail. The plastic deformation that accompanies slip also distorts the wafer in plane and out of plane. That distortion cannot be removed by later steps, so patterns printed afterwards no longer line up with earlier layers, producing overlay errors that the scanner can only partly correct.

Process engineers limit ramp-up and ramp-down rates, design furnace boats and RTP susceptors that spread support loads and keep temperature uniform, and position support points where the combined thermal and gravitational stress is lowest. Wafer material also matters. Interstitial oxygen in Czochralski (CZ) silicon gathers on dislocations and pins them, so CZ wafers resist slip better than low-oxygen float-zone (FZ) wafers, one reason CZ is used for large-diameter IC production. Excessive oxygen precipitation, however, can make wafers more prone to warpage.

faq.q: What is slip in a silicon wafer?
faq.a: Slip is plastic deformation in which dislocations form and glide along {111} crystal planes when thermal or gravitational stress exceeds silicon's strength at high temperature. It shows up as straight slip lines, usually starting near the wafer edge or support points.

faq.q: Why are CZ wafers more resistant to slip than FZ wafers?
faq.a: CZ silicon contains interstitial oxygen from the quartz crucible, and these oxygen atoms pin dislocations so they move less easily. Low-oxygen FZ silicon lacks this pinning and slips more readily during thermal processing.

faq.q: What is the difference between slip and warp?
faq.a: Slip is a crystallographic defect, the creation and motion of dislocations along slip planes. Warp is a measure of the wafer's overall out-of-plane shape; slip can cause warpage, but warp can also come from film stress without any slip.

サーマルドナー.desc: Oxygen clusters that act as donors when CZ silicon is heated around 450°C. Because they change the wafer's resistivity, they are annihilated by a higher-temperature treatment.

モニターウエハ.desc: A wafer run through a process separately from products to check equipment or measure film thickness and particles. Also called a test wafer, it is often stripped, repolished and reused as a reclaimed wafer.

Deal-Groveモデル.desc: A model of thermal oxidation in which the oxidant diffuses through the oxide and reacts with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. Thickness grows linearly with time for thin oxides and with the square root of time for thick ones.

about.p: The Deal-Grove model, published in 1965, treats thermal oxidation as three steps in series: oxidant moves from the gas to the oxide surface, diffuses through the existing oxide, and reacts with silicon at the Si/SiO2 interface. In steady state the three fluxes are equal, and dividing the flux by the number of oxidant molecules incorporated per unit volume of oxide gives the growth rate. Solving this yields x² + Ax = B(t + τ), where x is oxide thickness, B is the parabolic rate constant, B/A is the linear rate constant and τ accounts for any oxide present at the start.

When the oxide is thin, oxidant crosses it easily and the interface reaction limits growth, so x ≈ (B/A)t: thickness grows linearly with time. When the oxide is thick, diffusion through it limits growth, so x² ≈ Bt and thickness grows with the square root of time; doubling the thickness then takes about four times as long. The crossover occurs near a thickness of A/2, from tens of nanometers to about 100 nm for dry oxidation depending on temperature. Both constants rise steeply with temperature and roughly in proportion to oxidant partial pressure.

Because new oxide forms at the interface, the interface is always freshly made, and silicon is consumed: about 0.44 of the final oxide thickness comes from silicon below the original surface. Wet oxidation in steam is much faster than dry oxidation in oxygen, largely because water dissolves in SiO2 at far higher concentration, which is why thick isolation or masking oxides are grown wet and at high pressure, while denser dry oxides were preferred for gates. The linear constant depends on crystal orientation, with (111) silicon oxidizing faster than (100), while the parabolic constant does not.

For dry oxidation below a few tens of nanometers, real growth is faster than the model predicts. Proposed explanations include additional oxidant transport mechanisms in very thin films and stress effects at the interface. The original model handles this by assuming an effective initial thickness, roughly 20 to 25 nm for dry oxygen, but gate oxides only a few nanometers thick still require empirical calibration. Heavy doping, chlorine additions and two-dimensional geometries such as corners, where stress slows growth, also need corrections.

faq.q: What are the linear and parabolic rate constants in the Deal-Grove model?
faq.a: B/A is the linear rate constant, governing thin oxides where the interface reaction limits growth. B is the parabolic rate constant, governing thick oxides where diffusion through the oxide limits growth.

faq.q: Why is wet oxidation faster than dry oxidation?
faq.a: Water vapor dissolves in SiO2 at a much higher concentration than oxygen, so far more oxidant reaches the interface. Both rate constants are therefore larger for wet oxidation.

faq.q: How much silicon is consumed during thermal oxidation?
faq.a: About 0.44 of the grown oxide thickness, so growing 100 nm of SiO2 consumes roughly 44 nm of silicon.

STI(シャロートレンチ分離).desc: Isolating devices by etching shallow trenches in silicon, filling them with insulator and planarizing by CMP. It has no bird's beak like LOCOS and is the standard isolation for fine-pitch ICs.

about.p: A thin pad oxide and a silicon nitride layer are deposited, then lithography and etching open trenches about 200 to 300 nm deep into the silicon. A thin liner oxide is grown, often by thermal or ISSG oxidation, to repair etch damage and round the trench corners. The trench is filled with CVD oxide and annealed to densify it. Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess oxide and stops on the nitride, often using ceria slurries with oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100. Finally the nitride is stripped in hot phosphoric acid at about 160 °C.

In local oxidation of silicon (LOCOS), nitride masks the active areas while exposed silicon is thermally oxidized, but oxidant diffuses sideways under the nitride edge and grows a bird's beak that can encroach about half the oxide thickness on each side. That eats into active area, limits how close devices can be placed and leaves surface steps. STI isolates with an etched and filled trench, so the surface stays flat and isolation width is set by lithography. It replaced LOCOS around the 0.25 µm generation and is used today to isolate FinFET fins as well.

Ordinary CVD tends to pinch off at the trench opening and trap a void. From about the 0.25 µm to 65 nm generations, high-density plasma CVD filled STI by sputtering the corners while depositing; narrower trenches, down to around 10 nm, use flowable CVD or spin-on dielectrics that fill from the bottom and are then converted to oxide. Corners matter as well: a sharp top corner concentrates the gate field and creates a parasitic edge transistor, and an oxide divot from later wet cleans makes this worse, so corner rounding and recess control are tuned carefully.

The oxide in STI trenches stresses the neighboring silicon, and the amount depends on how far a transistor sits from the trench edge, so drive current can vary with active-area size and layout. Circuit models and design rules account for this. Trench etch must also avoid microtrenching at the bottom corners, which can create later filling or field concentration problems. In FinFET flows, the STI oxide is recessed after CMP to expose the upper part of each fin, and the recess depth sets the active fin height.

faq.q: What is the difference between STI and LOCOS?
faq.a: LOCOS grows thick thermal oxide in unmasked regions and suffers bird's-beak encroachment and surface steps. STI etches trenches, fills them with oxide and planarizes by CMP, giving flat surfaces and much narrower isolation.

faq.q: Why is it called shallow trench isolation?
faq.a: Its trenches are only a few hundred nanometers deep, shallow compared with the deep trench isolation, several micrometers deep, used in some bipolar, power, image sensor and older DRAM technologies.

faq.q: Why is ceria slurry used in STI CMP?
faq.a: Ceria removes silicon oxide efficiently, and with suitable additives it barely polishes silicon nitride. The high oxide-to-nitride selectivity lets polishing stop reliably on the nitride layer.

バーズビーク.desc: In LOCOS, the beak-shaped encroachment of oxide under the edge of the nitride mask. Because it wastes active area, it led to the switch to STI at finer geometries.

フォーミングガスアニール.desc: Heat treatment in a mixture of hydrogen and nitrogen (forming gas). Hydrogen terminates dangling bonds at the Si/SiO2 interface, reducing interface states.

界面準位.desc: Energy levels within the band gap at a semiconductor-insulator interface, created by broken bonds and similar defects. They trap and release carriers, causing threshold shifts, lower mobility and noise.

about.p: At the Si/SiO2 interface not every silicon atom finds an oxygen partner, leaving unsatisfied dangling bonds. These defects create allowed energy levels spread across the silicon band gap. As-oxidized interfaces typically carry about 10¹¹ to 10¹² cm⁻²eV⁻¹, and the density depends on crystal orientation, which is one reason MOSFETs are built on (100) wafers. Unlike fixed oxide charge, the charge in interface states changes with gate bias, because whether each level is filled depends on where the Fermi level sits at the surface.

Charge trapped in interface states shifts the flat-band and threshold voltages and stretches the capacitance-voltage (C-V) curve. Because the traps must be charged as the gate sweeps the surface potential, they add a capacitance that degrades subthreshold slope, so more gate voltage is needed per decade of current. Charged traps also scatter channel carriers and reduce mobility. Capture and emission of carriers produce low-frequency 1/f noise, and states near midgap act as generation centers that create leakage and dark current in image sensors.

A forming gas anneal at about 400 to 450 °C, in nitrogen with a few percent hydrogen, ties hydrogen to dangling bonds and lowers the density to around 10¹⁰ cm⁻²eV⁻¹. Those Si-H bonds can later break: hot carriers near the drain, negative bias temperature instability (NBTI) in p-channel devices and ionizing radiation all generate new interface states, causing threshold drift over the device's life. High-k gate dielectrics form poorer interfaces with silicon, so a thin SiO2 interlayer is normally kept between them.

Interface trap charge (Qit) is one of four standard MOS oxide charge types, together with fixed charge (Qf), mobile ionic charge (Qm) and oxide trapped charge (Qot). It is distinguished by its bias and frequency dependence. Common methods compare high-frequency and quasi-static C-V curves, analyze the conductance of a MOS capacitor versus frequency, or use charge pumping, which pulses a transistor's gate and measures the resulting substrate current to obtain trap density directly on small devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between interface states and fixed oxide charge?
faq.a: Fixed oxide charge sits in the oxide near the interface and does not change with bias, so it only shifts the C-V curve. Interface states exchange carriers with the silicon, so their charge varies with gate bias and they also distort the curve and degrade subthreshold slope.

faq.q: Why does forming gas anneal reduce interface traps?
faq.a: Hydrogen diffuses to the Si/SiO2 interface during the anneal and bonds to silicon dangling bonds, removing their energy levels from the band gap.

faq.q: How do interface states affect subthreshold slope?
faq.a: They add a trap capacitance in parallel with the depletion capacitance, so the gate controls the surface potential less efficiently and more millivolts are needed per decade of drain current.

RTP(急速熱処理).desc: Heating single wafers to high temperature for a few seconds, typically with lamps. It allows annealing and thin oxide growth while limiting unwanted dopant diffusion.

about.h: How an RTP chamber heats a wafer
about.p: Rapid thermal processing (RTP) treats one wafer at a time in a chamber whose walls stay relatively cool. An array of tungsten-halogen lamps shines through a quartz window, and the wafer absorbs the radiation and heats at tens to hundreds of degrees per second, holds above 1000 °C for seconds, and cools quickly when the lamps dim. Because only the wafer has to change temperature, the thermal mass is tiny. Temperature is usually read by pyrometers, and since emissivity depends on films and patterns on the wafer, accurate temperature control is one of the main engineering challenges.

about.h: Why short times help: thermal budget
about.p: Dopant activation after ion implantation needs high temperature, but every second at temperature also lets dopants diffuse. Diffusion length grows roughly as the square root of diffusivity times time, so cutting time from many minutes to seconds sharply limits junction movement while activation still proceeds. A spike anneal ramps up and immediately down with essentially no hold. For even shallower junctions, flash-lamp and laser anneals shorten heating to milliseconds or less, heating mainly the near-surface region while the bulk of the wafer stays cooler.

Typical jobs include activation anneals after implantation, growth of thin oxides by rapid thermal oxidation, nitridation of thin dielectrics, and the anneals that react deposited metal with silicon to form silicides, often in two steps with a selective etch between them. RTP is also used on bare wafers to engineer oxygen precipitation, for example to form a near-surface denuded zone free of precipitates above a bulk gettering region. In each case the attraction is precise, short exposure to high temperature with fast switching of gas ambient.

A vertical furnace stacks around 100 wafers in a quartz tube and ramps slowly, so it suits long processes such as thick oxidation and long anneals, offering excellent temperature uniformity and high throughput per run. RTP processes wafers singly and quickly, which favors short, tightly controlled steps but makes uniformity harder: the wafer edge loses heat differently from the center, and steep temperature gradients at high temperature can generate slip dislocations. Fabs use both, choosing by required time at temperature and diffusion tolerance.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTP and RTA?
faq.a: RTP is the general family of lamp-based single-wafer thermal processes. RTA (rapid thermal anneal) is one application of it, used for implant activation or silicide formation, while rapid thermal oxidation is another.

faq.q: What is a spike anneal?
faq.a: A spike anneal is an RTP recipe that ramps quickly to peak temperature and immediately cools with essentially no hold time, activating dopants while minimizing diffusion.

faq.q: Why use RTP instead of a furnace?
faq.a: RTP limits the time at high temperature to seconds, keeping dopant diffusion small, and lets each wafer get a precisely controlled thermal profile. Furnaces remain better for long, batch processes.

可動イオン.desc: Ions such as sodium and potassium that can move within the gate oxide. They drift with field and temperature and shift the threshold voltage. Because they can come from sources such as human sweat, they are tightly controlled.
可動イオン.title: Mobile Ions in Gate Oxide: Na+, Vth Shift and Measurement
可動イオン.description: Mobile ions such as Na+ and K+ drift through gate oxide and shift MOSFET threshold voltage. Their sources, how they are measured, and how fabs control them.

about.p: Mobile ions are alkali metal ions, chiefly sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+), that can migrate through silicon dioxide because they are small and only weakly bound in the oxide network. At room temperature they move slowly, but at moderately elevated temperatures, around 200 °C, and under an electric field they drift readily across a gate oxide. Common sources are human sweat and skin, process chemicals, tools, quartzware and furnace components, which is why the semiconductor industry treats alkali metals as critical contaminants.

about.h: How mobile ions shift the threshold voltage
about.p: A charge in the gate oxide shifts the flat-band voltage, and therefore the threshold voltage, by roughly the charge divided by the oxide capacitance, weighted by how close the charge sits to the silicon. Ions near the gate electrode have little effect, but under positive gate bias positive ions drift toward the Si/SiO2 interface, where they have full effect and lower the nMOS threshold voltage. Reversing the bias pulls them back, so the shift is reversible and depends on the bias and temperature history, the signature that distinguishes mobile ions from fixed oxide charge.

The standard check is a bias-temperature stress test on a MOS capacitor. The capacitor is heated, commonly to about 200 °C or more, with a positive gate bias applied, then cooled under bias and measured with a capacitance-voltage (C–V) sweep; the procedure is repeated with negative bias. The difference in flat-band voltage between the two states gives the mobile ion charge per area. Monitor wafers processed through furnaces and other tools are tested this way to detect contamination sources early.

about.h: How the industry brought them under control
about.p: Mobile ions were the main cause of unstable MOS transistors in the 1960s, and several countermeasures made MOS technology practical. Cleanroom discipline, gloves and high-purity chemicals limit sources, and metal-free chemicals such as TMAH replace sodium hydroxide as photoresist developer. Adding a chlorine source such as HCl during thermal oxidation removes sodium as volatile chlorides or immobilizes it in the oxide. Phosphosilicate glass (PSG) layers getter sodium, and silicon nitride films act as barriers in passivation layers.

faq.q: Why is sodium contamination bad for MOS transistors?
faq.a: Sodium ions move through the gate oxide under electric fields and heat, and when they accumulate near the silicon interface their positive charge shifts the threshold voltage, making devices unstable.

faq.q: What is the difference between mobile ions and fixed oxide charge?
faq.a: Mobile ions can drift through the oxide, so the threshold shift they cause changes with bias and temperature and can be reversed. Fixed oxide charge stays near the interface and gives a constant shift.

faq.q: Why is HCl added during gate oxidation?
faq.a: Chlorine binds alkali and metal contaminants, removing them as volatile chlorides or immobilizing them in the oxide, which reduces mobile ion effects and improves oxide reliability.

ドライブイン.desc: In thermal diffusion, the high-temperature step after a fixed amount of dopant has been introduced at the surface (predeposition), which pushes the dopant deeper.

about.h: Where drive-in fits in two-step diffusion
about.p: Classical thermal diffusion separates dose control from depth control. First, predeposition exposes the wafer to a dopant source, such as phosphorus oxychloride for phosphorus or a boron compound for boron, while the surface stays at a constant concentration, typically the solid solubility at that temperature. This gives a shallow complementary error function (erfc) profile. The doped glass left on the surface is then etched off, and drive-in heats the wafer with no further supply, so the fixed dose spreads deeper to set the final junction depth.

about.h: The Gaussian profile and junction depth
about.p: With a fixed dose Q and no surface supply, the concentration follows a Gaussian: C(x,t) = Q/√(πDt) · exp(−x²/4Dt), where D is the diffusion coefficient. As drive-in continues, the profile broadens with the diffusion length √(Dt) while the surface concentration falls in proportion to 1/√(Dt). The junction lies where the dopant concentration equals the background doping of opposite type. Because D rises exponentially with temperature following an Arrhenius law, temperature control matters more than time, and the product Dt is called the thermal budget.

Drive-in is often done in an oxidizing ambient so a masking or passivating oxide grows at the same time, which couples it to oxidation physics. Dopants redistribute at the moving silicon-oxide interface: boron tends to be absorbed into the oxide, depleting the silicon surface, while phosphorus piles up on the silicon side. Oxidation also injects silicon interstitials, which enhances the diffusion of boron and phosphorus, an effect called oxidation-enhanced diffusion. Real profiles at high concentrations therefore deviate from the ideal Gaussian.

In modern CMOS, ion implantation replaced predeposition because it sets the dose precisely, and short rapid thermal, spike or laser anneals activate dopants while minimizing their movement. Long drive-in style anneals remain useful wherever deep junctions are the goal: wells in mature processes, the deep diffused regions of power devices, and emitters of crystalline silicon solar cells, which are still commonly formed by phosphorus diffusion. Whatever the dose source, the same diffusion equations describe how dopants move during any high-temperature step.

faq.q: What is the difference between predeposition and drive-in?
faq.a: Predeposition introduces dopant at a constant surface concentration and controls the dose, giving an erfc profile. Drive-in removes the source and heats the wafer to push that fixed dose deeper, giving a Gaussian profile.

faq.q: Why does drive-in produce a Gaussian profile?
faq.a: The total amount of dopant is fixed and only redistributes by diffusion, which is the classic solution of the diffusion equation for a constant-dose source at the surface.

faq.q: Is drive-in still used after ion implantation?
faq.a: Yes, long anneals still drive implanted dopants deep in wells and power devices, though advanced transistors use very short anneals to keep junctions shallow.

酸化増速拡散(OED).desc: Faster diffusion of boron and phosphorus during oxidation than without it, caused by silicon interstitials injected into the silicon by the oxidation.

酸窒化膜(SiON).desc: Gate oxide with nitrogen incorporated. It blocks boron penetration from the gate electrode and has a slightly higher permittivity, so it was used as the gate insulator before high-k films.

about.h: Why nitrogen was added to gate oxides
about.p: pMOS transistors with p+ polysilicon gates are doped with boron, and during the dopant activation anneal boron can diffuse through a gate oxide only about 2 nm thick into the channel, shifting the threshold voltage and degrading reliability. Nitrogen in the film strongly blocks boron diffusion. It also raises the relative permittivity from 3.9 for SiO2 to roughly 5 to 6, so for the same equivalent oxide thickness (EOT) the physical film can be thicker, and direct-tunneling leakage, which falls steeply with thickness, is reduced. Resistance to hot-carrier damage also improves.

Annealing an oxide in NO or N2O incorporates nitrogen that piles up at the Si/SiO2 interface. Plasma nitridation instead exposes the oxide to active nitrogen from a plasma at a few hundred °C, placing roughly 10 to 20% nitrogen near the top surface. That location blocks boron arriving from the gate and raises permittivity while leaving the channel interface close to pure oxide. Too much nitrogen near the channel lowers carrier mobility and can worsen negative-bias temperature instability (NBTI) in pMOS devices, so the nitrogen profile is tuned carefully.

SiON was the standard gate dielectric in the generations just before high-k. As EOT approached about 1 nm, even nitrided films leaked too much gate current, and the industry moved to hafnium-based oxides with permittivity around 20 to 25 combined with metal gates, which also removed the boron-penetration problem of polysilicon. A thin silicon oxide-based interfacial layer still sits beneath the high-k film to keep a good interface with the channel. For comparison, silicon nitride (Si3N4) has a permittivity of about 7.

Silicon oxynitride is also deposited by plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) from silane with nitrous oxide, sometimes with ammonia, at about 300 to 400 °C. Adjusting the gas ratio tunes the refractive index anywhere between oxide (about 1.46) and nitride (about 2.0), so SiON serves as a dielectric antireflective coating under photoresist, as well as a hard mask and passivation layer. These deposited films are much thicker and differ in composition from nitrided gate oxides.

faq.q: Why is nitrogen added to gate oxide?
faq.a: Nitrogen blocks boron diffusion from p+ polysilicon gates into the channel and raises the dielectric constant, allowing a physically thicker film with lower leakage at the same EOT. It also improves hot-carrier reliability.

faq.q: What is the dielectric constant of SiON?
faq.a: It depends on nitrogen content, but gate-quality SiON is typically about 5 to 6, between SiO2 at about 3.9 and silicon nitride at about 7.

faq.q: Why was SiON replaced by high-k dielectrics?
faq.a: At an EOT near 1 nm, SiON films became so thin that tunneling leakage was too high. Hafnium-based high-k oxides, with permittivity around 20 to 25, give the same EOT with a much thicker physical film.

過渡増速拡散(TED).desc: A temporary speed-up of boron and other dopant diffusion early in post-implant annealing, caused by excess silicon interstitials from the implant. It hinders the formation of shallow junctions.

about.h: Where the excess interstitials come from
about.p: Each implanted ion knocks silicon atoms off their lattice sites, creating Frenkel pairs of vacancies and interstitials, often hundreds to thousands per ion. Most pairs recombine early in the anneal, but the implanted atoms themselves add extra atoms to the lattice, so a net excess of silicon interstitials remains, commonly approximated as about one per implanted ion. Boron and phosphorus diffuse mainly by pairing with interstitials, so a supersaturation of interstitials raises their diffusivity well above the normal value for that temperature.

The excess interstitials do not last. They cluster into extended defects such as {311} rod-like defects and dislocation loops, which slowly dissolve, and they are annihilated at the wafer surface and other sinks. While the supersaturation persists, boron diffusion can be enhanced by factors of tens to about a thousand; once it decays, diffusion returns to its normal rate. The effect is worst for long anneals at relatively low temperature, where enhancement lasts long compared with normal diffusion, whereas at high temperature the transient is over quickly. Interstitials can also trap boron in immobile, inactive clusters near the implant peak.

Transient enhanced diffusion (TED) pushes the tail of a boron profile deeper during the first moments of annealing, so a junction implanted shallow ends up deeper than intrinsic diffusion data predict. In transistors, deeper source/drain extensions worsen short-channel effects such as threshold voltage roll-off and drain-induced barrier lowering. Because the enhancement depends on implant dose, energy and anneal history, process simulators must model the interstitial population explicitly, not just a constant diffusivity, to predict final junction depth.

One approach shortens the thermal step: spike anneals, flash-lamp anneals and laser anneals activate dopants while giving the transient little time to act. Another removes the interstitials directly: co-implanting carbon at around 1e15 cm⁻² traps them and keeps boron in place, and fluorine or nitrogen co-implants serve similar roles. Lower implant energies also place damage close to the surface, where interstitials are lost quickly. Pre-amorphizing implants followed by solid-phase epitaxial regrowth help activation, but the end-of-range defects left below the original amorphous layer can still feed TED.

faq.q: Why does boron diffuse faster after ion implantation?
faq.a: Implant damage leaves a supersaturation of silicon interstitials, and boron diffuses by pairing with interstitials, so its diffusivity rises temporarily until the excess interstitials are annihilated.

faq.q: Is TED worse at high or low anneal temperature?
faq.a: Relative to normal diffusion it is worse at lower temperatures with longer anneal times, because the transient lasts much longer. High-temperature, very short anneals finish the transient quickly.

faq.q: How does carbon co-implantation reduce TED?
faq.a: Substitutional carbon captures silicon interstitials, so fewer of them are available to assist boron diffusion, and the junction stays shallower after annealing.

プリアモルファス化注入(PAI).desc: Implanting germanium or similar first to make the surface amorphous, so that the following implant does not channel and a shallow junction results.

ハロー注入(ポケット注入).desc: Angled implantation of dopant of the same type as the channel near the source and drain edges. It limits the spread of the drain depletion region and suppresses short-channel effects.

レトログレードウェル.desc: A well whose doping is higher deeper below the surface, made by high-energy implantation. It suppresses punch-through and latch-up while keeping the channel doping at the surface low.

固溶度.desc: The maximum concentration of an impurity that can dissolve in a crystal at a given temperature. It sets the upper limit of electrically active dopant concentration.

about.h: An equilibrium limit that depends on temperature
about.p: Solid solubility is the largest concentration of an impurity that a crystal can hold in equilibrium at a given temperature without forming a second phase. For dopants in silicon it varies with temperature, typically reaching its maximum in the range of roughly 1000-1300 °C and falling at lower temperatures. Near 1000 °C, boron's solubility is about 2e20 cm⁻³, while arsenic and phosphorus reach around 1e21 cm⁻³. Compared with silicon's atomic density of 5e22 cm⁻³, these limits correspond to at most about 2 atomic percent, and only about 0.4 percent for boron.

Dopant above the solubility limit does not sit on lattice sites as a donor or acceptor; it forms clusters or precipitates and contributes no carriers. Implanted dose can easily exceed solubility, so the total concentration measured by secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) can be much higher than the active carrier concentration measured electrically. This is why sheet resistance falls with dose at first and then saturates: additional dopant stays inactive, and mobility also drops at high doping because of ionized-impurity scattering.

Very fast thermal processes can trap dopants on substitutional sites before they have time to cluster. Millisecond flash and laser anneals, and solid-phase epitaxial regrowth of a layer amorphized by implantation, can activate concentrations above the equilibrium solubility. These states are metastable: later thermal steps at moderate temperature give the dopants time to deactivate by clustering, so the whole downstream thermal budget has to be considered when relying on above-solubility activation.

Source/drain regions and contact areas are doped to around 1e20 cm⁻³ or higher, which is close to solid solubility for boron. Specific contact resistivity between a silicide or metal and silicon falls steeply as active doping rises, because the Schottky barrier becomes thin enough for carriers to tunnel through it. At small contact areas, contact resistance becomes a large part of total transistor series resistance, so maximizing active dopant concentration at the interface is a recurring target in junction engineering.

faq.q: What is the solid solubility of boron in silicon?
faq.a: It is about 2e20 cm⁻³ near 1000 °C. Phosphorus and arsenic have higher limits, on the order of 1e21 cm⁻³.

faq.q: Why does sheet resistance stop decreasing at high implant dose?
faq.a: Once the dopant concentration exceeds solid solubility, the extra atoms cluster or precipitate and remain electrically inactive, and mobility also declines at high doping. Additional dose therefore gives diminishing returns.

faq.q: Can active dopant concentration exceed solid solubility?
faq.a: Yes, temporarily. Millisecond anneals and solid-phase epitaxial regrowth can freeze in metastable concentrations above solubility, but later heating can deactivate them.

スパイクアニール.desc: An anneal that ramps the wafer quickly to a high temperature and cools it again with almost no hold time. It activates dopants while limiting diffusion, for shallow junctions.

レーザーアニール.desc: Heating only the near-surface region of a wafer for an extremely short time with laser light. It achieves high activation with almost no diffusion.

about.p: Laser annealing is a heat treatment in which laser light is absorbed at the wafer surface, bringing only the near-surface region to a high temperature for a short time. Because the distance heat spreads in depth is roughly proportional to the square root of the heating time, shortening the heating time to the millisecond-to-nanosecond range heats only a shallow region near the surface while most of the wafer stays cool. The surface reaches above 1000 °C, in some conditions near silicon's melting point, but the time at high temperature is so short that implanted dopants can be activated before they diffuse appreciably. This makes shallow, low-resistance junctions possible.

There are two broad approaches. In non-melt annealing, continuous-wave laser light focused into a narrow line is scanned across the wafer, heating each point below the melting point for about a millisecond or less; this is called laser spike annealing, among other names. In melt annealing, nanosecond pulses from an excimer laser or similar melt a very shallow surface layer, which then recrystallizes on cooling using the crystal below as a seed. Melt annealing gives a nearly box-shaped dopant profile and can achieve activation above the equilibrium solid solubility, but that state tends to deactivate during later heat treatments.

In logic LSIs, laser annealing is combined with spike annealing to form shallow source/drain junctions and to reach high activation that lowers contact resistance. Because heat does not reach deep, it is also used in steps where underlying layers must not be damaged, such as forming backside layers on thinned wafers for IGBTs and other power devices, or building transistors in an upper tier of a stacked structure. Outside semiconductor manufacturing, excimer laser annealing (ELA), which converts amorphous silicon on glass substrates into polycrystalline silicon, is used to produce low-temperature polysilicon (LTPS) for LCD and OLED displays.

about.h: Challenges and comparison with other anneals
about.p: One challenge is the pattern effect: reflectivity and absorption vary with the materials and structures on the surface, so peak temperature varies from place to place. It is reduced by choosing the wavelength and angle of incidence or by adding a light-absorbing film. Care is also needed so that stress from rapid heating and cooling does not cause slip or warpage in the wafer. Anneal times get shorter in the order furnace anneal (tens of minutes or more), RTA and spike anneal (around seconds), flash-lamp anneal (around milliseconds) and laser anneal (milliseconds to nanoseconds); the shorter the time, the less diffusion.

faq.q: What is the difference between laser annealing and RTA (rapid thermal annealing)?
faq.a: RTA heats the whole wafer with lamps for around seconds, while laser annealing heats only the near-surface region for milliseconds to nanoseconds. Because the time at high temperature is far shorter, high activation is achieved with little dopant diffusion, and heat has less effect on underlying layers.

faq.q: How do melt and non-melt laser annealing differ?
faq.a: Non-melt annealing activates dopants in the solid state below the melting point, while melt annealing melts a shallow surface layer and lets it recrystallize. Melt annealing gives abrupt profiles and high activation, but the melt depth and changes in surface shape need careful control.

faq.q: Why is laser annealing also used in display manufacturing?
faq.a: Glass substrates cannot withstand high temperatures, so an excimer laser momentarily melts only the thin amorphous silicon film and converts it into polycrystalline silicon. This yields low-temperature polysilicon (LTPS) TFTs with high electron mobility, used in high-resolution LCD and OLED displays.

ファラデーカップ.desc: A device that collects an ion beam and measures the resulting current. In ion implanters it is used to determine the implanted dose.

プラズマドーピング.desc: Implanting low-energy ions by exposing the wafer directly to a plasma containing the dopant. It delivers high doses quickly and dopes 3D structures such as fins fairly uniformly.

シャドウイング.desc: When implanting at a tilt, the effect of tall patterns such as resist casting shadows so that some areas receive no implant.

about.h: Why implants are tilted at all
about.p: Silicon is a crystal, and along its major axes the atoms line up into open channels. An ion beam aimed straight down a channel can travel much deeper than the intended profile, an effect called channeling. Tilting the wafer by a few degrees, typically around 7°, and adding a twist angle makes the crystal look more random to the beam. Some implants are tilted on purpose for a different reason: halo or pocket implants use larger tilts so dopant lands under the gate edge to suppress short-channel effects. Every tilt, whatever its purpose, opens the door to shadowing.

about.h: The geometry of an implant shadow
about.p: A mask feature of height h, such as a resist line or a gate stack, blocks ions over a lateral distance of roughly h × tan(θ) on its far side, where θ is the tilt angle. With 500 nm of resist and a 7° tilt the unimplanted strip is about 60 nm wide; at the larger angles used for halos it grows quickly. Because the shadow falls on only one side, the source and drain of the same transistor receive different doping, so their characteristics no longer match and device behavior can depend on its orientation on the wafer.

The standard fix is quad-mode implantation: the total dose is split into four parts with the wafer rotated by 90° between them, so every side of a feature is exposed from some direction and the result is symmetric on average. Engineers also co-design resist thickness, opening width and tilt angle so that the shadow never reaches the region that matters. Channeling can alternatively be suppressed with a thin screen oxide or a pre-amorphization implant, which allows smaller tilts and therefore shorter shadows in densely packed layouts.

The same word describes a deposition problem. In physical vapor deposition (PVD), such as sputtering and evaporation, atoms fly in nearly straight lines and hardly move after landing. The top surface and the trench mouth collect film, while sidewalls and bottoms outside the line of sight receive little; the overhang at the opening can even pinch off and leave a void. Collimators and ionized PVD make the flux more directional and help bottom coverage, but conformal coatings in deep features usually call for CVD or ALD, where gas-phase precursors reach every surface.

faq.q: What causes shadowing in tilted ion implantation?
faq.a: When the wafer is tilted, tall structures such as resist or gate stacks block the ion beam on one side, leaving a strip roughly the feature height times tan(tilt) unimplanted. The result is asymmetric doping between the two sides of a feature.

faq.q: How is implant shadowing reduced?
faq.a: The dose is usually split into four implants with 90° wafer rotations (quad mode), and resist height, opening width and tilt are chosen together. Using a screen oxide or pre-amorphization to control channeling also allows smaller tilt angles.

faq.q: Is shadowing the same as channeling?
faq.a: No. Channeling is ions penetrating too deep along open crystal directions, and tilting the wafer is one way to avoid it; shadowing is the side effect of that tilt, where parts of the wafer receive no ions at all.

LPCVD(減圧CVD).desc: Thermal CVD performed under reduced pressure. Faster gas diffusion gives good thickness uniformity and step coverage, and many wafers can be processed at once in a vertical furnace. It is used for polysilicon and nitride films.

about.h: Why low pressure gives uniform films
about.p: Low-pressure chemical vapor deposition (LPCVD) runs thermal CVD at roughly tens to hundreds of pascals. Gas diffusivity rises as pressure falls, so reactants reach every surface quickly and the growth rate is set by the surface reaction rather than by gas transport. A surface-reaction-limited process depends mainly on temperature, and a hot-wall tube furnace holds temperature very uniform. That is why wafers can stand only a few millimetres apart, often more than a hundred per run, and still receive uniform, conformal films with good step coverage.

Polysilicon is deposited by decomposing silane (SiH4) at about 600 to 650 °C; below about 580 °C the film is amorphous. Silicon nitride comes from dichlorosilane and ammonia at about 700 to 800 °C, and oxide from TEOS decomposition at similar furnace temperatures. Polysilicon can be doped in situ by adding phosphine or diborane, which is useful for films lining deep trenches. Deposition rates are modest, typically a few to tens of nanometres per minute, which the large batch size compensates for.

Plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) uses a plasma to drive reactions at a few hundred degrees, which makes it usable after metallization, but its films are less dense, contain more hydrogen and etch faster. LPCVD films are dense and close to stoichiometric; LPCVD nitride holds only a few percent hydrogen compared with around 20% in PECVD nitride. Stoichiometric LPCVD nitride also has high tensile stress, so silicon-rich low-stress variants are often used in MEMS membranes. The price of LPCVD quality is its thermal budget.

Because it needs 600 to 800 °C, LPCVD belongs to the front end, before aluminum or copper wiring exists. Typical uses are polysilicon gates and resistors, nitride hard masks and spacers, pad nitride for isolation, capacitor electrodes in DRAM and floating gates or electrodes in flash, and structural layers in MEMS. Film also deposits on the furnace tube and on both sides of every wafer, so tubes need periodic cleaning and backside films sometimes must be stripped.

faq.q: What is the difference between LPCVD and PECVD?
faq.a: LPCVD uses heat alone at about 600 to 800 °C and gives dense, low-hydrogen, uniform films in large batches. PECVD uses a plasma to deposit at a few hundred degrees, enabling use over metal at the cost of film density and purity.

faq.q: Why is LPCVD deposition so uniform?
faq.a: At low pressure gas diffusion is fast, so growth is limited by the surface reaction, which depends mainly on temperature. A hot-wall furnace keeps temperature uniform across all wafers in the load.

faq.q: At what temperature is LPCVD polysilicon deposited?
faq.a: Typically about 600 to 650 °C from silane. Depositing below roughly 580 °C produces amorphous silicon, which can be crystallized by a later anneal.

TEOS.desc: Short for tetraethoxysilane, a liquid organosilicon compound widely used as the source for CVD silicon oxide. It gives oxide films with good step coverage.

about.p: Tetraethoxysilane (TEOS), Si(OC2H5)4, is a liquid at room temperature with a boiling point of about 168 °C. Each silicon atom is already bonded to four oxygen atoms, so silicon dioxide can form when the ethoxy groups decompose and leave as volatile organic byproducts, with oxygen or ozone added to help the reaction and burn off carbon. Unlike silane (SiH4), which is a pyrophoric gas, TEOS is comparatively safe to store and handle. The name is so common that the deposited film itself is often called TEOS oxide, or just TEOS.

Oxide from TEOS forms mainly through reactions on the surface, and the reactive intermediates have a low sticking probability, so they bounce around before reacting and reach sidewalls and the bottoms of trenches. The result is a conformal film whose thickness is similar on top, side and bottom surfaces. Oxide deposited from silane and oxygen at low temperature, by contrast, involves species that stick where they first land, giving thicker deposits at upper corners and poorer coverage. This difference is the main reason TEOS became the standard source for CVD oxide.

Low-pressure CVD (LPCVD) TEOS runs in a furnace at about 700 °C and gives conformal, good-quality oxide, but that temperature rules it out once metal is present, so it is used in the front end, for example for sidewall spacers. Plasma-enhanced CVD (PECVD) TEOS deposits at about 400 °C for interlayer dielectrics in the back end. TEOS with ozone at atmospheric or sub-atmospheric pressure gives flowing, gap-filling films. Adding boron and phosphorus sources produces doped oxides such as borophosphosilicate glass, which soften and reflow when heated.

TEOS oxide is less dense than thermal oxide and can contain hydrogen, moisture or residual carbon depending on conditions, so it typically etches faster in dilute hydrofluoric acid; annealing densifies it toward thermal-oxide behavior. As a liquid, the precursor reaches the chamber either by bubbling a carrier gas through a temperature-controlled container or by metering the liquid into a vaporizer, which gives tighter flow control. Delivery lines are heated so the vapor does not recondense before it reaches the reactor.

faq.q: What does TEOS stand for?
faq.a: TEOS stands for tetraethoxysilane, also called tetraethyl orthosilicate, with the formula Si(OC2H5)4. It is the most common liquid precursor for CVD silicon dioxide.

faq.q: What is the difference between TEOS oxide and silane oxide?
faq.a: TEOS oxide forms through surface reactions with low sticking intermediates, so it is more conformal; silane-based oxide tends to deposit more at the top of features. Silane is also a pyrophoric gas, whereas TEOS is a safer liquid.

faq.q: Is TEOS oxide the same as thermal oxide?
faq.a: Both are silicon dioxide, but thermal oxide is grown by consuming silicon and is denser and cleaner. Deposited TEOS oxide usually etches faster in HF and is used where oxide must be added on top of other layers.

電解めっき.desc: Depositing metal by passing current through a plating bath with the wafer as the cathode. It fills copper interconnect trenches, with additives making the fill proceed from the bottom up.

マグネトロンスパッタリング.desc: Sputtering with magnets behind the target that trap electrons near it and raise plasma density. It increases deposition rate and is the mainstream sputtering method today.

about.p: In plain diode sputtering, secondary electrons knocked out of the target race away to the chamber walls after few ionizing collisions, so the plasma is thin and needs relatively high gas pressure. A magnetron places permanent magnets behind the target so that the magnetic field lines arch over its surface, crossing the electric field. Electrons are forced into spiraling, drifting orbits that keep them close to the target, where each one ionizes many more argon atoms. The resulting dense plasma supplies a large ion current to the target and therefore a high deposition rate.

Magnetrons sustain a plasma at about 0.1–1 Pa, lower than diode sputtering needs. At these pressures sputtered atoms undergo fewer gas collisions on the way to the wafer, so they arrive with more energy and more directionality, which tends to give denser films. Because energetic electrons are trapped near the target rather than reaching the wafer, substrate heating from electron bombardment is also reduced. DC power is used for conductive metal targets, while insulating targets need RF power, commonly at 13.56 MHz, to avoid charge buildup on the target surface.

Ionization is strongest where the magnetic field runs parallel to the target, so erosion concentrates there and carves a ring-shaped groove often called the racetrack. A fixed magnet set would consume only a fraction of the target before the groove broke through, and would also deposit a nonuniform film. Production tools therefore rotate or sweep the magnet assembly behind the target to spread erosion, raise material utilization and improve thickness uniformity across the wafer. Large-area coaters often use rotating cylindrical targets for the same reason.

Magnetron sputtering is the workhorse of metal PVD in semiconductor fabs.
