Typical films include Ti and TiN liners, Ta and TaN diffusion barriers, copper seed layers for electroplating and aluminum interconnect. Target plates of Ti, Ta, Cu or Al must be highly pure with uniform grain structure, because impurities and grain variation are transferred directly into the film. For high-aspect-ratio features, ionized magnetron variants ionize much of the sputtered metal and attract it to the wafer with a bias to improve bottom coverage.

faq.q: Why is magnetron sputtering faster than diode sputtering?
faq.a: The magnetic field traps electrons near the target so each one causes many more ionizing collisions, creating a much denser plasma. More argon ions hit the target per second, so more atoms are sputtered even at lower pressure.

faq.q: Can magnetron sputtering deposit insulating films?
faq.a: Yes, either by RF sputtering an insulating target, which avoids charge buildup, or by reactive sputtering of a metal target in oxygen or nitrogen.

faq.q: What is the racetrack on a sputtering target?
faq.a: It is the ring-shaped erosion groove that forms under the region of strongest magnetic confinement. Rotating the magnets behind the target spreads the erosion and extends target life.

反応性スパッタリング.desc: Sputtering a metal target in an atmosphere containing a reactive gas such as nitrogen or oxygen to form nitride or oxide films. It is used for films such as titanium nitride (TiN).

about.p: A metal target, such as titanium, is sputtered in argon mixed with a reactive gas such as nitrogen or oxygen. Metal atoms leaving the target combine with the reactive species, mainly on the growing film surface but also partly on the target itself, producing nitride or oxide films such as TiN, TaN or AlN. Film stoichiometry, resistivity and stress are tuned through the reactive gas flow or partial pressure. The method avoids compound targets, which are often brittle, hard to manufacture and poorly conducting, so a robust metal target can run on simple DC power.

As reactive gas flow rises, the target surface itself becomes covered with compound. Compounds have a much lower sputter yield than metals, so the deposition rate suddenly drops to a fraction of its metallic value; this is target poisoning. Reducing the gas does not immediately reverse it, because the compound layer must be sputtered away first, so rate and partial pressure versus flow trace a hysteresis loop. The highest-rate stoichiometric films lie in the unstable transition region, which is held with feedback that monitors plasma optical emission or gas partial pressure and adjusts the flow.

about.h: Reactive sputtering vs. sputtering a compound target
about.p: Sputtering a ceramic compound target directly gives composition close to the target, but insulating targets need RF power, deposition is slow and targets can crack. Reactive sputtering trades this for process-control complexity: composition depends on gas flow, pumping speed and power, and must be managed against poisoning. For insulating products such as oxides, compound buildup on target areas that are not fully cleaned can charge up and cause arcing, so pulsed DC or mid-frequency AC power supplies are often used to discharge the surface periodically.

Titanium nitride is the classic example: reactively sputtered TiN serves as a diffusion barrier and adhesion layer, a metal hard mask for etching, and a work-function layer in high-k metal gates, where its composition shifts the effective work function. TaN barriers under copper are made the same way. Outside logic, reactively sputtered aluminum nitride is used as a piezoelectric film in acoustic-wave RF filters, and a variety of oxide films are produced for optical and dielectric coatings.

faq.q: What is target poisoning in reactive sputtering?
faq.a: It is the coating of the target surface with nitride or oxide when reactive gas flow is too high. Because compounds sputter much more slowly than metal, the deposition rate drops sharply.

faq.q: Why does reactive sputtering show hysteresis?
faq.a: Once the target is poisoned, the compound layer must be sputtered off before the target returns to metallic mode, so the transition happens at different gas flows when increasing and decreasing the flow.

faq.q: How is TiN deposited by sputtering?
faq.a: A titanium target is sputtered in an argon and nitrogen mixture, and the titanium reacts with nitrogen to form TiN on the wafer. The nitrogen flow sets the film's composition and properties.

真空蒸着.desc: Forming a film by heating a material in vacuum until it evaporates and condenses on the substrate. Electron-beam heating handles high-melting-point materials, but step coverage is poor.

about.p: The source material is heated in a chamber pumped to about 1e-4 Pa or better until its vapor pressure becomes significant and atoms leave its surface. At that pressure the mean free path of the atoms is much longer than the distance to the substrate, so they travel in straight lines without collisions and condense where they land. They arrive with only thermal energy, around 0.1 eV. Deposition rate and thickness are commonly monitored with a quartz crystal microbalance, whose resonant frequency falls as film accumulates on it.

Resistive evaporation passes current through a boat or filament of a refractory metal such as tungsten or molybdenum holding the source; it is simple but limited to materials that evaporate below the boat's temperature, and the boat can contaminate the film. Electron-beam evaporation instead focuses electrons accelerated through several kilovolts onto the source in a water-cooled crucible, melting only a small spot. It can evaporate refractory metals and oxides with little crucible contamination, though the electron impact also generates X-rays that can create charge traps in sensitive gate dielectrics.

Because atoms fly straight from the source, surfaces facing away from it receive little material, so step coverage over topography is poor and sidewalls stay thin. Rotating planetary substrate holders improve uniformity across wafers but cannot make the coating conformal. Lift-off turns this weakness into a patterning method: resist is patterned with an undercut profile, metal is evaporated over everything, and the film breaks cleanly at the resist edges, so dissolving the resist removes unwanted metal. This is widely used for electrodes on compound semiconductors, where etching the metal would be difficult.

Sputtering ejects atoms from a target by ion bombardment, and they arrive with several to tens of eV, giving denser films with better adhesion. In evaporation, components of an alloy with different vapor pressures leave at different rates, so film composition drifts, whereas a sputtered film closely matches the target once its surface stabilizes. Sputtering also covers large areas more uniformly, so it dominates silicon IC metallization. Evaporation remains common for lift-off metal stacks, research, and thermal evaporation of organic layers in OLED displays.

faq.q: What is the difference between evaporation and sputtering?
faq.a: Evaporation boils material off a heated source and the atoms arrive gently by line of sight; sputtering knocks atoms off a target with ions and they arrive with more energy. Sputtering gives better adhesion and alloy composition control, while evaporation suits lift-off and high-purity films.

faq.q: Why does evaporation give poor step coverage?
faq.a: In high vacuum the evaporated atoms travel in straight lines without scattering, so features shadow one another and vertical sidewalls receive very little material.

faq.q: What is e-beam evaporation used for?
faq.a: It is used to deposit high-melting-point metals and oxides with low contamination, and it is common for lift-off patterning of contacts on compound semiconductors and for optical coatings.

HDP-CVD(高密度プラズマCVD).desc: CVD using a high-density plasma that deposits while ion sputtering trims film at the trench openings. It has been used to fill narrow trenches with insulator without voids.
HDP-CVD(高密度プラズマCVD).title: HDP-CVD: High-Density Plasma CVD for Void-Free Gap Fill
HDP-CVD(高密度プラズマCVD).description: HDP-CVD deposits oxide while ion sputtering trims the film at trench openings, filling narrow gaps without voids. How it works and where it is used.

about.h: Deposition and sputtering at the same time
about.p: HDP-CVD is a CVD process that uses a source such as an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) to create a dense plasma, above 10¹¹ cm⁻³, at low pressure, depositing SiO2 from gases such as SiH4 and O2. Separately from the power that generates the plasma, an RF bias on the substrate draws in ions such as argon. Its defining feature is that plasma density and ion energy can be tuned independently: while film deposits, ions simultaneously sputter it away. The ratio of deposition rate to sputter rate (the D/S ratio) is a key parameter that determines how a trench fills.

When ordinary CVD fills a narrow trench, film can build up thickly at the opening corners and overhang, sealing the entrance before the bottom fills and leaving a void. In HDP-CVD the sputter yield is higher on sloped surfaces than on flat ones, so the opening corners are cut back into facets and the entrance stays open. Ions also arrive nearly perpendicular to the substrate, so film builds quickly on the trench bottom and less on the sidewalls. Some of the sputtered material redeposits on the opposite sidewall. In this way the trench fills from the bottom up.

From roughly the 0.25 µm generation to around the 65 nm generation, HDP-CVD was widely used to fill STI (shallow trench isolation) trenches, for the pre-metal dielectric (PMD) between transistors and wiring, and for the inter-metal dielectric (IMD) between aluminum lines. Because the surface is etched during deposition, the film is relatively dense, and the process can also deposit fluorine-doped FSG with a lower dielectric constant and phosphorus-doped PSG. After gap fill the surface keeps bumps that follow the underlying topography, so it is generally planarized by CMP before the next step.

As trenches become narrower and deeper, with higher aspect ratios, sputtering alone can no longer keep the entrance from closing. Stronger sputtering brings its own problems: clipping trench corners and underlying films (such as the nitride liner in STI or the corners of metal lines), plus plasma damage and charging. Finer generations have therefore turned to alternating deposition and etch steps, sub-atmospheric CVD using ozone and TEOS, flowable CVD that fills trenches with a film that flows and then cures it, spin-on dielectrics, and ALD.

faq.q: What is the difference between HDP-CVD and PECVD?
faq.a: Both are plasma CVD, but compared with typical parallel-plate PECVD, HDP-CVD creates a denser plasma at lower pressure and controls ion energy separately with a substrate bias. Because sputtering occurs during deposition, it is suited to filling narrow trenches.

faq.q: What is the D/S ratio in HDP-CVD?
faq.a: It is the ratio of the deposition rate to the sputtering rate. If it is too high, openings tend to close and leave voids; if too low, deposition is slow and trench corners or underlying layers get etched. It is tuned to the trench shape through gas flows and bias power.

faq.q: Is HDP-CVD still used?
faq.a: It may still be used for gap fill in trenches with relatively low aspect ratios and between interconnect lines. For very narrow STI at leading-edge nodes, however, methods with better gap fill, such as flowable CVD, ALD and alternating deposition-etch processes, have come into use.

静電チャック.desc: A mechanism that holds the wafer to its stage by electrostatic force. It works in vacuum and allows backside gas for temperature control; it is widely used in deposition and etch tools.

スピンコート.desc: Dispensing a liquid at the center of the wafer and spinning it at high speed so centrifugal force spreads a thin, uniform film. It is used for photoresist and spin-on dielectrics.

about.p: Liquid is dispensed at the center of the wafer, either while it is stationary or slowly turning. The wafer then accelerates and the liquid spreads outward to cover the surface. At the final speed, typically thousands of revolutions per minute, centrifugal force flings excess liquid off the edge and the film thins rapidly. As it thins, solvent evaporation takes over, the viscosity rises, and the film sets. A bake afterward, called a soft bake or post-apply bake for photoresist, drives out remaining solvent before the next step.

Final thickness depends on the liquid's viscosity and solids content and on spin speed, scaling roughly as the inverse square root of speed, so engineers use a measured spin curve to choose speed for a target. Solvent evaporation rate, set by exhaust flow, temperature and humidity, also matters. Within-wafer variation of a few nanometers is achievable. For photoresist, thickness control is especially important because light reflecting inside the film causes linewidth to oscillate with thickness, a behavior known as the swing curve.

Surface tension leaves a thicker rim of material, the edge bead, around the wafer perimeter, and some liquid can wrap around to the back side. Left in place, this material can flake off as particles during handling, contaminate chucks and scanner stages, and upset focus near the edge. Coater tracks therefore spray solvent onto the outer few millimeters while spinning, called edge bead removal (EBR), and rinse the backside. Optical edge exposure of resist is an alternative way to clear the rim.

Spin coating applies photoresist, bottom anti-reflective coatings, spin-on carbon hard masks, spin-on glass and polyimide passivation. It is fast and gives excellent uniformity on flat round wafers, but most of the dispensed liquid is thrown off, so material efficiency is low. Over topography the film partially planarizes, ending up thicker in trenches and thinner over raised features. Square or very large substrates and deep structures are better served by alternatives such as slit coating or spray coating.

faq.q: How does spin speed affect film thickness?
faq.a: Higher speed gives a thinner film, with thickness falling roughly in proportion to one over the square root of spin speed for a given liquid. Viscosity and solids content set the overall thickness range.

faq.q: What is edge bead removal?
faq.a: It is a step in which solvent is applied to the outer few millimeters of a spinning wafer to remove the thick rim of resist left by spin coating, preventing particles and contamination of tools.

faq.q: Why is spin coating wasteful?
faq.a: Most of the dispensed liquid is flung off the wafer during spinning, so only a small fraction ends up in the film. Dispense volume and recipe are optimized to reduce waste of expensive resists.

領域選択成膜.desc: Growing a film only in certain places by exploiting differences in the underlying materials. Because it can save lithography and etch steps, it is being researched and introduced for advanced interconnects.

ArFエキシマレーザー.desc: A laser using argon and fluorine that emits 193 nm ultraviolet light. Combined with immersion, ArF immersion lithography is a leading-edge technique alongside EUV. The 248 nm version is the KrF excimer laser.

about.h: How an ArF laser produces 193 nm light
about.p: The laser chamber holds a gas mixture of a small amount of argon and fluorine diluted in neon as a buffer gas. A fast electrical discharge excites the mixture and forms ArF molecules that are bound only in the excited state, an excimer or excited dimer. When the molecule emits a 193 nm photon it drops to a repulsive ground state and immediately falls apart, so the lower laser level is effectively always empty and population inversion is easy to achieve. The laser is pulsed, with lithography lasers running at repetition rates of several kHz.

about.h: Why lithography needs a narrow line
about.p: Few materials are transparent at 193 nm, so projection lenses are built from fused silica with some calcium fluoride elements. With so little choice of glass, chromatic aberration cannot be corrected the way it is in visible optics, and the laser output must instead be line-narrowed to a bandwidth of well under a picometer. Lithography lasers also stabilize pulse energy and wavelength from pulse to pulse, and the fluorine-based gas fill degrades over time and is periodically refreshed. Photoresists had to change as well, because phenolic KrF resists absorb too strongly at 193 nm.

Resolution follows the Rayleigh relation R = k1·λ/NA. Dry ArF scanners reach a numerical aperture (NA) of about 0.93. ArF immersion fills the gap between the final lens and the wafer with water, whose refractive index at 193 nm is about 1.44, allowing NA up to 1.35. With k1 near its practical limit, single exposures resolve roughly 38 to 40 nm half-pitch. Smaller pitches are made with multiple patterning, such as litho-etch-litho-etch or self-aligned double and quadruple patterning, which is how ArF immersion reached nodes far below its single-exposure limit.

The KrF excimer laser uses krypton and fluorine to emit 248 nm and serves less critical layers where cost matters more than resolution. EUV lithography at 13.5 nm does not use an excimer laser at all: its light comes from a tin plasma, and its optics are reflective mirrors. Even in leading-edge chips patterned with EUV for the tightest layers, many other layers are still exposed with ArF immersion, which has higher throughput and a mature infrastructure.

faq.q: What wavelength does an ArF excimer laser emit?
faq.a: It emits deep-ultraviolet light at 193 nm. The KrF excimer laser, the previous lithography generation, emits at 248 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry ArF and ArF immersion lithography?
faq.a: Dry ArF has air between the lens and the wafer, limiting the numerical aperture to about 0.93. Immersion fills that gap with water, raising NA to about 1.35 so that features roughly 30 percent smaller can be resolved at the same wavelength.

faq.q: Why is it called an excimer laser?
faq.a: Excimer is short for excited dimer, a molecule such as ArF that is bound only in its excited state. Because it dissociates as soon as it emits, the lower laser level stays empty, making efficient ultraviolet lasing possible.

化学増幅型レジスト.desc: A resist in which acid generated by exposure catalyzes a chain of reactions during the post-exposure bake (PEB). It needs little exposure dose and is widely used from KrF onward, but is sensitive to basic contamination.

about.p: A chemically amplified resist (CAR) contains a polymer whose alkali-soluble groups are blocked by acid-labile protecting groups, plus a photoacid generator (PAG). Exposure produces only a small amount of acid. During the post-exposure bake (PEB), typically around 90–130 °C, each acid molecule catalytically removes protecting groups again and again, tens to hundreds of times, without being consumed. In a positive-tone CAR the deprotected regions become soluble in aqueous TMAH developer. One absorbed photon therefore drives many chemical events, which is the amplification.

about.h: Why KrF, ArF and EUV need it
about.p: Older i-line resists based on novolak and a diazonaphthoquinone sensitizer produce at most one photochemical event per absorbed photon, and novolak absorbs too strongly at deep-UV wavelengths. Excimer laser and EUV sources deliver comparatively little usable dose, so throughput depends on resist sensitivity. Chemical amplification, a concept developed at IBM in the 1980s, made practical doses possible and became standard from KrF (248 nm) onward. ArF resists use different, transparent polymer platforms, but the acid-catalyzed mechanism is the same.

Because the image is formed by acid moving during PEB, diffusion blurs the latent image and roughens line edges, so PEB temperature and time are tightly controlled and base quenchers are added to limit how far acid travels. The same sensitivity makes CARs vulnerable to airborne bases such as amines. Contaminants neutralize acid at the resist surface, leaving an insoluble skin that develops into T-shaped profiles, called T-topping, and the effect worsens with delay between exposure and PEB. Lithography tracks therefore use chemical filters to remove amines.

The trade-off is often summarized as resolution, line-edge roughness and sensitivity: improving one tends to worsen another, a tension that is especially visible in EUV. A positive CAR can also be developed in an organic solvent that dissolves the unexposed regions instead, called negative-tone development (NTD), which gives better image contrast for small contact holes and narrow trenches. Non-amplified resists, such as novolak for i-line, have no acid diffusion step and are simpler to control but need far higher doses at short wavelengths.

faq.q: What is a photoacid generator in a chemically amplified resist?
faq.a: A photoacid generator (PAG) is a compound that releases a strong acid when it absorbs exposure light; that acid then catalyzes the deprotection reaction during the post-exposure bake.

faq.q: Why is the post-exposure bake so critical for chemically amplified resists?
faq.a: The amplification reaction and acid diffusion both happen during PEB, so small changes in its temperature or time change the dose response and the printed linewidth.

faq.q: What causes T-topping in photoresist?
faq.a: T-topping occurs when airborne bases such as amines neutralize the photogenerated acid at the top of a chemically amplified resist, leaving an insoluble surface layer that overhangs the developed pattern.

ポジ型フォトレジスト.desc: A photoresist whose exposed areas dissolve and are removed during development. One whose exposed areas remain is a negative resist.

位相シフトマスク.desc: A photomask that shifts the phase of light passing through neighboring openings, using interference to improve image contrast and resolution.

マルチパターニング.desc: Forming patterns with a pitch too fine for a single exposure by splitting them across several exposures or process steps. Splitting into two is double patterning.

about.h: Why one exposure is not enough
about.p: Resolution follows R = k1·λ/NA. Argon fluoride (ArF) immersion lithography combines a 193 nm wavelength with NA 1.35, and with k1 near its practical limit of about 0.27 the finest half-pitch is roughly 39 nm, a pitch of about 80 nm. Layers in advanced logic and memory need tighter pitches than that. Multiple patterning reaches them by building the final pattern from several exposures or from process steps that multiply a relaxed pattern, so no single exposure has to resolve the final pitch.

In litho-etch-litho-etch (LELE), the layout is decomposed into two masks, often described as coloring, so that features closer than the single-exposure limit land on different masks; each is printed and etched in turn. Three masks (LELELE) extend the idea. Two catches dominate. Overlay error between exposures directly changes the spacing between neighboring features, demanding very tight alignment. And some layouts, such as three mutually close features, cannot be split into two colors, so design rules must forbid them.

about.h: SADP and SAQP: spacers set the pitch
about.p: Self-aligned double patterning (SADP) prints mandrel lines at a relaxed pitch, coats them with a conformal film, usually by atomic layer deposition (ALD), and etches it back to leave spacers on both sidewalls. Removing the mandrels leaves spacer lines at half the original pitch, with widths set by film thickness, giving excellent uniformity and no overlay between halves. Repeating the process gives self-aligned quadruple patterning (SAQP). The result is a regular grating, so additional cut or block masks remove unwanted segments, which pushes designs toward unidirectional lines.

Every extra mask, deposition and etch adds cost, cycle time and opportunities for defects, and each step contributes variation: in spacer schemes, for example, mandrel width errors make alternate spaces unequal, known as pitch walking. These costs drove adoption of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography at 13.5 nm, which returns many layers to a single exposure. At the very tightest pitches, EUV itself can again be combined with multiple patterning.

faq.q: What is the difference between LELE and SADP?
faq.a: LELE splits the layout into two masks that are exposed and etched separately, so overlay between them matters. SADP uses sidewall spacers on a single printed pattern to halve the pitch in a self-aligned way, with line width set by film thickness.

faq.q: Why is multiple patterning expensive?
faq.a: Each layer needs extra masks, lithography passes, depositions, etches and inspections, which raise cost and cycle time and add sources of variation and defects.

faq.q: Does EUV eliminate multiple patterning?
faq.a: EUV allows many layers to be printed in a single exposure, greatly reducing the need for multiple patterning. At the finest pitches, however, EUV can still be combined with double patterning.

ペリクル.desc: A thin membrane stretched a short distance above a photomask. It keeps particles off the mask surface, and particles landing on the pellicle are out of focus and do not print.
ペリクル.title: Pellicle: How It Protects Photomasks (and Why EUV Is Hard)
ペリクル.description: A pellicle is a thin membrane above a photomask that keeps particles out of focus so they don't print. How it works and why EUV pellicles are so hard to make.

about.p: A photomask, or reticle, is imaged onto every exposure field of every wafer it prints. A single particle on its patterned surface therefore becomes a repeating defect that can kill the same die location across thousands of wafers. Masks are expensive, and cleaning them repeatedly risks damaging the pattern. The pellicle solves this by keeping particles off the patterned surface entirely, so that contamination arriving during handling, storage and exposure lands somewhere harmless.

The pellicle is a thin transparent membrane, under 1 µm thick for deep-ultraviolet tools, stretched on a frame about 6 mm from the patterned surface. The projection lens is focused on the pattern, and its depth of focus at the mask side is a tiny fraction of a millimeter. A particle on the pellicle is therefore millimeters out of focus; its image is so blurred that it only slightly dims a wide area instead of printing as a sharp defect. The membrane must transmit the exposure light with minimal loss and stay stable under prolonged irradiation.

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light at 13.5 nm is strongly absorbed by every material, so an EUV pellicle must be only tens of nanometers thick, made from materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotube films, and still transmits only around 90% per pass. Because EUV masks are reflective, light crosses the pellicle twice, compounding the loss. The membrane also absorbs part of the high source power and heats up, so it must survive high temperatures while remaining mechanically intact across the full mask area.

The pellicle protects the mask, not the wafer. In ArF immersion lithography, a topcoat over the photoresist keeps immersion water from leaching resist components, and a bottom antireflective coating (BARC) under the resist controls reflections; neither has anything to do with mask contamination. A pellicle also cannot fix defects already present in the mask pattern or particles trapped under it during mounting, so masks are inspected before the pellicle is attached.

faq.q: What is a pellicle in lithography?
faq.a: A pellicle is a thin transparent membrane mounted on a frame a few millimeters above a photomask's pattern. Particles land on the membrane instead of the mask, where they are out of focus and do not print.

faq.q: Why is an EUV pellicle hard to make?
faq.a: All materials absorb EUV strongly, so the membrane must be only tens of nanometers thick yet span the whole mask, survive heating from absorbed power, and still transmit around 90% of the light on each pass.

faq.q: Does a pellicle prevent all mask defects?
faq.a: No. It only keeps new particles off the patterned surface after mounting; pattern defects, or particles trapped underneath when the pellicle is attached, still print.

フォトマスク(レチクル).desc: The master pattern used for exposure, typically a light-blocking pattern on a quartz substrate (reflective for EUV). For reduction scanners it is made four times larger than the pattern on the wafer.

about.p: Mask making starts from a mask blank: a low-defect, very flat quartz plate 6 inches square and about 6 mm thick, coated with a chromium or MoSi absorber film and resist. An electron-beam writer exposes the pattern directly into the resist. Single-beam writers can take over ten hours for a complex mask, so advanced masks with heavy optical proximity correction (OPC) or curvilinear shapes use multi-beam writers with hundreds of thousands of beamlets. After development and etching, the mask is measured, inspected for defects, repaired where possible and fitted with a pellicle.

Scanners project the mask through reduction optics, so mask features are four times larger than on the wafer, which makes them easier to write and makes small mask errors shrink on the wafer. One exposure covers a field of about 26 mm by 33 mm, roughly 858 mm², on the wafer. This reticle limit caps the size of a single die, which is why very large processors approach it and why larger systems use chiplets. Silicon interposers bigger than one field are made by stitching wiring across adjacent exposures. High-NA EUV fields are half the standard size.

A binary mask simply blocks light with chromium. An attenuated phase-shift mask uses a partially transmitting MoSi film that also shifts the light phase by 180 degrees, sharpening the image at feature edges. Because EUV light at 13.5 nm is absorbed by almost every material, EUV masks are reflective: a multilayer stack of molybdenum and silicon acts as a mirror, and a patterned absorber on top defines dark regions. EUV blanks must be nearly free of defects, since a buried flaw in the multilayer cannot be removed later.

Any defect on a mask prints in every field of every wafer exposed with it, appearing on wafer maps as a failure at the same position in each shot. A pellicle, a transparent membrane under 1 µm thick stretched on a frame about 6 mm above the patterned surface, keeps particles away from the focal plane so they are blurred and do not print. EUV pellicles must be only tens of nanometers thick, made of materials such as polysilicon or carbon nanotubes, to transmit around 90 percent of the light and survive heating.

faq.q: What is the difference between a photomask and a reticle?
faq.a: Historically a photomask carried the pattern for an entire wafer at 1:1, while a reticle carried one or a few dies for a stepper that repeats it across the wafer. Today the terms are used almost interchangeably for the master plate used in scanners.

faq.q: Why are photomask patterns four times larger than on the wafer?
faq.a: Scanners use 4x reduction projection optics. Larger features are easier to write and inspect on the mask, and errors in mask dimensions are reduced by the same factor when printed.

faq.q: What is a pellicle on a photomask?
faq.a: It is a thin transparent membrane mounted a few millimeters above the mask pattern. Particles that land on it are out of focus during exposure and therefore do not print on the wafer.

スキャナー.desc: An exposure tool that moves the mask and wafer in sync under a slit of light. It is the mainstream production lithography tool and generally projects the mask pattern at 1/4 size.

about.p: A scanner never illuminates the whole mask at once. Light passes through a slit a few millimeters wide, and the reticle and wafer stages move synchronously in opposite directions so the image sweeps across the field. Because the projection optics reduce the pattern by 4×, the reticle stage travels four times faster than the wafer stage. A standard field is about 26 mm × 33 mm, roughly 858 mm², with the long side in the scan direction. After each field the wafer steps to the next position, which is why the method is called step-and-scan.

A stepper exposes an entire field in one static flash, so its lens must be nearly perfect over the full field area. A scanner only needs a good image over a narrow slit, using the lens's best central region, and it averages lens and illumination variations along the scan direction. The trade-off is mechanical: both stages must accelerate at several m/s² and still track each other with nanometer accuracy during the scan. That capability made larger fields and better uniformity possible, and scanners replaced steppers for critical layers in high-volume manufacturing.

about.h: What happens before the light turns on
about.p: Each wafer is measured before exposure. Alignment sensors read marks from earlier layers to correct position, rotation and expansion, and a level sensor maps surface height so the image stays within the shallow depth of focus as the wafer moves. Overlay results from downstream metrology are fed back as corrections for later lots. Many scanners carry two wafer stages so one wafer is measured while another is exposed. The tool is linked to a coater/developer track, and temperatures around it are held to about ±0.1 °C to limit thermal distortion.

Deep-ultraviolet (DUV) scanners use KrF (248 nm) or ArF (193 nm) excimer lasers with refractive lenses; ArF immersion fills the gap under the lens with water to reach a numerical aperture of about 1.35. Extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) scanners use 13.5 nm light, which every material absorbs, so they rely on mirrors and reflective masks coated with molybdenum/silicon multilayers reflecting about 70%. High-NA EUV halves the exposure field. The field size sets the reticle limit on die area, one reason very large designs are split into chiplets.

faq.q: What is the difference between a scanner and a stepper?
faq.a: A stepper exposes each field in one static shot, while a scanner moves the reticle and wafer in sync under a narrow slit of light, which uses less lens area and gives larger, more uniform fields.

faq.q: What is the maximum field size of a lithography scanner?
faq.a: About 26 mm × 33 mm per exposure on standard scanners, which effectively limits the largest die that can be printed; high-NA EUV fields are half that size.

faq.q: Why does the reticle move faster than the wafer in a scanner?
faq.a: The projection lens shrinks the pattern by 4×, so the reticle must travel four times the distance, and thus four times the speed, of the wafer during each scan.

焦点深度(DOF).desc: The range of focus over which a pattern prints with acceptable quality. Raising the numerical aperture improves resolution but reduces DOF, which makes wafer planarity important.

about.p: Lithography is governed by two Rayleigh relations: resolution R = k1·λ/NA and depth of focus DOF = k2·λ/NA², where λ is the exposure wavelength, NA the numerical aperture of the projection lens, and k1 and k2 process-dependent factors. Raising NA improves resolution in proportion to NA but shrinks DOF with its square. Shortening the wavelength helps resolution while reducing DOF only linearly. Leading-edge processes are left with a DOF of roughly 100 nm, which must cover every source of height and focus error.

about.h: What uses up the focus budget
about.p: The usable DOF has to absorb wafer non-flatness within each exposure field, topography left by underlying layers, resist thickness, chucking distortion, lens field curvature and the scanner's own focus-control errors. Site flatness over a field such as 26 × 33 mm is therefore held to tens of nanometres or less. Engineers measure the process window with a focus–exposure matrix: linewidth is plotted against focus for several doses (Bossung curves), and the overlapping range that keeps linewidth and profile within specification defines the practical DOF and exposure latitude.

about.h: How fabs protect depth of focus
about.p: Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) planarizes each interconnect level globally, removing the millimetre-to-centimetre topography that reflow or etch-back cannot, which made stacks of ten or more wiring levels practical. Scanners measure wafer height and tilt before each shot and level the wafer so the image plane follows the surface. Thinner resist films reduce the vertical range that must stay in focus. Resolution enhancement techniques such as off-axis illumination can also enlarge DOF for dense periodic patterns.

about.h: Why High-NA EUV makes DOF harder
about.p: Standard EUV scanners use NA 0.33 at a 13.5 nm wavelength, and High-NA EUV raises NA to 0.55 for about 1.7× better resolution. Because DOF scales with 1/NA², the same k2 gives roughly (0.55/0.33)² ≈ 2.8 times less depth of focus. That tightens every item in the focus budget, pushing toward thinner resists, flatter wafers and more precise focus control. High resolution and generous DOF pull in opposite directions, and much of lithography engineering is managing that conflict.

faq.q: What is the formula for depth of focus in lithography?
faq.a: The usual expression is DOF = k2·λ/NA², where λ is the wavelength, NA the numerical aperture and k2 a process factor. It shows that DOF falls with the square of NA.

faq.q: Is depth of focus the same as depth of field?
faq.a: No. Depth of field is the range of object distances that appear sharp, while depth of focus is the tolerance in the position of the image plane. In lithography the wafer sits in the image plane, so depth of focus is the relevant quantity.

faq.q: Why does a higher NA reduce depth of focus?
faq.a: A higher NA collects light over a wider cone of angles, so rays converge more steeply onto the image. A small shift away from best focus then spreads those rays more, blurring the image sooner.

オーバーレイ(重ね合わせ精度).desc: How accurately a new pattern is placed relative to the patterns made in earlier steps. Misalignment causes defects such as missed contacts, so it is controlled at the nanometer level.

about.p: Overlay is checked with dedicated targets, usually placed in the scribe lines between dies, that combine a feature printed in the previous layer with one printed in the current layer. Image-based tools find the center of each pattern and report the offset between them, while diffraction-based tools infer the shift from intensity differences in light diffracted by stacked gratings. Measurements from many sites are fitted to a wafer-level model, and the correction terms are fed back to the exposure tool so that later lots are printed closer to the ideal position.

Error accumulates from many sources: stage and reticle positioning, lens distortion, differences between the tools that exposed each layer, and distortion of the wafer itself. Film stress bows the wafer, high-temperature steps can introduce slip dislocations, and temperature matters directly: silicon expands by about 2.6 ppm/K, so a 0.1 °C change moves the edge of a 300 mm wafer by tens of nanometers. Scanners therefore measure alignment marks on every wafer and correct translation, rotation, magnification and higher-order terms, and the exposure area is held within about ±0.1 °C.

A common rule is that overlay must be held to roughly a quarter or a fifth of the minimum feature size, which means a few nanometers or less at advanced nodes. The budget is tightest in multiple patterning. In litho-etch-litho-etch (LELE) double patterning, any shift of the second exposure changes the spacing to neighboring lines directly: a 2 nm error on a 20 nm space is a 10% change in spacing, affecting wire capacitance and short risk. Spacer-based self-aligned double patterning (SADP) avoids this because line positions are set by deposition, not by a second alignment.

about.h: Overlay vs. CD, and design for misalignment
about.p: Overlay describes where a pattern lands; critical dimension (CD) describes how large it is. Both consume the same edge-placement margin, since a contact can miss its target because it is misplaced or because it is too small. Designers and process engineers buy back margin with self-aligned schemes. In a self-aligned contact (SAC), the gate is capped with silicon nitride, so a misaligned contact etch stops on the nitride instead of shorting to the gate. This lets gate-to-contact spacing shrink without demanding impossible alignment.

faq.q: What is the difference between overlay and alignment in lithography?
faq.a: Alignment is the act of measuring wafer marks and positioning the wafer before exposure; overlay is the resulting placement error between the new layer and earlier layers, measured afterwards on dedicated targets.

faq.q: How tight is overlay at advanced nodes?
faq.a: Requirements are roughly one quarter to one fifth of the smallest feature size, which works out to a few nanometers or less, and even tighter between the two exposures of LELE double patterning.

faq.q: Why does temperature affect overlay?
faq.a: Wafers, reticles and tool structures expand with temperature; for silicon at about 2.6 ppm/K, a 0.1 °C change shifts features at the edge of a 300 mm wafer by tens of nanometers, which is larger than the overlay budget.

ラインエッジラフネス(LER).desc: Nanometer-scale roughness along the edges of fine resist lines. It causes line-width variation (LWR) and leads to variation in transistor characteristics.

about.p: Line edge roughness (LER) measures how far a single pattern edge wanders from a straight line, usually reported as three standard deviations (3σ) of the edge position. Line width roughness (LWR) measures the variation of the distance between the two edges of a line. If the two edges roughen independently, LWR is about √2 times LER; correlated edges give less. Roughness is also characterized by its spatial frequency content: long-wavelength variation changes the effective width of a transistor or wire, while very short-wavelength wiggles tend to average out over the device.

Several sources add together. Resist polymers and their aggregates are a few nanometers across, setting a floor on edge smoothness. In chemically amplified resists, photogenerated acid diffuses during the post-exposure bake, blurring the latent image. The number of photons absorbed and acid generator molecules activated in each small area fluctuates statistically, called shot noise. A low-contrast aerial image makes all of these worse, because a small change in local dose then moves the edge further. Etch can then transfer, amplify or partly smooth the resulting roughness.

Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength, so a 13.5 nm EUV photon carries about 92 eV, roughly 14 times the 6.4 eV of a 193 nm ArF photon. At the same dose, only about one fourteenth as many photons arrive, perhaps a few hundred to a few thousand in a 20 nm square, and the relative fluctuation scales as 1/√N. These stochastic effects show up as LER, missing or bridging features and unopened contacts. Raising dose reduces them but lowers throughput, an instance of the trade-off between resolution, roughness and sensitivity.

Roughness of 2-3 nm is minor at large dimensions but exceeds 10 percent of a 20 nm line. In transistors, gate-length variation along the width causes threshold-voltage and leakage variation between nominally identical devices, and in interconnects it raises wire resistance and its spread. Trimming or shrinking a pattern does not remove roughness, so it becomes a larger fraction of the final width. LER is typically measured from top-down critical-dimension scanning electron microscope (CD-SEM) images, with corrections for image noise, which otherwise inflates the result.

faq.q: What is the difference between LER and LWR?
faq.a: LER describes the roughness of one edge of a line, while LWR describes the variation in the line's width, combining both edges. For uncorrelated edges LWR is about √2 times LER.

faq.q: Why is line edge roughness worse with EUV?
faq.a: Each EUV photon carries about 14 times the energy of an ArF photon, so far fewer photons deliver the same dose, and the statistical fluctuation in photon count shows up as rough edges and random defects.

faq.q: How is LER measured?
faq.a: It is usually extracted from top-down CD-SEM images by detecting edge positions along a line and computing their 3σ deviation, with care taken to remove the contribution of SEM image noise.

プロセスウィンドウ.desc: The range of exposure dose and focus over which pattern dimensions stay within tolerance. The wider it is, the more robust manufacturing is to variation.

about.p: The process window is usually found by exposing a focus-exposure matrix, a wafer on which each field receives a different combination of dose and focus, and measuring the resulting critical dimension (CD). Plotting CD against focus for several doses gives Bossung curves. The region of dose and focus where CD stays within tolerance, for example ±10 percent of target, is the exposure-defocus window. It is often summarized by exposure latitude, the allowed dose range as a percentage, and depth of focus (DOF), the usable focus range at a given exposure latitude.

Resolution and process window are different things: a pattern may print at best dose and focus yet fail with small deviations. Pushing the resolution factor k1 lower reduces image contrast and narrows the window. DOF scales roughly as wavelength divided by the square of numerical aperture, so higher-NA optics give less focus margin. In production, focus and dose drift with scanner variation, wafer flatness, underlying topography and resist-thickness changes, all of which consume margin before any pattern-specific weakness is considered.

Every pattern on a mask has its own window. Dense lines, isolated lines, line ends and contact holes have different best focus and dose, so the usable process window is the overlap of all of them, and a few weak layout spots, often called hotspots, can set the limit for the whole layer. Optical proximity correction (OPC), sub-resolution assist features, and source-mask optimization, which jointly tunes illumination shape and mask pattern, aim largely to enlarge this common window rather than just to improve best-case resolution.

Engineers center production on the middle of the window so that normal variation leaves margin on all sides, and they track dose and focus with monitoring patterns and scanner leveling data. A larger window means fewer wafers drift out of specification and less rework. When a new layout or resist is introduced, comparing the size and shape of windows gives a direct, quantitative way to judge which option is more manufacturable, beyond simply whether the smallest feature resolves.

faq.q: What is a Bossung curve?
faq.a: A Bossung curve plots critical dimension against focus, with one curve per exposure dose. A set of them shows how sensitive a pattern is to focus and dose and is used to determine the process window.

faq.q: What are exposure latitude and depth of focus?
faq.a: Exposure latitude is the range of dose, as a percentage, over which CD stays within tolerance; depth of focus is the corresponding usable focus range. Together they describe the size of the process window.

faq.q: How can the lithography process window be widened?
faq.a: Common methods include optical proximity correction, sub-resolution assist features, optimized illumination and source-mask optimization, better resist contrast, and reducing wafer topography and focus errors.

High-NA EUV.desc: Next-generation EUV lithography that raises the projection optics' numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 to improve resolution.

about.p: Resolution follows R = k1 × λ / NA, where λ is wavelength and NA is the numerical aperture of the projection optics. EUV already uses the 13.5 nm wavelength, so High-NA EUV improves resolution by raising NA from 0.33 to 0.55, about 1.7 times finer for the same k1. That brings pitches in the low 20 nm range within reach of a single exposure, instead of splitting a layer into several exposures with standard EUV. The wavelength, the reflective mirror optics and the vacuum environment stay the same as in standard EUV.

about.h: Anamorphic optics and a half-size field
about.p: EUV masks are reflective multilayer mirrors illuminated at an oblique angle. A larger NA would require light cones at angles the mask cannot reflect efficiently with 4× reduction in both directions. High-NA optics therefore reduce by 4× in one direction and 8× in the other, keeping the standard 6-inch mask. The cost is that the exposure field on the wafer shrinks to half of the usual 26 × 33 mm. Dies larger than this half field must be split and stitched from two exposures, or the design must be partitioned, for example into chiplets.

about.h: Trade-offs that come with higher NA
about.p: Depth of focus shrinks roughly with the square of NA, so higher-NA patterning tolerates less wafer non-flatness and calls for thinner resists. Thinner resists absorb fewer photons, and smaller features contain fewer photons per edge, so stochastic effects such as line edge roughness and random missing or bridging features become harder to control without higher dose, which costs throughput. The tools are larger and far more expensive than standard EUV scanners, so whether High-NA is cheaper than multi-patterning depends on the layer and the number of exposures it replaces.

faq.q: What is the numerical aperture of High-NA EUV?
faq.a: High-NA EUV uses projection optics with an NA of 0.55, compared with 0.33 for standard EUV scanners, at the same 13.5 nm wavelength.

faq.q: Why is the High-NA EUV exposure field half size?
faq.a: The optics use 8× reduction in one direction and 4× in the other to keep mask reflection angles workable with standard 6-inch masks. With 8× in one direction, the same mask covers only half the usual 26 × 33 mm field on the wafer.

faq.q: Does High-NA EUV use a shorter wavelength?
faq.a: No. It keeps the 13.5 nm EUV wavelength and improves resolution solely by increasing the numerical aperture of the optics.

反射防止膜(BARC).desc: A layer coated under the resist that suppresses standing waves in the resist and dimension variation over topography caused by light reflected from the substrate.

about.h: What substrate reflection does to resist
about.p: Exposure light that passes through the photoresist reflects from the layers below, and silicon and metal films reflect strongly. The reflected wave interferes with the incoming wave and sets up standing waves, so the dose varies periodically through the resist thickness and developed sidewalls show ripples. The total energy coupled into the resist also oscillates with resist thickness, making linewidth swing periodically with small thickness changes, which is called the swing curve. Over topography, light reflected sideways from sloped edges exposes regions under the mask and causes notching.

A bottom anti-reflective coating (BARC) is a thin layer placed between the substrate and the resist. Its refractive index n, absorption coefficient k and thickness are chosen so that light entering it is absorbed and the residual reflections from its top and bottom surfaces largely cancel by destructive interference. A well-tuned BARC reduces reflectivity back into the resist to below about 1%, which flattens the swing curve and removes most standing-wave and notching effects. Because the optimum thickness depends on wavelength and the underlying stack, BARC thickness is specified for each layer.

Organic BARCs are spin-coated and baked polymers containing light-absorbing groups; they also smooth small topography and provide a good surface for resist adhesion, a role otherwise played by HMDS priming. Most do not dissolve in developer, so after lithography the BARC exposed in the resist openings is removed by a short plasma etch before the underlying film is etched, which consumes some resist. Inorganic BARCs, such as silicon oxynitride deposited by CVD, are tuned through composition and can remain in the film stack or double as a hard mask.

about.h: BARC vs. TARC and top coat
about.p: A top anti-reflective coating (TARC) sits on top of the resist and reduces reflection at the air-resist interface, which mainly reduces the swing effect; it does not stop reflection from the substrate. A top coat in ArF immersion lithography serves a different purpose: it keeps the immersion water from leaching resist components such as the photoacid generator and keeps the surface hydrophobic for fast stage motion. A pellicle, by contrast, is a membrane that protects the photomask from particles, not part of the wafer film stack.

faq.q: What does BARC stand for in lithography?
faq.a: BARC stands for bottom anti-reflective coating, an absorbing layer coated under the photoresist to suppress reflections from the substrate during exposure.

faq.q: What is the difference between BARC and TARC?
faq.a: A BARC sits below the resist and suppresses substrate reflection, standing waves and notching, while a TARC sits on top of the resist and reduces reflection at the top surface, mainly reducing swing-curve variation.

faq.q: How is a BARC removed after lithography?
faq.a: Most organic BARCs are not removed by the developer, so the BARC in the resist openings is opened with a short plasma etch before the underlying film is etched, and the remainder is stripped with the resist.

ナノインプリントリソグラフィ.desc: Transferring patterns by pressing a mold with fine features into resist on the wafer. It can make fine patterns without expensive optics.

プラズマ.desc: A state in which a gas is ionized into a mixture of electrons, ions and radicals (reactive neutrals). It is used in many processes, including dry etching, plasma CVD and ashing.

about.h: What is inside a process plasma
about.p: Process plasmas are weakly ionized: only a small fraction of the gas molecules are ionized, while the rest are neutral molecules and radicals. An applied radio-frequency or microwave field accelerates the light electrons to energies of a few electronvolts, and their collisions break up and ionize the gas, while the heavy ions and neutrals stay relatively cool. This non-equilibrium state lets chemistry that would otherwise need hundreds of degrees run on a cool wafer. Between the glowing plasma and any surface forms a thin sheath whose electric field accelerates positive ions toward the wafer.

The two active ingredients do different jobs. Radicals are electrically neutral, chemically reactive fragments that drift in all directions and react isotropically. Ions are accelerated across the sheath and strike the wafer nearly vertically, adding physical energy and directionality. Reactive ion etching combines them to get vertical profiles, and the Bosch process for deep silicon etching takes this further by alternating SF6 etch steps with C4F8 passivation steps every few seconds; ions clear the passivation only at the bottom, giving trenches with aspect ratios above 20 and small sidewall ripples called scallops.

Plasma appears throughout the fab. Plasma CVD (PECVD) deposits films at about 300 to 400 °C instead of the 600 to 800 °C of thermal CVD, and high-density plasma CVD combines deposition with ion sputtering to fill narrow gaps. Magnetron sputtering confines electrons with magnets to sustain a dense argon plasma at about 0.1 to 1 Pa. Oxygen plasma ashing strips photoresist. Plasma nitridation and radical oxidation modify thin dielectrics at low temperature, plasma doping implants dopants at sub-keV energies, and ion implanters extract their ions from a plasma source.

Plasmas also cause problems. Charge collecting on isolated gates or resist can stress gate oxides only a few nanometres thick; in ion implantation a plasma flood gun supplies low-energy electrons to neutralize this charge. Energetic ion bombardment can damage crystals, and PECVD films usually contain hydrogen from the precursors, so their quality is below that of thermal CVD films. Plasma density and gas flow must be uniform across the wafer to keep etch and deposition rates even. Note that the plasma dispersion effect in silicon photonics refers to free carriers in a solid, not to a gas discharge.

faq.q: Why is plasma used in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: Energetic electrons in a plasma create reactive radicals and ions without heating the wafer, enabling etching, deposition and surface treatment at low temperature. Ions accelerated by the sheath also make vertical, anisotropic etching possible.

faq.q: What is the difference between radicals and ions in a plasma?
faq.a: Radicals are neutral, highly reactive species that move randomly and etch isotropically, while ions carry charge, are accelerated by the sheath field and hit the wafer nearly vertically. Dry etching balances the two to control profile and selectivity.

faq.q: What is plasma damage?
faq.a: It is degradation caused by the plasma itself, mainly charge buildup that stresses thin gate oxides and lattice damage from ion bombardment. Process tuning, charge neutralization and layout rules are used to limit it.

ラジカル.desc: A neutral atom or molecule with an unpaired electron that is highly reactive chemically. Plasmas contain far more radicals than ions, and they drive chemical etching and deposition.

about.p: In a processing plasma, energetic electrons collide with feed-gas molecules. Some collisions ionize a molecule, but more of them simply break it apart into neutral fragments, because dissociation requires less energy than ionization; CF4 yields CF3 and F, and O2 yields atomic O. These fragments, with unpaired electrons, are radicals. Being uncharged, they are not pulled to the walls by the plasma sheath and survive longer than ions, so their density typically exceeds the ion density by two to three orders of magnitude or more.

Radicals arrive at the wafer from all directions and react spontaneously with suitable surfaces; fluorine radicals, for instance, convert silicon into volatile SiF4. On its own this chemistry is isotropic and highly selective. Ions are fewer, but the sheath accelerates them vertically, so they strike horizontal surfaces with tens to hundreds of electronvolts, enhancing reactions there and clearing passivation from trench bottoms. Anisotropic etching relies on this division of labour: radicals supply most of the chemistry, ions decide where it proceeds fastest, and sidewall passivation protects the vertical walls.

Some steps deliberately exclude ions. In a downstream or remote plasma, the plasma is generated away from the wafer so ions recombine before arriving and only long-lived radicals reach the surface. This gives damage-free resist ashing and isotropic cleans. Radical oxidation uses oxygen radicals to grow good-quality oxide at about 400–600 °C with little dependence on crystal orientation, which makes it suitable for FinFET fins and 3D NAND structures and for steps with tight thermal budgets.

Radical density depends on gas chemistry, pressure, RF power and how quickly radicals are consumed. Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) sources let engineers set plasma density, and with it radical and ion flux, separately from ion energy, and pulsed plasmas shift the mix of radical species. Consumption leads to loading effects: when a wafer exposes more etchable area, radicals are depleted and the etch rate falls. In deep, narrow features radicals must diffuse down the hole, so etch rate often decreases with aspect ratio.

faq.q: What is the difference between a radical and an ion in a plasma?
faq.a: A radical is an electrically neutral atom or molecule with an unpaired electron, so it is chemically reactive but not steered by electric fields. An ion carries charge and is accelerated by the sheath toward the wafer, giving directional bombardment.

faq.q: Why are there more radicals than ions in an etching plasma?
faq.a: Breaking a molecule apart takes less electron energy than ionizing it, so dissociation happens more often. Radicals also live longer because they are not drawn to the walls, so they accumulate to much higher densities than ions.

faq.q: Do radicals cause isotropic etching?
faq.a: Etching by radicals alone is isotropic because neutral radicals arrive from all directions. Directionality comes from ion bombardment combined with sidewall passivation.

ドライエッチング.desc: Removing material with plasma or gas instead of liquid chemicals. Combining ion bombardment allows anisotropic etching, which is essential for fine patterns.

about.h: What does the etching in a plasma
about.p: Etch plasmas are weakly ionized, typically about 0.01% or less, and contain electrons, positive ions, highly reactive radicals and neutral molecules. Radicals supply the chemistry and ions supply directional energy. Etching works only if the reaction product is volatile: silicon leaves as SiF4, SiCl4 or SiBr4, silicon dioxide etched with fluorocarbon gases such as CF4 or C4F8 leaves as SiF4 plus CO or CO2, and GaN etched with Cl2 and BCl3 leaves as GaCl3. Copper chlorides are not volatile at normal process temperatures, which is why copper lines are formed by damascene instead.

Ions and radicals together etch much faster than either alone; in a classic experiment, XeF2 gas plus an argon ion beam etched silicon about ten times faster than the sum of the two separately. Because ions arrive vertically, feature bottoms etch quickly while sidewalls do not. In addition, polymer from fluorocarbon gases or HBr-derived byproducts coats the sidewalls and blocks lateral attack, while ion bombardment clears it from the bottom. Too much passivation tapers the profile and too little causes bowing, so chemistry, bias and temperature are balanced.

Key figures are etch rate, uniformity, profile and selectivity; Cl2 and HBr etch polysilicon with selectivity above 100 to thin gate oxide. Endpoint is detected by optical emission spectroscopy (OES), watching emission lines that change when the film clears, such as CO at 483 nm dropping at the end of an oxide etch; interferometry helps when the open area is too small for a clear signal. Typical defects include microtrenching at feature corners and sidewall residues, which are removed by ashing and wet cleans to avoid corrosion and high contact resistance.

Wet etching dissolves films in liquid, usually isotropically, undercutting the mask by roughly the film thickness, but it is cheap, can process many wafers at once and gives high selectivity. Dry etching, including reactive ion etching (RIE) and high-density ICP etching, transfers mask patterns with little dimensional loss and is essential below a few micrometers. Fabs therefore use dry etching for patterning and wet processes for blanket film removal and cleaning. Many etch gases, especially fluorocarbons, have very high global warming potentials, so exhaust passes through abatement systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between dry etching and wet etching?
faq.a: Dry etching removes material with plasma or reactive gas and, with ion bombardment, can etch vertically for fine patterns. Wet etching uses liquid chemicals, is usually isotropic and undercuts the mask, but is simple, high-throughput and highly selective.

faq.q: Why can copper not be patterned by dry etching?
faq.a: Copper chlorides and fluorides do not evaporate below several hundred degrees Celsius, so reaction products stay on the surface instead of being pumped away. Copper wiring is therefore made by etching trenches in the dielectric, filling them with copper and polishing off the excess.

faq.q: How is the endpoint of a dry etch detected?
faq.a: Most tools monitor the plasma's optical emission at wavelengths tied to reaction products, which change sharply when the film clears and the underlayer is exposed. Laser or broadband interferometry of film thickness is used when the exposed area is small.

アッシング.desc: Removing photoresist that is no longer needed after etching or implantation by oxidizing it to ash, typically with an oxygen plasma.

about.p: Photoresist is an organic polymer of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. In an oxygen plasma, atomic oxygen radicals attack it and convert it into volatile CO, CO2 and H2O, which are pumped away; the name comes from this burning of the resist, as if to ash. Heating the wafer speeds the reaction. Many ashers are downstream (remote) designs in which the plasma is generated away from the wafer, so ions recombine before arriving and only radicals reach the surface, avoiding ion damage and charging of sensitive devices. Ashing is used after the resist has served as an etch or implant mask.

High-dose ion implantation drives hydrogen out of the resist surface and carbonizes it into a hard crust tens of nanometres thick, while the resist underneath stays soft. If the wafer is ashed hot immediately, gas released from the soft layer bursts through the crust, an effect called popping, scattering residue and particles. Post-implant strips therefore start at low temperature and ramp up, or remove the crust first with hydrogen-based plasma chemistry. The resist used for implant masking must also be thick enough to stop the ions, several times the projected range.

Oxygen plasma is a problem in copper interconnect stacks. SiOC low-k films owe their low dielectric constant to Si-CH3 (methyl) groups, and oxygen radicals strip these into Si-OH, which absorbs moisture and can raise the dielectric constant from about 3.0 to above 4. Porous films are damaged deeper because radicals penetrate through the pores. Reducing chemistries based on hydrogen replace oxygen in these steps, and silylation treatments and post-process dehydration bakes are used to repair or limit damage.

Ashing removes the organic bulk of the resist but not everything. Inorganic residues, metals introduced during implant or etch, and sidewall polymer from dry etching remain and are removed by a wet clean that follows. SPM (sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide, often about 4:1 at 120–150 °C), nicknamed piranha, oxidizes remaining organics. Chlorine-bearing etch residue must be removed promptly because it corrodes aluminium wiring. Ash-and-clean sequences are repeated throughout the flow, so their efficiency and gentleness affect both yield and cost.

faq.q: Why is it called ashing?
faq.a: The process burns the organic resist in an oxygen plasma, much like reducing material to ash, converting it into gases such as CO2 and H2O that are pumped away.

faq.q: What is the difference between ashing and wet resist stripping?
faq.a: Ashing removes resist dry, using plasma radicals, while wet stripping dissolves or oxidizes it with liquid chemistries such as SPM or organic strippers. In practice the two are often combined: ash first, then wet-clean the residue.

faq.q: Why are downstream ashers used?
faq.a: A downstream asher generates the plasma away from the wafer so only neutral radicals reach it. This avoids ion bombardment and charging damage to transistors and sensitive films.

終点検出.desc: Detecting the moment when the target film has been fully etched, commonly by monitoring changes in the plasma's emission spectrum.

アスペクト比.desc: The ratio of a hole's or trench's depth to its width. Higher ratios make etching and deposition harder; memory holes in 3D NAND reach several tens or more.

about.p: Aspect ratio is depth divided by width. A hole 100 nm across and 1 µm deep has an aspect ratio of 10. Memory holes in 3D NAND, about 100 nm wide and several µm deep, reach 50 to 100, and DRAM capacitor holes are also extremely tall and narrow. The same idea applies to lines: a copper interconnect's thickness-to-width ratio is often around 2. Aspect ratio should not be confused with selectivity, which is the ratio of etch rates of two materials, or with the overall shape of a die.

about.h: Why deep, narrow features are hard to etch
about.p: As aspect ratio rises, fewer reactive radicals reach the bottom because they react with or stick to the walls along the way, ions are deflected by charge built up on insulating sidewalls, and reaction products escape slowly. The etch rate therefore falls with depth, an effect called aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) or microloading, so narrow holes end up shallower than wide ones etched at the same time. Deep etches also suffer bowing, twisting and tapered bottoms, which is why high-aspect-ratio etching is one of the hardest steps in memory fabrication.

Physical vapor deposition (PVD) atoms travel in nearly straight lines, so sidewalls and bottoms of deep features are shadowed and receive little film. CVD under surface-reaction-limited conditions coats much more uniformly, and ALD can coat features with aspect ratios of several tens because each step is self-limiting. Filling a gap completely is harder than lining it: film builds up at the opening and pinches off, trapping a void. High-density plasma CVD, which sputters back the corners, and flowable CVD, which fills from the bottom, were developed for this.

Tall, thin structures can be pulled together during drying by the surface tension of liquid between them, and the force grows with aspect ratio and with narrower gaps. Low-surface-tension rinses such as IPA, hydrophobic surface treatments and supercritical CO2 drying reduce pattern collapse. In interconnects, raising aspect ratio lowers resistance but increases sidewall capacitance to neighbors, so it is balanced per metal level. In DRAM, capacitor aspect ratio is approaching practical limits, one motivation for stacking cells in 3D DRAM.

faq.q: How is aspect ratio calculated in semiconductor etching?
faq.a: Divide the depth of the hole or trench by its width or opening diameter. For example, a trench 50 nm wide and 500 nm deep has an aspect ratio of 10.

faq.q: What is ARDE in plasma etching?
faq.a: Aspect-ratio-dependent etching (ARDE) is the slowing of etch rate as features become narrower and deeper, because fewer radicals and ions reach the bottom and products escape more slowly. It makes narrow features shallower than wide ones etched at the same time.

faq.q: Why do high-aspect-ratio patterns collapse?
faq.a: When rinse liquid dries between tall, narrow structures, capillary forces from surface tension pull neighboring structures together. Higher aspect ratio and narrower spacing increase the risk.

ARDE(アスペクト比依存エッチング).desc: The slowdown of etch rate in narrower, deeper features because ions and radicals reach the bottom less easily. Also called the microloading effect.

ハードマスク.desc: A durable mask of nitride, carbon, metal or similar used when photoresist alone cannot survive the etch, for example in deep-hole etching.
ハードマスク.title: Hard Mask in Semiconductor Etching: Materials and Uses
ハードマスク.description: A hard mask of nitride, carbon or metal takes over when photoresist can't survive the etch. Why it's needed, how materials are chosen, and self-aligned uses.

about.p: Resist for fine patterns is thin, often around 100 nm, partly because tall narrow resist lines collapse. Etching consumes the mask too, and selectivity, the target etch rate divided by the mask etch rate, sets how much is lost: at 100 nm/min for oxide and 20 nm/min for the mask, selectivity is 5, so etching 500 nm of oxide consumes 100 nm of mask, and with overetch and edge erosion about 150–200 nm is needed. A hard mask, an inorganic or carbon film that resists the main etch far better, removes this limit.

about.h: How a hard mask is used
about.p: The film stack is deposited first, then lithography patterns the resist. A short etch transfers the pattern into the hard mask, the resist can be stripped, and the hard mask defines the main etch. Multilayer schemes chain this idea: in a tri-layer stack, resist patterns a thin silicon-containing antireflective layer, which in turn masks an oxygen-based etch of a thick carbon layer, because oxygen plasma removes carbon but barely attacks silicon-containing films. The thick carbon then masks the target film.

The hard mask must resist the chemistry that etches the target. Silicon nitride, oxide or oxynitride mask silicon and polysilicon etches; amorphous carbon or polysilicon masks oxide etches with fluorocarbon gases; titanium nitride has been used as a metal hard mask for trenches in low-k dielectrics. For the very deep, high-aspect-ratio holes of 3D NAND, amorphous-carbon hard masks several micrometers thick are used, so their deposition, etch and removal are major process steps. Carbon is easy to strip by oxygen ashing, while metal masks need wet removal.

Hard masks also define geometry beyond simple etch resistance. In self-aligned double or quadruple patterning, spacers deposited on mandrels and then etched back become the hard mask that sets line width. In self-aligned via schemes, the hard mask used to pattern wiring trenches is kept, or materially distinct caps are placed over lines, so a via etch stays confined within the target line's width even with a few nanometers of misalignment, avoiding shorts to neighboring lines at tight pitches.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hard mask and a photoresist mask?
faq.a: Photoresist is a light-sensitive polymer patterned directly by lithography but erodes quickly in plasma. A hard mask is a durable film such as nitride, oxide, carbon or metal that is patterned using the resist and then survives long, aggressive etches.

faq.q: Why is amorphous carbon used as a hard mask?
faq.a: Amorphous carbon etches very slowly in the fluorocarbon plasmas used for oxide and nitride, so a thick layer can last through deep etches, and it is removed easily afterward by oxygen ashing without damaging the patterned film.

faq.q: How thick should an etch mask be?
faq.a: Divide the target etch depth by the selectivity to estimate mask consumption, then add margin for overetch and corner erosion. For 500 nm of oxide at selectivity 5, about 100 nm is consumed, so roughly 150–200 nm is a safe thickness.

オーバーエッチング.desc: Continuing to etch for a set time after endpoint so the film is removed everywhere on the wafer. It is done under conditions with high selectivity to the underlying layer.

about.h: Why etching must continue past endpoint
about.p: No film is perfectly uniform. Thickness varies across the wafer, the etch rate varies from center to edge, and film deposited over steps is effectively thicker along the step sidewalls. Endpoint detection, typically by watching the plasma's optical emission change when the underlayer is exposed, signals that some areas have cleared, not all. If etching stopped there, residues and stringers along steps could short neighboring lines. Overetch continues for a set time, often about 20–50% of the main etch time, so that the film is cleared everywhere on the wafer.

about.h: Planning the time and the mask
about.p: Etch time is simply thickness divided by rate: a 500 nm film at 100 nm/min needs 5 minutes, and a 20% overetch makes it about 6 minutes. The mask is consumed throughout, so its thickness must be budgeted using selectivity, the ratio of the target film's etch rate to the mask's. With selectivity 5, etching 500 nm of oxide consumes about 100 nm of mask, so allowing for overetch and erosion at feature edges the mask should be at least about 150–200 nm thick. When photoresist cannot survive, a hard mask is used instead.

During overetch the underlying layer is exposed in the areas that cleared first and keeps being attacked, so loss there is roughly the overetch time multiplied by the underlayer etch rate. Processes therefore switch to high-selectivity conditions after endpoint. Gate etching is the classic case: a fast main etch sets the vertical profile through the gate material, then a gentler overetch with very high selectivity to the gate dielectric clears residues while barely touching the few-nanometre insulator. Punching through it would gouge the silicon underneath and ruin the transistor.

Extra etch time is not free. Once an insulating underlayer is exposed, positive charge can build up on it and deflect incoming ions sideways, undercutting the base of the pattern, a defect called notching that locally changes gate length; pulsed plasma or low-frequency bias reduces this charging. In isotropic wet etching, lateral undercut already equals roughly the film thickness at clearing and grows further during overetch. The overetch amount is therefore a compromise between complete clearing and the damage, linewidth change and underlayer loss it causes.

faq.q: Why is overetching necessary?
faq.a: Film thickness and etch rate vary across the wafer, and material on step sidewalls is effectively thicker, so some film remains when the endpoint is first detected. Overetching removes these residues everywhere.

faq.q: How much overetch is typically used?
faq.a: Overetch is often specified as a percentage of the main etch time, commonly around 20–50%, depending on film uniformity, topography and how much underlayer loss the device can tolerate.

faq.q: What is the difference between endpoint and overetch?
faq.a: Endpoint is the moment the etch tool detects that the underlayer has started to be exposed, while overetch is the additional, usually higher-selectivity etching performed after endpoint to clear the remaining film.

ICP(誘導結合プラズマ).desc: A method that generates a high-density plasma with RF current in a coil. It makes it easy to control plasma density and the energy of ions reaching the wafer independently.

about.p: An inductively coupled plasma (ICP) source drives RF current, commonly at 13.56 MHz, through a flat spiral or cylindrical coil placed outside a dielectric window of quartz or ceramic. The coil's oscillating magnetic field induces a circulating electric field inside the chamber, which accelerates electrons and keeps the gas ionized. Because power is transferred to the electrons inductively instead of through a high-voltage sheath at an electrode, the discharge reaches densities of about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ while operating at low pressures of a few pascals or less.

about.h: Separate knobs for density and ion energy
about.p: An ICP etcher uses two RF supplies. Source power to the coil sets plasma density, and therefore the flux of ions and radicals. A separate bias supply on the wafer chuck sets the DC self-bias and therefore the energy of ions striking the wafer. Engineers can etch fast with low ion energy to protect the underlayer and limit damage, or raise bias for more vertical profiles. Low pressure gives a long mean free path, so ions cross the sheath with few collisions and arrive nearly perpendicular, which supports anisotropic etching.

In a capacitively coupled plasma (CCP), RF power is applied between parallel-plate electrodes, so the same power that sustains the plasma also sets the sheath voltage; density and ion energy rise together. CCP densities are typically around 10⁹–10¹⁰ cm⁻³ with higher ion energies, and CCP tools, often with two frequencies to partly decouple the two, are widely used for oxide and nitride etching with fluorocarbon gases. ICP tools are favored for silicon, polysilicon gates, metals and compound semiconductors, where high radical flux and modest ion energy are wanted.

In fabs, ICP etchers handle shallow trench isolation, gate and fin etching, and metal lines. For GaN, chlorine-based ICP plasmas (Cl2, BCl3) etch LED and laser mesas and HEMT gate recesses at low ion energy to keep damage from degrading devices. High-density plasma CVD for gap fill also uses inductive sources. Outside processing, the same principle appears in ICP-MS, where an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma ionizes samples for trace-metal analysis, for example of droplets collected from wafer surfaces by vapor phase decomposition (VPD).
