faq.q: What is the difference between ICP and CCP etching?
faq.a: ICP sustains the plasma with an inductive coil and biases the wafer with a separate RF supply, so plasma density and ion energy can be set independently and density is high. CCP drives parallel-plate electrodes, so density and ion energy are coupled and density is lower, which suits energetic dielectric etching.

faq.q: What plasma density does an ICP etcher reach?
faq.a: Typical ICP etch plasmas reach about 10¹¹–10¹² cm⁻³ at pressures of a few pascals or below, roughly one to two orders of magnitude denser than a conventional capacitively coupled plasma.

faq.q: Is the ICP in ICP-MS the same as in ICP etching?
faq.a: Both use an inductively coupled plasma, but ICP-MS runs an atmospheric-pressure argon plasma to ionize a liquid sample for mass spectrometry, while an ICP etcher runs a low-pressure reactive plasma to remove material from a wafer.

ALE(原子層エッチング).desc: Etching by alternating surface modification and removal so that each cycle removes about one atomic layer. It gives extremely precise control of etch depth.

about.p: Atomic layer etching (ALE) divides etching into separate, self-limiting half-steps. In a typical plasma ALE of silicon, chlorine is first introduced and adsorbs on the surface until it saturates, converting only the top layer into a weakly bonded chlorinated layer. After a purge, low-energy argon ions are applied with energy high enough to remove the modified layer but below the threshold for sputtering the unmodified silicon. Another purge follows and the cycle repeats. Each cycle removes a fixed amount, typically about 0.1–0.5 nm.

Because each step stops by itself, the etched depth is set by counting cycles rather than by timing a continuous etch. Removal per cycle is nearly the same in dense and isolated features, surfaces stay smooth, and the low ion energy causes little lattice damage. This makes ALE suited to steps that must stop within a few nanometers or etch films only a few atomic layers thick. The drawback is speed: gas switching and purges make each cycle slow, so ALE is usually reserved for the final, critical part of an etch.

Plasma ALE, which uses ions in the removal step, is directional and can etch the bottom of a feature without attacking its sidewalls. Thermal ALE instead uses purely chemical reactions, for example fluorinating a metal oxide surface and then removing the fluoride with a ligand-exchange precursor, so it etches isotropically. Thermal ALE is useful where a precise, uniform lateral recess is needed inside three-dimensional structures that ions cannot reach directly.

ALE is the etching counterpart of atomic layer deposition (ALD), which builds films by alternating self-limiting precursor exposures. Both trade speed for atomic-scale control and uniformity. As transistor structures move to gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets with layers only a few nanometers thick, ALE is entering use in gate-region processing and other steps where overetch must be minimal, and it is also studied for low-damage recess etching in compound-semiconductor devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between ALE and ALD?
faq.a: Both rely on alternating self-limiting surface reactions, but ALD adds material a fraction of a nanometer per cycle while ALE removes it. They are often described as mirror-image processes.

faq.q: How much material does one ALE cycle remove?
faq.a: Typically about 0.1–0.5 nm per cycle, roughly one atomic layer or less, depending on the material and chemistry. Total depth is set by the number of cycles.

faq.q: Why is atomic layer etching not used for every etch step?
faq.a: Each cycle needs separate modification, purge and removal steps, so the net etch rate is far lower than continuous plasma etching. It is used where precision and low damage justify the lower throughput.

アンテナ効果.desc: Damage to a gate oxide when a connected conductor, such as a long wire, collects charge like an antenna during plasma processing. Design rules limit the area ratio of such wires to prevent it.

バッファードフッ酸(BHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid buffered with ammonium fluoride. It is used for wet etching of SiO2 with a stable etch rate and little damage to resist.

シーズニング.desc: Running dummy wafers before product to stabilize the condition of an etch (or similar) chamber's walls, since wall changes alter process results.

セルフバイアス.desc: The negative DC potential that the wafer electrode naturally acquires in a capacitively coupled plasma. It accelerates positive ions toward the wafer, aiding anisotropic etching.

SC-1(APM).desc: A mixture of ammonia, hydrogen peroxide and water used first in RCA cleaning. It removes particles and organics while lightly etching the surface.

about.p: SC-1, also called APM (ammonia-peroxide mixture), is NH4OH, H2O2 and water, classically about 1:1:5 at around 70 °C. Peroxide continuously oxidizes the silicon surface to a thin oxide about 1 nm thick, while ammonia slowly dissolves that oxide at roughly 0.1–1 nm per minute. This gentle simultaneous oxidation and etching undercuts particles and lifts them off. In the alkaline solution both the silicon surface and most particles carry negative zeta potential, so detached particles are repelled rather than redeposited. The oxidizing chemistry also removes light organic contamination.

The RCA clean, published by Kern and colleagues in 1970, runs SC-1 first for particles and organics, then SC-2 (HCl, H2O2 and water) to dissolve metal contamination as chlorides, since metals tend to remain after the alkaline step. A dilute hydrofluoric acid (DHF) dip can be inserted to strip oxide, leaving a hydrogen-terminated, hydrophobic surface, and ultrapure-water rinses separate the steps. Heavier organics and resist residues are usually handled by sulfuric-peroxide mixture (SPM). Refined versions of this sequence remain the basis of front-end wafer cleaning.

The peroxide is what keeps SC-1 gentle. If its concentration is too low relative to ammonia, ammonia attacks bare silicon directly and roughens the surface, which can degrade a gate oxide grown later. Too aggressive a mix or too long a time removes more silicon or oxide than wanted. Ratios and temperature are therefore optimized, and modern fabs often use far more dilute SC-1 than the original recipe to limit material loss and roughening while still lifting particles.

SC-1 is often combined with megasonic agitation at around 1 MHz. At tens of kilohertz, collapsing cavitation bubbles deliver shocks strong enough to break fine patterns; at megahertz frequencies, fast acoustic streaming and a thin boundary layer instead dislodge particles below 0.1 µm with far less damage. The chemistry loosens and electrostatically repels particles, and the acoustic energy carries them away, which is why the pairing is so effective. Batch tanks and single-wafer spray tools both use this approach.

faq.q: What is SC-1 cleaning used for?
faq.a: Removing particles and light organic contamination from silicon wafers. It is the first step of the RCA clean and is followed by SC-2 for metals.

faq.q: What is the difference between SC-1 and SC-2?
faq.a: SC-1 is alkaline (ammonia plus peroxide) and removes particles and organics; SC-2 is acidic (hydrochloric acid plus peroxide) and removes metal contamination.

faq.q: Why does SC-1 contain hydrogen peroxide?
faq.a: Peroxide keeps the silicon covered with about 1 nm of oxide that ammonia slowly etches, so the surface is removed gently and evenly. Without enough peroxide, ammonia etches silicon directly and roughens it.

SC-2(HPM).desc: A mixture of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen peroxide and water used after SC-1 in RCA cleaning to remove metal contamination.

about.p: SC-2, Standard Clean 2, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid, hydrogen peroxide and water, also called HPM (hydrochloric acid/peroxide mixture). The classic RCA recipe uses volume ratios around 1:1:6 at about 70 to 80 °C for several minutes. It is the acidic, oxidizing companion to SC-1, the ammonia/peroxide mixture (APM). SC-2 does not measurably etch silicon or silicon dioxide, and it leaves a thin chemical oxide that makes the surface hydrophilic.

Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes metallic contaminants on the surface to ions, and the acidic chloride solution keeps them dissolved, partly as soluble chloride complexes, so they are rinsed away rather than redepositing. This targets alkali metals such as sodium and transition metals such as iron, nickel and zinc, as well as aluminum. In the alkaline SC-1 bath some of these metals, for example iron and aluminum, tend to form hydroxides that stay on or return to the wafer, which is why the acidic step follows.

The RCA clean, published by Kern and colleagues in 1970, runs SC-1 first to remove particles and organics, then SC-2 to strip metals, with ultrapure-water rinses between steps and a dilute hydrofluoric acid (HF) dip optionally inserted to remove oxide. A sulfuric acid/peroxide mixture (SPM) may precede everything when heavy organics such as resist residue are present. SC-2 is not effective for particles; particles adhere more readily in acidic solutions, so particle removal relies on SC-1 and physical action such as megasonics.

Refined versions of the sequence remain the basis of front-end cleaning, especially before gate oxidation and other high-temperature steps where metal contamination degrades oxide integrity and carrier lifetime. Fabs often use much more dilute mixtures and lower temperatures than the original recipe, which cut chemical use while still removing metals effectively, and many cleans now run in single-wafer spin processors instead of immersion baths. HCl fumes are corrosive, so baths and tools need good exhaust.

faq.q: What does SC-2 remove in wafer cleaning?
faq.a: SC-2 removes metal contamination, such as sodium, iron, nickel and aluminum, by oxidizing the metals and keeping them dissolved as ions in the acidic chloride solution. It does not remove particles effectively.

faq.q: Why is SC-2 done after SC-1?
faq.a: SC-1 removes particles and organics but can leave some metals behind as hydroxides in its alkaline solution. The acidic SC-2 step then dissolves those metals.

faq.q: What do HPM, APM and SPM stand for?
faq.a: HPM is the hydrochloric acid/hydrogen peroxide mixture (SC-2), APM is the ammonia/hydrogen peroxide mixture (SC-1), and SPM is the sulfuric acid/hydrogen peroxide mixture used to strip heavy organics.

SPM(硫酸過水).desc: A mixture of sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide. Its strong oxidizing power removes organics such as resist.

about.p: Mixing concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4) with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) forms peroxymonosulfuric acid (H2SO5, Caro's acid), an extremely strong oxidizer. Sulfuric acid also dehydrates hydrocarbons, so photoresist and other organic films are broken down and oxidized to carbon dioxide and water. Typical mixtures run from about 2:1 to 4:1 acid to peroxide at roughly 120–150 °C; mixing is strongly exothermic, which supplies part of the heat. Because peroxide decomposes during use, baths are replenished with fresh H2O2 to keep their stripping power.

about.h: Where SPM sits in a process flow
about.p: SPM is the workhorse for removing resist residue after plasma ashing and for stripping resist after ion implantation, where heavy implant doses harden the resist surface into a crust. It is often the first step of a pre-furnace clean, followed by SC-1 (ammonia and peroxide) for particles, SC-2 (hydrochloric acid and peroxide) for metals and dilute HF for oxide. SPM leaves a thin chemical oxide on silicon and barely etches silicon or SiO2, but it dissolves many metals, which is why it can strip unreacted nickel after silicide formation yet must not touch exposed copper or aluminum.

Ozonated water, ultrapure water carrying a few to tens of ppm of dissolved ozone, also oxidizes organics and works at room temperature. It reverts to oxygen after use, so waste treatment is simple, whereas SPM consumes large volumes of sulfuric acid and peroxide and needs heating, exhaust and acid recovery. SPM remains stronger for thick or implant-hardened resist, so fabs replace it with ozone-based or other sulfuric-acid-free cleans where the residue is light enough.

Sulfuric acid is viscous and adsorbs strongly, so a short or cold rinse leaves sulfate on the surface. That sulfate can later combine with airborne ammonia to grow ammonium sulfate crystals, seen as haze on wafers and, historically, as progressive haze defects on photomasks. Hot ultrapure-water rinses address this. Hot SPM is nicknamed piranha solution: it reacts violently with organic solvents, releases gas as peroxide decomposes, and must never be stored in sealed containers.

faq.q: Why is SPM called piranha solution?
faq.a: Because hot sulfuric acid and peroxide attack organic material so aggressively that resist and other organics are eaten away within minutes. The nickname is also a reminder that the mixture is dangerous to handle.

faq.q: What is the difference between SPM and SC-1 cleaning?
faq.a: SPM is an acidic, strongly oxidizing mixture aimed at heavy organic contamination such as resist. SC-1 is an alkaline ammonia-peroxide mixture aimed mainly at particles and light organics, using slight etching of the surface to lift particles off.

faq.q: Why must wafers be rinsed well after SPM?
faq.a: Residual sulfate stays on the surface and can later react with ammonia in the air to form ammonium sulfate crystals that appear as haze and defects. Thorough, typically hot, ultrapure-water rinsing removes it.

希フッ酸(DHF).desc: Hydrofluoric acid diluted with water. It removes native oxide from silicon and leaves a hydrophobic, hydrogen-terminated surface.

about.p: Hydrofluoric acid dissolves silicon dioxide, converting it to soluble fluorosilicic acid and water, while barely attacking silicon itself. Dilute HF (DHF), typically 0.5-1 percent, strips the roughly 1 nm native oxide from silicon in tens of seconds. Concentrations are often written as volume ratios of water to concentrated 49 percent HF, such as 50:1 or 100:1. Because the etch stops once the oxide is gone, the dip is a gentle and selective way to expose bare silicon, though prolonged exposure still thins any oxide layers present elsewhere on the wafer.

After the oxide is removed, the silicon surface is terminated with Si-H bonds and becomes hydrophobic: water beads up and runs off, a quick visual check that the oxide is gone. This passivation resists reoxidation in air for tens of minutes to hours, but a hydrophobic surface also attracts particles and is prone to watermarks during drying. Fabs therefore limit the queue time (Q-time) between the HF step and the next high-temperature process such as gate oxidation, epitaxy or silicide formation, and use carefully controlled drying.

In RCA-type cleaning, SC-1 (ammonia and hydrogen peroxide) removes particles and organics and SC-2 (hydrochloric acid and hydrogen peroxide) removes metals; both leave a thin chemical oxide that makes the surface hydrophilic. DHF may be inserted between steps to remove that oxide along with contaminants trapped in it, or used last, called an HF-last clean, when the following step needs a bare silicon surface. Buffered HF, which adds ammonium fluoride to stabilize the etch rate, is preferred for patterned oxide etching.

about.h: Etch rate as a film-quality probe
about.p: Thermal oxide is dense and nearly defect-free, so it etches slowly in dilute HF, only a few nanometers per minute in 1 percent HF. Deposited oxides that are less dense or contain hydrogen and moisture etch faster. The wet etch rate ratio relative to thermal oxide is therefore a simple index of film quality, and annealing a CVD oxide lowers its ratio toward 1. Silicon nitride etches far more slowly than oxide in HF, which allows oxide to be removed selectively from nitride.

faq.q: Why is silicon hydrophobic after an HF dip?
faq.a: HF removes the oxide and leaves the surface covered with Si-H bonds, which do not form hydrogen bonds with water. Water therefore beads up instead of wetting the surface.

faq.q: What is the difference between DHF and BHF?
faq.a: DHF is hydrofluoric acid simply diluted with water, used mainly for cleaning and native oxide removal. BHF adds ammonium fluoride as a buffer, giving a more stable etch rate for patterned oxide etching.

faq.q: How long does an HF-last silicon surface stay oxide-free?
faq.a: The hydrogen-terminated surface resists regrowth of native oxide for roughly tens of minutes to hours in clean air, which is why fabs set queue-time limits before the next process step.

自然酸化膜.desc: A thin oxide about 1 nm thick that forms naturally when silicon is exposed to air or water. Because it raises contact resistance and disturbs epitaxial growth, it is removed right before such steps.

about.p: Native oxide is not grown on purpose. When bare silicon meets air or water, oxygen and moisture react with the surface, and the film grows quickly at first, then nearly stops at around 1 nm because further growth requires oxidants to diffuse through the oxide. The result is thin, often non-stoichiometric and can trap water and carbon. Thermal oxide, by contrast, is grown deliberately at about 800–1,200 °C to a controlled thickness, forming a dense film with a high-quality interface. That excellent thermal oxide is one reason silicon displaced germanium, which lacks a comparably good oxide.

about.h: Why it gets in the way
about.p: Even 1 nm of insulator matters at an interface that must conduct or grow crystal. Under a contact or silicide it raises contact resistance and can block the metal-silicon reaction. Before epitaxy, residual oxide or carbon prevents proper single-crystal growth and seeds defects such as stacking faults. It also degrades the uniformity of very thin gate dielectrics and the quality of direct bonding. Because a cleaned surface starts reoxidizing immediately, fabs limit the queue time between the clean and the next step, or link the two in vacuum.

The standard wet method is dilute hydrofluoric acid (DHF), typically 0.5–1% for tens of seconds, which dissolves SiO2 and leaves a hydrogen-terminated, hydrophobic surface; water beading off the wafer confirms removal. In RCA-style cleaning it complements SC-1, which removes particles and organics, and SC-2, which removes metals. Dry cleans using HF vapor or NF3/NH3-based remote plasma avoid liquids, so tall, narrow structures cannot collapse, and can be clustered with deposition chambers. Before silicon epitaxy, a hydrogen bake near 1,100 °C converts the oxide to volatile SiO, with lower-temperature alternatives where thermal budget is tight.

Native oxide is not always a nuisance. In vapor phase decomposition (VPD), HF vapor dissolves the native oxide and a scanned droplet collects surface metals for ICP-MS or TXRF analysis, reaching sensitivities around 10⁸–10⁹ atoms/cm². On aluminium bond pads, a dense native oxide a few nanometres thick protects the metal from corrosion, although probe needles and bonding must break through it. Other semiconductors are less fortunate: GaAs and germanium lack a good native oxide, which complicates their surface passivation and gate dielectrics.

faq.q: How thick is native oxide on silicon?
faq.a: Typically about 1 nm. It forms quickly in air or water and then almost stops growing at room temperature.

faq.q: How do you remove native oxide from silicon?
faq.a: Dip the wafer in dilute HF (about 0.5–1%) for tens of seconds, or use HF vapor or a remote-plasma dry clean. Before epitaxy, a high-temperature hydrogen bake can also remove it.

faq.q: What is the difference between native oxide and thermal oxide?
faq.a: Native oxide forms uncontrolled at room temperature, stops at about 1 nm and is of poor quality. Thermal oxide is grown deliberately at about 800–1,200 °C to a chosen thickness and has a dense film and a good interface.

パッドコンディショニング.desc: Abrading the surface of a CMP polishing pad with a diamond tool to restore its texture and slurry-holding ability, stabilizing the removal rate. Also called dressing.

エロージョン.desc: In CMP, excessive polishing of an entire region of dense lines, insulator included, so it ends up lower than its surroundings. Along with dishing of wide lines, it is a typical CMP defect.

about.p: In damascene copper chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), polishing continues past the point where the field is cleared so that no metal residue remains. In a region of closely spaced lines, the narrow dielectric strips between the lines cannot hold the pad up on their own, and the slurry removes barrier and dielectric along with the copper. The whole array therefore sinks below the surrounding open dielectric. Erosion is usually measured as the dielectric thickness lost in the array relative to the field, and it grows with metal pattern density and overpolish time.

Dishing happens inside a single wide line or pad: the softer copper in the middle is polished below the adjacent dielectric, forming a dish whose depth increases with line width. Erosion is a regional effect across many narrow lines, metal and dielectric together, and depends on density rather than width. In a dense array both act at once, so the total copper thickness lost is roughly the erosion plus the dishing of each individual line. Together they are often reported as post-CMP topography.

Thinner copper means higher line resistance and wider resistance spread across the die, which shifts timing. The recessed array also passes its topography to the next level: the surface is no longer flat, consuming lithography depth of focus, and metal deposited for the next layer can remain in the low spots after its own CMP, leaving residues that short adjacent lines. Erosion therefore limits how much overpolish a process can afford.

Layout rules keep metal density within a window over each area of the chip, and dummy fill is inserted into sparse regions so that polishing sees a more uniform pattern. On the process side, polishing is split into steps with different slurries, a bulk copper step followed by a barrier step whose selectivity is tuned to stop on the dielectric, and endpoint detection limits overpolish. Harder pads also spread pressure more evenly across arrays.

faq.q: What is the difference between dishing and erosion in CMP?
faq.a: Dishing is the recess of metal inside one wide feature and grows with width. Erosion is the loss of metal and dielectric together over a dense array and grows with pattern density.

faq.q: How does dummy fill reduce CMP erosion?
faq.a: Dummy metal shapes make pattern density more uniform, so the pad removes material at a more even rate everywhere. That reduces the height difference between dense arrays and their surroundings.

faq.q: Does erosion mean anything else in semiconductor processing?
faq.a: Yes. The word is also used for the race-track groove worn into a magnetron sputtering target, for the gradual loss of an etch mask at its edges, and for plasma wear of chamber walls and parts.

プレストンの式.desc: The empirical rule that the CMP removal rate is proportional to the product of polishing pressure and the relative speed between pad and wafer.

about.p: Preston's equation states that removal rate equals Kp × P × V, where P is the pressure pressing the wafer against the pad and V is the relative velocity between them. It was introduced as an empirical rule for polishing glass in 1927 and carried over to chemical mechanical planarization (CMP). The Preston coefficient Kp lumps together everything else, including slurry chemistry and abrasive, pad material and conditioning, temperature and the film being polished, so it must be measured for each process. Doubling pressure or speed roughly doubles removal.

On a patterned wafer, raised features contact the pad first and carry a larger share of the applied load, so their local pressure is higher than in recessed areas. By Preston's equation they are removed faster, and the step height shrinks as polishing continues. Because the pad is not perfectly rigid, it also bends into wide recessed areas, which causes dishing of large metal pads and erosion of dense arrays. Layout rules on pattern density and dummy fill exist largely to keep local pressure, and therefore removal, uniform.

The linear law is an approximation. Many processes show little removal below a threshold pressure, deviations at high speed when the slurry film thickens between pad and wafer, and temperature effects as chemical reaction rates rise with heating from friction. Slurries designed for selectivity, such as ceria with additives used for shallow trench isolation, are strongly non-Prestonian because additive layers suppress removal at low pressure. Engineers still use the equation as the starting model and fit corrections from experiments.

If the platen and the wafer carrier rotate in the same direction at nearly the same speed, the relative velocity becomes nearly uniform across the wafer, removing one source of non-uniformity. Pressure is then the main knob. Modern heads divide their membrane into several concentric zones, roughly five to ten, each with independently set air pressure. Incoming thickness profiles are fed forward and in-situ measurements adjust zone pressures in real time, bringing post-CMP thickness variation down to a few nanometers.

faq.q: What is the Preston coefficient?
faq.a: It is the empirical constant Kp in removal rate = Kp × P × V. It captures the effects of slurry, pad, conditioning and film material and is determined experimentally for each process.

faq.q: Does doubling pressure double the CMP removal rate?
faq.a: Approximately, within the range where Preston's equation holds. Real processes deviate at very low pressure, very high speed and with selectivity-tuned slurries.

faq.q: Why do CMP platen and head rotate at similar speeds?
faq.a: Matching rotation speed and direction makes the relative pad-to-wafer velocity nearly the same at every point on the wafer, which by Preston's equation helps make removal uniform.

セリア(酸化セリウム).desc: An abrasive used in CMP slurries. It reacts chemically with oxide and gives high selectivity to nitride, so it is used for STI CMP.

about.p: Ceria, cerium dioxide (CeO2), polishes silicon dioxide by a combined chemical and mechanical action. Its surface reacts with the oxide to form Ce-O-Si bonds, an activity commonly attributed in part to Ce3+ sites, so when the particle moves it tears away silica units rather than simply scratching. Because the removal is so chemically assisted, ceria slurries can polish oxide quickly at abrasive concentrations much lower than typical silica slurries. Ceria was used to polish optical glass long before it was adopted in semiconductor chemical mechanical planarization (CMP).

In shallow trench isolation (STI), trenches etched into silicon are overfilled with oxide, and CMP must remove the excess down to a silicon nitride layer that protects the active areas. Ceria slurries contain additives, such as amino acids or other surfactants, that adsorb on the nitride and suppress its removal while oxide continues to polish, giving oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100. The nitride then works as a reliable stop. Afterwards the nitride is stripped, typically in hot phosphoric acid, leaving oxide-filled isolation trenches.

Colloidal or fumed silica is the general-purpose abrasive, used for oxide interlayer dielectric CMP and, with oxidizers, for tungsten and copper. Alumina is harder and has been used in some metal slurries. Ceria is chosen when high oxide removal and selectivity to nitride matter most. With additives that adsorb on the surface, ceria slurries also tend to self-stop on patterns: once the surface is nearly flat, the local pressure drops and removal slows sharply, which helps reduce dishing compared with simple Preston-like behavior.

The strong chemical affinity that makes ceria effective also makes particles cling to oxide surfaces after polishing, so post-CMP cleaning must remove residual ceria thoroughly, typically with dedicated chemistries and brush scrubbing. Large or agglomerated particles cause micro-scratches, so particle size distribution and filtration are tightly controlled. Fixed-abrasive pads embed ceria in the pad and supply only particle-free chemistry, giving strong planarization and less slurry waste, though pad-induced defects must be managed.

faq.q: Why is ceria used instead of silica for STI CMP?
faq.a: Ceria reacts chemically with oxide for fast removal, and with additives it barely polishes silicon nitride, so it can stop reliably on the nitride layer. Silica slurries give much lower oxide-to-nitride selectivity.

faq.q: What is the oxide to nitride selectivity of ceria slurry?
faq.a: With selectivity-enhancing additives, ceria slurries typically reach oxide-to-nitride selectivity of tens to over 100.

faq.q: Is cerium oxide the same as ceria?
faq.a: Yes. Ceria is the common name for cerium dioxide, CeO2, the cerium oxide used as an abrasive in CMP and glass polishing.

パターン倒壊.desc: A defect in which tall, fine patterns topple or stick together during cleaning and drying because of the surface tension of liquid left between them.

about.p: When a rinse liquid dries out of the gap between two tall lines, the curved liquid surface creates a pressure difference (Laplace pressure) proportional to the surface tension times the cosine of the contact angle, divided by the gap width. If the liquid level differs on the two sides of a line, the line feels a net sideways force. Treating the line as a cantilever, the bending stress grows roughly with the square of its height-to-width ratio and inversely with the spacing, so shrinking pitch while keeping height makes collapse much more likely.

Resist patterns are the classic case: after development and rinse, thin, tall resist lines lean and touch their neighbors, which is one reason resist thickness is kept only a few times the line width. The same failure appears after wet cleaning of etched structures such as silicon fins, DRAM capacitor pillars and deep stacked features. Collapsed lines may stay stuck together after drying through adhesion, a related effect often called stiction.

Each term of the capillary force can be attacked. Replacing water (about 72 mN/m at room temperature) with isopropyl alcohol (IPA, about 22 mN/m) before drying cuts surface tension; treating surfaces so the contact angle approaches 90° drives the cosine toward zero. Supercritical carbon dioxide drying removes the liquid-gas interface altogether, and dry methods such as cryogenic aerosol cleaning avoid liquid entirely. For lithography, thinner resists with high etch resistance, such as metal-oxide resists, reduce aspect ratio.

Pattern collapse is a mechanical failure of features caused by capillary forces, so it depends strongly on aspect ratio and spacing and appears as leaning or merged lines in top-down inspection. Watermarks, by contrast, are residues left where droplets dried, usually on hydrophobic surfaces, and do not involve deformation. Marangoni drying with IPA vapor helps against both by pulling water off the surface before it can evaporate in place.

faq.q: Why does IPA drying prevent pattern collapse?
faq.a: IPA has roughly a third of the surface tension of water, so the capillary force pulling neighboring features together while the liquid evaporates is much smaller. It also mixes readily with water, so it can displace the rinse water completely.

faq.q: What aspect ratio causes resist pattern collapse?
faq.a: There is no single threshold, because the risk depends on spacing, resist stiffness, adhesion and the rinse liquid. Since the bending stress scales roughly with the square of aspect ratio, processes keep resist only a few times taller than it is wide.

faq.q: How does supercritical CO2 drying avoid pattern collapse?
faq.a: Above its critical point carbon dioxide has no distinct liquid and gas phases, so no meniscus forms as it is removed. Without a meniscus there is no capillary force on the features.

枚葉式洗浄.desc: A cleaning method that processes one wafer at a time. It minimizes cross-contamination and allows per-wafer control. Immersing many wafers in a tank at once is batch cleaning.

MBE(分子線エピタキシー).desc: Epitaxial growth in ultra-high vacuum by supplying source materials to the substrate as molecular beams. It controls thickness and composition at the atomic-layer level and is used in compound-semiconductor research and quantum structures.

about.p: Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) takes place in ultra-high vacuum, around 1e-8 Pa. Source materials such as gallium, aluminum, indium and arsenic are heated in effusion cells, and the evaporated atoms or molecules travel as beams to a heated substrate without colliding with gas molecules. Mechanical shutters in front of each cell switch a source on or off in a fraction of a second. Growth is slow, around 1 µm per hour, roughly one atomic layer per second for GaAs, so layer thickness can be set at the atomic-layer level and interfaces are abrupt.

Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) directs a 10-30 keV electron beam at a grazing angle of about 1-3° onto the surface and displays the diffraction pattern on a phosphor screen. The pattern reveals whether the surface is smooth or rough and which surface reconstruction is present. During layer-by-layer growth, the intensity oscillates once per completed monolayer, so operators can count layers and calibrate growth rate in real time. RHEED needs ultra-high vacuum to keep the electron beam from scattering, which is why it pairs naturally with MBE.

Metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) supplies metal-organic and hydride gases in a flowing ambient at much higher pressure; it grows faster, handles multiple large wafers and dominates production of LEDs and many lasers. Liquid-phase epitaxy (LPE) grows near equilibrium from a metal solution and gives excellent crystal quality with simple equipment, but it is poor at very thin layers and abrupt interfaces. MBE trades throughput for control and cleanliness, making it the tool of choice for research and for devices that need atomically sharp layers.

MBE builds quantum wells, superlattices, modulation-doped heterostructures for high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs), and other quantum structures in III-V compound semiconductors. Very thin, sharply confined doping layers, known as delta doping, are another strength. Variants extend the method to other materials, such as plasma-assisted MBE that supplies active nitrogen for nitride growth. The ultra-high vacuum also lets researchers combine growth with surface analysis tools without exposing samples to air.

faq.q: What is the difference between MBE and MOCVD?
faq.a: MBE evaporates elemental sources into ultra-high vacuum and grows slowly with atomic-layer control, while MOCVD uses reactive gases at much higher pressure and offers higher throughput. MBE is favored for research and precise heterostructures, MOCVD for volume production.

faq.q: Why does MBE need ultra-high vacuum?
faq.a: The vacuum lets source atoms travel as collision-free beams to the substrate, keeps the growing surface free of contamination, and allows in-situ electron diffraction monitoring such as RHEED.

faq.q: What do RHEED oscillations mean?
faq.a: Each oscillation period of the RHEED intensity corresponds to the completion of one monolayer, so counting oscillations gives the number of layers grown and the growth rate.

オートドーピング.desc: Unintended incorporation into a growing epitaxial layer of dopant from the substrate or elsewhere via the gas phase. It is a problem when growing lightly doped layers on heavily doped substrates.

about.h: How dopant travels through the gas
about.p: During silicon epitaxy at high temperature in hydrogen, dopant atoms evaporate from exposed heavily doped surfaces: the substrate front before it is covered, its back side and edges, and deposits on the susceptor. These atoms enter the gas boundary layer above the wafer and are incorporated into the growing film along with the intended dopant. The effect is strongest at the start of growth, so the epi layer shows a doping tail near the interface and its overall doping can drift from target.

Out-diffusion moves substrate dopant into the epi layer through the solid by thermal diffusion, producing a graded transition a short distance from the interface that grows with thermal budget. Autodoping moves dopant through the gas phase and can raise doping far from the interface, sometimes throughout a thin layer. Both blur the junction between substrate and epi and effectively thin the lightly doped region, but they are fought with different measures.

The back side of a heavily doped wafer is commonly sealed with an oxide or polysilicon film so it cannot release dopant. Growing at reduced pressure, several to tens of kPa, speeds gas diffusion so evaporated dopant does not linger near the surface. Purging after the pre-growth hydrogen bake, or depositing a thin undoped cap layer first and purging before continuing, also helps. Lower growth temperatures reduce evaporation, at the cost of growth rate.

Lightly doped epi on heavily doped substrates is standard for vertical power MOSFETs and diodes, which use n+ substrates of about 0.001–0.01 Ω·cm, and for CMOS wafers built on p+ substrates. In both, the epi doping sets breakdown voltage or device behavior, so autodoping directly shifts electrical results. Bipolar processes with patterned buried layers also suffer lateral autodoping, where dopant from a buried region spreads sideways into neighboring areas.

faq.q: What causes autodoping in epitaxial growth?
faq.a: Dopant evaporates from heavily doped surfaces such as the substrate back side, edges or susceptor at growth temperature, travels through the gas and is reincorporated into the growing layer.

faq.q: Why is backside sealing used on epitaxial substrates?
faq.a: An oxide or polysilicon film on the back of a heavily doped wafer blocks dopant evaporation from that surface, which is one of the largest sources of autodoping.

faq.q: Is autodoping the same as out-diffusion?
faq.a: No. Autodoping transfers dopant through the gas phase during growth, while out-diffusion is solid-state diffusion from the substrate across the interface during high-temperature steps.

臨界膜厚.desc: The maximum thickness to which a lattice-mismatched layer can be grown while staying strained without forming dislocations. Beyond it, misfit dislocations appear.

about.p: When a film with a different lattice constant grows on a substrate, its first layers stretch or compress in-plane to match the substrate atom spacing; this is coherent or pseudomorphic growth. The elastic strain energy stored per unit area grows in proportion to film thickness. A misfit dislocation at the interface costs energy to create but relieves some of that strain. Once the film is thick enough that relieving strain pays for the dislocation, relaxation becomes favorable, and that crossover is the critical thickness. Energy-balance models such as Matthews–Blakeslee describe this trade-off quantitatively.

Critical thickness falls steeply as mismatch grows. Si and Ge differ in lattice constant by about 4%, so a SiGe alloy has a mismatch of roughly 4% times its Ge fraction. For about 20% Ge the critical thickness is on the order of tens of nanometers, while pure Ge on Si relaxes after only a few monolayers. Layers grown at low temperature can stay strained beyond the equilibrium value because dislocation formation is kinetically slow; such metastable films may relax later during high-temperature steps, so the thermal budget after growth matters.

Exceeding the critical thickness creates misfit dislocations along the interface. Their ends cannot stop inside the crystal, so many continue as threading dislocations that run up through the film to the surface and through any device built on it. They act as leakage paths and recombination centers, cutting carrier lifetime, raising junction leakage, reducing light output in LEDs and lasers and shortening device lifetime. Relaxation also removes the strain itself, which is often the very property the layer was designed to provide.

Strained-silicon channels, SiGe source/drain stressors, SiGe and III–V quantum wells all depend on keeping each strained layer below its critical thickness, or on strain-compensating alternating layers. When a thick layer of a mismatched material is genuinely needed, the opposite strategy is used: a graded buffer raises the composition slowly so that relaxation happens gradually and misfit dislocations can glide long distances, leaving fewer threading segments in a relaxed virtual substrate. Superlattices that bend threading dislocations and selective-area growth on small regions further reduce the defect density reaching the active layer.

faq.q: What happens when a strained layer exceeds its critical thickness?
faq.a: Misfit dislocations form at the interface to relieve the strain, and many extend as threading dislocations through the film. The layer loses its strain and gains defects that cause leakage and reduced lifetime.

faq.q: What is the critical thickness of SiGe on silicon?
faq.a: It depends strongly on Ge content; for around 20% Ge it is on the order of tens of nanometers, and it shrinks rapidly as the Ge fraction and therefore the mismatch increase.

faq.q: Can a film be grown thicker than the critical thickness without dislocations?
faq.a: Temporarily, yes: at low growth temperature dislocation formation is kinetically slow, giving a metastable strained film. Such films can relax if they later see high-temperature processing.

ミスフィット転位.desc: A dislocation at the interface between crystals with different lattice constants that relieves strain. It forms when the grown layer exceeds the critical thickness.

貫通転位.desc: A dislocation that runs up through the grown layer to the surface. GaN on sapphire or silicon has high densities (about 10⁸-10⁹ cm⁻²), which degrade device performance and reliability.

積層欠陥.desc: A planar defect in which the stacking order of atomic planes is disrupted. It is a concern in epitaxial layers, thermal oxidation (OSF) and SiC crystals.

横方向エピタキシャル成長(ELO).desc: Growing crystal from mask openings and letting it spread sideways over the mask. Dislocations from below do not propagate into the overgrown regions, reducing dislocations in materials such as GaN.

超格子.desc: A periodic structure of alternating layers of different materials, each a few nanometers thick. It shows electronic properties absent in bulk crystals and is used in lasers, buffer layers and more.

SiGe(シリコンゲルマニウム).desc: An alloy of silicon and germanium with a larger lattice constant than silicon. Grown epitaxially, it is used to strain channels, as the base of HBTs and as the sacrificial layer in GAA transistors.

about.p: Silicon and germanium are both group IV elements with the diamond structure and mix in any ratio, so SiGe is a continuous alloy rather than a compound. Adding germanium enlarges the lattice constant from about 0.543 nm for silicon toward 0.566 nm for germanium, roughly 4% larger, and lowers the band gap from 1.12 eV toward 0.66 eV. SiGe also has higher hole mobility than silicon. It is grown by chemical vapor deposition using germane (GeH4) with silane or dichlorosilane, and the gas flow ratio sets the germanium content, which high-resolution X-ray diffraction can then measure together with strain.

SiGe grown on silicon is compressively strained because its larger lattice is squeezed to match the substrate, and this strain stays coherent only up to a critical thickness, roughly tens of nanometers at 20% germanium. Selective epitaxy embeds boron-doped SiGe in pMOS source and drain regions, which squeezes the channel and raises hole mobility; advanced processes also use SiGe as the pMOS channel itself. The reverse trick serves nMOS: a thin silicon layer grown on relaxed SiGe, reached through a graded buffer several micrometers thick, is stretched into tensile strain that raises electron mobility.

In a SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT), the base is an epitaxial SiGe layer tens of nanometers thick, boron-doped during growth. Its narrower band gap blocks holes from flowing back into the emitter, so the base can be thin and heavily doped without losing injection efficiency. Grading the germanium from near 0% at the emitter side to 20 to 30% at the collector side builds in an electric field that speeds electrons across. A little carbon limits boron diffusion. Transition frequencies of hundreds of gigahertz suit SiGe BiCMOS to RF front ends, optical links and automotive radar.

Nanosheet gate-all-around (GAA) transistors start from an epitaxial stack of alternating silicon and SiGe layers, with about 25 to 30% germanium. The SiGe ends are first recessed and filled with dielectric inner spacers. After the dummy gate is removed, the remaining SiGe is etched away with high selectivity, often by remote-plasma or chemical etching, leaving suspended silicon sheets that high-k dielectric and metal gate then wrap on all sides. Because high temperature would relax strain or intermix the layers, later steps are held to a thermal budget of about 600 to 700 °C or less.

faq.q: Why is SiGe used in pMOS transistors?
faq.a: SiGe has a larger lattice constant than silicon, so SiGe embedded in the source and drain compresses the silicon channel, and compressive strain raises hole mobility. SiGe also has higher intrinsic hole mobility, so it is used as a pMOS channel material as well.

faq.q: What is a SiGe HBT?
faq.a: It is a bipolar transistor whose base is made of SiGe, whose narrower band gap than the silicon emitter forms a heterojunction. This allows a thin, heavily doped base and, with graded germanium, a built-in accelerating field, giving transition frequencies of hundreds of gigahertz.

faq.q: Is SiGe a compound semiconductor?
faq.a: No, it is an alloy of two group IV elements that mix in any proportion, not a compound of elements from different groups like GaAs. Its properties vary continuously with germanium content, and it is processed with silicon-compatible equipment.

ひずみシリコン.desc: Silicon whose band structure is modified by strain to raise carrier mobility. Tensile strain helps nMOS and compressive strain helps pMOS; it is applied with SiGe source/drain regions, nitride films and the like.

HVPE(ハイドライド気相成長).desc: Vapor-phase growth using gallium chloride, formed by reacting HCl with gallium, together with ammonia. Its very high growth rate is used to grow thick GaN crystals for free-standing substrates.

ステップフロー成長.desc: A growth mode in which the crystal extends sideways from atomic steps on a slightly off-axis substrate. In SiC it is used so the layer inherits the substrate's polytype.

4H-SiC.desc: The SiC polytype mainly used for power devices. It has a wide band gap of about 3.3 eV and relatively high electron mobility.

about.p: Silicon carbide is built from Si–C bilayers that can stack in many different sequences, giving more than 200 polytypes with identical chemistry but different crystal structures and properties. In Ramsdell notation the number is the count of bilayers in one repeat period and the letter gives the lattice symmetry. 4H-SiC repeats every four bilayers in a hexagonal lattice, 6H-SiC every six, and 3C-SiC every three in a cubic arrangement. The stacking sequence changes the band gap and electron mobility, so the polytype matters as much as the material.

4H-SiC combines a band gap of about 3.26 eV, an electron mobility of roughly 1000 cm²/V·s and only modest anisotropy. Its wide gap gives a critical electric field around ten times that of silicon, so a drift layer for a given blocking voltage can be about a tenth as thick and much more heavily doped, sharply reducing on-resistance. 6H-SiC has strongly direction-dependent mobility and 3C-SiC a smaller gap near 2.4 eV. Thermal conductivity several times higher than silicon's and mature substrate and epitaxy supply complete the case.

On an exactly on-axis surface, new islands nucleate on flat terraces and can adopt the wrong stacking, often 3C-SiC. Substrates are therefore cut about 4° off the c-axis toward a ⟨11-20⟩ direction, which creates a dense staircase of atomic steps. Adatoms diffuse to step edges and attach there, so each step advances sideways and copies the substrate's stacking sequence. This step-flow growth, typically by CVD with silane and a hydrocarbon in hydrogen at temperatures above 1500 °C, reproduces the 4H polytype in the drift layer.

Crystal defects remain a concern. Basal-plane dislocations in the drift layer can expand into stacking faults under forward bipolar current, raising on-voltage over time, so epitaxial processes aim to convert them into less harmful threading edge dislocations. In MOSFETs, traps at the SiO2/SiC interface make the inversion-channel mobility far lower than bulk mobility, which is an active area of gate-oxide process development. Compared with GaN, which is mostly used in lateral transistors, 4H-SiC is favored for vertical devices blocking several hundred volts to kilovolts.

faq.q: What is the band gap of 4H-SiC?
faq.a: About 3.26 eV at room temperature, roughly three times that of silicon (1.12 eV). This is often rounded to 3.2 or 3.3 eV.

faq.q: Why is 4H-SiC preferred over 6H-SiC for power devices?
faq.a: 4H-SiC has a slightly wider band gap, higher electron mobility and much less mobility anisotropy than 6H-SiC, and high-quality 4H substrates and epitaxy are mature.

faq.q: Why are SiC wafers cut off-axis for epitaxy?
faq.a: An off-angle of about 4° creates many atomic steps so growth proceeds by step flow, which copies the substrate's 4H stacking instead of nucleating other polytypes such as 3C-SiC.

ビア.desc: A conductor that electrically connects the wiring layers above and below it in a multilevel interconnect. It is made by filling a hole in the insulator with metal.

コンタクト.desc: The connection between a transistor's source, drain or gate and the lowest wiring layer. It is made by filling a contact hole in the insulator with tungsten or similar metal.

シリサイド.desc: A compound of silicon and a metal, such as NiSi or TiSi2. It is formed on source, drain and gate surfaces to reduce resistance and contact resistance.

about.p: After gates and sidewall spacers are formed, a thin metal film is deposited over the whole wafer, often with a cap layer to prevent oxidation. A rapid thermal anneal makes the metal react only where it touches silicon, on the source, drain and, in older flows, the polysilicon gate; it does not react with oxide or nitride spacers and isolation. A selective wet etch then removes the unreacted metal, and a second anneal may convert the film to its low-resistivity phase. No mask is needed, hence the name salicide.

about.h: Why the material changed: TiSi2, CoSi2, NiSi
about.p: Titanium disilicide must transform into a low-resistivity phase, and that transformation becomes difficult on narrow lines, so resistance rose as dimensions shrank. Cobalt disilicide avoided this linewidth problem but consumes a relatively large amount of silicon. Nickel monosilicide (NiSi) forms at lower temperature, consumes less silicon and has low resistivity, around 15 µΩ·cm. Its weakness is thermal stability: at higher temperatures it can agglomerate or convert to the high-resistivity NiSi2 phase, so later process steps must stay cool.

A metal on silicon forms a Schottky barrier. Heavy doping, around 10²⁰ cm⁻³ at the surface, thins that barrier enough for carriers to tunnel, and the silicide provides an intimate, low-resistance metal interface right at that doped silicon. Silicide also lowers the sheet resistance of source and drain regions by over an order of magnitude compared with doped silicon. In advanced transistors, where contacts account for a large share of total resistance, specific contact resistivities near 10⁻⁹ Ω·cm² are targeted, and titanium-based silicide formed at the bottom of contact trenches is common.

A silicide is an intermetallic compound grown by consuming silicon, unlike a deposited metal or barrier film such as TiN. Silicided polysilicon gate lines were once called polycide. In replacement metal gate processes, the gate is metal from the start, so silicide is needed only on source and drain contacts. Silicides are not used for long interconnects, which rely on copper or other metals with much lower resistivity.

faq.q: What does salicide mean?
faq.a: Salicide stands for self-aligned silicide: metal is deposited everywhere, reacts only where it contacts silicon, and the unreacted metal is etched away, so the silicide aligns to the silicon regions without a lithography step.

faq.q: Why is NiSi used instead of TiSi2?
faq.a: NiSi keeps low resistance on narrow lines, forms at lower temperature and consumes less silicon. TiSi2 has trouble reaching its low-resistivity phase on very narrow lines.

faq.q: Does silicide make a contact ohmic by itself?
faq.a: Not by itself; a silicide-silicon interface still has a Schottky barrier. Heavy doping under the silicide thins that barrier so carriers tunnel through, giving a low-resistance ohmic contact.

デュアルダマシン法.desc: Forming both the trench for a wire and the hole for a via in the insulator, filling them with copper together and finishing with a single CMP step. It reduces process steps.

about.h: How dual damascene builds a wiring level
about.p: A dielectric stack, usually a low-k film with thin etch-stop or cap layers, is deposited first. Lithography and etching then open two kinds of features in it: via holes that reach down to the wiring level below, and trenches shaped like the wires of the current level. A thin diffusion barrier such as TaN/Ta and a copper seed layer are sputtered, copper is electroplated to fill vias and trenches together, and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) removes the excess copper and barrier from the top surface, leaving metal inlaid only where it was patterned.

about.h: Why copper needs a damascene process
about.p: Aluminum wiring was made by depositing a metal film and etching it into lines. Copper is difficult to pattern that way because its reaction products with common plasma etch chemistries are not volatile at normal process temperatures. Damascene processing sidesteps the problem by etching the dielectric instead and filling it with metal, much like the inlay craft of Damascus that gave the method its name. The barrier layer is essential because copper diffuses readily into silicon and dielectrics, where it degrades devices and insulation.

Single damascene builds vias and lines in separate passes, each with its own dielectric patterning, barrier and seed deposition, plating and CMP. Dual damascene patterns both features before a single metallization, saving one round each of deposition, plating and CMP per wiring level. Because the via and the line above it are one continuous piece of copper, there is no barrier interface between them, which lowers via resistance and helps electromigration reliability. Advanced chips repeat this module for each of their many copper levels.

Dual damascene comes in variants that differ in which feature is opened first: via-first etches the holes before the trenches, trench-first does the reverse, and hard-mask schemes help align vias to the trench above. At advanced nodes vias are only about 20 nm across and a chip contains billions of them, so void-free filling, uniform CMP and avoiding damage to fragile low-k dielectrics during etch and resist removal strongly affect both performance and yield. A single open via can kill a circuit.

faq.q: What is the difference between single and dual damascene?
faq.a: Single damascene forms vias and wiring lines in separate deposition, plating and CMP sequences. Dual damascene opens both in the dielectric first and fills them with copper in one sequence, saving steps and avoiding a barrier layer between via and line.

faq.q: Why is copper wiring not made by etching like aluminum?
faq.a: Copper does not form volatile etch products easily with standard plasma chemistries, so patterning a copper film by dry etching is impractical. Instead, the dielectric is patterned and filled with copper, then polished flat.

faq.q: Where does the name damascene come from?
faq.a: It comes from the traditional inlay craft associated with Damascus, in which gold or silver was set into grooves cut in a metal surface, just as copper is inlaid into grooves in the dielectric.

シード層.desc: A thin copper film deposited by sputtering or similar before copper electroplating. It provides the conductive path for the plating current.

about.h: Why a seed layer is needed
about.p: Electroplating that fills copper trenches and vias makes the wafer the cathode and passes current so that copper ions in the plating bath are reduced and deposited on the surface. That requires an unbroken conductive layer over the whole wafer, including the inside of every trench. The barrier layer (such as Ta/TaN) that stops copper diffusion has high resistance and readily forms surface oxides, so plating directly on it does not start uniformly. A thin copper film is therefore sputtered on top to carry the plating current and give copper a surface on which to start depositing. This is the seed layer, named because it seeds the growth.

The seed layer is typically deposited a few nanometers to a few tens of nanometers thick, often by ionized sputtering (iPVD), which ionizes atoms ejected from the target and draws them vertically onto the wafer. If it is too thick, film overhangs at the trench opening and narrows it, so the opening closes before plating fills the trench and a void remains. If it is too thin, the film breaks up low on the sidewalls, copper does not deposit there and voids form. The narrower the lines, the harder this balance becomes. Remedies include ruthenium or cobalt liners, which copper wets readily, underneath the seed, and seed enhancement by CVD or similar methods.

about.h: The seed layer in the plating sequence
about.p: In the damascene process, trenches and vias are formed in the dielectric, the barrier and seed layers are deposited, copper is filled by electroplating, and after annealing, CMP removes the excess copper and barrier. The seed layer merges with the plated copper and remains inside the trenches as part of the wiring. If the seed is thin, voltage drops as current flows from contacts at the wafer edge toward the center, so the edge tends to plate thicker (the terminal effect); plating tools adjust the current distribution to compensate. Because a long wait between seed deposition and plating lets the surface oxidize and causes plating defects, that time is controlled.

about.h: Seed layers in packaging and TSVs
about.p: Seed layers are also used to form package redistribution layers (RDL) and bumps. There, an adhesion layer of Ti and a copper seed are first sputtered over the whole wafer, resist is patterned in the shape of the wiring or bumps, and copper is plated thick only in the openings (semi-additive process). After the resist is removed, the seed left between the lines must be wet-etched away or it will short them, so removing only the seed without thinning the lines is a challenge. In TSVs, getting a continuous seed all the way to the bottom of deep holes is critical.

faq.q: What is a seed layer?
faq.a: It is a thin metal film deposited on the underlying surface before growing copper or other metals by electroplating. It is both the conductive layer that carries the plating current and the base on which the metal begins to deposit. For copper interconnects, a thin copper film is usually sputtered on top of the barrier layer.

faq.q: Why not plate directly on the barrier layer?
faq.a: Barrier layers such as Ta and TaN have high resistance and oxidize easily, so current does not flow uniformly and copper deposition does not start uniformly. A seed layer in between lets plating start evenly across the wafer. Plating directly on liners such as ruthenium is also being researched.

faq.q: What happens to the seed layer after plating?
faq.a: In the damascene process the seed merges with the plated copper and becomes part of the wiring, and the portion outside the trenches is removed by CMP along with the excess copper. In semi-additive processes such as package redistribution, the seed in the areas that were not plated is etched away.

エアギャップ.desc: Leaving part of the insulator between wires as empty space. Since air has a relative permittivity of about 1, it greatly reduces capacitance between wires.

about.h: Why air between wires lowers capacitance
about.p: The capacitance between neighboring wires is proportional to the relative permittivity (k) of the material between them. Silicon dioxide has k of about 3.9, carbon-doped low-k films reach roughly 2.5 to 3, and air or vacuum sits at about 1, lower than any solid. Replacing part of the inter-wire dielectric with an air gap therefore cuts inter-wire capacitance by about 20 to 30% in practical structures, which reduces RC delay, dynamic switching power and crosstalk between adjacent signals.

One approach finishes the copper lines first, removes the dielectric between them by etching, and then deposits a cap film with poor step coverage so that it pinches off at the top and seals a void below. Another deliberately deposits a dielectric that cannot fill narrow spaces conformally, leaving voids between closely spaced lines. Either way, the gap forms naturally only where lines are tight, which matches where capacitance matters most. Air-gap ideas are also applied to the spacers beside transistor gates to cut gate-to-contact capacitance.

A cavity weakens the wiring stack mechanically, which matters during CMP, wafer dicing and packaging stress. Air conducts heat poorly, so wires surrounded by gaps run hotter. A via landing from the level above must not punch into a gap, so layouts keep gaps away from via landing areas, sometimes with an extra mask. Moisture and process chemicals must not get trapped inside. For these reasons air gaps are typically used only on the dense, tight-pitch levels where capacitance reduction pays off most, while other levels keep solid low-k dielectric.

about.h: Intended air gaps vs. unwanted ones
about.p: Outside interconnect design, an air gap is usually a defect. In packages, delamination between mold compound and die or lead frame leaves a thin air layer that weakens the joint and can lead to cracking. Scanning acoustic microscopy (SAT) detects it non-destructively: solids and air differ so strongly in acoustic impedance that an air gap reflects nearly all of the ultrasound, making delaminations, cracks and voids stand out clearly. Unintended voids in metal or dielectric fill are similarly treated as defects.

faq.q: Why do air gaps reduce interconnect capacitance?
faq.a: Capacitance scales with the permittivity of the material between conductors, and air has a relative permittivity of about 1, lower than any solid dielectric. Replacing part of the dielectric with air lowers inter-wire capacitance, typically by about 20 to 30%.

faq.q: What is the difference between an air gap and a low-k dielectric?
faq.a: A low-k dielectric is a solid film with reduced permittivity, typically around 2.5 to 3, that fills the space between wires. An air gap leaves part of that space empty, reaching lower effective capacitance but with weaker mechanical strength and heat conduction.

faq.q: What are the disadvantages of air gaps?
faq.a: They reduce mechanical strength, worsen heat dissipation, and create a risk that vias land in the cavity. These issues limit air gaps to the densest wiring levels.

IRドロップ.desc: The drop in supply voltage reaching a circuit because current (I) flows through the resistance (R) of the power wiring. It increases delay and can cause malfunctions.

about.p: Current reaches a transistor through a long chain: package balls or bumps, thick upper-level metal straps, stacks of vias, and finally the thin power rails that run along each row of standard cells. Every segment has resistance, and the lowest layers, being thinnest, contribute a disproportionate share. Ground has the same problem in reverse: current returning through VSS wiring raises the local ground. A cell therefore sees its supply squeezed from both sides, reduced VDD and elevated ground.

Static IR drop is computed from average current flowing through the grid resistance and shows regions that are chronically starved, such as the middle of a large block far from supply bumps. Dynamic IR drop captures short, local dips when many cells switch in the same clock edge and draw a burst of current. It is closely tied to inductive drop (L·di/dt) in the package and to how much decoupling capacitance sits nearby to supply charge during the burst.

Gate delay rises as supply voltage falls, so even a drop of about 5% (35 mV on a 0.7 V supply) can slow paths by several percent and break timing that passed at nominal voltage. For this reason sign-off before tape-out includes power-grid analysis of IR drop alongside electromigration checks, and the voltage maps may be fed back into timing analysis. Designers also keep voltage margin, which costs power, so a stronger grid lets that margin shrink.

The power grid is made wider and denser, with upper metal layers devoted largely to power and many parallel vias between layers. Packages assign a large fraction of balls or bumps to power and ground to spread current. Decoupling capacitor cells placed near busy logic supply charge during switching bursts, and placement can spread highly active cells apart. Power-gating switches add series resistance, so they are sized with IR drop in mind.

faq.q: What is an acceptable IR drop in chip design?
faq.a: Budgets depend on the design and process, but drops of a few percent up to around 10% of the nominal supply are typical targets, with timing analyzed at the resulting lower voltage.

faq.q: What is the difference between IR drop and electromigration?
faq.a: IR drop is a voltage loss that slows circuits immediately, while electromigration is gradual metal damage from high current density that can open or short wires over the chip's lifetime. Both are checked on the power grid at sign-off.

faq.q: What is ground bounce?
faq.a: Ground bounce is the rise of the local ground voltage when current flows back through the resistance and inductance of the ground network, the counterpart of supply droop on VDD.

クロストーク.desc: Noise that appears on one wire when the signal on a neighboring wire changes, mainly through capacitive coupling. Wider spacing and shield wires reduce it.

about.p: Two neighboring wires form a capacitor. When the aggressor wire switches, it injects charge through the coupling capacitance Cc into the victim wire. If the victim is floating or only weakly driven, the resulting glitch is roughly the aggressor swing multiplied by Cc / (Cc + Cg), where Cg is the victim's capacitance to ground and other wires. A driven victim pulls back toward its level at a rate set by its driver resistance, so weak drivers and long parallel runs give the largest and longest glitches. A glitch that reaches a latch, clock or dynamic node can flip a stored value.

Crosstalk matters even when nothing glitches, because it alters timing. If the victim and aggressor switch in the same direction at the same time, the voltage across Cc barely changes and the coupling capacitance effectively vanishes, speeding the victim. If they switch in opposite directions, the voltage across Cc changes by twice the swing, so the capacitance effectively doubles, a Miller-factor effect, slowing the victim. Static timing analysis with signal-integrity awareness therefore uses extracted coupling capacitances and switching windows to bound the best and worst cases.

A wire's capacitance has lateral components to neighbors on the same layer, vertical components to layers above and below and to the substrate, and fringe components from fields curling around its edges. In a parallel-plate approximation C = εS/d, so halving spacing roughly doubles lateral capacitance. Advanced metal layers use tight pitch and tall wires, with thickness-to-width ratios around 2, to keep resistance down, which further enlarges facing sidewall area. Lateral coupling thus becomes the dominant share of total capacitance, and parasitic extraction with field solvers after place and route quantifies it.

The main levers are spacing, shielding and dielectric constant. Wider spacing on critical nets, power or ground shield wires between sensitive signals, and low-k dielectrics such as carbon-doped oxide (about 2.7–3.0) or porous films (about 2.2–2.5) instead of SiO2 (about 3.9) all reduce coupling. Stronger victim drivers recover faster, and avoiding long parallel runs limits the coupling length. The word is used beyond wiring: image-sensor pixels leak light and charge into neighbors, and multiplexed sample-and-hold inputs can carry residue from a previous channel.

faq.q: What are aggressor and victim nets in crosstalk analysis?
faq.a: The aggressor is the switching net that injects noise, and the victim is the neighboring net that receives it through coupling capacitance. The same net can be an aggressor in one analysis and a victim in another.

faq.q: How do you reduce crosstalk in chip layout?
faq.a: Increase spacing, insert grounded or power shield wires, shorten parallel routes, and strengthen victim drivers. Low-k dielectrics reduce coupling capacitance at the process level.

faq.q: Is on-chip crosstalk capacitive or inductive?
faq.a: On-chip crosstalk in short and medium wires is dominated by capacitive coupling. Inductive coupling becomes significant for long, fast global wires, packages and circuit boards.

パッシベーション膜.desc: A film formed as the topmost layer of a chip to protect the circuitry from moisture, contamination and mechanical damage. Silicon nitride and polyimide are typical materials.

about.p: The passivation layer is a protective film covering the chip's top metal layer, also called final passivation. It keeps moisture and mobile ions such as sodium from reaching the circuitry, preventing wiring corrosion and shifts in transistor characteristics. It also protects the circuitry from scratches and particles during wafer handling and assembly. Only over the bond pads used for wire bonding or bumps is the film opened by lithography and etching (pad opening) to expose the metal. The layer is essential for surviving high-temperature, high-humidity reliability tests.

The typical material is silicon nitride, which is hard and resists moisture and ions, at a thickness of several hundred nanometers to about 1 µm. Because the aluminum or copper wiring underneath cannot tolerate high temperatures, plasma CVD, which deposits films at a low 300–400 °C, is used. Plasma CVD nitride contains a lot of hydrogen and deviates from Si3N4 stoichiometry, but it performs well as a protective film. Oxide and nitride may be stacked, or oxynitride used, to tune film stress and optical transmission. A resin film such as polyimide is often added on top to relieve stress from the package molding compound.

Cracks or pinholes in the passivation let moisture in and corrode aluminum wiring and pads. Moisture resistance is therefore checked with temperature-humidity-bias (THB) testing, which applies voltage at 85 °C and 85% RH, and with HAST, which accelerates the test under harsher conditions. Excessive film stress can crack the film itself or cause stress migration, in which metal in the wiring below moves and forms voids. Hydrogen in the nitride can also affect transistor characteristics, so film composition and process order are taken into account in the design.

In semiconductors, the word passivation is used more broadly for any treatment that makes a surface inactive and stable. For example, forming gas annealing, in which hydrogen terminates unbonded orbitals (dangling bonds) left at the silicon-oxide interface to reduce interface states, is also called passivation. In crystalline silicon solar cells, surface passivation with films such as aluminum oxide, which reduces recombination at the surface, strongly affects efficiency. In GaN HEMTs, nitride films suppress the effect of surface states and reduce current collapse. Forming protective films on sidewalls during dry etching is also called passivation.

faq.q: Why is silicon nitride so often used for passivation?
faq.a: It resists moisture and ions such as sodium and is hard and scratch-resistant. Plasma CVD can also deposit it at a low 300–400 °C, so it can cover the top of the chip without damaging the aluminum or copper wiring already formed.

faq.q: Why is polyimide added on top?
faq.a: It relieves the stress on the chip surface when the package molding compound shrinks during curing and temperature changes, preventing nitride cracks and shifting of the wiring. It also protects against scratches during assembly. It is sometimes used as a stress-buffer layer under flip-chip bumps as well.

faq.q: Are surface passivation and a passivation layer the same thing?
faq.a: Their aims are similar, but they refer to different things. A passivation layer is the protective film covering the top of the chip against moisture, contamination and scratches. Surface passivation is the treatment of defects at semiconductor surfaces and interfaces with hydrogen or films to make them inactive, reducing carrier recombination and interface states; it is important for solar cells and transistor interfaces.

裏面電源供給.desc: Placing the power wiring on the back of the wafer so the front-side wiring can be used for signals. It reduces voltage drop and routing congestion.

about.h: Why move power to the back
about.p: In a conventional chip, both signal and power wiring sit above the transistors in a back-end-of-line (BEOL) stack of about 15 levels. Power enters at the top through thick wires and then descends through more than ten levels of increasingly fine wires and vias to reach each transistor, losing voltage along the way (IR drop). Power rails also occupy routing tracks inside every standard cell, crowding the signal wiring. Backside power delivery separates the two networks: signals stay on the front, while power is delivered from the back of the wafer.

The front side, transistors and signal wiring, is processed first. The wafer is then bonded face-down to a carrier wafer and the original silicon is thinned from the back to hundreds of nanometers or a few micrometers. Very small vias are etched from the back to reach buried power rails or the transistors' source and drain contacts directly, and thick, low-resistance power wiring is built on the back. Announced implementations include Intel's PowerVia and TSMC's A16 process, among others.

Feeding transistors from directly below shortens the power path and lowers IR drop, freeing front-side tracks for signals, which eases routing congestion and allows smaller standard cells. The costs are extra process complexity: wafer bonding and thinning, alignment of backside features to front-side devices despite distortion from bonding, and new approaches to failure analysis. Heat removal also changes, because the active layer ends up sandwiched between bonding and wiring layers, so thermal design must be reconsidered.

about.h: Why it matters for scaling now
about.p: As transistors shrink, performance is increasingly limited by parasitics rather than the channel: source, drain and contact resistance can approach half of total on-resistance, and wiring resistance rises as pitches shrink into the 20 nm range. Gains therefore come from extrinsic improvements such as better contact materials, low-k or air-gap spacers and backside power delivery. It is often paired with gate-all-around transistors and is considered especially important for stacked CFET devices, whose lower tier is hard to reach from above.

faq.q: What is a backside power delivery network (BSPDN)?
faq.a: It is a chip wiring scheme that places the power distribution network on the back of a thinned wafer and connects it to transistors from below, leaving the front-side metal levels for signals.

faq.q: What is the difference between backside power delivery and a buried power rail?
faq.a: A buried power rail embeds the cell's power lines below the transistors instead of in the first metal level. Backside power delivery moves the whole power network to the back of the wafer and can feed buried rails or transistor contacts directly through backside vias.

faq.q: Why does backside power delivery reduce IR drop?
faq.a: Power no longer has to descend through ten or more thin front-side metal levels and vias; it arrives through short, thick backside wires, so the resistance between the supply and each transistor is much lower.

MOL(ミドル・オブ・ライン).desc: The contacts and local interconnects that link transistors (FEOL) to the multilevel wiring (BEOL). With scaling, their resistance has grown and now limits performance.

表皮効果.desc: The concentration of high-frequency current near the surface of a conductor, which raises its effective resistance. The higher the frequency, the thinner the surface layer carrying the current.

about.h: Why current crowds to the surface
about.p: An alternating current produces a changing magnetic field inside the conductor itself. That changing field induces eddy currents that oppose the current flow near the center and reinforce it near the surface. The net result is that current density falls off roughly exponentially with depth from the surface. The characteristic depth, where density has dropped to about 37% (1/e) of its surface value, is the skin depth δ = √(ρ / (π f μ)), with ρ the resistivity, f the frequency and μ the permeability. At DC there is no skin effect and current uses the whole cross-section.

For copper, skin depth is roughly 66 µm divided by the square root of frequency in MHz: about 8.5 mm at 60 Hz, about 66 µm at 1 MHz, about 2 µm at 1 GHz and about 0.66 µm at 10 GHz. Once δ is much smaller than the conductor's thickness, the effective resistance rises in proportion to √f. At multi-gigahertz frequencies the current also follows the microscopic roughness of copper foil surfaces, adding further loss, which is why smooth low-profile copper is used in high-speed boards.

Signal loss on a board trace or cable has two main frequency-dependent parts. Conductor loss from the skin effect grows roughly as √f, while dielectric loss, set by the loss tangent of the insulating material, grows roughly in proportion to f and tends to dominate at the highest frequencies. Both make a faster signal lose more over the same length. The resulting inter-symbol interference must be recovered by equalizers, low-loss laminate materials, or retimers that receive and retransmit a clean signal partway along the channel.

Skin effect limits the reach of high-speed copper links in servers and data centers, one reason optical fiber, with loss of only about 0.2–0.35 dB/km almost independent of modulation rate, takes over for rack-scale and longer distances. On chips, ordinary interconnect is thinner than the skin depth at typical clock frequencies, but thick top-metal layers used for RF inductors and transmission lines at multi-gigahertz frequencies see raised resistance and lower quality factor. A related effect, proximity effect, pushes current to one side when neighboring conductors carry current.

faq.q: What is the skin depth of copper at 1 GHz?
