faq.a: About 2 µm. It scales with 1/√f, so it is about 0.66 µm at 10 GHz and about 66 µm at 1 MHz.

faq.q: Does skin effect happen with DC current?
faq.a: No. Skin effect needs a time-varying current to induce opposing eddy currents, so DC current spreads uniformly over the conductor cross-section.

faq.q: Why does trace loss increase at higher data rates?
faq.a: Skin effect raises conductor resistance roughly as the square root of frequency and dielectric loss rises roughly linearly with frequency, so faster signals with higher-frequency content are attenuated more.

ブラックの式.desc: An empirical formula for interconnect lifetime under electromigration in terms of current density and temperature. Lifetime is inversely proportional to a power of current density and falls exponentially as temperature rises.
ブラックの式.title: Black's Equation for Electromigration: MTTF Formula Explained
ブラックの式.description: Black's equation, MTTF = A·J^(−n)·exp(Ea/kT), links wire lifetime to current density and temperature. Its terms, the physics, and how it extrapolates test data.

about.p: Black's equation is an empirical model for the median or mean time to failure of a wire under electromigration: MTTF = A·J^(−n)·exp(Ea/kT). J is the current density, n the current-density exponent (2 in Black's original form, with values between about 1 and 2 reported), Ea the activation energy of the dominant atomic diffusion path, k Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature, and A a constant that captures material, geometry and microstructure. Ea is on the order of 0.5 to 1 eV, depending on the metal and on whether atoms move mainly along grain boundaries or interfaces.

about.h: Using it to extrapolate test data
about.p: Electromigration failures at use conditions would take years to appear, so test structures are stressed at elevated temperatures, around 300 °C, and high current densities, then the equation extrapolates the results. The acceleration factor is (J_test/J_use)^n multiplied by exp[(Ea/k)(1/T_use − 1/T_test)]. The sensitivity is large: with n = 2, halving current density quadruples lifetime, and with Ea near 0.9 eV, raising temperature from 105 °C to 125 °C shortens lifetime by roughly a factor of four. Fitting n and Ea requires tests at several currents and temperatures.

Electromigration happens because conduction electrons transfer momentum to metal atoms, slowly pushing them in the direction of electron flow. Where more atoms leave a region than arrive, such as at a via or grain-boundary junction, voids form and eventually open the line; where atoms pile up, hillocks can short to neighbours. In copper, transport is dominated by the top interface with the dielectric cap, so cobalt caps can extend lifetime substantially. Black's equation does not capture back-stress effects: very short lines can be immune because opposing mechanical stress halts atom flow (the Blech effect).

Foundries translate Black's equation and test data into maximum allowed current densities per metal layer, width and temperature, typically on the order of MA/cm². Power and ground lines carrying steady DC current in one direction are the most critical. Signal lines with alternating current partly recover because atoms move back and forth, so their limits are less strict. Joule heating raises the local temperature of heavily loaded wires, which feeds back through the exponential term. Sign-off flows therefore check electromigration together with IR drop on the power grid.

faq.q: What is Black's equation used for?
faq.a: It estimates interconnect lifetime under electromigration as a function of current density and temperature. Engineers use it to extrapolate accelerated test results to operating conditions and to set current-density limits for wires.

faq.q: How does temperature affect electromigration lifetime?
faq.a: Lifetime falls exponentially with temperature through the exp(Ea/kT) term. For an activation energy near 0.9 eV, a 20 °C rise around 105 to 125 °C cuts lifetime by roughly four times.

faq.q: What is the current density exponent n in Black's equation?
faq.a: It describes how strongly lifetime depends on current density; Black originally used n = 2. Measured values range roughly from 1 to 2 depending on whether void nucleation or void growth limits lifetime.

ダイシング.desc: Cutting a wafer into individual chips (dies). Besides sawing with a rotating blade, there are methods such as stealth dicing, which forms a modified layer inside the wafer with a laser.

about.p: The wafer is first mounted on adhesive dicing tape stretched across a ring frame so the dies stay in place once cut. A diamond blade tens of micrometres thick, spinning at high speed, cuts along the scribe lines (streets) while water cools it and flushes away debris. The cut removes a kerf tens of micrometres wide, so streets must allow for kerf plus edge chipping, and test structures (TEGs) placed there are destroyed. With fragile low-k dielectric stacks, a laser usually grooves the surface first so the blade does not chip or delaminate them.

Stealth dicing focuses an infrared laser, at a wavelength silicon largely transmits, inside the wafer to create a modified layer along each street; expanding the tape then cleaves the wafer along it. The surface is not cut, so the process is dry, produces almost no debris and has nearly zero kerf. It suits contamination- and vibration-sensitive MEMS, thin wafers and very small dies, where narrower streets raise dies per wafer. Laser ablation grooving is different: it removes surface material, mainly to open the top layers before blade dicing.

about.h: Where dicing sits in the flow
about.p: Dicing follows wafer test and back grinding, which thins the wafer from about 750 µm to its target, down to tens of micrometres for stacked memory. Dies are then picked from the tape for die bonding, wire bonding or flip-chip attach, and encapsulation. In dicing before grinding (DBG), partial-depth grooves are cut first and grinding separates the dies, reducing breakage of very thin chips. In wafer-level packaging, redistribution layers and solder balls are formed before singulation. Slicing an ingot into wafers is a different step, done with a multi-wire saw.

Dicing leaves damage at die edges: front-side and backside chipping, microcracks and a damaged sidewall layer. These flaws can grow under thermal cycling or handling and lower die strength, so cut quality is inspected and blade type, feed speed and cut depth are tuned to each wafer stack. Seal rings around each die help stop cracks and moisture from reaching active circuitry. In silicon photonics, edge couplers need a clean facet after singulation, while grating couplers allow optical testing on the wafer before dicing.

faq.q: What is the difference between blade dicing and stealth dicing?
faq.a: Blade dicing removes a kerf tens of micrometres wide with a spinning diamond blade and water, while stealth dicing forms a modified layer inside the wafer with an infrared laser and cleaves it by expanding the tape. Stealth dicing is dry, with almost no kerf or debris.

faq.q: Is back grinding done before or after dicing?
faq.a: Usually before: the wafer is thinned first and then diced. In dicing before grinding (DBG) the grooves are cut first and grinding completes the separation, which suits very thin chips.

faq.q: What is kerf in wafer dicing?
faq.a: Kerf is the width of material removed by the cut. With blade dicing it is tens of micrometres, which sets a minimum width for the scribe lines between dies.

ダイボンディング.desc: Attaching and fixing a diced chip at its position on a lead frame or package substrate, using adhesive, solder or sintered material.

バックグラインド.desc: Grinding the back of a wafer before dicing to thin it for packaging. Chips for stacking are thinned to a few tens of micrometers.

about.p: Wafers arrive from the fab at roughly 725–775 µm thick, depending on diameter, because they must survive front-side processing. Before dicing, a protective backgrind tape is laminated over the circuit side and the wafer is held face-down on a vacuum chuck. A rotating diamond grinding wheel first removes most of the material in a coarse grind, then a finer-grit wheel brings it to the target thickness with a smoother surface. Thickness is measured during grinding, and afterwards the wafer is transferred to dicing tape on a frame before the backgrind tape is removed.

Grinding leaves a thin layer of microcracks and crystal damage on the back surface. This layer weakens the die, acts as a starting point for fractures and contributes to wafer warpage, which becomes severe as the wafer gets thinner. It is therefore removed by a stress-relief step such as polishing, dry polishing or wet or plasma etching. Note the contrast with CMP, which planarizes front-side films during wafer processing, and with etch-back, which uniformly removes a deposited film; backgrinding removes bulk silicon from the back.

about.h: Typical thicknesses and why they matter
about.p: Thin packages for mobile devices often use dies of around 100 µm or less, and dies for stacked memory may be thinned to tens of micrometers so many layers fit in one package height. Thinning also shortens the heat path from the active layer, and in vertical power devices it reduces the substrate's contribution to on-resistance. In through-silicon via (TSV) processing, backgrinding exposes the via tips from the back. Very thin wafers are fragile, so they are often bonded temporarily to a rigid carrier during processing.

Dicing an already thinned wafer risks breakage and backside chipping. In dicing before grinding (DBG), grooves slightly deeper than the final die thickness are cut into the front first; when backgrinding reaches the grooves, the dies separate cleanly while still held by tape. A variant replaces the grooves with a laser-modified layer formed inside the silicon, which splits during grinding. These approaches are favored for dies tens of micrometers thick used in stacked memory.

faq.q: Why are wafers thinned before packaging?
faq.a: Thinner dies allow thinner packages and more dies per stack, improve heat removal and, in vertical power devices, lower on-resistance. Full-thickness wafers are only needed for mechanical strength during fab processing.

faq.q: What is DBG (dicing before grinding)?
faq.a: A method that cuts partial-depth grooves from the front first and then backgrinds until the grooves are reached, separating the dies. It reduces chipping and breakage for very thin dies.

faq.q: Is backgrinding the same as CMP?
faq.a: No. Backgrinding mechanically removes bulk silicon from the wafer back to thin it, while CMP planarizes films on the front side during wafer fabrication.

WLP(ウエハレベルパッケージ).desc: A package in which redistribution wiring and external terminals are formed while the chips are still in wafer form, before dicing. The result is a small package about the size of the chip.

about.h: How a wafer-level package is built
about.p: In a wafer-level package (WLP), packaging steps run on the whole wafer at once instead of on individual dies. On top of the chip's passivation, a polymer dielectric is coated, and copper redistribution layers (RDL) are plated to route signals from the fine-pitch bond pads to a coarser array of terminal positions. Under-bump metallization is formed at those positions and solder balls are attached. Only then is the wafer diced. Because every die is processed in parallel by wafer-fab-like lithography and plating, the package adds almost no area and the cost per die falls as die count per wafer rises.

In fan-in WLP the redistribution wiring and solder balls must fit inside the die outline, so the package is exactly die-sized and the number of terminals is limited by the die area and ball pitch. Fan-out WLP removes that limit: diced, known-good dies are placed on a carrier with space between them and embedded in mold compound to form a reconstituted wafer. The RDL can then extend beyond the die edge onto the mold area, allowing more I/O. Fan-out needs no laminate substrate and is thin, so it is used even for smartphone processors.

A chip-scale package (CSP) is any package no larger than about 1.2 times the die area, usually with BGA-style ball terminals underneath. Many CSPs still mount the die on a small substrate with wire bonds or flip-chip bumps. A fan-in WLP is the limiting case of a CSP: there is no separate substrate at all, and the package outline equals the die. That makes it the smallest and thinnest option, with very short connections that keep parasitic inductance low, which suits high-frequency and power-management parts.

Without a substrate in between, the silicon is soldered almost directly to the printed circuit board. Silicon and board materials expand differently with temperature, so thermal cycling strains the solder joints, and the strain grows with die size. Fan-in WLP is therefore most common for relatively small dies with modest pin counts, such as power-management chips, sensors and RF components in phones and wearables. Larger or higher-I/O dies move to fan-out WLP or to conventional flip-chip packages. The bare silicon edges also need care during handling and board assembly.

faq.q: What does WLP stand for in semiconductor packaging?
faq.a: WLP stands for wafer-level package, a package whose redistribution wiring and solder terminals are formed on the whole wafer before it is diced into individual chips.

faq.q: What is the difference between fan-in and fan-out WLP?
faq.a: Fan-in WLP keeps all terminals within the die outline, so the package is exactly die-sized but I/O count is limited. Fan-out WLP embeds dies in mold compound so wiring and balls can extend beyond the die edge.

faq.q: Is WLP the same as CSP?
faq.a: WLP is one type of chip-scale package. CSP covers any package up to roughly 1.2 times the die area, while a fan-in WLP matches the die size exactly and has no separate substrate.

CSP(チップサイズパッケージ).desc: A general term for packages shrunk to nearly the size of the chip. They are widely used in compact devices such as smartphones.

about.p: CSP is a family name rather than a single structure. A package counts as chip-scale when its footprint is only slightly larger than the die, commonly no more than about 1.2 times the die area. Several constructions meet that definition: a die mounted on a small substrate with an array of solder balls underneath, lead-frame-based packages with terminals on the bottom, and wafer-level CSP (WLCSP), where redistribution wiring and solder balls are formed directly on the wafer so the finished package is exactly the size of the die.

Traditional packages such as the DIP (dual in-line package) and QFP (quad flat package) bring leads out from the body edges, so pin count is tied to perimeter and the body is much larger than the die. CSPs use an area array of terminals on the bottom, like a BGA (ball grid array) but scaled down to the die footprint. Short connections between die and board give lower parasitic inductance and capacitance. The trade-off is that the terminal pitch must be fine, commonly about 0.4–0.5 mm, which demands precise board design and assembly.

Silicon expands with temperature far less than an FR-4 circuit board, roughly 3 ppm/K versus around 15 ppm/K. In a WLCSP the die is soldered almost directly to the board, so thermal cycling strains the solder joints, especially the outermost balls. Large-die WLCSPs are therefore limited in size or reinforced with underfill, an epoxy flowed beneath the package to share the stress. Mechanical drop shock is another key qualification test for CSPs in handheld products.

about.h: Fan-in limits and where you will meet it
about.p: A fan-in WLCSP can only place balls within the die outline, so dies with many I/O but a small area run out of room; fan-out packages extend the redistribution layer beyond the die edge to solve this. CSPs are everywhere that board area and height are scarce: smartphones, wearables, earbuds and camera modules, typically for power management chips, sensors, RF parts and memory. Large processors with very high pin counts generally use larger flip-chip BGA packages instead.

faq.q: What is the difference between CSP and BGA?
faq.a: BGA describes the terminal style, an array of solder balls under the package, while CSP describes the size, a footprint close to the die. Many CSPs use BGA-style balls, but a BGA package is often much larger than its die.

faq.q: Is WLCSP a type of CSP?
faq.a: Yes. A wafer-level CSP forms its wiring and solder balls while still on the wafer, so after dicing the package is exactly the size of the die.

faq.q: How big is a chip-scale package compared with the die?
faq.a: It is commonly defined as no larger than about 1.2 times the die area, and a wafer-level CSP is the same size as the die.

リフローはんだ付け.desc: Printing solder paste on a circuit board, placing components and heating everything in an oven to melt the solder. It is the standard method for surface mounting.

熱抵抗.desc: A measure of how hard it is for heat to flow, in °C/W. Multiplying dissipated power by thermal resistance gives the temperature rise. Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance is written θJA.

about.p: Thermal resistance treats heat flow like current in a circuit: power plays the role of current, temperature difference plays the role of voltage, and the temperature rise across a path is power multiplied by thermal resistance. Because only differences matter, °C/W and K/W are the same unit. Resistances along one path add in series, so a device on a heatsink sees junction-to-case, case-to-heatsink and heatsink-to-air terms summed. Parallel heat paths, such as heat leaving through both the package top and the board, combine like parallel resistors and lower the total.

θJA is junction-to-ambient resistance measured on a standardized test board in still air, so it depends strongly on board copper area, layer count and airflow, and is best used for comparing packages. θJC is junction-to-case resistance measured with the case held at a fixed temperature, and is the starting point when a heatsink is attached. ψJT is not a true resistance but a characterization parameter: it relates junction temperature to the measured top-of-package temperature when most heat actually flows into the board, so Tj ≈ Ttop + P × ψJT.

A transistor dissipating 0.5 W in a small TO-92 package with θJA around 200 °C/W rises about 100 °C above ambient, which can exceed a typical 150 °C junction limit on a warm day. A power device with θJC = 1.0 °C/W, 0.5 °C/W of thermal grease and a 3.0 °C/W heatsink has 4.5 °C/W in total, so 10 W of loss raises the junction 45 °C above ambient. A 50 W processor on a 0.5 K/W cooler runs about 25 °C above the surrounding air.

about.h: Steady state vs. transients, and reliability
about.p: Thermal resistance describes steady state. Real packages also store heat, so for short power pulses designers use transient thermal impedance curves, which start low and approach the steady-state value as pulse length grows. Over a product's life, thermal resistance can increase: in power modules, repeated heating and cooling cracks solder layers and lifts bond wires because silicon, aluminum and copper expand at different rates. Heat spreaders, thermal interface materials (TIMs) and better die attach keep resistance low, and lower junction temperature generally extends lifetime.

faq.q: How do you calculate junction temperature from thermal resistance?
faq.a: Add the ambient temperature to power times the junction-to-ambient thermal resistance: Tj = Ta + P × θ. For example, 2 W in a 40 °C/W package runs 80 °C above ambient.

faq.q: Can I use the datasheet θJA for my own board?
faq.a: Only as a rough guide. It is measured on a standard test board in still air, and a real board with different copper area, layer count or airflow can change it by up to around a factor of two, so verify by measurement.

faq.q: Is °C/W the same as K/W?
faq.a: Yes. Thermal resistance relates a temperature difference to power, and a difference of 1 °C equals a difference of 1 K.

ウエハテスト(プローブテスト).desc: Checking the electrical characteristics of each chip on the wafer by touching probes to its pads before dicing. It finds bad chips before assembly so they are not packaged needlessly.

about.p: A prober loads the wafer onto a chuck, aligns it optically and steps it so that the needles of a probe card land on each die's pads, which are tens of micrometres square. After first touch, the needles are pushed a little further, called overdrive, so the tips scrub through the aluminium oxide and make stable contact. Automatic test equipment (ATE) with hundreds to thousands of channels then supplies power, drives patterns and measures responses. The chuck can be heated or cooled, roughly −40 to 150 °C, and many probe cards contact several dies at once to cut test time.

Typical wafer-level tests check continuity, opens and shorts, supply and leakage currents, and logic function through scan patterns or built-in self-test, plus analog and memory blocks. Memory testing also finds failing cells whose addresses are programmed into fuses or antifuses, redirecting accesses to spare rows and columns (redundancy repair). Analog references are often trimmed the same way. Some products also write the lot number, wafer number and die coordinates into on-chip fuses, so a field return can be traced back to its manufacturing and test history.

The usual sequence is wafer test, assembly, final test and shipment, sometimes with burn-in or system-level test added. Wafer test screens out bad dies before money is spent packaging them, since defects cost more the later they are found. Final test checks the packaged part and confirms nothing was damaged in assembly; some high-speed measurements are also easier through a socket than through probe needles. In multi-die packages, wafer test must deliver known good die, because one bad die can scrap the whole assembly. Stage yields multiply: 95% process yield times 90% test yield gives about 85.5%.

Results are stored as electronic wafer maps rather than the ink dots once used to mark bad dies; die bonders read the map and pick only good, correctly graded dies. The maps are also a diagnostic tool. Failures clustered at the wafer edge point to deposition or etch uniformity, failures repeating at the same position in every exposure shot point to a reticle defect, and streaks suggest scratches. Adaptive test changes limits based on upstream data, and part average testing rejects in-spec dies that are statistical outliers, a common practice for automotive parts.

faq.q: What is the difference between wafer test and final test?
faq.a: Wafer test probes each die on the uncut wafer to screen out bad dies before packaging, while final test checks the finished, packaged part before shipment. Both use automatic test equipment, paired with a prober and a handler respectively.

faq.q: What is a probe card?
faq.a: A probe card is the interface between the tester and the wafer, carrying many fine needles or MEMS contacts laid out to match the pad positions of one or more dies. It is custom-made for each product.

faq.q: Why test chips on the wafer before packaging?
faq.a: Packaging a defective die wastes materials and assembly cost, and in multi-die packages one bad die can ruin the whole module. Wafer test also enables memory repair, trimming and early feedback on process problems.

BIST(組み込み自己テスト).desc: Test circuitry built into the chip so that it generates test patterns and checks results by itself. It is widely used, for example, to test memories.

about.p: A BIST controller, a test pattern generator and a response analyzer are built onto the chip. In logic BIST the pattern generator is usually a linear feedback shift register (LFSR), which produces pseudo-random bits that are shifted into the scan chains. After each capture clock, the chain outputs are compacted by a multiple-input signature register (MISR) into a short signature that is compared with the value expected from a fault-free design. Any unknown value, for example from an uninitialized memory, would corrupt the signature, so such sources must be blocked during test.

Embedded memories are dense and regular, so they are tested with algorithmic patterns rather than random ones. March tests walk through all addresses in ascending and descending order, writing and reading complementary data, and detect stuck-at, transition, coupling and address-decoder faults in a number of operations proportional to the memory size. Memory BIST runs at full speed from an on-chip clock. Combined with built-in redundancy analysis, it can decide which spare rows or columns should replace failing cells, and the repair is then programmed into fuses.

about.h: Why build test into the chip
about.p: BIST reduces the need for expensive tester channels, pattern memory and test time, which makes it easier to test many chips in parallel on one tester. It also enables at-speed testing with on-chip clocks and self-testing after the chip is in a product. Automotive microcontrollers run logic and memory BIST at power-up to find latent faults, including faults in the safety mechanisms themselves, which raises the latent fault metric required by functional safety standards. The costs are added area, startup time and a small chance that a faulty circuit produces the correct signature (aliasing).

In scan testing driven by automatic test pattern generation (ATPG), software computes deterministic patterns that target specific faults, and the tester applies them, usually through on-chip compression. That reaches high coverage with relatively few patterns. Logic BIST's pseudo-random patterns need many more cycles and miss random-pattern-resistant faults unless extra test points are inserted, but they require almost nothing from outside the chip. In practice, production test commonly uses compressed ATPG for logic and memory BIST for memories, with logic BIST added where in-system self-test is needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between logic BIST and memory BIST?
faq.a: Logic BIST applies pseudo-random patterns from an LFSR through scan chains and compresses responses into a signature. Memory BIST applies deterministic algorithms such as March tests to embedded memories and can also identify cells to repair.

faq.q: Why do automotive chips run BIST at power-up?
faq.a: Faults in safety mechanisms such as ECC logic or comparators stay hidden during normal operation. Running BIST at every start finds these latent faults before driving, as functional safety standards require.

faq.q: Does BIST replace automatic test equipment?
faq.a: Not entirely. BIST reduces tester requirements and test time, but production testing still uses testers for scan patterns, parametric measurements and to start BIST and read its results.

ATPG(自動テストパターン生成).desc: Automatically generating test patterns that detect faults from a circuit's netlist. It is used together with scan design.

about.p: Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) works from the gate-level netlist and a fault model. For each target fault it must activate the fault, driving the faulty line to the opposite of its stuck value, and propagate the difference along a sensitized path to an observable output, while finding primary-input values that justify both. Classic algorithms such as the D-algorithm and PODEM search this space. Each new pattern is fault-simulated to mark every other fault it happens to detect, and patterns are compacted, because test time and tester memory grow with pattern count.

The stuck-at model assumes a line is permanently 0 or 1, giving 2n faults for n lines. It is abstract, yet patterns that detect stuck-at faults also catch many real shorts and opens, and it remains the baseline for measuring fault coverage, the fraction of modeled faults the pattern set detects. Defects that only slow a signal are invisible to static tests, so delay fault models such as transition faults add at-speed patterns that launch a transition and capture the result one clock later. Coverage is always relative to a model, not to every possible physical defect.

Generating tests for a deep sequential circuit is very hard, because internal states can be reached only through many clock cycles. Scan design, a design-for-testability (DFT) technique, adds a multiplexer at each flip-flop input so that in test mode the flip-flops link into shift-register chains. The tester shifts a state in, applies one functional capture clock and shifts the result out. ATPG then only has to solve combinational logic between scan cells, which is what makes high coverage practical for chips with hundreds of millions of gates.

Functional verification asks whether the design is correct; ATPG assumes the design is correct and asks whether each manufactured chip matches it. Its output is test patterns, also called test vectors: input values per time step plus the expected responses, which automatic test equipment applies and compares. Other screens complement it. Part average testing (PAT) rejects chips whose measurements are statistical outliers even though they pass, a practice common for automotive parts, while automatic defect classification (ADC) belongs to wafer inspection, not to electrical test.

faq.q: What is ATPG in VLSI testing?
faq.a: It is software that automatically generates input patterns and expected outputs that detect modeled manufacturing faults, such as stuck-at faults, from a circuit's netlist.

faq.q: Why does ATPG need scan chains?
faq.a: Scan chains let the tester set and read every flip-flop directly, turning a hard sequential test problem into a combinational one that ATPG can solve efficiently with high coverage.

faq.q: What is the difference between stuck-at and transition fault models?
faq.a: Stuck-at faults model a line fixed at 0 or 1 and are found with static tests. Transition faults model a line that switches too slowly and need at-speed launch-and-capture patterns.

縮退故障.desc: The basic fault model in logic testing, which assumes a signal line is stuck at 0 or 1.

故障検出率(フォールトカバレッジ).desc: The fraction of modeled faults that a set of test patterns can detect. The higher it is, the less likely defective chips are to escape.

about.p: Fault coverage is always relative to a fault model, an abstraction of how physical defects affect logic. The classic stuck-at model assumes each circuit node may be permanently stuck at 0 or 1. Transition-delay faults model nodes that switch too slowly, bridging faults model shorts between nets, and cell-aware models target defects inside standard cells. Coverage is the number of detected faults divided by the number of modeled faults. Many tools also report test coverage, which removes faults proven untestable from the denominator and therefore reads higher than fault coverage.

about.h: Reaching high coverage with scan and ATPG
about.p: Testing a sequential circuit directly is hard, because internal states can be reached only through long input sequences. Scan design adds a multiplexer at each flip-flop input so that, in test mode, flip-flops are chained into shift registers. Arbitrary states can then be shifted in and results shifted out, turning the problem into testing combinational logic. Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) then produces patterns targeting each modeled fault. Hard-to-reach faults can be made testable by inserting test points, and stuck-at coverage targets of well above 99 percent are common for production.

The Williams-Brown relation estimates the defect level of shipped parts as DL = 1 − Y^(1−T), where Y is yield and T is fault coverage. With Y = 0.5 and T = 0.99, DL is about 0.7 percent, or roughly 7,000 defective parts per million (DPPM), which shows why the last fraction of a percent matters. The relation assumes defects behave like modeled faults, which real defects do not always do, so manufacturers add at-speed tests, additional fault models and other screens to catch defects that stuck-at patterns miss.

Manufacturing fault coverage describes how many defective chips a test finds before shipment. Diagnostic coverage, used in functional safety standards for automotive electronics, describes the fraction of faults that an on-chip safety mechanism detects or controls during operation. For example, a block with a failure rate of 200 FIT protected by a mechanism with 99 percent diagnostic coverage leaves a residual undetected failure rate of 200 × 0.01 = 2 FIT, where 1 FIT is one failure per billion device-hours. Both use similar arithmetic but answer different questions.

faq.q: What is the difference between fault coverage and test coverage?
faq.a: Fault coverage divides detected faults by all modeled faults, while test coverage excludes faults that are proven untestable from the denominator. Test coverage is therefore equal to or higher than fault coverage.

faq.q: How does fault coverage relate to DPPM?
faq.a: The Williams-Brown model gives defect level as 1 − Y^(1−T). For 50 percent yield and 99 percent coverage this is about 0.7 percent, around 7,000 DPPM, so very high coverage is needed for low escape rates.

faq.q: What is a good fault coverage for scan ATPG?
faq.a: Stuck-at coverage well above 99 percent is a typical production target, and automotive products push higher still and add transition-delay and other fault models.

IDDQテスト.desc: A test that measures the supply current of a CMOS circuit at rest and flags defects such as bridging faults when it is abnormally high.

KGD(ノウングッドダイ).desc: A chip confirmed to be good before packaging. It matters when several chips go into one package, because a single bad chip ruins the whole module.

about.p: When several dies share one package, the package works only if every die works, so yields multiply. Eight dies that are each 99% good give 0.99⁸, about 92%, chance that all are good; four dies at 95% each give only about 81%. One bad die scraps the whole assembly, including expensive good dies such as a large processor or other HBM layers. Spending more on test before assembly is cheaper than discarding finished modules, which is why multi-chip modules, HBM and chiplet-based processors depend on known good dies.

about.h: Why wafer sort is not automatically enough
about.p: In a single-chip product, wafer probe screens out obvious failures and the package-level final test does the thorough job, including at-speed tests across temperature and often burn-in. A die is truly known good only after that. For multi-die assembly the thorough test must move before assembly, onto a bare die that is hard to contact: microbumps are tiny and fragile, probe cards have limited high-speed capability, and burn-in is difficult at wafer level. KGD therefore relies on higher-coverage wafer test, built-in self-test and design-for-test features, dedicated probe pads and sometimes wafer-level burn-in.

In co-packaged optics, silicon photonic chips are tested at wafer level before joining a costly switch IC. Fiber probes launch light through grating couplers from above the wafer while electrical probes contact the pads, so waveguide loss and modulator and photodetector performance can be measured automatically. For stacked memory the idea extends to a known good stack, a fully tested die stack, and built-in redundancy lets some defects be repaired after stacking rather than scrapping the part.

about.h: KGD does not replace final test
about.p: Assembly itself can introduce defects: cracked bumps, poor joints, warpage, contamination or damage from handling and bonding. A final test of the completed package is still indispensable, and its results feed back into deciding how much test effort to spend at the die level. The economic balance is set by die cost, the number of dies per package, defect rates at each stage and the cost of the test steps.

faq.q: What does known good die mean?
faq.a: It is a bare die that has been tested thoroughly enough before assembly to be trusted as good, so it can be combined with other dies in one package without risking the whole assembly.

faq.q: Why is KGD important for HBM and chiplets?
faq.a: Package yield is the product of all die yields, so one failing die among many ruins the entire module and every good die in it. Screening dies before assembly keeps multi-die yield economical.

faq.q: Is final test still needed if all dies are KGD?
faq.a: Yes. Bonding and assembly can create new defects, so the finished package must still be tested.

パレート図.desc: A chart that lists items such as defect types as bars in descending order of count, with a line for the cumulative share. It shows which items to tackle first.

about.h: How a Pareto chart is built
about.p: Start by tallying occurrences per category over a fixed period, for example defect types found at inspection or failure bins at wafer test. Plot the categories as bars in descending order, largest on the left, with small categories often grouped into an "other" bar at the far right. Then overlay a line showing the cumulative percentage against a second axis from 0 to 100%. The bars show which category is biggest; the line shows how many categories you must address to cover a given share of the problem.

The chart is named after the Pareto principle, the empirical observation that a few causes often account for most of the effect. In defect data it is common for the top two or three categories to make up 70–80% of the total, which tells an engineering team where limited effort pays off first. It is a tendency, not a law. A flat Pareto chart, where no category dominates, is itself informative: it suggests a broad, systemic cause rather than one dominant failure mode.

Counting alone can mislead, so bars are often weighted by impact, such as yield loss, scrap cost or the fraction of defects that actually kill a die. A frequent but harmless defect may then drop below a rarer killer defect. Engineers also stratify: the top bar is broken down into a second-level Pareto chart by tool, chamber, layer or product to narrow the cause. After a fix, a new chart over the same period length shows whether the target bar shrank and what has become the next priority.

about.h: Pareto chart vs. other quality tools
about.p: A Pareto chart is one of the classic seven basic quality-control tools, and each answers a different question. A histogram shows the distribution of a continuous measurement in ordered bins, while a Pareto chart sorts discrete categories by size. A scatter plot reveals correlation between two variables, a control chart tracks stability over time, a wafer map shows where failures occur on the wafer, and a shmoo plot shows pass/fail across supply voltage and frequency. Pareto analysis decides which problem to attack first; the others help explain it.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Pareto chart and a histogram?
faq.a: A histogram groups a continuous variable into ordered bins to show its distribution, so bar order follows the value axis. A Pareto chart plots discrete categories sorted from largest to smallest and adds a cumulative-percentage line.

faq.q: Why does a Pareto chart have a cumulative line?
faq.a: The cumulative percentage line shows how much of the total is covered by the top categories combined. It lets you read off, for example, that fixing the first three causes would address about 75% of all defects.

faq.q: What is the Pareto principle?
faq.a: It is the observation, often summarized as the 80/20 rule, that a small number of causes produce most of the effects. The exact ratio varies and should be checked with data rather than assumed.

管理図.desc: A chart that plots process measurements over time against a center line and control limits (usually ±3σ) to judge whether the process is stable. Points outside the limits or runs on one side signal problems.

about.p: A control chart plots a statistic, such as an individual measurement, a subgroup mean or a defect count, in time order against a center line at the process average. The upper and lower control limits sit three standard deviations of that plotted statistic away from the center; for subgroup means, this is the process standard deviation divided by the square root of the subgroup size. When the process is stable and roughly normal, only about 0.27% of points fall outside the limits by chance, so a point beyond them is strong evidence that something has changed.

Points inside the limits can still signal trouble when their pattern is unlikely to be random. Common rule sets, such as the Western Electric or Nelson rules, flag a long run on one side of the center line, a steady upward or downward trend, or several points clustered near one limit. Nine consecutive points on the same side of the center, for example, occur by chance less than 1% of the time in a stable process, so they suggest a shift in the mean before any product goes out of specification. Each added rule also raises the false-alarm rate.

Variables such as film thickness or line width use an X-bar and R chart, which tracks subgroup mean and range on separate panels to catch both shifts in center and changes in spread. Larger subgroups use standard deviation instead of range, and processes with one measurement per lot use an individuals and moving-range chart. Attribute data use a p chart for fraction defective, whose limits vary with sample size, an np chart for defective counts, and c or u charts for defect counts. EWMA and CUSUM charts detect small, gradual shifts faster.

Limits are first calculated in a setup phase from roughly 20 to 25 subgroups of a process believed to be stable, after removing points with known special causes; the chart is then used for ongoing monitoring. Control limits must not be confused with specification limits: a process can be stable yet produce out-of-spec parts, or be within spec while drifting out of control. Specification limits for individual parts also should not be drawn on a chart of subgroup means. Limits are recalculated after intentional process changes.

faq.q: Why are control limits set at three sigma?
faq.a: Three-sigma limits balance sensitivity against false alarms: a stable process puts only about 0.27% of points outside them by chance, while real shifts of meaningful size are detected quickly.

faq.q: When should I use a p chart instead of an X-bar R chart?
faq.a: Use a p chart when each item is classified as good or defective and you track the fraction defective. Use an X-bar and R chart when you have continuous measurements, such as thickness or dimensions, taken in subgroups.

faq.q: Can a process be in control but out of specification?
faq.a: Yes. Being in control means the process varies only randomly around a stable mean; if that spread is wider than the specification, or the mean is off target, it will still produce defects consistently.

特性要因図.desc: A diagram that organizes the causes affecting a problem (the effect) in the shape of a fish skeleton. Also called a fishbone diagram.

about.p: The problem being studied, called the effect, is written at the head on the right side, and a horizontal spine runs to it. Major bones branch off the spine for categories of causes, classically the 4Ms: man (people), machine, material and method. Many teams add measurement and environment to make 5M+E or 6M. Each major bone carries smaller bones for more specific causes, and those can branch further, so the diagram shows a hierarchy from broad category to concrete, checkable cause. It is also called an Ishikawa diagram after the quality engineer Kaoru Ishikawa.

Start by stating the effect narrowly and measurably, for example a rise in particle defects after a particular etch step rather than simply low yield. The team then brainstorms causes under each category, asking why repeatedly to move from vague items to specific ones, and avoids judging ideas while the diagram is being filled. Once the list is reasonably exhaustive, the most plausible causes are marked and each is checked against data, such as tool logs, inspection results or a designed experiment. The diagram generates hypotheses; it does not prove which cause is responsible.

Suppose wafer edge yield has dropped on one product. Under machine the team might list chamber wall flaking, a worn edge ring or a change in maintenance interval. Under material: a new photoresist lot or incoming wafer flatness. Under method: a recent recipe change or different chamber seasoning. Under measurement: a changed inspection threshold. Under man: a manual handling step done differently by shifts. Wafer maps, tool history and lot genealogy are then used to narrow the list to the cause that actually matches the failure pattern.

about.h: Place among the seven QC tools
about.p: The cause-and-effect diagram is one of the seven basic quality control tools, together with the check sheet, Pareto chart, histogram, scatter diagram, control chart and stratification (some lists use a flowchart or graph instead). The tools complement each other: a Pareto chart ranks defect types by count to pick which effect to attack, the fishbone lists candidate causes, a scatter diagram tests whether a suspected cause correlates with the result, and a histogram shows the distribution, where two peaks often mean data from two tools or materials are mixed and should be stratified.

faq.q: Why is it called a fishbone diagram?
faq.a: The effect sits at the head on the right, the main line forms the spine, and the cause categories branch off at an angle like ribs, so the finished drawing looks like a fish skeleton.

faq.q: What are the 4Ms in a cause-and-effect diagram?
faq.a: They are man (people), machine, material and method, the standard categories for the major bones. Measurement and environment are often added, giving 5M+E.

faq.q: What is the difference between a fishbone diagram and a Pareto chart?
faq.a: A Pareto chart ranks problems or defect categories by frequency to show which few matter most. A fishbone diagram takes one chosen problem and organizes its possible causes so they can be investigated.

FMEA(故障モード影響解析).desc: A method that lists the possible failure modes of a product or process, evaluates their effects and severity, and plans countermeasures in advance.

about.p: Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a structured, team-based review carried out before problems occur. For each component of a design or each step of a process, the team lists the ways it could fail (failure modes), the consequences of each failure (effects), the likely causes and the controls already in place. Each mode is then scored for severity, occurrence and detection, commonly on 1-to-10 scales, where a high detection score means the failure is hard to catch. Multiplying the three gives the risk priority number (RPN), which ranks where countermeasures should go first.

A design FMEA examines a product's design, such as a chip, package or module, asking how each function could fail and what the user would experience. A process FMEA examines manufacturing steps. In a wafer fab, for example, a CMP step might fail by over-polishing, with the effect of thin copper lines and high resistance, caused by an incorrect endpoint, and detected by thickness metrology. Countermeasures can lower occurrence, for instance through automated run-to-run control, or improve detection through added inspection. After actions are taken, the scores are re-evaluated and the document is kept current.

about.h: Limits of the risk priority number
about.p: The RPN is convenient but crude. Very different risks can share the same product: a severe failure that is rare and easily detected may score the same as a trivial one that happens often. For this reason teams usually treat high-severity modes, especially those affecting safety, as requiring action regardless of RPN. Some newer guidelines, notably in the automotive industry, replace the RPN with an action-priority table that weights severity first. Scores are also subjective, so consistent rating criteria and cross-functional review matter as much as the arithmetic.

FMEA is proactive and works bottom-up from individual failure modes to their effects. Fault tree analysis (FTA) works top-down, starting from one undesired event and tracing the combinations of causes that could produce it. Pareto charts and histograms analyze defects that have already occurred, statistical process control (SPC) watches running processes for abnormalities, advanced process control (APC) actively corrects tool settings, and gage R&R checks whether a measurement system is precise enough. In semiconductor ramp-up, FMEA results often decide where those other controls are applied.

faq.q: What does FMEA stand for?
faq.a: FMEA stands for failure mode and effects analysis. It is a method for listing possible failures of a product or process, evaluating their effects and planning countermeasures before they happen.

faq.q: How is the risk priority number calculated in FMEA?
faq.a: The RPN is the product of the severity, occurrence and detection scores, each commonly rated from 1 to 10. Higher numbers indicate risks to address first, although high-severity items usually need action regardless of RPN.

faq.q: What is the difference between FMEA and FTA?
faq.a: FMEA starts from individual failure modes and works forward to their effects, covering the whole design or process. FTA starts from one specific undesired event and works backward through a logic tree of causes.

APC(先進的プロセス制御).desc: Automatically adjusting the process settings for the next lot or wafer based on earlier measurements, as in run-to-run control. It reduces variation.

about.p: Advanced process control (APC) closes a loop between metrology and the process tool. In run-to-run (R2R) control, a simple model links a recipe knob to the result, for example polish time to removed thickness in CMP. After each lot or wafer is measured, the controller updates its estimate of the tool's current behaviour, often with an exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) to filter measurement noise, and computes the setting for the next run. A heavier weight on recent data tracks drift quickly but also chases noise; a lighter weight is smoother but slower to react.

APC uses information from two directions. Feedforward control uses measurements taken before the step on the same wafer: if the incoming film is measured thick, the next CMP polish time is extended so the final thickness still hits target. Feedback control uses results measured after processing earlier wafers to correct slow changes in the tool, such as a falling removal rate as a pad or chamber ages. Lithography overlay and critical-dimension control, where exposure dose, focus and alignment offsets are adjusted lot by lot, are classic examples of combining both.

Statistical process control (SPC) watches a process with control charts and raises an alarm or stops the tool when a parameter drifts outside its limits; it detects problems but does not fix them. APC actively steers the process back toward target on every run, which shrinks variation without waiting for an excursion. The two work together: SPC limits are still applied to APC-controlled outputs, and in many fabs the APC umbrella also includes fault detection and classification (FDC), which monitors tool sensor traces in real time.

Several yield-related acronyms sit close to APC but do different jobs. Automatic defect classification (ADC) sorts review-SEM images of defects into categories such as particles or scratches. Part average testing (PAT) rejects chips whose test results are statistical outliers within their lot even though they meet specification, a technique used for automotive quality. ATPG, automatic test pattern generation, creates test vectors for logic. Only APC changes how wafers are processed; the others classify defects or screen finished chips.

faq.q: What is the difference between APC and SPC in semiconductor manufacturing?
faq.a: SPC monitors process data with control charts and flags or stops the process when it goes out of control. APC uses the same kind of measurements to adjust the recipe automatically for the next lot or wafer, actively reducing variation.

faq.q: What is run-to-run control?
faq.a: Run-to-run control is a form of APC that updates a tool's recipe between runs based on measurements of previous runs, for example adjusting CMP polish time from the measured removal of earlier wafers. It corrects slow drift without changing anything during a single run.

faq.q: What is feedforward control in APC?
faq.a: Feedforward control uses a measurement of the incoming wafer, taken at an earlier step, to choose settings for the current step. A thicker-than-normal incoming film, for example, leads to a longer polish so the final thickness stays on target.

システマティック不良.desc: A defect that occurs repeatedly at particular patterns or locations because of interactions between design and process. It is distinguished from random defects caused by chance particles.

アレニウスモデル.desc: A model in which reaction or degradation rates vary with temperature as exp(−Ea/kT). It is used to estimate lifetime at operating temperature from accelerated tests at higher temperatures.

about.h: The equation and the acceleration factor
about.p: The Arrhenius model states that the rate of a thermally activated process is proportional to exp(−Ea/kT), where Ea is the activation energy, k is Boltzmann's constant (about 8.62e-5 eV/K) and T is absolute temperature. If lifetime is inversely proportional to the degradation rate, the acceleration factor between a stress temperature and a use temperature is AF = exp[(Ea/k)(1/Tuse − 1/Tstress)], with both temperatures in kelvin. For example, with Ea = 0.7 eV, stressing at 125 °C instead of using at 55 °C accelerates aging by roughly 78 times.

Because Ea sits in the exponent, the acceleration factor is very sensitive to it, and each failure mechanism has its own value; figures around 0.5-1 eV are commonly used. A mistaken Ea can change a lifetime estimate by an order of magnitude or more. The stress temperature must also be low enough that the same mechanism dominates as in use; if a new mechanism appears only at high temperature, extrapolation becomes invalid. Many models combine the Arrhenius term with other stresses, for example current density in Black's equation for electromigration.

A familiar shortcut says reaction rates roughly double for every 10 °C rise, so lowering operating temperature by 10 °C roughly doubles lifetime. Near room temperature this corresponds to an activation energy of about 0.55 eV. For mechanisms with larger Ea the temperature sensitivity is greater, and at higher temperatures the same Ea gives a smaller factor per 10 °C, so the rule is only a rough guide. It still explains clearly why cooling electronics extends their life.

High-temperature operating life (HTOL) tests run devices under bias at elevated temperature, often 125 °C, for on the order of 1000 hours, and the acceleration factor converts that to equivalent years at use conditions. Data-retention bakes for flash memory use the same idea, because stored charge leaks out faster when hot. Where voltage or humidity also accelerates failure, the Arrhenius term is combined with additional factors, as in Eyring-type or humidity models, to estimate field lifetime.

faq.q: How do you calculate the Arrhenius acceleration factor?
faq.a: Use AF = exp[(Ea/k)(1/Tuse − 1/Tstress)] with temperatures in kelvin and k = 8.62e-5 eV/K. For Ea = 0.7 eV, 125 °C stress versus 55 °C use gives about 78.

faq.q: What activation energy should be used in reliability tests?
faq.a: It depends on the failure mechanism and should come from data or established values for that mechanism; numbers around 0.5-1 eV are common. Using a generic value without justification can badly misestimate lifetime.

faq.q: Does lifetime double for every 10 °C decrease in temperature?
faq.a: Roughly, for an activation energy near 0.55 eV around room temperature. Mechanisms with higher activation energy are more temperature-sensitive, so the rule is only an approximation.

FIT.desc: A unit of failure rate: 1 FIT is one failure per billion (10⁹) device-hours. It is used for parts with very low failure rates, such as semiconductors.

ワイブル分布.desc: A probability distribution widely used to analyze lifetime data. Its shape parameter can represent early-failure, random-failure and wear-out behavior.

about.p: The Weibull distribution gives the fraction failed by time t (cumulative failure probability) as F(t) = 1 − exp[−(t/η)^m]. Here m is the shape parameter (also written β) and η is the scale parameter. At t = η, F = 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.632, so η is the time by which about 63.2% of the population has failed, also called the characteristic life. The failure rate (hazard function) is λ(t) = (m/η)(t/η)^(m−1), and the value of m determines how it changes with time. There is also a three-parameter form that adds a location parameter representing the time before any failures can occur.

When the shape parameter m is less than 1, the failure rate falls over time, representing early failures from manufacturing defects. When m equals 1, the failure rate is constant and the distribution is identical to the exponential distribution, representing random failures. When m is greater than 1, the failure rate rises over time, representing wear-out. Around m = 3.5, the shape of the distribution approaches a normal distribution. Being able to represent all three periods of the bathtub curve with one distribution is a major strength of the Weibull distribution. A larger m means failure times are more tightly clustered, so it also serves as a measure of spread.

Rearranging F(t) = 1 − exp[−(t/η)^m] gives ln(−ln(1 − F)) = m·ln t − m·ln η, which is a straight line when ln t is plotted on the horizontal axis and ln(−ln(1 − F)) on the vertical axis. This is the Weibull plot (Weibull probability paper), and the slope of the line is the shape parameter m. Failure times are sorted in ascending order, and the cumulative failure probability of the i-th failure is estimated with a median-rank approximation such as (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4) before plotting. When the data include tests stopped before every unit failed, maximum likelihood estimation is generally used. A bent plot may indicate a mix of failure modes.

Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) of gate dielectrics follows weakest-link behavior, failing first at the weakest spot in the film, so it is often described by a Weibull distribution. Lifetime then scales with area to the power −1/m: for example, with m = 1.5, a 1000-fold increase in area cuts lifetime to 1/100. This relation converts results from small test structures to the total gate area of a product. Thinner dielectrics tend to have smaller m. The Weibull distribution is also used for analyses such as thermal fatigue of solder joints, but electromigration lifetimes are often described with a lognormal distribution, so it is important to choose the distribution that fits the failure mechanism.

faq.q: What happens when the shape parameter m is 1?
faq.a: The failure rate becomes constant over time and the Weibull distribution is identical to the exponential distribution. It represents failures in the random-failure period, and the mean time to failure (MTTF) then equals the scale parameter η.

faq.q: What does the scale parameter η represent?
faq.a: It is the time by which about 63.2% of the population has failed, also called the characteristic life. Substituting t = η into the formula gives F = 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.632 regardless of the shape parameter.

faq.q: When should you use a Weibull versus a lognormal distribution?
faq.a: The Weibull distribution is commonly used for dielectric breakdown, where failure is set by the weakest spot, and when you want to describe how the failure rate changes over time. Degradation driven by many accumulating factors, such as diffusion and chemical reactions, often fits a lognormal distribution, which is widely used for electromigration lifetimes. In practice, the data are plotted on each type of probability paper to check the fit as well.

ホットキャリア注入(HCI).desc: Degradation in which carriers accelerated by the strong field near the drain are injected into the gate insulator, shifting the threshold voltage and reducing drive current.

ラッチアップ.desc: A condition in which a parasitic thyristor structure in a CMOS circuit turns on and a large current keeps flowing between supply and ground. It is prevented by well-contact placement, guard rings and similar measures.

about.p: A bulk CMOS inverter places a pMOS in an n-well on a p-type substrate next to an nMOS. The p+ source of the pMOS, the n-well and the p-substrate form a vertical PNP transistor, while the n+ source of the nMOS, the p-substrate and the n-well form a lateral NPN transistor. Each one's collector drives the other's base, making a PNPN thyristor between the supply and ground. Normally it stays off because well and substrate contacts hold both bases at their rail potentials, but the resistance of the well and substrate between those contacts and the transistors leaves room for a local voltage drop.

about.h: How latch-up is triggered and sustained
about.p: If current is injected into the well or substrate, for example when an input pin is driven above the supply or below ground, by electrostatic discharge, by a radiation strike or by incorrect power sequencing, the voltage drop across the well or substrate resistance can forward-bias one parasitic base-emitter junction. That transistor's collector current then turns on the other, and if the loop gain exceeds one the pair feeds itself. A low-resistance path from supply to ground then stays on even after the trigger disappears and persists until power is removed, often overheating and destroying metal lines or junctions.

Most defenses lower the well and substrate resistances or the parasitic gains. In layout, well and substrate contacts are placed frequently, which is why standard-cell libraries include tap cells, and I/O transistors are enclosed in guard rings that collect injected carriers before they reach the core. Increasing the spacing between nMOS and pMOS also helps. In the process, retrograde wells with heavy doping deep below the surface and p/p+ epitaxial wafers with a low-resistance substrate shunt parasitic current. Silicon on insulator (SOI) removes the substrate path entirely, so SOI circuits are essentially immune.

Latch-up is an event, not gradual wear. Hot carrier injection (HCI) and bias temperature instability (NBTI in pMOS, PBTI in high-k nMOS) slowly shift threshold voltage over years, and electromigration slowly erodes metal lines, whereas latch-up can destroy a chip within moments of a single trigger. For this reason latch-up immunity is tested directly: qualification standards such as AEC-Q100 for automotive ICs include latch-up tests, which inject current into pins and apply overvoltage to supplies while checking that the supply current returns to normal afterward.

faq.q: What causes latch-up in CMOS?
faq.a: A parasitic PNPN thyristor formed by the wells and substrate turns on when injected current, for example from an input overvoltage or ESD, forward-biases one of its junctions. The two parasitic bipolar transistors then sustain each other, keeping a large current flowing from supply to ground.

faq.q: How do you recover from latch-up?
faq.a: The latched state persists until the supply voltage is removed or reduced enough to stop the current, so power must be cycled. If the current has already overheated metal or junctions, the damage is permanent.

faq.q: Why does SOI prevent latch-up?
faq.a: In silicon on insulator, each transistor sits in a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide, so there is no continuous well and substrate path to form the parasitic thyristor. Without that path, the regenerative loop cannot exist.

ESD(静電気放電).desc: A sudden discharge of static electricity from a charged person or object. Applied to an IC pin it can destroy gate oxides and other structures, so I/O pins have protection circuits.

about.p: A person or object can easily charge to thousands of volts, while a gate dielectric a few nanometres thick breaks down at around 10 MV/cm, only a few volts for a 2 nm film. An electrostatic discharge into a pin can therefore rupture gate oxides instantly, and the peak current can melt junctions or metal lines. Not every hit kills a part outright: some leave latent damage, such as increased leakage, that fails later in the field. Factories therefore use grounded wrist straps, conductive floors and work surfaces, and ionizers.

Each I/O pin has diodes to the supply and ground rails, which turn on when the pin is driven beyond the rails and steer the discharge current away from internal circuits. A power clamp between the rails, often a large transistor triggered by the fast edge of an ESD event, completes the current path. Protection must trigger above the normal operating voltage but below the level that damages the circuit it guards. Protection devices add capacitance, so high-speed I/O keeps them small. A 5 V tolerant input omits the diode to VDD so a higher input voltage does not flow into the supply.

Component ratings describe handling in ESD-controlled factories. The human body model (HBM), a 100 pF capacitor discharged through 1.5 kΩ, represents a charged person touching a pin; about 2 kV is a common target. The charged device model (CDM) represents a charged IC discharging when a pin touches metal, with events around a nanosecond or shorter, and is the main concern in automated handling. A datasheet rating such as HBM ±2 kV and CDM ±500 V does not cover finished equipment, where system-level tests like IEC 61000-4-2 apply ±8 kV contact discharges and board-level TVS diodes are needed.

The two are often tested together, as in automotive AEC-Q100 qualification, but they are different failures. ESD is a brief, high-energy transient that damages structures directly. Latch-up is a sustained high-current state in which parasitic pnp and npn transistors in CMOS form a thyristor and turn each other on, triggered by current injection or overvoltage on a pin. Once latched, current keeps flowing until power is removed and can overheat the chip. Higher temperature raises the parasitic gains and well resistance, so latch-up testing is done at maximum operating temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between HBM and CDM ESD?
faq.a: HBM models a charged person discharging into a pin through 1.5 kΩ from 100 pF. CDM models the IC itself being charged and discharging very quickly when a pin touches metal, which is the dominant risk in automated assembly.

faq.q: Is an IC's HBM rating enough to pass system-level ESD tests?
faq.a: No. HBM and CDM ratings cover factory handling, while system-level tests such as IEC 61000-4-2 deliver much more energy. Pins exposed to the outside world normally need external protection such as TVS diodes.

faq.q: What is the difference between ESD and latch-up?
faq.a: ESD is a brief static discharge that destroys oxides or junctions directly. Latch-up is a parasitic thyristor in CMOS turning on and holding a large current until power is cycled.

ソフトエラー.desc: A temporary flip of data stored in memory or flip-flops caused by neutrons from cosmic rays, alpha particles and the like. The device is not damaged, so rewriting restores correct operation.

about.h: How a particle flips a bit
about.p: An energetic charged particle passing through silicon leaves a trail of electron-hole pairs, about one pair for every 3.6 eV it deposits. If a sensitive junction, such as the storage node of an SRAM cell or flip-flop, collects more than its critical charge, the stored value flips. Alpha particles come from trace uranium and thorium in package materials and solder. Cosmic-ray neutrons do not ionize directly but undergo nuclear reactions with silicon that produce charged fragments. Thermal neutrons captured by boron-10, once present in borophosphosilicate glass, are another historical source.

A soft error, also called a single-event upset (SEU), corrupts data without damaging the device, so rewriting the location restores correct behavior. A hard error is a permanent failure from a manufacturing defect or wear-out. As cells shrink and supply voltage falls, critical charge drops, and one particle can upset several neighboring cells at once, called a multi-cell upset. Some radiation effects are not soft: single-event latch-up can trigger a parasitic thyristor and destroy a device unless power is removed.

Soft error rate is usually expressed in FIT, failures per billion device-hours, often normalized per megabit. Ground-level neutron flux is low, about 13 neutrons per square centimeter per hour above 10 MeV at the New York City sea-level reference used in JEDEC standards, so field measurements take a long time. Instead, devices are irradiated with neutron beams at accelerator facilities, far more intense than the natural flux, and alpha sources are used for package effects. Neutron flux rises steeply with altitude, reaching hundreds of times ground level at airliner cruising altitude.

Error-correcting codes (ECC) are the main defense for memories: single-error-correct, double-error-detect codes fix any one flipped bit per word, and periodic scrubbing rewrites corrected data before a second upset accumulates. Physically interleaving the bits of a word spreads a multi-cell upset across several words so each remains correctable. Low-alpha materials reduce package emissions. For logic, hardened flip-flop designs, parity on registers and triple modular redundancy in critical paths are used, and silicon-on-insulator (SOI) reduces the volume from which charge is collected.

faq.q: What causes soft errors in memory?
faq.a: They are caused by alpha particles from trace radioactive impurities in packaging and by secondary particles from cosmic-ray neutrons, which generate enough charge in the silicon to flip a stored bit.

faq.q: What is the difference between a soft error and a hard error?
faq.a: A soft error is a temporary data upset that leaves the device undamaged and is cleared by rewriting. A hard error is a permanent fault caused by a defect or wear-out.

faq.q: Does ECC protect against soft errors?
faq.a: Yes. ECC corrects single-bit upsets and detects double-bit errors in each word, and combining it with scrubbing and bit interleaving handles most soft errors in memories.

ネットリスト.desc: Data describing the elements (cells) of a circuit and how they are connected. It is the output of logic synthesis and the input to place-and-route and timing analysis.

about.p: A netlist lists instances, the cells or transistors in a circuit, and nets, the electrical connections between their pins, plus the ports that connect the circuit to the outside. It is pure connectivity: it says that the output pin of one NAND gate drives the inputs of two flip-flops, but nothing about where those cells sit or how the wires are drawn. A gate-level netlist references cells from a standard-cell library and is usually written as structural Verilog, while a transistor-level SPICE netlist lists individual MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their parameters for circuit simulation.

about.h: Where netlists appear in the design flow
about.p: Logic synthesis converts register-transfer level (RTL) code into a gate-level netlist that meets timing, area and power constraints. Place-and-route reads that netlist, then adds buffers and a synthesized clock tree, producing an updated post-layout netlist. Parasitic resistance and capacitance extracted from the layout are attached for static timing analysis. Formal equivalence checking compares the netlist against the RTL, automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) works on the netlist to target faults such as stuck-at faults, and layout-versus-schematic (LVS) checking compares a netlist extracted from the layout with the reference netlist.

RTL simulation is fast but abstract, so some bugs only appear after synthesis. Simulating the gate-level netlist exercises the actual gates and flip-flops, exposing reset and initialization problems that X-optimism hides in RTL, and cases where the synthesized logic differs from the designer's intent. When gate and wire delays from the layout are back-annotated in SDF (Standard Delay Format), timing-related problems also show up. Because gate-level simulation is far slower than RTL simulation, it is usually run on a limited set of tests.

The netlist and the layout describe the same chip in different ways. The netlist captures what is connected to what, while layout data in GDSII or OASIS format holds the polygons on each mask layer that will actually be printed on the wafer. Verification ties them together: LVS proves that the drawn shapes implement exactly the connections in the netlist, and design rule checking (DRC) separately confirms that the shapes obey manufacturing rules. Only layout data goes to mask making after tape-out.

faq.q: What is the difference between RTL and a netlist?
faq.a: RTL describes behavior as registers and the logic operations between them in a language like Verilog or VHDL. A netlist is the structural result after synthesis, listing specific library cells and the wires connecting them.

faq.q: What is a SPICE netlist?
faq.a: It is a transistor-level netlist in the input format of SPICE circuit simulators, listing devices such as MOSFETs, resistors and capacitors with their node connections and model parameters, used for analog and cell-level simulation.

faq.q: Does a netlist contain physical layout information?
faq.a: No. A netlist contains only components and connectivity. Cell positions and wire shapes live in the layout database and in GDSII or OASIS files, although parasitics extracted from the layout can be attached to the netlist for timing analysis.

スタンダードセル.desc: A pre-designed, pre-verified building block such as a logic gate or flip-flop. Cells share a common height so automatic place-and-route can line them up to build large circuits.

about.p: A standard cell implements a small function, such as a NAND gate, multiplexer or flip-flop, as a fixed transistor layout. All cells in a library share the same height, while widths vary in multiples of a placement grid tied to the gate pitch. Power and ground rails run along the top and bottom edges, and alternate rows are flipped so neighboring rows share rails. Cells snap side by side into rows like bricks, with input and output pins on the lower metal layers for the router to reach. Each function usually comes in several drive strengths and threshold-voltage flavors to trade speed against leakage.

Cell height is quoted in tracks, the number of minimum-pitch routing wires that fit across it. Six tracks at a 28 nm metal pitch is about 170 nm. Fewer tracks give shorter cells and denser logic, and advanced nodes have moved from around 7.5 tracks toward 6 and 5. The cost is less room for internal wiring and pin access, which raises routing congestion, and fewer fins or nanosheets per transistor, which reduces drive strength. Low-track libraries therefore depend on features such as buried or backside power rails and careful pin design.

A library is delivered as several views of each cell: the transistor netlist and layout (GDS), an abstract physical view (LEF) giving size and pin shapes for place-and-route, functional models for simulation, and timing and power tables, typically in Liberty format. Library characterization fills those tables by circuit-simulating each cell across combinations of input transition time and output load, repeated at every process, voltage and temperature (PVT) corner. Synthesis and static timing analysis (STA) then look up and interpolate the tables to time millions of cells quickly.

In a standard-cell flow, synthesis maps register-transfer-level (RTL) code onto library cells, and automatic tools place them in rows, build the clock tree and route the wires. This semi-custom approach scales to billions of transistors with modest design effort. Full-custom design, where engineers draw each transistor, is reserved for structures where density or analog behavior justify the effort, such as SRAM bit cells, analog blocks and some high-performance datapaths. Libraries also include utility cells: fillers, well taps, decoupling capacitors and tie-high or tie-low cells.

faq.q: What does 6T or 7.5T mean for a standard cell library?
faq.a: It is the cell height expressed in routing tracks, the number of minimum-pitch metal lines that fit over the cell. Fewer tracks mean a shorter cell and higher logic density but less routing room and lower drive strength.

faq.q: What is a Liberty (.lib) file?
faq.a: It is the library view containing each cell's timing, power and functional data, tabulated against input transition and output load at a given PVT corner, and used by synthesis and static timing analysis.

faq.q: Why do all standard cells have the same height?
faq.a: A common height lets cells abut in uniform rows that share power and ground rails and well regions, which makes automatic placement and routing possible.

PDK(プロセスデザインキット).desc: The set of design data a foundry gives to designers, including design rules, device models, cell libraries and verification rule decks.

about.p: A process design kit (PDK) packages everything needed to design for one specific foundry process. It includes the design rules, which give minimum widths, spacings and enclosures for every layer; SPICE models for transistors, resistors, capacitors and diodes; rule decks that DRC (design rule check) and LVS (layout versus schematic) tools run; technology files for parasitic extraction; and layout generators, often parameterized cells, for basic devices. Digital standard-cell libraries with their timing and physical views are sometimes included and sometimes supplied separately by the foundry or a library vendor.

In a custom or analog flow, the designer draws a schematic using PDK device symbols, simulates it with the PDK's SPICE models, builds the layout from the PDK's device cells, and runs the PDK's DRC and LVS decks to verify it. Extraction with the PDK's technology data then adds wire parasitics for post-layout simulation. Digital flows use the same rule decks and extraction data at sign-off, plus cell libraries for synthesis and place and route. Because every step relies on foundry data, a design that passes PDK checks is one the foundry can manufacture.

Manufacturing varies from lot to lot, wafer to wafer and transistor to transistor, so a PDK models devices at process corners as well as typical conditions. Corners are named by the speed of NMOS and PMOS, such as TT, FF, SS, FS and SF, and are combined with voltage and temperature extremes. For random device-to-device variation, statistical models support Monte Carlo simulation, which reruns a circuit hundreds or thousands of times with randomly perturbed parameters such as threshold voltage to estimate the spread of offset, gain or timing and the resulting parametric yield.

about.h: PDK vs. cell library vs. IP
about.p: The PDK describes the process itself: its devices, rules and verification data. A standard-cell library is a set of pre-designed logic gates built with that PDK, characterized for timing and power. An IP core is a larger reusable circuit block, such as an interface or processor, that is delivered for a given process. Timing constraints, usually written in SDC format, are created by the design team for their own chip and are not part of the PDK.
