With several cache levels, the formula is applied recursively: the L1 miss penalty is the average access time of L2. Using an L1 hit time of 1 ns and miss rate of 5%, an L2 hit time of 10 ns and local miss rate of 20%, and 100 ns main memory, the L2 average is 10 + 0.2 × 100 = 30 ns, so AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 30 = 2.5 ns. The L2 local miss rate counts misses among accesses reaching L2; the global miss rate, 0.05 × 0.2 = 1%, counts them among all accesses.

Larger or more associative caches lower the miss rate but often lengthen the hit time. Compare a cache with a 1-cycle hit and 5% miss rate against one with a 2-cycle hit and 4% miss rate, both with a 20-cycle miss penalty: AMAT is 2.0 versus 2.8 cycles, so the cache with fewer misses is slower. Designers therefore work on three levers together: shorten hit time with small, simple L1 caches, reduce miss rate with capacity, associativity and prefetching, and reduce miss penalty with additional cache levels.

AMAT is a clean way to compare memory hierarchies, but it is not the same as program run time. Out-of-order processors can keep executing independent instructions and overlap several outstanding misses, so not all of the miss penalty turns into stall time. To estimate CPU time, memory stall cycles are usually expressed per instruction, as memory accesses per instruction times miss rate times miss penalty. Miss rates for these calculations are typically obtained from simulation or from hardware performance counters.

faq.q: What is the formula for average memory access time?
faq.a: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. For multi-level caches, the miss penalty of each level is itself the AMAT of the next level.

faq.q: What is the difference between local and global miss rate?
faq.a: The local miss rate of a cache is its misses divided by the accesses that reach it, while the global miss rate divides those misses by all accesses issued by the processor; the global L2 rate equals the L1 miss rate times the L2 local miss rate.

faq.q: Can a lower miss rate give a higher AMAT?
faq.a: Yes. If reducing misses requires a longer hit time, the extra time paid on every access can outweigh the savings on the few accesses that would have missed.

ミスペナルティ.desc: The extra time needed to fetch data from the next level when a cache miss occurs, determined by the lower level's access time and the line transfer time.

about.p: The miss penalty is the time to fetch the missing line from the next level of the hierarchy. It has two parts: the latency until the first data arrives and the transfer time for the rest of the line, which is line size divided by bandwidth. In a multilevel hierarchy, the L1 miss penalty is simply the average access time of L2. With a 10 ns L2 hit time, a 20% L2 local miss rate and 100 ns main memory, the L1 miss penalty is 10 + 0.2 × 100 = 30 ns, far shorter than going straight to memory.

about.h: How it enters AMAT and CPI
about.p: Average memory access time (AMAT) is hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With a 2-cycle hit time, a 4% miss rate and a 150-cycle penalty, AMAT is 2 + 0.04 × 150 = 8 cycles, four times the hit time. In CPI terms, an ideal CPI of 1.0 with 1.3 memory accesses per instruction, a 2% miss rate and a 100-cycle penalty gains 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6 stall cycles, giving a CPI of 3.6. A large penalty turns even small miss rates into large slowdowns.

about.h: Why miss rate alone can mislead
about.p: Larger or more associative caches reduce the miss rate but may lengthen the hit time, and larger lines exploit spatial locality but raise the miss penalty because each miss transfers more data. Designs must therefore be compared by AMAT, not miss rate. With a 20-cycle penalty, a cache with a 1-cycle hit and 5% miss rate averages 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2.0 cycles, while one with a 2-cycle hit and 4% miss rate averages 2 + 0.04 × 20 = 2.8 cycles, so the cache with the lower miss rate is slower.

about.h: Techniques that cut the effective penalty
about.p: Adding cache levels shortens the trip for most misses. Critical word first sends the word the CPU requested before the rest of the line, and early restart lets execution resume as soon as that word arrives. Non-blocking caches keep serving hits while a miss is outstanding, and out-of-order cores overlap several misses so their latencies partly hide one another. Prefetching hides the penalty by fetching ahead; a useful rule of thumb sets the prefetch distance to roughly the miss penalty divided by the time per loop iteration.

faq.q: How do you calculate miss penalty in a two-level cache?
faq.a: The L1 miss penalty equals the L2 average access time: L2 hit time plus L2 local miss rate times the main memory access time. For example, 10 ns + 0.2 × 100 ns = 30 ns.

faq.q: What is the difference between miss rate and miss penalty?
faq.a: Miss rate is the fraction of accesses that miss in the cache, while miss penalty is the extra time each miss costs. Average access time depends on their product plus the hit time.

faq.q: Does a larger cache line increase the miss penalty?
faq.a: Yes. Each miss must transfer more bytes, so the transfer part of the penalty grows, even though larger lines can reduce the number of misses for code with good spatial locality.

ループブロッキング.desc: An optimization that processes large arrays in small blocks that fit in the cache so loaded data is reused many times before eviction. Very effective for matrix multiplication.

about.p: Consider C = A × B for N × N matrices of doubles with the textbook triple loop. Each element of C needs a full row of A and a full column of B, and walking down a column of B in row-major storage touches a different cache line for every element. When N is large, a column of B and the rows of A do not stay in cache long enough to be reused, so the same data is reloaded from main memory again and again. These are capacity misses: making the cache more associative does not help, because the working set is simply too big.

Loop blocking, or tiling, splits each matrix into b × b tiles and reorders the loops so that one tile product, C-tile += A-tile × B-tile, is completed while all three tiles are resident in cache. Each loaded element is then reused about b times before eviction, and memory traffic falls from on the order of N³ elements to about N³/b. The arithmetic and the total memory footprint are unchanged; only the order of operations changes. Arithmetic intensity, operations per byte moved, rises roughly in proportion to the tile size.

A first estimate is that three tiles must fit in the target cache: 3 × b² × 8 bytes for doubles. For a 32 KB L1 cache that gives b of about 36, so a tile of around 32 is a natural choice, leaving room for other data. In practice, conflict misses from power-of-two strides, TLB reach and hardware prefetching also matter, so tile sizes are tuned empirically, and tiles are sometimes copied into contiguous buffers. High-performance libraries block at several levels at once: registers, L1, L2 and L3.

Loop unrolling replicates the loop body to cut loop overhead and expose instruction-level parallelism; it does not improve cache reuse by itself. Loop interchange swaps nesting order so the innermost loop walks memory contiguously, improving spatial locality. Blocking targets temporal locality across large data sets and is often combined with both. The same idea appears on GPUs, where tiles are staged in on-chip shared memory, and in stencil codes, convolutions and many dense linear-algebra kernels.

faq.q: What is loop tiling used for?
faq.a: It restructures loops to work on cache-sized blocks of data so that each loaded element is reused many times before eviction, sharply reducing capacity misses and memory traffic.

faq.q: How do you choose the block size for matrix multiplication?
faq.a: Start with a size where the working tiles fit in the target cache, for example three b × b tiles of doubles in a 32 KB L1 gives b around 32, then tune empirically for conflicts, TLB and prefetching.

faq.q: Is loop blocking the same as loop unrolling?
faq.a: No. Unrolling reduces loop overhead and branches, while blocking reorders iterations to improve cache reuse.

ノンブロッキングキャッシュ.desc: A cache that keeps servicing other accesses while a miss is outstanding. It can handle multiple misses at once, overlapping and hiding memory latency.

特権モード.desc: A CPU operating mode reserved for the OS kernel, in which dangerous operations such as setting page tables and controlling I/O are allowed. It is distinguished from user mode, where applications run.

about.p: Certain operations would let one program take over the whole machine: changing page tables or the register that points to them, accessing I/O devices directly, disabling interrupts, reprogramming the timer that lets the OS regain control, or halting the CPU. The processor allows these only in privileged mode, also called kernel or supervisor mode. If code running in user mode attempts one, the CPU raises an exception and the OS decides what to do, typically terminating the program.

User code cannot simply jump into privileged mode. The only ways in are exceptions, interrupts and deliberate traps such as system calls, and each one transfers control to an entry point the OS configured in advance. The CPU saves the return address, previous mode and interrupt-enable state in dedicated registers. A special return instruction, such as sret or mret on RISC-V, restores all of these at once, so execution never resumes in user code while still holding privileges.

Many architectures have more than two levels. RISC-V defines machine, supervisor and user modes; x86 has rings 0 to 3, with operating systems mainly using ring 0 for the kernel and ring 3 for applications; Arm uses exception levels EL0 to EL3. A hypervisor runs above guest kernels, and when a guest executes a privileged instruction it traps to the hypervisor, which emulates the effect. This trap-and-emulate scheme reuses the same protection idea one level higher.

Privileged mode is a hardware state of the CPU, not a user account. A process run by an administrator or root user still executes in user mode; its extra rights are permissions the kernel checks when it handles that process's system calls. Only kernel code, and in some systems firmware or a hypervisor, runs in privileged mode. Memory protection complements the mode bit: page-table entries mark which pages user mode may access.

faq.q: What is the difference between kernel mode and user mode?
faq.a: In kernel (privileged) mode the CPU allows operations such as changing page tables, controlling devices and disabling interrupts. In user mode these raise an exception, so applications must ask the kernel through system calls.

faq.q: Does running as root mean running in kernel mode?
faq.a: No. Root is an operating-system permission level, and root processes still run in user mode; only the kernel executes in privileged mode.

faq.q: How does a program switch to kernel mode?
faq.a: Only through a trap, such as executing a system call instruction, or through an exception or interrupt, all of which enter the kernel at entry points the OS has set up.

システムコール.desc: The mechanism by which applications ask the OS for services such as file I/O or memory allocation. A dedicated instruction raises an exception that switches to privileged mode and invokes the kernel.

about.h: A system call step by step
about.p: On RISC-V Linux, a program places the system call number in register a7 and its arguments in a0 onward, then executes ecall. The instruction deliberately raises an exception: the CPU records the address of the ecall, switches to supervisor mode and jumps to the kernel's trap entry. The kernel saves user registers, looks up the handler by number, checks the arguments, does the work and puts the result in a0. It then advances the saved address past the ecall and returns to user mode with sret. Other architectures use instructions such as syscall on x86-64 and svc on Arm.

Programs usually reach system calls through library wrappers, so the boundary is easy to miss. A function such as printf runs entirely in user space, formatting text into a buffer, and only occasionally calls the write system call to pass that buffer to the kernel. Many library functions, such as string handling or math routines, never enter the kernel at all. A system call is defined by the switch into privileged mode, not by how the function is named.

Each call pays a fixed overhead: the mode switch, saving and restoring registers, argument validation and the return. Entering the kernel also disturbs caches and the TLB, and countermeasures for speculative-execution attacks, such as kernel page-table isolation (KPTI), add a page-table switch on every entry. Writing one byte per call therefore runs far slower than buffering several kilobytes in user space and writing them in one call.

Besides buffering, programs can map a file into memory with mmap, after which reads are ordinary loads served by page faults on first touch rather than a call per read. Interfaces that submit several operations in one call reduce crossings further. Some operating systems also map read-only kernel data, such as the current time, into user space so frequent queries need no trap at all.

faq.q: What is the difference between a system call and an interrupt?
faq.a: A system call is a synchronous trap the program triggers on purpose with a dedicated instruction. An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from hardware, such as a timer or device, that arrives regardless of what the program is doing.

faq.q: Is printf a system call?
faq.a: No. printf is a C library function that formats output in user space; it eventually calls the write system call to hand the buffered data to the kernel.

faq.q: Why are system calls slow?
faq.a: Each one switches into privileged mode, saves state, validates arguments and returns, and it disturbs caches and the TLB. The cost is fixed per call, so many tiny calls add up.

割り込みハンドラ.desc: The routine a CPU runs when an interrupt or exception occurs. It saves the interrupted state, handles the cause and returns. Handlers should be kept as short as possible.

about.h: What happens when an interrupt is accepted
about.p: When a device signals an interrupt, the CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the address it would have executed next along with state such as the operating mode and flags, and jumps to the interrupt handler, also called an interrupt service routine (ISR), usually found through an interrupt vector table. The handler saves any registers it uses, services the cause, clears the device's interrupt flag, restores state and executes a return-from-interrupt instruction. The interrupted program then resumes exactly where it stopped; it is neither discarded nor restarted.

While a handler runs, other interrupts of the same or lower priority are typically held off and the main code is stalled, so a long handler increases latency for everything else. Slow calls such as printf are especially risky because they take time and may themselves depend on interrupts. A good handler does the minimum, such as moving received data into a buffer or setting a flag, and leaves heavy processing to the main loop or a task. Operating system kernels formalize this by splitting work into an immediate part and a deferred part.

Variables shared between a handler and the main program cause classic bugs. If main spins on a flag that only the handler sets, an optimizing compiler may load it into a register once and never see the update; declaring it volatile forces every access to go to memory. A read-modify-write such as reg |= mask can be interrupted between the read and the write, wiping out a change the handler made to another bit. Briefly disabling interrupts or using hardware set and clear registers avoids this, and multi-byte variables need protection against torn reads.

A periodic timer interrupt is what lets an operating system take back the CPU from a program that never yields, enabling preemptive scheduling and context switches. Interrupts are asynchronous events from hardware, whereas exceptions such as page faults or divide-by-zero arise synchronously from the instruction being executed, though both enter the kernel through similar handlers. One common mistake is kicking a watchdog timer unconditionally inside a timer interrupt: the interrupt keeps firing even if the main loop has hung, so the watchdog never detects the failure.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt handler and an ISR?
faq.a: There is no real difference: interrupt service routine (ISR) is another name for the interrupt handler, the code the CPU runs in response to an interrupt.

faq.q: Why should a variable shared with an interrupt handler be declared volatile?
faq.a: Without volatile, the compiler may assume the variable cannot change inside a loop and keep it in a register, so the main code never sees the handler's update. Volatile forces each access to read or write memory.

faq.q: What is the difference between an interrupt and an exception?
faq.a: An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from hardware such as a timer or peripheral, unrelated to the current instruction. An exception is raised synchronously by the instruction being executed, for example a page fault or an illegal operation.

割り込みベクタテーブル.desc: A table listing, for each type of interrupt or exception, the start address of its handler. The CPU indexes it by the cause number to find where to begin handling.

about.h: How the CPU uses the table
about.p: When an interrupt or exception is accepted, hardware determines a number, called the vector, that identifies its cause: a timer, a particular peripheral, a page fault, an illegal instruction or a system call. The CPU saves the address of the next instruction and status such as the operating mode, then uses the vector as an index into the interrupt vector table, typically reading the entry at base + vector × entry size. That entry holds the handler's start address. The handler saves the registers it uses, services the event and executes a return-from-interrupt instruction.

Architectures differ in detail. On Arm Cortex-M microcontrollers the table sits at the start of the code memory: its first word is the initial stack pointer, the second is the reset handler address, and later words point to fault and peripheral handlers; on most cores a vector table offset register (VTOR) lets software move it. In x86 real mode the table occupies the first 1 KB of memory with 256 four-byte entries, while protected and long modes use an interrupt descriptor table (IDT) located by the IDTR register. RISC-V uses the mtvec register, which can send all traps to one handler or vector interrupts to separate addresses.

about.h: Setting it up in embedded firmware
about.p: On a microcontroller with no operating system, the vector table must be at the address the hardware expects from the moment of reset. The startup code defines it as an array of function pointers in its own section, and the linker script places that section at the required flash address. Typical startup files give every entry a weak default handler, often an infinite loop, so the application overrides only the interrupts it uses by defining functions with matching names. A misspelled handler name therefore compiles cleanly but silently routes the interrupt to the default loop.

A vectored scheme sends each cause straight to its own handler, so the CPU does not need to read status registers to discover what happened, which shortens interrupt latency. The alternative is a single entry point whose handler reads a cause register and dispatches in software, as RISC-V's direct mode does. On a general-purpose operating system, the kernel fills the table at boot so timer ticks, device interrupts, page faults and system calls each reach the correct kernel routine.

faq.q: What is an interrupt vector?
faq.a: An interrupt vector is the number assigned to an interrupt or exception source, used as an index into the vector table. The term is also used loosely for the table entry itself, which holds the handler address.

faq.q: Where is the vector table on an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller?
faq.a: By default it is at the start of the boot memory, usually flash. Its first entry is the initial stack pointer value and its second is the reset handler, and on most cores the vector table offset register (VTOR) can relocate it, for example to RAM.

faq.q: What is the difference between the IVT and the IDT on x86?
faq.a: The interrupt vector table (IVT) is the real-mode table of 256 segment:offset addresses at the bottom of memory. The interrupt descriptor table (IDT) replaces it in protected and long modes, holding descriptors with privilege information, and can be placed anywhere via the IDTR register.

ページテーブル.desc: A table recording the mapping from virtual page numbers to physical page numbers. The OS builds one per process, and the CPU's MMU walks it to translate addresses. Each entry also holds protection bits.

about.h: How translation uses the page table
about.p: A virtual address is split into a virtual page number (VPN) and a page offset; with 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset. The memory management unit (MMU) looks up the VPN in the page table to obtain the physical frame number, then appends the unchanged offset. Each page-table entry (PTE) also holds a valid or present bit, read, write and execute permissions, a user or kernel flag, and accessed and dirty bits used by the operating system. A register points to the current process's top-level table and is switched on each context switch.

A flat table must have an entry for every possible page. With 32-bit addresses, 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries that is 2²⁰ entries, or 4 MB per process, mostly describing unused space. Multilevel tables form a tree in which an absent upper-level entry means a whole region is unmapped, so no lower table is needed. A typical 64-bit design translates 48 address bits with four levels of 512 eight-byte entries, each table filling exactly one 4 KB page. Ending the walk one or two levels early yields large pages, such as 2 MB.

The page table lives in ordinary memory, so a full walk can cost several dependent memory accesses: up to four in the four-level case, and many more under virtualization, where guest and host tables are both walked. The translation lookaside buffer (TLB) is a small cache of recent translations inside the CPU that avoids most walks. On a TLB miss, a hardware page walker in most modern processors reads the table, helped by caches of upper-level entries. Large pages increase how much memory each TLB entry covers.

about.h: What the OS does with it
about.p: If a PTE is not present, the access raises a page fault and the operating system decides what to do: load the page from storage, allocate a zero-filled page, or kill the process for an illegal access. Pointing several processes' entries at the same frame enables shared libraries, and marking shared pages read-only enables copy-on-write after a fork. When the OS revokes or changes a mapping on a multicore system, it must also invalidate stale TLB copies on other cores, an operation known as a TLB shootdown.

faq.q: Why are multilevel page tables used instead of a single table?
faq.a: A single table needs an entry for every possible virtual page, which is megabytes per process even for 32-bit addresses. A multilevel tree only allocates lower-level tables for regions actually in use.

faq.q: What is the difference between a page table and a TLB?
faq.a: The page table is the complete mapping kept in memory by the operating system. The TLB is a small hardware cache in the CPU that holds recently used translations so most accesses avoid walking the table.

faq.q: What happens when a page table entry is not present?
faq.a: The MMU raises a page fault and the operating system handles it, for example by reading the page in from storage and updating the entry, then restarting the faulting instruction.

ページフォルト.desc: An exception raised when an accessed page is not mapped to physical memory or the access type is not permitted. The OS either supplies the page and retries the instruction or treats it as an illegal access.

about.h: What happens during a page fault
about.p: When the memory management unit (MMU) translates a virtual address, it checks the page-table entry. If the entry is not valid or the access type is not allowed, the MMU raises a page fault, a synchronous exception tied to the faulting instruction. The OS handler checks whether the address belongs to a region the process may use. If so, it finds a free physical frame, evicting another page if necessary, fills it from disk or with zeros, marks the entry valid and restarts the faulting instruction. If not, the process receives a segmentation fault.

Not every page fault touches the disk. A minor (soft) fault is resolved without I/O, for example when a page is already in memory in the file cache, needs only a fresh zero-filled frame, or must be copied for copy-on-write. A major (hard) fault must read the page from storage and costs milliseconds. The difference matters enormously: with a 100 ns memory access and an 8 ms fault service time, a major fault rate of just one per million accesses raises the average access time from 100 ns to about 108 ns.

Operating systems rely on faults as a lazy-evaluation tool. Demand paging maps a program without loading it, then loads each page on first touch. Memory-mapped files (mmap) read file contents in the same way. Copy-on-write lets fork share pages read-only and copy only the pages that are later written. Guard pages with no access rights sit beyond the stack so runaway recursion faults instead of corrupting data. On NUMA systems, Linux places a page on the node of the thread that first writes it, so initialization order affects performance.

about.h: Page fault vs. TLB miss vs. cache miss
about.p: These three are often confused. A cache miss is handled entirely by hardware, which fetches the line from a lower memory level. A TLB miss means the translation is not cached in the translation lookaside buffer; on most modern CPUs a hardware page-table walker fetches it, and if the entry is valid, no exception occurs. Only when the page-table entry itself is invalid or forbids the access does a page fault reach the OS. When faults become so frequent that the system spends most of its time paging, the condition is called thrashing.

faq.q: Is a page fault an error?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Most page faults are normal events used for demand paging, copy-on-write and memory-mapped files; only a fault on an address the process is not allowed to access becomes an error such as a segmentation fault.

faq.q: What is the difference between a minor and a major page fault?
faq.a: A minor fault is resolved without disk I/O, for example by mapping a page already in memory, while a major fault must read the page from storage and is thousands of times slower.

faq.q: Why does a page fault restart the instruction instead of skipping it?
faq.a: The faulting access never completed, so the OS fixes the mapping and re-executes the instruction from the start, letting the program continue as if nothing had happened.

デマンドページング.desc: Loading a program's pages into physical memory only when first accessed and a page fault occurs, rather than all at once. It speeds startup and saves memory for unused parts.

about.h: What happens on a page fault
about.p: When a program starts, the OS sets up page tables describing its address space but marks most pages as not present. The first access to such a page makes the memory management unit (MMU) raise a page fault. The kernel checks that the address belongs to a valid region (if not, the program gets a segmentation fault), finds a free physical frame, fills it from the executable, a file or with zeros, updates the page-table entry and re-executes the faulting instruction, which now succeeds.

If the needed data is already in memory, for example in the OS file cache or as a shared library page another process loaded, the kernel only has to map it: a minor fault costing roughly a microsecond. A major fault must read from storage and costs far more, from tens of microseconds on fast flash to milliseconds on a hard disk. Kernels reduce major faults by reading ahead neighboring pages of a file when sequential access is detected.

Loading a whole program at startup wastes time and memory on code paths and data that are never used, such as error handlers or optional features. Demand paging loads only what is touched, so programs start quickly and more processes fit in memory. The downside is unpredictable latency on first touch, which is why real-time systems often lock or pre-touch their pages. If the active working sets exceed physical memory, the system thrashes, spending most of its time paging.

Memory-mapped files use the same machinery: mmap only records the mapping, and the first read of each page faults the file data in. Copy-on-write lets a newly created process share its parent's pages until one side writes, at which point a fault creates a private copy. Large memory allocations often receive physical pages only when first touched, so allocating memory and actually using it are different events.

faq.q: What is the difference between demand paging and swapping?
faq.a: Demand paging brings individual pages into memory when they are first used. Swapping, in its original sense, moves whole processes between memory and disk; modern systems page individual pages out and in instead.

faq.q: Is a page fault an error?
faq.a: Usually not. Under demand paging a page fault is the normal way a page gets loaded; only an access to an address outside any valid region is turned into an error such as a segmentation fault.

faq.q: Why does demand paging make programs start faster?
faq.a: The OS only builds page tables at startup and loads pages as they are touched, so parts of the program that are never used are never read from storage.

コピーオンライト.desc: Sharing duplicated memory with the original at first and copying a page only when either side tries to write it. It speeds process creation and saves memory.
コピーオンライト.title: Copy-on-Write (COW): How It Works, fork() and Pitfalls
コピーオンライト.description: Copy-on-write shares memory pages until one side writes, then copies just that page. See how it speeds up fork(), where else it is used, and its costs.

about.p: When a process is duplicated, the kernel copies only the page tables. Parent and child entries point to the same physical frames, and every writable private page is temporarily marked read-only while the kernel keeps a reference count per frame. Reads proceed at full speed. The first write by either process causes a protection fault; the kernel recognizes a copy-on-write page, allocates a new frame, copies the page, maps the copy as writable for the writer and restarts the faulting instruction. If the reference count shows the page is no longer shared, it can simply be made writable again without copying.

about.h: Why it pays off for process creation
about.p: A common pattern on Unix-like systems is fork followed almost immediately by exec, for example when a shell starts a command. Exec throws away the entire address space and loads a new program, so eagerly copying the parent's memory would be pure waste. With copy-on-write, fork costs roughly the time to duplicate page tables, and only pages that are actually modified before exec, typically a few stack and data pages, are ever copied. Memory is saved too, because pages that neither side writes, such as code and read-only data, remain shared for the lifetime of both processes.

about.h: Where else you will meet it
about.p: The same idea appears whenever data is logically duplicated but usually left unmodified. Private file mappings use it: a shared library's writable data section starts out shared with the file cache and each process gets its own copy of a page only when it writes. Many kernels map freshly allocated anonymous memory to a single shared zero page until it is written. Copy-on-write file systems and storage snapshots write modified blocks to new locations instead of overwriting, and virtual machine snapshots and some language runtimes apply the principle to disk images and strings.

Copy-on-write moves cost rather than eliminating it. Each first write to a shared page takes a fault, a trap into the kernel and a page copy, which is far slower than an ordinary store. If a large process forks and the parent keeps writing to most of its memory, nearly every page is eventually copied and memory use can approach double. Marking pages read-only at fork also requires invalidating stale TLB entries on other cores. Copy-on-write must not be confused with shared memory: with shared memory both processes see each other's writes, while copy-on-write gives each writer a private copy.

faq.q: Does fork copy all of the parent's memory?
faq.a: Not on modern systems. Fork duplicates the page tables and shares physical pages marked read-only; a page is copied only when one of the processes first writes to it.

faq.q: What happens when a child process writes to memory after fork?
faq.a: The write triggers a page fault, the kernel copies that single page into a new frame and maps it writable for the child. The parent keeps the original, so neither process sees the other's change.

faq.q: Is copy-on-write the same as shared memory?
faq.a: No. Shared memory is deliberately visible to both processes after writes, whereas copy-on-write only shares pages until someone writes, at which point the writer gets a private copy.

スラッシング.desc: A state in which physical memory is so short that pages are constantly evicted and reloaded, and little useful work gets done. It is relieved by running fewer processes or adding memory.

about.p: Each process has a working set, the pages it actively uses over a short time window. When the combined working sets of all running processes exceed physical memory, loading a page for one process evicts a page that another, or the same, process will need almost immediately. That page then faults back in, evicting yet another needed page. Page faults go to disk or SSD, which takes from tens of microseconds to milliseconds, compared with around 100 ns for DRAM, so the system spends nearly all its time waiting for paging I/O.

A classic textbook scenario shows how thrashing can feed itself. As processes wait on page faults, CPU utilization drops. A naive scheduler that tries to raise utilization by admitting more processes shrinks the memory available to each one, causing even more faults and lower utilization. Throughput collapses rather than degrading gracefully. The symptoms are a very high page-fault rate, saturated swap I/O, high time spent waiting on I/O and little useful computation, even though the machine appears busy.

The fundamental cure is to make memory demand fit: run fewer processes at once by suspending or swapping out entire processes, or add physical memory. Working-set based policies admit a process only when its working set can be held. Page-fault-frequency control gives a process more frames when its fault rate exceeds an upper threshold and takes frames away when it falls below a lower one. Programs can help themselves by improving locality so their working sets are smaller.

Thrashing is a sustained throughput collapse due to memory shortage. It differs from Bélády's anomaly, the specific case where FIFO replacement produces more faults when given more frames; stack algorithms such as LRU cannot show that anomaly. It also differs from deadlock, where tasks stop because each waits for resources another holds. The word is also used for caches and TLBs: cache thrashing describes lines repeatedly evicting each other, often addresses mapping to the same set, which is the same pattern at a smaller scale.

faq.q: What causes thrashing in an operating system?
faq.a: Running processes whose combined working sets exceed physical memory, so pages are evicted and then needed again almost immediately, keeping the system busy with paging I/O instead of useful work.

faq.q: How do you stop thrashing?
faq.a: Reduce the number of active processes, add physical memory, or use working-set or page-fault-frequency policies that allocate frames according to each process's actual needs.

faq.q: What is the difference between thrashing and Bélády's anomaly?
faq.a: Thrashing is performance collapse from memory overcommitment, while Bélády's anomaly is the counterintuitive case where FIFO replacement causes more page faults when more frames are available.

コンテキストスイッチ.desc: Switching the process or thread running on a CPU. Registers, the program counter and other state are saved and restored, and switching processes also switches address spaces.

about.p: The kernel saves the outgoing thread's CPU state, meaning its general-purpose registers, program counter, stack pointer and status bits such as the previous mode, and later reloads it so the thread resumes exactly where it stopped. Floating-point and vector registers are part of the state too, and some kernels save them lazily only when the next thread actually uses them. When the switch is between processes, the register pointing to the page table is also changed, giving the new process its own address space. Memory contents and open files stay in place and are not copied.

A switch is triggered when the running thread blocks, for example waiting for disk I/O or a lock, when it voluntarily yields, or when a timer interrupt tells the scheduler its time slice has expired and another thread should run. In each case the CPU is already in the kernel, handling a system call or interrupt, and the scheduler picks the next thread. Switching between threads of the same process is cheaper because the address space does not change.

Saving and loading registers takes little time; the whole kernel path, including scheduling, typically costs on the order of microseconds. The larger cost is often indirect: the new process finds caches and the TLB filled with the previous process's data and translations, so it misses repeatedly until they warm up. CPUs that tag TLB entries with an address-space identifier (ASID) avoid flushing the TLB on each switch, but cache warm-up remains. Frequent switching therefore lowers throughput more than the switch time alone suggests.

A system call or interrupt moves the CPU from user mode to privileged mode and back, but the same process continues afterward; that is a mode switch, not a context switch. A context switch changes which thread or process owns the CPU. The two often happen together, since a switch always takes place inside the kernel, but a system call that returns to its caller involves no context switch at all.

faq.q: What is saved during a context switch?
faq.a: The CPU state of the outgoing thread: registers, program counter, stack pointer and status information, plus the page-table pointer when switching processes. Memory itself is not saved because it stays in place.

faq.q: Why are context switches expensive?
faq.a: Beyond the kernel work itself, the incoming process starts with caches and the TLB holding another process's contents, so it suffers many misses until they are refilled.

faq.q: Is a system call a context switch?
faq.a: No. A system call is a mode switch within the same process; a context switch occurs only if the kernel decides to run a different thread or process before returning.

ASID(アドレス空間識別子).desc: A number tagged onto each TLB entry indicating which process's address space the translation belongs to. The TLB need not be flushed on a process switch, reducing TLB misses afterward.

TLBシュートダウン.desc: On a multiprocessor, the procedure for making other cores discard stale translations from their TLBs after a page table is modified. It uses inter-processor interrupts or instructions that broadcast the invalidation to all cores, and is costly.
TLBシュートダウン.title: TLB Shootdown: How Multicore CPUs Keep TLBs Coherent
TLBシュートダウン.description: After a page-table change, other cores must drop stale TLB entries. How shootdowns use inter-processor interrupts or broadcast invalidation, and their cost.

about.p: A TLB is a cache in which each core keeps virtual-to-physical address translations close at hand. On many CPUs, unlike data caches, TLB contents are not kept coherent with the page tables by hardware. Even after the OS revokes a mapping or removes write permission, the old translation can remain in other cores' TLBs, letting those cores write to a physical page that should already have been freed. So when the page tables change, for example through munmap, mprotect, page migration or eviction, the OS has the other cores discard their stale entries and confirms that all of them have finished before reusing the page.

A typical x86 procedure goes as follows. The OS first updates the page-table entry and removes the entry from its own TLB with an instruction such as INVLPG. It then sends inter-processor interrupts (IPIs) to the cores that may be using the address space. Each receiving core, in its interrupt handler, removes the relevant entry or flushes its whole TLB and reports completion. The initiating core waits for every response before continuing. Because this requires sending and receiving interrupts, interrupting running work and waiting for acknowledgments, it becomes a major source of slowdown on systems with many cores and in programs that free memory frequently.

Some instruction sets have instructions that propagate TLB invalidation to other cores. In the Arm architecture, issuing the form of the TLBI instruction that broadcasts to all cores in the shareability domain (the Inner Shareable variants) and waiting with a DSB instruction performs a shootdown without IPIs. Some AMD x86 CPUs have also added an INVLPGB instruction that broadcasts invalidation to all cores and a TLBSYNC instruction that waits for it to complete. RISC-V's SFENCE.VMA, by contrast, affects only the executing core, so other cores are asked through IPIs (such as SBI remote fence calls).

Operating systems try to reduce the number and scope of shootdowns: batching changes to several pages into one shootdown, sending requests only to cores that have actually used the address space, and flushing the entire TLB instead of page by page when many pages change. Changes that only widen permissions, such as allowing writes, can sometimes skip the shootdown, because a fault caused by the stale entry can simply be handled later. In virtual machines, IPIs sent by the guest OS are expensive, so paravirtualized methods in which the hypervisor performs the invalidation on the guest's behalf are also used.

faq.q: What is a TLB shootdown?
faq.a: On a multiprocessor system, it is the procedure for making other cores discard stale address translations left in their TLBs after the page tables are modified. It is done either by asking each core with inter-processor interrupts or by using instructions that broadcast the invalidation to all cores.

faq.q: Why aren't TLBs kept coherent by hardware like data caches?
faq.a: Monitoring every write to the page tables and updating every core's TLB would cost circuitry and inter-core communication. Many instruction sets are instead designed so that the OS explicitly specifies when and which translations to invalidate, and some, such as Arm, assist only by broadcasting the invalidation in hardware.

faq.q: When do TLB shootdowns hurt performance?
faq.a: When memory is allocated and freed frequently, when many threads share the same address space, or when there is a lot of page migration or reclamation. The more cores there are, the more responses must be awaited and the larger the impact.

メモリマップドI/O.desc: Assigning peripheral registers to specific addresses in the same address space as memory and accessing them with ordinary load and store instructions. That region is configured as uncached.

about.p: The processor's address decoder routes certain address ranges not to RAM but to peripheral devices. A timer's control register, a UART's data register or a GPIO port each appears at a fixed address, and ordinary load and store instructions become read and write transactions to that device. Unlike memory, these accesses can have side effects: reading a status or data register may clear a flag or pop a FIFO, writing a 1 may clear an interrupt, and the value can change at any moment because the hardware updates it independently of the program.

Port-mapped I/O gives devices a separate address space reached only through dedicated instructions, such as IN and OUT on x86. Memory-mapped I/O needs no special instructions, so every addressing mode, pointer and C struct can be used to reach registers, keeping the instruction set simple. It is the standard on ARM and RISC-V microcontrollers, and even on x86 systems PCI Express devices expose most of their registers through memory-mapped regions, while legacy port I/O remains mainly for compatibility.

Device regions must be configured as uncached; otherwise the CPU might keep rereading a stale cached copy and never see the device change, or hold writes in the cache. In C, register pointers are declared volatile so the compiler performs every access exactly as written, rather than reading once and looping forever or dropping repeated writes. volatile does not, however, control hardware reordering or write buffering. Processors and buses may post writes, so drivers use memory barriers or device memory attributes, and sometimes a read-back, to guarantee ordering and completion.

On systems with virtual memory, a device's physical register addresses are mapped into the kernel's virtual address space with uncached attributes before a driver can use them, and occasionally into a user process for user-space drivers. MMIO is typically used for control and status: configuring a device, starting operations and acknowledging interrupts. Bulk data usually moves by DMA (direct memory access), where the device itself reads and writes main memory, rather than by the CPU copying through registers.

faq.q: What is the difference between memory-mapped I/O and port-mapped I/O?
faq.a: Memory-mapped I/O places device registers in the normal memory address space and accesses them with ordinary loads and stores, while port-mapped I/O uses a separate address space and special instructions such as x86 IN and OUT.

faq.q: Why must memory-mapped registers be declared volatile?
faq.a: The device can change register values independently of the program, so volatile forces the compiler to perform every read and write rather than caching values in registers or removing apparently redundant accesses.

faq.q: Why is memory-mapped I/O space uncached?
faq.a: A cache would return stale values instead of the device's current state and could delay or merge writes, so device regions are mapped with uncached or device attributes.

デバイスドライバ.desc: An OS component that operates a specific peripheral. It handles the device's registers and interrupts and lets applications use the device through a common interface.

about.p: A driver translates generic requests from the kernel into the exact sequence a particular device expects. At start-up it probes the device, maps its registers into the address space (memory-mapped I/O) and puts the hardware into a known state. During operation it writes command and status registers, prepares DMA (direct memory access) descriptors so the device can move data to and from memory without the CPU copying it, and services the interrupts the device raises when work completes. Upward it plugs into a common framework, such as a block, network or character-device interface, so applications see ordinary reads, writes and control calls.

Interrupt handlers run while normal work on that CPU is suspended, so drivers keep them short: acknowledge the device, note what happened and schedule the rest. The heavier processing, such as passing received packets up the protocol stack or completing a disk request, runs later in a context that can be scheduled. This split is often called top half and bottom half. Very high-rate devices such as fast network cards may switch from one interrupt per event to polling under load, because taking an interrupt for every packet would waste more CPU time than checking a queue in a loop.

Most drivers run in kernel mode with the same privileges as the rest of the kernel. A stray pointer, a missed lock or a DMA buffer programmed with the wrong address can therefore corrupt memory anywhere or crash the whole system rather than just one program. For this reason drivers are a common source of system instability and security flaws. Some designs move drivers into user-space processes, trading extra context switches for isolation, and an IOMMU can limit which memory a device is allowed to reach even when its driver misbehaves.

Firmware is code that runs on the device itself, for example on a controller inside an SSD or a network card; the driver runs on the host CPU and talks to that firmware through registers and shared memory. A hypervisor sits below whole operating systems and shares hardware among virtual machines. Inside a virtual machine, the guest either uses paravirtual drivers that talk efficiently to the hypervisor, or, with device assignment, runs the ordinary driver for a real device handed to it.

faq.q: Is a device driver part of the operating system?
faq.a: Usually yes. Most drivers are kernel modules that run with kernel privileges and plug into the OS's device frameworks, although some systems also support drivers that run as user-space processes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a driver and firmware?
faq.a: Firmware runs on a processor inside the device and controls the hardware directly. The driver runs on the host CPU as part of the OS and communicates with the device and its firmware through registers, DMA buffers and interrupts.

faq.q: Why can a bad driver crash the whole computer?
faq.a: Kernel-mode drivers share the kernel's address space and privileges, so a bug can overwrite any kernel data or leave hardware in an inconsistent state. A user program's bug, by contrast, is confined to its own process.

IOMMU.desc: A unit that translates and protects the addresses peripherals use for DMA. It keeps devices from writing to unauthorized memory and is also used when assigning devices to virtual machines.
IOMMU.title: IOMMU: DMA Address Translation and Protection
IOMMU.description: An IOMMU translates and checks the addresses devices use for DMA. How it differs from the MMU, how it blocks DMA attacks, and device assignment to VMs.

about.p: With an IOMMU (input-output memory management unit), a device no longer issues raw physical addresses. Its DMA requests carry I/O virtual addresses, and the IOMMU looks them up in page tables that the OS has set up for that device or group of devices, identified on PCIe by the requester's bus, device and function numbers. Recent translations are cached in an IOTLB (I/O translation lookaside buffer). An access to an address with no valid mapping, or with the wrong read/write permission, is blocked and reported to the OS as a fault instead of reaching memory.

Both translate addresses through page tables, but they serve different masters. The CPU's MMU translates virtual addresses for each process so that programs are isolated from one another. The IOMMU translates addresses for each device, so that DMA engines are confined to the buffers their driver mapped. Because the mappings are independent, the OS can hand a device a buffer that is scattered across many physical pages but appears contiguous in the device's address space, which simplifies devices that cannot do scatter-gather transfers themselves.

DMA bypasses the CPU and its memory protection, so without an IOMMU any device that can master the bus can read keys or patch kernel code. This is a practical risk with external ports that expose PCIe-style DMA to plugged-in hardware. With the IOMMU enabled, the OS maps only the specific buffers each driver uses, typically for the duration of each transfer, and everything else is unreachable from that device. Many platforms also use the IOMMU to remap device interrupts so that a device cannot forge arbitrary interrupt messages.

A guest OS programs a device with what it believes are physical addresses, but they are really guest-physical addresses. When a hypervisor passes a real device such as a GPU or network card straight through to a virtual machine, it configures the IOMMU to translate those guest-physical addresses to the host-physical pages backing that VM. The device can then use DMA at full speed without the hypervisor intercepting each transfer, while remaining unable to touch other VMs' memory. The price is some translation overhead, mainly IOTLB misses and the cost of mapping and unmapping buffers.

faq.q: Do I need an IOMMU for GPU passthrough?
faq.a: Yes. Passing a physical device to a virtual machine relies on the IOMMU to translate the guest's DMA addresses and to keep the device from reaching memory outside that VM, so it must be supported and enabled in firmware and the OS.

faq.q: Does enabling the IOMMU slow down I/O?
faq.a: It adds some cost for translation misses and for creating and removing mappings, which can matter for very high-rate devices. Caching in the IOTLB and longer-lived mappings keep the overhead modest in most workloads.

faq.q: What is the difference between an IOMMU and an MMU?
faq.a: The MMU translates addresses issued by the CPU on behalf of processes, while the IOMMU translates addresses issued by devices doing DMA. Both use page tables and permission bits, but the IOMMU's tables are per device or device group.

ハイパーバイザ.desc: Software that runs multiple virtual machines on one computer, allocating CPU, memory and devices to each guest OS and isolating them from one another. Also called a virtual machine monitor.

about.h: How it keeps control of the CPU
about.p: A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, runs at a higher privilege level than the guest operating systems. Guest kernels believe they control the hardware, but when one executes a privileged instruction or touches a protected resource, the CPU traps to the hypervisor, which reproduces the effect on that virtual machine's state and resumes the guest. This is trap-and-emulate. Hardware virtualization extensions add a dedicated mode and save and restore guest state quickly on each transition; RISC-V, for example, adds hypervisor modes to its machine, supervisor and user modes.

Each guest manages page tables that map guest virtual addresses to what it believes are physical addresses. Those guest physical addresses must in turn map to real host memory. With nested paging, hardware performs both stages automatically: guest virtual to guest physical through the guest's tables, then to host physical through the hypervisor's tables. Earlier systems used shadow page tables maintained in software, forcing the hypervisor to intervene whenever a guest edited its tables. The cost of two-stage translation is a longer page-table walk on TLB misses, which larger pages help reduce.

Emulating a real device register by register is fully transparent but slow, since every register access exits to the hypervisor. Paravirtualization instead installs virtualization-aware drivers in the guest that exchange batched requests with the hypervisor through queues in shared memory, which is the common choice for virtual disks and network cards. For the highest performance, a physical device can be assigned directly to one guest, with an I/O memory management unit (IOMMU) restricting its DMA to that guest's memory so isolation is preserved.

A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, as in cloud servers, while a type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host OS. Containers are different again: they share one kernel and only partition processes, file systems and resources, so they are lighter but isolate less strongly than virtual machines, each of which boots its own kernel. Hypervisors also partition mixed-criticality software on automotive SoCs. Normally the hypervisor can read all guest memory; confidential-computing features encrypt VM memory so even the host cannot.

faq.q: What is the difference between a hypervisor and a virtual machine?
faq.a: The hypervisor is the software layer that creates and runs virtual machines and divides hardware among them; each virtual machine is one isolated guest environment running its own OS.

faq.q: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 hypervisors?
faq.a: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware, while a type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on top of an ordinary operating system.

faq.q: Are containers the same as virtual machines?
faq.a: No. Containers share the host kernel and are lightweight, while virtual machines each run their own kernel on a hypervisor, giving stronger isolation and the ability to run different operating systems.

入れ子ページング.desc: Hardware that walks two levels of page tables in succession, one managed by the guest OS and one by the hypervisor. It reduces hypervisor intervention and speeds up virtualization.
入れ子ページング.title: Nested Paging (EPT/NPT): Two-Level Address Translation
入れ子ページング.description: Nested paging (Intel EPT, AMD NPT) walks guest and hypervisor page tables in hardware, replacing shadow page tables. Why a TLB miss can cost 24 memory accesses.

about.h: Two translations in one hardware walk
about.p: A guest operating system inside a virtual machine manages page tables that map guest virtual addresses to what it believes are physical addresses, called guest physical addresses. That memory actually lives wherever the hypervisor placed it. With nested paging, also known as two-stage translation, the hardware walks the guest's page tables and then the hypervisor's own tables, translating guest virtual to guest physical to host physical automatically. The common implementations are Intel's Extended Page Tables (EPT), AMD's Nested Page Tables (NPT) and Arm's stage-2 translation.

about.h: What it replaced: shadow page tables
about.p: Before hardware support, hypervisors used shadow page tables: software-maintained tables mapping guest virtual addresses directly to host physical addresses, which the real MMU used. To keep them correct, the hypervisor had to trap the guest's page-table writes and address-space switches, causing frequent and expensive exits from the virtual machine. Nested paging lets the guest edit its own tables freely, removing most of those exits and simplifying the hypervisor. The trade-off moves to the cost of a TLB miss.

about.h: Why a TLB miss can cost 24 memory accesses
about.p: Each entry the guest walker needs is located by a guest physical address, which must itself be translated through the host's tables before it can be read. With four-level tables on both sides, each guest level costs four host reads plus one guest-table read, five in all, for 20 across four levels, and translating the final data address through the host adds four more: (4 + 1) × (4 + 1) − 1 = 24, versus four for a native walk. Page-walk caches, TLBs that cache the final combined translation and large pages on the host side keep the average cost far lower.

faq.q: What is the difference between nested paging and shadow paging?
faq.a: Shadow paging has the hypervisor maintain combined guest-virtual-to-host-physical tables in software and trap guest page-table updates. Nested paging lets the hardware walk the guest and host tables in succession, so the guest updates its own tables without hypervisor intervention.

faq.q: How many memory accesses does a nested page walk need?
faq.a: With four-level page tables in both guest and host, a TLB miss can require up to 24 memory accesses in the worst case, compared with four for a non-virtualized walk.

faq.q: Is nested paging the same as nested virtualization?
faq.a: No. Nested paging is two-stage address translation for ordinary virtual machines, while nested virtualization means running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine.

NMI(マスク不可能割り込み).desc: An interrupt that is always accepted regardless of interrupt masking. It is used to report uncorrectable memory errors, serious hardware faults and watchdog events.

字句解析.desc: The first compiler phase, which splits the characters of source code into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, operators and keywords. Whitespace and comments are removed here.

about.p: The lexical analyzer, or lexer, reads source text character by character and groups it into tokens, each with a type and often a value. For count = count + 1; it produces identifier count, operator =, identifier count, operator +, number 1 and the semicolon. Whitespace and comments are dropped, identifiers may be entered into a symbol table, and line numbers are recorded so later phases can report errors precisely. The parser then works only with the token stream.

Token patterns are written as regular expressions, for example a letter followed by letters or digits for identifiers and one or more digits for integers. These can be converted into a nondeterministic finite automaton, then into a deterministic one (DFA) that changes state on each character, so the lexer runs in time proportional to input length. Generator tools such as lex and flex build this automaton automatically from a list of patterns, although many production compilers use hand-written lexers.

Two rules settle which token to produce. Longest match, also called maximal munch, takes the longest string that matches any pattern, so >= becomes one token rather than > followed by =, and ifx is an identifier rather than the keyword if followed by x. When two patterns match the same longest string, the one listed first wins, which is how keywords take priority over the general identifier pattern.

Regular expressions cannot count nesting, so they cannot check matched parentheses or if statements inside if statements. That job belongs to parsing, which uses a context-free grammar to build a syntax tree from the tokens. Lexical errors are things like an illegal character or an unterminated string literal; a missing semicolon or unbalanced bracket is a syntax error found by the parser, and an undeclared variable is caught later by semantic analysis.

faq.q: What is the difference between a lexer and a parser?
faq.a: A lexer turns characters into tokens using regular patterns, while a parser checks the token sequence against a context-free grammar and builds a syntax tree.

faq.q: What is a token in a compiler?
faq.a: A token is the smallest meaningful unit of source code, such as an identifier, keyword, number, operator or punctuation mark, usually stored as a type plus its text or value.

faq.q: What is the maximal munch rule?
faq.a: It is the lexer rule of always taking the longest possible match, so that inputs such as ++ or >= become single tokens instead of being split.

構文解析.desc: The compiler phase that checks whether the token sequence follows the language grammar and builds the program's structure as a tree. Grammar errors are detected here.

about.h: Where parsing sits in a compiler
about.p: A compiler front end works in stages. Lexical analysis turns the character stream into tokens such as identifiers, numbers and symbols, discarding whitespace and comments. Syntax analysis, or parsing, then checks whether that token sequence forms a valid program according to the language grammar and records how the pieces nest: which statements form a loop body, which operands belong to which operator. Errors such as a missing semicolon or unbalanced parentheses are reported here. Semantic analysis follows, checking types and whether names are declared, before the program is lowered to an intermediate representation for optimization and code generation.

Token rules are simple enough for regular expressions and fast finite automata, but program structure is not. Nested parentheses and if statements inside if statements require counting to unlimited depth, which no regular expression can do. Programming languages are therefore described with context-free grammars, sets of rewriting rules such as expr → expr + term, often written in Backus-Naur form. A well-designed grammar also encodes operator precedence and associativity, so that a + b * c groups the multiplication first. Ambiguous grammars, where one input has two possible trees, must be avoided or resolved with extra rules.

about.h: Top-down LL vs. bottom-up LR parsing
about.p: LL parsers work top-down: starting from the start symbol, they predict which rule to apply by looking at the next token or few tokens. Hand-written recursive-descent parsers, with one function per grammar rule, are LL in style and are widely used for their clarity and good error messages, but they require left-recursive rules to be rewritten. LR parsers work bottom-up: they shift tokens onto a stack and reduce them to rules once a complete right-hand side is recognized. LR handles a wider class of grammars, and parser generators such as yacc and Bison build LALR tables automatically.

about.h: Parse trees vs. abstract syntax trees
about.p: Following the grammar literally yields a concrete syntax tree, or parse tree, containing every parenthesis, separator and intermediate rule. Later phases need far less, so parsers usually build an abstract syntax tree (AST) instead. In the AST for (a + b) * c, the addition node simply sits beneath the multiplication node; the tree shape now carries the evaluation order, and the parentheses disappear. The AST is the data structure that semantic analysis annotates with types and scopes and that the compiler later translates into intermediate code.

faq.q: What is the difference between lexical analysis and syntax analysis?
faq.a: Lexical analysis splits source text into tokens and discards whitespace and comments. Syntax analysis takes those tokens, checks them against the grammar and builds a tree describing the program structure.

faq.q: What is an abstract syntax tree?
faq.a: An abstract syntax tree is a tree representation of a program that keeps only the operations and statements needed for meaning. Grouping symbols like parentheses are dropped because the tree shape itself expresses precedence and nesting.

faq.q: What is the difference between LL and LR parsers?
faq.a: LL parsers build the tree top-down, predicting rules from upcoming tokens, and include hand-written recursive-descent parsers. LR parsers build bottom-up by shifting tokens onto a stack and reducing them to rules, and accept a broader class of grammars.

抽象構文木(AST).desc: A tree representing program structure with operations and statements as nodes. Meaningless details such as parentheses and separators are omitted, and operator precedence is expressed by the tree's shape.

about.p: A parser that follows the grammar literally produces a concrete syntax tree (parse tree), with a node for every grammar rule applied and a leaf for every token, including parentheses, commas and semicolons. Grammars that encode precedence with separate rules for expressions, terms and factors also create long chains of single-child nodes. An AST (abstract syntax tree) discards all of this. Each node is a meaningful construct, such as a binary operation, a function call, an if statement or a variable reference, with exactly the children that construct needs.

about.h: How the shape encodes precedence and associativity
about.p: Operations evaluated first sit deeper in the tree. For 2 + 3 * 4 the root is + with children 2 and a * node over 3 and 4; for (2 + 3) * 4 the root is * instead, and the parentheses have done their job and vanish. Associativity is encoded the same way: a - b - c means (a - b) - c, so the left child of the root is another subtraction, giving a left-leaning tree. A post-order walk, children before parent, therefore evaluates the expression in the correct order.

about.h: What compilers do with an AST
about.p: After parsing, semantic analysis walks the AST to resolve each name to its declaration, check and infer types, insert implicit conversions and report errors such as using an undeclared variable. Nodes are typically annotated with this information. The annotated tree is then lowered into an intermediate representation (IR), such as three-address code or SSA form, where control flow becomes explicit branches between basic blocks. Simple tree-walking interpreters execute the AST directly, and tools such as formatters, linters and refactoring engines also operate on ASTs.

An AST mirrors the source language: it still has nested loops, structured if statements and source-level expressions, which makes it ideal for checks and transformations that refer to the program as written. An IR is closer to the machine, with flat sequences of simple operations and explicit jumps, which suits data-flow analysis and optimization. Confusing the two is common, but the dividing line is roughly this: the AST answers what the programmer wrote, the IR answers what must be computed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a parse tree and an abstract syntax tree?
faq.a: A parse tree records every grammar rule and token, including punctuation, while an AST keeps only the constructs that carry meaning. Precedence that the parse tree shows through rule chains is shown in the AST simply by which node is the parent.

faq.q: How are parentheses represented in an AST?
faq.a: They are not stored as nodes. Their effect is captured by the tree structure: a parenthesized subexpression becomes a subtree that is evaluated before its parent operation.

faq.q: Do interpreters use an AST?
faq.a: Many do. A tree-walking interpreter evaluates the AST directly, while faster interpreters usually compile the AST into bytecode first and execute that.

中間表現.desc: A form of the program inside a compiler that depends on neither the source language nor the target CPU. Most optimizations operate on it, separating language-specific front ends from CPU-specific back ends.

about.p: Supporting M source languages on N processors with separate compilers would require M × N of them. With a shared intermediate representation (IR), each language needs only a front end that translates into the IR and each processor only a back end that translates out of it, M + N pieces in total. Optimizations written once on the IR then benefit every language and target. LLVM is the best-known example: front ends such as Clang emit LLVM IR, and back ends generate code for x86, Arm, RISC-V and other targets.

Compilers often use several IR levels. Close to the source sits an abstract syntax tree. Lower down, three-address code breaks expressions into simple steps such as t1 = a + b; x = t1 * c, with temporaries for intermediate values. These instructions are grouped into basic blocks connected by a control-flow graph. Many modern IRs, including LLVM IR, use static single assignment (SSA) form, where each variable is assigned exactly once and special phi nodes merge values where control paths join.

Most optimization passes run on the IR: constant propagation, dead code elimination, common subexpression elimination, moving loop-invariant computations out of loops, and function inlining. SSA form makes many of these simpler because every use points to exactly one definition. Link-time optimization (LTO) stores IR instead of machine code in object files so that the whole program can be optimized together, enabling inlining and dead-function removal across source files.

about.h: IR vs. bytecode and machine code
about.p: A compiler's internal IR is a working form for analysis and transformation; the CPU cannot execute it, and the back end must still select instructions, allocate registers and schedule code. Portable bytecodes, such as Java bytecode or WebAssembly, are related but serve a different purpose: they are stable distribution formats that a virtual machine interprets or compiles just in time, whereas internal IRs may change between compiler versions.

faq.q: What is an intermediate representation in a compiler?
faq.a: It is the form a compiler translates source code into before generating machine code, independent of both the source language and the target CPU, so optimizations can be shared.

faq.q: What is SSA form?
faq.a: Static single assignment is an IR form in which every variable is assigned exactly once, with phi nodes selecting values where control flow merges, which simplifies many optimizations.

faq.q: Is LLVM IR machine code?
faq.a: No. LLVM IR is a target-independent intermediate representation; a back end must translate it into machine code for a specific processor.

SSA形式.desc: An IR form in which variables are renamed so each is assigned exactly once, with φ functions selecting values at join points. Clear definition-use relationships make optimization easier.

about.p: SSA (static single assignment) form gives every assignment its own variable name. In straight-line code this is just renaming: x = 1; x = x + 2 becomes x1 = 1; x2 = x1 + 2, and each later use refers to whichever version reaches it. The word static matters: each name has exactly one assignment in the program text, even if that assignment executes many times in a loop. Because every use has exactly one definition, the definition-use relationships that optimizers need are explicit in the names themselves rather than computed by separate analysis.

Renaming alone fails where control flow merges, because the value of x after an if-else depends on which branch ran. SSA inserts a φ (phi) function at the start of the join block, x3 = φ(x1, x2), with one argument per incoming edge; it yields the argument for the edge actually taken. Loops need the same thing at the loop header, merging the initial value with the value from the previous iteration. Standard construction algorithms place φ functions only where definitions from different paths actually meet, using the control-flow graph's dominance information.

With a single definition per name, many optimizations become simple and fast. Constant propagation just follows each definition to its uses; dead-code elimination removes definitions with no uses; global value numbering detects redundant computations by comparing operations on the same named values. Analyses can be sparse, working along definition-use edges instead of iterating over every program point. For these reasons the IRs of many production compilers, LLVM IR among them, are in SSA form, usually for scalar values held in virtual registers while memory is accessed through explicit loads and stores.

Processors have no φ instruction, so before or during register allocation the compiler converts out of SSA. Each φ is replaced by copy instructions at the end of the predecessor blocks, so every incoming path writes the chosen value into a common location. Edges that leave a block with several successors and enter one with several predecessors may need to be split to have a place for those copies. Register allocation then tries to coalesce the copies, assigning both sides the same register so that most of them disappear.

faq.q: What does SSA stand for in compilers?
faq.a: Static single assignment. Each variable in the IR is assigned in exactly one place in the program text, and φ functions merge values where control-flow paths join.

faq.q: How can SSA work with loops if a variable can only be assigned once?
faq.a: The single assignment is static, not dynamic. A φ function at the loop header merges the value entering the loop with the value computed in the previous iteration, and that one definition executes on every iteration.

faq.q: Where are φ functions placed?
faq.a: At the beginning of blocks where different definitions of the same original variable can arrive along different incoming edges. Algorithms based on dominance frontiers find these points without inserting unnecessary φs.

基本ブロック.desc: A sequence of instructions with no branch entering or leaving in the middle, always executed from start to end. Basic blocks are the nodes of a control-flow graph and units of local optimization.

制御フローグラフ.desc: A graph representing a program's execution flow, with basic blocks as nodes and branches between them as edges. It is used to detect loops and analyze data flow.

about.p: A control-flow graph (CFG) is built from basic blocks: maximal runs of instructions entered only at the first instruction and left only at the last. To form them, a compiler marks leaders, namely the first instruction of a function, every branch target and every instruction immediately following a branch. Each block runs from a leader up to the next leader. Since instructions inside a block always execute in order, local optimizations such as common subexpression elimination are easy to apply within one block.

about.h: Edges and what the shape reveals
about.p: Edges represent possible transfers of control: a conditional branch gives a block two successors, the taken target and the fall-through block, while an unconditional jump gives one. Many analyses add a single entry and exit node. The graph's shape exposes structure. A block d dominates block n if every path from entry to n passes through d, and an edge whose target dominates its source is a back edge that identifies a loop. Blocks unreachable from the entry are dead code that can be removed.

Many optimizations rely on data-flow analyses that propagate facts along CFG edges and iterate until nothing changes. Liveness analysis works backward to find, at each point, which values may still be read later, and its result builds the interference graph used for register allocation. Reaching definitions works forward to find which assignments may supply a variable's value. Static single assignment (SSA) form, used by most modern compilers, is also constructed on the CFG, inserting phi functions where control-flow paths merge.

A CFG describes flow inside a single function, whereas a call graph has whole functions as nodes and calls as edges; interprocedural analysis uses both. CFGs also appear outside compilers. Branch coverage in testing asks whether every CFG edge has been executed, binary analysis tools reconstruct CFGs from machine code, and control-flow integrity defenses restrict indirect jumps to edges the CFG allows, blocking attacks that redirect execution to unintended code.

faq.q: What is a basic block in a control-flow graph?
faq.a: A straight-line sequence of instructions with one entry at the top and one exit at the bottom, so that if its first instruction runs, all of them run in order.

faq.q: How do you find loops in a control-flow graph?
faq.a: Compute dominators and look for back edges, edges whose target dominates their source; each back edge defines a natural loop headed by its target block.

faq.q: What is the difference between a control-flow graph and a call graph?
faq.a: A control-flow graph shows the possible paths between basic blocks within one function, while a call graph shows which functions call which other functions.

定数畳み込み.desc: An optimization that evaluates expressions whose values are known at compile time and replaces them with the resulting constant, such as turning 3 * 4 into 12. It removes run-time computation.

about.p: During optimization the compiler scans its intermediate representation for operations whose operands are all constants, evaluates them, and replaces the operation with the resulting literal.
