Arithmetic, bit operations, shifts, casts and comparisons can all be folded. Folding a comparison is especially powerful: if a condition such as 10 > 100 becomes a known false, the branch it guards can never run. Compilers usually fold together with algebraic simplification, rewriting expressions like x * 1 or x + 0 into x, although strictly that is a separate transformation because x itself is not constant.

about.h: Working with propagation, inlining and dead-code elimination
about.p: Constant folding rarely acts alone. Constant propagation replaces uses of a variable known to hold a constant with that constant, which creates new opportunities for folding, whose results can be propagated again. For example, n = 8; m = n * 2; return m + 1 collapses to return 17, after which dead-code elimination removes the unused assignments. Inlining feeds the loop: once a call sq(6) is replaced by its body, 6 * 6 + 1 folds to 37. Compilers based on SSA form often combine propagation, folding and unreachable-branch removal in one algorithm called sparse conditional constant propagation.

A folded result must be exactly what the target machine would have computed at run time. The compiler must therefore emulate the target's integer widths and wraparound, which matters when cross-compiling from a 64-bit host to a 32-bit target. Floating-point folding must reproduce IEEE 754 rounding for each operation in source order, which is why compilers do not reassociate floating-point expressions unless options such as fast-math permit it. Operations that would fault, such as integer division by zero, must not be turned into a compile-time error unless the code is certain to execute.

about.h: Constant folding versus language-level constant expressions
about.p: Some evaluation at compile time is required by the language rather than chosen by the optimizer. In C, array sizes, case labels and initializers of static variables must be constant expressions, and C++ constexpr functions can be evaluated at compile time on request. Optimization-level constant folding is broader and optional: it applies anywhere in the program, including values that only became constant after propagation or inlining, and it can happen at several stages, from the front end through the intermediate representation to instruction selection, where an address offset plus a constant may be merged into one immediate.

faq.q: What is the difference between constant folding and constant propagation?
faq.a: Constant folding evaluates an expression whose operands are all constants, such as 3 * 4 becoming 12. Constant propagation substitutes a variable's known constant value into its uses, which often creates new expressions that can then be folded.

faq.q: Does constant folding happen with optimization turned off?
faq.a: Simple literal expressions are often folded even without optimization, because front ends evaluate them while parsing. Folding through variables, function inlining and branch removal generally require optimization to be enabled.

faq.q: Can constant folding change floating-point results?
faq.a: A conforming compiler folds floating-point operations with the same IEEE 754 rounding the hardware would use, so results do not change. Options that relax floating-point rules, such as fast-math, allow reassociation and can change the last bits of results.

共通部分式の削除.desc: An optimization that computes a repeatedly evaluated expression once and reuses the result, after confirming its operands do not change in between.

インライン展開.desc: Replacing a function call with the body of the called function. It removes call overhead and enables further optimizations but enlarges the code.

ループ展開.desc: Replicating a loop body several times to reduce the number of iterations. It cuts branch and counter overhead and gives more freedom to reorder instructions, at the cost of larger code.

about.h: What unrolling does to a loop
about.p: A loop that adds two arrays element by element normally performs, for every element, a counter increment, a comparison and a conditional branch in addition to the useful work. Unrolling by four writes the body four times, handling elements i through i+3 in one pass and incrementing i by 4, so the loop runs a quarter as many iterations and the overhead is paid once per four elements. When the trip count is not a multiple of the unroll factor, a short remainder loop handles the leftover elements. Small loops with a known constant trip count can be unrolled completely.

Besides cutting branch and counter overhead, unrolling places several independent copies of the work in one basic block, giving the compiler's instruction scheduler freedom to interleave them. A load from one copy can be issued while arithmetic from another proceeds, hiding latencies. For reductions such as sums, unrolling with several separate accumulators breaks a single long dependency chain; for floating point this changes the rounding order, so compilers do it only when allowed. Unrolling also exposes groups of operations that can be combined into SIMD vector instructions.

Each extra copy enlarges the code, which can push hot loops out of the instruction cache, and more simultaneous values raise register pressure, which can force spills to memory that undo the gain. Modern out-of-order processors with accurate branch prediction already hide much loop overhead, so heavy unrolling often brings little benefit. Compilers therefore choose unroll factors heuristically, and programmers can request specific behavior through compiler options or pragmas when measurements justify it.

Loop unrolling targets control overhead and scheduling freedom. Strength reduction is different: it replaces an expensive operation with a cheaper one, such as computing i * 4 by adding 4 to a separate variable each iteration or by a shift. Loop blocking, or tiling, restructures loops such as matrix multiplication to work on cache-sized blocks and increase data reuse, attacking memory misses rather than branches. Compilers often apply several of these together to the same loop.

faq.q: What is loop unrolling?
faq.a: Loop unrolling is a compiler or manual optimization that replicates the loop body several times and reduces the number of iterations accordingly, cutting counter updates and branches and exposing more instructions for scheduling.

faq.q: Does loop unrolling always improve performance?
faq.a: No. It increases code size and register usage, which can cause instruction cache misses or register spills, and on modern CPUs the remaining loop overhead is often small, so the benefit must be measured.

faq.q: What is the difference between loop unrolling and loop tiling?
faq.a: Unrolling replicates the loop body to reduce branch overhead and increase instruction-level parallelism. Tiling splits the iteration space into cache-sized blocks to improve data reuse and reduce cache misses.

ベクトル化.desc: Transforming a loop that performs the same computation on each element so that SIMD instructions process several elements at once. It requires no data dependence between iterations.

about.h: How a loop becomes SIMD code
about.p: SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) instructions operate on several values packed into one wide register. A 128-bit register holds four 32-bit numbers, so one SIMD add replaces four scalar adds, and 256-bit or 512-bit units do eight or sixteen. A vectorizing compiler rewrites a loop so each iteration of the new loop handles one register's worth of elements. When the trip count is unknown at compile time or not a multiple of the vector width, it adds a scalar remainder loop, or uses masked operations, for the leftover elements.

The key requirement is that iterations be independent. A loop such as a[i] = a[i-1] + b[i] has a loop-carried dependence, because each element needs the previous result, so several elements cannot be computed at once. Possible aliasing is another obstacle: if two pointers might refer to overlapping memory, the compiler must either add a run-time overlap check or give up; C's restrict qualifier promises no overlap. Non-contiguous or indirect accesses, function calls the compiler cannot inline, and complex control flow also reduce or prevent vectorization.

Summing an array into one variable is itself a dependence, yet compilers vectorize it by keeping several partial sums in the vector lanes and combining them at the end. For integers the result is identical. For floating-point numbers it is not guaranteed, because every addition rounds, so (a + b) + c can differ slightly from a + (b + c). Under strict settings the compiler therefore keeps the original order and may not vectorize such reductions; options such as fast-math allow reassociation in exchange for tiny numerical differences.

Memory layout often decides whether vectorized code is fast. In an array of structures (AoS), each record stores x, y, z and mass together, so a loop that reads only x uses a quarter of every 64-byte cache line it fetches. In a structure of arrays (SoA), all x values are contiguous: every fetched line is fully used, memory traffic drops to about a quarter, and a single vector load picks up consecutive x values without gather instructions. Changing the layout does not change numerical results.

faq.q: What is the difference between vectorization and multithreading?
faq.a: Vectorization speeds up a single thread by using SIMD instructions that process several data elements per instruction. Multithreading runs separate instruction streams on different cores, and the two are routinely combined.

faq.q: Why won't my compiler vectorize a loop?
faq.a: Common reasons are a dependence between iterations, possible pointer aliasing, non-contiguous memory access, calls to functions that cannot be inlined, or a floating-point reduction that would require reordering additions under strict settings. Most compilers can print a vectorization report explaining their decision.

faq.q: Can vectorization change floating-point results?
faq.a: Element-wise operations give the same results, but vectorized reductions add numbers in a different order, and because floating-point addition is not associative the final sum can differ in the last bits.

強度低減.desc: Replacing expensive operations such as multiplication with cheaper ones such as addition or shifts, for example adding 4 each iteration instead of computing i * 4 every time.

about.p: The classic case is an expression that grows linearly with a loop counter, such as the byte offset i * 4 for an array of 4-byte elements. The compiler recognizes i as an induction variable, one that changes by a fixed amount each iteration, and introduces a new variable that starts at 0 and has 4 added each time round. The multiplication disappears from the loop body. Often the original counter then becomes unnecessary except for the exit test, and induction-variable elimination rewrites that test against the new variable so the old one can be removed.

Strength reduction also applies to single operations with constant operands. Multiplying by a power of two becomes a left shift, and x * 2 can become x + x. Unsigned division by a power of two becomes a logical right shift and unsigned remainder becomes a bitwise AND with a mask. Signed division needs a small correction, because division in C rounds toward zero while an arithmetic shift rounds toward negative infinity. Division by other constants is commonly replaced with multiplication by a precomputed fixed-point reciprocal followed by a shift.

Strength reduction keeps the same number of computations but makes each one cheaper. Common subexpression elimination is different: it removes repeated evaluations of the same expression by computing it once into a temporary. Loop unrolling is different again: it replicates the loop body to cut per-iteration overhead and expose parallelism. In practice they interact; after unrolling, for example, several strength-reduced address computations can share one base pointer with different constant offsets folded into the load instructions.

On modern processors integer multiplication is pipelined and typically takes only a few cycles, so replacing it inside a loop gains less than it once did, though it can still shorten dependency chains and free multiplier units. Integer division remains much slower, often tens of cycles, so turning division by a constant into multiply and shift is still valuable. For floating point, care is needed: multiplying by 0.5 instead of dividing by 2.0 gives identical results, but replacing division by a general constant with multiplication by its rounded reciprocal can change the last bit.

faq.q: Should I write x shifted left by 1 instead of x * 2 for speed?
faq.a: Generally no. Compilers apply this strength reduction automatically when it is profitable, and writing the multiplication keeps the code clear. Hand-written shifts on signed values can even change results for negative numbers in the division case.

faq.q: What is an induction variable?
faq.a: A variable whose value changes by a constant amount on every loop iteration, such as a loop counter or a pointer stepped by a fixed stride. Strength reduction targets expressions that are linear functions of induction variables.

faq.q: Does strength reduction change program results?
faq.a: For integer arithmetic with the language's overflow rules it gives identical results. For floating point, compilers only apply it when exact, such as multiplication by a power of two, unless relaxed math options are enabled.

レジスタ割り当て.desc: Assigning program variables and temporaries to the CPU's limited registers, ensuring values in use at the same time get different registers, often via coloring an interference graph.

about.p: Compilers generate intermediate code using an unlimited supply of virtual registers or temporaries, but a real CPU has only a small fixed set, typically 16 to 32 general-purpose registers. Register allocation decides which values live in which physical registers at each point and which must be kept in memory instead. Because registers are far faster than even an L1 cache access, good allocation has a large effect on speed, especially inside loops. The hard rule is that two values needed at the same time cannot share a register.

The allocator first runs liveness analysis over the control-flow graph to find, at every point, which values may still be read later. It then builds an interference graph: each value is a node, and an edge joins two values that are live at the same time. Assigning registers becomes coloring the graph with k colors, where k is the number of available registers, so that no neighbors share a color. Optimal coloring is NP-complete in general, so compilers use heuristics such as Chaitin-style simplification, repeatedly removing nodes with fewer than k neighbors.

When the graph cannot be colored with k colors, some values are spilled: they are kept in a stack slot, with a store after each definition and a load before each use. Spills add instructions and memory traffic, so the allocator estimates a spill cost for each candidate, weighting uses by loop nesting depth, and prefers to spill values that are used rarely but interfere with many others. Splitting a long live range into shorter pieces can also let a value stay in a register where it matters most.

about.h: Calling conventions, coalescing and linear scan
about.p: Real allocators must respect the calling convention: arguments and return values use specific registers, caller-saved registers are clobbered by calls, and callee-saved registers must be restored before returning. Coalescing assigns the same register to the source and destination of a copy when they do not interfere, deleting the move instruction. Just-in-time (JIT) compilers often use linear-scan allocation instead of graph coloring, walking sorted live intervals in a single pass, which is much faster to run at the cost of somewhat lower code quality.

faq.q: What is register spilling?
faq.a: Spilling is keeping a value in memory, usually a stack slot, because there are not enough registers for everything live at that point; the compiler inserts stores and loads around its uses, which slows the code.

faq.q: Why is register allocation a graph coloring problem?
faq.a: Values live at the same time interfere and need different registers, so if values are nodes and interferences are edges, giving each node one of k colors with no neighbors alike is exactly assigning k registers.

faq.q: What is the difference between graph coloring and linear scan register allocation?
faq.a: Graph coloring builds a full interference graph and usually produces better code but takes longer; linear scan allocates in one pass over sorted live intervals, trading some code quality for much faster compilation.

スピル.desc: Saving some values to memory (the stack) during register allocation when more values are live than there are registers. The extra stores and reloads slow the code.

命令スケジューリング.desc: Reordering instructions without changing results so that latencies of operations and memory accesses are filled with independent instructions.

LLVM.desc: A compiler infrastructure built around a common intermediate representation (LLVM IR), combining language front ends, optimization passes and CPU back ends. It is used for many languages and CPUs.

JITコンパイル.desc: Compiling frequently executed parts of a program to machine code while it runs, enabling optimizations based on run-time information. Used in runtimes for Java, JavaScript and others.

about.p: A typical JIT (just-in-time) runtime starts by interpreting bytecode, which costs nothing up front but runs slowly. While interpreting, it counts how often each method is called and each loop iterates. Code that crosses a threshold is handed to a quick baseline compiler, and code that stays hot is later recompiled by an optimizing compiler that spends much more time per function. Long-running loops can be switched to compiled code in the middle of execution, a technique called on-stack replacement. Compilation usually happens on background threads so the program keeps running meanwhile.

The interpreter and baseline code collect profiles: which branches are taken, which object types appear at each call site, whether integers have ever overflowed. The optimizing compiler bets on these observations, for example inlining the one method a virtual call has always reached and dropping code for types never seen. Each bet is protected by a cheap guard. If a guard fails, the runtime deoptimizes: it rebuilds the interpreter's view of the current frame, continues in slower code and may later recompile with the new information. Ahead-of-time compilers cannot make such bets so freely.

A pure interpreter starts instantly and needs no compiler at run time, but executes each operation slowly. AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation produces machine code before the program runs, giving fast start-up, predictable performance and no compiler in memory, but it must optimize without knowing actual inputs, unless profile-guided optimization supplies training-run data. A JIT pays for warm-up time, compilation CPU time and memory for the code cache, and in return can reach high peak speed on long-running programs. Many runtimes combine approaches, for example caching or AOT-compiling start-up code.

A JIT writes machine code into memory and then executes it, which conflicts with the security rule that memory should not be writable and executable at the same time. Runtimes handle this by switching page permissions after emitting code, or by mapping the same physical memory twice with different permissions, and some locked-down platforms forbid run-time code generation entirely. Because compiled code depends on run-time profiles, performance can vary between runs and can drop suddenly when deoptimization occurs, which makes benchmarking JIT-based systems require proper warm-up.

faq.q: Is JIT compilation faster than AOT compilation?
faq.a: It depends on the workload. JIT code can match or beat AOT code on long-running programs because it optimizes using real profiles, but AOT wins on start-up time, memory use and predictability.

faq.q: What is JIT warm-up?
faq.a: The initial period in which code runs in the interpreter or a baseline tier while the runtime profiles it and compiles hot parts. Performance measured during warm-up underestimates steady-state speed.

faq.q: What is deoptimization in a JIT?
faq.a: Abandoning optimized code when an assumption it was built on turns out false, and continuing execution in the interpreter or less-optimized code from the equivalent point. The runtime may then recompile with updated profile information.

固定小数点.desc: Representing fractions with ordinary integer bit patterns and an agreed binary-point position. Integer arithmetic circuits suffice, giving small, low-power hardware, but the range is narrow. Formats are often named by fraction bits, as in Q15.

about.h: How a fixed-point number is stored
about.p: A fixed-point number is an ordinary integer that the programmer agrees to divide by a fixed power of two. With 8 bits and 4 fraction bits, the pattern 0011 1000 reads as the integer 56, and dividing by 2⁴ = 16 gives 3.5: the upper bits are the integer part and the first fraction bit weighs 0.5. Q notation names the format: Q15 is a 16-bit signed number with 15 fraction bits, covering −1 to just under +1 with a step of 2⁻¹⁵, about 3.05 × 10⁻⁵. Qm.n states integer and fraction bits explicitly.

Two numbers in the same format can be added with an ordinary integer adder, since their binary points already line up. Multiplication doubles the fraction bits: two Q15 values give a 32-bit product with 30 fraction bits, which is shifted right by 15 to return to Q15, with rounding if needed. Overflow is the main hazard. Ordinary integer hardware wraps around, turning a large positive result into a negative one, so DSPs provide saturating arithmetic that clamps to the largest representable value. In Q15, even −1 × −1 overflows because +1 cannot be represented.

Because the contents are just integers, fixed point needs no exponent alignment, normalization or special-value handling, all of which make floating-point units larger and more power-hungry. Integer multipliers and adders are small and fast, which suits low-cost microcontrollers without a floating-point unit, signal-processing DSPs, and custom datapaths on FPGAs and ASICs where the designer can choose exactly as many bits as the algorithm needs. The price is design effort: every intermediate value must be scaled so it neither overflows nor loses too much precision.

Fixed-point values are evenly spaced, so absolute precision is the same everywhere but the range is narrow. Floating point stores a significand and an exponent, so spacing doubles each time the exponent rises: in single precision the gap between neighbors is about 1.2 × 10⁻⁷ near 1 but 8 near 100 million. Floating point therefore keeps relative precision roughly constant over an enormous range. Both formats have rounding error; the difference is that fixed point trades range for simple hardware and predictable, uniform resolution.

faq.q: What does Q15 mean in fixed-point arithmetic?
faq.a: Q15 is a 16-bit signed fixed-point format with 15 fraction bits and one sign bit. It represents values from −1 up to 1 − 2⁻¹⁵ in steps of about 3.05 × 10⁻⁵.

faq.q: How do you convert a fixed-point value to decimal?
faq.a: Read the bit pattern as an integer and divide by 2 raised to the number of fraction bits. For example, 0011 1000 with 4 fraction bits is 56 ÷ 16 = 3.5.

faq.q: What is the difference between fixed point and floating point?
faq.a: Fixed point uses a binary point at an agreed fixed position, giving uniform spacing and simple integer hardware but a narrow range. Floating point adds an exponent, giving a wide range with roughly constant relative precision at the cost of more complex hardware.

IEEE 754.desc: The international standard defining floating-point formats and arithmetic, including single (32-bit) and double (64-bit) precision, rounding, and special values such as infinity and NaN, so results agree across computers.

about.h: How the bits encode a value
about.p: A binary IEEE 754 number stores a sign bit, a biased exponent field and a fraction, and for normal numbers represents (−1)^sign × 1.fraction × 2^(exponent − bias). Single precision (FP32) uses 1, 8 and 23 bits with a bias of 127; double precision (FP64) uses 1, 11 and 52 bits with a bias of 1023. The leading 1 is implied (the hidden bit), giving 24 and 53 bits of precision, about 7 and 15–16 decimal digits. For example, 1.0 has a stored exponent of 127 and an all-zero fraction, which is 0x3F800000 in FP32.

The extreme exponent codes are reserved. An all-zero exponent encodes ±0 and subnormal numbers, which drop the hidden 1 to fill the gap below the smallest normal value with evenly spaced tiny values (gradual underflow). An all-ones exponent encodes ±infinity when the fraction is zero and NaN (not a number) otherwise. Dividing a nonzero number by zero gives infinity, while 0 ÷ 0 or ∞ − ∞ gives NaN, which compares unequal even to itself. +0 and −0 compare equal but give opposite infinities as divisors. By default these events set status flags instead of stopping the program.

The basic operations, including addition, multiplication, division and square root, must be correctly rounded: the result equals the exact value rounded to a representable one. The default mode rounds to nearest with ties to even, which avoids a systematic upward drift. Machine epsilon, the gap above 1.0, is 2⁻²³ (about 1.19 × 10⁻⁷) in FP32 and 2⁻⁵² in FP64, and every integer is exact only up to 2²⁴ and 2⁵³ respectively. Decimal fractions such as 0.1 are not exactly representable, and floating-point addition is not associative, so results should be compared with a tolerance.

Fixed-point numbers have uniformly spaced values, so absolute error is constant and the range is narrow. Floating point keeps the relative error roughly constant across an enormous range, about 10⁻³⁰⁸ to 10³⁰⁸ for FP64, at the cost of more complex hardware for alignment, normalization and rounding. The standard also defines half precision with a 5-bit exponent and a fused multiply-add that rounds only once. Machine-learning hardware often uses bfloat16, which keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent with a 7-bit fraction; it follows the same encoding ideas but is not one of the standard's formats.

faq.q: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in floating point?
faq.a: None of these decimal values has an exact binary representation, so each is stored rounded and the rounding errors do not cancel. In double precision the sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004, so equality tests should use a tolerance.

faq.q: What is the exponent bias in IEEE 754 single precision?
faq.a: The bias is 127, so the true exponent is the stored 8-bit value minus 127. Stored values 0 and 255 are reserved for zero, subnormals, infinity and NaN, leaving 1–254 for normal numbers.

faq.q: Why is NaN not equal to itself?
faq.a: IEEE 754 defines every comparison involving NaN as unordered, so x == x is false when x is NaN. Use a dedicated function such as isnan rather than relying on this trick.

仮数.desc: The bits of a floating-point number holding its significant digits. For normalized numbers the leading 1 is implied, so single precision stores 23 bits but has 24 bits of precision.

about.h: Where the significand sits in IEEE 754
about.p: An IEEE 754 binary floating-point number stores a sign bit, an exponent field and a significand field, and a normalized value equals (−1)^sign × 1.f × 2^(exponent − bias), where f is the stored significand. Single precision (FP32) allots 1, 8 and 23 bits; double precision (FP64) allots 1, 11 and 52. Because a normalized binary number always begins with 1, that leading bit is implied rather than stored, so FP32 has 24 bits of precision and FP64 has 53. When the exponent field is all zeros, the number is subnormal and the leading digit is 0 instead.

about.h: Significand sets precision, exponent sets range
about.p: The exponent decides how large or small a number can be; the significand decides how many digits are kept. With 24 bits, FP32 resolves about 7 decimal digits, since 2²⁴ is about 1.7×10⁷, and FP64's 53 bits give about 15 to 16. Machine epsilon, the gap between 1 and the next representable number, is 2⁻²³ ≈ 1.19×10⁻⁷ for FP32 and 2⁻⁵² for FP64. Storing 123456789 in FP32 yields 123456792. Values whose fractions do not have power-of-two denominators, like 0.1, become repeating binary fractions and are rounded.

To encode −6.25 in FP32, write 6.25 in binary as 110.01 and normalize it to 1.1001 × 2². The sign bit is 1, the stored exponent is 2 + 127 = 129 (1000 0001), and the significand field holds the bits after the binary point, 1001 followed by zeros. The full pattern 1 10000001 1001000…0 is 0xC0C80000 in hexadecimal. For 1.0 the significand field is all zeros and the stored exponent is 127, giving 0x3F800000. With the exponent field all ones, a zero significand means infinity and a nonzero one means NaN.

about.h: Trading significand bits in AI formats
about.p: Machine-learning hardware often shortens the significand to halve memory and arithmetic cost. FP16 uses 1 sign, 5 exponent and 10 significand bits, keeping reasonable precision but a narrow range, so small gradients can underflow and training uses loss scaling. bfloat16 uses 1, 8 and 7 bits: the same exponent width and nearly the same range as FP32, but only 8 bits of precision. Training tolerates this coarse precision, so bfloat16 trades significand bits for range, while FP16 does the opposite.

faq.q: Is the significand the same as the mantissa?
faq.a: In everyday use, yes; mantissa is the older term for the stored fraction of a floating-point number. IEEE 754 prefers significand, partly because mantissa traditionally means the fractional part of a logarithm.

faq.q: Why does single precision have 24 bits of precision when only 23 are stored?
faq.a: Normalized binary numbers always start with 1, so that leading bit is implied rather than stored. The 23 stored bits plus the hidden 1 give 24 bits of precision.

faq.q: How many decimal digits does a float have?
faq.a: Single precision keeps about 7 significant decimal digits and double precision about 15 to 16. The limit comes from the significand width: 24 and 53 bits including the hidden bit.

指数部.desc: The bits of a floating-point number giving the power of two. To represent negative exponents, the true exponent plus a bias (127 for single precision) is stored.

about.p: The exponent field is an unsigned integer that stores the true exponent plus a fixed bias, so negative exponents need no sign. Single precision (FP32) uses 8 bits with bias 127, double precision (FP64) 11 bits with bias 1023, and half precision (FP16) 5 bits with bias 15. In FP32, stored values 1 to 254 cover true exponents −126 to +127; a stored 130 means 2³. Forgetting to subtract the bias is the most common decoding mistake.

Two exponent patterns are special. All zeros means zero or a subnormal number: the implicit leading 1 is dropped and the exponent is fixed at the minimum normal value (−126 in FP32), letting values shrink gradually toward zero. All ones means infinity when the significand is zero and NaN (not a number) otherwise. Hence the largest normal FP32 exponent field is 254, and FP16 tops out at 65504 because its exponent field stops at 30.

Exponent width sets range; significand width sets precision. FP32's 8 exponent bits reach about 3.4 × 10³⁸ with normals down to about 1.2 × 10⁻³⁸, while FP16's 5 bits stop at 65504, which is why FP16 training must watch for overflow. The bfloat16 format keeps FP32's 8-bit exponent with only 7 significand bits, giving the same range as FP32 with far less precision, a trade-off that suits many neural-network workloads.

about.h: Why biased rather than two's complement
about.p: Placing the biased exponent just below the sign bit and above the significand means that, for positive numbers, a larger value always has a larger bit pattern when read as an integer. Comparisons and sorting can therefore use integer hardware with only sign handling added. A worked example: 10.0 is 1.25 × 2³, so the sign is 0, the exponent field is 130 (binary 10000010) and the fraction is .01, giving the FP32 pattern 0x41200000.

faq.q: Why is the exponent biased in IEEE 754?
faq.a: A bias lets the field be stored as an unsigned number while still representing negative exponents, and it makes positive floats order the same way as their bit patterns read as integers.

faq.q: What is the exponent bias for double precision?
faq.a: 1023, with an 11-bit exponent field; single precision uses 127 with 8 bits, and half precision uses 15 with 5 bits.

faq.q: What does an exponent field of all zeros mean?
faq.a: It encodes zero when the significand is zero and a subnormal number otherwise, with no implicit leading 1 and the exponent fixed at the minimum normal value.

非正規化数.desc: A floating-point number whose exponent field is all zeros, without an implied leading 1, representing values smaller than the smallest normal number. It fills the gap to zero gradually (gradual underflow), so x − y = 0 implies x = y.

NaN.desc: Short for Not a Number, a floating-point special value produced by operations with no numeric result, such as 0 ÷ 0 or the square root of a negative number. It has an all-ones exponent and a nonzero significand, and compares unequal even to itself.

about.p: In IEEE 754 binary formats, an all-ones exponent field is reserved for special values: a zero significand means infinity and any nonzero significand means NaN. The sign bit is not meaningful for NaN. There are two kinds. A quiet NaN passes silently through arithmetic, while a signaling NaN raises the invalid-operation exception when used. In the encoding recommended by the 2008 revision and used by common processors, a 1 in the most significant significand bit marks a quiet NaN, and the remaining bits form a payload that can carry diagnostic information.

NaN is the default result of an invalid operation, one with no meaningful numeric answer: 0 ÷ 0, ∞ − ∞, 0 × ∞, ∞ ÷ ∞, the square root of a negative number, and similar cases. These also set the invalid-operation status flag. Dividing a nonzero number by zero is different: it returns a signed infinity and sets the divide-by-zero flag. Once created, a NaN propagates, so almost any arithmetic involving it returns NaN, which lets a calculation finish and the problem be detected at the end.

NaN is unordered with respect to every value, itself included. Every ordered comparison such as <, <= or == with a NaN operand is false, and != is true, which is why x != x is a classic NaN test. Because of this, a single NaN can break sorting routines or searches that assume consistent ordering. Library functions such as isnan are the safer test, since aggressive compiler optimization options may assume NaNs never occur and remove x != x checks. Minimum and maximum functions also differ in whether they return the NaN or the other operand.

In machine learning with 16-bit floats, whose largest finite value is 65504, an overflow first produces infinity, and a later operation such as ∞ − ∞ or 0 × ∞ turns it into NaN that spreads through the loss and weights; loss scaling and overflow checks guard against this. In numerical code, enabling traps on the invalid-operation exception stops execution at the first NaN to locate the cause. Integers have no NaN at all: integer division by zero is typically trapped or undefined rather than producing a special value.

faq.q: Why does NaN not equal itself?
faq.a: IEEE 754 defines NaN as unordered, meaning it represents no particular number, so every equality and ordering comparison involving it is false. As a result x == x is false and x != x is true when x is NaN.

faq.q: What is the difference between NaN and infinity?
faq.a: Infinity is a legitimate result of overflow or of dividing a nonzero number by zero and still has a sign and an order. NaN results from operations with no defined value, such as 0 ÷ 0, and cannot be ordered.

faq.q: What is the difference between a quiet NaN and a signaling NaN?
faq.a: A quiet NaN propagates through calculations without raising an exception. A signaling NaN raises the invalid-operation exception when used, which is useful for catching uninitialized data.

最近接偶数丸め.desc: Rounding to the nearest representable value and, on an exact tie, to the one whose last bit is even (0). It is the IEEE 754 default and keeps rounding errors from accumulating in one direction.

about.p: An exact result usually has more significand bits than the destination format can hold. Besides the bits it keeps, the hardware tracks the first discarded bit, called the round (or guard) bit, and a sticky bit that is the OR of all bits below it. If the round bit is 0 the result is truncated; if the round bit is 1 and the sticky bit is 1, the result is rounded up in magnitude. Only when the round bit is 1 and the sticky bit is 0 is the value exactly halfway, and then the last kept bit decides: if it is 1, round up to make it 0.

Rounding every tie upward adds a small positive error each time, and over many operations those errors pile up in one direction. Sending ties to the even neighbor rounds them up about half the time and down the other half, so the errors tend to cancel. In decimal terms, 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4, preserving their sum of 6, whereas always rounding up would give 7. The method is also called banker's rounding, and in binary floating point the even choice is the one whose least significant significand bit is 0.

IEEE 754 also defines directed rounding: toward zero (truncation), toward positive infinity and toward negative infinity. These are selected explicitly for special purposes; for example, interval arithmetic computes a lower bound rounded down and an upper bound rounded up so the true result is guaranteed to lie between them. The 2008 revision added round half away from zero for ties, required mainly for decimal formats. Round half to even remains the default for both arithmetic and conversions, and correctly rounded operations are defined as the exact result rounded in the current mode.

Python 3's built-in round follows ties-to-even, so round(2.5) returns 2, which looks like a bug to anyone expecting school rounding. A second surprise comes from representation: a decimal value such as 2.675 cannot be stored exactly in binary, and the nearest double is slightly below it, so rounding to two decimal places gives 2.67 regardless of the tie rule. When results must follow a specific decimal rounding convention, such as in financial calculations, decimal arithmetic types with an explicit rounding mode are the usual solution.

faq.q: Why does Python round(2.5) return 2?
faq.a: Python 3 rounds exact ties to the nearest even value, the same rule IEEE 754 uses by default, so 2.5 goes to 2 and 3.5 goes to 4. This avoids a systematic upward bias when many values are rounded.

faq.q: Is banker's rounding the same as round half to even?
faq.a: Yes. Both names describe rounding to the nearest value and, on an exact tie, choosing the neighbor with an even last digit or bit.

faq.q: What is the default rounding mode in IEEE 754?
faq.a: Round to nearest, ties to even. Directed modes toward zero, positive infinity and negative infinity are available but must be selected explicitly.

桁落ち.desc: Loss of significant digits when subtracting two nearly equal numbers, as their leading digits cancel and the relative weight of existing rounding error grows. It is avoided by rearranging formulas.

about.h: The subtraction is not the culprit
about.p: Surprisingly, subtracting two nearby floating-point numbers is usually exact: if x and y are within a factor of two of each other, x minus y is exactly representable and the hardware returns it without rounding (a result known as Sterbenz's lemma). The damage comes from errors already present in the operands, from earlier rounding, measurement or conversion. When the leading digits cancel, those small absolute errors remain while the result itself becomes tiny, so the relative error is magnified. Cancellation exposes old errors rather than creating new ones.

If a and b each carry a relative error of about e, the error in a minus b is roughly e multiplied by (|a| + |b|) / |a - b|. Subtracting numbers that agree in their first six significant digits therefore amplifies the relative error by about a million, which consumes six decimal digits of a double's roughly sixteen. If the operands agree to all their digits, the result can be pure noise or exactly zero. This ratio is the condition number of subtraction, and it explains why the effect depends on how close the inputs are, not on the format alone.

The cure is algebra that avoids subtracting close values. Rationalizing turns √(x + 1) − √x into 1 / (√(x + 1) + √x). In the quadratic formula, when b² is much larger than 4ac, one root suffers cancellation; computing the other root first and obtaining the troublesome one from the product of roots, c / a divided by the first root, avoids it. For small x, 1 − cos x becomes 2 sin²(x / 2), and math libraries provide expm1(x) and log1p(x) to compute exp(x) − 1 and log(1 + x) accurately near zero.

Cancellation and absorption are the two classic ways floating point loses information, and they are easily confused. Cancellation happens when subtracting nearly equal numbers and leaves too few meaningful digits in the result. Absorption happens when adding numbers of very different magnitude: the smaller operand's low digits fall off the end of the significand, as when 1.0e16 + 1 evaluates to exactly 1.0e16 in double precision. Moving to a wider format postpones both problems but does not remove them; reformulating the computation does.

faq.q: Why does subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers lose precision?
faq.a: The matching leading digits cancel, leaving a small result made mostly of the low-order digits, which are the ones already contaminated by rounding error. The absolute error stays the same while the value shrinks, so the relative error grows sharply.

faq.q: Does switching from float to double fix catastrophic cancellation?
faq.a: It helps by giving more digits to lose, but the same cancellation reappears when the operands are closer still. Rewriting the formula to avoid the subtraction is the real fix.

faq.q: How do you avoid cancellation in the quadratic formula?
faq.a: Compute the root in which -b and the square root term have the same sign, so they add rather than cancel, then get the other root from the relation that the product of the roots equals c / a.

情報落ち.desc: Loss of the smaller operand's low-order digits when adding numbers of very different magnitude, because they do not fit in the significand. It matters when summing many small values.

マシンイプシロン.desc: The difference between 1 and the next larger representable floating-point number, a measure of relative precision: 2⁻²³ (about 1.19 × 10⁻⁷) in single precision and 2⁻⁵² (about 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶) in double.

FMA(融合積和演算).desc: An operation computing a × b + c in one instruction, rounding only once at the end without rounding the intermediate product. It is faster and more accurate than separate multiply and add and is heavily used in matrix computation.

about.p: Multiplying two p-bit significands produces an exact product of up to 2p bits. A separate multiply instruction rounds that product to p bits, and the following add rounds again. An FMA (fused multiply-add) unit keeps the full-width product, aligns c against it, adds, and rounds only once, so the result is the exact value of a × b + c correctly rounded. IEEE 754-2008 standardized this operation, C provides it as the fma function, and most current CPU and GPU instruction sets include it, for example fmadd.s and fmadd.d in RISC-V's F and D extensions.

Dot products, matrix multiplication and convolution are long chains of multiply-accumulate steps, so FMA both halves the instruction count and improves accuracy. Polynomial evaluation by Horner's method has the form r = r × x + c at every step, a perfect fit. Iterative division and square-root algorithms rely on FMA to compute residuals accurately. A neat trick: if p is the rounded product of a and b, then fma(a, b, -p) gives the exact rounding error of that product, a building block for extended-precision arithmetic. Peak floating-point performance figures conventionally count each FMA as two operations.

Because FMA rounds differently, enabling it can change the last bits of results compared with separate multiply and add. Compilers may contract a * b + c into an FMA automatically, depending on language rules and flags (in GCC and Clang, -ffp-contract controls this), so the same source can give slightly different answers on different targets or optimization levels. FMA can also break expected symmetries: computing a * a - b * b as fma(a, a, -(b * b)) when a equals b returns the rounding error of b * b rather than exactly zero.

about.h: FMA vs. a multiply-accumulate in integers
about.p: Integer multiply-accumulate instructions also compute a × b + c, but integer arithmetic has no rounding, so fusing them only saves time and registers. The accuracy argument is specific to floating point. In digital signal processors and AI accelerators, wide accumulators play a similar role: products of narrow values are summed in a wider register so precision is not lost at every step, and only the final total is rounded or scaled down.

faq.q: Why do my floating-point results change when FMA is enabled?
faq.a: FMA rounds a × b + c once instead of twice, so its result can differ in the last bits from separate multiply and add. The FMA result is usually the more accurate one, but it is not bit-identical.

faq.q: Is an FMA counted as one or two FLOPs?
faq.a: Conventionally two, one multiply and one add, which is why peak throughput figures for hardware with FMA units are twice the number of FMA instructions per second.

faq.q: What does the fma function do in C?
faq.a: fma(x, y, z) from math.h returns x × y + z computed as if with infinite precision and rounded once to the result type. On hardware without an FMA instruction it is emulated in software and can be slow.

bfloat16.desc: A 16-bit floating-point format with 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 significand bits. Sharing FP32's exponent width gives it a wide range, so despite low precision it is used for AI training. FP16, with 5 exponent and 10 significand bits, is more precise but has a narrow range.

about.p: bfloat16 (brain floating point) is simply the upper 16 bits of an FP32 number: the same sign bit and 8-bit exponent, with the significand cut from 23 bits to 7. Converting from bfloat16 to FP32 is exact, done by appending 16 zero bits, and converting the other way only requires rounding off the low 16 bits. The range matches FP32, roughly 1e-38 to 3e38 for normal numbers, but with 8 significant bits including the hidden bit, values carry only about two to three decimal digits; the spacing just above 1.0 is 2 to the power -7, about 0.0078.

FP16 spends its bits the other way, with a 5-bit exponent and a 10-bit significand. It is more precise, about three decimal digits, but its largest value is 65504 and its smallest normal value is about 6e-5. In training, small gradients can underflow to zero in FP16, so FP16 training usually needs loss scaling, multiplying the loss by a large factor and later dividing the gradients back. bfloat16's FP32-sized range generally makes that unnecessary and makes conversion from existing FP32 models straightforward, which is why it is popular for training.

about.h: Why master weights stay in FP32
about.p: Low precision fails when tiny updates are added to large values. With a weight of 1.0 stored in bfloat16, the next representable value is 1.0078125, so an update of 0.001 is less than half a step and the sum rounds back to exactly 1.0: the update is absorbed. Mixed-precision training therefore keeps master weights and optimizer state in FP32 and uses bfloat16 copies for the forward and backward passes. Matrix units likewise typically multiply bfloat16 inputs but accumulate the products in FP32, so long sums do not lose their small contributions.

bfloat16 is supported by the matrix units of many current GPUs and AI accelerators, and by vector extensions on some CPUs, for both training and inference. Halving the size of each value relative to FP32 halves memory capacity and bandwidth needs and allows more multipliers per unit of chip area. It is not a good general-purpose format, though: with so few significand bits, sums of many values, small differences and anything needing more than a few digits of accuracy must be done in a wider type.

faq.q: Is bfloat16 the same as FP16?
faq.a: No. Both are 16 bits, but bfloat16 has an 8-bit exponent and 7-bit significand, while FP16 has a 5-bit exponent and 10-bit significand. bfloat16 trades precision for FP32's range.

faq.q: How do you convert FP32 to bfloat16?
faq.a: Keep the top 16 bits of the FP32 bit pattern, ideally rounding to nearest even based on the discarded 16 bits rather than just truncating. Converting back is exact: append 16 zero bits.

faq.q: Why does bfloat16 training usually not need loss scaling?
faq.a: Loss scaling exists to keep small gradients from underflowing in FP16's narrow range. bfloat16 has the same exponent range as FP32, so such gradients normally remain representable.

FP8.desc: 8-bit floating-point formats: E4M3 (4 exponent, 3 significand bits) and E5M2 (5 exponent, 2 significand bits), chosen to trade precision against range. Used to make AI training and inference faster and more power-efficient.

about.p: Both FP8 formats have a sign bit; they differ in how the other seven bits are split. E4M3 has a 4-bit exponent and 3-bit significand; in the widely used definition it gives up infinities and keeps only one NaN pattern per sign in order to extend its largest finite value to 448. E5M2 has a 5-bit exponent and 2-bit significand and follows IEEE 754 conventions with infinities and NaNs, reaching about 57344. With 3 significand bits, adjacent E4M3 values within a binade differ by 12.5 percent of the binade's lower bound; with 2 bits, E5M2 steps are 25 percent.

Weights and activations in a trained network usually have a fairly predictable spread of magnitudes, so the extra precision of E4M3 is worth more than range. Gradients during backpropagation can vary over many orders of magnitude between layers and steps, so E5M2's extra exponent bit matters more there. A common recipe is therefore E4M3 for the forward pass and E5M2 for gradients, though some systems use E4M3 throughout. Either way, only the matrix multiply inputs are FP8; master weights, optimizer state and many sensitive operations remain in higher precision.

Eight bits cannot cover the values of a real tensor without help. Before casting, software multiplies each tensor, or each block of a tensor, by a scale factor chosen from its recently observed maximum absolute value, so that the largest elements land near the top of the FP8 range and small ones are not flushed to zero. The scale is stored in higher precision and divided out after the matrix multiply. Matrix units multiply the FP8 inputs but accumulate products in a wider format, such as FP16 or FP32, so long dot products do not lose precision step by step.

INT8 quantization spaces its 256 values uniformly, which suits tensors with a bounded, even distribution but wastes resolution when a few outliers set the scale. FP8 values are spaced roughly logarithmically, with fine steps near zero and coarse steps for large magnitudes, which better matches the bell-shaped distributions with long tails common in neural networks and often reduces calibration effort. Both halve memory and bandwidth relative to 16-bit formats and allow more multiply-accumulate units per area and watt. Which is more accurate depends on the model.

faq.q: What is the difference between E4M3 and E5M2?
faq.a: E4M3 uses 4 exponent bits and 3 significand bits, giving more precision but a smaller range, with a maximum of 448. E5M2 uses 5 exponent bits and 2 significand bits, giving a much wider range but coarser steps.

faq.q: Why does FP8 training need scaling factors?
faq.a: FP8's representable range is so narrow that unscaled tensors would overflow or underflow. A per-tensor or per-block scale shifts the values into the usable range before conversion and is removed after the computation.

faq.q: Is FP8 better than INT8 for inference?
faq.a: Not universally. FP8 handles wide, outlier-prone value distributions with less calibration, while INT8 is widely supported and accurate for many models when quantized carefully.

INT8.desc: An 8-bit signed integer (−128 to 127). In AI inference, quantizing weights and activations to INT8 with a scale factor greatly cuts computation and memory and allows fast processing on small integer circuits.

about.h: How real values are mapped to 8-bit integers
about.p: INT8 is an 8-bit two's-complement integer from -128 to 127. To use it for a neural network, each tensor gets a scale factor so that real value is approximately scale times the integer, sometimes after subtracting a zero point. Symmetric quantization fixes the zero point at 0 and usually uses -127 to 127 so the range is balanced; the scale is the maximum absolute value divided by 127. For data spanning -6.35 to 6.35 the scale is 0.05, so 1.0 maps to 20. Asymmetric quantization adds a zero point, which suits activations that are always non-negative after ReLU.

Compared with FP32, INT8 cuts weight storage and memory traffic to one quarter, which matters most when inference is limited by memory bandwidth. The arithmetic is also cheaper: multiplier area grows roughly with the square of operand width, and an 8-bit integer multiplier has no exponent handling or normalization, so it is far smaller and more energy-efficient than an FP32 unit. A product of two INT8 values fits in 16 bits, and long dot products are accumulated in 32-bit integers to avoid overflow. The 32-bit result is then rescaled, or requantized, back to INT8 for the next layer.

Only 256 levels are available, so rounding and clipping errors are unavoidable. Weights are fixed after training, so their scales can be chosen directly, often per output channel to fit each channel's range. Activations depend on the input, so post-training quantization runs a few hundred representative samples through the model to observe each layer's range, a step called calibration. Matching the absolute maximum lets rare outliers waste resolution, so the range is often clipped to cover most of the distribution. If accuracy still drops too much, quantization-aware training simulates rounding during training so the network learns to tolerate it.

INT8 has uniformly spaced levels, so its precision is the same everywhere in its range, which works well for weights and activations with modest dynamic range. Floating-point formats such as FP16, BF16 and FP8 spend bits on an exponent, giving wider dynamic range with spacing that grows with magnitude. Many accelerators support several of these formats, and performance figures quoted in TOPS are usually given at INT8 or lower. Even narrower integers, such as INT4, are used mainly for weights when memory capacity is the main constraint, at the price of more quantization error.

faq.q: What is the range of INT8?
faq.a: A signed 8-bit integer covers -128 to 127. Symmetric quantization schemes often restrict themselves to -127 to 127 so that positive and negative ranges are equal and zero maps exactly to 0.

faq.q: Why are INT8 products accumulated in 32-bit integers?
faq.a: Each INT8 by INT8 product needs up to 16 bits, and a dot product adds hundreds or thousands of them, which would overflow a narrow accumulator. A 32-bit accumulator keeps the sum exact before it is rescaled back to INT8.

faq.q: How much accuracy is lost by quantizing a model to INT8?
faq.a: It depends on the model and how carefully scales are chosen. With good calibration and per-channel weight scales the loss is often small, and quantization-aware training can recover more when post-training quantization is not good enough.

桁上げ先見加算器.desc: An adder that computes carries in parallel from each bit's generate signal g = a·b and propagate signal p = a ⊕ b, without waiting for carries to ripple. Delay stays small even for wide operands.
桁上げ先見加算器.title: Carry-Lookahead Adder: Generate, Propagate and Delay
桁上げ先見加算器.description: A carry-lookahead adder computes carries in parallel from generate (g = a·b) and propagate (p = a⊕b) signals. Why ripple carry is slow, and wide adders.

about.p: For each bit with inputs a and b, the generate signal g = a·b is 1 when the bit produces a carry regardless of the carry coming in, and the propagate signal p = a ⊕ b is 1 when an incoming carry will pass through. The carry out is c(i+1) = g(i) + p(i)·c(i), and the sum is s(i) = p(i) ⊕ c(i). Expanding the recurrence gives c1 = g0 + p0·c0 and c2 = g1 + p1·g0 + p1·p0·c0, so every carry can be written in two-level logic using only the g and p signals and the input carry c0.

In a ripple-carry adder, each full adder must wait for the carry from the bit below. In the worst case, such as adding 1 to a word of all ones, the carry travels through every bit, so delay grows linearly with width; a 64-bit ripple-carry adder is far too slow for a processor clocked at gigahertz rates. A carry-lookahead adder (CLA) computes the carries directly from the inputs in parallel, and with hierarchical lookahead its delay grows only with the logarithm of the width.

Fully expanded carry equations quickly need gates with too many inputs, so practical designs use blocks of about 4 bits. Each block produces a group generate, G = g3 + p3·g2 + p3·p2·g1 + p3·p2·p1·g0, and a group propagate, P = p3·p2·p1·p0. A second-level lookahead unit treats these exactly like single-bit g and p signals to compute the carries into each block, and a third level extends the scheme to 64 bits. Parallel prefix adders such as Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung generalize the same idea, trading wiring and area for logic depth.

Fast adders sit in ALUs, address generators and floating-point units, and in the last stage of multipliers. A multiplier first reduces its many partial products with carry-save adders, which are independent full adders that turn three numbers into two with only one full-adder delay and no carry propagation. Only the final two numbers need a carry-propagating addition, which is done once by a carry-lookahead or prefix adder. Other compromises, such as carry-select and carry-skip adders, sit between ripple-carry and full lookahead in speed and area.

faq.q: Why is a carry-lookahead adder faster than a ripple-carry adder?
faq.a: A ripple-carry adder waits for the carry to pass through every bit in turn, so delay grows linearly with width. A carry-lookahead adder computes all carries in parallel from generate and propagate signals, so delay grows roughly with the logarithm of the width.

faq.q: Can the propagate signal use OR instead of XOR?
faq.a: Yes, for the carry chain: p = a + b gives the same carries because when both inputs are 1 the generate term already produces the carry. The sum bit still needs a ⊕ b, so many designs compute XOR for p and use it for both.

faq.q: What is group generate and group propagate?
faq.a: They summarize a block of bits: group generate is 1 if the block produces a carry out by itself, and group propagate is 1 if a carry entering the block will pass all the way through. Higher lookahead levels use them to compute block carries quickly.

桁上げ保存加算器.desc: An adder that reduces three numbers to two, a sum and a carry, without propagating carries. Made of independent full adders per bit, its delay is constant, so multipliers use it to add many partial products.
桁上げ保存加算器.title: Carry-Save Adder (CSA): How It Speeds Up Multipliers
桁上げ保存加算器.description: A carry-save adder reduces three numbers to two without propagating carries, so its delay does not grow with width. How it works and why multipliers use it.

about.p: A carry-save adder (CSA) is simply full adders placed independently, one per bit. Feeding the same bit position of three numbers A, B and C into each full adder, and collecting the sum bits into a number S and the carry bits, shifted one place left, into a number Cy, gives A + B + C = S + Cy. For example, with the 4-bit numbers 5 (0101), 6 (0110) and 7 (0111), S = 0100 (4) and Cy = 1110 (14), and 4 + 14 = 18 = 5 + 6 + 7. Because no carry passes to the neighboring bit, the delay is a constant one full adder regardless of width.

about.h: How it differs from a ripple-carry adder
about.p: In an ordinary ripple-carry adder, each bit's result waits for the carry from the bit below, so in the worst case a carry travels from the least to the most significant bit and delay is proportional to width. Even sped up with a carry-lookahead adder, delay still grows roughly with the logarithm of the width. A carry-save adder simply saves the carries and passes them to the next stage, so no matter how many numbers are added, the intermediate additions never wait for carry propagation. The price is a redundant result split into two numbers, sum and carry, which must finally be added once by an ordinary adder to give a single number.

An n-bit multiplication produces n partial products, and adding them one after another is slow. Instead, carry-save adders are arranged in a tree, reducing three numbers to two in parallel at each level. Each level cuts the count to about two-thirds, so the number of levels needed to reach two is roughly logarithmic in the width. This is the Wallace tree; the Dadda tree reduces hardware by using full adders more economically. 4:2 compressors, which reduce four numbers to two, are also common. A fast adder such as a carry-lookahead adder then sums the final two numbers to complete the product. Combining this with Booth's algorithm to reduce the number of partial products is also common.

The carry-save form works for any process that keeps adding many numbers. A multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit may keep its accumulator in sum-and-carry form to avoid carry propagation every cycle. Large-integer Montgomery multiplication in cryptography, and division and square-root computation, also gain speed by holding intermediate values in redundant form. In redundant form, though, magnitude, sign and overflow cannot be determined immediately, and registers holding the value need roughly twice as many bits. So when such a decision is needed, the value is converted back into a single number with an ordinary adder.

faq.q: What is a carry-save adder?
faq.a: It is an adder that reduces three numbers to two, a sum and a carry, without propagating carries. Made simply of full adders per bit, its delay is constant, so multipliers use it to add many partial products.

faq.q: What is the difference between a carry-save adder and a ripple-carry adder?
faq.a: A ripple-carry adder adds two numbers to give one result, but carries pass from low to high bits in sequence, so delay is proportional to width. A carry-save adder only reduces three numbers to two and does not propagate carries, so its delay is constant regardless of width.

faq.q: Why can't a carry-save adder finish an addition on its own?
faq.a: Because its output is split into two numbers, a sum and a carry. To use the result as a single value, the two must finally be added by an ordinary adder that propagates carries. Even when many numbers are added, this final addition is needed only once.

ウォレスツリー.desc: A multiplier structure that reduces many partial products in parallel with a tree of carry-save adders. Its depth grows only logarithmically with width, so it is used in fast multipliers; a final adder sums the last two numbers.

ブースのアルゴリズム.desc: A multiplication method that recodes the multiplier's bits, for example in pairs, into signed digits to reduce the number of partial products. Radix-4 Booth encoding roughly halves them.

飽和演算.desc: Arithmetic that clamps results exceeding the representable range to the maximum or minimum instead of wrapping around. Used in audio and image signal processing to avoid large errors.

算術シフト.desc: A right shift of a signed integer that copies the sign bit into the vacated high bits. Shifting a negative number right by one divides by 2, rounding toward negative infinity. Filling with zeros is a logical shift.
算術シフト.title: Arithmetic Shift vs. Logical Shift: Sign Extension Explained
算術シフト.description: An arithmetic right shift copies the sign bit, so it divides a negative number by 2 rounding toward negative infinity. How it differs from a logical shift.

about.h: How an arithmetic right shift works
about.p: An arithmetic right shift moves the bits of a two's-complement signed integer to the right and copies the original most significant bit (the sign bit) into the vacated high bits. Positive numbers get 0s and negative numbers get 1s, so the sign is preserved. For example, shifting 8-bit −8 (1111 1000) right by one gives 1111 1100, which is −4. An n-bit arithmetic right shift equals the original value divided by 2 to the n, rounded downward (toward negative infinity). A logical right shift, which inserts 0s at the top, is meant for unsigned integers; applied to a negative number it produces a large positive one.

Because an arithmetic right shift rounds toward negative infinity, it can give a different result from division that truncates toward zero when the value is negative. In C (since C99), −7 / 2 is −3, but arithmetic-shifting −7 (1111 1001) right by one gives 1111 1100, which is −4. So when a compiler replaces division of a signed integer by 2 to the n with a shift, it adds correction instructions, such as first adding 2 to the n minus 1 when the value is negative and then shifting. For unsigned integers or values known to be non-negative, the shift can replace the division without correction.

For left shifts, both arithmetic and logical shifts insert 0s at the bottom, so the bits move the same way; that is why x86's SAL and SHL instructions behave identically. The value is multiplied by 2 to the n, but for signed integers, if the bits shifted out or the new top bit differ from the original sign, overflow occurs and the sign changes. For example, shifting 8-bit 64 (0100 0000) left by one gives 1000 0000, which is −128. Note that in C, left-shifting a negative value, or left-shifting a signed integer so the result does not fit the type, is undefined behavior.

Most instruction sets provide arithmetic and logical right shifts as separate instructions: SRA/SRAI and SRL/SRLI in RISC-V, ASR and LSR in Arm, and SAR and SHR in x86. Among programming languages, Java distinguishes >> as the arithmetic right shift and >>> as the logical one. In hardware, a barrel shifter supports both simply by switching whether the bits fed in at the top are the sign bit or 0. Fixed-point DSP code uses arithmetic right shifts to scale values down, but because the rounding is biased toward negative values, 2 to the (n−1) is sometimes added first to approximate round-to-nearest.

faq.q: What is the difference between an arithmetic shift and a logical shift?
faq.a: In a right shift, an arithmetic shift copies the sign bit into the vacated high bits, while a logical shift inserts 0s. Arithmetic shifts are used for signed integers, logical shifts for unsigned integers and bit manipulation. In a left shift, both insert 0s at the bottom, so the bits move the same way.

faq.q: Is an arithmetic right shift the same as dividing by 2?
faq.a: For positive numbers yes, but for negative numbers it can differ. An arithmetic right shift rounds toward negative infinity, so −7 becomes −4, whereas C's division, which truncates toward zero, gives −3.

faq.q: Is C's >> an arithmetic shift?
faq.a: For unsigned integers and non-negative signed integers, the result is defined to equal division by a power of two. Right-shifting a negative signed integer is implementation-defined; most compilers use an arithmetic shift, but portable code is safer not relying on it.

ロード・ストア・アーキテクチャ.desc: An ISA style in which only load and store instructions access memory and arithmetic works only on registers. Used by RISC-V and Arm, it gives instructions a uniform shape that is easy to pipeline.
ロード・ストア・アーキテクチャ.title: Load-Store Architecture: Definition and Why RISC Uses It
ロード・ストア・アーキテクチャ.description: In a load-store ISA only loads and stores touch memory; arithmetic works on registers. Why RISC-V and Arm use it, and how it compares with register-memory ISAs.

about.p: In a load-store architecture, only load and store instructions can read or write memory, and operations such as add and compare work between registers. For example, adding variables b and c in memory and writing the result to a takes four instructions in RISC-V: lw to load b and c into registers, add to sum them, and sw to store the result to a. By contrast, designs such as x86, where an arithmetic instruction like "add eax, [mem]" can read memory directly, are called register-memory architectures, the opposite approach.

Because arithmetic instructions never touch memory, every instruction accesses memory at most once, and instruction formats and processing flow are uniform. In the classic five-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write-back), only loads and stores use the memory-access stage; other instructions pass straight through it. Memory-related exceptions such as translation failures and page faults can arise only from loads and stores, which simplifies exception handling. Fixed-length instructions are also easier to adopt, making decoding simple.

Because values are placed in registers before being operated on, load-store ISAs generally have many general-purpose registers: RISC-V has 32 integer registers and Arm's 64-bit instruction set (AArch64) has 31 general-purpose registers. Compilers allocate frequently used values to registers to reduce loads and stores. On the other hand, instruction counts rise and code tends to grow, so there are short instruction formats to improve code density, such as RISC-V's C extension (compressed instructions) and Arm's Thumb.

about.h: Relation to CISC and exceptional instructions
about.p: Load-store design is a hallmark of RISC, adopted by RISC-V, Arm, MIPS, Power and others. Even register-memory x86 CPUs today internally split arithmetic instructions that read memory into load and compute micro-operations, so at the execution level they look much like a load-store machine. Load-store ISAs do, however, include atomic instructions that read a memory value, operate on it and write it back (such as the AMO instructions of RISC-V's A extension), provided as an exception for multicore synchronization.

faq.q: What is a load-store architecture?
faq.a: It is an instruction-set style in which only load and store instructions access memory and all arithmetic is done between registers. RISC-V and Arm are leading examples, and the uniform instruction shape makes pipelining easier.

faq.q: Does load-store architecture mean the same as RISC?
faq.a: No. Load-store describes how memory is accessed, while RISC is a broader design philosophy that also includes simple instructions, fixed-length encoding and more. Because many RISC designs adopt the load-store approach, however, the two are often discussed together.

faq.q: Is x86 a load-store architecture?
faq.a: Not as an instruction set: it is a register-memory architecture in which arithmetic instructions can read and write memory directly. Today's x86 CPUs, however, internally split such instructions into load, compute and store micro-operations.

アドレッシングモード.desc: The way an instruction specifies the address of data or a jump target. Examples include immediate, register, base register plus offset and PC-relative.

PC相対アドレッシング.desc: Specifying a branch target or data address as a distance from the current instruction's address (PC). The distance is unchanged wherever the program is loaded, so it underpins position-independent code.

about.p: The instruction holds a signed offset, and the hardware adds it, after sign extension, to a reference address derived from the program counter (PC). In RISC-V the reference is the address of the branch itself. Conditional branches encode a 13-bit even offset, reaching about ±4 KiB, and jal encodes a 21-bit offset, about ±1 MiB. For anything farther, auipc adds a 20-bit upper immediate shifted left by 12 to the PC, and a following jalr, addi or load supplies the low 12 bits, together reaching about ±2 GiB. Other ISAs use different reference points, such as the address of the next instruction on x86.

Position-independent code (PIC) must run correctly at whatever address it is loaded. With absolute addresses, the loader would have to patch every instruction that names an address, which takes time, makes each process's copy of the code different and prevents sharing the same physical pages among processes. PC-relative offsets between parts of the same image do not change when the whole image moves, so no patching is needed. Shared libraries and executables loaded at randomized addresses for security (address space layout randomization) depend on this.

PC-relative addressing is equally important for data. x86-64 introduced RIP-relative addressing so that loads and stores can name global variables relative to the instruction pointer, something 32-bit x86 lacked, forcing PIC on that architecture to obtain the PC with a call trick and dedicate a register to it. For symbols whose final address is only known at run time, such as variables in another shared library, the code uses a PC-relative load from the global offset table (GOT), a table of addresses that the dynamic linker fills in once at load time.

Absolute addressing names a fixed address and must be relocated if the code moves. Register-indirect addressing jumps or loads through an address held in a register, which is how function pointers, virtual calls and returns work, since their targets are not known when the code is assembled. PC-relative addressing covers the large middle ground of targets that are fixed relative to the code: loop branches, calls within a program and accesses to its own constants and globals. Its limitation is the offset field's width, which is why long-range sequences such as auipc plus jalr exist.

faq.q: What is the range of a RISC-V branch instruction?
faq.a: Conditional branches such as beq have a 13-bit signed offset in multiples of 2 bytes, about ±4 KiB from the branch. jal reaches about ±1 MiB, and auipc combined with jalr reaches about ±2 GiB.

faq.q: Why does x86-64 use RIP-relative addressing?
faq.a: It lets code access global data relative to the current instruction, so position-independent code needs no load-time patching and no dedicated base register. 32-bit x86 had no such mode for data.

faq.q: Is PC-relative addressing required for shared libraries?
faq.a: In practice yes. Shared libraries are loaded at different addresses in different processes, and PC-relative branches and data references, plus indirection through tables like the GOT, let the same code pages work everywhere.

即値.desc: A constant embedded directly in an instruction. In RISC-V addi it is a 12-bit signed integer that is sign-extended before use.

符号拡張.desc: Widening a signed integer to more bits by copying its top (sign) bit into all the new upper bits, which preserves its value. Filling the upper bits with zeros is zero extension.

about.h: Why copying the sign bit preserves the value
about.p: In n-bit two's complement, the top bit carries a weight of minus 2 to the power n-1 and the others carry their usual positive weights. Extending a negative number by one bit adds a new top bit worth minus 2 to the power n and turns the old top bit into a positive 2 to the power n-1; together they still contribute minus 2 to the power n-1, so the value is unchanged. Repeating this for every added bit justifies the rule. For example, 4-bit 1010 (-6) becomes 8-bit 11111010, still -6.

Immediates are the most common case: RISC-V's 12-bit I-type immediate is sign-extended, so addi accepts -2048 to 2047 and negative constants work without a separate subtract instruction. Loads come in pairs, lb and lh sign-extend while lbu and lhu zero-extend. On RV64, lw sign-extends a 32-bit value to 64 bits and lwu zero-extends it, and word instructions such as addw sign-extend their 32-bit results. x86 provides movsx and movzx for the same purpose. In hardware, sign extension costs nothing more than wiring the top bit to all the new positions.

about.h: A classic pitfall: lui plus addi
about.p: To build a 32-bit constant, RISC-V code uses lui for the upper 20 bits and addi for the lower 12. Because addi sign-extends its immediate, a low part of 0x800 or more is treated as a negative number, its value minus 4096. Assemblers compensate by adding 1 to the upper part whenever bit 11 of the constant is set, and the %hi and %lo relocation operators do this automatically. Hand-written code that splits the constant naively produces a value that is off by exactly 4096, a bug that is easy to miss in testing.

about.h: Sign vs. zero extension in C
about.p: C chooses the extension from the source type: converting a signed char or int16_t to int sign-extends, while converting an unsigned type zero-extends. Plain char is signed on some platforms and unsigned on others, for example signed on x86 but unsigned on most Arm Linux systems, so a byte value of 0xFF may become -1 or 255 depending on the target. That difference causes bugs when bytes are compared with constants or used as array indices. Using unsigned char or uint8_t for raw bytes avoids the ambiguity.

faq.q: What is the difference between sign extension and zero extension?
faq.a: Sign extension fills the new upper bits with copies of the original top bit, preserving the value of a signed number. Zero extension fills them with zeros, preserving the value of an unsigned number.

faq.q: Why does RISC-V addi sign-extend its immediate?
faq.a: So that a single instruction can add negative constants, such as addi sp, sp, -16. The 12-bit field then covers -2048 to 2047 rather than only non-negative values.

faq.q: How do I sign-extend a value in C?
faq.a: Store it in a signed type of the original width, such as int8_t or int16_t, and assign it to a wider signed type; the conversion sign-extends automatically and compilers emit the matching sign-extending instruction.

疑似命令.desc: Something written like an instruction in assembly that the assembler replaces with one or more real instructions, such as RISC-V nop, mv, li, j and ret.
疑似命令.title: Pseudo-Instructions in Assembly (RISC-V li, mv, ret)
疑似命令.description: A pseudo-instruction is expanded by the assembler into real instructions, like RISC-V nop, mv, li and ret. How they work and how they differ from directives.

about.p: A pseudo-instruction is assembly syntax with no encoding of its own; the assembler replaces it with one or more real instructions. In RISC-V, nop becomes addi x0, x0, 0, mv rd, rs becomes addi rd, rs, 0, j label becomes jal x0, label, ret becomes jalr x0, 0(ra), and bnez rs, label becomes bne rs, x0, label. Many rely on register x0, which always reads as zero and discards writes. Disassemblers usually print the pseudo form back, which makes listings easier to read.
