Some pseudo-instructions expand to a variable number of real instructions. li (load immediate) becomes a single addi when the constant fits in a 12-bit signed immediate but lui followed by addi for a larger 32-bit value, and longer sequences for 64-bit constants. la (load address) and call for a distant function use auipc plus a second instruction to form a PC-relative address. Hand-computed code sizes and offsets must account for this.

Defining nop, mv or a plain jump as separate hardware instructions would add opcodes and decoder logic without adding capability, since existing instructions with x0 already do the job. Pseudo-instructions keep the hardware instruction set small, a core RISC-V design goal, while giving programmers readable names for common idioms such as returning from a function or comparing against zero.

Assembler directives such as .text, .globl or .word are instructions to the assembler itself: they choose sections, export symbols or emit data, and do not correspond to machine instructions. A pseudo-instruction always turns into real instructions with a fixed meaning defined by the toolchain. Macros are similar expansions but defined by the programmer. Toolchains may also shorten some expansions later, for example turning an auipc-plus-jalr call into a single jal at link time when the target is close enough.

faq.q: What is the difference between a pseudo-instruction and a real instruction?
faq.a: A real instruction has its own machine encoding that the CPU executes. A pseudo-instruction is only assembler syntax that is translated into one or more real instructions before execution.

faq.q: What does li expand to in RISC-V?
faq.a: For a small constant that fits in 12 signed bits, a single addi from x0; for larger 32-bit values, lui followed by addi, and longer sequences for 64-bit constants.

faq.q: Is nop a real instruction in RISC-V?
faq.a: No. nop is a pseudo-instruction encoded as addi x0, x0, 0, which changes nothing because writes to x0 are discarded.

アセンブラ.desc: Software that converts a program written in assembly language into machine instruction bit patterns. It turns labels into addresses and expands pseudo-instructions into real instructions.

about.p: An assembler reads assembly source line by line. For each instruction it looks up the mnemonic, checks the operands, and packs the opcode, register numbers and immediate values into the fixed fields of the instruction format, for example a 32-bit RISC-V word. Directives such as .text, .data, .word and .globl tell it which section to emit into, which data to lay down and which symbols to export. Because assembly maps almost one-to-one onto machine instructions, every instruction set architecture (ISA) has its own assembly language.

Labels let programmers write branch targets and data names instead of numeric addresses. A label may be used before it is defined, so a classic assembler makes two passes: the first walks the source assigning an address to every label and building a symbol table, and the second encodes each instruction using those addresses. Distances to labels in the same section are filled in directly. References to symbols in other files, or to addresses that depend on final placement, cannot be resolved yet, so the assembler leaves a placeholder and records a relocation entry for the linker in the output object file.

Assemblers accept convenient pseudo-instructions that do not exist in hardware. In RISC-V, nop becomes addi x0, x0, 0, mv rd, rs becomes addi rd, rs, 0, j label becomes jal x0, label, and ret becomes jalr x0, 0(ra). li loads any constant: small values need one addi, while a full 32-bit value becomes lui for the upper 20 bits plus addi for the lower 12, with the upper part adjusted by one when the lower part is negative because addi sign-extends its immediate. Assemblers may also rewrite a conditional branch whose target lies beyond its roughly 4 KiB reach into an inverted branch skipping over a jal.

about.h: Assembler versus compiler, linker and disassembler
about.p: A compiler translates a high-level language, where one statement can become many instructions and the mapping involves real decisions about registers and optimization. An assembler makes almost no such choices; its job is encoding, label resolution and pseudo-instruction expansion. Its output is an object file, not a runnable program: the linker still has to combine object files and libraries and fix final addresses. A disassembler performs the reverse translation from bit patterns back to mnemonics, but it cannot recover comments or, without a symbol table, the original label names.

faq.q: What is the difference between an assembler and a compiler?
faq.a: A compiler translates a high-level language such as C into assembly or machine code, making decisions about register use and optimization. An assembler translates assembly language almost one-to-one into machine code, mainly encoding instructions and turning labels into addresses.

faq.q: What is a pseudo-instruction in assembly language?
faq.a: It is a convenient mnemonic that the hardware does not implement directly; the assembler replaces it with one or more real instructions. In RISC-V, for example, nop is assembled as addi x0, x0, 0 and li may become lui followed by addi.

faq.q: Does the assembler produce an executable file?
faq.a: Usually not. It produces an object file with machine code, a symbol table and relocation entries, and the linker turns one or more object files into an executable.

呼び出し規約.desc: The agreement on how arguments and return values are passed in registers or on the stack, and who saves which registers, when calling a function. It is a key part of the ABI.

about.p: A calling convention fixes the low-level details of a function call: which registers carry the arguments, where the return value is placed, how the return address is saved, which registers a called function may overwrite, and how the stack frame is laid out and aligned. The caller and the callee are often compiled separately, perhaps by different compilers or hand-written in assembly, so neither can see how the other was built. As long as both obey the same convention, a C function can call a library routine or an assembly function and the values arrive where expected.

RISC-V has 32 integer registers, x0 to x31, and the convention gives them role names. Up to eight integer arguments travel in a0 to a7 (x10 to x17); a ninth or tenth argument goes on the stack at a fixed offset from sp. The result returns in a0, or in a0 and a1 for a 64-bit value on RV32. Floating-point arguments use fa0 to fa7. A call is jal ra, func, which writes the return address into ra (x1). The stack pointer must be a multiple of 16 bytes on entry, so frames are allocated in 16-byte steps.

Registers are split into two groups. Caller-saved temporaries, t0 to t6 in RISC-V along with the argument registers, may be overwritten freely by any callee, so a caller that still needs such a value after the call must save it first. Callee-saved registers, s0 to s11, must look unchanged when the call returns, so a function that wants to use one saves it in its prologue and restores it in its epilogue. The split lets short leaf functions run on temporaries with no saving at all, while long-lived values such as loop counters live safely in s registers.

about.h: Calling convention vs. ABI and API
about.p: The calling convention is one part of the application binary interface (ABI), which also fixes the sizes and alignment of data types, struct layout and how system calls are made. An API, by contrast, describes how functions are used at the source level. Two builds can share an API yet be incompatible at the binary level because their ABIs differ, so a library must then be recompiled. Different platforms define different conventions for the same ISA family: on x86-64, Linux passes the first six integer arguments in registers, while Windows uses four.

faq.q: What is a calling convention?
faq.a: It is the agreement on how a function call passes arguments and return values, saves the return address and divides register-saving duties between caller and callee. It lets separately compiled code, including libraries and assembly routines, call each other correctly.

faq.q: What is the difference between caller-saved and callee-saved registers?
faq.a: A caller-saved register may be overwritten by the called function, so the caller must save it if it needs the value afterward. A callee-saved register must be preserved by the called function, which saves and restores it if it uses it.

faq.q: Where are function arguments passed in RISC-V?
faq.a: The first eight integer arguments go in registers a0 to a7 and any further arguments go on the stack. The return value comes back in a0, or a0 and a1 for a value twice the register width.

スタックフレーム.desc: The area reserved on the stack each time a function is called. It holds the return address, saved registers and local variables and is freed when the function returns.

about.p: A frame is the slice of stack a single function call owns. Depending on the function it contains the return address, the old values of callee-saved registers the function intends to use, local variables that do not fit in registers or whose address is taken, spill slots for temporaries, and arguments beyond those passed in registers; An optional frame pointer register, s0 in RISC-V, can mark a fixed reference point in the frame. Because every call gets a fresh frame, each recursive invocation has its own independent copy of the locals.

By the usual convention the stack grows toward lower addresses, so a function allocates its frame by subtracting from the stack pointer. A typical RISC-V prologue is addi sp, sp, -16 followed by sw ra, 12(sp) and sw s0, 8(sp). The matching epilogue reloads s0 and ra, executes addi sp, sp, 16 and returns with ret. The standard RISC-V calling convention keeps sp aligned to 16 bytes, which is why small frames are rounded up to 16. Allocation and release cost only an add, which is why stack storage is far cheaper than heap allocation.

In RISC-V, a call made with jal writes the return address into register ra, so a function that calls others must save ra in its frame before the first call. A leaf function, which calls nothing, never overwrites ra and can return without saving it; if it also uses only caller-saved registers and keeps its locals in registers, it needs no frame at all. On x86 the situation differs: the call instruction always pushes the return address onto the stack, so every call touches memory. Tail-call optimization turns a final call into a jump that reuses the current frame, so deep tail recursion does not grow the stack.

about.h: Stack frames versus the heap, and common bugs
about.p: Frame contents live only until the function returns, while heap objects persist until freed. Returning a pointer to a local variable is therefore a bug: the memory belongs to whatever frame is pushed next. Unbounded or very deep recursion exhausts the stack, whose size per thread is fixed and commonly a few megabytes or less, causing a stack overflow. Writing past the end of a local array can overwrite the saved return address, a classic security vulnerability; compilers counter it with stack canaries, guard values checked in the epilogue before returning.

faq.q: What is the difference between the stack pointer and the frame pointer?
faq.a: The stack pointer marks the current top of the stack and may move during a function. The frame pointer, when used, holds a fixed address inside the current frame so locals and saved registers can be found at constant offsets, which also helps debuggers walk the call chain.

faq.q: Why does deep recursion cause a stack overflow?
faq.a: Each recursive call allocates a new stack frame, and the stack has a fixed maximum size. If the recursion is deep enough, the frames exceed that space; tail-call optimization or rewriting the recursion as a loop avoids the growth.

faq.q: Why should a function not return a pointer to a local variable?
faq.a: The local lives in the function's stack frame, which is released on return and reused by later calls. The pointer then refers to memory whose contents can change at any time.

スタックポインタ.desc: The register that points to the current top of the stack; sp (x2) in RISC-V. In many ISAs the stack grows toward lower addresses.

about.p: The stack is a last-in, first-out region of memory used for function calls, and the stack pointer is the register holding the address of its current top. In RISC-V it is register x2, named sp; on x86-64 it is RSP. In most ABIs the stack grows toward lower addresses, so allocating space means subtracting from the stack pointer and freeing it means adding back. x86 has dedicated push and pop instructions that adjust RSP automatically, while RISC-V uses ordinary instructions, such as addi sp, sp, -16 followed by stores at offsets from sp.

When a function is entered, its prologue moves the stack pointer down to reserve a stack frame. The frame holds the return address if the function makes further calls, callee-saved registers it will use, and local variables that do not fit in registers. In the standard RISC-V calling convention, the first eight integer arguments travel in registers a0–a7, and further arguments are placed on the stack at fixed offsets from sp. The epilogue restores registers and adds the frame size back. Because each call gets its own frame, recursion works naturally.

The stack has a finite size, set by the operating system for each thread or, on a microcontroller, by the linker script and start-up code that initialize the stack pointer. Deep recursion or large local arrays can push the stack pointer past its limit, a stack overflow that corrupts other memory or triggers a fault. Because return addresses sit on the stack next to local buffers, writing past the end of a local array can overwrite a return address, a classic attack. Stack canaries and non-executable stacks are standard defenses.

The stack pointer moves whenever space is allocated, so offsets to a given variable can change within a function. A frame pointer, s0/fp in RISC-V or RBP on x86-64, can be set once at function entry to a fixed point in the frame, making local and argument addresses constant and stack traces easy to walk; optimizing compilers often omit it to free a register. During a context switch, the stack pointer is saved along with the program counter and other registers, because each thread has its own stack and must resume on it.

faq.q: Which register is the stack pointer in RISC-V?
faq.a: In RISC-V the stack pointer is x2, given the ABI name sp. The standard calling convention keeps it 16-byte aligned and the stack grows toward lower addresses.

faq.q: Why does the stack grow downward?
faq.a: It is a convention adopted by most ABIs, historically convenient because the heap can grow upward from low memory while the stack grows downward from high memory, using the free space between them. The hardware or ABI defines the direction, and grows-down is by far the most common.

faq.q: What is the difference between the stack pointer and the frame pointer?
faq.a: The stack pointer always marks the current top of the stack and moves as space is allocated. The frame pointer stays fixed for the duration of a function call, giving stable offsets to locals and making it easy to walk the chain of frames when debugging.

フレームポインタ.desc: A register that keeps pointing at the stack position on function entry; s0 (fp) in RISC-V. Locals can be addressed at fixed offsets, and the call chain is easy to walk.

呼び出し先保存レジスタ.desc: A register guaranteed to keep its value across a call; if the called function uses it, the function saves and restores it. In RISC-V these are s0-s11.

呼び出し元保存レジスタ.desc: A register the called function may overwrite freely; if the caller needs its value after the call, the caller saves it. In RISC-V these include t0-t6 and a0-a7.

リターンアドレス.desc: The address to go back to when a function finishes. In RISC-V, jal puts the next instruction's address in ra (x1); in x86, call pushes it on the stack.

about.p: A call must record where execution should resume, which is the address of the instruction after the call. In RISC-V, jal (jump and link) writes PC + 4 into a register, by convention ra (x1), and jumps; the return is ret, a pseudo-instruction for jalr x0, 0(ra). Calls through function pointers, virtual functions and shared-library stubs use jalr with a register target. In x86, call pushes the return address onto the stack and ret pops it back into the instruction pointer, so the stack always holds it.

Because every jal overwrites ra, a RISC-V function that calls other functions must save its own return address first. A typical prologue is addi sp, sp, -16 to allocate a frame on the downward-growing stack, then sw ra, 12(sp) and sw s0, 8(sp) to save ra and a callee-saved register. The epilogue reloads them, restores sp and executes ret. A leaf function, which calls nothing, can leave ra in its register and may need no stack frame at all, which makes small functions cheap.

A return address stored on the stack sits next to local buffers, so a buffer overflow can overwrite it and redirect execution when the function returns. Classic attacks wrote machine code onto the stack and jumped to it; W^X policies with the page-table no-execute bit block that. Attackers then shifted to return-oriented programming, chaining existing code fragments. Further defenses include stack canaries checked before return, address-space layout randomization and hardware shadow stacks that keep a protected second copy of each return address.

Out-of-order CPUs predict where a return will go long before ra or the stack is read. A return address stack (RAS) in the branch predictor pushes the fall-through address on each call and pops it on each return, giving very accurate predictions for well-nested code. Exceptions and interrupts are different: the CPU saves the interrupted PC in a dedicated register such as RISC-V mepc or sepc, together with the previous privilege mode, and mret or sret restores all of them at once rather than a plain ret.

faq.q: Where is the return address stored in RISC-V?
faq.a: In register ra (x1), written by jal or jalr at the call. A non-leaf function copies it to its stack frame before making its own calls and restores it before ret.

faq.q: What is the difference between call/ret in x86 and jal/ret in RISC-V?
faq.a: x86 call always pushes the return address onto the stack and ret pops it, while RISC-V jal places it in a register and only touches memory if the function chooses to save it.

faq.q: Why is overwriting the return address dangerous?
faq.a: When the function returns, the CPU jumps to whatever address is there, so an attacker who overwrites it through a buffer overflow can take control of the program.

葉関数.desc: A function that calls no other functions. Its return address is never overwritten, so it need not be saved, and it often needs no stack frame at all.

ABI(アプリケーションバイナリインターフェース).desc: The machine-level agreement that lets compiled programs and libraries work together, covering the calling convention, data type sizes and alignment, how system calls are made and more.

about.p: An application binary interface (ABI) fixes everything two pieces of compiled code must agree on to call each other without being rebuilt. That includes the calling convention (which registers carry arguments and return values, which registers a callee must preserve, how the stack is aligned and laid out), the size and alignment of basic types such as int, long and pointers, the layout and padding of structs, how C++ names are mangled, how exceptions unwind, the object-file format and the instruction sequence used to make a system call into the operating system.

An application programming interface (API) is a source-level contract: function names, parameter types and behaviour as a programmer sees them. An ABI is the same contract after compilation. A library can keep its API unchanged yet break its ABI, for instance by adding a field to a public struct, which changes the struct's size and the offsets of later fields. Programs then compile fine against the new header, but binaries built against the old version misread memory unless they are recompiled. Shared-library version numbers exist largely to signal such ABI breaks.

The instruction set architecture (ISA) defines what the processor executes; the ABI is a software convention layered on top, so one ISA can have several. On x86-64, the System V ABI used by Linux passes the first six integer arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8 and R9 and makes long 64 bits, while the Windows x64 ABI uses RCX, RDX, R8 and R9 and keeps long at 32 bits. RISC-V defines ABIs such as ilp32, lp64 and lp64d, the last passing floating-point arguments in floating-point registers.

Every symbol a shared library exports becomes part of its ABI and must stay compatible. Exported functions can also be overridden by a same-named symbol in another module, so even calls inside the library must go through the procedure linkage table (PLT) or global offset table (GOT). Marking internal functions with hidden visibility removes them from the public interface: the dynamic linker has fewer symbols to resolve, internal calls become direct PC-relative calls, name collisions with other libraries are avoided, and the library is free to change those functions later.

faq.q: What is the difference between an API and an ABI?
faq.a: An API is the source-code interface a programmer writes against, while an ABI is the binary-level agreement on registers, data layout and calling sequence that compiled code relies on. Keeping the API but changing the ABI forces dependent programs to be recompiled.

faq.q: Why can a library update break programs that were not changed?
faq.a: If the update changes the ABI, for example a struct's size or a function's argument types, existing binaries still use the old layout and pass data in the wrong form. The source may compile unchanged, but already-built programs fail until they are rebuilt.

faq.q: Is a calling convention part of the ABI?
faq.a: Yes. The calling convention, which specifies where arguments and return values go and which registers each side must preserve, is one of the central parts of an ABI.

マイクロオペレーション.desc: A simple internal operation into which a CPU decodes an instruction, also written μop. x86 CPUs split complex instructions into μops and execute them with RISC-like fast techniques.

圧縮命令.desc: An instruction that encodes a common operation in fewer bits than usual. The RISC-V C extension adds 16-bit instructions and cuts code size by roughly 25-30%.

分岐遅延スロット.desc: An ISA rule that the instruction right after a branch always executes, taken or not. Found in older ISAs such as MIPS, it exposed a pipeline detail in the ISA and later became a burden.

条件コード.desc: Flags such as zero, negative, carry and overflow that record the outcome of a compare or arithmetic operation. Conditional branches in x86 and Arm test them; RISC-V has none.

オブジェクトファイル.desc: The file a compiler produces from one source file. It contains machine code, initial data, a symbol table and relocation entries, but addresses in other files are unresolved, so it cannot run until linked.

about.h: What is inside an object file
about.p: An object file is organized into sections. The text section holds machine code; the data section holds initialized writable variables; a read-only data section holds constants and string literals; and the bss section records only the size of zero-initialized variables, so it takes no space in the file. Alongside these, the symbol table lists every name the file defines and every name it uses but does not define, and the relocation entries list each place whose address must be filled in later. Debug information is optional. Common formats are ELF on Linux, Mach-O on macOS and COFF/PE on Windows.

about.h: Why it cannot run by itself
about.p: The compiler or assembler builds each object file in isolation, laying out its sections as if they began at address 0. When code calls a function in another file, such as printf, its address is unknown, so the instruction contains a placeholder, often 0, plus a relocation entry describing what must go there. Only the linker sees all object files and libraries together. It matches every undefined symbol with a definition, decides where each section will live in memory, patches the placeholders and adds the startup code and headers the operating system needs to load a program.

about.h: Typical link errors and what they mean
about.p: An error such as undefined reference to foo means some object file uses foo but nothing in the link defines it. Common causes are forgetting to link the file that defines it, omitting a library option such as -lm, a misspelled name, or calling C code from C++ without extern "C", which makes the names differ after C++ name mangling. The reverse, multiple definition, usually comes from defining a variable in a header included by several source files. With the GNU linker, static libraries should appear after the object files that use them on the command line.

about.h: Object files, static libraries and shared libraries
about.p: A static library is simply an archive of object files. The linker extracts only the members that resolve currently undefined symbols, which is why command-line order matters. A shared library is different: it is already the output of a link, built from position-independent code, and it is mapped into memory at run time, with remaining addresses filled in by the dynamic linker. Tools such as nm, objdump and readelf display an object file's sections, symbols and relocation entries, and are the quickest way to see why a link fails.

faq.q: What is the difference between an object file and an executable?
faq.a: An object file contains machine code for one source file but leaves references to other files unresolved and has no final addresses. An executable is the linker's output, with all symbols resolved, addresses fixed and headers that tell the operating system how to load it.

faq.q: How can I list the symbols in an object file?
faq.a: Use nm, objdump -t or readelf -s. In nm output, symbols marked U are undefined, meaning the file references them and expects another object file or library to define them.

faq.q: What is the bss section?
faq.a: It holds global and static variables that start at zero. The object file records only its size, and the loader allocates and zero-fills the memory when the program starts.

リンカ.desc: Software that combines object files and libraries, performs symbol resolution and relocation, and produces an executable or shared library.

about.h: Where the linker fits in the build
about.p: Building a C program normally runs the compiler, which produces assembly or object code, the assembler, which produces a machine-code object file, and finally the linker. Each object file is compiled in isolation, so it contains machine code and data, a symbol table of names it defines and references, and relocation entries marking every place where an address is still unknown, such as a call to printf in another file. The linker combines many such object files and libraries into one executable or shared library that the operating system can load.

The linker's core work has three parts. Symbol resolution binds every referenced name to exactly one definition, reporting undefined-reference or multiple-definition errors otherwise. Layout merges like sections from all inputs, such as .text for code, .rodata for constants, .data for initialized variables and .bss for zero-initialized ones, and assigns their final addresses, often under the control of a linker script. Relocation then visits each relocation entry and writes the correct absolute address or PC-relative distance into the instruction or data word.

A static library (.a on Linux) is an archive of object files, and the linker copies in only the members needed to resolve references that are still undefined, scanning inputs left to right; that is why libraries are listed after the files that use them. Static linking produces a self-contained executable but duplicates library code in every program, and library fixes require relinking. With shared libraries (.so), the linker records dependencies and the dynamic linker binds library functions at load or run time through PLT stubs and the GOT.

The linker also adds start-up objects from the C runtime, such as crt1.o, and makes their _start symbol the entry point. _start sets up arguments, initializes the library and global objects, then calls main and passes its return value to exit. C++ global constructors are collected into an .init_array table that start-up code calls before main. C++ compilers mangle names to encode argument types so overloaded functions get distinct symbols, and extern "C" disables mangling for functions shared with C code.

faq.q: What is the difference between a compiler and a linker?
faq.a: A compiler translates one source file into an object file with unresolved addresses, while a linker combines many object files and libraries, resolves names between them and fixes final addresses to produce an executable.

faq.q: Why does library order matter when linking with GCC?
faq.a: The GNU linker scans inputs left to right and extracts members from a static library only for symbols that are already undefined, so a library listed before the objects that use it contributes nothing.

faq.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic linking?
faq.a: Static linking copies the needed library code into the executable at build time, while dynamic linking leaves references to shared libraries that the dynamic linker binds when the program is loaded or run.

ローダ.desc: The OS function that reads an executable into memory, maps its parts with the right permissions, sets up arguments on the stack and starts the program.

シンボル解決.desc: The linker step that matches each function or variable name referenced in a file with its definition. No definition gives an undefined-reference error; more than one gives a multiple-definition error.

about.p: Each object file carries a symbol table listing the names it defines, such as functions and global variables, and the names it references but does not define. If main.c calls sum and sum.c defines it, main.o records an undefined reference to sum and sum.o records a definition. Symbol resolution is the linker step that gathers all symbol tables and binds every reference to exactly one definition. It comes before relocation, which then writes the final addresses of those definitions into the instructions and data that refer to them.

If no definition exists for a reference, the linker reports an undefined reference, typically because a source file or library was not linked or a name is misspelled. If two non-static global definitions share a name, it reports a multiple-definition error, because it cannot decide which one references should bind to. Declaring a function static gives it internal linkage, hiding it from other files so the same name can be reused. A declaration such as extern int count; reserves no storage and simply promises that a definition exists elsewhere.

A weak symbol is a fallback definition that is used only if no ordinary (strong) definition with the same name exists, a pattern embedded code uses for default interrupt handlers. Static libraries are archives of object files, and the GNU linker processes its inputs from left to right, extracting a library member only if it defines a symbol that is undefined at that moment. A command such as gcc -lmylib main.o therefore fails, because nothing in main.o is unresolved yet when the library is scanned. Libraries go after the files that use them.

The linker matches symbols purely by name strings. C++ allows overloaded functions such as print(int) and print(double), so the compiler encodes argument types and namespaces into the symbol name, which is called name mangling. C does not mangle names, so C++ code declares C functions with extern "C" to make the names match. With shared libraries, part of symbol resolution is postponed: the dynamic linker binds references to library functions at load time or on first call, typically through PLT stubs and GOT entries.

faq.q: What causes an undefined reference error?
faq.a: The linker found a reference to a function or variable but no definition in any linked object file or library, often because a file or library is missing from the link command, is listed in the wrong order, or a name does not match.

faq.q: What is the difference between symbol resolution and relocation?
faq.a: Symbol resolution decides which definition each referenced name refers to. Relocation then patches the actual addresses of those definitions into the machine code and data that use them.

faq.q: How do I fix a multiple definition error?
faq.a: Make sure each non-static global function or variable is defined in exactly one source file, use extern declarations in headers, and mark file-local items static so their names do not collide.

再配置.desc: Rewriting placeholder addresses in instructions and data with correct values once final addresses are decided. The linker does it, and with dynamic linking part of it is done at run time by the dynamic linker.

about.p: Separate compilation means each source file is translated without knowing where its code and data will finally sit in memory, or where functions and variables defined in other files will be. The compiler therefore assumes each section starts at address 0 and, wherever an instruction or data word needs an address it cannot know, writes a placeholder and records a relocation entry. After the linker has laid out every section of every object file and decided final addresses, it walks these entries and writes the correct values. Without this step, independently compiled pieces could not be combined into one program.

Each entry names the location to patch, given as an offset within a section, the symbol whose address is needed, an addend, and a type. The type tells the linker how to compute the value and how to encode it: an absolute 32- or 64-bit address, a PC-relative distance for branches and calls, or a value split across two instructions. RISC-V, for example, builds addresses with pairs such as lui plus addi or auipc plus jalr, so separate relocation types fill the upper 20 bits and the lower 12 bits.

In a fully static link, the linker resolves every relocation and the executable runs as is. Shared libraries change this, because their load addresses are not fixed until run time. Position-independent code reaches global data through a table of addresses, the global offset table (GOT), and calls library functions through small stubs in the procedure linkage table (PLT). The dynamic linker fills the GOT when the program loads, or lazily on the first call. Position-independent executables loaded at randomized addresses also carry simple relative relocations that the loader applies by adding the actual base address.

The two steps are easily confused. Symbol resolution matches each referenced name with exactly one definition, and its failures appear as undefined-reference or multiple-definition errors. Relocation comes afterwards and is purely about patching bits: once the address of every symbol is known, it writes the right numbers into the recorded fields. Relocation has failures of its own. If the computed value does not fit in the instruction field, for instance a branch target beyond its reach, the GNU linker reports relocation truncated to fit, which usually calls for a different code model or a longer instruction sequence.

faq.q: What is the difference between symbol resolution and relocation?
faq.a: Symbol resolution decides which definition each referenced name refers to. Relocation then writes the final addresses or distances of those symbols into the instructions and data that use them.

faq.q: What does the linker error relocation truncated to fit mean?
faq.a: The linker computed an address or offset that is too large for the instruction field it must go into, such as a branch whose target is out of range. Changing the code model or memory layout, or using a longer instruction sequence, usually fixes it.

faq.q: Does relocation happen at run time?
faq.a: Partly. The static linker does most of it, but with shared libraries and position-independent executables the dynamic linker applies the remaining relocations when the program is loaded or when a library function is first called.

シンボルテーブル.desc: The list of function and variable names, with their addresses and attributes, contained in object files and executables. Used for linking and debugging; strip can remove it.

about.p: Each symbol table entry describes one named entity. In the ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) used on Linux, an entry records the name (as an offset into a string table), the value (an address, or an offset within a section in an object file), the size, the type such as function or data object, the binding (local, global or weak) and the section where the symbol is defined. A symbol that is referenced but not defined in this file is marked undefined; these are the references the linker must satisfy from other object files or libraries.

Linking starts with symbol resolution: the linker collects the symbol tables of all input files and matches every undefined reference with exactly one definition. Two strong global definitions of the same name produce a multiple-definition error, a weak definition yields to a strong one, and a reference with no definition produces an undefined-reference error. Once each symbol has a final address, the linker processes relocation entries, patching every instruction and data word that refers to a symbol. Local symbols, such as static functions in C, never take part in cross-file matching.

about.h: Static symbols, dynamic symbols and strip
about.p: ELF files carry two symbol tables. The full table (.symtab) serves the static linker and debuggers; the dynamic table (.dynsym) lists only the symbols that must be resolved at load time between an executable and its shared libraries. Running strip removes .symtab and debug sections such as DWARF line information, shrinking the file, but leaves .dynsym because the program cannot run without it. Developers often save the debug information to a separate file before stripping so that crashes in shipped binaries can still be symbolized. Tools such as nm and readelf -s list a file's symbols.

The same term also names a different structure inside the compiler. During semantic analysis, the compiler keeps a table, typically hash tables organized by nested scope, that maps each identifier to its declaration, type and storage. It answers questions such as which variable x means at this point and whether a function was declared with matching arguments. That table exists only while compiling. The object-file symbol table is its persistent output, containing just the names that matter for linking, relocation and debugging.

faq.q: How do I view the symbol table of an executable or object file?
faq.a: On Linux, nm lists symbols with a one-letter type, and readelf -s shows the full ELF symbol tables including size, type and binding. objdump -t is another option.

faq.q: What do T and U mean in nm output?
faq.a: T marks a symbol defined in the text (code) section, typically a global function, and U marks an undefined symbol that this file references but does not define. Lowercase letters indicate local symbols.

faq.q: Can a stripped binary still be debugged?
faq.a: Yes, but stack traces show addresses instead of function names unless separately saved debug information or symbol files are available to the debugger.

ELF.desc: The file format used for object files, executables and shared libraries on Linux and other UNIX-like systems and in embedded devices.

about.h: What is inside an ELF file
about.p: An Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) file starts with an ELF header beginning with the magic bytes 0x7F followed by the letters E, L and F. The header records whether the file is 32- or 64-bit, its byte order, the target CPU, the file type and the entry point address where execution begins. The same format covers relocatable object files produced by the compiler, executables, shared libraries and core dumps. After the header come a program header table, the contents themselves and a section header table describing each section.

ELF offers two views of the same bytes. The linker works with fine-grained sections such as .text for code, .rodata for constants, .data for initialized variables and .bss for zero-initialized variables, which takes no space in the file and is zero-filled at load time. The loader works with segments listed in the program headers, which group sections by permission: .text and .rodata typically go into a read-execute segment, .data and .bss into a read-write one. Grouping by permission makes it simple to set page-level memory protection.

about.h: How ELF supports linking and loading
about.p: Object files carry symbol tables and relocation entries that tell the linker which addresses to patch when code and data are combined. Dynamically linked executables name an interpreter, the dynamic loader, in a program header, and include a dynamic section listing required shared libraries; calls into those libraries usually go through a procedure linkage table (PLT) and global offset table (GOT) so addresses can be resolved at run time. Debug information is stored in additional sections that tools can strip. Embedded toolchains often output ELF and then convert it to a raw binary or hex file for flashing.

Linux, the BSDs and many embedded systems use ELF, Windows uses the Portable Executable (PE) format for .exe and .dll files, and macOS and iOS use Mach-O. The underlying ideas of code and data regions, symbols, relocations and dynamic-linking information are similar, but the formats differ, and so do the system call interfaces and libraries the programs expect. That is why a compiled program does not run unchanged on a different operating system even on the same CPU.

faq.q: What does ELF stand for?
faq.a: ELF stands for Executable and Linkable Format, the standard file format for object files, executables and shared libraries on Linux and many other UNIX-like and embedded systems.

faq.q: What is the difference between sections and segments in ELF?
faq.a: Sections are fine-grained units such as .text and .data that the linker combines and relocates. Segments, described by program headers, group sections with the same permissions into the units the loader maps into memory.

faq.q: Can an ELF executable run on Windows?
faq.a: Not natively. Windows expects the PE format and its own system interfaces, so an ELF program needs a compatibility layer, a virtual machine running Linux, or recompilation for Windows.

BSSセクション.desc: The area for global and static variables with no initializer (or zero). Only its size is recorded in the file and it is zero-filled at load time, so it does not enlarge the executable.
BSSセクション.title: .bss Section: What It Is and Why It Takes No File Space
BSSセクション.description: The .bss section holds zero-initialized globals and statics. Why it adds no size to the executable, how startup code clears it, and where the name comes from.

about.p: The C language requires every object with static storage duration, meaning globals and static variables, to start at zero if no initializer is given. Compilers place such variables, and usually also those explicitly initialized to 0, in the .bss section. Globals with a nonzero initial value go in .data, and const-qualified constants go in read-only .rodata. The static keyword does not choose the section; it only limits visibility to one file. Local automatic variables never appear in .bss, because they live on the stack and have no defined initial value.

Storing a long run of zeros in the executable would only waste disk space and load time, so the .bss section records only its size and alignment. In ELF it is marked as occupying no file bytes. The loader maps the read-write segment containing .data and .bss, and where the segment's memory size exceeds its file size, the extra bytes are provided as zero-filled pages. As a result, a declaration such as static char buf[1000000]; adds about 1 MB to memory use but almost nothing to the file.

On a microcontroller without an operating system, nobody else zero-fills memory, so the start-up code does it. Before calling main, the reset handler typically copies initial values of .data from flash into RAM and clears the .bss range in RAM, using start and end addresses that the linker script exports as symbols. Forgetting either step leads to globals with garbage values. Tools such as the size command report text, data and bss separately, which helps estimate flash and RAM usage.

BSS is commonly expanded as block started by symbol, a name inherited from an assembler directive on early IBM mainframes that reserved an uninitialized block of storage under a label. The meaning survived into Unix object formats and later ELF, even though the directive itself is long gone. Today the name simply refers to the zero-initialized data section, alongside .text for code, .data for initialized data and .rodata for constants.

faq.q: What does BSS stand for?
faq.a: BSS is usually expanded as block started by symbol, after an old assembler directive. In modern toolchains it simply names the section for zero-initialized global and static variables.

faq.q: Does a large uninitialized array make the executable bigger?
faq.a: No. A global or static array without an initializer goes in .bss, where only its size is recorded; the memory is allocated and zero-filled when the program is loaded.

faq.q: What is the difference between .data and .bss?
faq.a: The .data section holds globals and statics with nonzero initial values, which must be stored in the file. The .bss section holds those that start at zero, so it occupies memory at run time but no space for contents in the file.

ヒープ.desc: The area from which a running program obtains memory of any size with malloc and the like and returns it with free. Repeated allocation and release can cause fragmentation.

静的リンク.desc: Linking that copies the code of the libraries used into the executable. It runs without the libraries present, but the file is larger and library fixes require rebuilding.

about.p: In static linking the linker reads the program's object files and the static libraries named on the command line, pulls in the archive members needed to resolve undefined symbols, and merges like sections together: all code into one text section, all initialized data into one data section, and so on. It then assigns final addresses, patches every reference using the relocation entries and writes a single executable. With GCC, the -static option requests this for all libraries, including the C standard library, provided static versions of them are installed.

A statically linked executable is self-contained: nothing has to be found at start-up, there is no symbol binding by a dynamic linker and calls into library code are direct. The costs are size and maintenance. Each program carries its own copy of every library routine it uses, so copies are not shared in memory across processes as shared-library pages are, and a security fix in a library reaches the program only when it is relinked. Dynamic linking reverses these trade-offs, at the price of depending on compatible library versions on every machine where the program runs.

A static executable still depends on the CPU architecture and on the operating system's system-call interface, so it cannot simply run on another OS. Some library features also assume dynamic loading behind the scenes. GNU libc, for example, warns that functions such as getaddrinfo, used in statically linked programs, still require shared libraries at run time for name-service lookups. Static linking also means the program cannot use dlopen-style plug-ins as easily, since those are shared objects expecting a dynamic linker.

Firmware for microcontrollers is almost always statically linked into one image, because there is no loader or file system to supply libraries at run time. On servers and in minimal container images, static executables are valued because a single file can be copied anywhere with a compatible kernel. Developers also use static linking for command-line tools that must run on many distributions without worrying about library versions, accepting a larger file in exchange for avoiding problems such as a missing or incompatible shared library.

faq.q: How do I statically link a C program with gcc?
faq.a: Add -static to the link command, for example gcc -static main.c -o main. Static (.a) versions of every library involved, including the C library, must be installed for this to succeed.

faq.q: Why is my statically linked executable so much bigger?
faq.a: It contains copies of all library code it uses, including parts of the C runtime, instead of referring to shared libraries already on the system. Stripping symbols and linking with section garbage collection can reduce the size.

faq.q: Is a statically linked program faster?
faq.a: Start-up is usually faster because no shared libraries need loading and binding, and calls avoid an indirection. For most long-running programs the difference in steady-state speed is small.

動的リンク.desc: Linking that loads and binds shared libraries at run time. Libraries can be shared between processes and fixed by replacement, but a compatible library must be present on the system.

about.p: A dynamically linked executable does not contain library code. It records which shared libraries it needs and which of their symbols it uses, and on Linux it names a program interpreter, the dynamic linker. When the program starts, the kernel maps the executable and the dynamic linker, which then locates each library along a search path, maps it into memory, resolves symbol references, applies the remaining relocations and runs library initializers before jumping to the program's entry point. Windows does the same job for DLLs using each executable's import table.

For one physical copy of library code to serve many processes, the code pages must never be patched, even though the library may load at a different address in each process. Shared libraries are therefore compiled as position-independent code (PIC), and addresses that vary go into a data table, the global offset table (GOT). Calls to external functions go through small procedure linkage table (PLT) stubs that jump via the GOT. With lazy binding the GOT entry is filled on first call; resolving everything at start-up and then making the GOT read-only is a common hardening choice.

Static linking copies the needed object code into the executable at build time. The result is self-contained and avoids run-time symbol lookup, but it is larger and must be rebuilt to pick up a library fix. Dynamic linking shares library pages across processes, saves disk space and lets a security fix reach every program by replacing one file. The costs are start-up work and dependency on the target system: a missing or incompatible library stops the program from launching, which is why libraries carry version names and versioned symbols.

Beyond the libraries fixed at start-up, a running program can load one explicitly with dlopen on POSIX systems or LoadLibrary on Windows, then look up functions by name with dlsym or GetProcAddress. This is how plug-in architectures and optional features work. Because symbol binding happens at run time, a preloaded library can also interpose its own version of a function, a mechanism used by profilers and memory debuggers. Tools such as ldd list the shared libraries an executable will load and where they are found.

faq.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic linking?
faq.a: Static linking copies library code into the executable at build time, so it runs without external libraries. Dynamic linking leaves references that the dynamic linker resolves at run time, letting processes share one library copy and receive fixes by replacing it.

faq.q: What are the PLT and GOT?
faq.a: The global offset table (GOT) is a writable data table holding run-time addresses of external functions and variables. The procedure linkage table (PLT) contains small stubs that code calls, which jump through the GOT to the actual library function.

faq.q: What does error while loading shared libraries: cannot open shared object file mean?
faq.a: The dynamic linker could not find a library the program depends on in its search path. It is fixed by installing the library or adding its location to the search path, for example through the system linker configuration or an rpath.

共有ライブラリ.desc: A library loaded at run time by dynamic linking: .so on Linux, .dll on Windows. Built as position-independent code, its code pages can be shared by many processes.

about.p: When a program is linked against a shared library, the executable records only which libraries it needs, identified by their soname, and which symbols it imports. At start-up the dynamic linker (ld.so on Linux) finds each library, maps it into the process's address space, resolves symbol references and applies relocations. Calls to library functions typically go through the procedure linkage table (PLT), which can resolve each function lazily on its first call. The ldd command shows which file each needed library resolves to and flags missing ones as "not found"; it should not be run on untrusted binaries, since that can execute their code.

A shared library may land at a different address in every process, so it is compiled as position-independent code (PIC). Code reaches its own functions and data with PC-relative addressing and reaches external symbols through the global offset table (GOT), a per-process data area that the dynamic linker fills in. The code pages therefore never need patching and can be mapped read-only and executable. The OS points every process's mapping at the same physical pages, so 100 processes using one library hold its code once, while writable data pages are kept per process, typically with copy-on-write.

On Linux a library file such as libfoo.so.1.2.3 carries a soname such as libfoo.so.1, and programs record the soname. A bug fix or security patch that keeps the ABI (application binary interface) compatible keeps the soname, so replacing one file updates every program that uses it. Changing argument types, struct layouts or removing functions breaks old binaries, so the soname number is raised and the new library is installed alongside the old one.

A static library is an archive of object files whose needed parts are copied into the executable at link time, giving a self-contained binary with no start-up binding, but every program carries its own copy and a fix requires relinking. Shared libraries save memory and disk and allow in-place updates, at the price of start-up binding work, an indirection on cross-module calls, and missing-dependency failures. Giving internal functions hidden visibility and exporting only the public API reduces the symbols the dynamic linker must process, lets internal calls skip the PLT, avoids name clashes and keeps the ABI small.

faq.q: What is the difference between a static library and a shared library?
faq.a: A static library (.a or .lib) is copied into the executable at link time. A shared library (.so or .dll) stays a separate file loaded at run time and can be shared in memory by many processes.

faq.q: Why do shared libraries need -fPIC?
faq.a: The library can be loaded at any address, so its code must avoid absolute addresses. PIC uses PC-relative addressing and the GOT so code pages need no modification and can be shared.

faq.q: What does "not found" in ldd output mean?
faq.a: The dynamic linker cannot locate that shared library in its search path, so the program will fail to start until the library is installed or the path is fixed.

静的ライブラリ.desc: An archive bundling many object files (.a on Linux). During static linking, the linker extracts only the objects it needs into the executable.

about.p: On Unix-like systems a static library is an archive created with the ar tool, for example ar rcs libfoo.a a.o b.o. It is little more than the object files concatenated with headers, plus an index mapping each defined global symbol to the member that defines it, so the linker can find definitions without scanning every member. The command-line option -lfoo makes the linker look for libfoo.so or libfoo.a in the library search path; GNU ld prefers the shared version when both exist unless static linking is requested. Windows toolchains use .lib files for the same purpose.

about.h: The unit of extraction is the object file
about.p: When a member is needed, the linker includes the whole object file, not just the one function that was referenced. If a library's source file defines twenty functions and a program calls one, all twenty land in the executable, along with anything they reference in turn. Libraries such as the C standard library are therefore often built from many small source files, sometimes one function each. Alternatively, compiling with -ffunction-sections and -fdata-sections and linking with --gc-sections lets the linker drop unreferenced functions within a member.

The GNU linker scans inputs left to right and, on reaching an archive, extracts only members that resolve references undefined at that moment, then never revisits it. Libraries must therefore come after the objects that use them, and a library that depends on another must come before it. When two libraries depend on each other, the usual fixes are listing one twice or wrapping both in --start-group and --end-group so the linker rescans them until nothing new is resolved. Some linkers, such as LLVM's lld, remember all archive symbols and do not need this ordering.

A static library is consumed only at build time: its code is copied into each executable, and the .a file is not needed when the program runs. A shared library (.so on Linux, .dll on Windows) is a single linked file, built as position-independent code, that is loaded at run time and whose pages are shared among all processes using it. Static libraries suit self-contained deployment and embedded firmware, while shared libraries save disk and memory and let a fix reach every program by replacing one file.

faq.q: How do I create a static library in Linux?
faq.a: Compile the sources to object files with gcc -c, then bundle them with ar rcs libname.a file1.o file2.o. Link against it with -L pointing to its directory and -lname.

faq.q: What is the difference between a .a and a .so file?
faq.a: A .a file is an archive of object files whose needed members are copied into the executable at link time. A .so file is a shared library loaded at run time and shared among processes.

faq.q: Why do I get undefined reference errors even though I linked the library?
faq.a: With the GNU linker the most common cause is order: the library appears on the command line before the object files that use it. Move -lname after the objects, and check the library actually defines the symbol with nm.

位置独立コード.desc: Machine code that runs without modification at any load address, also called PIC. It uses PC-relative references and the GOT and is used for shared libraries and PIEs.

about.h: How PIC addresses code and data
about.p: Position-independent code (PIC) never embeds absolute addresses in its instructions. Branches and calls name their targets as distances from the program counter, which stay the same wherever the whole module is placed. For targets farther than a branch field can reach, RISC-V pairs auipc, which adds a 20-bit immediate shifted left by 12 bits to the PC, with jalr or a load that supplies the low 12 bits, covering about ±2 GiB from the current instruction. x86-64 offers RIP-relative addressing for the same purpose, which makes position-independent code nearly as fast as fixed-address code.

PC-relative distances work within one module, but the address of a variable or function in another shared library is not known until run time. PIC therefore reaches such symbols through the global offset table (GOT), a per-module table of addresses placed at a fixed distance from the code. The code loads the needed address from the GOT, and the dynamic linker fills in the real addresses at load time. On ELF systems, calls to external functions additionally go through small stubs in the procedure linkage table (PLT), which can resolve each function lazily on its first call.

A shared library may be mapped at a different virtual address in every process that uses it. If its code contained absolute addresses, the loader would have to patch the instructions for each address, turning shared read-only pages into private writable copies and defeating the purpose of sharing. With PIC, only the small writable GOT differs between processes, so the code pages need no changes and a single physical copy is mapped into all of them. This saves memory and lets the library load quickly no matter where it lands.

about.h: PIC vs. PIE and the security link
about.p: A position-independent executable (PIE) applies the same technique to the main program, typically built with the -fPIE and -pie options in GCC or Clang, while shared libraries use -fPIC. Older executables assumed a fixed load address, so address space layout randomization (ASLR) could move libraries and the stack but not the main program's code, leaving its addresses predictable to attackers. A PIE can be loaded anywhere, so its code is randomized too, and many current Linux distributions build PIEs by default. The cost is a small overhead from GOT indirection, which was noticeably larger on 32-bit x86.

faq.q: What does PIC stand for?
faq.a: PIC stands for position-independent code, machine code that runs correctly without modification at any load address. It relies on PC-relative addressing and the global offset table.

faq.q: What is the difference between -fPIC and -fPIE?
faq.a: Both generate position-independent code; -fPIC is meant for shared libraries, whose symbols may be overridden by other modules, while -fPIE targets the main executable and can use slightly cheaper direct references to its own symbols. An executable built with -fPIE is linked with -pie to produce a PIE.

faq.q: Why is the global offset table needed?
faq.a: Code cannot embed the address of a symbol in another module, because that address is only known after loading. The GOT holds those addresses, filled in by the dynamic linker, and the code reaches the GOT through a PC-relative reference.

GOT(グローバルオフセットテーブル).desc: A table of the actual addresses of external variables and functions, filled in by the dynamic linker at run time. Position-independent code refers to them through it, so code pages need no patching.

PLT(プロシージャリンケージテーブル).desc: A table of small stubs used to call shared-library functions. With lazy binding, the dynamic linker resolves the address on the first call and writes it into the GOT.

about.h: Why calls go through a stub
about.p: A shared library can be loaded at a different address in each process, so the address of a function like printf is unknown when the program is linked. Patching every call instruction at load time would make code pages writable and unshareable between processes. Instead, the linker points each external call at a small stub in the procedure linkage table (PLT). The stub performs an indirect jump through a slot in the global offset table (GOT), a writable data area that the dynamic linker fills with real addresses.

With lazy binding, each GOT slot initially points back into its own PLT stub. On the first call, the stub pushes an index identifying the function's relocation entry and jumps to a common PLT header, which enters the dynamic linker's resolver. The resolver looks up the symbol in the loaded libraries, writes its address into the GOT slot and jumps to the function. Every later call goes stub, GOT, function with no further lookup. Functions that are never called are never resolved, which shortens program start-up.

Because the GOT is writable and holds code addresses, an attacker who can overwrite memory may redirect a GOT entry to hijack control flow. Many systems therefore resolve all symbols at start-up, for example by linking with -z now or setting LD_BIND_NOW on Linux, and then mark the GOT read-only, a hardening known as full RELRO (relocation read-only). The trade-off is a slower start for programs that import many functions, in exchange for removing a common attack target.

Exported functions in a shared library can be overridden, or interposed, by a definition with the same name in another module, so even calls from inside the library must normally go through the PLT. Giving internal functions hidden visibility removes them from the dynamic symbol table, so calls to them become direct PC-relative calls, the dynamic linker has fewer symbols to process and name clashes with other libraries are avoided. The GOT also holds addresses of external data, but data accesses read the GOT directly without a PLT stub.

faq.q: What is the difference between the PLT and the GOT?
faq.a: The PLT contains small executable stubs that external calls jump to, while the GOT is a data table holding the resolved addresses; each PLT stub jumps indirectly through its GOT entry.

faq.q: What is lazy binding in dynamic linking?
faq.a: Lazy binding defers resolving a shared-library function's address until the first time it is called, when the dynamic linker looks it up and stores it in the GOT for all later calls.

faq.q: What does full RELRO do?
faq.a: It makes the dynamic linker resolve all symbols at start-up and then remaps the GOT read-only, so attackers cannot overwrite GOT entries to redirect function calls.

動的リンカ.desc: Software that, when a dynamically linked program starts, finds and loads shared libraries, applies relocations and binds symbols before starting the program, such as ld.so on Linux.

about.p: A dynamically linked ELF executable names an interpreter in its program headers, such as ld-linux on Linux. After execve maps the program, the kernel also maps that dynamic linker and transfers control to it rather than to the program. The dynamic linker reads the list of needed libraries, searches for them in configured paths and its cache, maps them into the address space, applies relocations, binds symbols, runs the libraries' initialization functions (listed in sections such as .init_array), and finally jumps to the program's entry point. Libraries opened later with dlopen go through the same machinery.

Shared libraries are built as position-independent code, so their code pages contain no absolute addresses of other modules. Instead, code reads addresses from the global offset table (GOT), a writable data table the dynamic linker fills in. Function calls go through procedure linkage table (PLT) stubs. With lazy binding, the first call through a stub enters the linker's resolver, which writes the real address into the GOT, and later calls jump straight there. Many systems instead bind everything at start-up and then make the GOT read-only (full RELRO) to block GOT-overwrite attacks.

The static linker (ld) runs at build time: it combines object files, resolves symbols and applies most relocations, producing an executable. The dynamic linker runs every time the program starts and finishes the job for shared libraries. That split is what lets one physical copy of a library's code be shared by many processes and lets a security fix reach every program by replacing one file. The price is extra start-up work and a dependency on the right library versions being present on the target machine.

Most start-up failures of dynamically linked programs are missing or incompatible libraries; the ldd command lists the dependencies and shows which ones cannot be found. On Linux, environment variables such as LD_LIBRARY_PATH add search directories and LD_PRELOAD injects a library ahead of others, which is useful for debugging and instrumentation. Library authors can speed up loading by exporting only public functions and marking internal symbols hidden, which reduces the symbols the dynamic linker must process and lets internal calls skip the PLT.

faq.q: What is ld.so on Linux?
faq.a: It is the dynamic linker/loader: the program the kernel runs first for a dynamically linked executable, which loads shared libraries, resolves symbols and then starts the program.

faq.q: Why does my program say a shared library cannot be found?
faq.a: The dynamic linker could not locate a required library, or found only an incompatible version, in its search paths. Running ldd on the program shows which dependency is missing.

faq.q: What is the difference between the GOT and the PLT?
faq.a: The GOT is a data table of resolved addresses filled by the dynamic linker, while the PLT is a set of small code stubs that external function calls jump through, reading their targets from the GOT.

ASLR.desc: A countermeasure that changes the addresses of the stack, heap, shared libraries and executable every run so attackers cannot easily predict them.
ASLR.title: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization): How It Works
ASLR.description: ASLR randomizes the addresses of the stack, heap, libraries and executable on every run. Why attackers need addresses, the role of PIE, and ASLR's limits.

about.p: When a program starts, the kernel and the dynamic loader choose random, page-aligned base offsets for each major region of the address space: the stack, the heap, the mmap area where shared libraries are mapped, and the executable itself if it was built as a position-independent executable (PIE). The relative order of the regions stays the usual one (text, data, BSS and heap at low addresses, stack at the top), but their absolute addresses differ on every run. Address space layout randomization (ASLR) therefore changes where things are, not what the program does.

Memory-corruption exploits such as stack buffer overflows usually overwrite a return address or function pointer with the address of something useful: shellcode on the stack, a library function like system() in a return-to-libc attack, or a chain of instruction snippets in return-oriented programming (ROP). Each of these needs exact addresses. With ASLR the attacker must guess them, and a wrong guess typically crashes the process instead of handing over control. The protection is probabilistic, so its strength depends on how many random bits are available, which is much more limited on 32-bit address spaces than on 64-bit ones.

ASLR can only move code that does not assume a fixed load address. Shared libraries have long been compiled as position-independent code (PIC), reaching their data through PC-relative addressing and the global offset table (GOT). Older executables, however, were linked for a fixed address, so the main program's code stayed at a known location and gave attackers a reliable source of ROP gadgets. Building with -fPIE and -pie makes the executable relocatable as well, so the loader can randomize it too. On x86-64 the cost is small because PC-relative data access is native.

Randomization is applied per region, so leaking a single pointer from a library reveals the offset of that whole library, and from there every function in it. Child processes created by fork() inherit the parent's layout, which lets attackers probe a forking server repeatedly. For these reasons ASLR is combined with non-executable writable memory (W^X or NX), stack canaries and control-flow protections. The operating-system kernel can be randomized too, which is called KASLR. On Linux the setting is visible in /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space.

faq.q: Does ASLR prevent buffer overflow attacks?
faq.a: No. ASLR does not stop the overflow itself; it only makes it hard to know which address to jump to, so most attempts crash instead of succeeding. An information leak that reveals one real address can defeat it, which is why it is paired with NX memory and stack canaries.

faq.q: What is the difference between ASLR and PIE?
faq.a: ASLR is the operating-system mechanism that loads memory regions at random addresses on each run. PIE is a way of compiling and linking the executable so that its code works at any address, which allows ASLR to randomize the main program as well as libraries, stack and heap.

faq.q: How do I check whether ASLR is enabled on Linux?
faq.a: Read /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space: 0 means disabled, 1 randomizes the stack, mmap region and shared libraries, and 2 additionally randomizes the brk-based heap. Most distributions default to 2.

PIE(位置独立実行ファイル).desc: An executable whose main program is also built as position-independent code. It runs at any address, so ASLR can randomize the main program's code too.

エントリポイント.desc: The address where a program begins execution, recorded in the ELF header. In C it is usually start-up code such as _start, which initializes and then calls main.

about.p: The entry point is the address of the first instruction the loader transfers control to, stored in the executable's header, such as the e_entry field of an ELF file. For a C program it is normally not main. The linker adds start-up objects from the C runtime, such as crt1.o, and makes the _start symbol inside them the entry point. To C code, main looks like the beginning, but it is just an ordinary function called by this start-up code. Linkers let you choose a different entry symbol when needed.

On Linux the kernel starts a new process with argc, the argv pointers, the environment pointers and an auxiliary vector laid out on the stack. The _start routine gathers these, aligns the stack and calls the C library's initialization, which sets up the standard library, runs constructors and initializers for global objects, and then calls main. When main returns, its return value is passed to exit, which runs registered atexit handlers, flushes buffered output and finally asks the kernel to terminate the process.

A dynamically linked executable names its dynamic linker, such as ld.so on Linux, in a program header. The kernel maps both the program and the dynamic linker and starts execution at the dynamic linker's own entry point, not the program's. The dynamic linker loads the required shared libraries, applies relocations, binds symbols and runs the libraries' initialization functions, then jumps to the program's entry point, _start. So in a dynamically linked process, a substantial amount of code runs before the program's own first instruction.

about.h: Entry points in kernels and microcontrollers
about.p: The term also covers other places where execution begins. An operating system registers exception and interrupt entry points with the CPU; on RISC-V, for example, an ecall instruction raises an exception that switches to a higher privilege mode and jumps to the trap vector the OS configured. On a bare-metal microcontroller, the reset vector points to start-up code that prepares the stack, copies initialized data from flash to RAM, zeroes the uninitialized .bss section and only then calls main.

faq.q: Is main the entry point of a C program?
faq.a: Usually not. The executable's entry point is start-up code such as _start, which prepares arguments and the runtime, calls main and then passes main's return value to exit.

faq.q: Where is the entry point stored in an ELF file?
faq.a: In the e_entry field of the ELF header, which holds the virtual address at which execution begins after the program is loaded.

faq.q: What runs before main in a C program?
faq.a: The C runtime start-up code, library initialization and constructors for global objects; in a dynamically linked program, the dynamic linker also loads and relocates shared libraries first.

名前修飾.desc: A C++ compiler's encoding of argument types and namespaces into a function's symbol name, so the linker can tell overloaded functions apart.

about.p: A mangled name packs into one linker symbol everything that distinguishes C++ entities sharing a source-level name: enclosing namespaces and classes, the function name, the parameter types, const or volatile qualification of member functions and template arguments. The return type is normally omitted, since overloads cannot differ only by return type, although function template instances do include it. Under the Itanium C++ ABI, used by GCC and Clang on Linux and many other platforms, print(int) becomes _Z5printi and ns::f(double) becomes _ZN2ns1fEd, where lengths prefix each name and single letters encode built-in types.

C has no overloading, so C compilers emit plain function names. When C++ code calls a C library, its declarations must be wrapped in extern "C" so that the C++ compiler looks for the unmangled name; otherwise it looks for something like _Z3fooi, finds only foo, and the link fails with an undefined reference. Headers shared between the languages usually wrap their declarations in extern "C" guarded by a check for the __cplusplus macro. Functions declared extern "C" cannot be overloaded, because two of them would map to the same symbol.

Mangled names show up in nm output, disassembly, crash reports and linker errors. The c++filt tool converts them back to readable declarations, nm -C does the same in its listing, and most debuggers and linkers demangle automatically when printing diagnostics. Being able to read the raw form still helps: two symbols that look identical once demangled may differ in a const qualifier or a parameter type, which reveals that a declaration in a header does not match the definition that was actually compiled.

about.h: Mangling is part of the ABI
about.p: Each compiler family defines its own scheme, and Microsoft's compiler uses a completely different encoding from the Itanium ABI. The scheme is part of the application binary interface (ABI), so object files from compilers with different schemes cannot be linked directly even if the source is identical. Changes to a library's C++ interface, such as altering a parameter type, change the mangled names and break binary compatibility with programs built against the old version. Other languages with overloading or modules, such as Rust, mangle names for the same reasons.

faq.q: How do I demangle a C++ symbol name?
faq.a: Pipe it through c++filt, for example echo _Z5printi | c++filt prints print(int). nm -C and objdump -C demangle while listing symbols.

faq.q: What does extern "C" do in C++?
faq.a: It gives the declared functions C linkage, so the compiler uses the plain unmangled name. This lets C++ code call C libraries and lets C code call C++ functions exported this way.

faq.q: Why is the return type not part of a mangled function name?
faq.a: C++ overloads must differ in their parameters, so the parameters alone identify the function. Function template instances are the exception and do encode the return type.

弱いシンボル.desc: A fallback definition replaced by any ordinary (strong) definition with the same name. Embedded code uses it for default interrupt handlers and similar.

リンカスクリプト.desc: A file telling the linker at which memory addresses to place each section. Embedded development uses it to lay out flash and RAM and to fix the interrupt vector address.
