about.p: The compiler produces object files whose code and data are grouped into sections such as .text (instructions), .rodata (constants), .data (initialized variables) and .bss (zero-initialized variables), but without final addresses. A linker script tells the linker how to combine them. In GNU ld syntax, a MEMORY block declares regions with an origin and length, for example flash at one address and RAM at another, and a SECTIONS block maps input sections into output sections and assigns each to a region. The linker reports an error if a region overflows.

On a PC the operating system's loader decides where a program sits in memory, and a default linker script works for nearly everything. A microcontroller without an OS starts executing from fixed addresses at power-on, so the program must be built for its exact memory map. The interrupt vector table has to sit where the hardware expects it, code and constants belong in non-volatile flash, and writable variables, the heap and the stack must be in RAM. Different chips in the same family often need only a different linker script because their memory sizes differ.

Initialized variables pose a special problem: their initial values must survive power-off, so they are stored in flash, yet the program writes to them, so they must live in RAM at run time. The linker script therefore gives .data two addresses: a load address in flash and a run address in RAM. It also defines symbols marking the start and end of .data and .bss and often the top of the stack. Start-up code uses those symbols to copy .data from flash to RAM and fill .bss with zeros before calling main, giving C its promised initial state.

Many problems in bare-metal projects trace back to the linker script. When unused-section removal is enabled, the vector table or other sections referenced only by hardware can be discarded unless marked to be kept. A stack region sized too small does not cause a link error but silently overwrites other data at run time. Placing a section at the wrong load address leaves variables with garbage initial values. Reading the map file the linker can produce, which lists every symbol's address and each region's usage, is the standard way to check the result.

faq.q: What is a linker script used for?
faq.a: A linker script tells the linker which memory regions exist and at which addresses to place each code and data section. Embedded projects use it to put code in flash, variables in RAM and the interrupt vector table at its required address.

faq.q: What is the difference between .data and .bss?
faq.a: .data holds variables with nonzero initial values, which are stored in flash and copied to RAM at start-up. .bss holds variables that start at zero, so it takes no space in flash and is simply cleared in RAM before main runs.

faq.q: Why does .data have two addresses in a linker script?
faq.a: Its initial values must be stored in non-volatile flash, but the variables are modified at run time and so must live in RAM. The load address points to the flash copy and the run address to the RAM location the code actually uses.

断片化.desc: The condition in which repeated allocation and release split free memory into small pieces, so a large contiguous block cannot be allocated even though the total is sufficient.

MESIプロトコル.desc: A coherence protocol that tracks each cache line in one of four states: Modified, Exclusive, Shared or Invalid. On a write it invalidates other cores' copies.

about.p: Modified (M): this cache holds the only copy and has written it, so memory is stale and the data must be written back or supplied to others. Exclusive (E): the only copy, but identical to memory. Shared (S): an unmodified copy that other caches may also hold. Invalid (I): the line holds no usable data. The protocol guarantees a single-writer, multiple-reader rule for each line: at any time either one cache may write it (M or E) or any number may read it (S), never both.

On a read miss the cache requests the line; if no other cache has it, it is loaded in E, otherwise in S. If another cache holds it in M, that cache supplies the data or writes it back and drops to S. A write to an S line must first invalidate all other copies, an upgrade request, before moving to M. A write miss issues a read-for-ownership that fetches the line and invalidates other copies in one step. When another core's write request is observed, any local copy goes to I, and an M copy hands over its data first.

The simpler MSI protocol has no E state, so a core that reads private data and then writes it must send an extra invalidation on the bus even though no other cache holds a copy. E records that the line is clean and unshared, allowing the later write to move silently to M. Since much data is private to one core, this saves a large amount of coherence traffic. Variants add more states: MOESI adds Owned, letting a dirty line be shared without first updating memory, and MESIF adds Forward, naming the one sharer that answers requests.

Coherence works per cache line, typically 64 bytes, not per variable. If two cores repeatedly write different variables that happen to share a line, each write must invalidate the other core's copy, so the line bounces between M in one cache and I in the other even though the threads never touch the same data. This false sharing can make parallel code slower than sequential code. The fix is to separate frequently written per-thread data, such as counters, onto different lines by padding or alignment.

faq.q: What is the difference between MESI and MSI?
faq.a: MESI adds the Exclusive state for clean lines that no other cache holds. A core can then write such a line without broadcasting an invalidation, which MSI would require.

faq.q: What does the Modified state mean in MESI?
faq.a: This cache has the only valid copy and has changed it, so main memory is out of date. The line must be written back on eviction or supplied to another core that requests it.

faq.q: What is false sharing?
faq.a: A slowdown that occurs when threads on different cores write separate variables located in the same cache line, forcing the coherence protocol to move the line back and forth between their caches.

スヌーピング.desc: A coherence approach in which each cache watches other cores' reads and writes on a shared bus or similar and updates its own line states. It suits small core counts.

ディレクトリ方式.desc: A coherence approach that records in a table which cores hold each line and notifies only those cores. Used in systems with many cores.

about.p: Every memory line has a home node, usually determined by its address, and the home keeps a directory entry for it: a coherence state such as uncached, shared or exclusive, plus a record of which caches hold copies. The simplest record is a full bit vector with one bit per core or cache. Entries live beside the memory controllers or in the shared last-level cache. Since requests go to one home rather than to everyone, the interconnect can be a mesh of point-to-point links rather than a broadcast bus.

A core that wants to write a line it does not own sends a request to the line's home. The home consults the directory and sends invalidations only to the caches marked as sharers; they drop their copies and acknowledge, either to the home or directly to the requester. Once all acknowledgments arrive, the requester gets exclusive ownership and the directory records it as the owner. If another cache held the line modified, the home forwards the request to that owner, which sends the data to the requester, a so-called three-hop transaction.

Snooping broadcasts every miss to every cache, giving low latency because there is no extra lookup, but traffic and snoop work grow with the number of cores, which limits it to small systems. A directory adds the latency of a lookup at the home and sometimes an extra hop, but sends messages only where needed, so traffic grows with actual sharing rather than with core count. Large multicore chips and multi-socket systems therefore use directories or hybrids, such as snoop filters that track which caches might hold a line so that most broadcasts can be skipped.

A full bit vector for every memory line would cost too much storage as core counts rise, so practical designs economize. Limited-pointer schemes store a few sharer IDs and fall back to broadcast if more caches share the line; coarse vectors use one bit per group of cores. Sparse directories track only lines that are actually cached, organized like a cache themselves. When a sparse directory runs out of entries it must evict one, which forces invalidation of that line in every cache that holds it, so its capacity must be sized generously relative to the caches it tracks.

faq.q: Why does directory-based coherence scale better than snooping?
faq.a: It sends invalidations and requests only to the caches that actually hold a line instead of broadcasting to all of them. Traffic therefore follows real sharing rather than growing with the number of cores.

faq.q: Is directory-based coherence slower than snooping?
faq.a: Each miss may take longer because the home's directory must be consulted and requests may be forwarded, but in large systems the reduced traffic and contention usually outweigh that added latency.

faq.q: What is a snoop filter?
faq.a: A structure that records which caches might hold each line so that coherence requests are sent only to those caches. It is essentially a directory used to cut broadcast traffic in a snooping-style design.

偽共有.desc: A slowdown in which threads update different variables that happen to share a cache line, so the line bounces between cores.

about.h: Why coherence works per line, not per variable
about.p: Cache coherence protocols such as MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) track ownership of whole cache lines, typically 64 bytes, rather than individual variables. Before a core can write, it must hold the line exclusively, which invalidates every other core's copy. If core 0 keeps writing variable a and core 1 keeps writing variable b in the same line, each write forces the line to move between the two caches. Neither thread reads the other's data, so the results stay correct, but an access that would be a few-cycle L1 hit becomes a slow cross-core transfer.

True sharing means threads really do access the same variable, such as a global counter or a lock word; the contention is inherent and can only be removed by changing the algorithm, for example by splitting the counter. False sharing means the data are logically independent and merely happen to be neighbors in memory, so the cure is a change of data layout. Both produce the same symptom: heavy coherence traffic on a few lines. Read-only sharing causes neither problem, because many caches can hold a line in the Shared state at once; only writes force invalidations.

The classic case is an array of per-thread counters: with 8-byte elements, eight of them fit in one 64-byte line, so up to eight threads fight over it. Other common sources are structs whose fields are updated by different threads, a lock placed in the same line as data guarded by a different lock, and work queues whose head and tail indices, written by producer and consumer, sit side by side. The usual sign is a program whose speedup flattens or even falls as threads are added although each thread appears to touch only its own data.

about.h: How to fix and find it
about.p: Pad or align each independently written item to the cache-line size, for example with alignas(64) in C or C++, so every thread owns its own line. Some processors fetch adjacent pairs of lines together, which is why 128-byte separation is sometimes used. Better still, let each thread accumulate in a local variable or register and write the shared location once at the end. Hardware performance counters can expose the problem; on Linux, the perf c2c tool reports cache lines that are frequently modified by one core and then hit by another.

faq.q: Does false sharing cause wrong results?
faq.a: No. The coherence protocol keeps every variable correct; false sharing only costs time, because the cache line holding the variables keeps moving between cores.

faq.q: How much padding do I need to avoid false sharing?
faq.a: Enough that each independently written variable occupies its own cache line, usually 64 bytes. Some code uses 128 bytes because certain CPUs prefetch adjacent line pairs together.

faq.q: Can read-only shared data cause false sharing?
faq.a: No. Several cores can keep the same line in a shared state simultaneously; the problem appears only when at least one thread writes to the line.

データ競合.desc: A situation in which threads access the same variable concurrently without synchronization and at least one access is a write. Results vary between runs; in C and C++ it is undefined behavior.

about.p: The statement counter++ looks atomic but compiles to three steps: load the value, add 1, store it back. Suppose two threads each increment a shared counter 100,000 times. If thread A loads 100 and thread B also loads 100 before A stores, both store 101 and one increment disappears. Depending on how the threads interleave, the final value can be anywhere below 200,000 and differs from run to run. Nothing crashes, so the bug is easy to miss, and it may vanish when the program is slowed down by a debugger or logging.

A data race is precisely defined: two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and no synchronization orders them. A race condition is broader: any bug whose outcome depends on timing. The two overlap but are not identical. A check-then-act sequence built from individually atomic operations has no data race yet can still be a race condition, because another thread can act between the check and the act. Languages treat data races differently: in C and C++ a program containing one has undefined behavior, while Java gives racy programs defined but weak semantics.

The cure is to impose an order on the conflicting accesses. A lock (mutex) turns the update into a critical section that only one thread executes at a time; keeping critical sections short limits waiting. For simple operations, atomic instructions are faster: fetch-and-add, such as x86 lock xadd or RISC-V amoadd.w, performs the read, add and write indivisibly and returns the old value, so it never needs to retry. More complex updates use compare-and-swap loops. Declaring a variable volatile in C or C++ does not prevent a data race, because it provides neither atomicity nor ordering between threads.

about.h: Why compilers and hardware make races worse
about.p: Because C and C++ assume race-free programs, compilers may legally keep a shared variable in a register, hoist a load out of a loop or merge stores, so a thread spinning on a flag written by another thread without synchronization might never see the change. Hardware adds its own reordering through store buffers and caches. Synchronization operations, such as lock acquisition and atomics with the appropriate memory ordering, are what tell both compiler and hardware where ordering must be preserved. Dynamic race detectors such as ThreadSanitizer help find races that testing alone rarely exposes.

faq.q: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
faq.a: A data race is concurrent, unsynchronized access to the same memory location where at least one access is a write. A race condition is any timing-dependent bug, which can exist even when every individual access is properly synchronized.

faq.q: Can a data race happen on a single-core CPU?
faq.a: Yes. If the operating system preempts a thread between its load and store, another thread can run and update the same variable, so an increment can still be lost without any true parallelism.

faq.q: Does the volatile keyword prevent data races in C and C++?
faq.a: No. Volatile only forces the compiler to perform each access; it does not make read-modify-write sequences atomic or order them between threads. Use atomics or locks instead.

アトミック命令.desc: An instruction that performs a memory read and write as one operation no other core can interrupt, such as CAS, fetch-and-add and LR/SC.
アトミック命令.title: Atomic Instructions: CAS, Fetch-and-Add and LR/SC Explained
アトミック命令.description: Atomic instructions read and write memory as one indivisible step. Why plain loads and stores fall short, the common kinds, and how hardware does it.

about.h: Why ordinary loads and stores are not enough
about.p: A statement like counter++ compiles into a load, an add and a store. If two cores run it at the same time, both can load the same old value and both store old + 1, losing one increment. An atomic instruction performs the whole read-modify-write as one indivisible operation: no other core's access to that location can slip in between, and other cores observe only the value before or after it. This guarantee is the foundation for locks, counters and lock-free data structures on multicore processors.

Test-and-set and atomic swap write a new value and return the old one. Fetch-and-add adds to memory and returns the previous value. Compare-and-swap (CAS) writes a new value only if memory still holds an expected value, reporting whether it succeeded. Load-reserved/store-conditional (LR/SC) splits the operation into a reserving load and a store that fails if the reservation was lost. RISC-V also provides atomic memory operation (AMO) instructions such as amoadd and amoswap, while x86 applies a LOCK prefix to instructions such as cmpxchg and xadd.

Early systems locked the shared bus for the duration of the operation. Modern cores instead use the cache coherence protocol: the core obtains exclusive ownership of the cache line, in the Modified or Exclusive state of a MESI-style protocol, and delays other cores' requests for that line until the read-modify-write finishes. An atomic is therefore much slower than a plain cached load, and under contention the line bounces between cores. Atomics also interact with memory ordering; on x86, locked instructions act as full memory barriers.

A spinlock tries to set a lock variable with an atomic instruction and retries in a loop if it is already taken. Retrying the atomic write directly causes heavy coherence traffic, because every attempt demands exclusive ownership. The test-and-test-and-set pattern spins with ordinary reads on a shared copy in the local cache and attempts the atomic only when the lock appears free. Lock-free structures use CAS or LR/SC directly, but CAS-based designs must guard against the ABA problem, where a value changes and changes back unnoticed.

faq.q: What is the difference between an atomic instruction and a lock?
faq.a: An atomic instruction makes a single read-modify-write on one memory location indivisible in hardware; a lock is a software construct, built from atomics, that protects a longer section of code touching many locations.

faq.q: What is compare-and-swap?
faq.a: Compare-and-swap writes a new value to a memory location only if it still contains an expected value, and reports success or failure, all as one atomic operation.

faq.q: Why are atomic operations slow?
faq.a: The core must gain exclusive ownership of the cache line and often enforce memory ordering, and when several cores contend for the same line it is repeatedly transferred and invalidated between them.

コンペア・アンド・スワップ.desc: An atomic instruction that writes a new value only if memory still holds an expected value. Wrapped in a retry loop, it enables lock-free updates.

about.p: CAS (compare-and-swap) takes an address, an expected value and a new value. In one indivisible step it reads the location, compares it with the expected value and, only if they match, stores the new value; it reports success or failure, often by returning the value it found. On x86 this is the lock cmpxchg instruction. C11 exposes it as atomic_compare_exchange_strong and _weak, and C++ as compare_exchange_strong and compare_exchange_weak on std::atomic. In hardware, the core obtains the cache line in an exclusive state so no other core can write it during the operation.

A lock-free update reads the current value, computes the new value from it and attempts a CAS with the value read as the expected value. If another thread changed the location in the meantime, the CAS fails and the loop rereads and tries again. Some thread always succeeds, so the system as a whole makes progress without locks, which makes such code lock-free but not wait-free: one unlucky thread can retry indefinitely. Under heavy contention many retries and the cache line bouncing between cores can make a CAS loop slower than a simple lock.

CAS checks only that the value is equal, not that it was never changed. If a location changes from A to B and back to A between a thread's read and its CAS, the CAS succeeds even though the data structure may now be different. The classic case is a lock-free stack where a node is popped, freed and reallocated at the same address before another thread's pop completes. Common remedies are pairing the pointer with a version counter updated on every change, and safe memory reclamation schemes such as hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation.

Many RISC architectures provide load-linked/store-conditional (LL/SC) instead: in RISC-V, lr reserves an address and sc stores only if no other write to it has occurred since, failing otherwise. Because it detects any intervening write rather than comparing values, it avoids ABA in principle, but the reservation can be lost for unrelated reasons, which is why compare_exchange_weak is allowed to fail spuriously. For simple operations such as counters, atomic fetch-and-add, or RISC-V AMO instructions like amoadd, is better than a CAS loop because it never needs to retry.

faq.q: What is the ABA problem in compare-and-swap?
faq.a: A CAS succeeds because the location holds the expected value again, even though it was changed to something else and back in between. This can corrupt lock-free structures that reuse memory, and is usually prevented with version counters or safe memory reclamation.

faq.q: Is a CAS loop lock-free or wait-free?
faq.a: Lock-free. Apart from spurious failures of weak forms, a CAS fails only because another thread's update succeeded, so the system progresses, but an individual thread has no bound on how many retries it may need.

faq.q: What is the difference between compare_exchange_weak and compare_exchange_strong?
faq.a: The weak form may fail even when the value matches, which lets it map directly to LL/SC instructions and suits retry loops. The strong form fails only on a real mismatch, at the cost of an internal loop on LL/SC machines.

LR/SC.desc: A pair of instructions, also called LL/SC: if another core writes the address after the load-reserved, the store-conditional fails, enabling atomic updates.

about.p: Load-reserved (LR) reads a memory word and at the same time registers a reservation on that address, usually covering its cache line. The program computes a new value in registers, then store-conditional (SC) attempts to write it. SC writes only if the reservation is still intact and returns a status code indicating success or failure; on RISC-V, zero means success. Software wraps the sequence in a retry loop. RISC-V calls the pair lr and sc, Arm provides equivalent load-exclusive and store-exclusive instructions, and the general name is LL/SC.

The main cause of failure is another core writing to the reserved location between the LR and the SC. The core detects this through cache coherence: the write invalidates its copy of the line and clears the reservation. The reservation may also be cleared by an interrupt or context switch, another SC, or eviction of the line, so SC can fail even without a real conflict. Correct code must always be prepared to retry, and RISC-V guarantees eventual success only for short loops that follow specified restrictions.

about.h: LR/SC vs. CAS and the ABA problem
about.p: Compare-and-swap (CAS) checks whether memory still holds an expected value. If another thread changes a value from A to B and back to A, CAS cannot tell and succeeds, which can corrupt lock-free structures such as linked lists: the ABA problem. LR/SC checks whether any write happened, not what the value is, so an A-B-A sequence still breaks the reservation. LR/SC can also build any single-word read-modify-write in software, including CAS itself and fetch-and-add. Its weaknesses are spurious failures and possible livelock under heavy contention.

A single CAS instruction must read, compare and write memory in one step, which fits awkwardly into a pipeline where each instruction performs at most one memory access. LR/SC keeps that load/store discipline: LR behaves like a load plus a reservation register, and SC like a store gated by that register. No bus locking is needed, because the coherence protocol already tells the core when another processor writes the line. For this reason the pair has long been used in RISC instruction sets, often alongside single-instruction atomics.

faq.q: When does a store-conditional fail?
faq.a: It fails when the reservation set by the load-reserved has been lost, most commonly because another core wrote the address, but also possibly due to an interrupt, context switch or cache eviction.

faq.q: Does LR/SC solve the ABA problem?
faq.a: Yes. LR/SC detects any intervening write to the reserved location, so a value that changes and changes back still causes the store-conditional to fail, unlike compare-and-swap.

faq.q: What is the difference between LL/SC and LR/SC?
faq.a: They are the same idea under different names: load-linked/store-conditional is the traditional term, and load-reserved/store-conditional is the RISC-V name.

ABA問題.desc: The problem that when a value changes from A to B and back to A, a CAS comparing only values fails to notice and succeeds. Lock-free data structures must guard against it.
ABA問題.title: ABA Problem in Lock-Free Programming: Cause and Fixes
ABA問題.description: Why a compare-and-swap can succeed after a value changes A→B→A, why memory reuse causes it, and the fixes: tagged pointers, hazard pointers and epochs.

about.p: Compare-and-swap (CAS) writes a new value only if a location still holds an expected value, and it compares values, not history. Consider a lock-free stack whose head points to node A, with A's next pointer pointing to B. Thread 1 reads head = A and next = B, then is preempted. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, and pushes A back, or pushes a new node that happens to reuse A's address. Thread 1 resumes, its CAS(head, A, B) succeeds because head is still A, and head now points to B, a node that is no longer in the stack.

about.h: Why memory reuse makes it likely
about.p: The problem is most common in languages with manual memory management. When a node is freed, the allocator readily hands the same address to the next allocation, so a pointer value can return to A even though it refers to a different node. In garbage-collected languages a node cannot be reclaimed while a thread still holds a reference to it, which largely removes the address-reuse form of ABA, although the logical form can still occur if the same node is deliberately reinserted.

The classic fix pairs the pointer with a modification counter and compares both in one atomic operation, using a double-width CAS or spare pointer bits; every update increments the counter, so A with tag 5 differs from A with tag 7. Load-linked/store-conditional (LL/SC, called LR/SC in RISC-V) fails if the location was written at all since the load, even when the value is the same. Safe memory reclamation schemes, such as hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation, prevent a node from being freed and reused while any thread may still access it.

A lock-free algorithm guarantees that some thread always makes progress even if others stall, because a CAS fails only when another thread's update succeeded. That progress guarantee says nothing about correctness, and ABA is the classic way a seemingly correct CAS loop corrupts a data structure. It is hard to catch in testing because it needs a specific interleaving plus memory reuse, so lock-free code should be designed with an explicit ABA strategy from the start.

faq.q: What is the ABA problem in simple terms?
faq.a: A thread sees value A, another thread changes it to B and back to A, and the first thread's compare-and-swap succeeds as if nothing had happened. The value matches, but the state behind it has changed.

faq.q: How does LL/SC avoid the ABA problem?
faq.a: Store-conditional succeeds only if no write has occurred to the location since the matching load-linked, regardless of the value written. A change from A to B and back to A therefore still makes the store fail.

faq.q: Does a version counter fully solve ABA?
faq.a: In practice yes, as long as the counter is wide enough that it cannot wrap around to the same value while a thread is stalled. A very narrow counter can in principle wrap and reintroduce the problem.

スピンロック.desc: A lock that waits by repeatedly checking the lock variable in a loop. Fast for short waits, but it keeps using the CPU while waiting.

about.h: How a spinlock acquires and releases
about.p: A spinlock is a shared variable, typically 0 when free and 1 when held. To acquire it, a thread uses an atomic read-modify-write instruction such as test-and-set, swap or compare-and-swap, which sets the variable to 1 and returns the old value in one indivisible step; on RISC-V this is an atomic swap or a load-reserved/store-conditional pair. If the old value was 0, the thread owns the lock; otherwise it tries again in a loop. Releasing simply stores 0. Acquire and release must also act as memory barriers, so that accesses inside the critical section stay between them.

Retrying the atomic instruction in a tight loop performs poorly on multicore chips. Every atomic operation needs exclusive ownership of the cache line, so waiting cores keep pulling the line into the modified (M) state and invalidating each other's copies, flooding the coherence fabric. The test-and-test-and-set pattern waits with ordinary loads instead: each waiter reads its own shared copy in its cache, generating no traffic, and attempts the atomic operation only when it sees the lock become free. Exponential backoff and ticket or queue-based locks further reduce contention and add fairness.

A mutex that sleeps puts a waiting thread into a blocked state and hands the CPU to other threads; the operating system wakes it when the lock is released. That wastes no CPU time but costs a system call, scheduling and a context switch, typically several microseconds. A spinlock avoids that overhead entirely and wins when the lock is held for only a short time, shorter than a sleep and wake cycle would take. For long hold times the balance reverses, so many library mutexes spin briefly first and then sleep, combining the strengths of both.

about.h: Where spinlocks fit and where they fail
about.p: Spinlocks are common inside operating system kernels, for short critical sections on multiprocessors and for data shared with interrupt handlers, which cannot sleep. Code holding a spinlock must not sleep, and kernels usually disable preemption, and interrupts where needed, while it is held, so that an interrupt handler on the same core cannot spin forever on a lock its own core holds. On a single-core system a user-level spinlock is especially wasteful: the holder cannot run to release the lock while the waiter spins, so the waiter burns its entire time slice.

faq.q: What is the difference between a spinlock and a mutex?
faq.a: A spinlock waits by looping on the lock variable and keeps the CPU busy, which is efficient only for very short waits. A mutex puts the waiting thread to sleep and lets other threads run, which suits longer waits but adds the cost of sleeping, waking and context switching.

faq.q: When should you use a spinlock?
faq.a: Use one when the critical section is very short and threads run on different cores, or in kernel contexts such as interrupt handlers that are not allowed to sleep. Avoid it when the lock may be held for long or on single-core systems.

faq.q: What is test-and-test-and-set?
faq.a: It is a spinlock technique in which waiters repeatedly read the lock with ordinary loads from their own caches and attempt the atomic test-and-set only when the lock appears free. This avoids constant cache-line invalidations and greatly reduces coherence traffic.

ミューテックス.desc: A lock that only one thread can hold at a time. Typically a thread that cannot get it sleeps and yields the CPU, and the OS wakes it when the lock is released.

about.p: A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is usually a memory word recording whether the lock is held and whether anyone waits. Acquiring it in the uncontended case is a single atomic instruction such as compare-and-swap, done in user space and costing on the order of tens of nanoseconds. Only when the lock is held does the thread ask the operating system to sleep on a wait queue; on Linux this is built on the futex system call. Unlocking checks for waiters and, if there are any, asks the kernel to wake one. A mutex has an owner: only the thread that locked it should unlock it.

A spinlock waiter keeps executing a loop that retries the lock, so it reacts within nanoseconds of the release but burns its CPU the whole time. A mutex waiter gives up the CPU, which is efficient for long waits but costs a system call, a context switch and a later wake-up, typically several microseconds in total. Spinlocks therefore suit very short critical sections on multicore machines, and places where sleeping is not allowed, such as kernel interrupt handlers. On a single core spinning is pointless, because the holder cannot release the lock while the waiter occupies the CPU. Many library mutexes are adaptive: they spin briefly, then sleep.

A counting semaphore holds an integer and lets up to N threads pass, which makes it a tool for limiting access to a pool of resources or for signaling between threads. Any thread may post a semaphore, so it has no concept of an owner. A mutex is restricted to one holder and is tied to the thread that locked it. That ownership enables error checking and, in real-time systems, priority inheritance, which a plain semaphore cannot offer because the system cannot know which thread to boost.

In a real-time operating system (RTOS), priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits for a mutex held by a low-priority task, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one, delaying the high task indefinitely. This caused repeated resets on the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997. Priority inheritance fixes it by temporarily raising the holder to the waiter's priority. The other classic hazard is deadlock: two threads each holding one mutex and waiting for the other's. The standard prevention is to acquire multiple mutexes in a single, fixed global order.

faq.q: What is the difference between a mutex and a binary semaphore?
faq.a: Both admit one thread at a time, but a mutex has an owner that must release it, while any thread can signal a semaphore. Ownership is what makes priority inheritance and error checking possible for a mutex.

faq.q: When should I use a spinlock instead of a mutex?
faq.a: Use a spinlock only when the critical section is a handful of instructions, the holder is running on another core, and sleeping is impossible or too slow. For anything that might wait longer than a few microseconds, a sleeping mutex is the better choice.

faq.q: Why is my mutex slow under contention?
faq.a: Each contended acquisition can involve a system call, a context switch and a wake-up, and the lock's cache line bounces between cores. Shortening the critical section or splitting one lock into several finer-grained locks usually helps more than changing the lock type.

デッドロック.desc: A state in which threads each hold a resource while waiting for one held by another, so none can proceed. Fixing a global lock order prevents it.

about.p: Deadlock can occur only when four conditions, often called the Coffman conditions, hold together. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps what it has while waiting for more. No preemption: resources cannot be taken away forcibly. Circular wait: a cycle of threads exists in which each waits for a resource held by the next. Because all four are required, every prevention technique works by making at least one of them impossible.

The classic case involves two locks. Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for lock B, while thread 2 holds B and waits for A; neither releases what it holds, so both wait forever. With locks that put waiting threads to sleep, the CPU goes idle and the program simply appears frozen. Livelock differs: threads stay busy, for example repeatedly backing off and retrying in step, yet make no progress. Starvation is when one thread never gets a resource while others proceed, and thrashing is a memory-paging problem, not a lock problem.

The most common practical rule is a global lock order: if every thread always acquires A before B, no thread can hold B while waiting for A, so no cycle can form. Other approaches acquire all needed locks at once, or use a try-lock and release everything held when a lock is unavailable, then retry after a delay. Some systems instead detect deadlock by finding cycles in a wait-for graph and break it by aborting one participant, as databases do with transactions. Lock-order checking tools can flag violations during testing.

Hardware interconnects can deadlock too. In an on-chip network, packets occupy buffers while waiting for buffers ahead of them; if those dependencies form a cycle, traffic stops permanently. Designers prevent this with routing rules that rule out cycles, such as dimension-order routing on a mesh, or with virtual channels that break the dependency chain. Protocol deadlock, where responses cannot proceed because requests fill the same buffers, is avoided by giving request and response messages separate buffers or channels.

faq.q: What are the four conditions for deadlock?
faq.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait; all four must hold at once, so breaking any one prevents deadlock.

faq.q: How do you prevent deadlock with multiple locks?
faq.a: Define one global order for acquiring locks and make every thread follow it, which makes a circular wait impossible; acquiring all locks at once or backing off with try-lock are alternatives.

faq.q: What is the difference between deadlock and livelock?
faq.a: In deadlock the threads are blocked and do nothing; in livelock they keep running and changing state, for example retrying in response to each other, but still never make progress.

メモリ一貫性モデル.desc: The contract specifying in what order a core's reads and writes to multiple addresses may be observed by other cores. Examples include sequential consistency, x86 TSO and the weak models of Arm and RISC-V.

about.p: Modern cores do not perform loads and stores strictly in program order. A store is often parked in a store buffer while the core moves on, and loads may be issued early or out of order to hide cache latency. These optimizations are invisible inside a single thread, because the core always forwards its own pending writes and preserves its own results. Another core, however, can see the same operations in a different order. A memory consistency model is the contract stating exactly which of these reorderings may become visible, so programmers and compilers know when synchronization is required.

about.h: Sequential consistency, TSO and weak models
about.p: Sequential consistency (SC) is the strictest model: all operations appear to occur in one global order that respects each core's program order. x86 uses total store order (TSO), which is nearly as strong: the only visible reordering is a later load to a different address completing before an earlier store, exactly what a FIFO store buffer produces. Arm and RISC-V use weak models that allow loads and stores to different addresses to be reordered in most combinations. Ordering must then be requested explicitly with fence or barrier instructions or with acquire and release operations.

about.h: A classic example: the store-buffer test
about.p: Let core 0 execute x = 1 then read y, while core 1 executes y = 1 then read x, with x and y initially 0. Under sequential consistency at least one core must read 1. Under TSO both can read 0, because each store may still sit in its own core's store buffer when the other core's load runs. Lock algorithms such as Dekker's and Peterson's fail in exactly this way unless a full fence is placed between the store and the load. On a weak model, even passing data with a flag can fail unless barriers order the accesses.

Cache coherence is a guarantee about a single address: all cores agree on the order of writes to that location and eventually see the latest value. A consistency model covers ordering across different addresses, such as whether a write to x becomes visible before a later write to y. A system can be fully coherent and still show such reorderings, which is why barriers exist alongside coherence protocols. High-level languages define their own models, such as C11 and C++11 atomics, and compilers translate them into the barrier instructions the hardware model requires.

faq.q: What is the difference between cache coherence and memory consistency?
faq.a: Coherence ensures that all cores see writes to one address in the same order and eventually read the latest value. Consistency defines the order in which accesses to different addresses may be observed by other cores.

faq.q: What does TSO stand for?
faq.a: TSO stands for total store order, the memory model used by x86 processors. It allows only a later load to a different address to be observed before an earlier store, an effect of the store buffer.

faq.q: Why do Arm and RISC-V programs need more memory barriers than x86 programs?
faq.a: Arm and RISC-V use weak memory models that permit most reorderings of loads and stores to different addresses, so ordering must be requested explicitly. x86 TSO already keeps most orderings, so barriers are needed only in cases such as a store followed by a load to another address.

逐次一貫性.desc: The most intuitive memory consistency model: all cores' operations appear in one order in which each core's operations keep their program order.

about.p: Sequential consistency, defined by Leslie Lamport in 1979, requires that the result of any execution be the same as if all cores' memory operations were interleaved into one global sequence, with each core's operations appearing in that sequence in program order. Like shuffling several decks of cards together without reordering any single deck, the interleaving may be anything, but every core sees the same one. Programmers can reason about concurrent code by imagining the threads taking turns, which is why it is considered the most intuitive memory consistency model.

Strictly preserving program order across all memory accesses forbids many hardware optimizations. A store buffer lets a core continue executing after a write without waiting for it to reach the cache, and out-of-order execution lets later loads complete before earlier stores. Both break sequential consistency. Most processors therefore implement weaker models: x86 uses total store order (TSO), which allows a later load to pass an earlier store to a different address, and Arm and RISC-V use still weaker models that permit more reordering unless the program inserts fences.

Suppose core 0 executes x = 1 then r1 = y, while core 1 executes y = 1 then r2 = x, with x and y initially 0. Under sequential consistency one of the writes must come first in the global order, so at least one read sees 1, and r1 = r2 = 0 is impossible. On x86, each write can sit in its core's store buffer while the following read fetches the old value from cache, so both reads can return 0. Placing a full memory barrier between the write and the read on each core restores the sequentially consistent outcome.

Cache coherence concerns a single memory location: all cores agree on the order of writes to that address and eventually see the latest value. A memory consistency model such as sequential consistency concerns the ordering of accesses to different addresses, which coherence alone does not constrain. Languages bridge the gap: C11 and C++11 atomics default to memory_order_seq_cst, and programs free of data races behave as if sequentially consistent. Weaker orders such as acquire/release or relaxed let the compiler emit fewer barriers when full ordering is unnecessary.

faq.q: Is x86 sequentially consistent?
faq.a: No. x86 implements total store order (TSO), which lets a load complete before an earlier store to a different address becomes visible to other cores, so the store-buffer litmus outcome r1 = r2 = 0 can occur. A fence such as MFENCE or a locked instruction prevents it.

faq.q: What is the difference between sequential consistency and cache coherence?
faq.a: Coherence guarantees a single agreed order of writes for each individual address. Sequential consistency is stronger and covers the relative order of operations on all addresses, as one global interleaving that respects every core's program order.

faq.q: What does memory_order_seq_cst mean in C++?
faq.a: It is the default ordering for std::atomic operations and makes all seq_cst operations appear in one total order consistent with each thread's program order. It is the easiest to reason about but may require the most expensive barrier instructions.

TSO(トータルストアオーダー).desc: The x86 memory consistency model. It allows only a later read of a different address to overtake an earlier write, reflecting the presence of a store buffer.

ストアバッファ.desc: A small buffer in which a core holds writes temporarily. The core can move on without waiting for writes to complete, but other cores see the writes later.

about.p: When a core executes a store, the target cache line may be missing or held by another core, and gaining write ownership through the coherence protocol can take many cycles. Rather than stall, the core places the address and data in a store buffer and continues executing. Entries drain into the L1 cache later, typically in program order on x86. In out-of-order processors the store buffer also holds speculative stores, which cannot be written to the cache until the store instruction commits and is known not to be squashed.

Because recent stores may still be sitting in the buffer, every load checks it for a matching address. If it finds one, the load takes the data from the newest matching entry instead of from the cache, a mechanism called store-to-load forwarding. This keeps single-threaded behavior intact: a core always sees its own writes immediately, in program order. Forwarding works best when the load reads exactly the bytes a single earlier store wrote; partial overlaps between a load and buffered stores often force the load to wait until those stores drain.

about.h: Why other cores see writes late
about.p: Other cores cannot look into a core's store buffer, so a buffered write is invisible to them until it drains. Consider x and y both 0, with core 1 running x = 1 then r1 = y, and core 2 running y = 1 then r2 = x. Under sequential consistency at least one load must see 1. With store buffers, both stores can wait in their buffers while both loads read 0 from the caches, so r1 = r2 = 0 occurs on real x86 machines. A memory barrier between the store and the load, which waits for the buffer to drain, forbids this result.

about.h: Store buffers and memory consistency models
about.p: The x86 model, total store order (TSO), essentially describes a first-in, first-out store buffer: stores stay ordered with stores and loads with loads, and only a later load to a different address may appear to pass an earlier store. Weaker models such as those of Arm and RISC-V also allow stores to become visible out of order, among other reorderings, so they need fences or acquire/release instructions more often. Programmers normally rely on language-level atomics, which the compiler maps to the right fences.

faq.q: What is store-to-load forwarding?
faq.a: It is when a load finds a matching earlier store still waiting in the store buffer and takes its data directly from there, so the core sees its own pending writes without waiting for them to reach the cache.

faq.q: Why can both threads read 0 in the store buffering litmus test?
faq.a: Each core's write sits in its own store buffer, invisible to the other core, while its following load reads the old value from cache; a memory fence between the store and load prevents this.

faq.q: How does the store buffer relate to TSO?
faq.a: Total store order is essentially the behavior of a FIFO store buffer: the only reordering it allows is a later load to a different address completing before an earlier store becomes visible.

メモリバリア.desc: An instruction guaranteeing that memory operations before it become visible to other cores before those after it, also called a fence, such as RISC-V fence.

about.p: A memory barrier, also called a fence, is an instruction that splits a thread's memory operations into those before it and those after it, and guarantees that the earlier ones become visible to other cores before the later ones are performed. Without it, a processor may let loads and stores to different addresses complete out of order, for example by keeping stores in a store buffer while later loads proceed. Results seen by the issuing thread itself never change, so barriers matter only when data is shared between cores or with devices such as DMA engines.

Suppose core 0 runs x = 1 and then r1 = y, while core 1 runs y = 1 and then r2 = x, with x and y starting at 0. Under sequential consistency one store happens first, so at least one load must return 1. On real processors, including x86, each store can wait in its core's store buffer while the following load reads the old value from cache, so both r1 and r2 can be 0. Placing a full barrier between the store and the load in each thread forces the store to become visible before the load runs, which rules out that outcome.

RISC-V provides fence, whose operands state which earlier accesses must be ordered before which later ones, so fence rw, rw orders all reads and writes, and its atomic and load-reserved/store-conditional instructions carry acquire and release bits. Arm has dmb (data memory barrier) for ordering, dsb when completion must be awaited, and load-acquire and store-release instructions. On x86, whose total store order (TSO) already preserves most orderings, mfence or a locked instruction is needed mainly to order a store before a later load. Barriers are not free, because they can stall the core until pending stores drain.

Most programmers never write a barrier directly. Lock acquisition includes acquire semantics, so later accesses cannot move before it, and release includes release semantics, so earlier writes are visible before the lock is freed; this is why data protected by a lock passes correctly between threads. Languages expose the same ideas through atomics with memory orders, such as C11 and C++11. A compiler barrier is a different thing: it stops the compiler from reordering accesses across a point but emits no instruction, so it does not constrain the hardware.

faq.q: What is the difference between a memory barrier and a fence?
faq.a: They are the same concept under two names. Both refer to an instruction that keeps memory operations before it ordered ahead of those after it as observed by other cores; RISC-V calls its instruction fence, and Arm calls its instructions barriers.

faq.q: Does x86 need memory barriers?
faq.a: Less often than weakly ordered architectures, because x86 total store order keeps most loads and stores in program order. A barrier such as mfence, or a locked instruction, is still needed when a store must become visible before a later load to a different address.

faq.q: What is the difference between a compiler barrier and a memory barrier?
faq.a: A compiler barrier only prevents the compiler from moving memory accesses across it and generates no machine instruction. A memory barrier is a hardware instruction that constrains the order in which the processor makes accesses visible to other cores.

アクワイア・リリース.desc: An ordering guarantee: operations after an acquire cannot move before it, and operations before a release cannot move after it. Used for lock acquire and release, it is lighter than a full barrier.

クリティカルセクション.desc: A part of a program that operates on shared data and must be run by only one thread at a time. It is protected by a lock and kept as short as possible.

about.p: Even a simple statement like count++ compiles to a read, a modify and a write. If two threads run it at the same time, both may read the same old value and one increment is lost. Code that reads and updates shared data in this way is a critical section, and the bug that occurs when two threads enter it together is a data race or race condition. A correct solution must guarantee mutual exclusion, so only one thread is inside at a time, while still letting waiting threads make progress rather than wait forever.

The usual tool is a lock: a thread acquires a mutex before entering and releases it on exit, and any other thread trying to acquire it blocks or spins until it is free. Locks are built from atomic hardware instructions such as test-and-set, compare-and-swap, or load-linked/store-conditional, which read and update a memory word without interference. A spinlock busy-waits and suits very short sections on multicore systems, while a mutex that puts the waiting thread to sleep suits longer waits. Acquiring several locks in inconsistent orders can cause deadlock.

On a single-core microcontroller, the competing code is often an interrupt handler rather than another thread, so a critical section is commonly protected by disabling interrupts and re-enabling them afterward. Interrupts that arrive meanwhile are normally held pending and serviced on re-enable, but long masked periods delay timer and communication handling and can overflow buffers. The section must therefore be as short as possible. On a multicore system disabling interrupts on one core is not enough, because another core can still access the data, so a spinlock or atomic operation is also needed.

about.h: Keeping sections short and transactional memory
about.p: While one thread holds a lock, others wait, so long critical sections serialize a program and erase the benefit of extra cores. Designers shorten them, split one coarse lock into finer locks for independent data, or use lock-free atomic operations. Hardware transactional memory offers another route: the critical section runs speculatively as a transaction whose writes stay invisible to other threads. If no other thread touched the same data it commits all at once; on conflict it aborts, rolls back and retries or falls back to a normal lock.

faq.q: What is the difference between a critical section and a mutex?
faq.a: A critical section is the region of code that accesses shared data and must not run concurrently. A mutex is one mechanism for enforcing that, by letting only the thread holding it enter the region.

faq.q: Why should critical sections be kept short?
faq.a: Other threads must wait while one is inside, and interrupts may be disabled during it on microcontrollers. Long sections reduce parallelism and delay response to other events.

faq.q: Is disabling interrupts enough to protect a critical section?
faq.a: On a single-core system where the only competitor is an interrupt handler, it usually is. On a multicore system other cores can still run, so a lock or atomic operation is required as well.

ロックフリー.desc: A property of an algorithm that some thread can always make progress even if others stall partway. Built with atomic instructions such as CAS.

バリア同期.desc: Synchronization in which threads that arrive first wait until all threads reach the same point, keeping them in step phase by phase. Distinct from a memory barrier.

NUMA.desc: An organization in which each core has near and far memory, and far accesses take longer. Placing data and threads on the same side is faster.

about.p: Modern processors integrate their memory controllers, so in a multi-socket server each socket has its own directly attached DRAM. A core reaching memory on its own socket goes straight through its local controller; reaching memory on another socket requires a trip across the inter-socket link and through the remote controller. The group of cores plus their local memory is called a NUMA node. Remote accesses typically show noticeably higher latency, often in the range of roughly 1.3 to 2 times local, and lower bandwidth, with the exact ratio depending on the platform and how heavily the link is loaded.

about.h: NUMA vs. UMA and vs. clusters
about.p: In a uniform memory access (UMA) system, often a single-socket machine with one memory controller complex, every core sees every address at about the same cost. A cache-coherent NUMA (ccNUMA) system keeps a single shared address space and hardware cache coherence, so unmodified programs run correctly; only their speed depends on where data lives. That distinguishes it from a cluster of separate computers, where each node has a private address space and data must be exchanged explicitly by message passing. Large chiplet-based processors can also expose more than one NUMA node within a single socket.

Linux usually places a page on the node of the thread that first writes it, not the one that allocated it, since malloc only reserves virtual addresses. If a single thread zero-initializes a large array, every page lands on that thread's node, and later parallel loops on other nodes run almost entirely from remote memory, while one memory controller is saturated and the others sit idle. The fix is to initialize data in parallel with the same work partitioning as the computation, so that each thread's portion ends up local to it.

On Linux, numactl --hardware lists the nodes, their memory and a distance table in which local access is conventionally 10 and remote values are larger. The same tool can bind a process to a node's CPUs and memory, or interleave pages across nodes, which suits data that every thread reads evenly. Pinning threads (setting CPU affinity) keeps the scheduler from migrating a thread away from its data and makes benchmarks reproducible. The kernel can also migrate pages automatically toward the threads using them, but explicit placement is more predictable for performance-critical code.

faq.q: How do I check whether my machine is NUMA?
faq.a: On Linux, run lscpu or numactl --hardware; more than one NUMA node listed means memory access cost depends on location. Most dual-socket servers show at least two nodes.

faq.q: Do programs need to be rewritten for NUMA?
faq.a: No, a ccNUMA machine presents one coherent address space, so programs run correctly as is. Rewriting matters only for performance, mainly by keeping each thread's data on its own node.

faq.q: What is the first-touch policy?
faq.a: It is the common rule that a physical page is allocated on the NUMA node of the thread that first writes to it. It is why parallel initialization of arrays matters on NUMA systems.

セマフォ.desc: A synchronization mechanism holding a counter of remaining units: decrement before use (waiting at 0) and increment when done. Used to manage resources with a fixed number of units.

条件変数.desc: A synchronization mechanism that puts a thread to sleep until a condition holds and wakes it on a signal from another thread. The condition must be rechecked after waking.

読み書きロック.desc: A lock that admits any number of readers together but only one writer at a time, excluding everyone else while writing.

トランザクショナルメモリ.desc: A mechanism that runs critical sections speculatively, committing them as a whole if there is no conflict and rolling back and retrying if there is.

SerDes.desc: Serializer/deserializer: a circuit that turns parallel on-chip data into a fast serial bit stream for transmission and restores the parallel data at the receiver. It is the heart of high-speed serial physical layers.

about.p: On chip, data moves over wide, relatively slow buses. A serializer multiplexes that parallel word into one fast bit stream, clocked by a phase-locked loop (PLL) that multiplies a reference clock up to the line rate. Before serializing, data is usually line-coded or scrambled, for example with 8b/10b, 64b/66b or 128b/130b codes, so the stream has frequent transitions and no long DC runs. The output driver then shapes the waveform with feed-forward equalization (pre-emphasis), boosting transitions to offset the high-frequency loss of board traces, cables and connectors.

about.h: The receive side and clock recovery
about.p: No separate clock travels with the data, so the receiver must recover it. Equalizers such as a continuous-time linear equalizer (CTLE) and a decision-feedback equalizer (DFE) undo channel loss and reflections, and a clock and data recovery (CDR) circuit locks a sampling clock to the incoming transitions so each bit is sampled near the center of its eye. The deserializer then rebuilds the original wide words. In multi-lane links, the receiver also deskews and realigns lanes, since each lane recovers its own clock and arrives with a different delay.

Per-lane speed is limited by circuits and channel loss, so high bandwidth comes from both faster lanes and more of them. 100-gigabit Ethernet can be built from four 25 Gb/s lanes, or a single 100 Gb/s lane using four-level pulse-amplitude modulation (PAM4) can carry it. PAM4 sends two bits per symbol, halving the symbol rate compared with two-level NRZ signaling, but its smaller eye openings demand forward error correction. PCI Express, USB, Ethernet, storage links and GPU-to-GPU links all build their physical layers from SerDes lanes.

Testers cannot easily probe tens of gigabits per second directly, so SerDes include built-in test features. In loopback mode, the transmitter sends a pseudo-random bit sequence that is routed back to the receiver, internally or through load-board traces, and on-chip checkers count bit errors. Power is another constant concern, since PLLs, CDRs and equalizers run even when no data flows; link power states such as PCI Express L0s and L1 shut parts down when idle at the cost of exit latency. Linear-drive optics remove the module DSP and rely on host SerDes equalization.

faq.q: What does a SerDes do?
faq.a: It converts wide parallel data into a single high-speed serial stream for transmission and, at the receiver, recovers the clock and converts the stream back into parallel words.

faq.q: Why is serial faster than parallel for chip-to-chip links?
faq.a: Wide parallel buses suffer from skew between wires and need many pins; a serial lane embeds its clock in the data and can be equalized individually, so a few fast lanes outperform many slow wires.

faq.q: What is the difference between NRZ and PAM4 in SerDes?
faq.a: NRZ uses two voltage levels to send one bit per symbol, while PAM4 uses four levels to send two bits per symbol, doubling data rate at the same symbol rate at the cost of noise margin.

差動信号.desc: Signaling that sends opposite signals on two wires and represents 0 and 1 by their voltage difference. Noise picked up equally on both cancels, allowing fast transmission with small swings.

クロック・データ・リカバリ.desc: A receiver circuit that extracts clock timing from transitions in the received data and decides each bit, removing the need for a dedicated clock wire.

about.h: Why recover the clock from the data
about.p: At rates of tens of gigabits per second a bit lasts only tens of picoseconds, and a separately routed clock would arrive with skew relative to the data lanes that consumes a large part of that bit time. High-speed serial links therefore send no clock at all. Each receiver lane includes a clock and data recovery (CDR) circuit that derives timing from the data transitions themselves, so every lane aligns independently. Source-synchronous interfaces such as DDR memory take the other approach and forward a strobe alongside the data.

A CDR is a feedback loop. A phase detector compares where data transitions occur with the local sampling clock and decides whether the clock is early or late; a bang-bang detector of this kind uses samples taken at the bit centers and at the edges. A loop filter smooths these decisions and steers either a voltage-controlled oscillator, as in a PLL-based CDR, or a phase interpolator that rotates the phase of a reference clock. The goal is to sample each bit near the center of the data eye, where the margin is largest.

The phase detector gets information only when the data changes, so long runs of identical bits let the clock drift and also shift the average voltage on AC-coupled links. Line coding guarantees enough transitions. 8b/10b coding maps 8 data bits to 10-bit symbols with balanced ones and zeros and short run lengths, costing 25% extra bits for 80% efficiency; it was used in PCI Express generations 1 and 2 and USB 3.0. Later links use scrambling with lighter framing, such as 128b/130b, which provides transitions statistically with far less overhead.

Transmitter and receiver reference clocks are never exactly equal, so a CDR must track a small frequency offset as well as phase. With spread-spectrum clocking (SSC), the transmit clock is swept slowly by about 0.5% to lower electromagnetic emission peaks, and the CDR must follow that sweep too. Loop bandwidth is a trade-off: jitter slower than the loop bandwidth is tracked out, while faster jitter must fit inside the eye margin. Standards specify jitter tolerance masks that a receiver must meet across frequency.

faq.q: What does a CDR do in a SerDes receiver?
faq.a: It extracts a clock aligned to the incoming bit stream from the data transitions and uses it to sample each bit near the center of the eye, so no separate clock wire is needed.

faq.q: Why do serial links need 8b/10b or 128b/130b encoding?
faq.a: The coding guarantees frequent transitions and DC balance so the receiver's CDR can stay locked and AC-coupled signals stay centered; 128b/130b achieves this with scrambling at much lower overhead than 8b/10b.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CDR and a PLL?
faq.a: A PLL locks an oscillator to a clean periodic reference clock, while a CDR locks to random data, whose transitions occur irregularly; many CDRs are built around a PLL with a phase detector designed for data.

8b/10b符号化.desc: Line coding that sends 8 data bits as a 10-bit code with balanced 0s and 1s and short runs. It eases clock recovery but limits efficiency to 80%.

128b/130b符号化.desc: Line coding that sends 128 data bits with a 2-bit header, about 98.5% efficient, relying on scrambling for transitions. Used from PCI Express 3.0 onward.

about.p: 128b/130b encoding groups data into blocks of 130 bits: a 2-bit sync header followed by a 128-bit payload. Only the header values 01 and 10 are legal, so every block is guaranteed at least one transition at its start, which lets the receiver find block boundaries. The header also tells the receiver whether the payload carries data or an ordered set, the special symbols used for link training and clock compensation. The payload itself is passed through a scrambler, which XORs it with a pseudo-random sequence from a linear feedback shift register, and the receiver descrambles it with the same sequence.

A serial receiver recovers its clock from data transitions and AC-coupled links need roughly equal numbers of ones and zeros. 8b/10b encoding guarantees both by construction: no run longer than five identical bits and a running disparity that keeps the line DC-balanced, at the cost of two extra bits per byte. 128b/130b instead relies on scrambling to make long runs and imbalance statistically very unlikely. The guarantee is weaker, so equalization and clock recovery must tolerate occasional longer runs, but the overhead drops from 20% to about 1.5%.

about.h: What the efficiency means for PCI Express
about.p: Efficiency is 128/130, about 98.5%, versus 80% for 8b/10b. That is why PCI Express 3.0 nearly doubled usable bandwidth while raising the signaling rate only from 5 to 8 GT/s: a PCIe 2.0 lane carries 5 × 0.8 = 4 Gb/s of data, while a PCIe 3.0 lane carries 8 × 128/130 ≈ 7.88 Gb/s, or about 0.985 GB/s. A x16 link therefore gives about 15.8 GB/s in each direction before packet headers and protocol overhead, which reduce the delivered figure somewhat.

128b/130b is used by PCI Express 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0, which kept the encoding while doubling the transfer rate each generation. It belongs to the same family as 64b/66b, used in 10 Gigabit Ethernet, which also pairs a 2-bit sync header with a scrambled payload. PCI Express 6.0 moved to PAM4 signaling with fixed-size flits and forward error correction, so it no longer uses 128b/130b blocks. When comparing link speeds, always check which encoding applies, because the raw rate in GT/s is not the data rate.

faq.q: Why is 128b/130b more efficient than 8b/10b?
faq.a: 8b/10b spends 2 extra bits on every 8 data bits, a 20% overhead, while 128b/130b spends 2 header bits on every 128 data bits, about 1.5%. It can do this because scrambling, rather than the code itself, provides the transitions and balance the receiver needs.

faq.q: What is the sync header in 128b/130b encoding?
faq.a: It is the 2-bit prefix of each 130-bit block, either 01 or 10, which marks the block boundary with a guaranteed transition and indicates whether the block carries data or an ordered set.

faq.q: How much bandwidth does a PCIe 3.0 x16 link have?
faq.a: About 15.8 GB/s in each direction, from 8 GT/s × 128/130 ÷ 8 bits per byte × 16 lanes. Packet overhead makes the usable throughput slightly lower.

PCI Express.desc: A high-speed serial expansion interface connecting the CPU with GPUs, SSDs, network cards and more, also written PCIe. Lanes are bundled for bandwidth, and speed roughly doubles each generation.

about.p: A PCI Express lane is one differential pair for transmitting plus one for receiving, four wires that carry data in both directions at once. Lanes are bundled into links of x1, x4, x8 or x16, with data striped across them so bandwidth scales with lane count. Unlike the old parallel PCI bus, where devices shared one bus and contended for it, PCIe is a tree of point-to-point links: the root complex beside the CPU and memory connects through switches to endpoints, and each link has its bandwidth to itself.

Bandwidth is the per-lane signaling rate times the coding efficiency times the lane count. Generations 1 and 2 used 8b/10b encoding, so a 5 GT/s Gen 2 lane carries 4 Gb/s, or 500 MB/s per direction. From Gen 3 on, 128b/130b encoding with scrambling raised efficiency to about 98.5 percent, so an 8 GT/s Gen 3 x16 link gives about 15.8 GB/s per direction. Signaling rates have roughly doubled each generation, from 8 to 16, 32 and 64 GT/s for Gen 3 through Gen 6. Packet headers make real throughput somewhat lower.

Each lane is driven by a SerDes (serializer/deserializer) that turns wide on-chip buses into a single fast bit stream, while the receiver recovers the clock from the data itself, so transitions must occur often enough. To reach 64 GT/s without raising the symbol rate, Gen 6 switched from two-level NRZ to four-level PAM4, sending two bits per symbol. Squeezing four levels into the same swing leaves about one third of the spacing, roughly 9.5 dB less noise margin, so Gen 6 adds lightweight forward error correction (FEC). At start-up, link training settles on the widest lane count and fastest generation both ends support.

Graphics cards typically use x16 slots, NVMe SSDs x4 and network cards x1 to x8. NVMe, designed for flash over PCIe with many parallel command queues, reaches about 7 GB/s on Gen 4 x4, far beyond SATA's roughly 600 MB/s. For discrete GPUs, data must be copied across PCIe into GPU memory before computing, and PCIe bandwidth is more than ten times lower than the GPU's own memory bandwidth, so offloading pays only when much computation is done per transferred byte or data stays on the GPU.

faq.q: Can an x4 PCIe card work in an x16 slot?
faq.a: Yes. Link training negotiates the largest lane count and speed both sides support, so an x4 card in an x16 slot simply runs with four lanes. The same negotiation lets newer and older generations interoperate at the lower common speed.

faq.q: What is the difference between GT/s and GB/s in PCIe?
faq.a: GT/s is the raw signaling rate per lane, counting encoding overhead, while GB/s is usable data bandwidth. Convert by multiplying by the coding efficiency (0.8 for 8b/10b, about 0.985 for 128b/130b) and the lane count, then dividing by 8.

faq.q: Why did PCIe 6.0 switch to PAM4?
faq.a: Doubling the bit rate with NRZ would require doubling the symbol rate, and channel loss grows sharply with frequency. PAM4 sends two bits per symbol at the same symbol rate as Gen 5, at the cost of smaller noise margin, which FEC compensates for.

PAM4.desc: Four-level pulse amplitude modulation, sending 2 bits per symbol. It doubles the bit rate at the same symbol rate but reduces noise margin.

about.p: Non-return-to-zero (NRZ) signaling uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol. PAM4 uses four evenly spaced levels, so each symbol carries two bits, and the levels are usually Gray-coded (00, 01, 11, 10) so that mistaking a symbol for its neighbor corrupts only one bit. The symbol rate, measured in baud, is therefore half the bit rate: a 106 Gb/s lane runs at about 53 GBd. Halving the symbol rate halves the Nyquist frequency the channel must pass, and because copper traces and connectors lose much more at high frequencies, this is the main reason PAM4 is adopted.

With the same peak-to-peak swing, PAM4 fits three eyes where NRZ has one, so the spacing between adjacent levels is one third. That costs about 9.5 dB of signal-to-noise ratio, which is 20 log10 of 3. PAM4 is also more sensitive to nonlinearity, since the levels must stay evenly spaced, and to reflections and crosstalk. Receivers therefore rely on strong equalization, often with analog-to-digital converters and digital signal processing in high-rate SerDes, and links accept a higher raw bit error rate that forward error correction (FEC) then cleans up.

PCI Express 6.0 moved to PAM4 to reach 64 GT/s at the same symbol rate as the NRZ-based 5.0 generation and added a lightweight FEC to handle the higher raw error rate. High-speed Ethernet electrical lanes and the optical links inside data centers also use it. In intensity modulation with direct detection (IM-DD), the transmitter sets the optical power to four levels and a photodiode converts power directly into current, which keeps transceivers simple and low-power. Long-haul links instead use coherent detection, which also encodes information in the phase and polarization of light.

about.h: When to choose PAM4 over NRZ
about.p: The decision is a trade between channel bandwidth and noise margin. If a channel's loss at the Nyquist frequency needed for NRZ would exceed what equalization can recover, halving that frequency with PAM4 wins despite the smaller eyes. On short, clean channels NRZ remains simpler, more power-efficient and more robust. Higher-order formats such as PAM8 or 16-level schemes push further in the same direction, cutting symbol rate again but shrinking level spacing more, which is why each step up requires better signal-to-noise ratio and more error correction.

faq.q: What is the difference between baud and bit rate in PAM4?
faq.a: Baud counts symbols per second, and each PAM4 symbol carries two bits, so the bit rate is twice the baud rate. A 106 Gb/s PAM4 signal runs at about 53 GBd.

faq.q: Why is PAM4 more susceptible to noise than NRZ?
faq.a: Four levels share the same voltage or optical power swing, so adjacent levels are only one third as far apart as the two NRZ levels. This corresponds to about a 9.5 dB loss in signal-to-noise ratio.

faq.q: Why do PAM4 links need forward error correction?
faq.a: The reduced level spacing makes raw bit errors far more frequent than in comparable NRZ links. FEC lets the receiver correct those errors with modest overhead, so the link still delivers a very low error rate.

NRZ.desc: Non-return-to-zero: the most basic signaling scheme, sending 1 bit per symbol with two voltage levels.

about.p: In NRZ signaling, each bit is sent as one of two levels, for example high for 1 and low for 0, and the level is held for the entire bit period. The name contrasts it with return-to-zero (RZ) coding, in which each pulse returns to a rest level partway through the bit, roughly doubling the required bandwidth. Because NRZ sends 1 bit per symbol, the symbol rate in baud equals the bit rate. In the context of multilevel signaling it is also called PAM2, and in optics it corresponds to on-off keying.

The fastest-changing NRZ pattern, alternating 1010, is a square wave whose fundamental is half the bit rate. This Nyquist frequency is where channel loss is usually quoted: a 32 Gb/s NRZ link has a Nyquist frequency of 16 GHz. NRZ also has strong low-frequency content, since long runs of identical bits contain no transitions and shift the average level. That is why links add line coding or scrambling, to give the receiver's clock recovery enough edges and keep AC-coupled signals balanced.

Four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) carries 2 bits per symbol, so the same bit rate needs only half the symbol rate and half the Nyquist frequency. About 106 Gb/s, for example, needs about 53 GBd in PAM4 but about 106 GBd in NRZ. The price is noise margin: with the same voltage swing, PAM4's three eyes each get about one third of the height, a penalty of roughly 9.5 dB, which raises the bit error rate and makes forward error correction (FEC) necessary. PCI Express 6.0 doubled Gen 5's bit rate this way.

Related schemes appear in many interfaces. NRZI (non-return-to-zero inverted) encodes a 1 or a 0 as the presence or absence of a transition rather than as a level; USB 2.0 uses it, with bit stuffing to limit run length. Plain NRZ remains the simplest, most noise-tolerant choice whenever the channel can support the required Nyquist frequency, and it served PCI Express through generation 5. PAM4 takes over when channel loss at the NRZ Nyquist frequency becomes too high to equalize.

faq.q: What is the difference between NRZ and PAM4?
faq.a: NRZ uses two levels and sends 1 bit per symbol, while PAM4 uses four levels and sends 2 bits per symbol; PAM4 halves the required symbol rate but has about one third the eye height, so it needs error correction.

faq.q: Is the baud rate equal to the bit rate in NRZ?
faq.a: Yes. NRZ carries exactly one bit per symbol, so for example a 10 Gb/s NRZ signal runs at 10 GBd.

faq.q: What is the difference between NRZ and NRZI?
faq.a: NRZ represents bits by the signal level itself, while NRZI represents them by whether the level changes at the start of a bit period, which makes it independent of signal polarity.

ルートコンプレックス.desc: The root of the PCI Express tree, connected to the CPU and memory, from which links fan out through switches to devices (endpoints).
