MSI(メッセージシグナル割り込み).desc: A scheme in which a device signals an interrupt by writing to a designated address. It needs no dedicated interrupt wire and lets one device have many interrupts.

USB PD.desc: A specification in which source and sink negotiate voltage and current over USB, allowing up to 48 V and 240 W.

アイソクロナス転送.desc: A USB transfer type that reserves bandwidth and sends at fixed intervals without retrying on error. Used for audio and video.

ホットプラグ.desc: Connecting and disconnecting devices with power on while the OS automatically recognizes or detaches them. Used with USB, server SSDs and more.

AXI.desc: An on-chip bus from Arm's AMBA specifications that connects blocks in an SoC, with five independent channels and a VALID/READY handshake. Variants include AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream.

about.p: The Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) splits each connection into five one-directional channels: read address, read data, write address, write data and write response. Every channel transfers information with the same VALID/READY handshake, completing a transfer on a clock edge where both signals are high. A sender must not wait for READY before asserting VALID, which avoids deadlock, while a receiver may hold READY low to apply backpressure. Because each channel is a simple handshake, pipeline register slices can be inserted on any of them to ease timing closure without changing behaviour.

A single address handshake can start a burst of many data beats. The address channel carries the start address, burst length, beat size and burst type: fixed for a FIFO-like address, incrementing for ordinary memory blocks, or wrapping for cache-line fills that start at the critical word. In AXI4 an incrementing burst can be up to 256 beats, and a burst must not cross a 4 KB address boundary, so an interconnect never has to split one burst between two targets. Each read beat and each write burst returns a response code indicating success or an error.

Each transaction carries an ID. A manager can issue many requests before earlier ones complete, keeping the bus busy through long memory latency. Transactions with the same ID must complete in order, while different IDs may complete out of order, so a fast peripheral need not wait behind slow DRAM. In an SoC, an interconnect or crossbar decodes addresses, arbitrates between managers such as CPUs and DMA engines, and routes requests to subordinates such as memory controllers, often adding width, clock-domain and protocol converters.

AXI4-Lite keeps the five channels but drops bursts and most transaction options, moving one data word per transaction; it suits control and status registers. AXI4-Stream has no addresses at all: a single TVALID/TREADY channel carries continuous data, with TLAST marking packet ends, and it suits video, signal-processing and network data paths. The Advanced Peripheral Bus (APB), another member of the Arm AMBA specifications, is simpler still and non-pipelined, typically used behind a bridge for slow peripherals. Coherent extensions of AXI add snooping for cache coherency.

faq.q: What is the difference between AXI4, AXI4-Lite and AXI4-Stream?
faq.a: Full AXI4 supports bursts, IDs and multiple outstanding transactions for high-throughput memory traffic. AXI4-Lite handles one word per transaction for register access, and AXI4-Stream drops addresses entirely to carry continuous data flows.

faq.q: Can VALID depend on READY in AXI?
faq.a: No. A sender must assert VALID when it has data, without waiting for READY, otherwise both sides could wait forever. A receiver is allowed to wait for VALID before asserting READY.

faq.q: What is the difference between AXI and APB?
faq.a: AXI is a high-performance, pipelined interface with independent read and write channels and bursts. APB is a simple, low-speed bus for peripheral registers, usually connected to AXI through a bridge.

ネットワークオンチップ.desc: An on-chip interconnect of routers and links arranged as a network that carries data as packets, moving many transfers between blocks simultaneously.

CXL.desc: A standard on the PCI Express physical layer that enables coherent memory sharing between CPUs and accelerators or memory devices.

about.p: PCI Express (PCIe) moves data efficiently, but it does not keep device memory coherent with CPU caches, so software has to copy buffers and flush or invalidate caches to share data with an accelerator. Compute Express Link (CXL) reuses the PCIe physical layer, connectors and electrical signaling and adds protocols that keep caches coherent and let the CPU access device memory with ordinary loads and stores. CXL 1.x and 2.0 run at the PCIe 5.0 rate of 32 GT/s per lane, and CXL 3.x moves to the PCIe 6.0 rate of 64 GT/s.

CXL.io is essentially PCIe and handles device discovery, configuration, interrupts and DMA. CXL.cache lets a device cache CPU memory in its own cache while hardware keeps it coherent. CXL.mem lets the CPU read and write memory attached to the device as if it were part of system memory. Devices are commonly grouped into three types: Type 1 devices such as smart network cards use CXL.io and CXL.cache; Type 2 accelerators with their own memory use all three; Type 3 memory expanders use CXL.io and CXL.mem.

The DRAM a CPU can attach directly is limited by its number of memory channels and DIMM slots. A CXL memory expander adds capacity, and bandwidth, through PCIe-style links, and with CXL switches a pool of memory can be shared among several servers and assigned where it is needed. Access latency is higher than for directly attached DRAM, often compared with reaching memory on another CPU socket, so operating systems usually present CXL memory as a separate NUMA node and use it as a tier, keeping frequently accessed data in local DRAM.

DRAM and NAND flash differ by about 1000 times in access time, tens of nanoseconds versus tens of microseconds, and storage-class memory was proposed to fill that gap. After Intel announced in 2022 that it would discontinue its phase-change-based Optane products, much of this space has been taken by low-latency SLC NAND on the storage side and CXL-attached DRAM on the memory side. CXL also allows memory controllers on the device to use different memory types than the CPU supports natively.

faq.q: What does CXL stand for?
faq.a: CXL stands for Compute Express Link, an open interconnect standard built on the PCI Express physical layer that adds cache-coherent memory access between CPUs, accelerators and memory devices.

faq.q: What is the difference between CXL and PCIe?
faq.a: They share the same physical layer and slots, but plain PCIe transfers are not cache coherent. CXL adds the CXL.cache and CXL.mem protocols so devices and CPUs can share memory coherently with load/store semantics.

faq.q: What is a CXL Type 3 device?
faq.a: A Type 3 device is a memory expander that uses CXL.io and CXL.mem to give the host additional memory capacity, without caching host memory itself.

イコライザ.desc: A circuit that compensates for a channel attenuating high frequencies more, which smears the signal. Examples include receiver CTLE and DFE and transmitter de-emphasis.

アイパターン.desc: A plot overlaying many bit periods of a waveform. The height of the central eye shows noise margin and its width shows timing margin.

ビット誤り率.desc: The fraction of transmitted bits received incorrectly. High-speed serial links typically require values such as 10^-12 or lower.

特性インピーダンス.desc: The ratio of voltage to current seen by a wave traveling along a transmission line, set by trace width and layer spacing. Changes along the path cause reflections.

リタイマ.desc: A circuit that receives a high-speed serial signal, decides the bits and retransmits a clean signal. Inserted mid-channel to extend reach.

スペクトラム拡散クロック.desc: Slowly varying a clock's frequency slightly to spread electromagnetic emission energy across a wider band and lower its peaks.

クレジット方式のフロー制御.desc: A scheme in which the receiver advertises free buffer space as credits and the sender transmits only within them, so buffers never overflow.

GPIO.desc: General-purpose input/output: microcontroller pins that software can configure as inputs or outputs, used for reading switches, lighting LEDs and so on.

about.p: GPIO pins are controlled by a GPIO controller inside the microcontroller or SoC. The basic registers are a direction register that sets each pin as input or output, an output data register that holds the value to drive, and an input data register for reading the pin voltage. Other registers select internal pull-up or pull-down resistors, the output type (push-pull or open-drain), and output drive strength and slew rate. On many microcontrollers you can also choose whether a pin acts as GPIO or as a pin of another peripheral such as a UART or SPI. Some controllers provide set and reset registers that force only specific bits to 1 or 0, so bits can be changed safely without reading back the others.

about.h: Using a pin as an input
about.p: Input pins often use noise-tolerant Schmitt triggers, and the controller synchronizes the value to its clock before reading it. A pin connected to nothing has no defined voltage, so its value can change randomly and short-circuit current can flow; a pull-up or pull-down fixes its level. Mechanical switch contacts bounce, flipping between 0 and 1 several times (contact bounce), which is removed by waiting a set time in software or by filtering. Most GPIO controllers can raise interrupts on rising or falling edges or on levels, which can also wake the chip from low-power states.

A push-pull output actively drives the pin both toward the supply and toward ground, while an open-drain output drives only low and relies on a pull-up resistor for high. GPIO pins can supply only small currents, and the datasheet sets limits both per pin and for all pins combined. LEDs are connected with a series resistor to limit current. Loads needing large currents, such as motors and relays, and inductive loads such as coils are driven through a transistor or driver IC, with a diode to protect against back EMF. Applying a voltage above the supply to a pin forces current through its protection diodes, which can cause malfunction or damage.

On SoCs running Linux and similar systems, a pin controller assigns pin functions and the GPIO controller driver handles GPIO input and output, with pin usage described in a device tree or similar. From Linux applications, the current standard approach is a library such as libgpiod that uses the GPIO character device; the older sysfs interface is deprecated. When pins run short, GPIO expanders connected over I2C or SPI add more. Because going through the OS adds response delay, signals that need precise timing are usually generated by dedicated peripherals.

faq.q: What is GPIO?
faq.a: GPIO stands for general-purpose input/output: pins that software can configure as either inputs or outputs. They are widely used for signals without a fixed purpose, such as reading switch states, lighting LEDs, or sending reset or select signals to other ICs.

faq.q: What is a GPIO controller?
faq.a: It is the circuit that controls a group of GPIO pins, with registers setting each pin's direction, output value, input value, pull-up or pull-down and interrupt conditions. The CPU operates the pins by reading and writing these registers. GPIO expanders attached over I2C or SPI are also treated as a kind of GPIO controller.

faq.q: Can a GPIO pin drive a motor directly?
faq.a: Generally no. GPIO pins can supply only small currents, while motors need large currents and produce back EMF when they stop, which can damage the pin. Drive them through a transistor or motor driver IC, adding a protection diode where needed.

プルアップ抵抗.desc: A resistor connecting a signal line to the supply so it rests at logic 1 when nothing drives it. It keeps input pins from floating and is used on I2C lines and elsewhere.

about.h: Why inputs need a defined level
about.p: A CMOS input draws almost no current, so if nothing drives it, its voltage is undefined. Coupled noise or even a nearby hand can make it read 0 and 1 at random, and an input resting at an intermediate voltage can turn on both transistors of the input stage, wasting shoot-through current. A pull-up resistor connects the line to the supply so it reads 1 by default. A switch wired from the pin to ground then reads 1 when open and 0 when pressed. A pull-down resistor does the mirror-image job.

An open-drain (or open-collector) output can only pull a line to ground or release it; it never drives high. The pull-up resistor supplies the high level. When several such outputs share one line, the line is high only if all of them release it and goes low if any one pulls down, forming a wired-AND. Multiple devices can therefore drive the line simultaneously without damaging each other, which is why I²C, shared interrupt lines and reset lines use this arrangement. Pulling up to a different supply also provides simple level shifting.

The rising edge is an RC charge of the line capacitance through the pull-up, so the time constant is R × C: 10 kΩ and 100 pF give 1 µs, with the 10–90% rise taking about 2.2 time constants. A smaller resistor speeds this up, but whenever an output holds the line low, current V/R flows, for example 3.3 mA from 3.3 V through 1 kΩ. That current must stay within the sink current at which the datasheet guarantees the low output voltage VOL, and it wastes power. Buses like I²C specify both maximum rise time and sink current.

A pull-up is deliberately weak, so any active driver can override it; it only sets the default state. A push-pull output, by contrast, actively drives both high and low with low impedance and must never be tied to another push-pull output. Most microcontrollers offer internal pull-ups, typically in the tens of kilohms, which are fine for buttons but often too weak for fast buses that need external resistors. Pull-ups and pull-downs also hold enable, reset and configuration pins in a known state during power-up.

faq.q: Why do I2C lines need pull-up resistors?
faq.a: I²C devices have open-drain outputs that can only pull SDA and SCL low, so external pull-ups are needed to create the high level and allow several devices to share the lines safely.

faq.q: What happens if a pull-up resistor value is too small?
faq.a: Edges get faster, but more current flows whenever a device holds the line low, which wastes power and can push the low voltage above its specified VOL if the driver's sink rating is exceeded.

faq.q: What happens if a microcontroller input is left floating?
faq.a: The pin's level is undefined, so noise makes it read 0 and 1 unpredictably and an intermediate voltage can cause extra current in the input buffer; a pull-up or pull-down resistor fixes it.

チャタリング.desc: The rapid on-off flickering of a mechanical switch's contacts when pressed or released, removed by debouncing.

デバウンス.desc: Processing that removes switch bounce, by software that accepts a change only after repeated identical readings or by hardware filtering.

プリスケーラ.desc: A circuit that divides the clock fed to a timer or similar by a fixed ratio, bringing a fast clock into a range the timer can count.
プリスケーラ.title: Prescaler: Clock Divider for Timers and Counters
プリスケーラ.description: A prescaler divides a fast clock by a fixed ratio so a timer or counter can handle it. How it works and how the ratio trades timing resolution for range.

about.p: A prescaler is a circuit placed in front of a timer or counter that divides the input clock by a fixed ratio N. For example, dividing a 16 MHz clock by 16 gives 1 MHz, so one timer count is 1 µs. Setting an interrupt every 1000 counts then gives an interrupt every 1 ms. Because a counter has a limited number of bits, counting a fast clock directly makes it wrap around quickly, so long intervals cannot be measured. Coarsening the tick with a prescaler matches the counter's range to the time needed.

A larger division ratio lengthens the time that can be measured but coarsens the time per count (resolution). With a 16-bit counter at 1 µs per count, the counter wraps after about 65.5 ms. The timer period is division ratio × count ÷ input clock frequency. Configuration differs by microcontroller: some choose from fixed values such as 1, 8, 64, 256 and 1024 (as on AVR), while others allow any ratio through a 16-bit register. Some, like STM32 timers, divide by the register value plus 1, so checking the datasheet is important.

Power-of-two division can be done with a counter made of a few chained flip-flops, each stage halving the frequency. To divide by an arbitrary ratio N, a counter resets to 0 after counting to N−1 and emits a pulse at that point. In synchronous microcontroller designs, the divided signal is often not used as a new clock but fed to the timer as an enable signal synchronized to the original clock that is active once every N cycles, avoiding clock skew and multiple-clock-domain problems. The same idea is used to generate ADC clocks, watchdog timer ticks and UART baud rates.

In radio frequency synthesizers, prescalers matter in another sense. VCO outputs are in the GHz range, too fast for a counter with a freely programmable division ratio to run at directly, so a fast prescaler first divides by a fixed ratio P and a slower counter then counts the result. To allow fine selection of the division ratio, a dual-modulus prescaler that can switch between dividing by P and P+1 is used, with a swallow counter setting how many times it divides by P+1, so the overall ratio can be set in steps of 1 as P × N + A. Prescalers are also used to extend the range of frequency counters.

faq.q: What is a prescaler?
faq.a: It is a circuit that divides the clock fed to a timer or counter by a fixed ratio. It coarsens the tick of a clock that is too fast so the time until the counter wraps matches the length needed. The correct English spelling is prescaler.

faq.q: What is the difference between a prescaler and a postscaler?
faq.a: A prescaler divides the clock before the counter, changing the time per count. A postscaler sits after the counter and counts matches or wraparounds to thin out interrupts and similar events, changing only how often they occur. Some timers have both, such as Timer2 on PIC microcontrollers.

faq.q: How do I calculate prescaler settings?
faq.a: Multiply the desired period by the input clock frequency to get the number of clock cycles needed, then split it into division ratio × count that fits the counter's range. For example, 1 ms at 16 MHz is 16000 cycles, which can be a divide-by-16 prescaler and 1000 counts. Watch out for schemes in which the value written to the register is N−1.

PWM(パルス幅変調).desc: A method that adjusts average voltage or power by varying the high time of an output while keeping the period constant. Used to dim LEDs and control motor speed.

about.p: Pulse-width modulation (PWM) keeps the switching period T fixed and varies the high time t_on. The duty cycle D = t_on/T sets the average output, which is D times the pulse amplitude: a 5 V signal at 40% duty averages 2 V. The information is carried entirely in the timing, so the output stage only ever sits at two levels. A load that responds slowly compared with the period, such as a motor, a heater, the human eye looking at an LED, or an RC or LC filter, sees mainly this average value.

about.h: How a microcontroller timer generates PWM
about.p: A hardware timer counts clock pulses from zero up to a period value and then restarts. The output is set at the start of each period and cleared when the counter matches a compare register. With a period of 1000 counts and a compare value of 250, the output is high 25% of the time. Resolution is set by the number of counts per period, so for a fixed timer clock, higher PWM frequency means coarser duty steps. Once configured, the timer runs without CPU involvement. Analog PWM circuits do the same job by comparing a control voltage with a triangle or sawtooth wave.

The switching transistor is either fully on, with little voltage across it, or fully off, with almost no current, so it dissipates far less power than a transistor held at an intermediate voltage in a linear circuit. Losses come mainly from on-resistance and the brief transitions between states. The frequency is chosen for the load: high enough that LED flicker is not visible and motor current is smoothed by winding inductance, and often above the audible range to avoid motor whine, but not so high that switching losses dominate.

about.h: PWM as a DAC and in power electronics
about.p: Passing PWM through a low-pass filter gives a crude digital-to-analog converter without dedicated DAC hardware; placing the PWM frequency well above the filter cutoff reduces ripple, at the cost of slower response. The same principle runs switch-mode power supplies, where an ideal buck converter outputs D times its input voltage, and inverters, which switch power devices at several kHz to tens of kHz while varying pulse widths to synthesize AC. A three-phase motor inverter uses six switches, two per leg.

faq.q: How do you calculate PWM duty cycle?
faq.a: Divide the high time by the period: duty cycle = t_on / T. For example, 250 counts high out of a 1000-count period is 25%, and the average output is 25% of the pulse amplitude.

faq.q: Does PWM change the frequency or the voltage?
faq.a: Neither, in its basic form: frequency and pulse amplitude stay constant and only the pulse width changes. The average voltage or power delivered to the load changes because the fraction of on time changes.

faq.q: Why is PWM more efficient than a linear regulator for driving a motor?
faq.a: A linear regulator drops the excess voltage across a transistor that carries full current, wasting it as heat. With PWM the transistor is either fully on or fully off, so its voltage-current product, and thus its loss, stays small.

デューティ比.desc: The fraction of each period during which a periodic pulse signal is high. In PWM it sets the average power.

about.p: Duty cycle D is the high time divided by the period, D = t_high / T, usually expressed in percent. A signal with a 1000-count period that is high for 250 counts has D = 25%. For a pulse switching between 0 and an amplitude V, the average value is D × V, which is why duty cycle is the knob for average power. Duty cycle and frequency are independent: two signals at the same frequency can have very different duty cycles, and changing the period while keeping the high time fixed changes the duty cycle.

Pulse-width modulation (PWM) keeps the period fixed and varies the high time. A microcontroller timer compares its counter with a compare register and toggles the output, so PWM runs continuously without CPU involvement, and the counter range sets the resolution. Passing PWM through a low-pass filter yields roughly D times the amplitude, about 2 V for 40% of 5 V, giving a crude DAC. Placing the PWM frequency well above the filter cutoff reduces ripple at the cost of slower response. LED dimming and motor speed control often use the pulses directly, relying on the load or the eye to average.

Switching DC-DC converters regulate output through duty cycle. In an ideal buck converter operating in continuous conduction, Vout = D × Vin, so 12 V at D = 0.25 gives 3 V; an inductor and capacitor smooth the switched waveform into DC. An ideal boost converter gives Vout = Vin / (1 − D), doubling the input at D = 0.5, because the inductor's stored energy adds to the input when the switch opens. Real converters deviate because of switch and inductor losses, which is why feedback continuously adjusts duty cycle.

For clocks, a 50% duty cycle matters whenever both edges are used. A path launched on a rising edge and captured on the falling edge gets only half a period: with a 2.0 ns clock and 0.1 ns setup time, at most 0.9 ns remains for clock-to-output and logic delay, and any duty-cycle distortion shrinks it further. Clock-gating checks likewise require an AND-gate enable to change only while the clock is low. A toggle flip-flop dividing by two naturally produces an exact 50% duty cycle, a common way to clean up a clock.

faq.q: How do you calculate duty cycle?
faq.a: Divide the time the signal is high by the full period and multiply by 100%. For example, 2 µs high in a 10 µs period is a 20% duty cycle.

faq.q: Does changing the duty cycle change the frequency?
faq.a: Not necessarily. In standard PWM the period stays fixed and only the high time changes, so frequency is constant while duty cycle varies.

faq.q: What output voltage does a buck converter give for a given duty cycle?
faq.a: Ideally Vout = D × Vin in continuous conduction, so a 50% duty cycle from 12 V gives 6 V. Losses make the required duty cycle slightly higher in practice.

インプットキャプチャ.desc: A timer function in which hardware records the counter value at the instant an input signal changes, allowing precise measurement of pulse width or frequency.

UART.desc: A circuit for asynchronous serial communication without a clock wire, in which both sides agree on a baud rate and characters are framed by start and stop bits.

about.p: A UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter) sends bytes one bit at a time over a transmit line and receives on a separate line, sharing only a ground with the other device. No clock is sent. The line idles at logic 1; a character begins with a start bit of 0, followed by usually eight data bits sent least significant bit first, an optional parity bit and one or more stop bits at 1. The most common format is written 8N1: eight data bits, no parity, one stop bit. Both ends must be configured to the same baud rate in advance, such as 9600 or 115200 bits per second.

Framing costs bandwidth: an 8N1 character takes ten bit times for eight bits of data. At 115200 bps that gives 115200 / 10 = 11,520 bytes per second, about 87 µs per byte, so heavy logging can stall a program. The receiver synchronizes on the falling edge of each start bit, typically by sampling the line at 16 times the baud rate, and then samples each bit near its center using its own clock. Any rate mismatch accumulates, and once the drift reaches half a bit by the stop bit the character is corrupted, so the combined error of both ends must stay within a few percent.

UART is the simplest of the common on-board serial links: two signal wires, point to point, with no clock and little protocol. SPI (serial peripheral interface) is synchronous, with a shared clock, data in each direction and a chip-select line per device, which allows clock rates of tens of megahertz but adds a wire for each additional device. I2C (inter-integrated circuit) connects many devices on two open-drain wires using addresses, at a few hundred kilohertz to a few megahertz. Choose UART to link two devices simply, SPI for speed and I2C for many devices on few wires.

Almost every microcontroller includes one or more UARTs, alongside SPI, I2C and often CAN. They provide debug consoles, connect GPS receivers, cellular and wireless modules, and serve as a recovery path through which a bootloader receives new firmware. The UART itself works at logic levels; standards such as RS-232 and RS-485 add line drivers with different voltage levels or differential signaling for longer cables. Because characters can arrive at any time, practical drivers use receive FIFOs with interrupts or DMA so that no byte is lost while the processor is busy.

faq.q: What does UART stand for?
faq.a: UART stands for universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter. It is the hardware block that converts bytes to and from a serial bit stream framed by start and stop bits, without a shared clock.

faq.q: How many bytes per second can a 115200 baud UART send?
faq.a: With 8N1 framing each byte takes 10 bits, so 115200 bps carries about 11,520 bytes per second, roughly 87 µs per byte. Adding parity or a second stop bit lowers this further.

faq.q: Why do both sides of a UART link need the same baud rate?
faq.a: No clock is transmitted, so the receiver times each bit with its own clock after the start bit. If the rates differ by more than a few percent, the sampling point drifts by half a bit or more before the end of the frame and bits are misread.

ボーレート.desc: The number of symbols sent per second in serial communication; for a UART it equals bits per second and must match on both sides.

SPI.desc: Serial Peripheral Interface: synchronous serial communication in which data is exchanged in both directions on a master-driven clock, with devices selected by chip-select lines. Used for fast parts.

about.p: SPI uses a clock (SCLK) driven by the master, a master-to-slave data line (MOSI, also called COPI or SDO), a slave-to-master line (MISO, also CIPO or SDI) and an active-low chip select (CS) per slave. Inside, master and slave each hold a shift register, and the two registers form a ring: on every clock one bit leaves the master while one bit enters it. Transfers are therefore always full duplex. To read from a device, the master must still clock out bytes, often dummy ones. SPI has no addresses and no acknowledge; selecting a device is done purely with its CS line.

about.h: Clock polarity and phase: the four modes
about.p: Two settings define an SPI mode. CPOL sets the idle level of the clock, and CPHA chooses whether data is sampled on the first or second clock edge after CS goes active. The four combinations are modes 0 to 3; in mode 0 the clock idles low and data is sampled on the rising edge, and in mode 3 it idles high and is also sampled on the rising edge. If master and device disagree, sampling shifts by half a clock period and bits are shifted or garbled, so the datasheet's mode, bit order and maximum clock rate are the first things to check.

SPI's push-pull outputs and dedicated lines allow clock rates of tens of MHz, which is why flash memory, displays and fast ADCs use it. The cost is wiring: every additional device needs another CS line. I2C shares two open-drain lines with pull-up resistors among many devices, selects them by address and acknowledges each byte, but the pull-ups limit it to a few hundred kHz to a few MHz. A UART links just two devices asynchronously, with no clock wire, relying on both sides agreeing on the baud rate. The choice depends on speed, pin count and what the parts support.

Serial flash and some displays extend the basic scheme. Dual and quad SPI turn the data lines into two or four bidirectional lines, multiplying throughput for reads, and some microcontrollers can execute code directly from quad SPI flash. Several devices can also be daisy-chained, passing data through each shift register in turn so they share one CS. Because SPI has no built-in flow control or error checking, protocols built on top often add status registers, busy flags or checksums.

faq.q: How many wires does SPI need?
faq.a: Basic SPI uses four signals, SCLK, MOSI, MISO and CS, plus ground. Each additional slave normally needs its own CS line, while three-wire variants combine the two data lines into one.

faq.q: What is SPI mode 0?
faq.a: Mode 0 means CPOL = 0 and CPHA = 0: the clock idles low and data is sampled on the rising edge. It is the most widely supported mode, but the device datasheet decides which mode must be used.

faq.q: Is SPI faster than I2C?
faq.a: Generally yes. SPI's push-pull signaling commonly runs at tens of MHz, while open-drain I2C buses typically run from about 100 kHz to a few MHz.

I2C.desc: A synchronous serial bus connecting several devices on two wires, clock (SCL) and data (SDA), selecting the partner by address. The lines are open-drain with pull-ups.

about.p: I2C (inter-integrated circuit) connects a controller and many target devices (historically called master and slaves) with just two lines: a serial clock, SCL, and serial data, SDA. Every device drives the lines only through open-drain outputs, which can pull a line low or release it; pull-up resistors return released lines high. This wired-AND arrangement means no two devices can fight with opposite levels. The pull-up value is a trade-off: smaller resistors charge the bus capacitance faster for cleaner rising edges but waste more current when a line is held low. Common speed grades are 100 kHz standard mode, 400 kHz fast mode and 1 MHz fast mode plus.

A transfer begins with a START condition, SDA falling while SCL is high; otherwise SDA may change only while SCL is low. The controller then sends a 7-bit address and a read/write bit. On the ninth clock of every byte, the receiver acknowledges by pulling SDA low (ACK); if SDA stays high, that is a NACK. Data bytes follow, each with its own acknowledge, and a STOP condition, SDA rising while SCL is high, ends the transfer. Reading a sensor register usually writes the register number first, then issues a repeated START to switch direction without releasing the bus.

Open-drain lines also let devices cooperate. A slow target can hold SCL low after a byte, known as clock stretching, and the controller waits until the line is released. When two controllers start at once, each watches SDA while transmitting; a controller that releases SDA for a 1 but sees it held at 0 knows another device is sending a 0, and it backs off. The winner's message is never corrupted. When troubleshooting, a missing ACK after the address points to a wrong address, a missing or unpowered device, or broken wiring.

about.h: Address conflicts and I2C versus SPI
about.p: Because devices are selected by address, two identical parts with the same fixed address cannot share a bus. Many parts provide address-select pins that change the low bits when tied to supply or ground; otherwise use a second I2C peripheral or an I2C multiplexer. Compared with SPI, which uses push-pull lines and a chip-select per device to reach tens of MHz, I2C is slower but needs only two wires however many devices are attached.

faq.q: Why does I2C need pull-up resistors?
faq.a: I2C devices use open-drain outputs that can only pull a line low, so resistors are needed to bring SDA and SCL back high when no device is driving them. Without pull-ups the lines would float and the bus would not work.

faq.q: How fast is I2C?
faq.a: Standard mode runs at up to 100 kHz, fast mode at 400 kHz and fast mode plus at 1 MHz, with a less common high-speed mode at 3.4 MHz. Actual speed is also limited by bus capacitance and pull-up strength.

faq.q: What is the difference between I2C and SPI?
faq.a: I2C shares two open-drain wires among many devices and selects them by address, which saves pins but limits speed. SPI uses a clock, separate data-in and data-out lines and a chip-select per device, allowing much higher speeds at the cost of more wires.

ポーリング.desc: A method in which the CPU repeatedly checks a peripheral's status to detect changes. Simple, but it consumes time and power even when nothing happens.

about.p: With polling, the CPU learns about a peripheral by reading its status register in a loop, for example checking a UART's "receive data ready" flag until it is set and then reading the byte. The check may be a tight busy-wait or a periodic test inside the main loop or a timer routine. Polling is simple to write and debug, and the timing is predictable because checks happen exactly where the program places them. In C, the register pointer must be declared volatile so the compiler actually re-reads the hardware on each pass instead of reusing a cached value.

With interrupts, the peripheral signals the CPU when something happens; the CPU suspends its current work, saves its state, runs a handler and resumes. That leaves the CPU free to do other work or sleep while waiting, which matters for battery-powered devices. Polling spends CPU time and energy even when nothing has changed, and its worst-case reaction time is set by the polling interval. Each interrupt, on the other hand, carries fixed overhead for entering and leaving the handler, which polling avoids.

about.h: When polling is the better choice
about.p: Polling wins when events are so frequent that per-interrupt overhead would dominate. High-speed network processing is the classic case: under heavy load, drivers switch from an interrupt per packet to polling batches of packets, and some packet-processing frameworks dedicate cores to continuous polling. Polling also suits very short waits, such as a status flag that will be ready within a few cycles, simple boot code where interrupts are not yet configured, and control loops that must sample at strictly fixed instants.

Real systems often combine the two. An interrupt wakes the CPU from sleep, and the handler then polls to drain all pending data before re-enabling the interrupt, so a burst of events costs one interrupt rather than many. DMA (direct memory access) reduces the need for either by moving data without CPU involvement and signalling only when a whole block is complete. Care is needed with status registers whose flags are cleared by the act of reading them, because an extra read can silently discard an event.

faq.q: What is the difference between polling and interrupts?
faq.a: With polling, the CPU repeatedly checks a device's status; with interrupts, the device notifies the CPU when its status changes. Polling is simpler and predictable, while interrupts let the CPU do other work or sleep in the meantime.

faq.q: Why should a polled register be declared volatile in C?
faq.a: Without volatile, the compiler may assume the value cannot change and read it only once, turning the polling loop into an infinite loop. Volatile forces a fresh read of the hardware register on every iteration.

faq.q: Is polling always inefficient?
faq.a: No. When events arrive at a very high rate, polling avoids the save-and-restore overhead of each interrupt and can process events in batches, making it more efficient than interrupts.

スーパーループ.desc: A firmware structure without an OS in which an infinite loop in main calls each task in turn, with urgent work done in interrupts.

RTOS(リアルタイムOS).desc: An embedded OS that switches tasks by priority so the system responds within set time limits, such as FreeRTOS and Zephyr.

about.p: A real-time operating system (RTOS) organizes firmware into tasks, each with a priority and a state such as ready, running or blocked. Most RTOSes use preemptive priority scheduling: when an interrupt or a message makes a higher-priority task ready, the kernel saves the running task's context and switches immediately, and the interrupted task later resumes where it stopped. A periodic tick from a hardware timer, often 1 ms, drives timeouts and delays; for example, 16 MHz divided by a prescaler of 16 gives 1 µs counts, and an interrupt every 1000 counts gives the 1 ms tick.

about.h: Real-time means predictable, not just fast
about.p: The goal is a bounded, predictable response time for critical work such as motor control or communication protocols, not maximum average throughput. A general-purpose OS optimizes fairness and throughput and may delay a task unpredictably; an RTOS keeps its kernel small and its scheduling decisions deterministic, which also lets it run on microcontrollers with little memory. Without any OS, firmware often uses a super loop: a while (1) loop calls each job in turn while interrupts handle urgent events and set flags. It is simple and lean, but one slow job delays everything, which is when an RTOS becomes worthwhile.

An RTOS supplies primitives so tasks can cooperate without busy-waiting. A message queue lets a sensor task post readings while a display task sleeps in the blocked state, using no CPU, until data arrives; buffering several items absorbs temporary speed differences so nothing is lost. Mutexes protect shared resources such as a bus or a buffer, semaphores signal events, often from interrupt handlers, and timed waits let a task block with a timeout. Using these instead of shared variables and polled flags avoids data races and wasted cycles.

Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority task waits for a mutex held by a low-priority task, and an unrelated medium-priority task preempts the low one. The low task cannot finish and release the mutex, so the high task is effectively blocked by the medium task for an unbounded time. This caused repeated system resets on the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997. Priority inheritance fixes it by temporarily raising the mutex holder to the waiting task's priority until it releases the resource, and many RTOS mutexes provide it as a built-in option.

faq.q: What is the difference between an RTOS and a general-purpose OS like Linux?
faq.a: An RTOS is designed for predictable worst-case response times with strict priority-based preemption and a small footprint. A general-purpose OS optimizes average throughput and fairness and offers richer services but less timing determinism.

faq.q: What is priority inversion in an RTOS?
faq.a: A high-priority task is stuck waiting for a resource held by a low-priority task, which is itself starved by a medium-priority task. Priority inheritance temporarily boosts the holder to prevent this.

faq.q: When should I use an RTOS instead of a super loop?
faq.a: When there are several activities with different timing requirements and a long job in a super loop would delay time-critical work. Simple, lightly loaded firmware is often fine with a super loop and interrupts.

優先度逆転.desc: A situation in which a high-priority task waiting for a resource held by a low-priority task is held up because a medium-priority task preempts the low one.

about.p: Consider three tasks in a preemptive real-time operating system (RTOS): high (H), medium (M) and low (L) priority. L locks a mutex protecting a shared resource. H becomes ready, needs the same mutex and blocks, waiting for L to release it. Now M, which has nothing to do with the resource, becomes ready. Because M outranks L, the scheduler runs M and L cannot reach the point where it releases the mutex. As long as M keeps running, H waits as well, so in effect a medium-priority task is delaying the highest-priority task, inverting the intended order.

Some blocking is unavoidable whenever tasks share a resource: if L holds the mutex, H must wait for L to finish its critical section. That delay is bounded by the length of the critical section and can be included in timing analysis. The problem is the medium-priority interference, which makes the delay unbounded, since any number of medium tasks can run in between. In a hard real-time system, where deadlines must be guaranteed, an unbounded delay can mean a missed deadline, a watchdog reset or unsafe behavior, which is why the issue receives so much attention.

Priority inheritance fixes the problem dynamically: when H blocks on a mutex held by L, L temporarily takes on H's priority, so M cannot preempt it. L finishes its critical section, releases the mutex, drops back to its own priority, and H runs. Many RTOS mutexes provide this option. The priority ceiling protocol is a static alternative: each mutex is assigned the priority of the highest task that may use it, and any task locking it is raised to that ceiling immediately. Ceiling protocols also prevent certain deadlocks, at the cost of analyzing which tasks use which resources.

A well-known example occurred on the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997. After landing, the spacecraft suffered repeated system resets. A high-priority task was waiting for a mutex held by a low-priority task, which was in turn preempted by medium-priority work, until a watchdog timer noticed that a periodic task had not completed in time and reset the system. Engineers reproduced the problem on a ground replica and fixed it by enabling priority inheritance on the mutex involved. Keeping critical sections short and minimizing resources shared across priority levels remain useful design rules.

faq.q: What is priority inversion in an RTOS?
faq.a: It is a situation in which a high-priority task waits for a resource held by a low-priority task, and a medium-priority task preempts the low one, so the high-priority task is effectively delayed by the medium one. The delay can become unbounded.

faq.q: What is the difference between priority inheritance and priority ceiling?
faq.a: Priority inheritance raises a lock holder's priority only when a higher-priority task actually blocks on that lock. Priority ceiling raises any task to a preset ceiling priority as soon as it takes the lock, which also helps prevent deadlocks.

faq.q: How was priority inversion fixed on Mars Pathfinder?
faq.a: The repeated resets were traced to priority inversion on a shared mutex, and engineers fixed them by enabling priority inheritance on that mutex in the flight software.

優先度継承.desc: Temporarily raising a low-priority task holding a resource to the priority of the high-priority task waiting for it, preventing priority inversion.

ハードリアルタイム.desc: A strict timing requirement in which missing a deadline even once is a system failure, as in automotive brake or airbag control. Where occasional lateness is acceptable, it is soft real-time.

ウォッチドッグタイマ.desc: A timer that resets the microcontroller if software does not kick it within a set time, recovering from runaway or hung programs.

about.p: A watchdog is a down-counter that runs independently of the program it supervises. Software must periodically "kick", "feed" or "service" it, typically by writing a specific key value to a register, which reloads the counter. If the counter reaches zero because the code has hung in a loop, crashed into a fault handler or been upset by noise, the watchdog asserts a reset (on some parts, first an early-warning interrupt) and the microcontroller restarts from a known state. Clocking it from its own low-speed oscillator means a failed main clock does not silence it as well.

A watchdog is only as good as the place where it is kicked. Kicking it unconditionally inside a periodic timer interrupt is a classic mistake: the interrupt keeps firing even when the main loop is stuck, so the counter never expires and the hang goes unnoticed. A better pattern has each task or main-loop stage set a check-in flag, and a supervisor routine kicks the watchdog only when every flag has been set within the period, then clears them. The timeout is chosen longer than the worst-case loop time but short enough to bound recovery time.

A standard watchdog only catches kicks that arrive too late. If a fault makes the program skip most of its work and spin in a short loop that still contains the kick, the timer is serviced more often than expected and nothing is detected. A window watchdog adds a lower bound: kicks are accepted only inside a defined time window, and a kick that comes too early is treated as a fault just like a missing one. This catches control-flow errors that a simple timeout misses, which is why window watchdogs are common in functional-safety designs.

In automotive and industrial equipment the watchdog is often placed in a separate supervisor or power-management IC running on its own clock, so a common cause such as a failed oscillator cannot stop both the processor and its monitor. Some external monitors use question-and-answer schemes in which the processor must return the correct response to a challenge within a time window. After a watchdog reset, firmware usually reads a reset-cause register so the event can be logged and analyzed instead of silently repeating.

faq.q: What does it mean to kick or feed a watchdog timer?
faq.a: It means writing to the watchdog's reload or service register so its counter restarts before it expires. Healthy software does this periodically; if it stops doing so, the watchdog resets the chip.

faq.q: Should I kick the watchdog inside a timer interrupt?
faq.a: Not unconditionally. A timer interrupt keeps running even when the main code is hung, so it would hide the fault; kick only after confirming that the main loop and each task have completed a normal cycle.

faq.q: What is the difference between a window watchdog and a normal watchdog?
faq.a: A normal watchdog resets only when the kick comes too late. A window watchdog also treats a kick that arrives too early as a fault, catching code that is looping abnormally fast.

ブートローダ.desc: A small program that runs first at power-on, verifying and starting the main firmware or updating it with new firmware.

about.p: After reset, a processor starts executing from a fixed address, and in many embedded devices the code there is the bootloader rather than the application. It initializes the minimum hardware it needs, checks whether a valid application image is present, usually by validating a header plus a CRC or signature, and then jumps to the application's entry point, typically after setting up the stack pointer and interrupt vector table. If no valid image exists, or an update has been requested, it stays in control and waits for new firmware instead.

about.h: Field updates and protecting the bootloader
about.p: A bootloader can receive firmware over UART, USB, CAN, Ethernet or a radio link and write it into flash, so products can be fixed after shipping without a hardware programmer. Because a corrupted bootloader would leave the device unrecoverable, or "bricked", it normally sits in a write-protected flash region and is excluded from updates. Many microcontrollers also contain a vendor bootloader in ROM, selected with a boot-mode pin, which is handy for first programming and for recovering a board whose flash is blank or damaged.

about.h: A/B slots for safe OTA updates
about.p: Overwriting the running firmware in place is risky: losing power or connectivity halfway leaves no bootable image. Over-the-air (OTA) designs therefore split flash into two slots. The new image is written into the inactive slot and verified, and only then does the bootloader switch which slot it boots. If the new version fails to start or never confirms that it is healthy, the bootloader rolls back to the previous slot. The price is roughly twice the flash space for firmware.

about.h: Secure boot and the chain of trust
about.p: In secure boot, immutable ROM code verifies the digital signature of the first-stage bootloader, that stage verifies the next stage or the operating-system kernel, and so on, forming a chain of trust. A failed check stops the boot, so tampered boot code never runs. A bootloader that checks only a CRC detects accidental corruption but not deliberate modification, because an attacker can simply recompute the CRC; authenticity needs a signature verified with a key the attacker does not have.

faq.q: What is the difference between a bootloader and firmware?
faq.a: The bootloader is a small, rarely changed program that runs first and decides what to start; the application firmware is the main program it verifies and launches. The bootloader can also install new application firmware.

faq.q: Why do OTA updates use two firmware slots?
faq.a: So the new image can be written and verified while the old one stays intact. If the update is interrupted or the new version fails, the device still boots from the original slot.

faq.q: Is a CRC check enough for secure boot?
faq.a: No. A CRC catches accidental corruption, but anyone who modifies the image can recompute it; secure boot requires verifying a cryptographic signature.

OTA更新.desc: Updating a device's firmware via wireless communication, often using two flash slots so the device can still boot if an update fails.

スリープモード.desc: A microcontroller state that stops clocks or power to the CPU and peripherals while idle to save power, waking on an interrupt or similar.

ブラウンアウト検出.desc: A function that resets the microcontroller when the supply voltage drops below the operating minimum, preventing unreliable behavior and corrupt flash writes.

JTAG.desc: A standard interface for chip testing and debugging that lets developers halt programs, inspect internal values and program flash. Arm also uses SWD, which needs fewer wires.

about.p: JTAG is named after the Joint Test Action Group, and the standard is IEEE 1149.1. Its original job was testing assembled boards. A boundary-scan cell sits just inside each I/O pin, and the cells are linked into a shift register. Through the test access port (TAP), test equipment shifts patterns in, drives them out of one chip's pins and captures them at another chip's pins, revealing solder opens and shorts even under BGA packages where no probe can reach.

about.h: The TAP signals and state machine
about.p: The TAP uses four signals: TDI (test data in), TDO (test data out), TCK (test clock) and TMS (test mode select), plus an optional TRST reset. TMS, sampled on TCK edges, steers a 16-state controller that decides whether bits shifted between TDI and TDO go into the instruction register or a selected data register. Several chips can be daisy-chained by connecting each TDO to the next TDI, so one connector reaches every device on the board.

about.h: Debugging and flash programming; JTAG vs. SWD
about.p: Chip vendors reuse the same port to reach on-chip debug logic. A debugger on a PC can halt the core, set breakpoints, single-step, read and write registers and memory, and program flash, exposing internal state where printf is unavailable. Arm's Serial Wire Debug (SWD) provides similar debug access over only two signals, SWDIO and SWCLK, saving pins on small microcontrollers, but it is a debug protocol and does not perform boundary scan. Many Arm devices support both on shared pins.

The access that helps developers also helps attackers. An open debug port lets anyone with a probe read out firmware, extract keys or bypass secure boot. Shipped products therefore disable the port permanently by blowing eFuses, apply read-out protection, or open it only after a cryptographic challenge-response authentication, so that authorized engineers can still analyze failed units returned from the field.

faq.q: What are the JTAG pins?
faq.a: TDI, TDO, TCK and TMS, plus an optional TRST reset, along with ground and usually a reference voltage on the debug connector.

faq.q: What is the difference between JTAG and SWD?
faq.a: SWD is Arm's two-wire debug interface offering similar halt, step and memory access with fewer pins. JTAG uses four or five signals and also supports boundary-scan board testing and daisy-chaining several chips.

faq.q: Why is JTAG disabled on production devices?
faq.a: Because it allows reading and writing memory and halting the processor, an open port lets attackers extract firmware and keys or bypass secure boot. Products disable it with fuses or require authentication to unlock it.

読み出し・変更・書き込み.desc: A sequence that reads a value, changes part of it and writes it back. If interrupted midway, other changes can be lost.

GPUカーネル.desc: A function that many threads execute simultaneously on a GPU. It is launched from the CPU-side program, and each thread uses its index to choose its data. Distinct from an OS kernel.

CUDA.desc: NVIDIA's platform for general-purpose computing on its GPUs. Kernels are written in an extended C++, with parallelism expressed as a grid, blocks and threads.

about.p: In CUDA, the CPU (host) launches a kernel, a function that many GPU threads execute at once. One launch creates a grid of blocks, and each block contains many threads. Each thread computes a unique global index, typically i = blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, to choose its data element: thread 5 of block 2 with 256 threads per block handles element 517. Because threads are launched in whole blocks, the last block usually has surplus threads, so kernels guard memory accesses with if (i < n) to avoid writing past the array.

about.h: How blocks map onto the GPU
about.p: Each block is assigned to one streaming multiprocessor (SM) and runs there to completion, and an SM can hold several blocks at once. Inside, threads execute in warps of 32. Occupancy, the ratio of resident warps to the SM's maximum, is limited by registers per thread, shared memory per block and block size; low occupancy leaves too few warps to hide memory latency. Blocks run independently and in any order, so waiting inside a kernel for all other blocks can deadlock; global synchronization is normally obtained by splitting the work into two kernel launches.

Global memory is the GPU's DRAM: high bandwidth, high latency, and fastest when adjacent threads access adjacent addresses. Shared memory is a small on-chip memory per block, managed explicitly by the program. It is divided into 32 banks, and threads of a warp hitting different addresses in the same bank are serialized. __syncthreads() makes every thread of a block wait until all arrive; placing it inside a branch that some threads skip causes hangs or undefined results. Unified memory lets host and device share one pointer, with pages migrated on demand.

Host-to-device copies cross PCI Express and are often the bottleneck. Streams, ordered queues of transfers and kernels, let work in different streams overlap, so the next chunk of data can be copied while the current one is computed. Each kernel launch also costs a few microseconds, so programs that launch thousands of tiny kernels benefit from fusing them, which also avoids writing intermediate results to memory, or from submitting recorded launch sequences at once with CUDA Graphs. CUDA itself runs only on NVIDIA GPUs; cross-vendor alternatives such as OpenCL follow a similar kernel-and-work-group model.

faq.q: What is the difference between a CUDA block and a warp?
faq.a: A block is a programmer-chosen group of threads that runs on one SM and can share memory and synchronize. A warp is the hardware's group of 32 threads within a block that execute instructions together in lockstep.

faq.q: How do I calculate the global thread index in CUDA?
faq.a: For a one-dimensional launch, use i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. Check i < n before accessing arrays, because the last block often contains more threads than remaining elements.

faq.q: What is CUDA shared memory used for?
faq.a: It is fast on-chip memory shared by the threads of one block, used to stage data from global memory for reuse and to exchange intermediate results. Unlike a cache, the program decides what goes into it, and __syncthreads() orders accesses.

スレッドブロック.desc: A group of GPU threads that runs on a single SM. Threads in a block can share data through shared memory and synchronize.

SIMT.desc: An execution model in which programs are written per thread while hardware bundles threads into warps (32 on NVIDIA) that execute the same instruction in lockstep.
SIMT.title: SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads): Warps, Divergence
SIMT.description: SIMT lets you write per-thread code while the GPU runs warps of threads in lockstep. How branch divergence works and how SIMT differs from CPU SIMD.

about.p: In the single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT) model, the programmer writes a kernel as ordinary code for one thread, and thousands of threads run it on different data. The hardware groups threads into fixed bundles, called warps of 32 threads on NVIDIA GPUs and wavefronts of 64 or 32 on AMD GPUs. One instruction is fetched and decoded for the whole bundle and executed by all its threads in lockstep, each with its own registers and data. This amortizes control logic over many arithmetic lanes, so most of the chip area goes to computation.

Because each thread is written independently, threads in one warp may take different branches. The hardware handles this by executing each path in turn, with the threads not on that path masked off, and then reconverging. Correctness is preserved, but if half the threads take each side of an if-else, the warp spends time on both and its throughput roughly halves. Performance-aware code arranges data so that threads in the same warp follow the same path, for example by making branch conditions depend on the warp index rather than on each thread's data.

CPU single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) extensions apply one instruction to a vector register holding a fixed number of elements, such as 4 or 8. The program or the compiler must be written around that width, with explicit vector instructions and masks for edge cases. SIMT hides the width: the code describes a scalar thread, and the hardware forms the vectors from many threads and manages masking on divergence. Underneath, the execution is similar, which is why SIMT performance still depends on keeping threads in a warp in step.

Several common GPU programming rules follow from SIMT. Thread-block sizes are normally multiples of 32 so no warp runs partly empty. Memory accesses are fastest when neighboring threads in a warp access neighboring addresses, letting the hardware combine them into a few wide transactions, a pattern called coalescing. And GPUs hide long memory latency by keeping many warps resident and switching to another ready warp whenever one stalls, which is why high occupancy, enough active warps per core, often matters for performance.

faq.q: What is a warp in GPU computing?
faq.a: A warp is a group of 32 threads on NVIDIA GPUs that execute the same instruction together in lockstep. It is the basic unit of instruction issue in the SIMT model; AMD's equivalent is called a wavefront.

faq.q: What is the difference between SIMT and SIMD?
faq.a: SIMD exposes fixed-width vector instructions that the programmer or compiler must use explicitly. SIMT lets each thread be written as independent scalar code while the hardware groups threads into warps and handles divergent branches.

faq.q: What is warp divergence?
faq.a: Warp divergence occurs when threads in the same warp take different branch paths. The hardware executes each path serially with inactive threads masked, which lowers efficiency until the paths reconverge.

ワープダイバージェンス.desc: The splitting of threads within one warp onto different paths at a conditional branch. The paths execute one after another, lowering efficiency.

メモリコアレッシング.desc: Combining accesses into a few memory transactions when adjacent threads in a warp access adjacent addresses.

about.p: GPU global memory is accessed in fixed-size chunks, typically 32-byte sectors within 128-byte cache lines, not in individual words. Threads execute in groups called warps, usually 32 threads issuing the same load instruction together. When thread i of a warp reads the 4-byte element at base + 4i, the 32 requests fall into 128 contiguous bytes, and the hardware combines them into one or a few memory transactions. This combining is memory coalescing, and it lets the GPU use nearly all the bytes it moves.

If threads access addresses with a stride, for example every fourth element, the warp touches four times as many sectors, and most of each fetched sector is discarded. Random or indirect accesses can require a separate transaction for every thread. Misaligned starting addresses can add one extra segment. In each case effective bandwidth drops to a fraction of the peak, and since many GPU kernels are limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic, uncoalesced access often slows a kernel by a large factor.

about.h: Array of structures vs. structure of arrays
about.p: Data layout largely decides whether accesses coalesce. With particle positions stored as an array of structures (AoS), the x, y and z of particle 0 are followed by those of particle 1, so when each thread reads x the addresses are 12 bytes apart. With a structure of arrays (SoA), all x values are contiguous, so adjacent threads read adjacent addresses and the warp's loads coalesce. SoA is also usually better for CPU SIMD vectorization, for the same reason: neighboring lanes want neighboring elements.

Common fixes include mapping the fastest-changing thread index, threadIdx.x in CUDA, to the contiguous dimension of an array, converting AoS data to SoA, and staging data through on-chip shared memory, for example loading a matrix tile with coalesced row reads and writing it out transposed. Coalescing concerns global memory transactions. It should not be confused with shared-memory bank conflicts, which occur when several threads of a warp hit different addresses in the same shared-memory bank and their accesses are serialized.

faq.q: What is memory coalescing in CUDA?
faq.a: It is the hardware combining the global memory accesses of a warp's threads into as few transactions as possible, which happens when adjacent threads access adjacent, aligned addresses.

faq.q: Why is a structure of arrays better for GPU memory access?
faq.a: In a structure of arrays, each field is stored contiguously, so adjacent threads reading the same field access consecutive addresses and their loads coalesce; an array of structures puts a stride between them.

faq.q: What is the difference between memory coalescing and bank conflicts?
faq.a: Coalescing concerns how a warp's global memory accesses map onto memory transactions, while bank conflicts concern multiple threads accessing the same bank of on-chip shared memory, which forces serialization.

シェアードメモリ.desc: Small, fast memory inside each GPU SM that threads of the same block can share. The program decides what is stored there.

バンク競合.desc: In GPU shared memory, multiple threads of a warp accessing different addresses in the same bank at once, which serializes the accesses. Padding can avoid it.

占有率.desc: The ratio of warps actually resident on a GPU SM to the maximum it can hold, determined by register and shared-memory use.

ストリーミングマルチプロセッサ.desc: On NVIDIA GPUs, a unit bundling arithmetic units, registers, shared memory and warp-scheduling circuitry. A GPU is built from many SMs.

レイテンシ隠蔽.desc: Keeping waits, such as for memory, from showing up in performance by doing other work in the meantime. GPUs do it by switching among many warps.

ピン留めメモリ.desc: Memory locked so the OS will not move or evict its physical pages. The GPU can access it directly by DMA, speeding transfers and enabling asynchronous copies.

ユニファイドメモリ.desc: Memory accessible from CPU and GPU through the same pointer, with data migrating automatically on access. It simplifies programs, but migration costs need attention.

テンソルコア.desc: A GPU unit that computes the product and sum of small matrices in one instruction, mainly with low-precision numbers, greatly speeding up AI.

混合精度.desc: Using different numeric precisions for different parts of a computation, such as multiplying in FP16 and accumulating in FP32, to balance speed and accuracy.

並列リダクション.desc: Computing a sum or similar over many values in parallel with a tree that repeatedly combines neighbors, finishing n values in log2 n stages.

プレフィックスサム.desc: Computing the running totals of an array from the start, also called a scan. It can be computed in parallel and is used to find write positions when compacting output.

グリッドストライドループ.desc: Writing a kernel as a loop in which each thread processes elements spaced by the total thread count, decoupling launch size from element count.

定数メモリ.desc: A small GPU region for values that do not change during a kernel. When every thread in a warp reads the same address, one read is broadcast to all, which is fast.

OpenCL.desc: A standard parallel-programming framework for GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs and more from multiple vendors, defined by the Khronos Group industry consortium.

推論.desc: Running only the forward pass with weights fixed by training to produce answers from inputs. It needs less computation and memory than training.

about.p: Training runs a forward pass, computes a loss, propagates gradients backward and updates the weights, repeated over the dataset many times. It must keep intermediate activations for the backward pass and store optimizer state, and it usually needs floating-point formats with enough range for small gradients. Inference runs the forward pass only, with frozen weights, one input or batch at a time. It needs far less memory and computation per sample and tolerates much lower precision, so 8-bit integers or narrower formats are common. Training happens once per model version, while inference runs every time the model is used.

Most of the arithmetic is multiply-accumulate operations inside matrix products and convolutions, which is why accelerators pack thousands of multiply-accumulate units. Feeding them is often the real bottleneck. With a batch of one, each weight fetched from memory is used for only one input, so performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic; generating text with a large language model, where every new token reads all the weights, is a typical example. Batching several requests reuses each fetched weight, raising throughput at the cost of latency. Latency and throughput therefore must be stated separately.

Quantization from FP32 to INT8 cuts weight storage and memory traffic to a quarter and lets compact integer units do the math, at the price of a small accuracy risk that calibration or quantization-aware training controls. Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a large teacher. Pruning removes weights or whole channels that contribute little, and structured sparsity patterns let hardware skip zeros. These techniques combine, and they are what makes running a model within the memory, power and heat budget of a phone or embedded device possible.

Data-center inference runs large models on GPUs or dedicated accelerators with plenty of memory and power. Edge inference runs on the device, typically on a neural processing unit (NPU) in the system-on-chip, which specializes in low-precision matrix math, reuses data on chip and omits general-purpose machinery such as branch prediction, giving much higher energy efficiency than a CPU. Running on the device avoids network latency, works offline, keeps photos and audio local and saves server cost. The trade-off is that very large models do not fit within the device's limits without heavy compression.

faq.q: What is the difference between AI training and inference?
faq.a: Training adjusts a model's weights using forward and backward passes over a dataset, which is very compute- and memory-intensive. Inference uses the trained, fixed weights to compute outputs for new inputs with forward passes only.

faq.q: Why is AI inference often limited by memory bandwidth?
faq.a: With small batches, each weight read from memory is used for only a few calculations, so the arithmetic units wait on data. Large models with batch size one, such as text generation, are the most memory-bound case.

faq.q: Why do phones use an NPU for inference instead of the CPU?
faq.a: An NPU packs many low-precision multiply-accumulate units and avoids general-purpose control overhead, so it spends far less energy per operation. That makes on-device features practical within battery and heat limits.

逆伝播.desc: The training computation that propagates the error between output and target backward from output to input to obtain each weight's gradient.

about.p: Training starts with a forward pass that computes the output and a loss measuring its error against the target. Backpropagation then applies the chain rule in reverse: starting from the loss, each layer receives the gradient with respect to its output and computes two things, the gradient with respect to its weights and the gradient with respect to its input, which it passes to the previous layer. For a fully connected layer, the weight gradient combines the incoming gradient with the input activations saved during the forward pass. An optimizer then nudges each weight against its gradient.

Frameworks represent a model as a computational graph, with operations such as matrix products, additions and activations as nodes and tensors as edges. Because each node knows its own local derivative, the framework can traverse the graph backward and compute all gradients automatically, a technique called reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The graph also exposes which operations are independent. Inference runtimes such as TensorRT or ONNX Runtime drop the bookkeeping needed for backpropagation, then fuse operations, lower precision and pick hardware-specific kernels, which is why they run faster than the training framework used for inference.

The backward pass costs about twice the forward pass, because each layer computes gradients for both its inputs and its weights. A forward pass is about 2N operations per token for N parameters, so training costs about 6N per token, or 6ND for D tokens; a 7-billion-parameter model on 1 trillion tokens needs about 4.2 × 10^22 operations. Memory grows even more: training stores intermediate activations, gradients equal in number to the weights, and optimizer state such as Adam's two moving averages. Gradient checkpointing saves only some activations and recomputes the rest, costing roughly one extra forward pass.

Gradients are often tiny. FP16 (1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 significand bits) covers positive values from only about 6 × 10^-8, including subnormals, up to 65504, so many gradients underflow to zero and learning stalls. Loss scaling multiplies the loss by a factor such as 1024 before backpropagation, lifting gradients into range, and divides it back out before the weight update. Mixed-precision training usually also keeps a higher-precision master copy of the weights. BF16, with 8 exponent bits like FP32, has a much wider range and rarely needs loss scaling.

faq.q: What is the difference between backpropagation and gradient descent?
faq.a: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Gradient descent, or another optimizer such as Adam, uses those gradients to update the weights.

faq.q: Why does training need more memory than inference?
faq.a: Training must keep forward activations for the backward pass, plus a gradient for every weight and optimizer state, while inference needs only the weights and transient activations.

faq.q: How expensive is the backward pass compared with the forward pass?
faq.a: Roughly twice as expensive, so one training step costs about three forward passes, which is the origin of the 6N operations-per-token rule of thumb.

演算強度.desc: Operations performed divided by bytes moved to and from memory. High values tend toward compute-bound, low values toward memory-bound.

about.p: Arithmetic intensity is operations performed divided by bytes moved between memory and the processor, usually counted as FLOP per byte of DRAM traffic. For the product of two N × N FP16 matrices, read once and written once, the work is 2N^3 operations and the traffic is 3N^2 elements or 6N^2 bytes, giving N/3, about 340 for N = 1024. A matrix-vector product reuses each weight only once, giving about 1 FLOP/byte in FP16, and element-wise operations such as ReLU fall below 1. Intensity depends on the algorithm, the data type and how well the implementation reuses data.

The roofline model, which sometimes uses the term operational intensity, plots attainable performance against arithmetic intensity. Performance is the smaller of peak compute and memory bandwidth times intensity, so the chart has a slanted bandwidth ceiling and a flat compute ceiling. They meet at the ridge point, peak divided by bandwidth. With 100 TFLOPS and 2 TB/s the ridge is at 50 FLOP/byte, so a workload at 10 FLOP/byte is memory-bound at 2 TB/s × 10 = 20 TFLOPS. Below the ridge, extra arithmetic units do not help; above it, memory bandwidth is no longer the limit.

When a workload sits under the slanted roof, the fix is to do more work per byte or move fewer bytes. Blocking (tiling) keeps sub-matrices in caches or on-chip memory so each value fetched from DRAM is used many times. Operator fusion applies element-wise steps such as activations or normalization while data is still on chip, instead of writing it out and reading it back. Batching lets one read of the weights serve several inputs. Lower-precision data types cut the bytes per value, which raises operations per byte for the same computation.

Arithmetic intensity explains much of AI accelerator behavior. Large matrix multiplications are compute-bound and can approach peak throughput, while element-wise layers can take a noticeable share of runtime despite few operations. Inference at batch size 1 is a matrix-vector workload with intensity near 1, so it is limited by how fast weights stream from memory, which is why batching and weight quantization help. Compare it with the hardware's ridge point: the intensity belongs to the workload, the ridge point to the machine, and their ratio tells you which resource to optimize.

faq.q: How do you calculate arithmetic intensity?
faq.a: Divide the number of operations (usually FLOPs) by the bytes transferred to and from memory. For an N × N FP16 matrix multiply this is 2N^3 / 6N^2 = N/3.

faq.q: What is the ridge point in a roofline model?
faq.a: It is peak compute divided by memory bandwidth, the arithmetic intensity at which a workload switches from memory-bound to compute-bound. For 100 TFLOPS and 2 TB/s it is 50 FLOP/byte.

faq.q: Why is batch-size-1 inference memory-bound?
faq.a: Each weight is read from memory and used for just one multiply-add, so arithmetic intensity is about 1 FLOP/byte in FP16, far below the ridge point of typical accelerators.

Rooflineモデル.desc: A model expressing attainable performance as the smaller of peak compute and memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity, used to tell compute-bound from memory-bound work.

about.p: The roofline model plots attainable performance (operations per second, usually FLOP/s) against arithmetic intensity (operations per byte moved to or from memory), normally on log-log axes. Two ceilings bound every workload: a sloped line equal to memory bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, and a flat line at peak compute. Attainable performance is the lower of the two. The corner where they meet, the ridge point, sits at peak compute divided by bandwidth. With 100 TFLOPS and 2 TB/s, the ridge is 50 FLOP/byte, so a kernel at 10 FLOP/byte is memory-bound at 20 TFLOPS.

Count the useful operations and divide by the bytes that actually cross the memory interface. Adding two arrays of 8-byte doubles into a third performs 1 FLOP while moving 24 bytes, about 0.04 FLOP/byte, so it is hopelessly memory-bound on any modern chip. Multiplying two n-by-n matrices performs about 2n³ FLOPs on roughly 3n² elements, so intensity grows with n, provided caches or tiling actually deliver that reuse. Because intensity depends on real traffic, the same algorithm can sit at different points depending on blocking, cache size and data type.

about.h: Reading the chart and acting on it
about.p: A kernel under the sloped roof will not speed up with more arithmetic units; it needs fewer bytes per operation. Blocking or tiling to reuse data in caches, fusing consecutive operations so intermediates never reach DRAM, and using lower-precision data all move the point right or up. A kernel near the flat roof needs better use of compute instead: vectorization, fused multiply-add, matrix units and enough parallelism. Extra lower ceilings are often drawn for missing optimizations, such as peak without SIMD, and separate rooflines can be drawn for each cache level.

about.h: Where the numbers come from and limits
about.p: The flat roof is usually the vendor's peak for the relevant data type; the slope is better taken from a measured bandwidth, such as the STREAM benchmark, than from the theoretical figure. The model is an upper bound, not a prediction: real kernels sit below the roof because of latency, imperfect overlap of memory and compute, synchronization and load imbalance.
