A familiar application is large language model inference at batch size one, where each weight is read for about two operations, giving intensity near 1 FLOP/byte at 16-bit precision and a firmly memory-bound result.

faq.q: What is the ridge point in a roofline model?
faq.a: It is the arithmetic intensity where the bandwidth slope meets the compute ceiling, equal to peak FLOP/s divided by memory bandwidth in bytes per second. Workloads below it are memory-bound, those above it can be compute-bound.

faq.q: How do I measure arithmetic intensity for a kernel?
faq.a: Divide the number of operations by the bytes actually transferred from DRAM, which you can estimate by hand or measure with hardware counters or a profiler. Use measured traffic when caches change the amount of data moved.

faq.q: Why is my workload memory-bound even on a fast GPU?
faq.a: Fast accelerators have very high ridge points, often tens to hundreds of FLOP per byte, so element-wise operations and small-batch matrix-vector work cannot reach peak. Fusing operations and increasing data reuse or batch size raise intensity.

バッチサイズ.desc: The number of inputs processed together. Larger batches reuse weights for efficiency but increase latency and memory.

about.p: In a neural-network layer, the weights are the same for every input. With batch size 1, a fully connected layer is a matrix-vector product: each weight is fetched from memory for a single multiply-add, giving an arithmetic intensity of about 1 FLOP/byte in FP16, so compute units mostly wait for memory. With batch size B, the layer becomes a matrix-matrix product: weight traffic stays the same while operations grow B-fold, so intensity rises roughly B-fold and the workload moves from memory-bound toward compute-bound. Servers exploit this by grouping requests from many users.

A bigger batch raises total throughput but not individual speed. Requests may wait for others to arrive, and each batch takes longer to compute, so per-request latency grows; interactive services raise the batch only as far as their response-time targets allow. Memory grows too. In LLM (large language model) inference the KV cache, which stores attention keys and values of earlier tokens so they are not recomputed, scales with layers, key and value dimensions, tokens, batch size and bytes per element. With long contexts or many requests it can reach tens of gigabytes, more than the weights.

During decoding at batch size 1, every generated token requires reading all the weights. A model with about 14 GB of FP16 weights on a GPU with 2 TB/s of bandwidth therefore needs at least 14 GB ÷ 2 TB/s = 7 ms per token, at most about 140 tokens per second. Quantizing weights to 4 bits, about 3.5 GB, lowers that bound to about 1.75 ms. A larger batch generates several tokens per weight read, multiplying aggregate throughput until compute or KV-cache memory becomes the limit. KV-cache pressure is eased by lower-precision caches, sharing keys and values across heads and block-based memory management.

In training, the batch (mini-batch) is the set of samples whose gradients are averaged for one weight update. Larger batches use hardware more efficiently and need fewer update steps per pass over the data (an epoch), but activation memory for backpropagation grows with batch size and model depth. Gradient checkpointing counters this by storing only some activations and recomputing the rest for roughly one extra forward pass. Changing the batch size substantially usually means retuning the learning rate, since it changes gradient noise.

faq.q: Does a larger batch size make inference faster?
faq.a: It increases total throughput because each weight read serves more inputs, but each individual request usually waits longer, so latency gets worse.

faq.q: Why does increasing batch size increase GPU memory use?
faq.a: Activations, and in LLMs the KV cache, are stored per input, so they scale linearly with batch size while the weights stay the same.

faq.q: What is the difference between batch size and epoch?
faq.a: Batch size is how many samples are processed per step or weight update; an epoch is one full pass over the training dataset, which takes dataset size divided by batch size steps.

KVキャッシュ.desc: Memory in LLM inference holding the attention keys and values of already processed tokens. It avoids recomputation but grows with context length and batch size.

about.h: Why LLM inference keeps keys and values
about.p: A transformer language model generates text one token at a time. In each attention layer the new token's query is compared with the keys of all earlier tokens, and the result weights their values. Because attention is causal, the keys and values of earlier tokens never change once computed. The KV cache stores them per layer, so each decoding step only computes the new token's query, key and value and appends the latter two, instead of reprocessing the entire sequence. This turns repeated full recomputation into a modest per-token cost.

about.h: How big the KV cache gets
about.p: Cache size is 2 (keys and values) × number of layers × key/value dimension per layer × number of tokens × batch size × bytes per element. As an illustration, a model with 32 layers, a hidden size of 4096 and standard multi-head attention needs about 0.5 MB per token in FP16. A 4096-token context then takes about 2 GB per sequence, and a batch of eight such sequences needs about 16 GB, more than the roughly 14 GB that the weights of a 7-billion-parameter FP16 model occupy.

Inference has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel and writes its keys and values into the cache; it is mostly limited by compute. Decode then produces one token per step, and each step must read the model weights plus the entire KV cache for that sequence, so it is usually limited by memory bandwidth. Larger batches share the weight reads among more requests and raise throughput, but they enlarge the KV cache and lengthen each step, increasing the latency of individual requests.

about.h: Ways to shrink or manage it
about.p: Several techniques reduce KV cache pressure. Grouped-query and multi-query attention let several query heads share one set of key and value heads, cutting cache size proportionally. Storing the cache in 8-bit or lower precision halves or further reduces memory relative to FP16. Allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, rather than one contiguous region per sequence sized for the maximum length, avoids fragmentation and lets more requests fit; it also allows sequences with a common prompt prefix to share blocks. Some models also limit attention to a sliding window of recent tokens.

faq.q: What is the KV cache in large language models?
faq.a: It is memory holding the attention keys and values of tokens already processed, so each newly generated token only needs its own keys and values computed instead of recomputing the whole sequence.

faq.q: Why does the KV cache use so much memory?
faq.a: Its size grows linearly with the number of layers, the attention width, the context length and the batch size, so long contexts or many concurrent requests can make it larger than the model weights.

faq.q: Does the KV cache affect output quality?
faq.a: Caching exact keys and values is mathematically equivalent to recomputing them; only approximations such as low-precision cache storage or dropping old tokens can change outputs.

プリフィル.desc: The first stage of LLM inference, processing all input prompt tokens together; it tends to be compute-bound. The following token-by-token generation is called decode.

アテンション.desc: The Transformer mechanism in which each token gathers information by computing its relationship to every other token. Its cost grows with the square of sequence length.

FlashAttention.desc: A fast attention implementation that tiles the computation in on-chip memory and never writes the large intermediate table to HBM. Its results match standard attention.

演算の融合.desc: An optimization that combines several operations into one kernel, avoiding writing intermediate results to memory and reading them back.

計算グラフ.desc: A representation of a model's computation with operations as nodes and tensor flows as edges, underpinning automatic differentiation and AI compiler optimization.

about.h: Nodes, edges and what they carry
about.p: A computational graph is usually a directed acyclic graph. Nodes are operations such as matrix multiplication, convolution, addition or an activation function; edges are tensors, each with a known shape and data type, flowing from the operation that produces them to the ones that consume them. Inputs and trainable weights appear as source nodes. Because dependencies are explicit, the graph shows at a glance which operations can run in parallel and which must wait, and it gives software a complete, analyzable description of the model independent of the Python code that created it.

Training needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. During the forward pass a framework records the graph; reverse-mode automatic differentiation then walks it backward from the loss, applying each operation's local derivative rule and the chain rule to accumulate gradients, which is backpropagation. This requires the intermediate outputs (activations) saved from the forward pass, which is why training uses far more memory than inference. Activation checkpointing trades compute for memory by discarding some activations and recomputing them during the backward pass.

In a static, define-and-run style, the whole graph is built first and then executed, which makes global optimization easy but complicates data-dependent control flow and debugging. In a dynamic, define-by-run or eager style, operations execute immediately as the program runs and the graph is recorded on the fly, which is flexible but leaves little room for optimization across operations. Modern frameworks commonly mix the two: code is written eagerly, and a compile step traces or captures the graph so that a compiler can optimize it before execution.

about.h: What compilers and runtimes do with it
about.p: AI compilers rewrite the graph before generating code. Operator fusion merges chains such as matrix multiply, bias add and activation into one kernel so intermediate tensors stay in on-chip memory instead of making a round trip to DRAM. Other passes include constant folding, removal of unused nodes, choice of tensor memory layout, tiling to fit caches or scratchpads, and memory planning that reuses buffers whose lifetimes do not overlap. Exchange formats such as ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) serialize the graph and weights so different runtimes and hardware toolchains can execute the same model.

faq.q: What is a computational graph in deep learning?
faq.a: It is a representation of a model as operations (nodes) connected by the tensors they pass to each other (edges). Frameworks use it to compute gradients automatically and compilers use it to optimize execution.

faq.q: Why does operator fusion speed up neural networks?
faq.a: Many operations, such as activations and normalization, are memory-bound, so writing their outputs to DRAM and reading them back dominates the time. Fusing them into one kernel keeps intermediates on chip and cuts memory traffic.

faq.q: What is the difference between eager execution and graph mode?
faq.a: Eager execution runs each operation immediately as Python reaches it, while graph mode builds or captures the whole graph first and then optimizes and runs it. Eager is easier to debug; graph mode allows fusion and other whole-model optimizations.

AIコンパイラ.desc: Software that analyzes a model's computational graph, optimizes fusion, data layout and tiling, and generates code for the target hardware, such as XLA and TVM.

ONNX.desc: Open Neural Network Exchange: a common model format for exchanging models between frameworks and inference runtimes.

推論ランタイム.desc: Software that loads a trained model and runs inference quickly through graph optimization, quantization and hardware-specific kernel selection.

学習後量子化.desc: Converting a trained model's weights and activations to lower precision after examining value ranges with representative data.

about.p: Post-training quantization (PTQ) starts from a model already trained in 32-bit floating point and maps each tensor onto a small integer grid, most often INT8. Every real value is represented as an integer times a scale factor, sometimes with a zero-point offset. Weights are fixed after training, so their scales can be computed directly from their stored values, often separately for each output channel to follow differences between filters. No gradient updates take place, so PTQ typically finishes in minutes and needs no labeled training data, only a small set of inputs for calibration.

Activations change with every input, so their range cannot be read from the model itself. Calibration runs a few hundred representative inputs through the network, records each layer's activation distribution and picks the range to map onto the symmetric INT8 grid of -127 to 127. Using the absolute maximum guarantees nothing is clipped, but a few rare outliers then stretch the scale and waste most of the available levels on values that almost never occur. Narrowing the range to cover most of the distribution clips the outliers while giving finer resolution to the common values.

Quantization-aware training (QAT) inserts simulated rounding into the forward pass during training or fine-tuning, so the weights learn to tolerate the quantization error. PTQ skips this step entirely, which makes it far cheaper and usable when the original training pipeline or dataset is not available. The price is accuracy: at INT8 the loss is often small, but as the bit width shrinks toward 4 bits rounding error grows quickly and PTQ alone may no longer be acceptable. QAT is the usual fallback, because it can preserve accuracy at precisions where PTQ breaks down.

about.h: Why it matters for inference hardware
about.p: An INT8 weight occupies a quarter of the memory of an FP32 weight, so the same model needs less DRAM capacity and, more importantly, less memory bandwidth per inference. Integer multiply-accumulate units are also much smaller and use less energy per operation than floating-point units, which is why neural processing units and edge accelerators are built around low-precision integer arrays. PTQ is the most common way to move an existing model onto such hardware, and deployment toolchains generally provide a calibration step for it.

faq.q: What is the difference between post-training quantization and quantization-aware training?
faq.a: Post-training quantization converts an already trained model to low precision without retraining, using only a small calibration set. Quantization-aware training simulates the rounding during training so the weights adapt, which costs a training run but keeps accuracy better at very low bit widths such as 4 bits.

faq.q: Why does post-training quantization need calibration data?
faq.a: Weights are known after training, but activation values depend on the input, so their ranges must be observed by running representative inputs through the model. Those observed ranges set the scale factors that map activations onto the integer grid.

faq.q: Does post-training quantization need the original training dataset?
faq.a: No full training dataset or labels are required. A few hundred unlabeled inputs that resemble real usage are normally enough to calibrate activation ranges.

量子化を考慮した学習.desc: Training that simulates quantization rounding so weights adapt to its error, preserving accuracy even at low bit widths.

プルーニング.desc: Zeroing out low-impact weights in a neural network to reduce computation and memory. Structured pruning, which follows fixed patterns, is easier to accelerate in hardware.

構造化スパース.desc: Sparsity in which zero weights follow a fixed pattern; 2:4 sparsity, with two zeros in every four weights, lets matrix units compute about twice as fast.

知識蒸留.desc: Training a small student model to mimic a large teacher model's outputs so the small model achieves similar performance.

データ並列.desc: Distributed training in which each GPU holds a full model replica, processes its share of the data, and gradients are averaged across GPUs before updating.

テンソル並列.desc: Splitting one layer's weight matrix by rows or columns across GPUs, computing partial products and combining them through communication.

パイプライン並列.desc: Splitting a model's layers across GPUs in sequence, streaming micro-batches to reduce the time GPUs sit idle (the bubble).

オールリデュース.desc: Communication that sums values held by all GPUs element by element and gives the result to every GPU, used to average gradients in data-parallel training.

勾配チェックポイント.desc: Storing only some intermediate forward results and recomputing the rest during backpropagation, trading extra computation for less memory.

TOPS.desc: Trillions of operations per second, a performance figure for AI accelerators, usually a theoretical peak counted at low precision.

about.h: How a TOPS figure is calculated
about.p: TOPS means tera, or trillion, operations per second. For an accelerator it is normally the peak value: number of multiply-accumulate (MAC) units, times two operations per MAC (one multiply and one add), times clock frequency. An array of 4,096 INT8 MAC units at 1 GHz therefore gives about 8.2 TOPS. The figure assumes every unit does useful work on every cycle, which a real workload never fully achieves. It is a statement of hardware capacity, not of how fast any particular model will run.

Always check the conditions behind the number. It is usually quoted at INT8 or lower; the same hardware may claim twice the TOPS at INT4 and far fewer at FP16. Some figures assume structured sparsity, where skipping zero weights is counted as doing the operations. The number says nothing about memory bandwidth, on-chip buffer size, which operators the hardware supports, or how much work falls back to a CPU. For energy efficiency, TOPS per watt is quoted, but it depends heavily on voltage, clock and which parts of the chip are included in the power.

about.h: Peak versus achieved: the roofline view
about.p: Achievable performance is the smaller of peak compute and memory bandwidth multiplied by arithmetic intensity, the number of operations performed per byte moved. An accelerator rated at 100 TOPS with 100 GB/s of memory bandwidth needs about 1,000 operations per byte fetched to reach its peak. Layers with little data reuse, such as small-batch fully connected layers or token-by-token generation in language models, fall far short and are bandwidth-bound. Convolutions with high reuse come closer. This is why measured throughput on the target model is the only fair comparison.

FLOPS counts floating-point operations per second, while TOPS is mostly used for integer or mixed low-precision operations, though vendors sometimes quote TOPS for low-precision floating point as well. The two are not interchangeable even when the numbers match, because an FP16 operation does more work and costs more area than an INT8 one. When comparing devices, convert both to the same precision, note whether sparsity is assumed, and look for benchmark results measured under identical conditions, such as the same model, batch size and accuracy target.

faq.q: What does TOPS stand for?
faq.a: Tera operations per second, meaning trillions of operations per second. For AI accelerators it is usually a theoretical peak counting each multiply-accumulate as two operations at a low precision such as INT8.

faq.q: Does a higher TOPS rating mean faster AI performance?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Real speed also depends on memory bandwidth, utilization of the compute units, supported operators and software, so a chip with fewer TOPS can outperform one with more on a given model.

faq.q: How is TOPS different from TFLOPS?
faq.a: TFLOPS counts floating-point operations, while TOPS usually counts integer or low-precision operations. Because the operation types differ, the numbers cannot be compared directly without stating the precision.

MFU.desc: The percentage of hardware peak performance achieved, computed from the operations a model actually requires.

投機的デコーディング.desc: Speeding up inference by having a small model draft several tokens ahead and a large model verify them together, accepting the correct ones at once.

ハードウェア記述言語.desc: A language for describing the structure and behavior of digital circuits, such as Verilog, SystemVerilog and VHDL, converted into circuits by logic synthesis.

about.p: A hardware description language describes circuits rather than a sequence of instructions. Every assign statement, always block and module instance represents hardware that operates all the time, so code order does not imply execution order. Designs are usually written at register-transfer level (RTL): registers updated on clock edges, with combinational logic computing their next values. The main languages are Verilog, its extension SystemVerilog, and VHDL, which is more strongly typed. Only a synthesizable subset of each language maps to gates; the rest exists for simulation and verification.

Clocked blocks such as always @(posedge clk) become flip-flops and conventionally use nonblocking assignments (<=). Combinational blocks should use @(*) or always_comb with blocking assignments (=) and must assign every output on every path, for example with a default case, or synthesis infers a latch. A for loop is unrolled into parallel hardware, so a loop over eight bits becomes eight adders. State machines combine a state register, next-state logic and output logic. Tri-state outputs are kept for off-chip bidirectional pins; internal selection uses multiplexers.

The same languages build the verification environment. A testbench instantiates the design under test, generates clocks, resets and stimulus, and checks outputs; since it is never synthesized, it can use delays, file I/O and display statements. SystemVerilog adds classes, constrained-random stimulus, functional coverage and assertions, and UVM provides a standard class library for reusable testbenches. Lint tools check code statically for width mismatches, inferred latches and unsynthesizable constructs. Verification often takes as much effort as the design itself, or more.

HDL sits between the specification and the gate-level netlist. Engineers write RTL from the specification, simulate it, then logic synthesis maps it onto cells from the foundry's library, guided by the process design kit (PDK) and timing constraints. Describing behavior this way is what makes large designs possible: even a 32-bit adder would need a truth table of 2⁶⁴ rows. High-level synthesis raises abstraction further by generating RTL from C or C++, while FPGA tools take the same HDL and map it to lookup tables instead of standard cells.

faq.q: What is the difference between Verilog and VHDL?
faq.a: Both describe hardware at RTL and are supported by synthesis and simulation tools. Verilog has a terse, C-like syntax, while VHDL is more verbose and strongly typed; SystemVerilog extends Verilog with major verification features.

faq.q: Is an HDL a programming language?
faq.a: It looks like one, but synthesizable HDL code describes hardware that runs concurrently, not instructions executed in order. Each line costs circuit area, so designers think in terms of registers and logic rather than steps.

faq.q: When should blocking and nonblocking assignments be used in Verilog?
faq.a: The common guideline is nonblocking (<=) in clocked always blocks and blocking (=) in combinational blocks. Mixing them in one block is a frequent source of simulation-synthesis mismatches.

Verilog.desc: A hardware description language widely used for digital design and verification, describing circuits as modules with behavior expressed through assign and always.

about.p: A Verilog design is built from modules, each a block of circuitry with declared input and output ports. A module can be instantiated inside another as many times as needed, with ports wired together, so a chip is described as a hierarchy of components. Inside a module, a continuous assignment such as assign y = (a & b) | c describes combinational logic whose output follows its inputs at all times. An always block describes behavior triggered by events: always @(posedge clk) becomes edge-triggered flip-flops, while always @(*) re-evaluates whenever any signal it reads changes and describes combinational logic.

Verilog looks like a programming language, but every assign statement and always block operates concurrently, regardless of its order in the file. In clocked blocks, nonblocking assignments (<=) evaluate all right-hand sides with pre-edge values and then update together, matching flip-flops that capture simultaneously; blocking assignments (=) suit combinational blocks that compute intermediate values top to bottom. A signal declared reg is not necessarily a register: assigned in always @(*), it is combinational. An if without an else in a combinational block implies memory and infers an unintended latch. Widths also matter, since assignments silently truncate, and signals are unsigned unless declared signed.

Verilog simulators are event-driven: they re-evaluate only the logic whose inputs changed, which is efficient because few signals toggle in any cycle. Signals take four values: 0, 1, X for unknown and Z for high impedance. Uninitialized registers and conflicting drivers produce X, and undriven nets produce Z, so seeing either in a waveform is a strong debugging clue. Some semantics are optimistic: an if statement treats an X condition as false, hiding bugs that real hardware would expose. The == operator returns X when operands contain X or Z, while === compares them literally and is used only in testbenches.

Only a subset of Verilog is synthesizable. Delays such as #10, $display and file I/O are simulation-only and are ignored by synthesis, so testbenches may use them freely but RTL should not. SystemVerilog, the successor standard, adds the logic type, which removes most of the wire/reg distinction, and always_ff and always_comb, which state the designer's intent so tools can flag an inferred latch. It also adds extensive verification features such as assertions and classes. VHDL is the other major hardware description language, with stricter typing and a more verbose style; both are used for RTL design.

faq.q: What is the difference between wire and reg in Verilog?
faq.a: A wire is driven by a continuous assignment or a module output, while a reg is assigned inside an always or initial block. A reg becomes a flip-flop only if it is updated on a clock edge; in always @(*) it is combinational logic.

faq.q: When should I use blocking (=) versus nonblocking (<=) assignments?
faq.a: Use nonblocking assignments in clocked always blocks that describe flip-flops, and blocking assignments in combinational always blocks. Mixing the two in one block or using blocking assignments for sequential logic can make simulation depend on statement order and differ from hardware.

faq.q: What is the difference between Verilog and SystemVerilog?
faq.a: SystemVerilog is a superset of Verilog that adds design conveniences such as the logic type, always_ff and always_comb, plus verification features like assertions, constrained random stimulus and object-oriented testbenches.

SystemVerilog.desc: An extension of Verilog adding design features such as the logic type and always_ff/always_comb, and verification features such as classes, constrained random and assertions.

about.p: SystemVerilog, standardized as IEEE 1800, is a superset of Verilog that adds features for both writing hardware and verifying it. On the design side, the logic type replaces Verilog's confusing wire and reg split for single-driver signals; always_ff, always_comb and always_latch state the intended hardware; and enums, structs, packages and interfaces make RTL more readable and less error-prone. In Verilog, reg merely means a signal assigned in an always block, not necessarily a flip-flop. Signals with multiple drivers, such as tri-state buses, still use wire, and logic is a four-state type that can hold X and Z.

A frequent Verilog bug is an unintended latch: a combinational always block that leaves an output unassigned on some path forces the tool to remember the old value. The standard cure is to assign default values to every output at the top of the block. With always_comb, tools also know combinational logic was intended and warn or error when a latch is inferred, and the sensitivity list is derived automatically from the signals read, avoiding the missing-signal mistakes of hand-written lists. always_ff similarly flags code that does not map to edge-triggered flip-flops.

Most of SystemVerilog's additions are for testbenches. Classes bring object-oriented programming; constrained random generation produces legal stimulus such as word-aligned addresses or lengths from 1 to 256; covergroups measure functional coverage to show which cases were exercised; and SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) express temporal properties, such as a response within three cycles of a request, that are checked in simulation or proven by formal tools. Clocking blocks define when testbench signals are driven and sampled, preventing races with the design. The Universal Verification Methodology (UVM, IEEE 1800.2) builds reusable testbenches on these features.

Only part of SystemVerilog describes hardware. The synthesizable subset, including logic, always_ff, always_comb, enums, structs, packages and interfaces, is accepted by synthesis tools and becomes gates. Classes, randomization, coverage and most dynamic data types exist only in simulation, where they describe the environment around the design. Assertions can be bound to RTL and used in simulation, formal verification and sometimes emulation, but they are not turned into functional logic. VHDL remains the main alternative language, especially in some FPGA and aerospace teams.

faq.q: What is the difference between Verilog and SystemVerilog?
faq.a: SystemVerilog is a superset of Verilog that adds safer design constructs such as logic, always_ff and always_comb, plus verification features such as classes, constrained random stimulus, functional coverage and assertions. Existing Verilog code is generally valid SystemVerilog.

faq.q: Is SystemVerilog synthesizable?
faq.a: Its design subset is, including logic, always_ff, always_comb, structs, enums and interfaces. Verification constructs such as classes, randomization and covergroups are for simulation only.

faq.q: Should I use logic instead of wire and reg?
faq.a: For signals with a single driver, logic works whether it is driven by an assign statement or an always block, so it replaces both in most code. Use wire for nets with multiple drivers, such as tri-state buses.

ノンブロッキング代入.desc: Verilog's "<=" assignment, which evaluates every right-hand side at a time step before updating all left-hand sides together. It matches flip-flop behavior and is used for sequential logic.

ブロッキング代入.desc: Verilog's "=" assignment, which updates the left side immediately so the next statement sees the new value. Used in combinational always blocks and testbenches.

about.p: A blocking assignment, written with a single equals sign, evaluates its right-hand side and updates the left-hand variable before the next statement in the same procedural block runs, much like assignment in C. Statements therefore act in order, and a later line sees the value an earlier line just wrote. A nonblocking assignment, by contrast, evaluates every right-hand side first and applies all the updates together later in the time step, so each statement sees the values from before the clock edge.

Inside a clocked always block, blocking assignments let one register see another's new value within the same edge. Writing "q1 = d; q2 = q1;" for a two-stage shift register gives q2 the freshly updated q1, which is d, so both simulation and the synthesized circuit delay by only one stage. Likewise "a = b; b = a;" leaves both equal to the old b instead of swapping them. Using nonblocking assignments for every register in a clocked block makes the code behave like parallel flip-flops regardless of statement order.

about.h: Where blocking is the right choice
about.p: Blocking assignment belongs in combinational always blocks, written as always @(*) or SystemVerilog always_comb, where an intermediate variable computed on one line feeds the next and the result describes a chain of gates. It is also natural in testbench procedural code and for temporary variables inside functions and tasks. The widely followed rules are: nonblocking for clocked logic, blocking for combinational logic, and never assign the same variable with both kinds.

Driving a design input with a blocking assignment at exactly the same simulation time as the active clock edge creates a race: whether the design's flip-flops capture the old or the new value depends on which process the simulator happens to execute first, and results can differ between simulators. Common fixes are changing stimulus on the opposite clock edge or a short delay after the active edge, driving inputs with nonblocking assignments, or using SystemVerilog clocking blocks.

faq.q: When should I use blocking vs nonblocking assignment in Verilog?
faq.a: Use nonblocking assignment for registers in clocked always blocks and blocking assignment in combinational blocks and for temporary variables. Do not mix both kinds on the same variable.

faq.q: Why does my Verilog shift register only delay by one clock?
faq.a: Most likely the stages are written with blocking assignments, so each stage receives the value the previous line just updated. Switching to nonblocking assignments makes every stage take the pre-edge value.

faq.q: Is a VHDL variable assignment like a Verilog blocking assignment?
faq.a: Yes, roughly: a VHDL variable assignment takes effect immediately within the process, while a VHDL signal assignment is scheduled and behaves more like a nonblocking assignment.

センシティビティリスト.desc: The list in @( ) after a Verilog always that names the signals triggering the block. Omissions in combinational logic make simulation and hardware disagree.

about.p: An event-driven simulator does not evaluate an always block continuously. It waits at the @( ) event control and wakes the block only when a listed signal changes, or, for posedge and negedge entries, only on that particular edge. Everything follows from this: if a signal that affects the outputs is missing from the list, the block simply does not run when that signal changes, and the outputs keep stale values until some listed signal moves.

Synthesis tools largely ignore the list for combinational logic and build gates from the block's statements, typically with only a warning. So "always @(a) y = a & b;" synthesizes to an AND gate in which y follows both inputs, while the simulator updates y only when a changes. Tests that happen to toggle a will pass, yet the hardware behaves differently from the RTL simulation. The mismatch is dangerous because it survives RTL verification and appears only in gate-level simulation or silicon.

Verilog-2001 introduced always @(*), which automatically includes every signal read inside the block and removes the risk of omissions. SystemVerilog's always_comb goes further: it also executes once at time zero so outputs start consistent, is sensitive to signals read inside called functions, and lets tools flag blocks that would infer a latch. Hand-written sensitivity lists for combinational logic are now a legacy style best avoided.

For flip-flops the list names edges rather than levels. "always @(posedge clk)" describes a register that samples on the rising clock edge. Adding "or negedge rst_n" gives an asynchronous active-low reset: the block also runs the instant rst_n falls, so the output clears without waiting for a clock, even when the clock is stopped. The "_n" suffix is a common convention for active-low signals. The reset's release still needs care, usually by synchronizing it to the clock to meet recovery and removal timing.

faq.q: What does always @(*) mean in Verilog?
faq.a: The block runs whenever any signal it reads changes, which is the correct behavior for combinational logic. The asterisk saves you from listing signals by hand and missing one.

faq.q: Does synthesis use the sensitivity list?
faq.a: For combinational logic, synthesis tools essentially ignore it and build logic from the statements, so an incomplete list causes simulation to disagree with the hardware. Edge keywords in clocked blocks are used to infer flip-flops and asynchronous resets.

faq.q: Does VHDL have a sensitivity list too?
faq.a: Yes. A VHDL process lists its triggering signals in parentheses after the process keyword, and VHDL-2008 adds process(all), the counterpart of Verilog's @(*).

意図しないラッチ.desc: A latch created by synthesis when a description intended as combinational logic fails to assign an output under some condition, so the value must be held.

非同期リセット.desc: A reset that initializes flip-flops as soon as the reset signal is asserted, regardless of the clock. Release should be synchronized to the clock.

about.h: How an asynchronous reset is written
about.p: In Verilog an asynchronous reset appears in the sensitivity list together with the clock, as in always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) followed by if (!rst_n) q <= 0; else q <= d;. Because the falling edge of rst_n also triggers the block, q clears the instant reset is asserted, without waiting for a clock edge. The _n suffix is a common naming convention for active-low signals. Synthesis maps this pattern onto flip-flops that have a dedicated reset or clear pin, so the reset does not pass through the data path logic.

A synchronous reset is just another input sampled at the clock edge: it passes through logic in front of the flip-flop's D input and takes effect only when the clock is running. That makes timing analysis simple, but it cannot initialize a block whose clock is stopped and adds logic to the data path. An asynchronous reset uses the flip-flop's reset pin, acting immediately even without a clock, which is useful at power-up or when clocks are gated. Its weakness is the moment of release, which has timing requirements of its own.

Flip-flops specify recovery and removal times, which play the role of setup and hold times for the deassertion of an asynchronous reset. If reset is released too close to a clock edge, a flip-flop may become metastable, or flip-flops at different points of the reset network may leave reset in different clock cycles. A state machine whose bits start one cycle apart can begin in an illegal state. Because the external reset source is not related to the clock, this situation cannot be ruled out without synchronizing the release.

The usual remedy is a reset synchronizer: two flip-flops in series, clocked by the destination clock, whose asynchronous reset pins are driven by the external reset, with the first stage's data input tied to the inactive level. Asserting reset clears both stages at once, so reset still acts immediately. On release, the inactive level must ripple through the two flip-flops, so the distributed reset deasserts in step with the clock, and the second stage gives the first time to resolve metastability. Each clock domain needs its own synchronizer.

faq.q: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous reset?
faq.a: A synchronous reset takes effect only at an active clock edge and needs a running clock, while an asynchronous reset acts immediately through the flip-flop's reset pin regardless of the clock.

faq.q: Why do we synchronize the release of an asynchronous reset?
faq.a: If reset is released near a clock edge, flip-flops can violate recovery or removal timing, become metastable or leave reset in different cycles; a two-flip-flop synchronizer aligns the release to the clock.

faq.q: What are recovery and removal times?
faq.a: They are the minimum times by which an asynchronous reset must be deasserted before (recovery) or held after (removal) an active clock edge, analogous to setup and hold times for data.

同期リセット.desc: A reset sampled at clock edges to initialize flip-flops. Timing is easier to analyze, but it does not act while the clock is stopped.

リセット同期化回路.desc: A circuit that applies an asynchronous reset immediately but aligns its release to the clock through two flip-flops before distributing it.

ミーリ型.desc: A state machine whose outputs depend on both the current state and the inputs. Input changes reach outputs within the same cycle, but so can input glitches. A Moore machine's outputs depend only on state.
ミーリ型.title: Mealy Machine vs. Moore Machine: Differences Explained
ミーリ型.description: A Mealy machine's outputs depend on the state and the inputs; a Moore machine's depend on the state only. Timing, glitches and when to choose each.

about.h: Definition and structure of a Mealy machine
about.p: In a Mealy state machine, outputs depend on both the current state and the current inputs. Like a Moore machine, it consists of a state register, combinational logic for the next state and combinational logic for the outputs, but the inputs connect directly to the output logic. In a state diagram, outputs are written on the transition arrows as input/output rather than inside the states. Because outputs change as soon as inputs change, without waiting for the next clock, a Mealy machine can react one cycle sooner than a Moore machine and often implements the same function with fewer states.

In a Moore machine, outputs depend only on the current state and are written inside the states in a state diagram. An input change reaches the outputs only after the clock changes the state, so the response is a cycle later, but input noise does not pass to the outputs and timing is easier to predict. Encoding the states so that outputs come directly from state-register bits also eliminates output glitches. In a Mealy machine, a combinational path runs from inputs to outputs, so input glitches appear at the outputs and timing paths that include the surrounding logic become longer.

Consider an overlapping sequence detector that outputs 1 when it finds 101 in an input bit stream. A Mealy machine needs only three states: nothing matched, matched 1, and matched 10. In the matched-10 state, the output goes to 1 as soon as a 1 arrives, and the machine moves to matched 1, treating that 1 as the start of the next candidate. A Moore machine needs an extra detected-101 state to represent output 1, giving four states, and its output becomes 1 only after the clock that captures the final 1. The Mealy machine thus uses fewer states and responds faster, while the Moore machine has the edge in output stability.

In Verilog or VHDL it is common to write a sequential block that updates the state register separately from a combinational block that determines the next state and outputs; if the output expressions include inputs, the machine is a Mealy machine. Using asynchronous inputs directly disturbs the outputs, so inputs should be synchronized first. Connecting a Mealy output to the input of another Mealy machine can create a combinational loop, so care is needed. Registering the outputs through flip-flops removes glitches, but the timing then lags by one cycle, just like a Moore machine.

faq.q: What is the difference between a Mealy machine and a Moore machine?
faq.a: A Mealy machine's outputs depend on both the current state and the inputs, while a Moore machine's depend only on the current state. A Mealy machine can respond to inputs in the same cycle and often needs fewer states, but input noise passes to its outputs more easily.

faq.q: Which should I use, Mealy or Moore?
faq.a: Mealy suits cases where response speed or fewer states matter; Moore suits cases where output stability and predictable timing matter. Real designs choose per output or combine both.

faq.q: Can a Mealy machine be converted to a Moore machine?
faq.a: Yes. Splitting each Mealy state according to the output of the transitions entering it into separate Moore states gives the same input-output relationship. The number of states may increase, however, and the outputs appear one clock later.

ワンホット符号化.desc: State encoding that assigns one flip-flop per state with exactly one set at a time. Logic tends to be simple and fast, and it is common on FPGAs.

about.p: In a finite state machine, one-hot encoding gives each state its own flip-flop, and exactly one flip-flop holds 1 at any time. Four states become 0001, 0010, 0100 and 1000. Testing whether the machine is in a given state means looking at a single bit, so outputs that depend on the state are often just one flip-flop or a small OR of a few. The next-state input of each flip-flop is the OR of the conditions on the transitions entering that state, each ANDed with the bit of the source state, which keeps the logic depth shallow and the machine fast.

Binary encoding numbers the states and needs only the ceiling of log2 N flip-flops: three states fit in two flip-flops, while one-hot needs three, and sixteen states need four flip-flops versus sixteen. The cost of binary encoding is wider decode logic, because recognizing a state means comparing all state bits. Gray-code encoding, a third option, assigns codes so that frequent transitions change one bit, reducing switching activity. Binary suits designs where flip-flops are scarce or the state count is large; one-hot suits speed and simplicity when flip-flops are plentiful.

An FPGA logic block pairs each small lookup table (LUT) with one or more flip-flops, so registers are abundant while wide logic functions must be split across several LUT levels. One-hot encoding fits this structure well: each state bit's next-state function usually involves only a few inputs and fits in a single LUT, which shortens critical paths. Synthesis tools commonly detect state machines and pick an encoding automatically, often one-hot for small and medium machines, though designers can override the choice. In ASICs, where flip-flops cost more area, binary or other compact encodings are more common.

With N flip-flops, one-hot uses only N of the 2^N possible patterns, so all-zero and multi-hot patterns are illegal. Noise, a glitch or a radiation-induced bit flip could put the machine into one of them, where it may stall or behave unpredictably. Binary encoding has the same issue with unused codes, such as 11 in a three-state machine. Robust designs therefore define a default branch that returns any unexpected state to a known one, and synthesis tools offer safe state-machine options that keep this recovery logic instead of optimizing it away.

faq.q: How many flip-flops does one-hot encoding need?
faq.a: One flip-flop per state, so a machine with N states needs N flip-flops. Binary encoding of the same machine needs only the ceiling of log2 N.

faq.q: What is the difference between one-hot and binary state encoding?
faq.a: One-hot uses one flip-flop per state with a single bit set, giving simple, fast decode logic at the cost of more registers. Binary encoding stores the state number in the fewest flip-flops but needs wider logic to decode each state.

faq.q: Is one-hot encoding in digital design the same as one-hot encoding in machine learning?
faq.a: The idea is the same: a vector with exactly one element set to 1 identifies one item from a set. In hardware it encodes the current state of a state machine or a select signal, while in machine learning it represents a categorical value as a numeric vector.

4値論理.desc: The four values used in HDL simulation: 0, 1, X (unknown) and Z (high impedance). Uninitialized or conflicting signals become X.

X楽観主義.desc: In HDL simulation, the tendency for conditions containing unknown X to resolve to definite values instead of propagating X, hiding bugs.

テストベンチ.desc: Simulation-only code that drives inputs to the design under test and checks its outputs. Since it is never synthesized, delays, display statements and similar can be used freely.
テストベンチ.title: Testbench in Verilog and SystemVerilog: What It Contains
テストベンチ.description: A testbench drives inputs into the design under test and checks outputs in simulation. What it contains, simulation-only code, races and self-checking tests.

about.p: A testbench is a top-level HDL module, usually without ports, that instantiates the design under test (DUT) and surrounds it with everything needed to exercise it. It generates the clock, for example always #5 clk = ~clk; which toggles every 5 time units and gives a 10 ns period with a 1 ns unit, applies reset, drives input stimulus, and observes the outputs. It may also read test vectors from files, write logs and dump waveforms. The DUT is the synthesizable design; the testbench exists only in simulation.

Because a testbench is never synthesized, it can use features that have no hardware meaning. Delay statements such as #10 advance simulation time, $display and file I/O print or record values, and the case-equality operator === compares X and Z bits literally, which lets a test detect an output that has become unknown. Synthesis ignores or rejects these constructs, so they must stay out of RTL. If they leak into the design code, simulation and hardware behavior can diverge in ways that are hard to debug.

about.h: Avoiding races at the clock edge
about.p: A common testbench bug is changing a DUT input with a blocking assignment at exactly the same simulation time as the rising clock edge. Whether the DUT flip-flops capture the old or new value then depends on the order in which the simulator executes events, a race whose result can even differ between simulators. Safer practice is to drive inputs on the opposite clock edge or a little after the active edge, to use nonblocking assignments, or to use SystemVerilog clocking blocks, which define sampling and driving times explicitly.

For a small block, inspecting waveforms by eye may be enough, but this does not scale. A self-checking testbench computes or looks up the expected result for each input, often with a reference model, compares it automatically with the DUT output and reports mismatches as errors. Thousands of tests can then run unattended, for example overnight in regression. Larger projects build on this with constrained-random stimulus, scoreboards and coverage collection, and verification effort often matches or exceeds design effort.

faq.q: Is a testbench synthesizable?
faq.a: No. A testbench is written only for simulation, so it freely uses delays, display statements, file I/O and other constructs that cannot become hardware.

faq.q: What is the DUT in a testbench?
faq.a: DUT stands for design under test, the synthesizable module that the testbench instantiates, drives with stimulus and checks.

faq.q: What is the difference between == and === in a Verilog testbench?
faq.a: The == operator returns X if either operand contains X or Z bits, like a hardware comparator. The === operator compares X and Z literally and always returns 0 or 1, so testbenches use it to detect unknown outputs.

参照モデル.desc: A separate model, often in C, implementing the same function as the circuit. Its results for the same inputs serve as expected values for the design's outputs.

制約付きランダム検証.desc: Verification that generates random input values within constraints allowed by the specification, broadly exercising cases people might not think of.

回帰テスト.desc: Re-running existing tests after each design change to confirm that previously working features still work.

Lint.desc: A tool that checks HDL or other code against rules without simulation, flagging problem-prone constructs such as width mismatches and unintended latches.

ゲートレベルシミュレーション.desc: Simulation of the post-synthesis or post-layout netlist, optionally with delay information, to catch problems invisible at RTL.
ゲートレベルシミュレーション.title: Gate-Level Simulation (GLS): What It Catches That RTL Misses
ゲートレベルシミュレーション.description: Gate-level simulation runs the synthesized or post-layout netlist, optionally with delays, to catch bugs RTL simulation can't see. When and why it's needed.

about.h: How it differs from RTL simulation
about.p: Gate-level simulation (GLS) runs the netlist produced by logic synthesis or place-and-route together with simulation models of the standard cells. RTL simulation checks the behavior as written, whereas GLS checks how the gates and flip-flops actually created are connected and how they behave. It can therefore reveal cases where the synthesis tool interpreted the description differently from the designer's intent, and verify circuitry that did not exist in the RTL, such as scan chains and clock-gating cells.

There are two broad kinds of GLS. Zero-delay GLS, which treats all delays as zero, mainly checks logical behavior, reset and initialization, and how unknown values (X) propagate. Timing GLS back-annotates each cell's and wire's delay onto the netlist using an SDF (Standard Delay Format) file output by a static timing analysis (STA) tool or similar. The cell models contain built-in setup and hold checks, so a violation produces a warning and drives the flip-flop output to X. Delays are generally checked at several corners, such as slow and fast conditions.

In RTL simulation, unknown values can be treated optimistically, for example an if statement taking one branch when its condition is X, hiding problems with uninitialized registers (X-optimism). GLS tends to expose such missing resets and power-up unknowns. It is also used to check mismatches between simulation and synthesis caused by incomplete sensitivity lists or synthesis directives, the connections of test circuitry such as scan chains, the behavior of asynchronous paths, and errors in timing constraints (such as a path that must work in one cycle being declared an exception).

about.h: Division of labor with STA and formal verification
about.p: Timing is checked exhaustively across all paths by static timing analysis, and logical equivalence between RTL and netlist by equivalence checking (formal verification), so GLS is not the only safeguard. GLS is far slower than RTL simulation, and the larger the circuit the longer it takes, so it is generally limited to selected tests such as reset and boot sequences, test patterns and representative functional tests. Cell models may also propagate unknowns pessimistically, spreading X where there is no real problem (X-pessimism), so results need careful interpretation.

faq.q: What is gate-level simulation?
faq.a: It is simulation of the gate-level netlist produced after logic synthesis or place-and-route. With delays supplied through SDF as needed, it checks for problems invisible in RTL simulation, such as initialization bugs, differences introduced by synthesis and timing-related issues.

faq.q: Why is GLS needed when there is STA?
faq.a: STA computes delays and exhaustively checks them against constraints, but it does not check how the circuit actually behaves. Constraint mistakes, asynchronous paths, reset and initialization problems, and test-circuit behavior can be caught by GLS, which actually exercises the circuit.

faq.q: What is SDF?
faq.a: SDF stands for Standard Delay Format, a file format describing cell and wire delays, timing-check values and the like. It is output by STA tools and similar and back-annotated onto the netlist in gate-level simulation to run timing simulation.

generate文.desc: A Verilog construct that expands hardware descriptions by loops or conditions, used for example to instantiate a module repeatedly in a regular pattern.

組み合わせループ.desc: A structure in which combinational output feeds back to its own input without a flip-flop. It can oscillate or fail to settle and defeats timing analysis, so it is avoided.

VCD.desc: A standard file format recording signal value changes during simulation, viewed in waveform tools for debugging.

サイドチャネル攻撃.desc: An attack inferring secrets such as keys from physical information other than the intended output, such as processing time, power consumption or electromagnetic emissions.

タイミング攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack exploiting processing time that varies with secret values, prevented by constant-time implementation.

定数時間実装.desc: A way of writing cryptographic code so that branch directions, loop counts and memory addresses accessed do not depend on secret values.

投機的実行.desc: A CPU technique that executes instructions ahead based on predictions, such as branch outcomes, before they are known. Wrong results are discarded, but traces such as cache state may remain.

about.h: Why CPUs execute ahead of time
about.p: A high-performance CPU has a deep pipeline and executes instructions out of order, so waiting for every branch to resolve would leave it idle for many cycles. Instead, a branch predictor guesses the outcome and the core keeps fetching and executing along the predicted path. These speculative results are held in internal buffers and committed, or retired, only once the guess is confirmed. If the prediction was wrong, the core discards the speculative work and restarts on the correct path, so the program's visible results are always correct.

Rolling back a misprediction restores the architectural state, meaning the registers and memory a program can observe directly. It does not undo changes to microarchitectural state such as which lines are in the cache, TLB contents or predictor history. Those changes are normally harmless because programs cannot read them directly, but timing can reveal them: an access to a cached line is measurably faster than one to main memory. This gap between what is rolled back and what is not is the root of speculative-execution vulnerabilities.

about.h: How Spectre and Meltdown exploit it
about.p: In Spectre, disclosed in 2018 along with Meltdown, an attacker trains the branch predictor so that a path which should never run, such as code past a bounds check, executes speculatively, reads a secret, and uses its value to touch a particular cache line. The results are discarded, but timing which line is cached reveals the secret through a cache side channel. Meltdown abused CPUs that let a speculative load return data from kernel memory before the permission check took effect. Nearly all high-performance CPUs were affected by at least one variant.

Mitigations span every layer: operating systems separated kernel and user page tables, compilers insert speculation barriers or use indirect-branch sequences that avoid poisoned predictions, microcode updates add controls over predictor behavior, and newer CPUs build in hardware fixes. Each restriction on speculation, prediction or shared caches reduces leakage but can cost performance, so designers choose how far to go based on what data is at stake. The episode showed that performance features can become security weaknesses even when software is bug-free.

faq.q: Is speculative execution the same as out-of-order execution?
faq.a: They are related but different. Out-of-order execution reorders instructions whose inputs are ready, while speculative execution runs instructions before it is known that they should execute at all, such as those after an unresolved branch; modern cores do both.

faq.q: What is the difference between Spectre and Meltdown?
faq.a: Spectre tricks the branch predictor into speculatively running legitimate code paths that leak data the victim program can access. Meltdown exploited CPUs whose speculative loads could read kernel memory before the permission check took effect, and it was largely fixed by kernel page-table isolation and later hardware changes.

faq.q: Why can discarded speculative results still leak data?
faq.a: The CPU discards register results but does not restore the cache, so data loaded during speculation leaves a trace that can be detected by measuring access times.

Spectre.desc: A class of vulnerabilities, disclosed in 2018, that induces mispredicted speculative execution to read secret data and infers its value from traces left in the cache.

about.p: The classic bounds-check-bypass form targets code like: if (x < size) y = table[data[x] * 4096]. The attacker first calls it many times with valid x, training the branch predictor to expect the check to pass. Then the attacker supplies an out-of-range x while size is not in the cache. Waiting for size, the CPU speculatively reads data[x], which is really a secret byte elsewhere in memory, and loads the table line chosen by that byte. When the check resolves, the work is discarded, but the line remains cached; timing accesses to each table line reveals which one is fast, and therefore the secret.

The instruction set architecture (ISA) promises that a mispredicted path leaves no trace in program-visible, or architectural, state: registers and memory are rolled back exactly. Microarchitectural state, such as cache contents, branch predictor tables and translation buffers, exists only for performance and is not restored. Spectre turns that hidden state into a covert channel by measuring timing differences, typically with flush-and-reload techniques. No ISA rule is broken, which is why the problem spans processors from many vendors and why it is described as a class of vulnerabilities rather than a single bug.

Meltdown, disclosed at the same time, abused out-of-order execution in certain designs that let a user-mode load forward kernel data to dependent instructions before the permission fault was raised. It was largely fixed by separating kernel and user page tables in operating systems and then by hardware changes. Spectre instead tricks a victim into speculatively accessing memory that the victim itself is allowed to address, steering it with branch predictors. Because it relies on speculation in general, not on one implementation shortcut, it affects nearly all high-performance CPUs and has no single complete fix.

Software defenses insert a speculation barrier such as x86 lfence after sensitive bounds checks, or clamp indices with a mask so even speculative accesses stay in range. The branch-target-injection variant, which poisons indirect branch predictions, is countered by retpoline code sequences and by microcode and hardware controls that restrict or flush predictor state across privilege or process boundaries. Browsers reduced timer precision and isolated websites in separate processes. Each measure costs some performance, so they are applied at vulnerable points rather than by disabling speculation altogether.

faq.q: Is Spectre fixed in modern CPUs?
faq.a: Specific variants are mitigated by microcode, compiler and operating system changes and by hardware updates, but the underlying class cannot be eliminated without giving up speculation. New variants have continued to be found since 2018.

faq.q: What is the difference between Spectre and Meltdown?
faq.a: Meltdown let user code read kernel memory by exploiting a delayed permission check in some processors, and was fixed fairly directly. Spectre misleads branch prediction so a program speculatively leaks data it can address, which makes it far broader and harder to mitigate.

faq.q: Why does Spectre need a cache timing measurement?
faq.a: Speculative results are discarded, so the secret never appears in a register the attacker can read. Encoding it in which cache line was loaded, and then timing loads, is how the value is recovered.

Meltdown.desc: A vulnerability in some CPUs where kernel memory could be read speculatively before the permission exception took effect, with values inferred from cache traces. Mitigated by KPTI and other measures.

about.p: Meltdown, disclosed in 2018, abuses out-of-order execution. A user program issues a load from a kernel address. Architecturally this must raise a permission fault and return nothing, but on affected processors the loaded value was forwarded to dependent instructions before the fault took effect. Those transient instructions use the secret byte as an index into a user-owned probe array, pulling one particular cache line into the cache. When the fault is finally raised, register results are discarded, but the cache state is not rolled back.

about.h: Reading the secret through the cache
about.p: The attacker then times an access to every entry of the probe array. The one entry that loads quickly, a cache hit instead of a slow trip to DRAM, reveals the value that was read transiently. This timing side channel, commonly built with a flush-and-reload technique, is repeated byte by byte to dump kernel memory. The permission fault itself can be caught with a signal handler or otherwise suppressed, so the leak can proceed at a useful rate.

Both attacks rely on transient execution leaving traces in the cache, but they bypass different things. Meltdown breaks the user/kernel privilege boundary directly by exploiting a permission check that completes too late, and it depended on specific microarchitectural behavior found in some processor designs. Spectre instead mistrains branch predictors so that a victim's own, legitimately privileged code speculatively accesses data the attacker chooses. Spectre affects nearly all high-performance speculative CPUs and is harder to eliminate completely.

The main software mitigation, kernel page-table isolation (KPTI), stops mapping most kernel memory into the page tables used while user code runs; only a small stub needed to enter the kernel stays mapped. Without an address translation, the data cannot be loaded even transiently. The cost is a page-table switch on every system call, interrupt and exception, which can noticeably slow syscall-heavy workloads; process-context identifiers (PCIDs) reduce the TLB-flush penalty. Processors fixed in hardware do not need KPTI.

faq.q: Is Meltdown the same as Spectre?
faq.a: No. Both leak data through cache traces of speculative execution, but Meltdown reads kernel memory past a delayed permission check, while Spectre tricks a victim program's own speculation into touching secret data.

faq.q: Why does the Meltdown patch slow down computers?
faq.a: KPTI switches page tables on every transition between user and kernel mode, adding overhead and TLB misses to each system call and interrupt. Programs that make many system calls are affected most.

faq.q: Are new CPUs still vulnerable to Meltdown?
faq.a: Processors designed after the disclosure generally block the faulting data from reaching dependent instructions, and operating systems detect such CPUs and skip KPTI. Older affected CPUs still rely on the software mitigation.

KPTI.desc: An OS countermeasure to Meltdown that removes most kernel memory from the page tables while user programs run.

電力解析攻撃.desc: A side-channel attack inferring secrets from a chip's power consumption traces. Differential power analysis (DPA), which processes many traces statistically, is especially powerful.

故障注入攻撃.desc: An attack that deliberately makes a chip malfunction with voltage or clock glitches, lasers and the like to bypass authentication or infer keys.

コールドブート攻撃.desc: An attack reading DRAM contents that persist briefly after power-off to extract keys and other secrets; cooling extends persistence. Prevented by memory encryption.

セキュアブート.desc: A mechanism that verifies the digital signature of the next software at each boot stage and starts only authentic software, forming a chain of trust.

about.h: How the chain of trust works
about.p: At power-on, boot code in the chip's ROM loads the first bootloader and checks its digital signature: it hashes the image and verifies the vendor's signature over that hash. Only if the check passes does it run the bootloader, which in turn verifies the next stage or the OS kernel before handing over control. Each link vouches for the next, forming a chain of trust. If any signature fails, boot stops, so malware that rewrites the bootloader or OS boot code cannot run. Smartphones, PCs and many embedded devices use this scheme.

about.h: The root of trust in silicon
about.p: The chain is only as strong as its first check, so the root of trust must be immutable: boot code in mask ROM, fixed at manufacture, plus the public key used to verify signatures, often stored as a hash in eFuses (one-time programmable fuses) to save space. Public-key cryptography matters here. With a symmetric scheme, the key that verifies could also sign, so extracting it from one device would allow fake firmware for all devices. With public-key signatures, devices hold only a verification key and the signing private key never leaves the vendor's secure facility.

Signature checks alone still accept old firmware, because the vendor legitimately signed it. After a vulnerability is fixed, an attacker could reinstall the vulnerable version, so images carry a version number and the chip stores a minimum allowed version in write-once storage such as eFuses, advancing it with each update. Debug ports such as JTAG and SWD can read and write memory and halt the processor, which would bypass secure boot entirely, so shipped products disable them with fuses or open them only after cryptographic authentication.

Secure boot enforces: unverified code does not start. Measured boot records: each stage hashes the next and extends the result into TPM (trusted platform module) platform configuration registers, where a new value can only be formed by combining the old value with a new hash. Boot continues regardless, but the record lets software or a remote server later verify exactly what ran. Note also that a signature proves authenticity, not confidentiality; keeping firmware secret needs encryption. Secure boot protects only the start-up path, so it is one layer in defense in depth alongside memory protection, trusted execution environments and tamper resistance.

faq.q: What is the root of trust in secure boot?
faq.a: Immutable code in the chip's mask ROM together with the public key, or its hash in eFuses, used to verify the first bootloader. Everything later in the chain depends on it being unchangeable.

faq.q: What is the difference between secure boot and measured boot?
faq.a: Secure boot refuses to run software whose signature fails. Measured boot lets everything run but records hashes in a TPM so the boot state can be checked or attested later.

faq.q: Why does secure boot need anti-rollback protection?
faq.a: Older firmware versions carry valid signatures too, so without a minimum-version counter an attacker could reinstall a version with a known vulnerability.

ルートオブトラスト.desc: The component unconditionally trusted as the starting point of security checks, such as immutable ROM boot code and a public key inside the chip.

about.h: Why a starting point of trust is needed
about.p: In secure boot, each stage verifies the signature of the next software before starting it, building a chain of trust. But the very first checker cannot be checked by anything else. This starting point, which must be trusted without verification, is the root of trust. If it is tampered with, every later check becomes meaningless. A root of trust is therefore kept as small and simple as possible to minimize bugs, placed where it cannot be rewritten, and protected from being read or written from outside.

A typical setup is boot code in mask ROM, fixed at manufacture and unchangeable, plus the public key used to verify signatures. To save space, the key's hash is often stored in one-time-programmable eFuses. Per-device secret keys are written into eFuses or OTP memory, or derived from manufacturing variation using a PUF. High-end SoCs increasingly include a security subsystem combining a dedicated processor, crypto engines, a true random number generator and key storage, which boots before the main CPU and verifies the startup of everything else. Open designs such as OpenTitan and Caliptra also exist.

Roots of trust are sometimes divided by the role they play. The TCG (Trusted Computing Group) distinguishes the root of trust for measurement (RTM), which first measures the software being booted; the root of trust for storage (RTS), which keeps keys and measurements safe; and the root of trust for reporting (RTR), which signs measurements and reports them externally. There is also a root of trust for verification, which checks signatures in secure boot. On PCs, the CPU or the first part of the firmware typically serves as the measurement root, while the TPM serves as the storage and reporting root. A single chip does not necessarily fill every role.

Boot ROM's strength is that it cannot be rewritten, but if a vulnerability is found there, shipped products cannot be fixed. ROM code is therefore kept small and verified thoroughly. Against fault-injection attacks, which apply momentary glitches to the supply voltage or clock to skip the signature check, designs perform checks twice or add glitch-detection circuits. These are combined with disabling debug ports such as JTAG before shipment, preventing rollback to older versions, and storing hashes of several keys in eFuses so that a leaked key can be revoked.

faq.q: What is a root of trust?
faq.a: It is the part trusted without verification as the starting point of security checks. Unchangeable ROM boot code, the public key used to check signatures and device-unique keys are placed in the chip, and the chain of trust is built from there.

faq.q: Why must it be in hardware?
faq.a: A starting point built only in software could be rewritten by an attacker who has taken over the OS or firmware. Using hardware properties such as ROM and eFuses fixed at manufacture and key storage that cannot be read from outside keeps the starting point safe even if software is compromised.

faq.q: Is a TPM a root of trust?
faq.a: A TPM serves as the root for storing keys and measurements and the root for signing and reporting measurements. However, the software being booted is usually first measured by the CPU or the first part of the firmware, so a TPM alone does not provide every root of trust.

ロールバック防止.desc: A mechanism recording a minimum version number in unchangeable storage so software cannot be reverted to older vulnerable versions.

TPM.desc: A security chip or function that generates and stores keys, records measurements of booted software and attests to platform state.

about.p: A Trusted Platform Module is a tamper-resistant security chip, or an equivalent function implemented in firmware on the main processor, often called fTPM. It contains a random-number generator, engines for hashing, signing and encryption, protected non-volatile storage and a set of platform configuration registers (PCRs). Keys can be generated inside the TPM and used there without the private part ever leaving in the clear. The interface is defined by the Trusted Computing Group, and current PCs use version 2.0.

In measured boot, each stage hashes the next piece of software before running it and extends the hash into a PCR. Extending means the new PCR value is the hash of the old value concatenated with the new measurement; software cannot write a PCR directly, and the boot-measurement PCRs are cleared only by a platform reset. The final values therefore summarize the whole boot sequence in order, and any change produces different values. Unlike secure boot, measured boot does not stop anything from running; it produces evidence for later checks.

Two uses follow from PCRs. Sealing binds data, such as a disk-encryption key, to specific PCR values, so the TPM releases it only when the platform booted the expected software; a removed disk or a modified bootloader gets nothing. In remote attestation, the TPM signs a report of its PCR values with a key that cannot be extracted, and a server checks the signature and measurements before granting secrets, services or network access. A fresh random challenge from the server prevents replaying an old report.

about.h: TPM vs. secure element and TEE
about.p: A TPM is a standardized platform-trust component focused on measurement, key protection and attestation, and it is relatively slow; bulk encryption runs on the CPU using keys the TPM has released. A secure element is a smart-card-class chip for payment or identity credentials, and a trusted execution environment (TEE) is an isolated mode of the main processor that runs trusted code. Systems often combine them, and attestation can be rooted in either a TPM or a TEE.

faq.q: What is the difference between TPM and secure boot?
faq.a: Secure boot blocks unsigned or altered boot software from running. A TPM records measurements of what booted, protects keys and can prove the platform state to others; the two are often used together.

faq.q: What is a PCR in a TPM?
faq.a: A platform configuration register holds a running hash of measured software. It can only be extended by hashing in new measurements, so its value reflects the exact sequence of what was loaded since reset.

faq.q: What is a firmware TPM (fTPM)?
faq.a: It is TPM functionality implemented in firmware running in an isolated environment of the main processor instead of a separate chip. It offers the same interface but different physical-attack resistance from a discrete TPM.

測定ブート.desc: A mechanism that cumulatively records hashes of each boot stage's software in a TPM or similar so the boot state can be verified later.
測定ブート.title: Measured Boot vs. Secure Boot: How TPM Measurements Work
測定ブート.description: Measured boot records a hash of each boot stage in a TPM so the boot state can be verified later. How it works and how it differs from secure boot.

about.p: In measured boot, a small piece of code that runs first at startup and serves as the root of trust computes (measures) the hash of the firmware to be run next, records it in the TPM and only then hands over control. Each subsequent stage, such as the bootloader and then the OS kernel, continues the measurement chain in the same way. The records go into the TPM's PCRs (platform configuration registers), where each new value is computed as the hash of the previous PCR value concatenated with the new hash (an extend operation). The PCRs that hold boot measurements cannot be reset without a reboot, so the record cannot later be rewritten to a convenient value.

Secure boot verifies the signature of the software to be started next and halts the boot if it is not properly signed. Measured boot, by contrast, does not stop the boot but records what started in a tamper-evident way. Secure boot only tells you whether something was signed with a trusted key, so it cannot distinguish an old, correctly signed but vulnerable version, or a configuration change. Measured boot keeps the values of what actually ran. The two are not in conflict and are used together: secure boot prevents unauthorized boot, and measured boot proves the boot state.

about.h: How the recorded values are used
about.p: PCR values are used in two main ways. One is remote attestation: the device sends a server the PCR values signed with a key inside the TPM (a quote) along with the record of each stage (the event log). The server checks that the PCR values computed from the event log match, and grants access only to devices that booted the expected software. The other is sealing: secrets such as disk-encryption keys are made releasable by the TPM only when the PCRs hold specific values. If any part of the boot is altered, the key cannot be released, protecting the data.
