Vapor pressure climbs steeply with temperature, so the same package can earn a worse MSL when classified at 260 °C than at 235 °C. An MSL is therefore always quoted together with the peak reflow temperature it was classified at.

faq.q: What does MSL 3 mean?
faq.a: After the dry bag is opened, the parts must be reflowed within 168 hours (one week) at 30 °C/60% RH or less. If that floor life is exceeded, they must be baked before mounting.

faq.q: What is the popcorn effect in IC packages?
faq.a: Moisture absorbed by a plastic package turns to vapor during reflow heating, and the pressure cracks the package or delaminates internal interfaces. MSL control and baking prevent it.

faq.q: Is MSL 1 better than MSL 3?
faq.a: Yes, in handling terms. MSL 1 parts have unlimited floor life under 30 °C/85% RH, while higher numbers mean the part absorbs moisture more critically and needs tighter time control.

露出パッド(エクスポーズドパッド).desc: A large metal area on the underside of packages such as QFN, connected to the die pad. Soldered to the board, it is the main path for removing heat and is usually tied to inner-layer planes with thermal vias.

レール・ツー・レール.desc: Describes an op amp or similar whose input or output range extends close to both supply rails. It allows large signal swings in single-supply, low-voltage circuits, although the output still saturates some tens of mV short of the rails depending on load current.

スラック.desc: A value expressing timing margin. For setup it is required time minus arrival time, and for hold it is arrival time minus required time; a negative value means a violation.

about.p: Static timing analysis (STA) compares when data arrives with when it is required. For setup, the data launched at one clock edge must arrive before the next capture edge minus the setup time, so slack = required − arrival. With a 2.0 ns period, 0.2 ns clock-to-output, 1.4 ns of logic and 0.1 ns setup, arrival is 1.6 ns, required is 1.9 ns and slack is +0.3 ns. Clock uncertainty for jitter and unbuilt clock trees is also subtracted from the required time, and a multicycle path of 2 moves the capture edge one extra period later.

about.h: Hold slack and why frequency does not help
about.p: Hold asks the opposite question: does new data launched by an edge arrive so early that it corrupts the value the same edge is capturing? Here slack = arrival − required, using minimum delays and required = capture clock arrival + hold time. Because both checks refer to the same edge, the clock period does not appear, so slowing the clock never fixes a hold violation; in silicon it is usually fatal. Hold problems appear on short paths such as shift registers and are normally fixed by inserting delay cells on the data path.

Clock skew moves the two checks in opposite directions. If the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock (positive skew), setup slack grows by that amount and hold slack shrinks by the same amount; negative skew does the reverse. On-chip variation (OCV) derating makes the analysis pessimistic, for setup slowing the launch clock and data paths and speeding the capture clock. Where both clock paths share buffers from the root, that shared section cannot be fast and slow at once, so common path pessimism removal (CRPR) adds the difference back.

Reports summarize slack per endpoint. WNS (worst negative slack) is the single worst value and indicates how far the clock is from closing; TNS (total negative slack) sums the negative slacks of all violating endpoints and indicates how much work remains. Three endpoints at −0.1 ns give WNS −0.1 ns and TNS −0.3 ns. Both are reported separately for setup and hold, and per clock group. Setup violations are attacked by shortening logic, upsizing cells or restructuring; a multicycle exception is legitimate only if the logic really captures every other cycle.

faq.q: What does negative slack mean in timing analysis?
faq.a: It means the path violates its constraint: for setup the data arrives too late for the capture edge, and for hold it arrives too early and could overwrite the value being captured. The magnitude tells how much delay must be removed or added.

faq.q: What is the difference between WNS and TNS?
faq.a: WNS is the slack of the single worst path, while TNS is the sum of all negative endpoint slacks. A design can have a small WNS but a large TNS when many paths fail by a little.

faq.q: How do you fix a hold violation?
faq.a: Add delay to the short data path, typically with buffer or delay cells, or reduce the skew that pushes the capture clock late. Lowering the clock frequency does not help because the hold check does not involve the period.

WNS(ワーストネガティブスラック).desc: In STA, the worst (smallest) slack among all paths. Together with TNS (total negative slack), the sum of negative slack over violating endpoints, it indicates how large and how widespread the timing violations are.

クリティカルパス.desc: The path with the largest delay in a circuit, which sets the maximum clock frequency. In STA it is the path with the smallest slack, and speeding up a design starts by reducing its delay.

クロックの不確かさ.desc: A margin subtracted from the available time in timing analysis to account for jitter and for clock skew not yet known. It is set with set_clock_uncertainty in SDC, and before the clock tree is built it is set larger to cover skew as well.

about.h: How it enters the timing checks
about.p: In static timing analysis, clock uncertainty is a user-specified margin that makes setup and hold checks stricter. For setup, it is subtracted from the time available before the capturing edge: with a 1.25 ns period, 0.05 ns setup time and 0.05 ns uncertainty, data must arrive by 1.15 ns. For hold, it is added to the hold requirement, so data must stay stable for longer after the edge. It is specified in SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) with commands such as set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.05 [get_clocks clk], with a separate -hold value.

Three ingredients are usually folded in. Jitter from the phase-locked loop (PLL) and clock distribution makes edges arrive early or late from cycle to cycle. Before clock tree synthesis (CTS), clocks are ideal and skew between flip-flops is unknown, so an estimate of it is added. Many teams also add a design margin for effects not modeled precisely at that stage, such as supply noise. Period jitter matters for setup, which spans two different edges, but almost cancels for hold, where launch and capture use the same edge; the skew estimate applies to both.

about.h: How the value changes through the flow
about.p: During synthesis and placement, with ideal clocks, uncertainty is set relatively large to cover jitter plus expected skew. After CTS the clocks become propagated: the tool computes each flip-flop's actual clock latency, so skew is analyzed explicitly and is removed from the uncertainty, leaving jitter and margin. Uncertainty can also be set between specific clock pairs with -from and -to options, for example for paths between related clocks generated by different PLL outputs. Too large a value over-constrains the design and costs area and power; too small risks failures in silicon.

Skew is a computed difference between the clock arrival times at two flip-flops, known only once a clock tree exists. Clock uncertainty is not computed; it is an assumed lump margin applied to every path of that clock. On-chip variation (OCV) derating is different again: it scales cell and wire delays by factors, making the launch path slower and the capture path faster, or vice versa, rather than subtracting a fixed time. A complete signoff setup typically combines propagated skew, derating and a small remaining uncertainty.

faq.q: Does clock uncertainty apply to hold checks?
faq.a: Yes, but it is set separately with set_clock_uncertainty -hold and is usually smaller, because period jitter largely cancels when launch and capture share the same edge. Before CTS it still includes the expected skew.

faq.q: Why is clock uncertainty reduced after clock tree synthesis?
faq.a: Once the clock tree exists, the tool calculates real clock skew from the tree's delays, so the part of the margin that estimated skew is no longer needed. Only jitter and any design margin remain.

faq.q: How do I calculate setup slack with clock uncertainty?
faq.a: Required time equals the clock period minus setup time minus uncertainty (adjusted for clock latencies), and slack is required time minus data arrival time. For example, 1.25 − 0.05 − 0.05 = 1.15 ns required versus 1.05 ns arrival gives 0.10 ns slack.

OCV(オンチップばらつき).desc: Variation in transistor and wire delay from place to place within a single chip. STA applies separate factors to launch and capture paths (for example 1.1× and 0.9×) to analyze the most pessimistic combination.

about.p: Even within one die, transistors and wires do not match exactly. Random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness and local lithography effects shift threshold voltage and channel length; wire width and thickness vary with local pattern density; and IR drop and hot spots make local supply voltage and temperature differ. Global PVT corners (process, voltage, temperature) cover chip-to-chip shifts, but two paths on the same chip can still differ, and setup and hold checks compare exactly such pairs of paths.

With flat OCV, STA multiplies delays by derating factors chosen pessimistically for each check. For setup, the launch clock and data paths are made slow (for example ×1.1) and the capture clock path fast (×0.9). With a 1.0 ns launch clock, 1.5 ns data path, 1.0 ns capture clock, 3.0 ns period and 0.1 ns setup time, arrival is 2.75 ns and required time is 3.8 ns, giving 1.05 ns slack instead of 1.40 ns without derating. For hold the factors are swapped.

When launch and capture clocks share a common path from the clock root to a branch point, flat derating treats that same buffer chain as both slow and fast in one check, which cannot happen for a single clock edge. Common path pessimism removal (CRPR, also called CPPR) adds the difference back to the slack. For a 1.0 ns common segment with 1.1 and 0.9 factors, it recovers 0.2 ns. It does not set the common delay to zero; it only removes the double counting.

Flat derating is crude. Random variation partly averages out along deep paths, while cells placed far apart see more systematic difference. Advanced OCV (AOCV) uses tables indexed by logic depth and distance, so long paths receive smaller derates. Parametric or statistical OCV (POCV, SOCV) gives each cell a delay mean and standard deviation and combines them statistically along the path. Both recover margin that flat OCV wastes while still covering variation to a chosen confidence level.

faq.q: What is the difference between OCV and PVT corners?
faq.a: PVT corners model the whole chip shifting together to a slow or fast condition. OCV models differences between paths on the same chip at a given corner, so it is applied on top of the corner analysis.

faq.q: What is CRPR in static timing analysis?
faq.a: Common path pessimism removal credits back the slack lost when OCV derating treats the shared part of the launch and capture clock paths as both slow and fast at the same time.

faq.q: Why are OCV derates applied differently for setup and hold?
faq.a: Each check assumes its own worst case: setup is hurt by a late launch and an early capture, while hold is hurt by an early launch and a late capture, so the slow and fast factors are swapped.

CRPR(共通パスの悲観性の除去).desc: A correction in OCV-based STA that adds back to the slack the difference caused by applying both slow and fast factors to the shared portion of the launch and capture clock paths. The shared portion is physically the same, so it cannot be both slow and fast within one clock edge.

マルチサイクルパス.desc: A timing exception telling STA that a path may take several clock cycles to transfer data. When setup is set to N cycles, hold is usually set to N − 1 to move the hold check edge back to its original position.

about.h: When a path really has more time
about.p: Some paths need not deliver data within one clock period because the destination captures only every N cycles, for example a register loaded through an enable that is asserted every other cycle, or a slow arithmetic block whose result is sampled two cycles after its inputs change. By default STA assumes single-cycle transfer and reports a violation. A multicycle path exception, set_multicycle_path in SDC, tells the tool that the capture edge is N periods after launch instead of one.

With a 2.0 ns clock, a data arrival time of 3.3 ns and a 0.1 ns setup time, the default single-cycle check gives a required time of 1.9 ns and a slack of −1.4 ns. A setup multicycle of 2 moves capture to 4.0 ns, so the required time becomes 3.9 ns and the slack +0.6 ns. The exception is valid only if the logic truly guarantees capture every second cycle; otherwise it hides a real failure that will appear in silicon.

STA checks hold against the edge one period before the setup capture edge. Moving setup capture to N periods therefore also drags the hold check to N − 1 periods after launch, which would demand that new data arrive at least that late, an absurdly strict requirement that usually fails. Adding a hold multicycle of N − 1 moves the hold check back to the launch edge at time zero, restoring the ordinary hold condition. It does not remove the hold check.

A multicycle path stays timed, just with a longer budget. A false path, set with set_false_path, is excluded from analysis entirely and is meant for paths that are structurally connected but can never carry a meaningful transition, for example through two multiplexers whose select conditions are mutually exclusive. Declaring a path false merely because it is hard to close hides real bugs, and declaring a genuine multicycle path false removes a check it still needs.

faq.q: Why is a hold multicycle of N − 1 set with a setup multicycle of N?
faq.a: Moving the setup capture edge also moves the default hold check later, making hold nearly impossible to meet. The N − 1 hold setting returns the hold check to its original edge.

faq.q: What is the difference between a multicycle path and a false path?
faq.a: A multicycle path is still analyzed but given several clock periods. A false path is not analyzed at all and should be used only for paths that can never functionally propagate.

faq.q: When is it safe to set a multicycle path?
faq.a: Only when the design guarantees the destination samples the data every N cycles, for example through an enable, and verification confirms that behavior. Otherwise the relaxed check can mask a real timing failure.

フォールスパス.desc: A path that exists structurally but along which no signal actually propagates in operation. It is excluded from STA as a timing exception, specified with set_false_path in SDC.

SDC.desc: A format for timing constraints that describes clock periods and waveforms, input and output delays, timing exceptions and so on. Written as Tcl commands, it is shared by logic synthesis, place-and-route and STA tools.

about.p: SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) is a Tcl-based format that originated at Synopsys and is now read by most synthesis, place-and-route and static timing analysis tools. Typical commands define clocks (create_clock with period and waveform), derived clocks (create_generated_clock), external timing at the ports (set_input_delay, set_output_delay), the electrical environment (set_load, set_driving_cell), clock quality (set_clock_uncertainty, set_clock_latency) and timing exceptions (set_false_path, set_multicycle_path, set_max_delay, set_clock_groups).

set_clock_uncertainty subtracts margin for jitter and, before clock-tree synthesis (CTS), for expected skew: with a 1 ns period and 50 ps of uncertainty, data must arrive within 0.95 ns. After CTS the tool computes the real skew from the built tree, so the uncertainty is reduced to jitter plus any deliberate margin. A divided clock must be declared with create_generated_clock relative to its source, for example divide-by-2 turning 500 MHz into 250 MHz, so the flip-flops it drives are analyzed with the correct period and phase relationship.

about.h: Why constraints are a sign-off risk
about.p: Tools optimize and verify only what the constraints describe. A missing clock leaves flip-flops unanalyzed, an over-broad false path silences real violations, and declaring synchronous clocks asynchronous drops paths that must be checked. Such a design can pass every tool report and still fail in silicon. Constraints are therefore reviewed as carefully as RTL, checked with constraint-linting tools for unclocked registers and unconstrained ports, and kept consistent between synthesis, implementation and sign-off.

SDC states requirements, not results. Calculated delays are exchanged in SDF (Standard Delay Format) for back-annotated gate-level simulation, and extracted parasitics in SPEF (Standard Parasitic Exchange Format). FPGA tools use SDC or close derivatives that add physical constraints such as pin assignments. Because SDC is Tcl, variables and loops can generate constraints compactly, though heavily scripted files become harder to review.

faq.q: What does SDC stand for in VLSI?
faq.a: Synopsys Design Constraints, a Tcl-based format for timing constraints such as clocks, input and output delays and timing exceptions, shared by synthesis, place-and-route and STA tools.

faq.q: What is the difference between SDC and SDF?
faq.a: SDC describes the timing requirements the design must meet, while SDF carries calculated cell and interconnect delays, mainly for back-annotated gate-level simulation.

faq.q: When do I need create_generated_clock?
faq.a: Whenever a clock is derived inside the design, for example by a divider or clock multiplexer. Without it, the derived net is not treated as a clock and the logic it drives is not timed correctly.

リカバリーチェック.desc: A timing check that the release of an asynchronous reset or similar does not come too soon before a clock edge; it corresponds to setup. It is paired with the removal check, which verifies that release does not come too soon after the edge and corresponds to hold.

クロックドメイン.desc: A group of flip-flops driven by the same clock, or by clocks with a fixed frequency and phase relationship. Passing a signal between clock domains that are asynchronous to each other requires a synchronizer.

about.h: What makes two clocks the same domain
about.p: Flip-flops belong to one domain when they share a clock, or clocks whose frequency and phase relationship is fixed, such as divided clocks from the same PLL. Static timing analysis (STA) can then check every path for setup and hold. Clocks from independent sources, or with no known phase relationship, are asynchronous: a data edge can arrive at any point relative to the capturing edge, so timing cannot be guaranteed. Such paths are excluded from normal timing checks, for example by declaring the clocks as asynchronous groups in the constraints, and must instead be made safe by design.

If data changes inside a flip-flop's setup and hold window, the output can hover between 0 and 1, a metastable state, before resolving. The standard single-bit synchronizer adds a second flip-flop in the receiving domain, giving the first one a full cycle to settle. The probability of failure falls exponentially with that settling time, so two stages usually give a mean time between failures far beyond the product lifetime, and three are used at high frequencies. A synchronizer lowers the probability; it does not remove it, and it decides only when a change is seen, not whether it was valid.

about.h: Crossing with multi-bit data and pulses
about.p: Synchronizing each bit of a bus separately fails because different bits may be captured on different edges: a change from 0111 to 1000 can arrive as 1111 or 0000 for a cycle. Counters crossing domains are therefore Gray-coded so only one bit changes at a time, and arbitrary data is held stable while a single valid or request bit is synchronized, through a handshake or an asynchronous FIFO. Pulses also need care: a 2 ns pulse from a 500 MHz domain can fall between 10 ns edges of a 100 MHz clock and vanish, so it is stretched or converted to a toggle.

Signals entering a synchronizer must come straight from a flip-flop in the sending domain, because combinational logic can glitch and an asynchronous edge may capture the glitch. Toggle synchronizers need a minimum spacing between events, several receiving cycles, or two toggles can cancel out. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model metastability and rarely exposes these bugs, so dedicated clock domain crossing (CDC) tools check structurally for missing synchronizers, logic in front of them and unsafe multi-bit crossings. Resets crossing domains need the same care, typically asserted asynchronously and released synchronously.

faq.q: What is a clock domain crossing?
faq.a: A clock domain crossing is any path where a signal launched by one clock is captured by another clock that is asynchronous to it. Such paths need synchronizers, handshakes or asynchronous FIFOs because timing analysis cannot guarantee them.

faq.q: Why does a synchronizer use two flip-flops?
faq.a: The first flip-flop may go metastable when its input changes near the clock edge; the second gives it a full clock period to settle before the value is used. This makes the failure probability extremely small, though never zero.

faq.q: Are clocks with different frequencies always in different clock domains?
faq.a: No. If they are derived from the same source with a fixed ratio and phase, such as a clock and its divide-by-two, timing analysis can check paths between them, so they can be treated as synchronous.

同期化回路.desc: A circuit that aligns an asynchronous signal to the receiving clock. The basic form is two flip-flops in series, which raises the probability that metastability in the first stage resolves before the next edge.

about.p: When an asynchronous input changes inside a flip-flop's setup–hold window, the flop can go metastable, its output hovering between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time. This cannot be prevented, but the probability that it is still unresolved falls exponentially with waiting time. A two-flop synchronizer exploits this: the first flop may go metastable, and the second samples it a full clock period later, by which time it has almost certainly settled. The rest of the receiving domain only ever sees the second flop's clean output.

Synchronizer reliability is expressed as mean time between failures, approximately MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data), where t_r is the time available to resolve and τ and T_0 are flip-flop constants. Because t_r sits in an exponent, small changes matter enormously: with τ = 20 ps, one extra nanosecond multiplies MTBF by e^50. Adding a third stage adds roughly one clock period of resolution time. Raising the receiving clock frequency hurts twice, by adding more sampling events and by shrinking the period, which is why very fast domains often use three stages.

Connect the first and second flops directly, with no combinational logic or buffering between them, and place them close together; any delay there is subtracted from t_r. Never fan the first-stage output out to other logic, since different loads could interpret a metastable level differently. The signal entering the synchronizer must come straight from a flip-flop in the sending domain, not from combinational logic, because an asynchronous edge can catch a momentary glitch as a valid pulse. Clock-domain-crossing (CDC) verification tools check these rules automatically.

A synchronizer handles one bit at a time. If each bit of a bus has its own synchronizer, bits can resolve in different cycles, so a change from 0111 to 1000 may briefly read as 1111 or 0000. Signals synchronized separately and recombined, called reconvergence, show the same hazard. Short pulses are another trap: a 2 ns pulse can fall entirely between edges of a 100 MHz clock and vanish. Remedies include Gray-coded counters, holding data while a single valid bit is synchronized, handshakes, asynchronous FIFOs, and stretching level signals to about 1.5 receiving periods or more.

faq.q: Is a two flip-flop synchronizer enough?
faq.a: For most designs at moderate clock rates, yes: a two-stage synchronizer typically pushes MTBF to thousands of years or more. At very high receiving frequencies or with flops having a large τ, a third stage is added to gain another clock period of resolution time.

faq.q: Can I synchronize a multi-bit bus with one synchronizer per bit?
faq.a: No, not for arbitrary data, because different bits may be captured in different cycles and produce values that never existed. Use Gray code for counters, or hold the data stable and synchronize a single control bit through a handshake, or use an asynchronous FIFO.

faq.q: Why does a pulse get lost when crossing from a fast to a slow clock?
faq.a: If the pulse is shorter than the receiving clock period it can start and end between two receiving edges and never be sampled. Stretch it to well beyond one receiving period, or convert it to a toggle that is then synchronized and edge-detected.

MTBF(平均故障間隔).desc: The average interval between failures. For a synchronizer it is the average time between metastable events that fail to resolve and propagate onward, given by MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) ÷ (T_0 × f_clk × f_data). Adding stages lengthens the resolution time t_r and increases it exponentially.

about.p: Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the average operating time between successive failures of a repairable system. For parts that are not repaired, the matching figure is mean time to failure (MTTF), and the average time to restore service is mean time to repair (MTTR). With a constant failure rate λ, MTBF = 1/λ, and since 1 FIT is one failure per 10⁹ device-hours, 100 FIT corresponds to 10⁷ hours. An average is not a guaranteed life: under a constant failure rate about 63% of units have failed by the time t equals MTBF.

Quality describes whether a product meets specification at shipment, tracked with figures such as DPPM (defective parts per million) or controlled by sampling with an acceptable quality level (AQL). Reliability is the time-dependent ability to keep working under stated conditions, expressed with FIT, MTTF and MTBF. Quality can be checked by testing finished parts, but reliability has to be predicted, usually from accelerated stress tests at elevated temperature or voltage whose results are extrapolated to use conditions.

In digital design MTBF has a special meaning: the average time between metastable events that fail to resolve before the next stage samples them. It is approximated by MTBF = e^(t_r/τ) / (T_0 × f_clk × f_data). Here t_r is the resolution time available, roughly a clock period minus overheads; τ is the flip-flop's regeneration time constant; and T_0 relates to the width of its metastability window. More sampling events from a faster clock or a busier data input reduce MTBF linearly, while t_r acts exponentially.

Because t_r sits in the exponent, adding one synchronizer stage, which adds roughly one clock period, typically multiplies MTBF by an astronomical factor; with τ = 20 ps, one extra nanosecond gives e^50, more than 10^21. Doubling the receive clock from 500 MHz to 1 GHz halves the period and cuts MTBF by far more than two. Failure rates add for parts in series, so a chip with many synchronizers has a system MTBF lower than any single one, and well-designed crossings aim for thousands of years or more.

faq.q: Does an MTBF of 1,000,000 hours mean a device will last 114 years?
faq.a: No. MTBF describes a population's failure rate during its useful life, not the lifetime of a single unit. With a constant failure rate, about 63% of units would have failed by one MTBF, and wear-out mechanisms usually end life much earlier.

faq.q: How do you convert FIT to MTBF?
faq.a: Under a constant failure rate, MTBF in hours equals 10⁹ divided by the FIT value. For example, 50 FIT corresponds to 2×10⁷ hours.

faq.q: What is the difference between MTBF and MTTF?
faq.a: MTBF applies to repairable systems and measures average operating time between failures, while MTTF applies to non-repairable parts and measures average time until their single failure. For a chip that is replaced rather than repaired, MTTF is the appropriate term.

非同期FIFO.desc: A FIFO written and read on separate clocks, used to pass multi-bit data between clock domains. Its pointers are converted to Gray code before being synchronized into the other domain to decide full and empty. The pointers have one more bit than the address to distinguish wrap-around.

about.h: How an asynchronous FIFO is built
about.p: An asynchronous FIFO is a dual-port memory written on the sender's clock and read on the receiver's clock. The write pointer lives in the write domain and the read pointer in the read domain. Each pointer is passed through a synchronizer into the opposite domain: the write side compares its own pointer with the synchronized read pointer to generate full, and the read side compares its pointer with the synchronized write pointer to generate empty. The data itself is never synchronized; it sits stable in memory until the pointers say it may be read.

A binary counter can flip many bits at once, such as 0111 to 1000, and bits synchronized separately may resolve in different cycles, producing a value unrelated to either. In Gray code only one bit changes per increment, so even if that bit is caught mid-change the receiver sees either the old or the new pointer, just possibly one step stale. Depth is normally a power of two so the sequence wraps cleanly. The pointer bits should not simply be declared false paths: a maximum-delay constraint keeps their skew within one sending period.

With 16 entries, a 4-bit address cannot distinguish an empty FIFO from one that has wrapped all the way round, because both show equal addresses. Adding a fifth lap bit solves this. In binary, all five bits equal means empty, and only the MSB differing means full. In Gray code the full condition becomes the top two bits inverted and the lower three equal; for a read pointer of 00000, full is 11000. Because each side sees a stale copy of the other pointer, full and empty may be held slightly too long but are never released too early, so it errs safe.

Depth must absorb the rate mismatch during a burst. If the writer sends 100 words at 100 MHz and the reader drains one word per cycle at 80 MHz, the burst lasts 1000 ns, the reader removes 80 words, and 20 remain, which follows from burst × (1 − read rate / write rate). Real designs add a few entries for the two-to-three-cycle pointer synchronization latency. Compared with a req/ack handshake, which needs eight or more cycles per item, an asynchronous FIFO sustains one word per cycle and is the standard choice for streaming data.

faq.q: Why does an asynchronous FIFO use Gray code pointers?
faq.a: Only one bit changes per increment, so a pointer sampled mid-change by the other clock still resolves to a valid value from just before or after the increment. A binary pointer could be captured as a completely wrong value and corrupt full or empty.

faq.q: Why is the FIFO pointer one bit wider than the address?
faq.a: The extra bit counts laps. When the addresses match, equal lap bits mean empty and different lap bits mean the writer has gone a full lap ahead, which means full.

faq.q: Asynchronous FIFO or handshake for clock domain crossing?
faq.a: Use a handshake for occasional transfers such as configuration registers, where a cost of eight or more cycles per item is acceptable. Use an asynchronous FIFO when data must flow continuously at up to one word per cycle.

トグル同期.desc: A scheme that turns each pulse on the sending side into a toggle of a level signal, synchronizes it, and recovers a pulse on the receiving side by XORing it with its value one cycle earlier. Pulses shorter than the receiving clock period are not lost, but pulses must be spaced several receiving cycles apart.

ハンドシェイク.desc: A scheme that transfers data reliably by exchanging a request (req) from the sender and an acknowledgment (ack) from the receiver. Across clock domains only req and ack are synchronized while the data is held stable, which is safe but takes several cycles or more per transfer.

about.p: In a four-phase (return-to-zero) handshake the sender first places data on the bus and holds it, then raises req. The receiver sees the synchronized req, captures the data and raises ack. The sender sees the synchronized ack and lowers req, and the receiver, seeing req fall, lowers ack. Each signal rises and falls once, four transitions per transfer. The critical rule is ordering: data must be stable before req rises and must not change until ack confirms capture, or the receiver may catch a value in transition.

about.h: Why it is safe across clock domains
about.p: Only req and ack cross between domains, and each is a single bit passed through an ordinary two-flop synchronizer. The multi-bit data is never synchronized; by the time the receiver sees req, the data has been stable for several cycles and can be captured directly. This removes the bit-skew problem that breaks per-bit synchronization of a bus, works for any frequency ratio, and never loses an event because the sender waits for confirmation. That waiting is what distinguishes it from toggle synchronization, which requires a guaranteed minimum spacing between events.

Every transition must pass through a synchronizer, typically two cycles each way, and four-phase signaling needs two round trips, so one transfer costs eight or more cycles in total across both domains. A two-phase variant treats each toggle of req or ack as an event, halving the transitions at the cost of edge-detection logic. Either way, throughput is far below one word per cycle, so handshakes suit occasional transfers such as control-register writes, while streaming data goes through an asynchronous FIFO.

The same request–acknowledge idea appears in synchronous buses, without synchronizers. In AXI, every channel uses VALID from the sender and READY from the receiver, and a transfer occurs on any clock edge where both are 1. Holding READY low applies backpressure, so blocks of different speeds connect without losing data. To avoid deadlock, the sender must not wait for READY before asserting VALID. AXI has five independent channels for read address, read data, write address, write data and write response; AXI4-Stream drops addresses for one-way data flow.

faq.q: What is the difference between two-phase and four-phase handshakes?
faq.a: In four-phase signaling req and ack each rise and then return to zero, so one transfer uses four transitions. In two-phase signaling every toggle is an event, so a transfer needs only two transitions, roughly halving latency but requiring edge detection.

faq.q: Does an AXI VALID/READY handshake need synchronizers?
faq.a: No, VALID/READY operates within a single clock domain and transfers on any edge where both are high. When AXI traffic must cross clock domains, an asynchronous bridge, usually built from asynchronous FIFOs, is inserted.

faq.q: Why is a req/ack handshake slow for clock domain crossing?
faq.a: Each req and ack transition passes through a multi-cycle synchronizer and the sender must wait for the reply, so a full transfer takes eight or more cycles. That is acceptable for occasional data but not for continuous streams.

AEC-Q100.desc: The qualification standard for reliability testing of automotive integrated circuits, defined by the Automotive Electronics Council (AEC). It has operating temperature grades: Grade 1 is −40 to 125 °C and Grade 0 is −40 to 150 °C. Discrete semiconductors are covered by AEC-Q101 and passive components by AEC-Q200.

about.p: AEC-Q100 is a set of stress tests an integrated circuit must pass before it is accepted for automotive use. Test groups cover accelerated lifetime, package integrity, temperature cycling, humidity, electrostatic discharge (ESD) and latch-up, among others. The best-known item is high temperature operating life (HTOL): parts run at around 125 °C and at least nominal voltage, with 77 units from each of three lots operated for 1,000 hours and zero failures allowed. Temperature and voltage acceleration let those hours stand in for years of field use.

Each part is qualified to an operating temperature grade defined by ambient temperature. Grade 0 is −40 to 150 °C, Grade 1 is −40 to 125 °C, Grade 2 is −40 to 105 °C and Grade 3 is −40 to 85 °C; the smaller the number, the hotter the upper limit. Because the grade refers to ambient, self-heating means the junction runs hotter still, so thermal design must budget for that rise. Parts are tested hot and cold, since leakage grows at high temperature and timing shifts at low temperature.

The Automotive Electronics Council splits its documents by component type because failure mechanisms differ. AEC-Q100 covers integrated circuits such as microcontrollers and power-management ICs. AEC-Q101 covers discrete semiconductors such as diodes, power MOSFETs and IGBTs. AEC-Q200 covers passive components such as resistors, capacitors, inductors and crystal resonators. None of these is a functional safety standard: they demonstrate that a part survives automotive stress, while ISO 26262 governs how safety requirements, safety mechanisms and failure-rate metrics are handled.

Qualification applies to a specific design, process, fab and package. Moving production to another fab, changing materials or modifying the package can alter reliability even if datasheet values are unchanged. Suppliers therefore issue a Product Change Notification (PCN) in advance, describing the change and its expected impact, repeat the relevant reliability tests, and switch only after customer agreement. AEC-Q100 includes guidance on which tests to repeat for each type of change. This discipline supports the very low defect rates, aimed at ppb levels, that automotive customers expect.

faq.q: What is the temperature range of AEC-Q100 Grade 1?
faq.a: Grade 1 covers an ambient temperature of −40 to 125 °C. Grade 0 extends to 150 °C, Grade 2 to 105 °C and Grade 3 to 85 °C, all starting at −40 °C.

faq.q: Is AEC-Q100 a certification?
faq.a: Not in the sense of a certificate issued by an outside body. The supplier runs the specified stress tests and declares the part qualified, providing the data to customers who may review it.

faq.q: What is the difference between AEC-Q100 and AEC-Q101?
faq.a: AEC-Q100 is for integrated circuits, while AEC-Q101 is for discrete semiconductors such as diodes, MOSFETs and IGBTs. Their test lists and conditions differ because the devices fail in different ways.

ゼロディフェクト.desc: An approach that aims for zero failures by combining design margin, process control and tests that remove outlier chips, preventing defects from being built in or shipped. Because a car uses thousands of semiconductors, automotive defect rates are managed in ppm (parts per million) with zero as the goal.

HAST(高度加速ストレス試験).desc: A test that applies bias in pressurized steam at high humidity and temperatures above 100 °C to evaluate moisture resistance quickly. For example, 96 hours at 130 °C/85% RH is treated as equivalent to 1000 hours of temperature-humidity-bias testing (THB) at 85 °C/85% RH.

about.h: How HAST speeds up moisture failures
about.p: HAST places packaged devices in a sealed pressure vessel filled with unsaturated steam, typically at 110 to 130 °C and 85% relative humidity (RH). Because the water vapor pressure at these temperatures is roughly two to five times that at 85 °C, moisture diffuses through the plastic mold compound and along interfaces to the die much faster. Electrical bias is applied during the test so that, once moisture and ionic contaminants arrive, electrochemical reactions proceed. Common conditions are 96 hours at 130 °C/85% RH, used as a substitute for 1000 hours of temperature-humidity-bias testing (THB) at 85 °C/85% RH.

The main targets are corrosion of aluminum bond pads and metal lines, especially when chloride or other ionic contaminants are present; ion migration that grows conductive paths between biased conductors; and rising leakage currents across surfaces and passivation defects. Delamination between mold compound and die or lead frame can open paths that let moisture in faster. Bias is usually arranged to put voltage between adjacent pins while keeping power dissipation low, since self-heating would dry out the die surface and hide humidity-driven failures.

about.h: HAST vs. THB, unbiased HAST and autoclave
about.p: THB uses the same 85% RH at 85 °C and atmospheric pressure, so it needs about 1000 hours to reach similar damage; HAST trades that time for a pressure chamber. Unbiased HAST uses the same temperature and humidity without bias, focusing on purely chemical corrosion and package integrity. The autoclave, or pressure cooker test, uses saturated steam at 100% RH, commonly 121 °C, also without bias, and is harsher on packaging materials. Results from these tests are not interchangeable, because condensation and bias change which mechanisms dominate.

Acceleration is commonly estimated with Peck's model, which multiplies a humidity term, relative humidity to the power of minus n with n around 3, by an Arrhenius temperature term. Using it, a qualification test can be mapped to an expected lifetime in a given climate. The conversion has limits: if the test temperature is so high that the mold compound's properties change markedly, or condensation forms, the test can trigger failure modes that would never occur in service. Test conditions are therefore chosen within ranges established by industry standards such as those from JEDEC.

faq.q: What is the difference between HAST and THB?
faq.a: Both apply bias in 85% relative humidity, but THB runs at 85 °C and atmospheric pressure for about 1000 hours, while HAST uses pressurized steam at around 110 to 130 °C to reach a comparable result in about 100 to 300 hours.

faq.q: Why is bias applied during HAST?
faq.a: Voltage between conductors drives the electrochemical reactions behind corrosion and ion migration once moisture reaches the die. Without bias the test mainly checks chemical attack and package integrity, which is what unbiased HAST does.

faq.q: Is HAST the same as a pressure cooker test?
faq.a: No. HAST uses unsaturated steam, typically 85% RH, and usually bias, while the pressure cooker or autoclave test uses saturated steam at 100% RH, commonly at 121 °C, without bias.

ISO 26262.desc: The international standard for automotive functional safety, aimed at reducing risks from failures of electrical and electronic systems to an acceptable level. It adapts IEC 61508 to road vehicles and covers the whole lifecycle from concept through development and production to decommissioning.

about.p: ISO 26262 defines functional safety as the absence of unreasonable risk due to hazards caused by malfunctioning behavior of electrical and electronic (E/E) systems. The aim is not zero failures, which is impossible, but making sure a failure does not turn into a hazardous situation. A typical pattern is detect and react: if electric power steering detects an anomaly in its motor control, it stops assist, lights a warning lamp and leaves the driver able to steer manually. Crash protection and general quality management are separate topics, the latter covered by IATF 16949.

Work starts with hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA). Each hazardous event is rated for severity (S1–S3), exposure (E1–E4) and controllability (C1–C3), which together give an ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level) from A to D, or QM when ordinary quality management is enough. A useful shortcut is that S + E + C of 10 gives D, 9 gives C, 8 gives B, 7 gives A. Each hazard becomes a safety goal, such as no unintended sudden acceleration, which inherits the ASIL and is refined into functional, technical, hardware and software safety requirements.

The standard treats two failure types differently. Random hardware failures, from wear-out or radiation-induced bit flips, are handled quantitatively with failure rates in FIT and metrics such as the single-point fault metric (SPFM), latent fault metric (LFM) and probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF). Systematic failures, from specification errors, design mistakes or software bugs, recur whenever the same conditions occur and are prevented through process rigor scaled to the ASIL. Safety mechanisms must detect a fault and reach a safe state within the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI), and latent faults, such as a broken ECC corrector, must be uncovered before a second fault arrives.

A general-purpose automotive microcontroller is designed before its final vehicle application is known, so it is developed as a Safety Element out of Context (SEooC): the supplier assumes safety requirements and usage conditions and documents them in a safety manual, and the system integrator checks those assumptions. ASIL decomposition lets a requirement be split across independent redundant elements, for example ASIL D into B(D) plus B(D), provided dependent failures are analyzed. Neighboring standards cover other risks: ISO 21448 (SOTIF) addresses performance limits of a non-failed system, and ISO/SAE 21434 addresses cyberattacks.

faq.q: What is the difference between ISO 26262 and IEC 61508?
faq.a: IEC 61508 is the generic functional safety standard for electrical, electronic and programmable electronic systems. ISO 26262 adapts it to series-production road vehicles, replacing its concepts with automotive ones such as the ASIL and covering the vehicle lifecycle from concept to decommissioning.

faq.q: Does ISO 26262 certification mean a car cannot have an accident?
faq.a: No. It only aims to reduce the risk from E/E malfunctions to an acceptable level, typically by detecting faults and moving to a safe state. Hazards from sensor limitations or attacks are handled by SOTIF and ISO/SAE 21434 respectively.

faq.q: Is AEC-Q100 the same as ISO 26262 compliance?
faq.a: No. AEC-Q100 is a stress-test qualification of an IC's reliability, while ISO 26262 governs the safety lifecycle, safety mechanisms and failure-rate metrics. Automotive chips are usually expected to satisfy both.

ASIL(自動車安全度水準).desc: In ISO 26262, the level of safety requirements assigned to each hazardous event from three factors: severity S, exposure E and controllability C. There are four levels, A to D, with D the most stringent; low-risk items that need no ASIL are classed as QM.

about.p: During hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA), each hazardous event is rated for severity of injury (S1–S3), exposure to the driving situation in which it can occur (E1–E4) and controllability by the driver or others (C1–C3). A table in ISO 26262 maps the combination to ASIL A, B, C or D, or to QM (Quality Management) when no ASIL is needed. A handy rule: S + E + C equal to 10 gives D, 9 gives C, 8 gives B and 7 gives A. Only S3/E4/C3 reaches D, and lowering any one factor by a step lowers the ASIL by one.

The ASIL attaches to the safety goal and is inherited by the requirements derived from it, then by the hardware and software that implement them. A higher ASIL demands more rigorous development and verification and tighter hardware metrics. Target guidelines for the single-point fault metric (SPFM) are 90% for B, 97% for C and 99% for D; for the latent fault metric (LFM), 60%, 80% and 90%. The probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF) target is below 100 FIT for B and C and below 10 FIT, or 10⁻⁸ per hour, for D. QM still requires normal quality work.

SPFM is one minus the fraction of safety-related failure rate that is single-point or residual, meaning faults that by themselves violate a safety goal or slip past safety mechanisms undetected. If a block has 1000 FIT of safety-related failures and 5 FIT of them are single-point or residual, SPFM = 1 − 5/1000 = 99.5%, which meets the ASIL D target. Improving it means adding safety mechanisms with higher diagnostic coverage, such as ECC on memories, lockstep cores or monitoring circuits, so that fewer faults remain undetected.

A requirement can be split across sufficiently independent redundant elements, written with the original level in parentheses: ASIL D may become B(D) + B(D), C(D) + A(D), or D(D) + QM(D). Dependent failure analysis must show the two cannot fail together from a common cause, and the random hardware metrics still follow the original ASIL. When software of different ASILs shares one SoC, freedom from interference must be shown with spatial partitioning, such as memory protection units or a hypervisor, and temporal partitioning by execution-time monitoring; otherwise everything must be developed to the highest ASIL.

faq.q: Which ASIL is the most stringent?
faq.a: ASIL D is the highest and ASIL A the lowest; QM means the risk is low enough that ordinary quality management suffices. Parts of brake, steering and airbag control are typical ASIL D examples.

faq.q: What does ASIL B(D) mean?
faq.a: It marks a requirement developed to ASIL B as a result of decomposing an original ASIL D requirement across two independent redundant elements. The parentheses keep the original level visible because some obligations, such as hardware metric targets, still follow ASIL D.

faq.q: Is ASIL the same as SIL?
faq.a: No. SIL levels 1–4 come from the generic standard IEC 61508, while ASIL A–D are defined by ISO 26262 for road vehicles using severity, exposure and controllability. They are related in spirit but not formally interchangeable.

HARA(ハザード分析とリスクアセスメント).desc: The ISO 26262 analysis that identifies hazardous events at the vehicle level and rates severity, exposure and controllability to determine ASILs and safety goals. It is done at the very start of development.

about.p: HARA is carried out in the concept phase of ISO 26262, after the item, the vehicle-level function under development such as electronic throttle control, has been defined and before any architecture exists. It considers malfunctioning behaviors of the item, for example unintended acceleration or loss of braking, and combines each with operational situations such as highway driving, parking or a wet road to form hazardous events. The analysis looks at effects at the vehicle level, not at how hardware or software might fail.

Each hazardous event is classified by severity S (S0 to S3, from no injuries to life-threatening or fatal injuries), exposure E (E0 to E4, how often or how long the vehicle is in the relevant situation) and controllability C (C0 to C3, how likely the driver or others can avoid harm). A table combines the three into QM (quality management, no ASIL-specific requirements) or ASIL A to D, with D the most demanding. Sudden loss of braking at high speed, severe and hard to control, lands at a high ASIL.

about.h: From hazardous events to safety goals
about.p: Hazardous events rated ASIL A to D are covered by safety goals, top-level requirements such as "avoid unintended sudden acceleration", each inheriting the highest ASIL of the events it addresses. Safety goals flow down into the functional safety concept, technical safety requirements and finally hardware and software requirements. Quantities such as failure rates, diagnostic coverage and the fault-tolerant time interval (FTTI) come later, when checking whether a design meets those requirements, not when determining the ASIL.

HARA addresses hazards caused by random hardware failures and systematic faults such as design errors. Intentional attacks are handled by ISO/SAE 21434 through threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA), which identifies assets, threat scenarios and attack feasibility. The two activities are coordinated, because an attack that disables a safety mechanism becomes a safety problem. Hazards arising from performance limits of an intended function, such as sensor misperception without any fault, fall under the separate SOTIF standard, ISO 21448.

faq.q: What are S, E and C in ISO 26262?
faq.a: Severity of potential harm, exposure to the driving situation in which the hazard can occur, and controllability by the driver or others. Together they determine the ASIL of a hazardous event.

faq.q: What does QM mean in ASIL classification?
faq.a: QM, quality management, means the risk is low enough that normal quality processes suffice and no ASIL-specific safety requirements apply.

faq.q: When is HARA performed?
faq.a: At the very start of development, in the concept phase, once the item is defined. Its safety goals and ASILs drive all later safety requirements and design work.

安全目標.desc: The top-level safety requirement defined for each hazardous event found in the HARA. It is phrased like "prevent unintended sudden acceleration" and inherits the ASIL of that event.

about.h: From hazard analysis to a safety goal
about.p: Under ISO 26262, functional safety work on a vehicle function, called the item, starts with hazard analysis and risk assessment (HARA). Engineers list malfunctioning behaviors, such as unintended acceleration or loss of braking, combine them with driving situations into hazardous events, and rate each for severity (S), exposure (E) and controllability (C). Those ratings give an ASIL (Automotive Safety Integrity Level) from A to D, or QM when ordinary quality management suffices. A safety goal is then written for each hazardous event; similar goals may be merged, keeping the highest ASIL.

about.h: What a good safety goal says
about.p: A safety goal states what must not happen at the vehicle level, not how to prevent it: "avoid unintended vehicle acceleration" rather than "add a redundant pedal sensor". It carries the ASIL of its hazardous event and is often accompanied by a safe state, such as cutting engine torque, and a fault tolerant time interval (FTTI), the time a fault can persist before the hazard occurs. Keeping goals technology-independent allows several different architectures to be compared against the same target.

about.h: How goals are refined into requirements
about.p: Safety goals sit at the top of a requirement hierarchy. The functional safety concept derives functional safety requirements, such as detecting implausible pedal signals and limiting torque. The technical safety concept allocates these to system elements as technical safety requirements, which are then refined into hardware and software safety requirements. The ASIL flows down with them, and ASIL decomposition can split a requirement across sufficiently independent redundant elements, for example turning an ASIL D requirement into two ASIL B(D) requirements.

Hardware metrics are evaluated against each safety goal. The single-point fault metric (SPFM), latent fault metric (LFM) and probabilistic metric for random hardware failures (PMHF) depend on which faults could violate that goal. PMHF guideline targets are below 100 FIT (10⁻⁷ per hour) for ASIL B and C and below 10 FIT for ASIL D. Semiconductor suppliers rarely know the final vehicle, so they often develop a chip as a safety element out of context (SEooC), documenting assumed safety goals and ASIL for the integrator to confirm.

faq.q: What is the difference between a safety goal and a safety requirement?
faq.a: A safety goal is the top-level requirement tied to one hazardous event and phrased at vehicle level. Functional, technical, hardware and software safety requirements are derived from it and describe progressively more concrete ways of achieving it.

faq.q: Where does the ASIL of a safety goal come from?
faq.a: It is inherited from the hazardous event the goal addresses, whose ASIL is set in HARA by rating severity, exposure and controllability.

faq.q: What is an example of an ISO 26262 safety goal?
faq.a: For an electronic throttle, a typical goal is to avoid unintended acceleration of the vehicle, often rated at a high ASIL, together with a safe state such as reducing engine torque.

SPFM(単一点故障指標).desc: An ISO 26262 hardware metric expressing how small the share of single-point faults (which alone violate a safety goal) and residual faults is among safety-related faults. Typical targets are at least 90% for ASIL B, 97% for ASIL C and 99% for ASIL D.

about.p: SPFM equals one minus the summed failure rate of single-point and residual faults divided by the total failure rate of the safety-related hardware elements. Failure rates are expressed in FIT, failures per 10⁹ device-hours. If the safety-related hardware totals 1000 FIT and 5 FIT of it is single-point or residual, SPFM is 1 − 5/1000 = 99.5%, meeting the ASIL D guideline of at least 99%. Because it is a ratio, SPFM measures architectural robustness and does not by itself show whether the absolute risk is acceptable; that is the role of PMHF.

A single-point fault occurs in an element with no safety mechanism and by itself violates the safety goal, such as an unprotected register in a steering controller's datapath. A residual fault is the portion of faults in a protected element that its safety mechanism fails to detect or control. Multiple-point faults violate a goal only in combination with another fault; the ones that stay hidden, latent faults, are assessed by the separate latent fault metric (LFM), with guideline targets of 60%, 80% and 90% for ASIL B, C and D.

In a failure modes, effects and diagnostic analysis (FMEDA), each block, such as SRAM, CPU, clock generation and power supply, gets a failure rate from handbooks or test data. That rate is split by failure mode, the safe fraction that cannot violate the goal is removed, and the diagnostic coverage (DC) of the relevant safety mechanism is applied. The residual rate is roughly the failure rate times the unsafe fraction times one minus DC. Summing over all blocks gives SPFM, LFM and PMHF, and any shortfall points to the blocks needing better protection.

The lever is diagnostic coverage on the blocks that dominate the residual rate. Typical mechanisms include error-correcting codes (ECC) on memories and buses, dual-core lockstep for CPUs, watchdog timers, voltage and clock monitors, and built-in self-tests. ISO 26262 broadly classes coverage as low, medium and high at about 60, 90 and 99%. Since an unprotected block with even a small failure rate can consume the budget, ASIL D designs aim to leave almost nothing without a mechanism.

faq.q: What SPFM is required for ASIL D?
faq.a: The ISO 26262 guideline is at least 99% for ASIL D, compared with 97% for ASIL C and 90% for ASIL B. ASIL A has no SPFM target.

faq.q: What is the difference between SPFM and LFM?
faq.a: SPFM covers faults that violate a safety goal on their own, directly or because a safety mechanism missed them. LFM covers multiple-point faults that remain hidden and could combine with a later fault.

faq.q: How do I calculate SPFM from FIT rates?
faq.a: Add the single-point and residual failure rates, divide by the total failure rate of safety-related hardware, and subtract the result from one. For 5 FIT out of 1000 FIT, SPFM is 99.5%.

診断カバレッジ.desc: The fraction of faults that a safety mechanism can detect or control, abbreviated DC. Adding a safety mechanism with 99% diagnostic coverage to a 200 FIT circuit leaves 2 FIT of undetected faults.

about.p: Diagnostic coverage (DC) is the share of a hardware element's failure rate, or of one failure mode's rate, that a safety mechanism detects or controls in time to prevent a safety goal violation. The uncovered part becomes residual faults: residual rate = failure rate × (1 − DC). A 200 FIT block with 99% coverage leaves 2 FIT; the same block with 90% leaves 20 FIT, ten times more. Detection alone is not enough: the system must also reach a safe state, such as resetting or disabling an output, within the fault tolerant time interval (FTTI).

about.h: Diagnostic coverage vs. test fault coverage
about.p: The two are easily confused because both are percentages of faults detected. Fault coverage in manufacturing test is the fraction of modeled faults, such as stuck-at faults, that test patterns can catch on a tester before shipment; it screens defective parts. Diagnostic coverage concerns faults that arise during use, in the vehicle, and must be caught on the spot by mechanisms built into the chip or system. Some techniques serve both purposes: logic built-in self-test (LBIST) run at power-up, for example, helps detect latent faults in the field.

Coverage depends on both the mechanism and the fault model. Parity detects any single-bit error in a word but misses double-bit errors; single-error-correct, double-error-detect (SECDED) ECC covers more. Dual-core lockstep compares two cores running the same instructions every cycle, giving high coverage for CPU logic, but common-cause faults that hit both cores alike, such as clock or supply disturbances, need extra measures like a cycle offset between cores and separate monitors. Watchdogs and program-flow monitoring typically reach lower coverage because they see only gross misbehavior.

ISO 26262 lists typical mechanisms and ranks the coverage they can be credited with as low, medium or high, corresponding to about 60, 90 and 99%. A claim must be backed by evidence: analysis of which faults the mechanism can observe, and often fault-injection simulation, where stuck-at and transient faults are injected into the RTL or gate-level netlist and the fraction detected is counted. Separate coverages are tracked for residual faults, which feed the single-point fault metric (SPFM), and for latent faults, which feed the latent fault metric (LFM).

faq.q: How do you calculate residual failure rate from diagnostic coverage?
faq.a: Multiply the element's relevant failure rate by one minus the diagnostic coverage. For example, 200 FIT with 99% coverage leaves 200 × 0.01 = 2 FIT undetected.

faq.q: What is high diagnostic coverage in ISO 26262?
faq.a: High coverage corresponds to about 99%, medium to about 90% and low to about 60%. ASIL D designs generally need high coverage on the blocks that dominate the failure rate.

faq.q: Is diagnostic coverage the same as fault coverage?
faq.a: No. Fault coverage measures how many modeled faults manufacturing test patterns detect before shipment, while diagnostic coverage measures how many faults occurring in operation are detected or controlled by on-board safety mechanisms.

安全機構.desc: A means of detecting faults and moving to a safe state, or containing their effects, before they lead to a hazardous event. Examples include ECC, lockstep CPUs, watchdog timers, voltage and clock monitors, and BIST.

about.h: What a safety mechanism must do
about.p: In functional safety standards such as ISO 26262 for road vehicles, a safety mechanism is a technical measure that detects a fault, or controls its effect, and brings the system to or keeps it in a safe state. Timing is part of the requirement. The fault tolerant time interval (FTTI) is the minimum time from a fault to a possible hazardous event, and fault detection plus reaction, such as shutting off outputs, resetting or switching to a degraded mode, must fit inside it. A diagnosis that runs too rarely fails this test even if it eventually catches the fault.

Error-correcting codes (ECC) on memories correct single-bit errors and detect double-bit errors. Lockstep CPUs run two identical cores on the same instructions and compare outputs every cycle, often with a small time offset so a single disturbance does not hit both identically. Watchdog timers catch software that stops servicing them, and windowed watchdogs also catch servicing that comes too early. Clock monitors and voltage monitors check for stoppage, drift, undervoltage and overvoltage. Built-in self-test (BIST) checks logic and memories at start-up or periodically, and CRCs protect communication.

Diagnostic coverage (DC) is the fraction of faults a mechanism detects or controls. Failure rates are expressed in FIT, failures per 10⁹ device-hours, and a block with 200 FIT protected at 99% DC leaves 200 × (1 − 0.99) = 2 FIT undetected. ISO 26262 aggregates such numbers into the single-point fault metric (SPFM) and latent fault metric (LFM). For the highest integrity level, ASIL D, the targets are at least 99% for SPFM and 90% for LFM, and a residual hardware failure rate budget also applies.

A mechanism must not fail together with what it monitors. A clock monitor needs a reference oscillator independent of the main clock, and a voltage monitor needs its own reference, otherwise a common fault moves both and goes unseen. The mechanism itself can also break silently: an ECC checker that has failed shows no symptom until a memory error arrives, which makes it a latent fault. Such mechanisms are therefore tested themselves, for example by injecting deliberate errors or running comparator self-tests at start-up.

faq.q: What is a safety mechanism in ISO 26262?
faq.a: It is a measure implemented in hardware or software that detects faults or controls their effects and achieves or maintains a safe state. Examples include ECC, lockstep cores, watchdogs and voltage or clock monitors.

faq.q: How is the residual failure rate calculated from diagnostic coverage?
faq.a: Multiply the failure rate by one minus the coverage. For example, 200 FIT with 99% diagnostic coverage leaves 2 FIT of undetected faults.

faq.q: Why can a lockstep CPU detect but not correct a fault?
faq.a: With only two cores, a mismatch shows that one is wrong but not which one, so the system must reset or move to a safe state. Correcting by majority vote requires at least three redundant channels.

FTTI(フォールトトレラント時間間隔).desc: The shortest time from the occurrence of a fault to a hazardous event if no safety mechanism acts. A safety mechanism must complete detection of the fault and transition to a safe state within the FTTI.

ロックステップ.desc: A scheme in which two identical CPU cores run the same program and a comparator checks their outputs to detect faults. To keep common-cause faults from corrupting both cores the same way, execution is offset by a few clocks or the cores are placed apart. Performance is that of one core.

ECU(電子制御ユニット).desc: An in-vehicle controller built around a microcontroller that controls the engine, brakes, doors and so on. ECUs multiplied with each new function, sometimes exceeding 100 per car, and are now being consolidated through zonal architectures and similar approaches.

CAN.desc: Short for Controller Area Network, an in-vehicle network that connects ECUs using differential signaling on two wires. Lower ID values have higher priority, and when nodes start transmitting at once, non-destructive arbitration leaves a single frame intact. Classical CAN runs at up to 1 Mbit/s, while CAN FD speeds up the data phase to several Mbit/s.

ゾーンアーキテクチャ.desc: A vehicle electronics layout in which zone ECUs placed in each area of the car connect nearby sensors and actuators, while control processing is concentrated in a central high-performance computer. It allows a shorter, lighter wiring harness than the traditional one-ECU-per-function approach.

SOTIF(意図した機能の安全性).desc: The concept that addresses hazards arising without any component failure, from sensor performance limits, insufficient specifications or reasonably foreseeable misuse. It is standardized as ISO 21448 and is central to developing automated driving and driver-assistance systems.

シリコンフォトニクス.desc: Technology for integrating optical circuits such as waveguides, modulators and photodetectors on silicon. It uses the materials and processes of CMOS fabs, enabling volume production on 200 mm or 300 mm wafers. Because silicon emits light poorly, lasers are added using compound semiconductors.

about.h: What gets built on the chip
about.p: Silicon photonics starts from an SOI (silicon-on-insulator) wafer whose top silicon layer, commonly 220 nm thick, is patterned into waveguides, with a 2–3 µm buried oxide as the lower cladding. Silicon is transparent at the 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm telecom bands, so it guides light with modest loss. On the same wafer go modulators based on carrier dispersion in pn junctions, germanium photodetectors grown by selective epitaxy, and passive filters such as ring resonators, arrayed waveguide gratings (AWGs) and Mach-Zehnder interferometers that combine or separate wavelengths.

Every main step reuses CMOS tooling: lithography and dry etching define waveguides, ion implantation forms modulator junctions, selective epitaxy grows germanium, and metal interconnects wire it up. That allows precise, reproducible volume production on 200 mm and 300 mm wafers. Feature sizes are a few hundred nanometres, so DUV lithography is sufficient and leading-edge logic nodes are not needed. What matters more is nanometre-level control of width and thickness, because small dimensional errors shift the wavelengths at which resonant devices operate.

Silicon is an indirect-gap semiconductor: the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum sit at different crystal momenta, so radiative recombination needs a phonon and is far less likely than non-radiative recombination. Efficient lasers therefore come from III-V compound semiconductors such as InP, either bonded onto the silicon wafer (heterogeneous integration) or attached as separate chips. Because III-V materials raise contamination concerns, they are usually processed apart from the CMOS line. Detection uses germanium because silicon barely absorbs beyond about 1.1 µm; discrete receivers often use InGaAs instead.

The main application is optical transceivers for data-center and AI networks, where wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) puts separate signals on several wavelengths in one fiber, for example four 100 Gb/s lanes for 400 Gb/s. Integration also enables co-packaged optics, which place optical engines beside a switch chip. Silicon nitride waveguides, with an index near 2.0, are often added to the same platform for lower loss and lower temperature sensitivity, though silicon nitride cannot form carrier-based modulators because it is an insulator.

faq.q: Why can't silicon be used to make lasers?
faq.a: Silicon has an indirect band gap, so an electron and hole can only recombine radiatively with the help of a phonon, which is rare. Silicon photonics therefore uses III-V lasers such as InP, bonded to the chip or supplied from outside.

faq.q: What is used as the photodetector in silicon photonics?
faq.a: Germanium grown by selective epitaxy on the silicon, because germanium absorbs at 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm while silicon is transparent there. Standalone receivers often use InGaAs.

faq.q: Does silicon photonics need advanced process nodes?
faq.a: No. Waveguides are a few hundred nanometres wide, so mature DUV lithography is enough. The demanding part is tight control of dimensions and thickness rather than minimum feature size.

導波路.desc: A structure that confines and guides light by surrounding a high-index core with a lower-index cladding. Silicon photonics commonly uses silicon about 0.5 µm × 0.22 µm in cross section surrounded by oxide, allowing bend radii of just a few µm.

about.p: Light launched along a high-index core is held there by total internal reflection at the boundary with the lower-index cladding; the guided pattern of the field is called a mode. A small part of the field, the evanescent tail, always extends into the cladding. Confinement grows with index contrast: silicon (about 3.48 at 1.55 µm) against oxide (about 1.45) differs by roughly 2, whereas the core and cladding of optical fiber differ by less than 1%. That is why a silicon strip only about 0.5 µm × 0.22 µm can guide light around bends of a few µm radius.

about.h: Why silicon works at telecom wavelengths
about.p: A photon at 1.55 µm carries about 1.24 / 1.55 ≈ 0.8 eV, less than silicon's band gap of about 1.12 eV, so it cannot excite band-to-band transitions and silicon is nearly transparent. Silicon only absorbs strongly below about 1.1 µm, which is also why a separate material such as germanium is needed for detectors. On an SOI (silicon-on-insulator) wafer the waveguide is patterned in the thin top silicon layer, commonly 220 nm, and the buried oxide (BOX), typically 2–3 µm thick, acts as the lower cladding so the evanescent field does not leak into the silicon substrate.

A strip waveguide is etched all the way through the silicon layer. Its large lateral contrast gives tight confinement and the smallest bends. A rib waveguide is etched only partway, leaving thin slabs on both sides. Confinement is weaker, so sharp bends leak light into the slab, but the slabs can be doped to carry current from electrodes placed well away from the optical mode to a pn junction in the core. Metal right next to the waveguide would absorb light, so modulators and other electrically driven devices are usually built on rib geometry.

The same high contrast that allows tight bends also makes the mode sensitive to sidewall roughness, which scatters light. Typical strip-waveguide loss is about 1–3 dB/cm depending on the process, with rib or optimized processes lower, against roughly 0.2 dB/km for fiber. Losses are tracked in decibels because they add along a path: transmittance T = 10^(−L/10). Two decibels per centimeter over 5 mm gives 1 dB, or about 79% of the power remaining; 3 dB is roughly half and 10 dB one-tenth. Fiber-to-chip coupling through a grating or edge coupler is usually a larger item in the budget than the waveguide itself.

faq.q: Why is silicon transparent at 1550 nm?
faq.a: A 1550 nm photon has about 0.8 eV of energy, below silicon's 1.12 eV band gap, so it cannot lift electrons across the gap and is not absorbed by band-to-band transitions. Silicon only absorbs strongly at wavelengths shorter than about 1.1 µm.

faq.q: What is the difference between a grating coupler and an edge coupler?
faq.a: A grating coupler diffracts light up to a fiber held above the chip, so it can sit anywhere and be tested on the wafer, but its bandwidth is only a few tens of nm and it is polarization sensitive. An edge coupler butts a fiber against a polished facet, usually through an inverse taper that enlarges the mode, giving lower, broadband loss at the cost of facet processing.

faq.q: Why are silicon waveguides polarization dependent?
faq.a: A flat waveguide about 0.5 µm wide and 0.22 µm thick confines TE (horizontal) and TM (vertical) polarizations very differently, so their effective indices and losses differ. Standard single-mode fiber does not hold polarization, so receivers use polarization splitter-rotators or two-dimensional grating couplers.

屈折率.desc: The speed of light in vacuum divided by its speed in a material. At a wavelength of 1.55 µm, silicon is about 3.48 and oxide (SiO2) about 1.45; the larger this contrast, the more tightly light can be confined in a small waveguide.

about.p: Refractive index n is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its phase speed in a material. The optical frequency does not change on entering a material, so the wavelength inside shrinks to λ/n: 1.55 µm light has a wavelength of about 0.45 µm in silicon. Index varies with wavelength (dispersion) and temperature, so values must be quoted with conditions. Useful reference points are silicon about 3.48 and SiO2 about 1.45 at 1.55 µm, silicon nitride about 2.0, and water about 1.44 at 193 nm.

about.h: Snell's law and total internal reflection
about.p: At an interface, n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2. Going from high to low index, rays beyond the critical angle, sinθc = n2/n1, cannot escape and are totally reflected. For silicon to oxide, 1.45 / 3.48 gives θc ≈ 25° from the normal, so most rays are trapped and waveguides can be tiny and sharply bent. In fiber the contrast is under 1%, θc exceeds 80°, and only near-grazing rays are guided. The reverse direction, low to high index, never gives total reflection. A guided mode sees an effective index between the core and cladding values.

Silicon's thermo-optic coefficient is large, about 1.8×10⁻⁴ per kelvin, which shifts a C-band ring resonance by roughly 0.07–0.08 nm per °C; heaters exploit this for tuning. For fast modulation, silicon lacks the Pockels effect because its crystal is centrosymmetric, so modulators rely on free-carrier (plasma) dispersion: adding electrons and holes lowers the index and raises absorption. The change is small, about 10⁻³ or less, so phase shifters are millimeters long. Lithium niobate, by contrast, has a strong Pockels effect.

about.h: Where index shows up in the fab
about.p: Index is central to several process tools. Ellipsometry fits the polarization change of reflected light to a model to extract both film thickness and index. FTIR measures epitaxial-layer thickness from interference, relying on the slight infrared index difference that free carriers create between a lightly doped epi layer and a heavily doped substrate. Immersion lithography fills the lens–wafer gap with water so that NA = n sinθ can exceed 1, reaching about 1.35. Silicon oxynitride films have a tunable index and serve as antireflective layers.

faq.q: What is the refractive index of silicon at 1550 nm?
faq.a: About 3.48 at room temperature, rising slightly with temperature at roughly 1.8×10⁻⁴ per kelvin. Silicon dioxide is about 1.45 at the same wavelength.

faq.q: Why does a higher index contrast allow smaller optical waveguides?
faq.a: A larger contrast lowers the critical angle and pulls the mode tightly into the core, so the core can be sub-micron and bends of a few µm radius do not radiate. The trade-off is greater sensitivity to sidewall roughness and dimensional variation.

faq.q: What is effective index?
faq.a: It is the index that a guided mode experiences as a whole, defined from its propagation constant, and it always lies between the cladding and core indices. It sets the phase accumulated along a waveguide and the resonance condition of rings and gratings.

Cバンド.desc: The optical fiber communication band around 1530 to 1565 nm. Silica fiber loss is lowest there (about 0.2 dB/km) and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) can amplify it, so it is used for long-haul links and dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM).

about.p: Loss in silica fiber comes mainly from Rayleigh scattering, which falls steeply as wavelength increases (roughly as the inverse fourth power), and from infrared absorption by the glass, which rises at longer wavelengths. The minimum, about 0.2 dB/km in standard single-mode fiber, lies near 1550 nm, so 100 km of fiber costs only about 20 dB. Just as important, erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs), pumped by lasers at 980 or 1480 nm, provide gain across roughly 1530 to 1565 nm, amplifying all channels at once in the optical domain without converting them to electrical signals.

about.h: C-band vs. the other telecom bands
about.p: The ITU (International Telecommunication Union) divides the low-loss region of fiber into bands: O (original, about 1260 to 1360 nm), E, S, C (conventional, 1530 to 1565 nm), L (long, about 1565 to 1625 nm) and U. In standard single-mode fiber, chromatic dispersion is close to zero around 1310 nm, in the O-band, which is why short-reach links such as those inside data centers often use it. The C-band has lower loss and EDFA gain but significant dispersion. The L-band extends capacity using amplifiers adapted to longer wavelengths.
