Dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) places many lasers on a frequency grid defined by ITU-T, anchored at 193.1 THz, with spacings such as 100 GHz (about 0.8 nm) or 50 GHz (about 0.4 nm). The C-band spans roughly 4.4 THz, so it holds about 40 channels at 100 GHz or about 80 at 50 GHz. Because the spacing is so narrow, laser wavelengths must be held stable, typically by temperature control, and filters, multiplexers and ring resonators must be tuned to the grid.

about.h: Dispersion and silicon photonics in the C-band
about.p: Standard single-mode fiber has a chromatic dispersion of around 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm, which broadens pulses over long distances. Older systems compensated it with special fiber; modern coherent receivers undo it with digital signal processing. For integrated photonics, the C-band photon energy of about 0.8 eV is below silicon's 1.12 eV band gap, so silicon waveguides are transparent, while germanium grown on silicon serves as the photodetector. Silicon's strong thermo-optic effect, however, shifts ring resonances by roughly 0.07 to 0.08 nm per °C.

faq.q: What wavelength range is the C-band?
faq.a: The C-band, or conventional band, covers about 1530 to 1565 nm, corresponding to roughly 191.6 to 195.9 THz in frequency.

faq.q: Why is 1550 nm used for long-distance fiber communication?
faq.a: Silica fiber has its lowest loss there, around 0.2 dB/km, and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers can boost signals across the band without electrical conversion.

faq.q: What is the difference between the O-band and the C-band?
faq.a: The O-band around 1310 nm has near-zero chromatic dispersion in standard fiber and suits short links, while the C-band around 1550 nm has lower loss and optical amplification, suiting long-haul and DWDM systems.

Oバンド.desc: The optical fiber communication band around 1260 to 1360 nm. It includes the region near 1.31 µm where chromatic dispersion in standard single-mode fiber is nearly zero, and is widely used for short links such as those inside data centers.

about.h: Where it sits in the spectrum
about.p: Fiber-optic bands are labeled by letter: O (original, about 1260–1360 nm), E (extended, 1360–1460 nm), S (short, 1460–1530 nm), C (conventional, 1530–1565 nm), L (long, 1565–1625 nm) and U (ultra-long, above that). The O-band was the first band used for single-mode fiber systems, hence its name. It contains the zero-dispersion wavelength of standard single-mode fiber near 1310 nm, where pulses spread the least as they travel.

Links inside and between nearby data center buildings run from a few hundred meters to roughly 10 km. At these distances fiber loss matters little, even though O-band loss, about 0.3–0.35 dB/km, is higher than the roughly 0.2 dB/km near 1550 nm. Near-zero chromatic dispersion matters more: fast intensity-modulated signals travel several kilometers without dispersion compensation, keeping transceivers simple and low in power. Coarse wavelength grids with 20 nm spacing are commonly placed in this band to carry several lanes on one fiber.

The C-band around 1550 nm wins for long-haul links thanks to the lowest loss and direct optical amplification by erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs). In return, standard single-mode fiber has about 17 ps/(nm·km) of dispersion there, which long links must compensate, today usually in the digital signal processor of a coherent receiver. The O-band lacks an equally mature and widespread amplifier, which together with its higher loss confines it mostly to shorter reaches.

At 1310 nm the photon energy is about 0.95 eV, below silicon's bandgap of about 1.12 eV, so silicon waveguides are transparent while germanium photodetectors still absorb the light. Many silicon photonic transceivers for data centers therefore operate in the O-band. Light reaches the chip through edge couplers, which give low loss over a broad range spanning the O- and C-bands, or grating couplers, which are more wavelength-selective but can be placed anywhere on the surface and tested on the wafer.

faq.q: What wavelength range is the O-band?
faq.a: Approximately 1260 to 1360 nm, centered around the 1310 nm zero-dispersion region of standard single-mode fiber.

faq.q: Why is 1310 nm used for short-reach optical links?
faq.a: Chromatic dispersion in standard single-mode fiber is nearly zero there, so high-speed signals keep their shape over several kilometers without compensation. The somewhat higher fiber loss is unimportant at those distances.

faq.q: What does the O in O-band stand for?
faq.a: Original: it was the first wavelength band used for single-mode fiber communication.

伝搬損失.desc: The fraction of optical power lost to scattering and absorption as light travels through a waveguide or fiber, expressed in dB/cm or dB/km. In silicon waveguides the main cause is scattering from sidewall roughness, with typical values around 1 to 3 dB/cm, far higher than fiber's roughly 0.2 dB/km.

about.p: Propagation loss is quoted per unit length in decibels, where loss in dB equals 10 log10(Pin/Pout). The total for a waveguide is simply the loss per length times the length, and the transmitted fraction is T = 10^(−L/10). A 5 mm silicon waveguide at 2 dB/cm therefore loses 1 dB and passes about 79% of the light; 3 dB is roughly half and 10 dB one-tenth. Because decibels add, a link budget is just the sum of propagation, coupling, bend and component losses, which is why the unit is used throughout photonics.

In silicon waveguides on oxide, the dominant mechanism is scattering from nanometer-scale sidewall roughness left by lithography and etching. The high index contrast and small cross section put strong optical field at the sidewalls, so even small roughness scatters noticeably. Other contributions are free-carrier absorption in doped regions such as modulators, leakage into the substrate if the buried oxide is too thin, and radiation at very tight bends. At telecom wavelengths, photons have less energy than silicon's band gap, so band-to-band absorption does not occur. In fiber, Rayleigh scattering and glass absorption dominate.

Propagation loss describes only what happens per unit length inside the guide. Insertion loss is the total measured from input to output of a device or chip, including fiber-to-chip coupling at each end, which is often a few dB per grating coupler, plus bends, splitters and junctions. To separate the two, the cutback method measures identical waveguides of several lengths: plotting total loss in dB against length gives propagation loss as the slope and the combined coupling loss as the intercept at zero length. Consistent coupling between measurements is essential.

about.h: Typical values and how to reduce them
about.p: A typical silicon strip waveguide of about 0.5 µm by 0.22 µm shows roughly 1 to 3 dB/cm, depending on the process. Rib waveguides, which etch only partway into the silicon, and wider waveguides reduce the field at the sidewalls and can reach below 1 dB/cm, though wider guides may support extra modes. Smoothing sidewalls by oxidation or hydrogen annealing also helps. Silicon nitride waveguides, with lower index contrast, can achieve much lower loss. For comparison, fiber at 1550 nm loses about 0.2 dB/km, some five to six orders of magnitude less per unit length.

faq.q: How do I convert dB/cm loss to percentage transmission?
faq.a: Multiply the loss per cm by the length to get total dB, then compute 10^(−dB/10). For example, 1 dB gives about 79% and 3 dB about 50%.

faq.q: Why do silicon waveguides have higher loss than optical fiber?
faq.a: The strong index contrast and tiny cross section concentrate light at the etched sidewalls, where nanometer roughness scatters it. Fiber has a weakly guiding, smooth glass core, so its loss is about 0.2 dB/km instead of dB/cm.

faq.q: What is the cutback method?
faq.a: It measures the total loss of otherwise identical waveguides with different lengths; the slope of loss versus length is the propagation loss and the zero-length intercept is the coupling loss.

グレーティングカプラ.desc: A device that etches a periodic grating into a waveguide so that diffraction redirects light to couple with an optical fiber positioned above the chip. Its advantage is that optical testing is possible on the wafer before dicing, but its coupling bandwidth is narrow and it is polarization dependent.

エッジカプラ.desc: A device that couples light by butting an optical fiber against the edge facet of the chip. An inverse taper that narrows the waveguide tip expands the optical mode to match the fiber. It offers low loss over a wide wavelength range but needs facet preparation and is hard to test at wafer level.

シングルモードファイバ.desc: Optical fiber that carries only one propagation mode, with a core diameter of about 9 µm. With no pulse spreading from different modes traveling at different speeds (modal dispersion), it is used for long-distance and high-speed links.

about.p: Standard single-mode fiber (SMF) is a silica fiber with a core about 9 µm across inside a 125 µm cladding, and a core index only a fraction of a percent higher than the cladding. A waveguide supports only its fundamental mode when its normalized frequency, which grows with core radius and index contrast and falls with wavelength, stays below a cutoff value. Standard SMF is designed so that this holds above a cutoff wavelength of roughly 1.26 µm. The guided light spreads slightly beyond the core, so its mode field diameter is about 9 to 10 µm.

Silica loss is lowest near 1.55 µm, about 0.2 dB/km, between Rayleigh scattering at shorter wavelengths and infrared absorption at longer ones; at 1.31 µm it is about 0.3 to 0.35 dB/km. Because there is only one mode, the remaining pulse spreading is chromatic dispersion, which in standard SMF is nearly zero around 1.31 µm and roughly 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1.55 µm. Long-haul links therefore use the 1.55 µm C-band, where erbium-doped fiber amplifiers work, while short data-center links favour the 1.31 µm O-band to avoid dispersion compensation.

Multimode fiber has a much larger core, typically 50 or 62.5 µm, so many modes travel along paths of different length and arrive at different times. This modal dispersion limits the bandwidth-distance product, restricting multimode links to short reaches, usually with low-cost 850 nm vertical-cavity lasers. Its large core tolerates loose alignment. Single-mode fiber eliminates modal dispersion and supports long distances, very high symbol rates and many wavelengths on one fiber, but needs precise alignment and more expensive optics.

The small mode makes connections unforgiving: a lateral offset of about 2.5 µm between two 10 µm modes adds roughly 1 dB of loss, so fibers are often actively aligned while light passes through. Silicon photonic chips have modes under 1 µm, so they use inverse tapers or grating couplers to enlarge the mode. Standard SMF also does not preserve polarization; bending and temperature change it randomly, so receivers must handle any polarization. Polarization-maintaining fiber is a separate, specialized type with deliberately built-in birefringence.

faq.q: What is the difference between single-mode and multimode fiber?
faq.a: Single-mode fiber has a core of about 9 µm and carries one mode, so it has no modal dispersion and suits long, fast links. Multimode fiber has a 50 or 62.5 µm core, is easier to couple to, but is limited to short distances by modal dispersion.

faq.q: Why are 1310 nm and 1550 nm used in single-mode fiber?
faq.a: Standard single-mode fiber has nearly zero chromatic dispersion near 1310 nm and its lowest loss, about 0.2 dB/km, near 1550 nm. Short links favour the former and long-haul links the latter.

faq.q: What is the core diameter of single-mode fiber?
faq.a: About 8 to 9 µm for standard telecom fiber, with a 125 µm cladding. The mode field diameter is slightly larger, around 9 to 10 µm.

マッハツェンダー変調器.desc: A modulator that splits incoming light into two arms, shifts the phase between them by changing the arms' refractive index with an electrical signal, and recombines them to turn the phase change into an intensity change. A phase difference of 0 gives maximum brightness and π gives minimum. Silicon versions use the plasma dispersion effect and are a few mm long.

キャリア分散効果(プラズマ分散効果).desc: The change in refractive index and optical absorption of a semiconductor when its free electron or hole concentration changes. Because silicon has almost no Pockels effect, this effect is used to shift phase in silicon modulators. Increasing the carrier concentration lowers the refractive index.

リング共振器.desc: A looped waveguide that resonates only at wavelengths for which one round trip's optical length is an integer number of wavelengths. It is used as a wavelength filter or compact modulator. In silicon the resonance shifts by about 0.08 nm per °C, so heaters are often used to control its temperature.

about.p: A ring resonator is a closed-loop waveguide placed next to a straight bus waveguide. Light couples across the narrow gap into the ring and circulates many times. When the round-trip optical length, effective index times circumference, equals an integer number of wavelengths, each pass adds in phase and power builds up. At those wavelengths the light passing along the bus shows sharp dips, while other wavelengths pass almost unaffected. Adding a second bus waveguide makes an add-drop filter that routes the resonant wavelength to a separate drop port.

Resonances repeat in wavelength. Their spacing, the free spectral range, is approximately FSR ≈ λ²/(ng·L), where ng is the group index and L the circumference. A silicon ring of about 10 µm radius (L ≈ 63 µm, ng ≈ 4.2) at 1.55 µm has an FSR near 9 nm; halving L roughly doubles it, helping WDM channels avoid neighboring resonances, though tighter bends add loss. Linewidths of about 0.1–0.3 nm are common, corresponding to quality factors Q, resonant wavelength divided by linewidth, of roughly 5,000 to 15,000.

Silicon's thermo-optic coefficient of about 1.8×10⁻⁴ per kelvin shifts a C-band ring's resonance toward longer wavelengths by roughly 0.07–0.08 nm per °C. With linewidths of a few tenths of a nanometer, a few degrees of drift detunes it from the laser. Fabrication is also unforgiving: a few nanometers of error in waveguide width or thickness moves the resonance by nanometers. Integrated heaters with feedback control therefore lock each ring to its wavelength, at the cost of extra power.

In a ring modulator, a PN junction in the ring changes the refractive index as carriers are depleted, shifting the resonance so that transmitted power at a fixed laser wavelength swings between high and low. Because the resonance magnifies a small index change, a ring is only tens of micrometers across with low capacitance, whereas a silicon Mach-Zehnder modulator is typically millimeters long. The tradeoffs are a narrow optical bandwidth, strong temperature sensitivity and the need for active wavelength locking.

faq.q: What is the free spectral range of a ring resonator?
faq.a: It is the wavelength spacing between adjacent resonances, approximately λ²/(ng·L). Smaller rings have a larger FSR.

faq.q: Why do silicon ring resonators need heaters?
faq.a: Their resonance shifts by about 0.08 nm per °C and also varies with fabrication, while resonances are only tenths of a nanometer wide. Heaters with feedback keep the resonance aligned to the laser wavelength.

faq.q: What is the difference between an all-pass and an add-drop ring?
faq.a: An all-pass ring couples to one bus waveguide and produces dips in its through transmission. An add-drop ring couples to two waveguides, sending the resonant wavelength out of a second drop port.

WDM(波長多重).desc: A method of carrying separate signals on different wavelengths of light and sending them together over a single fiber. CWDM uses wide 20 nm spacing, while DWDM packs many wavelengths at narrow spacings such as 100 GHz (about 0.8 nm).

about.p: Light of different wavelengths travels through the same fiber with almost no mutual interference at normal power levels, so each wavelength can carry an independent signal. At the transmitter, several lasers at distinct wavelengths are modulated separately and combined by a multiplexer; at the receiver, a demultiplexer separates the wavelengths and sends each to its own photodetector. Capacity scales with the channel count: four wavelengths at 100 Gb/s each deliver 400 Gb/s over one fiber. This differs from time-division multiplexing, which interleaves signals in time slots on a single carrier.

Coarse WDM (CWDM) spaces channels 20 nm apart, for example 1271, 1291, 1311 and 1331 nm, near the zero-dispersion region of standard single-mode fiber. A DFB laser's wavelength drifts by about 0.1 nm per degree Celsius, so tens of degrees shift it by only a few nanometers, well within the spacing; uncooled lasers keep cost and power low for data-center links. Dense WDM (DWDM) packs dozens of channels on the ITU-T frequency grid at spacings such as 100 GHz (about 0.8 nm) or 50 GHz (about 0.4 nm), so its lasers need active temperature control to stay on their channels.

Because frequency and wavelength are inversely related, a frequency spacing converts to a wavelength spacing as Δλ ≈ λ² × Δf / c. At 1.55 µm, 100 GHz gives (1.55×10⁻⁶ m)² × 10¹¹ Hz ÷ 3×10⁸ m/s, or about 0.8 nm. The same frequency spacing corresponds to a slightly narrower wavelength spacing at shorter wavelengths. Long-haul DWDM uses the C-band around 1530 to 1565 nm because fiber loss is lowest there and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) can amplify all channels at once without converting them to electrical signals.

Common wavelength filters include thin-film interference filters, arrayed waveguide gratings (AWGs), cascaded Mach-Zehnder interferometers and ring resonators. A ring passes wavelengths whose round trip fits an integer number of wavelengths, and its free spectral range is approximately λ² / (ng × L), so shrinking the circumference widens the spacing between resonances and keeps a ring from also responding to other channels. Smaller rings suffer more bending loss, however. Silicon's refractive index changes noticeably with temperature, so silicon ring filters are usually tuned and stabilized with integrated heaters.

faq.q: What is the difference between CWDM and DWDM?
faq.a: CWDM uses a few channels spaced 20 nm apart so inexpensive uncooled lasers can be used, typically for short reaches. DWDM packs many channels at spacings such as 100 GHz (about 0.8 nm) or 50 GHz, needs temperature-stabilized lasers and is used for long-haul, high-capacity links.

faq.q: How do you convert DWDM channel spacing from GHz to nm?
faq.a: Use Δλ ≈ λ² × Δf / c. Around 1550 nm, 100 GHz corresponds to about 0.8 nm and 50 GHz to about 0.4 nm.

faq.q: Why is DWDM used in the 1550 nm band?
faq.a: Silica fiber has its lowest loss near 1550 nm, and erbium-doped fiber amplifiers work in this C-band, amplifying every wavelength channel simultaneously. Together these allow long spans with many channels.

消光比.desc: In intensity modulation, the ratio of the optical power P1 for a "1" to the power P0 for a "0", expressed in dB as 10 log(P1/P0). The larger it is, the greater the difference between 1 and 0 and the fewer decision errors at the receiver.

CPO(コパッケージドオプティクス).desc: Technology that mounts the optical transceiver parts (optical engines) in the same package as a switch IC or similar. Shorter electrical connections lower the energy per bit, but the optics cannot be swapped out by unplugging, so testing before assembly and the use of external laser sources become important.

about.p: In a conventional switch, the switch IC drives electrical signals across the circuit board to pluggable optical transceivers in the front panel. These traces run from roughly a dozen to several tens of centimetres, and at high data rates the circuits that compensate their loss consume considerable power. Co-packaged optics (CPO) moves the optical engines into the same package as the switch IC, shrinking the electrical path to a few millimetres. That lowers energy per bit, reduces signal degradation and allows many optical links to be packed densely around the chip.

Link power is energy per bit multiplied by bit rate. A switch with 51.2 Tb/s of total bandwidth whose optical links consume 5 pJ/bit spends 5×10⁻¹² × 51.2×10¹² = 256 W on them, and at 15 pJ/bit it would spend about 768 W, so the difference is roughly 500 W per switch. Watch the prefixes, since mixing up T and G or p and n gives answers off by a factor of a thousand. CPO and linear-drive approaches both aim to cut pJ/bit by reducing long electrical paths and digital signal processing (DSP).

The price of integration is that a failed optical component can no longer be unplugged and replaced; a fault can take out the whole package, including an expensive switch IC. CPO therefore depends on known good die (KGD): photonic chips are tested at wafer level by bringing fiber probes down onto grating couplers alongside electrical probes, measuring waveguide loss, modulators and photodetectors before assembly. Final test after assembly is still required. Attaching many fibers precisely and keeping optics stable next to a hot processor are further engineering challenges.

about.h: Why the laser often sits outside
about.p: A semiconductor laser's threshold current rises and its efficiency falls as temperature increases, and degradation accelerates. Next to a switch IC dissipating several hundred watts, an in-package laser would face harsh conditions and would be the most failure-prone part. An external laser source places lasers in a cooler spot, often as front-panel modules that can still be swapped, and feeds continuous light to the optical engines by fiber, where modulators impose data. The cost is extra coupling loss, which must be offset by higher laser output.

faq.q: What is the difference between co-packaged optics and pluggable transceivers?
faq.a: Pluggable transceivers sit in the front panel and connect to the switch IC through long board traces, but they are easy to replace and mix. CPO puts the optics inside the switch package to shorten the electrical path and save power, at the cost of field replaceability.

faq.q: Why does co-packaged optics use an external laser source?
faq.a: Lasers lose efficiency and lifetime at high temperature and are among the least reliable components, so keeping them away from the hot switch IC and in a replaceable module improves both performance and serviceability.

faq.q: How do you calculate optical interconnect power from pJ/bit?
faq.a: Multiply energy per bit by total bit rate: for example, 5 pJ/bit × 51.2 Tb/s = 256 W. Keep units consistent, since pico is 10⁻¹² and tera is 10¹².

波長分散.desc: The broadening of light pulses in an optical fiber because light of different wavelengths travels at slightly different speeds. In standard single-mode fiber it is nearly zero near 1.31 µm and about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1.55 µm.

about.p: Any real optical signal occupies a range of wavelengths, from the laser's own linewidth and from the modulation itself. In fiber, group velocity depends on wavelength through two effects: material dispersion, because silica's refractive index varies with wavelength, and waveguide dispersion, because how tightly the mode is confined in the core changes with wavelength. Different spectral components therefore arrive at slightly different times, broadening each pulse. In standard single-mode fiber the two effects cancel near 1310 nm, the zero-dispersion wavelength.

The dispersion parameter D is quoted in ps/(nm·km): picoseconds of delay spread per nanometer of spectral width per kilometer. Standard single-mode fiber has about 17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm. Pulse spreading is roughly D × spectral width × length, so a signal 0.1 nm wide sent 100 km at 1550 nm spreads by about 170 ps, more than one full symbol at 10 Gbaud. Because spectral width also grows with symbol rate, dispersion-limited reach falls roughly with the square of the rate.

about.h: Dispersion vs. loss when choosing a band
about.p: Fiber loss is lowest near 1550 nm, about 0.2 dB/km, while dispersion is nearly zero near 1310 nm. Short links of a few kilometers to about 10 km, typical in data centers, favor the O-band so that simple intensity-modulation direct-detection (IM-DD) transceivers work without compensation. Long-haul systems use the C-band for its low loss and erbium-doped amplifiers and deal with the dispersion. Fiber that shifts the zero to 1550 nm exists, but it worsens nonlinear mixing between closely spaced WDM channels.

Older long-haul systems inserted spools of dispersion-compensating fiber with opposite-sign dispersion at amplifier sites. Coherent systems instead recover the full optical field, amplitude and phase on two polarizations, by mixing the signal with a local oscillator laser, so the receiver's digital signal processor (DSP) can undo chromatic dispersion as a linear filter. IM-DD receivers detect only optical power and lose the phase, so they cannot fully reverse dispersion electronically, which limits their reach at high rates.

faq.q: What is the chromatic dispersion of single-mode fiber at 1550 nm?
faq.a: About 17 ps/(nm·km) for standard single-mode fiber, compared with nearly zero around 1310 nm.

faq.q: What is the difference between chromatic dispersion and modal dispersion?
faq.a: Modal dispersion occurs in multimode fiber because different modes travel different effective paths. Single-mode fiber eliminates it, leaving chromatic dispersion, which comes from different wavelengths traveling at different speeds.

faq.q: Why can coherent receivers compensate dispersion digitally?
faq.a: They measure both amplitude and phase of the optical field, so dispersion appears as a known linear phase distortion that a DSP filter can reverse. Direct-detection receivers lose the phase and cannot undo it fully.

ラピダス(Rapidus).desc: A Japanese semiconductor manufacturer founded in 2022 to mass-produce leading-edge logic chips at the 2 nm generation. It has a fab in Chitose, Hokkaido, and plans to start volume production in 2027 as a foundry that manufactures chips designed by other companies.

about.h: What kind of company it is
about.p: Rapidus was founded in August 2022 with the aim of becoming a foundry that manufactures leading-edge logic chips under contract. Its goal is to bring up domestic Japanese production of logic chips using nanosheet GAA transistors, based on 2 nm-generation technology developed by IBM in the United States. In December 2022 it entered a strategic partnership with IBM, and it also works with the Belgian research institute imec. Its research and development receives government support as a project of NEDO (the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization).

The fab is IIM-1 in Chitose, Hokkaido, where construction began in September 2023. Delivery of EUV lithography tools began in December 2024, and the pilot line started operating in April 2025. Alongside the front-end fab, the company runs a back-end R&D site in the same city, and in April 2026 it opened Rapidus Chiplet Solutions, which handles the design and manufacture of chiplets and packages.

about.h: Single-wafer processing to shorten manufacturing time
about.p: Rapidus has said it will run every front-end step as single-wafer processing, handling one wafer at a time. Compared with batch processing, which treats many wafers together, this makes it easier to collect data on each wafer and adjust conditions quickly. The company calls its business model of linking design, front-end and back-end processing in a short time RUMS (Rapid and Unified Manufacturing Service), and aims to set itself apart from larger established foundries through a short turnaround time (TAT).

In July 2025 the company announced that 2 nm-generation GAA transistors prototyped at IIM-1 had been confirmed to work electrically. Volume production is scheduled to begin in 2027. To succeed as a foundry it needs more than transistor performance: a PDK (process design kit) that customers design with, partnerships with design-support companies and stable yields are all essential. In October 2026 it announced Rapidus CORE, a framework for working with design companies and other partners.

faq.q: What kind of company is Rapidus?
faq.a: It is a Japanese semiconductor manufacturer founded in 2022 that aims to be a foundry making 2 nm-generation logic chips designed by other companies. Its fab is in Chitose, Hokkaido, and it plans to start volume production in 2027.

faq.q: When will Rapidus start volume production?
faq.a: The company has said it plans to start volume production in 2027. It started its pilot line in April 2025 and announced in July 2025 that it had confirmed its 2 nm-generation GAA transistors work.

faq.q: How does Rapidus's 2 nm differ from TSMC's 2 nm?
faq.a: Both are generations that use nanosheet GAA transistors. Rapidus builds on IBM's technology and highlights running the entire front end as single-wafer processing to shorten the manufacturing turnaround time (TAT).

DRAM(ダイナミックRAM).desc: Volatile memory that stores each bit in a cell of one transistor and one capacitor and needs periodic refresh before the charge leaks away. It is used as main memory in PCs and servers.

about.h: What DRAM stands for and how a cell works
about.p: DRAM stands for dynamic random-access memory. Each bit is stored in a 1T1C cell made of one transistor and one capacitor, with the presence or absence of charge on the capacitor representing 0 or 1. Cells sit in a grid at the crossings of word lines and bit lines; turning on the transistor through the word line connects the capacitor to the bit line. Random access means any address can be reached regardless of order, and dynamic refers to the fact that the stored charge slowly leaks away, so the data has to be rewritten periodically.

To read a cell, its capacitor is connected to a bit line precharged to about half the supply voltage. The charge is shared, producing a small voltage difference that a sense amplifier amplifies to decide 0 or 1. Because this disturbs the stored charge (a destructive read), the amplified voltage is written back to the cell. Charge is also lost through junction and subthreshold leakage, so every row must be read and rewritten at intervals, which is called refresh. As a guide, standards up to DDR4 require all rows to be refreshed within 64 ms in the normal temperature range and DDR5 within 32 ms, with shorter intervals at high temperature.

about.h: DRAM vs. SRAM and flash memory
about.p: SRAM builds a latch from six transistors, so it needs no refresh and can be accessed in around 1 ns, but its cells are large and its cost per bit is high. DRAM's small 1T1C cell makes it roughly 20 times denser than SRAM, suiting it to large main memory, at the cost of access times of tens of nanoseconds because rows must be activated. NAND flash memory is nonvolatile, keeping data with power off, and offers even larger capacity at lower cost, but it writes and erases slowly and has a limited number of rewrite cycles. Systems therefore build a memory hierarchy with SRAM for caches, DRAM for main memory and SSDs for storage.

DRAM products include DDR SDRAM for PCs and servers, low-power LPDDR for smartphones and similar devices, GDDR for graphics, and HBM, which stacks several dies with TSVs to provide a very wide bus. The central scaling challenge is keeping enough charge on the capacitor to read the data as cells shrink. Tall, narrow cylindrical capacitors, high-dielectric-constant (high-k) insulators and buried-word-line transistors that reduce leakage have been introduced to meet it. Higher density also brings reliability issues such as Rowhammer, where repeatedly activating a row flips data in neighboring rows.

faq.q: What does DRAM stand for?
faq.a: Dynamic random-access memory. It is called dynamic because the stored charge is lost over time and must be refreshed periodically, unlike SRAM (static RAM), which keeps its data without refresh as long as power is applied.

faq.q: What is the difference between DRAM and SRAM?
faq.a: DRAM uses a small 1T1C cell, so it can be made large and cheap, but it needs refresh and takes tens of nanoseconds to access. SRAM uses a six-transistor cell that needs no refresh and is fast, but takes more area. That is why DRAM is used for main memory and SRAM for CPU caches.

faq.q: Does DRAM lose its data when power is turned off?
faq.a: Yes. DRAM is volatile: when power is removed, refresh stops and the charge leaks away. If the chips are cooled, however, data can persist for seconds to minutes, which cold boot attacks exploit to read encryption keys from memory.

HTOL(高温動作寿命試験).desc: A reliability test that operates products at high temperature under voltage for a long time to accelerate and evaluate chip lifetime and failure rate. A typical condition is 1000 hours at around 125 °C.

about.p: HTOL stands for high temperature operating life. Products are held at high temperature and operated for a long time with supply voltage and input signals applied, to see whether failures occur. Temperature and voltage accelerate degradation, so stress equivalent to years of field use is applied in a short time. The targets are degradation of the chip itself and latent defects, such as time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) of gate oxides, threshold voltage shifts from BTI and electromigration in interconnects. Electrical characteristics are measured during and after the test to check for parametric or functional failures.

Typical conditions are a junction temperature of around 125 °C, a supply voltage at or somewhat above the maximum operating voltage, and a duration of 1000 hours. Conditions like these are typical in JEDEC standards (the JESD22 series), and the automotive AEC-Q100 requires, for example, zero failures when 77 units from each of 3 lots are tested for 1000 hours, with higher temperatures for some temperature grades. High-power products can self-heat to excessive junction temperatures, so the oven temperature is lowered or devices are temperature-controlled individually to hit the target. Parts are pulled and measured at intermediate points such as 168 and 500 hours to track how degradation progresses.

Burn-in is a screen that applies short high-temperature, high-voltage stress to all or many shipped units to remove those prone to early failure. HTOL is a qualification test that applies long stress to a sample to confirm that the design and manufacturing process meet the target lifetime and failure rate; the units tested are not shipped. HAST adds humidity and pressure to evaluate the package's moisture resistance and targets different failures from HTOL, which operates parts at dry high temperature. Early-life failure rate is evaluated separately, for example with ELFR tests that run more units for a shorter time than HTOL.

about.h: Estimating failure rate from the results
about.p: HTOL results are converted to time under use conditions by estimating a temperature acceleration factor with the Arrhenius model and a voltage acceleration factor with a voltage model. For example, assuming an activation energy of 0.7 eV, one hour at 125 °C corresponds to roughly 80 hours at 55 °C. From a zero-failure result, the chi-square distribution gives an upper bound on the failure rate in FIT at a chosen confidence level. Activation energy differs by failure mechanism, however, and the assumed value changes the result greatly, so the figures are treated as estimates.

faq.q: What does HTOL stand for?
faq.a: High temperature operating life. Parts are operated continuously at high temperature under voltage to accelerate and evaluate chip lifetime and failure rate.

faq.q: What is the difference between HTOL and burn-in?
faq.a: Burn-in is a screen that removes early-failure units from products to be shipped, applied for a short time to many units. HTOL is a qualification test that confirms long-term lifetime on a sample, and the tested units are not shipped.

faq.q: How long does an HTOL test run?
faq.a: 1000 hours is a common benchmark, with measurements at intermediate points such as 168 and 500 hours. Temperature, voltage and duration depend on the applicable standard, the product's temperature grade and agreements with the customer.

高温高湿バイアス試験(THB).desc: A reliability test that applies voltage in a hot, humid environment, typically 85 °C/85% RH, to evaluate corrosion and increased leakage caused by moisture entering the package. It is also called the 85/85 test.

about.p: THB stands for temperature humidity bias. Products are placed in a temperature-humidity chamber at atmospheric pressure, typically at 85 °C and 85% RH, and held for about 1000 hours with voltage applied. Plastic packages sealed with mold compound are not hermetic, so moisture slowly reaches the die through the mold compound and along the interfaces between the compound and the lead frame. When voltage is present there, electrochemical reactions proceed and failures are accelerated. Electrical characteristics are measured before, during and after the test to check for rising leakage current or functional failures.

The main target is corrosion of aluminum bond pads and interconnects. When chloride or other ionic contaminants dissolve in the moisture, corrosion progresses much faster. Between adjacent biased conductors, ion migration can also occur: metal dissolves as ions, migrates and deposits as dendrites that cause shorts. Cracks and defects in the passivation film become paths for moisture, and delamination between mold compound and the die or lead frame speeds its entry. Increased leakage current along the die surface or package surface is also evaluated.

HAST (highly accelerated stress test) uses unsaturated steam at about 110 to 130 °C in a pressure vessel, accelerating humidity-driven failures more strongly than THB. The commonly used HAST at 130 °C/85% RH for 96 hours serves as a substitute for THB at 85 °C/85% RH for 1000 hours. HAST gives results quickly, but its higher temperature can change mold compound properties and cause failures that would not occur in service. THB runs at a lower temperature closer to real environments, so it takes longer. Which one is used depends on the applicable standard and agreements with the customer.

about.h: Biasing and converting to field life
about.p: Bias is applied so that as much voltage as possible appears between adjacent pins while power dissipation stays low. If the die heats up, its surface temperature rises and the local relative humidity falls, making moisture-driven failures less likely. Methods such as alternating supply and ground across the pins or applying voltage intermittently are therefore used. To estimate field life from the results, models such as Peck's model are used, expressing the humidity term as a power of relative humidity (exponent around 3) and the temperature term in Arrhenius form.

faq.q: What does 85/85 mean in THB testing?
faq.a: It refers to test conditions of 85 °C and 85% relative humidity. THB is often run for about 1000 hours under these conditions with voltage applied, which is why it is also called the 85/85 test.

faq.q: What is the difference between temperature-humidity-bias testing (THB) and HAST?
faq.a: Both apply voltage at high temperature and humidity, but THB runs at 85 °C and atmospheric pressure for about 1000 hours, while HAST uses pressurized steam at about 110 to 130 °C to reach a comparable evaluation in about 100 to 300 hours.

faq.q: Why is power dissipation kept low during THB?
faq.a: If the die heats up, it drives moisture away and lowers the relative humidity at its surface, making humidity-driven corrosion and ion migration less likely. Bias conditions are chosen to apply voltage while keeping self-heating small.

高温放置試験(高温保存試験).desc: A reliability test that keeps products at high temperature without applying voltage to evaluate degradation of wire-bond joints, data retention in nonvolatile memory and similar effects. It is also called HTS or HTSL.

about.h: A test that applies only temperature
about.p: The high-temperature storage test places products in an oven at high temperature without applying voltage and compares their electrical characteristics before, during and after the test. It is also called high temperature storage (HTS) or high temperature storage life (HTSL). In JEDEC standards (the JESD22 series) and elsewhere, 1000 hours at 150 °C, for example, is a typical condition, and some products or standards use higher temperatures for shorter times. Because no voltage or signals are applied, the equipment is simple, many samples can be tested at once, and degradation driven by temperature alone can be isolated.

A typical target is the wire-bond joint. Where a gold wire meets an aluminum pad, gold-aluminum intermetallic compounds grow at high temperature, and when the difference in diffusion rates creates voids (Kirkendall voids), the joint's resistance rises or the bond lifts. For copper wire bonds, intermetallic growth and corrosion are also important to evaluate. High-temperature storage is further used to evaluate thermal degradation of materials such as mold compound and die-attach material, as well as data retention in nonvolatile memory.

HTOL (high-temperature operating life test) operates parts at high temperature under voltage, so it also accelerates degradation driven by electric field or current, such as TDDB and electromigration. The high-temperature storage test applies no voltage, so it cannot evaluate those mechanisms, but in exchange it can single out degradation caused by temperature alone. The temperature-humidity-bias test (THB) accelerates corrosion with humidity and voltage, and temperature cycling applies strain from temperature changes. Because each targets different failures, qualification combines them. The storage temperature range in a datasheet specifies where parts may be stored and is separate from test conditions.

In flash memory and EEPROM, charge stored on a floating gate or in a charge-trap film leaks out faster at higher temperature. Products with data written are therefore stored at high temperature to check that they still read correctly after a specified time. Because repeated rewriting degrades the dielectrics and makes charge loss easier, a common approach is to wear the parts first with an endurance test and then bake them. Results are converted to retention time at use temperature with the Arrhenius model, using an activation energy assumed for the failure mechanism, but the assumption can change the result greatly.

faq.q: What is the difference between a high-temperature storage test and HTOL?
faq.a: A high-temperature storage test only holds parts at high temperature without voltage, evaluating degradation driven by temperature alone. HTOL operates parts at high temperature under voltage, so it also accelerates degradation driven by electric field and current.

faq.q: What are typical conditions for a high-temperature storage test?
faq.a: 1000 hours at 150 °C, for example, is a typical condition. Actual temperature and time depend on the applicable standard, the package materials and the product's temperature grade, and higher temperatures with shorter times are sometimes used.

faq.q: What kinds of accelerated tests are used for semiconductors?
faq.a: They include HTOL, which operates parts under temperature and voltage; the high-temperature storage test, which applies temperature only; temperature-humidity-bias testing (THB) and HAST, which apply temperature, humidity and voltage; and temperature cycling, which repeats temperature changes. Each intensifies the stresses that cause failures so that lifetime and failure rate can be evaluated in a short time.

温度サイクル試験.desc: A reliability test that repeatedly applies high and low temperatures to evaluate solder-joint fatigue and package cracking or delamination caused by differences in thermal expansion between materials.

about.p: A semiconductor package is built from materials with different coefficients of thermal expansion: the silicon die, mold compound, lead frame or substrate, solder and the printed circuit board. Silicon's coefficient is small, about 3 ppm/K, while the board and solder expand several times more, so every temperature change turns the difference in expansion into strain on joints and interfaces. Each strain cycle is small, but repetition drives metal fatigue until cracks form. Temperature cycling concentrates this repetition into a short period and finds how many cycles it takes to cause failure.

Parts are cycled in an air chamber and held for a set time at each of the high and low temperatures. In JEDEC standards (the JESD22 series), temperature ranges such as −55 to 125 °C or −65 to 150 °C are typical conditions, with hundreds to thousands of cycles. The automotive AEC-Q100 uses conditions that depend on the temperature grade. Besides component-level tests, after which the package and internal bonds are examined, there are board-level tests that mount parts on a printed circuit board and count the cycles until the solder joints fail.

about.h: Main failures and how they are found
about.p: A typical failure is a fatigue crack in a solder joint; in a BGA, balls near the package corners tend to fail first. Inside the package, cracks at wire-bond joints or at the wire heel, delamination between mold compound and the die or lead frame, and cracks in the die or passivation film occur. Board-level tests detect breaks by monitoring the resistance of a daisy chain that connects many joints in series. Delamination is checked with scanning acoustic microscopy and internal cracks with cross-sections.

about.h: Thermal shock, power cycling and life estimation
about.p: Thermal shock tests apply faster temperature changes than temperature cycling by quickly moving samples between hot and cold chambers or immersing them in liquids. Power cycling heats devices by passing current through them rather than heating them externally, repeating on-off cycles, and is important for evaluating power modules. To estimate field life from temperature-cycling results, the Coffin-Manson relation is used, in which cycles to failure are inversely proportional to a power of the temperature swing. For solder the exponent is said to be around 2, so halving the temperature swing increases cycle life about fourfold.

faq.q: What is the difference between temperature cycling and thermal shock testing?
faq.a: Both alternate between high and low temperatures, but thermal shock testing applies more abrupt changes, for example by moving samples between liquid baths. Temperature cycling changes temperature in air and holds each extreme for a set time, mainly evaluating joint fatigue from repetition.

faq.q: What temperature ranges are typical for temperature cycling?
faq.a: For example, −55 to 125 °C or −65 to 150 °C are typical. The range and number of cycles depend on the applicable standard, the product's temperature grade and whether the test is done on components alone or on board-mounted parts.

faq.q: How is field life estimated from temperature cycling results?
faq.a: The Coffin-Manson relation gives an acceleration factor from the ratio of test and field temperature swings. For solder the exponent is said to be around 2, and in practice models that also account for differences in mean temperature and cycles per day are used.

QFN.desc: A surface-mount package with terminals exposed around the perimeter of its underside and no leads projecting from the sides. The central thermal pad on the bottom can be soldered to the board, making it small with good heat dissipation.

about.p: QFN stands for quad flat no-lead and is a type of lead-frame package. The die is mounted on a die pad, wire-bonded to the surrounding leads and covered with mold compound, but the leads do not project from the sides; they are exposed as terminals along the four edges of the package's underside. The die pad is usually exposed at the center of the underside too, and is called the exposed pad or thermal pad. Terminal pitches of about 0.4 to 0.65 mm are common. Most QFNs are made by molding many units at once on a lead-frame strip and separating them with a dicing saw. Versions with terminals on only two sides are called DFN or SON.

Because the leads sit under the package and are short, their inductance and resistance are small, which suits RF circuits handling high frequencies and fast-switching power ICs. The central thermal pad is soldered to a pad on the printed circuit board, and multiple thermal vias beneath it carry heat to inner-layer or back-side copper, so thermal resistance can be lower than for a leaded package of the same size. The thermal pad is often tied to ground and doubles as an electrical connection. Its small footprint and low profile make QFN common in compact devices such as smartphones.

Since the terminals are on the underside, most of each solder joint is hidden, so inspection relies mainly on X-ray. Where joints must be confirmed by optical inspection, as in automotive use, wettable-flank versions are used, processed so that solder also wets the sides of the terminals. Too much solder on the thermal pad can float the package and cause poor perimeter joints, while too little hurts heat dissipation, so the stencil opening is split into a grid to control solder volume and voids. Because the solder layer is thin, joint fatigue under temperature cycling also needs attention in large packages.

about.h: Names like VQFN, and comparison with QFP and BGA
about.p: Letters such as V, W and U in front of QFN mainly denote thickness classes; VQFN is a very thin QFN, meaning a low-profile part with a mounted height of roughly 1 mm or less. Class boundaries and naming differ between manufacturers, so dimensions should be checked on each package drawing. QFP brings gull-wing leads out from four sides, making joints easy to inspect but taking more board area. BGA arranges solder balls in a grid across the whole underside and can provide many more terminals. Because QFN can place terminals only around the perimeter, it is used especially for ICs with relatively few pins.

faq.q: What does QFN stand for?
faq.a: Quad flat no-lead: a flat package with terminals on four sides that has no leads projecting from its sides. The terminals are exposed on the package's underside.

faq.q: What is the difference between VQFN and QFN?
faq.a: VQFN is the name for a thin (very thin) QFN; the structure is the same. Thickness classes and naming vary by manufacturer, so check dimensions on the package drawing.

faq.q: What is the pad in the center of a QFN's underside for?
faq.a: It is the exposed die pad that carries the die. Soldered to the printed circuit board, it becomes a heat path through thermal vias, and in many cases it is also connected to ground, serving as an electrical connection.

QFP.desc: A surface-mount package with gull-wing leads extending from all four sides. Its joints are easy to inspect visually, and it is widely used for microcontrollers and similar ICs.

about.p: QFP stands for quad flat package and is a type of lead-frame package. The die is mounted on a die pad, wire-bonded to the leads and covered with mold compound; the protruding leads are then trimmed and bent into a shape like a gull's wing. Lead pitches of about 0.4 to 0.8 mm are common, and pin counts range from a few dozen to several hundred. Variants are named by body thickness, such as LQFP at generally about 1.4 mm and TQFP at about 1.0 mm. It can be seen as an SOP, which has leads on two sides, extended to all four sides.

Because the lead tips and joints are visible, solder quality is easy to check by eye or with automated optical inspection, and hand repair or replacement is straightforward. The bent leads flex like springs and absorb thermal expansion mismatch, so solder joints tend to last longer under temperature cycling. On the other hand, terminals can be placed only around the perimeter, so the package grows as pin count rises. Narrower pitches make leads easier to bend, and controlling the height alignment of the lead tips (coplanarity) and solder bridging become problems.

In an ordinary QFP, heat from the die escapes mainly through the mold compound and the leads, so thermal resistance is relatively high. For higher-power products, versions with an exposed die pad on the underside soldered to the printed circuit board, or with a heat spreader built into the package, are used. Thermal vias under the exposed pad spread heat into inner-layer or back-side copper. In these versions, as with QFN, solder volume and voids at the pad must be controlled.

about.h: Choosing among QFP, QFN and BGA
about.p: QFP uses more board area because its leads extend outward, and the lead length adds inductance, but its ease of inspection and handling has kept it in long use for microcontrollers and ICs for industrial equipment. QFN tucks the terminals under the package for a smaller, thinner part with good thermal and high-frequency performance. BGA places balls across the whole underside, providing far more terminals than a QFP of the same size, and is the mainstream for high-performance, high-pin-count chips. The choice weighs pin count, board area, heat dissipation, inspection method and board cost.

faq.q: What is the difference between QFP and BGA?
faq.a: QFP brings leads out from four sides, so its joints are easy to inspect visually, but terminals can be placed only around the perimeter. BGA places solder balls across the whole underside, allowing many more terminals, but its joints are hidden and are inspected with X-ray.

faq.q: What is the difference between QFP and QFN?
faq.a: QFP has gull-wing leads extending from its sides, while QFN has no leads and exposes terminals on its underside. QFN is smaller, thinner and better at dissipating heat; QFP joints are easier to inspect visually and to rework after assembly.

faq.q: What is the difference between LQFP and TQFP?
faq.a: Mainly body thickness: LQFP generally refers to about 1.4 mm and TQFP to a thinner body of about 1.0 mm. Lead pitch and pin count vary by part, so check the package drawing.

SSD.desc: A storage device that stores data using NAND flash memory and a controller. It has no moving parts and offers faster random access and better shock resistance than an HDD.

about.p: An SSD (solid-state drive) is a storage device with several NAND flash memory chips, a controller that manages them and, in many cases, DRAM that holds the address mapping table, all on one board. The controller handles the FTL, which maps logical addresses to physical locations in flash, ECC to correct errors, wear leveling to spread writes across the whole device, and garbage collection to erase blocks that are no longer needed and create free space. By running many chips in parallel over multiple channels, it achieves higher transfer rates than a single chip could.

SSDs connect to the host through SATA, the same interface as HDDs, or NVMe, which runs over PCI Express. SATA is limited to 6 Gb/s by specification, and actual transfer rates stay in the 500 MB/s range. NVMe SSDs use several PCI Express lanes (usually x4) and, depending on the generation, can reach transfer rates of several GB/s; they can also process many commands in parallel, which keeps latency low. Form factors include the same size as a 2.5-inch HDD, the narrow M.2 board used in laptops and elsewhere, and form factors for data centers.

An HDD reads and writes by moving a head over spinning magnetic platters, so accessing a distant location takes several milliseconds. An SSD has no moving parts and responds to random reads in roughly tens to 100 µs, making it especially fast for workloads with many small files. It also uses less power, withstands shock and vibration and makes no noise. On the other hand, large-capacity HDDs are generally cheaper per unit of capacity, and data centers also use HDDs to store large volumes of data. An HDD can overwrite in place, but flash must be erased before it is written, which complicates an SSD's internal processing.

Each rewrite degrades the insulating films in NAND flash cells, so SSDs have a guideline for total writable data, expressed as TBW (terabytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day). TLC and QLC, which store more bits per cell, generally have lower rewrite limits. TRIM, which lets the host report deleted data, and spare area hidden from the user (over-provisioning) reduce write amplification and extend lifetime. How long data survives with power off varies greatly with wear and storage temperature, and a heavily worn SSD stored hot for a long time can lose data.

faq.q: Which is faster, an SSD or an HDD?
faq.a: An SSD is generally faster, especially for random access: an HDD needs several milliseconds to move its head, while an SSD responds in roughly tens to 100 µs. Large HDDs are cheaper per unit of capacity, so the two are used for different purposes.

faq.q: What is the difference between NVMe and SATA SSDs?
faq.a: SATA is an interface designed for HDDs and is limited to 6 Gb/s by specification. NVMe is a protocol for flash that runs over PCI Express, and multiple lanes plus parallel processing of many commands give higher transfer rates and lower latency.

faq.q: Does an SSD keep its data while powered off?
faq.a: NAND flash memory is nonvolatile, so data remains when power is off. How long it lasts depends on wear from rewriting and on storage temperature, however, and a worn SSD stored hot for a long time can lose data.

JFET(接合型FET).desc: A field-effect transistor whose gate is a pn junction, controlling channel current through the width of the depletion layer that grows under reverse bias. Most are depletion-mode devices that conduct at a gate voltage of 0 V.

about.p: A JFET (junction field-effect transistor) is a field-effect transistor whose gate is formed by a pn junction. In an n-channel JFET, p-type gate regions sit on both sides of an n-type channel connecting source and drain; reverse-biasing the gate-channel junction widens the depletion layer, narrowing the channel and reducing current. Current is highest at a gate voltage of 0 V (IDSS), and when the reverse bias reaches the pinch-off voltage, the channel closes and current almost stops. In the saturation region, drain current is roughly proportional to the square of the difference between the gate voltage and the pinch-off voltage.

A MOSFET separates the gate from the semiconductor with an insulating film, whereas a JFET's gate is a pn junction with no insulator. The junction must be kept reverse-biased; forward-biasing it causes gate current to flow. Reverse-biased gate leakage is small, around pA to nA at room temperature, but because it is junction leakage it rises sharply with temperature. JFETs are also fundamentally normally-on depletion-mode devices, which makes them unsuitable for integrated circuits like CMOS that combine normally-off n-type and p-type transistors. That is why MOSFETs dominate as the transistors in integrated circuits.

In a JFET, current flows inside the channel and is less affected by defects at an insulator interface than in a MOSFET, so low-frequency (1/f) noise tends to be small. This makes JFETs suited to audio preamplifiers, high-impedance input stages of sensors and instruments, and JFET-input op amps with input bias currents in the pA range. The impedance-converting element inside electret condenser microphones and the current-regulating diode, which ties gate to source to pass a constant current, are also based on JFETs.

SiC JFETs offer high breakdown voltage and low on-resistance and are also used as power devices. Because a normally-on device can be hazardous, for instance at power-up, a common approach is a cascode connection in series with a low-voltage Si MOSFET so that the pair can be treated as normally-off. In planar power MOSFETs, the region squeezed between adjacent p-type body regions acts like a JFET and narrows the current path, so its resistance is called JFET resistance. In compound semiconductors such as GaAs, the MESFET, whose gate is a Schottky junction, operates on the same principle.

faq.q: What is the difference between a MOSFET and a JFET?
faq.a: A MOSFET isolates the gate from the semiconductor with an insulating film, while a JFET forms its gate from a pn junction. A JFET is fundamentally a depletion-mode device that conducts at 0 V gate voltage and is used with its gate kept reverse-biased. MOSFETs are easy to make normally-off and are used in CMOS integrated circuits.

faq.q: Why is a JFET normally on?
faq.a: At 0 V gate voltage, an n-type (or p-type) channel already connects source and drain, so current flows. Current can be reduced only by reverse-biasing the gate to widen the depletion layer.

faq.q: What happens if a JFET's gate is forward-biased?
faq.a: The gate-channel pn junction becomes forward-biased, and in silicon gate current starts to flow once the voltage exceeds roughly 0.5 V. That loses the JFET's advantage of high input impedance, so the gate is normally used reverse-biased or near 0 V.

DUV(深紫外線).desc: Light in the deep-ultraviolet range used in semiconductor lithography. DUV lithography generally refers to exposure using KrF excimer lasers (248 nm) and ArF excimer lasers (193 nm) as light sources.

about.p: Lithography light sources moved from the g-line (436 nm) and i-line (365 nm) of mercury lamps to shorter-wavelength deep ultraviolet (DUV). DUV lithography uses excimer lasers: KrF, using krypton and fluorine, emits at 248 nm, and ArF, using argon and fluorine, at 193 nm. KrF came into full use from the 0.25 µm generation in the late 1990s and spread together with chemically amplified resists. A 157 nm F2 laser with an even shorter wavelength was also developed, but problems with lens materials and other issues, together with the arrival of ArF immersion lithography, kept it out of volume production.

The resolvable feature size is approximated by the Rayleigh equation R = k1·λ/NA: the shorter the wavelength λ and the larger the numerical aperture NA, the finer the patterns. In dry ArF, with air between lens and wafer, NA tops out at about 0.93, but ArF immersion lithography fills that gap with water and uses its refractive index at 193 nm (about 1.44) to raise NA to 1.35. With NA 1.35 and k1 0.27, for example, R ≈ 39 nm (half-pitch); finer patterns are made by combining multiple patterning such as SADP.

EUV lithography uses extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nm, roughly one-fourteenth of DUV's 193 nm, and can print finer patterns in a single exposure. EUV light is strongly absorbed even by air and glass, however, so it requires a vacuum, multilayer mirrors and reflective masks. DUV uses lenses of fused silica and calcium fluoride with transmissive masks and does not need a vacuum. EUV tools are far more expensive, while DUV is a mature technology with advantages in cost and productivity. EUV uses NA 0.33, and High-NA EUV with NA 0.55 began to be introduced in the mid-2020s.

Even in leading-edge logic and DRAM manufacturing, EUV is used only for the layers that need the finest patterns, while many other layers are exposed with ArF immersion, dry ArF or KrF. Layers that need less precision and implant patterns also use KrF or i-line. Mature-node logic, power semiconductors, analog, MEMS and silicon photonics are made mainly with DUV lithography. DUV scanners, excimer lasers and resists therefore remain essential technologies in semiconductor manufacturing even as EUV spreads.

faq.q: What is the difference between DUV and EUV?
faq.a: DUV uses KrF (248 nm) or ArF (193 nm) excimer lasers and exposes through lenses and transmissive masks. EUV uses 13.5 nm light, so it requires a vacuum, mirrors and reflective masks. EUV can print finer patterns in one exposure, but the tools are expensive.

faq.q: Is ArF immersion lithography a form of DUV?
faq.a: Yes. ArF immersion lithography is DUV lithography with an ArF excimer laser (193 nm) in which water fills the space between lens and wafer to raise the numerical aperture to 1.35.

faq.q: Is i-line lithography DUV?
faq.a: It is not usually counted as DUV. The i-line is 365 nm light from a mercury lamp, and DUV lithography normally refers to exposure with KrF or ArF excimer lasers.

AMHS(自動搬送システム).desc: The collective term for the equipment that automatically moves wafer carriers such as FOUPs between tools and storage in a semiconductor fab, and the control system that runs it. It consists of OHTs, stockers and related equipment.

about.p: AMHS stands for automated material handling system and refers to the whole system that automatically moves and stores wafer containers in a fab. In a 300 mm fab it consists of OHT vehicles that run on ceiling rails and lower FOUPs onto tool load ports, stockers that are automated warehouses where robots store and retrieve FOUPs, buffers that hold FOUPs temporarily near the rails, and lifters that move them between floors. A transport control system runs all this, receiving transport requests from the manufacturing execution system (MES) and assigning vehicles and storage locations.

Many fabs have used a layout of bays, each grouping tools of the same kind. In a bay layout, interbay transport links distant bays via stockers and similar equipment, while intrabay transport links tools within a bay to each other and to stockers. In 200 mm fabs, often only interbay transport was automated and lots were carried by hand within a bay. Because each transfer adds waiting time, modern 300 mm fabs widely use OHTs that handle both in a single system and carry FOUPs directly from tool to tool.

A FOUP holding 25 wafers of 300 mm weighs about 8 kg, which is a heavy load to carry all day, and a drop can destroy expensive wafers. A wafer passes through hundreds of process steps before completion and moves between tools at each one, so the number of moves is very large. Automation transports FOUPs at a steady pace around the clock, lets the fab track where each FOUP is at any time and prevents mistakes such as delivering one to the wrong tool. Fewer people moving around also reduces particle contamination.

In large fabs, hundreds or more OHT vehicles run on a single rail network, so congestion and route selection strongly affect delivery time. If a tool stops while waiting for a FOUP, capacity drops and the time wafers spend in the fab (cycle time) grows. Fabs therefore anticipate transport requests to dispatch vehicles in advance and place storage near tools to cut waiting time. During fab design, transport volume is simulated to decide rail layout, vehicle count and storage capacity. Redundancy so that a local failure does not stop the whole system is also important.

faq.q: What does AMHS stand for?
faq.a: Automated material handling system. In a semiconductor fab it refers collectively to the OHTs that carry FOUPs, the stockers that store them and the control system that runs them.

faq.q: What is the difference between AMHS and OHT?
faq.a: AMHS is the name for the whole transport and storage system, and OHT is the overhead vehicle within it that actually carries FOUPs. An AMHS also includes stockers, buffers and transport control software.

faq.q: What is a stocker in a semiconductor fab?
faq.a: An automated warehouse with shelves where robots store and retrieve FOUPs, temporarily holding those waiting for tools to become free. It is filled with clean air or nitrogen and connected to transport systems such as OHTs.
